en: Auspiciousness.
The *Mālatīmādhava*, composed by the great poet Śrī Bhavabhūti,
accompanied by the commentary named *Rasamañjarī* composed by Śrī Pūrṇasarasvatī.
May the Elephant-faced One (Gaṇeśa), whose form is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, be present.
May he always carry me across the obstruction of the array of obstacles.
Salutations to that Śrī Pūrṇajyotis, the enemy of ignorance, by whose light the world shines and by whose light that Great Splendor (Brahman) shines.

May that form of Īśa, which is skillful in playing within the small cavity of the sages’ hearts, burn away your fear of worldly existence— she who, through the artifice of speech, pours forth from her mouth the noble celestial river as if it were trickling from her head, and who is the very personification of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
When the blinding darkness of delusion is destroyed by the delight of hearing the meaning of her song, a man in the three worlds, rejoicing in Kṛṣṇa, attains the state of Viṣṇu.

May that one, the full light whose great universal form is manifested within Himself alone, whose eyes extend as far as a lotus, flash forth in my heart. May the wave of the great ocean of Consciousness— that splendor— spread for you,
which is the victory of Yaśodā’s infant and the wealth of Dhanañjaya.

In this work titled *Mālatīmādhava*, which is a crest-jewel among treatises on the abundant skill of bringing about the manifestation of existence through the equality of all states of being, I desire to undertake an immersion by means of a commentary; may the virtuous, who are captivated by even the most subtle qualities, take delight therein. //6//
If there should be any lapse here, whether in meaning or in word, may the noble ones—who possess intellects matured by extensive learning—rectify it;
for those wishing to leap suddenly upon the crags of a mountain in a narrow pass, only a friend provides a firm hand to grasp. //7//
The full expansion of the meaning cannot be expressed without an expansion of words; therefore, the fault of prolixity in this work should be readily forgiven by those of refined taste. (8)
Revealing its own intense fragrance of the *Mālatīmādhava*, this *Rasamañjarī* should be cherished with affection by those of refined taste and explained [to them]. 9.

At the outset of this work, the great poet Bhavabhūti—who is intent on composing this treatise for the sake of connoisseurs—offers a benediction to the audience, beginning with the words "sānandam" (with joy), which serves as a maṅgala consisting of the recollection of the Supreme Deity. The phrase "accompanied by joy" (*ānandasahitam*) is an adverbial qualifier for the act of striking.

This is illustrated by the lines: "by which [light] the rays from the nails of his thumb are split apart by the brilliant [flashes] struck from the strings of the lute he has been incessantly strumming," and "when the drum is being vigorously beaten."

It is as in the verse: "The betel-nut trees (*pūga-druma*), laden with clusters of betel leaves, are bending down under their fruit. The meaning is: "with a heart delighted by the opportunity to serve the uplifted axe of Śiva during his dance of bliss (*ānanda-tāṇḍava*). Nandin is Nandīśvara, the chief attendant of the Supreme Lord. "Struck" (*āhata*) means beaten; "the drum" (*murava*) is a specific type of percussion instrument. "Summoned" (*āhūta*) is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*): because he arrives joyfully immediately after hearing the smooth and deep sound of the drum, suspecting it to be the roar of a rain-cloud, he is as if called forth.

Nor does the fault of violating established usage (*prasiddhi-dhuta-doṣa*) apply here in the phrase *na ca muravaravā*; for we find it used in the *Raghuvaṃśa*: "The wealth of Naravāhana [Kubera] resounded with deep roars" (*ghanaravā naravāhanasampadaḥ*); and in the *Māghakāvya*: "In every direction, a cry is made by young elephants" (*pratidiśaṃ kriyate kalabhai ravaḥ*), and "the army was trampled by the sounds of trees shaken by playing elephants" (*balākrāntaṃ krīḍaddviradamathitorvīruharavaiḥ*). Furthermore, in the *Setu*, we have: "And bow to him whose roar is manifest" (*ṇamaha a jassa phuḍaravaṃ*), and "whose fame resounds clearly through its own cries" (*ṇiāravāhi phuḍaṇintajasaṇighghosaṃ*). Since its non-defectiveness is determined by hundreds of such usages by great poets in other poetic works as well, the objection is invalid.

This is because usage is stronger than mere definition; for this very reason, even though such a form is recorded in traditional grammars, it is disregarded by poets, which is why the fault of being "unemployed" (aprayukta) is mentioned. *Kaumāra* refers to the acceptance of a peacock (*barhin*) as a vehicle for the *subrahmaṇya*. A peacock is a *barhin*; therefore, there is fear from it, and for that reason [the elephant acts]. The "aperture at the tip of the trunk" (*nāsāgrarandhra*) is the opening at the tip of the hand (*hastāgra*), since for elephants the trunk itself is the nose, as seen in usages such as "one whose thighs are like the trunk of an elephant" (*nāganāsoru*). He enters—that is, he will enter—using the present participle (*śatṛ*) to denote proximity to the present time.

Regarding the lord of serpents, Vāsuki: the phrase "intent on the service of Śiva" implies that he is present there for that purpose. By the term *kaumārabarhin* (the peacock of Kumāra), it is suggested that even Śarva could not restrain his mischievous antics. The contraction of his coils (*bhoga-saṅkoca*)—the folding of his hoods into buds—is for the sake of facilitating his entry.
As for the word *bhoga*: "The word *bhoga* refers to a kingdom, wealth, happiness, protection, and eating;
also to the hood and the body of a serpent, and to the wages of courtesans and the like."

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*. "Uḍḍīnāḥ" means those that have flown up; it is a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) derived from the root *ḍīṅ*, meaning "to move through the air. "Mukharitāḥ" means made resonant or vocalized; [this refers to] those by which the quarters (*kakubhaḥ*), the directions, were made to resound. "Ghaṭṭanam" is the striking of the circle of the earth with the trunk (*śuṇḍā-daṇḍa*). "Vyastam" means having its joints and bonds loosened or shattered. "Viśvam" refers to the entire universe (*brahmāṇḍa*). Thus, they are "Vainākyas"; because he removes the obstacles of his devotees, Vināyaka is Gaṇapati; these are related to him. [The suffix -ika is applied according to the rule] *ṭiṭṭhāḍhāṇañ-*.

By [the rule] beginning with (4-1-15), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. "Tremors of the face" (*vadanavidhutayaḥ*) refers to the shaking of the mouth; from the root *dhunoti*, the suffix *ktin* is applied according to (3-3-14). The use of the plural number indicates an intensive repetition (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) for the sake of warding off [the elephants]. "Accompanied by *phīṭ* sounds" (*phīṭkāravatyaḥ*) is an imitation of the cries of young elephants who are agitated for some reason, making the sound *phīṭ*. As in the *Kādambarī*: "thickened by the *phīṭ* cries of terrified young elephants. The suffix *matup* is added here [to form *phīṭkāravat*]. In this context, the vowel substitution is governed by (1-1-1): "The augment *vṛddhi* is [substituted] for *āt* and *aiC*."

(1-1-1) Just as in the case of [the word] "it" (*it-i-vat*), because the work begins with the auspicious term "with joy" (*sānandaṃ*), one should understand that the Great Poet has employed this supreme benediction for the sake of accomplishing his intended purpose by addressing the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*). This is done through the recollection of the Nandin—a specific form of the Supreme Lord—whose dancing was suggested by the power of the drum-beating mentioned therein; and of the Kumāra, who is introduced as "Kaumāra" and is the primary subject of the poem; and of Vināyaka. Furthermore, it is done by means of a benedictory statement directed toward those sensitive readers. Thus, it should be known that the highest auspiciousness has been invoked.

Nor should it be thought that, by the consequence of entering the nostril at the tip of his trunk, the poet has indicated at the outset some misfortune for the face of the elephant, which is inauspicious for the lord of serpents; for that [incident] is described as a condition for the context of the Lord Vināyaka’s transcendent form, and the intended meaning lies precisely therein.

Having served as the footstep of the bowstring for the proud Śarva-dhanus—the mountain of the immortals rising a hundred thousand *yojanas* high—the hollow of the lotus is as vast as the subterranean abyss of Pātāla for the entry of the lord of serpents. By this, the remaining expanse of his body is explained. Through the mention of the "beaming of the face," the capacity of any divine activity whatsoever to protect devotees is revealed. May they protect—may they guard by warding off the undesirable and fulfilling the desired.

Here, by the phrase "with joy," Śailāda’s devotion toward Śiva is suggested (*dhvani*). By the word "from fear," the *bhayānaka-rasa* (the sentiment of terror) residing in the Lord of Serpents is expressed. By the phrase "shaking his face," the *raudra-rasa* (the sentiment of fury) residing in Vināyaka is conveyed. Through the expressions beginning with "flying from his temples" and so forth—which describe one who is skilled enough to shatter even the cosmic egg (*jagadaṇḍa*) through a sudden, dancing fit of anger—it is shown that what effort could there be for him to protect those who bow before him? Thus, due to the excellence of this inherent capacity (*vastusāmarthya*), there is the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction), as he is distinguished from other deities.

And thus, the poet imparts a threefold resonance to his own composition. By the words "May they protect you," the poet's devotion toward the deity is revealed. Here, because of the description of the natural character of the transformed elephant, there is the figure of speech *svabhāvokti* (description of nature). Due to the vivid manifestation of that natural character, there is the ornament *bhāvika*. //1//

Having offered a benediction through the mouth of Vināyaka for the sake of appropriately removing obstacles, the poet now offers a benediction through the mouth of his chosen supreme deity by means of three verses via the Sūtradhāra. At the conclusion of the *nāndī*, it follows the dramatic convention that the Sūtradhāra enters and speaks. He is called the *sūtradhāra* because he holds (*dhārayati*) the *sūtra*—the treatise on the characteristics of drama and other forms composed by the sage Bharata. [The Sūtradhāra speaks: "Cūḍāpīḍa... and so forth. At the end of the performance of the *nāndī*, the entry and speech of the Sūtradhāra occur according to the rules of the drama. He is the Sūtradhāra because he maintains the *sūtra*, the manual of dramaturgy authored by the sage Bharata.

The term *nāndī* is derived from the root *dhṛṅ* in the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇe*), forming a compound with its object as a subordinate member (*karmopapada-samāsa*). It refers to a specific auspicious performance (*prayoga-viśeṣa*) to be executed by the *sūtradhāra* while behind the curtain, during the preliminary ritual (*pūrvaraṅga-vidhāna*) which consists of twenty-two components beginning with the *pratyāhāra* and ending with the *prarocanā*. As stated by Kohala: "The recitation of auspicious beginnings consisting of salutations to deities and others at the start of a drama is what is praised; that, according to the wise, is called *nāndī*."

Thus [it is said]. And the word *nāndī* was derived by Bhaṭṭa Ghaṭṭu from the root *ṇadi* (meaning "to praise") according to the rule for words like *pṛṣodara*. Likewise, Bādarāyaṇa says: "Even though there are many ancillary elements of the *pūrvaraṅga* in a drama, nevertheless the *nāndī* must necessarily be performed for the pacification of obstacles.
Its four constituent parts are known as *utthāpana*, *parivartana*, *nāndī*, and *prarocanā*. Thus says Bharata: "Because the reciters of the *nāndī* first cause the performance to rise..."
Therefore, awakening should be understood as that which brings about the manifestation of speech and the limbs [of the body].
And because the world-protectors, having turned around in the four directions,
perform a salutation, therefore there should be a turning around.
Because it is always associated here with words of benediction for gods, brahmins, kings, and others, it is therefore called *nāndī*.
That which is an address using a word in its perfected form (*siddha*) should be understood as *prarocanā* (the act of arousing interest).

For example: "Viṣṇu is perfected in the three strides; Guha is perfected at Krauñcapada," and so forth. At the end, that is, upon the conclusion of such a *nāndī*, when the *nāndī-sūtradhāra* has exited, the *sthāpaka-sūtradhāra* enters and speaks—this is the meaning. As stated by Bharata: "Having employed the stage, the *sūtradhāra* should exit along with his followers."
"The *sthāpaka* should enter there, appearing identical in form to the *sūtradhāra*. And the *nāndī* is of two kinds: "one is to be employed in the *pūrvaraṅga*, and the other in the *sthāpanā*.

Furthermore, it is the tradition of poets that this must necessarily be performed with the name of the Moon (*candra*) inscribed upon it. Having entered, the *sthāpaka* performs the *nāndī* characterized by eight words and marked by the word "Moon"—beginning with "cūḍāpīḍa," and so forth. As Bharata says: "There, the *sūtradhāra* should recite [the *nāndī*] employing a medium pitch."
"The *nāndī* should be adorned with twelve or eight *padas*.
Here, *cūḍā* means a crest-lock;
as it is said: "The *cūḍā*, the *keśī*, the *keśapāśī*, the *śikhaṇḍī*, the *kamujā*, and the *śikhā* [are synonyms for a tuft of hair]."
Thus says the Vaijayantī: here, by the word *cūḍā*, the binding of matted hair (*jaṭābandha*) is indicated, or else the head;
as in the verse: "The moon, possessing the luster of a honey-colored parasol, goes to the peak (*cūḍa*) of the western mountain. *Āpīḍa* means a crest-jewel (*śekhara*).
"Furthermore, *vataṃsa*, *uttaṃsa*, and *śekhara* are synonyms for an ear-ornament," according to the *Vaijayantī*. *Saṃkulam* means agitated or confused.
*Prāyaḥ* is used in the senses of age, abundance, equality, fasting, and death.

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*. They are like lightning (*taṭittulyāḥ*) due to their tawny color and abundance of luster; their splendors are merged with the light from the interiors of their eyes. "Not harsh" means newly sprouted and indistinct—that is, doubtful. A "serpent-creeper" (*bhujaṅgavallī*) is a very long serpent, like a creeper; its "coil" (*valaya*) is the body arranged in a circle, and that itself is the "garland" (*srak*); those whose massed locks (*jūṭa*) are bound together by such a garland are so described.

By the word "tvām" (you), the Lord of the Assembly is appropriately addressed; by the word "vaḥ" (your), the members of the assembly are addressed. Here, through the description of the falling water, the flash of lightning, the budding *ketaka* flowers, and the encircling creepers, the forest ranges—resplendent during the rainy season—are brought to mind, and thus a relationship of simile (*upamāna-upameya-bhāva*) between the matted locks (*jaṭā*) and those [forests] is to be inferred. Consequently, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is illuminated through the figure of simile (*upamālaṅkāra*): just as such forest ranges remove the torment of all living beings, so too do the matted locks of the Supreme Lord. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) here is *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state). //2//

"Upon the rows of teeth," and so forth. The plural number is used because of the great number of skulls. They are agitated by rolling about amidst a spreading clamor of "kalakala" sounds. They possess a nature of resonating like rising bubbles within the cavities of the nostrils, eyes, and ears as they move obliquely. A "gaṇḍagranthi" is the protruding bone of the cheek. "Jarjaraśikhāḥ" means those with shattered tips. "Cūḍāsravantyūrmayaḥ" refers to the waves of the river of the topknot.

Because of the statement, "A break, a ripple, or a wave," there is a dual gender [for the word *taraṅga*]. The reading is: "In the cavernous region of Brahma’s skull, they are violent with throbbing. The skulls of the many past four-faced [Brahmas] are themselves the *kandarās*, meaning mountain caves, due to their depth. "In that region" means in that place; "violent with the onset" (*pravartanoddhatāḥ*). The root *spadi* is used in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the sense of "slight movement."

However, in the reading "kandaraparispande," since the skull-bones are separated by intervening spaces, one would face the fault of *abhavanmatayoga* (the impossibility of the intended connection), as to what the rows of teeth and so forth could possibly be connected. Here, by means of the subject matter (*vastu*), another subject matter is suggested: how can the irresistible, wicked sports of those who are proud of their great refuge [of the Lord] be described when their enemies have been conquered by sheer force? The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) here is *ullekha* (multiple description), because there is a depiction in various ways according to the distinction of the objects. //3//

"Of the tawny hue of the row of eyelashes," and so forth. Regarding the eye (*locana*): the "row of eyelashes" (*pakṣmālī*) refers to the fringe of the eye, that is, the line of hair; its "tawny hue" (*piṅgalimā*) is a brownish color. A "particle" (*kaṇaḥ*) is a drop (*binduḥ*). This is a suggestion (*dhvani*) based on metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇāmūla*), because the word "particle"—which denotes the smallness of a material object—is used here to express the smallness of the intangible tawny hue. "Entire" (*kṛtsnaḥ*) means all of it taken together: what has been, what is being, and what is yet to be.

Here, by the poetic conceit (*saṃbhāvanā*) of the effect—the state of the entire mass of lightning becoming as minute as a speck of dust—which is itself irrelevant to the context, the intended excellence of the cause—the tawny hue of the row of eyelashes—is understood through its abundance and the resulting difficulty of beholding the light. Thus, this is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) in the form of the cognition of a cause from an effect. The cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) has a breadth of five hundred million yojanas; its interior is filled with the fourteen worlds, and it is conceived as comprising everything from the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the specific elements (*viśeṣa*). It is the embryonic sphere (*peśī-maṇḍala*) from which Hiraṇyagarbha was born.
As it is said: "Between the sun and the cosmic egg, there are twenty-five crores [of yojanas]."

Thus it is said in the *Bhāgavata*. Regarding the phrase "in the slightly opened bud" (*īṣadvighaṭitamukule*): the word "bud" (*mukula*) indicates closing by way of similarity; the meaning is that the connection between the eyelashes is somewhat loosened. This is because at other times [the eyes] are closed for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world. As it is stated in the *Ambāstava*: "When You, O Goddess, caused the charming method of Your sidelong glances to sprout in many ways from the single burnt Madana, from that time forth the Moon-crested Lord bears the eye on His forehead as if truly closed in shame."

Thus, by the word "slightly" (*īṣat*), it is understood that the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is an object insufficient for complete unfolding. Kālayajvan [states]: "O twice-born one, from one place to the next, each is counted as ten times the former;
beyond that, eighteen..."

The meaning is that it refers to the time of the conclusion of the life-span of Brahmā, known as *para*, which consists of two *parārdhas* as stated [in the verse]: "In my portion (*ṛke*), a *parārdha* is designated. That very person is the sacrificer (*yajvā*), the one who performs the sacrifice (*yajamāna*). [This is derived from] the root *suyaj* with the suffix *ṅvanip*.

(3-2-103) He offers—that is, he gives by way of a sacrificial portion (*avadāna*). Because of the use of the present tense, it is indicated that within this beginningless *saṃsāra*, even during dissolution and emergence, the oblation (*homa*) is manifested at every cycle, as they revolve like a wheel. However, if the reading were *juhāva* (he offered), this meaning would not be established, as it would merely convey a sense of the past, non-contemporary, and non-evident. Time is said to be the offerer because Time alone is the impeller during creation, dissolution, and so forth.
[As stated: "O Mānavī, for Prakṛti, who is the equilibrium of the *guṇas* and devoid of distinctions..."
"Since all movement proceeds from him, that Blessed One is designated as Time"—
so it is stated in the *Bhāgavata*. "You too shall live for a hundred such years."

"And by the words of the venerable teacher Śrī Bhagavatpāda: 'Your life is my breath; it is impelled by Time alone. This statement is made because it is well known that the fire from the third eye of Hara is the destroyer of the universe. As Murāri has said: "Victorious is that indescribable fire upon the forehead-mark of Nīlalohita; for the sake of destroying the world once it has been protected, its kindling was performed by the Self-born (Brahmā)."

Thus, by the metaphorical representation of Time as a sacrificer (*yajvan*), it follows by implication that the eye is the sacrificial fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*) and the cosmic egg (*jagadaṇḍa*) is the oblation (*havya*); this is therefore a *ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka* (a metaphor based on a partial transformation). "Arcirniṣṭaptaḥ" means slightly heated by the flame; [this is according to the rule] "nisastapatāvanāsevane."

By [Pāṇini 8.3.102], there is a cerebral [ṇ]. "Cultivation" (*āsevana*) means repetition; it should be understood that non-repetition consists of occasional, slight glances. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the reduction to ashes of the young moon, which is as tender as a fragment of butter. "Essence of nectar" (*sudhāsāra*) means a rain of ambrosia. According to the *Vaijayantī*, "a *sāra* is a forceful downpour. A "sounding" (*sātkāra*) is an imitation of the sound of a fire being extinguished by the falling of drops of water; one who possesses this is "sounding" (*sātkārī*), referring to whose outer corner of the eye (*apāṅgadeśa*). "Tārtīyīka" means the third.
[This is according to the rule: "The suffix *īkak* may optionally be added after a word ending in *tīya* in the sense of itself."

(vā. 4-2-8) Thus, the suffix *ikak* [is applied]. "Of Purāri," meaning the enemy of the three cities of the Asuras; by this, his habitual nature (*tācchīlya*) of bestowing grace upon the world is suggested. "May he protect" (*avatu*); the verbal root is *ava* in the sense of "to protect. "The burner of Madana," meaning the one who incinerated Kāma; derived from the root *pluṣa* in the sense of "to burn" with the suffix *-ana* according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*.

(3-3-113) Thus, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). And here, this extremely secret meaning—which is accessible only through the mouth of the Guru—has been indicated in aphoristic form (*sūtrita*) by the moon among the assembly of poets, who has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of Sāṅkhya and Yoga, and who is the pleasure-pavilion for the rhythmic songs of the women that are all the Upaniṣads; it is to be investigated as follows: the word *pakṣman* denotes hair, as seen in the expression "by [the eye] with naturally variegated, brilliant, and fine *pakṣmans*"; and it also denotes a thread-like filament, as stated in the *Vaijayantī*: "The word *pakṣman* [is used] for a part of a thread and so forth, for a filament, and for the eyelashes."

And here, this continuous stream of radiance—extremely subtle like the tip of a hair or the awn of a grain of *nīvāra*, and yellow-hued like a thread of *trapuṣī* cotton—is called a "row of eyelashes" (*pakṣmālī*) due to its resemblance [to them]. This occurs when the bud [of the heart] has slightly opened, and the concealment by *māyā* has almost ceased through the instruction of a true guru and spiritual practice. The word "slightly" (*īṣat*) is used because the cognition of the sacrificer and the object of sacrifice still persists; for even that [cognition] is an effect of *māyā*.
As it is said: "The form of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-rūpa*) perishes through the scripture; that which is capable of causal efficiency perishes through direct realization (*aparokṣya*).
Upon the destruction of the *prārabdha* [karma], the appearance itself perishes; thus, the *māyā* of the Self perishes gradually."

This is because of the statement of the Teacher (*ācārya*) and the Śruti text: "Furthermore, at the end, there is the cessation of all illusion" (*bhūyaścānte viśvamāyānivṛttiḥ*). And when the bolt of the door of the *ādhāra* (the foundational center) has been loosened by the breath (*marut*) regulated within the channels (*nāḍī*), the person—acting as a "sacrificer of time" (*kālayajvan*) by worshipping the Lord through rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti without transgressing the fixed times—is a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*). By the term "sacrificer of time," it is indicated that such a person is one who, having abandoned prohibited and desire-driven acts, performs the enjoined duties for the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The meaning is that one offers the universe as an oblation so that it does not arise again, dissolving it through meditation. As the Teachers have said: "Having conceived the entire phenomenal world as the sacrificial offering, I offer it for the sake of liberation into the eternally blazing light within all, which is self-existent, by means of the ladle of wisdom."

Thus it is said; and in the *Ambāstava*: "O Mother, this ocean of illusion—crowded with a multitude of bubbles that are the cosmic eggs and possessing rows of waves that are the various principles—is, to our amazement, instantly reduced to dissolution in the great submarine fire of the continuous stream of meditation upon you."

Thus: "Arci" means that which has its edges saturated by a flood of the rain of supreme nectar flowing from the moon of the lotus at the *brahmarandhra*—the crown aperture—which is melted by the flame of one's own crest [of consciousness] delighting in wandering through the *suṣumṇā* channel. "Tārtīyīkam" (the third): according to the method of the Upaniṣads, "It is indeed other than the known, and moreover, above the unknown," it is that which is distinct from Māyā and its effects, being the third as the substratum upon which their superimposition occurs. Alternatively, according to the Śaiva Āgamas, there is a triad in sequence consisting of the Lord (*pati*), the individual soul (*paśu*), and the fetter (*pāśa*). It is the primary among these.

In the manner thus described, as the controller (*niyantṛ*) of the two things to be controlled—the individual soul (*paśu*) and its fetter (*pāśa*)—the city, which is the body, of the Enemy of Cities (*purāri*) stands transcendent. It is the burning of Madana, which uproots the bondage of the body fashioned by the pair of karmas that are the cause of ignorance for devotees; it is the crushing of Manmatha, who is the seed of the poisonous tree of *saṃsāra*.
As it is said: "This is desire, this is anger, born of the quality of passion (*rajas*);
it is the great devourer, the great sinner—know this to be the enemy here."

Thus, from the words of the Blessed One: *Locana* is derived from the root *locṛ* (to see) with the suffix *lyuṭ*. It is the inner light (*pratyag-jyotiḥ*), which is one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-bhūta*), consisting of the essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda-rasa*), and manifesting from the *mūlādhāra*. For the scripture states: "There is no loss of the vision of the Seer. As the Teachers have said: "From the *mūlādhāra*, she who is the subtle form of the radiance of a flashing lightning-streak, ascending to the crown of the head as the most minute root of all lights;
skilled in traversing the path of the *suṣumṇā*, joined with the Sun, when meditated upon, she immediately causes the nectar of the Sun together with the half-moon to flow forth."

Thus it is said. Herein, the sequence should be understood as follows: because matted locks (*jaṭā*) are the outward signs of dharma, there is the increase of dharma; because the waves of the flowing river remove misfortune, there is the removal of adharma; and because the eye is of the nature of knowledge, liberation—which is to be accomplished by that [knowledge]—is prayed for.

Having thus offered the benediction, the Sūtradhāra anticipates the distress of sensitive readers (sahṛdayas) caused by the interruption of aesthetic flavor (rasa) arising from the fault of unnecessary prolixity, and dispels it by saying: "Enough with excessive elaboration. By the word *ati* ("excessive"), he implies that there is no fault in this much verbal expansion as it does not abandon propriety (*aucitya*), whereas anything beyond this would indeed be a fault. As the author of the Dhvani says: "There is no cause for the disruption of rasa other than impropriety; the composition based on established propriety is the supreme secret of rasa."

Thus: because of the prohibition of the suffix *ghañ* by the rule "in the sense of expansion, provided it does not mean sound" (Pāṇini 3.3.33), the suffix *ap* [is applied] after the root *stṛñ* preceded by the prefix *vi-* when referring to sound, according to the rule "for roots ending in *ṛ* or *u*, the suffix *ap*" (Pāṇini 3.3.57).

(3-3-57) / Since it is stated that *alam* is used in the senses of "ornament," "sufficiency," and "prohibition," this indeclinable is employed here in the sense of prohibition. It is joined with the third case, as seen in such examples as "O protector of the earth, enough of your exertion" (*alam mahīpāla tava śrameṇa*). This [usage] is also a third case governed by the category of *prakṛti* and so forth. Now, keeping in mind the proper time for service as it arose at the conclusion of the morning twilight worship of the gods of the earth (*bhūmideva*), and desiring to approach the Sun for the attainment of his own desired goal, he says: *uditabhūyiṣṭha*...

Thus, "greatly risen" means having ascended from the mountain of sunrise to the expanse of the sky. He is "the lamp for all the continents of the world," meaning he is like a lamp because he illuminates all the specific regions of the earth—the various parts of the world consisting of the continents named Jambū, Plakṣa, Śālmalī, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara, whose boundaries are interspersed with oceans.
As it is said: "As far as the earth is illuminated by the rays of the sun and moon, including its oceans, rivers, and mountains, so far is the earth known to extend."

Thus, according to the statement of the Purāṇas. Furthermore, one should not suspect a deficiency on the part of the lamp; for it is logical that the lamp, the illuminator, may also be large in proportion to the greatness of the space to be illuminated. "I approach" (*upatiṣṭhe*) means "I worship. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used for the root *sthā* according to the rule: "The prefix *upa* [is used] in the senses of worshipping a deity, forming a connection, making a friend, and paths" (Pāṇini 1.3.25).

"Having prostrated," he says; thus he describes the manner of attendance with the words "of auspicious things," and so forth. "Of auspicious things" (*kalyāṇānām*) is an introduction of what is intended. It refers to those that are causes of well-being (*maṅgala*); this is a metaphorical designation of the effect by means of the cause. "Of great splendors" (*mahasām*) means of lights. By the use of the plural number, those belonging to the moon and other such sources are also included, as it is said:
"That light which, residing in the sun, illuminates the entire world—that which is in the moon and that which is in fire—know that light to be mine."

And because of the Lord’s own words: "Among luminaries, the sun is the radiant one. *Bhājana* means a receptacle or support. Since the word *bhājana* is invariably neuter, its coreferentiality with *tvam* (you) [is established]. O Viśvamūrti! [O you] whose body (*vigraha*) is the entire universe (*viśva*), consisting of the mobile and immobile world; the meaning is that [the world] is pervaded by you in the form of consciousness. This is according to the Vedic scripture: "That which is here in the person and that which is yonder in the sun, these are one. *Atha*—for this reason—O Deva! O you who delight in the play (*krīḍā*) of creating the world and so forth.

Be gracious—cast upon me a glance of compassion. Bestow *lakṣmī*—the prosperity consisting of fame, gain, and honor, produced by the application of superior knowledge—upon me as one who is *dhuryā*, capable of bearing the burden of serving virtuous people. [The suffix *yat* is applied here according to Pāṇini 4.4.77: *dhuro yaṭḍhakañau*. Cherish [this]—nourish it. [The rule *ghvasoreddhāvabhyāsalopaśca* applies.]

(6-4-119) *it* is substituted [for the final vowel] and there is elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*). The expression "whatever" (*yadyat*) refers to speech, mind, and body; by means of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), everything existing in whatever form is referred to. That which is of such a nature is referred to by the single word "that" (*tad*). This is because, in the illustrative sentence for the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the *Nyāyadīpāvalī*—"Whatever is perceptible is false, just like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell"—this is established in both ways; and because it has been explained accordingly in this verse through the application of logical principles (*nyāyabharabandha*).
"Sin"—that which is unprecedented, resulting from the practice of what is forbidden—"cast out"—render it struck down; [this is according to the rule] "the root *han* becomes *j*" (Pāṇini 6.4.36).

O Lord of the World! He is called *nātha* because he is entreated (*nāthyate*); he is one who is to be prayed to by the worlds, because he is the bestower of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*). [The word is derived] from the root *nāthṛ* in the sense of "begging," with the suffix *ghañ*. "Of the bowing one"—of one whose nature is to bow. [This is according to the rule] "after the roots *nam*, *kamp*, *sma*, *yaj*, *kam*, *hiṃs*, and *dīp*, the suffix *ra* is added. (Pāṇini 3.2.167).

By [Pāṇini 8.1.4], *ra* is substituted [for *m*]. "Bhadraṃ bhadram" means the sovereignty characterized by the arising of the knowledge of reality higher and higher; [this is an example of] the rule "nityavīpsayoḥ" [Pāṇini 8.1.4].

(8-1-4) Thus, there is reduplication (*dvitva*). *Vitara* means "give. The root *tṛ* preceded by *vi* is used in the sense of giving. O Blessed One! O treasury of the six qualities known as sovereignty, heroism, knowledge, splendor, fame, and dispassion! By this, the capacity for the gift of knowledge and so forth is implied; the sense is that the power to give belongs only to one who possesses wealth, not to one who is destitute. For the sake of greater auspiciousness (*bhūyase maṅgalāya*). By the word "auspiciousness" (*maṅgala*), happiness—the effect of auspiciousness—is figuratively expressed.

In order to attain liberation (*apavarga*), which consists in the cessation of all suffering without remainder and the attainment of unsurpassed bliss; [this is expressed by the rule: *kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi sthāninaḥ*.

(2-3-14) Thus ends the fourth [verse]. There is a vocative at the beginning of each sentence. It should be understood that, according to the principle that "a deity being praised indeed increases in power," these are intended for the increase of power and for the sake of [the deity's] grace and favor. Here, it should be understood that the awakening of power is effected by the first [sentence], the prayer for fruits in this world by the second, the hope for the destruction of sins by the third, and the prayer for the knowledge of reality—which is the means to that [destruction]—by the fourth. As it is said: "The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes."

This is because of the words of the Blessed One, and because it is heard that upon the realization of that [knowledge], there is the complete destruction of both the subsequent and the prior parts [of karma]. And herein, the preliminary benediction consisting of a salutation to the deity has been performed.

According to the statement: "That which is recited at the beginning of a drama, consisting of auspicious acts such as salutations to the deities and others, is called *nāndī* by the learned," and based on Bharata’s dictum that "the *miśra* [style] occurs in the *nepathya* (tiring room)," it should be understood that the salutation to the deities is performed in the *nepathya*. //5//

"Facing the *nepathya*," and so forth. *Nepathya* refers to the private area for actors where they assume their costumes. "Well-prepared" (*suvihitāni*) means properly executed according to the sequence prescribed in the *Nāṭya-veda*. "Descent" (*avataraṇa*) refers to the entrance of female singers whose mouths are resonant with sweet, auspicious songs; as stated by Bharata:
"Likewise, there is the descent and the entrance of the female singers.
Although other preliminary elements of the stage ritual (*pūrvaraṅga*) such as the *pratyāhāra* exist, the mention of "descent" here is due to its preeminence.
"Song (*geya*) is the life-breath of performance, or rather, everything is said to be song;
for the fourfold aims of life—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—are accomplished through song," according to the statement of Bharata. Likewise, Śārṅgadeva [says]:
"‘Dance is said to follow instrumental music, and instrumental music is bound to song;

therefore, because of its primacy, song is mentioned here at the beginning. Thus [it is said]. The *raṅgamaṅgalas* (auspicious stage-rites) consist of *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal of the senses) and so forth. *Sannipatitaḥ* means assembled or gathered together. *Kālapriya* is the name of a particular sanctuary (*devatāyatana*). “In connection with the festival (*yātrā*), that is, on the occasion of a divine celebration (*divyotsava*)”; as Murāri says: “The members of the assembly are present for the festival of Puruṣottama. *Nānādigantavāstavyaḥ* means a resident of various regions—that is, one dwelling in diverse lands. [The suffix] *-tavyat* is applied to the root *vas* (to dwell) in the sense of the agent, and it is also *ṇic*-derived.

(Vārttika 3.1.96). *Mahājana* means those people who are extraordinary (*lokottara*) by virtue of their lineage (*abhijana*), learning (*vidyā*), and conduct (*vṛtta*). *Samāja* means a multitude (*samūha*). Because the rule "after *sam* and *ud*, the suffix *ap* is used for animals" (3.3.61) prescribes the suffix *ap*, the suffix *ghañ* is used here as it does not refer to animals. *Kimiti* means for what purpose. *Udāsate* means they remain indifferent toward duties due to a lack of enthusiasm; this [statement] is intended to encourage them. *Bharatas* means actors. *By the performance of unprecedented subject matter* means by the dramatic representation of plots never before seen. Regarding the explanation of the word *vastu*, Dhanika says: "the varieties of plot. *Vinodanīyāḥ* means they should be made to pass the time.

By the phrase "by means of a continuous composition characterized by the qualities just specified," he indicates an injunction to the audience that there ought to be a composition distinguished by these very qualities. The word *prabandha* (composition) is common to poetry, drama, and so forth, as seen in such expressions as "Know our six *prabandhas*."

Having entered, [the stage direction] says "the *pāripārśvika*. His entrance is justified by his desire to hear the matter already indicated [by the *sūtradhāra*]. When it is said "having entered," the further specification of the character is appropriate because no verbal action has yet been stated. Since the suffix *-ktvā* is prescribed by the rule "when two actions have the same agent, the one occurring earlier takes *-ktvā*" (Pāṇini 3.4.21), the word "says" (*āha*) is established as an indispensable corollary; therefore, to specify the character again would be redundant and a mistake. This should be understood in all similar cases. "Standing at the side of the *sūtradhāra*" refers to the actor (*naṭa*). Because this is a dialogue between the *sūtradhāra* and the actor, it constitutes the *āmukha* (prologue).
As it is said: "The *sūtradhāra* addresses the *naṭī*, the *māriṣa*, or the *vidūṣaka*;

that which introduces the subject matter of his own business through striking speech is the *āmukha* (prologue). [In response to the question] "Sir, what are those qualities?"—this is the *prayogātiśaya* (excellence of performance), a constituent element (*aṅga*) of the *āmukha*, because of the entrance [of the characters].

"Where there is the entrance of a character accompanied by the expectation 'This is I,' following the direction of the stage-manager (sūtradhāra), this is considered *prayogātiśaya* (an excellence of performance). In dramatic terminology, *bhāva* refers to the state of being or the internal disposition.

By the statement, "The actor [addresses] the *sūtradhāra* as 'māriṣa' and likewise [the *sūtradhāra* addresses him as] 'bhāva'," the actor addresses the *sūtradhāra*. Who are they? Of what nature are they? "Āryamiśrāḥ"—those worthy of honor among those of virtuous conduct. The word *miśra* is used for those who are venerable, just like words such as *pāda* (used for the feet of a teacher). This is seen in examples such as *Kṛṣṇamiśra*. "Bhagavantaḥ"—[those who know] "the origin and dissolution of beings, as well as their coming and going."

"He who knows both knowledge and ignorance—he indeed is to be called Bhagavān. [The Brahmins] are distinguished by the aforementioned qualities. "Bhūmidevas" refers to the Brāhmaṇas; by the mention of "Brāhmaṇas," it is indicated that they alone possess the primary eligibility for the eighteen branches of learning, such as the Vedas and so forth, and since the performance of drama is the essence of the four Vedas, it is implied that it should be viewed by other castes only by following their lead. As stated by Bharata:
"From the Ṛgveda, the recited text (pāṭhya) emerged; from the Sāmaveda, the song (gīta) was produced."
"From the Yajus were born the dramatic gestures (abhinaya), and from the Atharvan came the aesthetic sentiments (rasas).
Thus it is said.

"By abundance," etc.—by "abundance" (bhūmnā) is meant by way of preponderance. Regarding "the sentiments" (rasānām): this refers to the primary sentiments such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), and those that serve as their subordinate members. Sentiments (*rasa*) are stable emotional states (*sthāyibhāva*)—such as love (*rati*) and the like—which consist of a delight directed toward objects such as the *ālambana* (the foundational stimulus), and which are colored by the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*), which are synonyms for cause, effect, and auxiliary factors. The mention of "sentiments" is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the emotional states (*bhāva*). They are "profound" (*gahanāḥ*)—difficult to fathom by those of limited intellect, and to be savored solely within the hearts of the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*). "Applications" (*prayogāḥ*) are the suggestive gestures and enactments (*abhinaya*), because they have as their sole nature the manifestation of what is to be suggested. [These are] "heart-pleasing through friendship."

(Viceṣṭitāni): The deeds of the hero, the supporting characters, and others, which are charming due to their genuine affection. *Autsukya* is the frustration of longing (*abhilāṣa-vipralambha*), as seen in such usages as "hastening through eagerness" (*autsukyena kṛtatvarā*) and "not taking account [of anything] out of eagerness" (*ity autsukyād aparigaṇayan*).

According to the *Vaijayantī*: "Syād āyallakaṃ autsukyaṃ utkaṇṭhā utkalikā ratiḥ. If the reading is *auddhatyam*, it means immodesty rooted in passion (*manmatha*). "In which the aphorisms of the *Kāmasūtra* are applied" means that the aphorisms of the science of love composed by the sage Vātsyāyana have been incorporated therein as examples throughout. "Variegated" (*citrā*) means producing wonder through skill in arrangement and brought forth by the poet’s creative genius. "Story" (*kathā*) refers to the body of the narrative (*itivṛtta*).

The term *vāci* (in speech) is used in the singular to denote the various utterances of the respective characters, and not the composition of the poet, since that [quality] will be discussed later in the passage beginning with "that which is maturity" (*yat prauḍhitvam*). *Vidagdhatā* (cleverness) is non-vulgarity by virtue of propriety (*aucitya*). By the word *iti*, the poet makes a formal declaration regarding the matters within the scope of his own creative effort, by way of the assembly's commission; for these are established as being inseparable from the application of grammar, political science, the *Bhārata*, and so forth. The words "these are those qualities" (*ete te guṇāḥ*) are to be understood as the ellipsis. And we shall demonstrate these qualities in their respective contexts. //6//

By the words "the story is varied," the actor is reminded of the definition of a *prakaraṇa* (drama) as having a plot that is invented rather than based on historical fact; he then asks, "In which *prakaraṇa* [are] these qualities?"—the word "these qualities" being the understood remainder of the sentence. Now, what indeed is this thing called a *prakaraṇa*? It is said in reply:

That in which the plot is fashioned by the poet’s imagination and accords with worldly propriety, where the hero—distinguished by general qualities such as modesty—is a *dhīrapraśānta* (calm and composed) type, being either a minister, a brahmin, or a merchant, and whose success in his undertakings is beset by obstacles; and where there are only two heroines, namely a lady of noble birth (*kulastrī*) or a courtesan (*gaṇikā*), while everything else is like that of a *nāṭaka*—that is the dramatic form called *prakaraṇa*. We shall apply the characteristics of the *nāṭaka*, which serve as the basis for it, in their respective places further on.

In this work, however, the hero is a young Brahmin named Mādhava, who is well-disposed, wise and tranquil, and devoted to the attainment of the three aims of life (trivarga) despite its dangers. The heroine is a Brahmin woman named Mālatī, endowed with virtues such as good character and sincerity, and remaining in a state of youthful innocence (mugdha). The erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa) is the primary theme, while the others are subordinate. It should be understood that the associate hero (upanāyaka)—a term synonymous with *pīṭhamarda*—is named Makaranda and possesses qualities slightly inferior to those of the hero; the antagonist (pratināyaka), named Nandana, is characterized by greed, stubbornness, and old age, and so forth.
"Having reflected"—the meaning is that he spoke after deliberating upon such a subject with a concentrated mind.

According to the *Vaijayantī*: "The region south of the Vindhya mountains is designated as the Dakṣiṇāpatha. The *Taittirīya* is a specific branch of the Yajurveda which, at the command of his guru, was disgorged by the lord of yogis, Yājñavalkya; it was then received by his disciples, who had become embodied partridges (*tittiri*), and set forth in the world. As Murāri has said:
"He who vomited forth the Taittirīya Yajus-mantras in bodily form—
that yogi Yājñavalkya taught you the Vedāntas.
Thus [it is said].

The suffix *chaṇ* is applied by the rule "tittirivaratantukhaṇḍikokhācchaṇ" (Pāṇini 4.3.102). Since he has grasped [the tradition] both in word and in meaning, those who possess that [tradition] take the suffix *ini*, resulting in "taittirīyiṇaḥ. By this, it is implied that his study is preceded by the study of his own specific recension (*svaśākhā*), because the study of other recensions and so forth will be mentioned later in the passage beginning with "bhūriśrutam. One who, standing in a row of a thousand outcasts (*pātakin*), purifies all of them is called a "purifier of the row" (*paṅktipāvana*), according to the Vedic scripture: "They purify the row up to a thousand [people]."

And from the words of Manu: "Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the expositions [of the scriptures], and who are born of a lineage of Vedic scholars (śrotriya), are to be known as the sanctifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvana). As for the Kāśyapas—those born of the Kāśyapa gotra. As for the "five-fire" practitioners (pañcāgnayaḥ)—those by whom the five fires, known as Gārhapatya, Āhavanīya, Dakṣiṇāgni, Sabhya, and Āvasathya, are worshipped. Alternatively...
"Five fires must be served with diligence by a man:
the father, the mother, the sacred fire, one's own self, and the teacher, O bull of the Bharatas.

Thus, they were devoted to the service of these five fires as described in the *Mahābhārata*. They were firm in their vows, their bodies purified by the practice of austerities such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances.

"Vrata, Viṣṇu, Ṛtu, Varṣa, Ijyā, Tapas, Māsa, Agni, and Bhukti"—thus says the *Vaijayantī*. "One who drinks Soma is a *somapa*"—thus says the *Vaijayantī*. Although the meaning is already conveyed by the term "those who maintain the five fires" (*pañcāgnayaḥ*), the mention of "those who drink Soma" (*somapīthinaḥ*) highlights their habitual practice. "Teachers of conduct" (*caraṇaguravaḥ*) refers to those preceptors who teach specific branches of the Veda (*vedaśākhā*).
"One should not inquire about [the other's] lineage, branch of study, sacred recitation, or traditional lore."

According to this statement; or else, as the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "Ācāra, vṛtta, cāritra, caritra, and caraṇa [are synonyms]. They are those who, by their own practice of worldly duties, teach the conduct of the virtuous (*sadācāra*).
"Revelation (Śruti), tradition (Smṛti), the conduct of the virtuous (Sadācāra), and what is pleasing to oneself—
these they declare to be the fourfold direct definition of Dharma," according to the words of Manu.
"Whatever a great man does, that very thing other people do;
whatever standard he sets, the world follows that."

And because of the words of the Blessed One: a householder who collects grain sufficient for only six months is called *audumbara* or *audumbra*. As the *Vaijayantī* states: "An *udumbara*, however, is one who stores [grain] for six months and eats at the same time. They became well-known by that name. *Brahmavāda* is discourse concerning Brahman, free from passion, consisting of those whose habit is to reflect upon the power and intended meaning of Vedāntic statements such as "One only, without a second. It is a discourse (*vada*) regarding Brahman.
The suffix *ṇini* [is applied] by [Pāṇini's rule] vā. 3-2-78.

"Those who are learned in the Vedas," and so forth. Although it is traditionally recorded that one becomes a *śrotriya* by studying a single branch (*śākhā*) of the Veda, here the word *śrotriya* refers merely to the status of being a Brāhmaṇa; for this is because qualities such as purifying the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*) and the like are established through the study of all the Vedas and other such attributes. "For the sake of determining reality"—that is, to effect a definitive determination of the true nature of the Lord (*īśvara*)—[the suffix is used] according to the rule: "And [the suffix *tumun* is used] after a word expressing an action when another word expressing purpose follows. (*Pāṇini 3.3.10*)

(2-3-15) Thus, the dative case [is used]. The meaning is: for the purpose of stabilizing the intellect, which has been rendered agitated by various mutually contradictory philosophical tenets established through fallacious conceptual constructions such as "existent" and "non-existent," "one" and "many," "eternal" and "non-eternal," and so forth. *Bhūri* means much. *Śāśvatam* means unshakable, through the removal of doubt and error. *Śrutam* refers to the hearing of the scriptures; they *ādriyante*, meaning they honor it by dispelling lack of desire to hear, haste, and pride. This is because of the saying: "One should hear from many, one should hear in many ways.
For indeed, "knowledge that is fully perfected cannot arise from a single teacher."
"Indeed, this Brahman is sung as non-dual by many sages," according to the statement in the *Bhāgavata*.

"The *iṣṭa* is action consisting of sacrifice, and the *pūrta* is action such as digging tanks," according to the *Vaijayantī*. *Karma* is that which is most desired by the agent, or that which is the non-inherent cause of conjunction and disjunction; [the compound] is for the sake of that. *Arthān* means riches.
"Of his six duties, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of pure gifts.

According to this sequence from the Smṛti, by means of acquiring and protecting [wealth] and so forth, he [should support] his *dārān*—that is, his wife (*patnīm*). The word *dārāḥ* is masculine and always plural, as per the rule "the word *dārāḥ* is masculine and used in the plural. The word *apatyam* (offspring) is common to both male and female, according to the rule "progeny (*apatyam*) and *tokam* apply equally to both"; it is for the sake of that [offspring].

"Women are said to be the glories of the home; therefore, they should be especially honored. According to this *smṛti* [text], [he honors them] with clothing, ornaments, and so forth, as well as by preserving their proper conduct. "For the sake of austerity" (*taportham*) means for the sake of all human goals, which are the source (*tīrtha*) of dharma, that is, for the performance of religious duty. The compound is a fourth-case (*caturthī*) tatpuruṣa, and its neuter gender is established by the rule: "A constant compound with *artha* should be stated to have all genders" (*Pāṇini* 2.1.36). "Aging" (*āyuḥ*) refers to the duration of life. [He honors them] through the study of the Vedas and so forth, and by following the sequence of instructions from the *Āyurveda*.

"Through the non-study of the Vedas, the abandonment of right conduct, laziness, and defects in food, death seeks to strike down the Brahmins"—so says the word of Manu. Here, by the phrase "for the sake of what is heard," the engagement in the discharge of debts toward the sages (*ṛṣis*), the gods (*devas*), and the ancestors (*pitṛs*) is established. Furthermore, by the phrases "for the sake of austerity," "wives," "wealth," and "for the sake of the determination of truth," the fulfillment of one's duties through the attainment of the four aims of human life—known as virtue (*dharma*), pleasure (*kāma*), wealth (*artha*), and liberation (*mokṣa*)—is illuminated. And the phrase "life for the sake of austerity" applies universally to all.

As it is said: "One who desires long life—the means for achieving dharma, artha, and sukha—should show the highest respect for the instructions of Ayurveda. Here, by the word *bhūmikā*, the composition of words—which constitutes the poet's activity and corresponds to those roles—is intended. This is because in the verse, "Listen with attentive minds to this work of Kālidāsa," the command is "listen" (*śṛṇuta*), and not "behold" (*paśyata*).

"At that very moment"—meaning immediately after he had offered his own composition—"the members of the group" (*vargyāḥ*), those belonging to our troop, [are so called] according to Pāṇini 4.3.54, *digādibhyo yat*.

They were "made to recite," that is, taught. This is based on the rule: "In a *ṇic*-formation, the agent of roots meaning motion, cognition, eating, or having sound as their object, or being intransitive, becomes the object. (Pāṇini 1.4.52)

(1-4-52) Because it has sound as its object (*śabdakarmaka*), there is a state of having two objects (*dvikarmakatā*). *Saugata-jarat-pravrājikā* refers to an elderly Buddhist female ascetic (*bauddha-siddhānta-vartinī*) who follows the Buddhist tenets; her name is Kāmandakī. *Prathamām* means "the first," being the foremost among all characters (*sarva-pātra-ādi-bhūtām*). *Adhīte* means she studies or recites. *Tad-antevāsinyāḥ* means "of her resident pupil" (*tac-chiṣyāyāḥ*). [The genitive case ending is not elided] because of the rule *śaya-vāsa-vāsiṣv akālāt* (Pāṇini 6.3.18). *Avalokitā* is her name. By the force of the context (*sāmarthyāt*), the word *adhīya* undergoes a change of gender to masculine. And by the word *tu*, the term *bhūmikām* is drawn in [from the previous verse].
Anticipating the objection that the subject (*anuvādya*) must look toward the predicate (*vidheya*), the Stage Manager asks: "Then what?"—meaning, "What do you wish to say regarding that?

He asks "How?"—that is, "In what manner?"—as a timely inquiry. He provides the answer: "At the occasion of the entrance of Kalahaṃsa and Makaranda. Kalahaṃsa is Mādhava’s servant; Makaranda is his friend. By mentioning them in the order of *Kalahaṃsa-Makaranda*, he indicates the order of their entrance. "That" means "that matter. "Well-arranged" (*suvihita*) means it has been thoroughly instructed as something to be done.

"By that means"—that is to say, by such well-prepared application. "To those venerable ones" (*atrabhavataḥ*): those who exist in the assembly (*sāmājikān*), i.e., those present in the assembly. The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.53, *tatra bhavaḥ*. "We attend upon" (*upāsmahe*) means we serve them.

"Firmly" (*bāḍham*) means resolutely, or appropriately. By the suddenness with which he assumes his role (*bhūmikā-parigraha-jhāṭityāt*), he demonstrates his proficiency in action—[expressed as] "Here I am. Because the predicate "Kāmandakī" finds its rest in the subject [of the sentence], this [subject] is qualified by the masculine gender.
The actor says with a smile: "I too," thus displaying his skill through rivalry. It is to be connected with "has occurred" (*saṃvṛttaḥ*), as before.

"Having turned around and gone to the dressing room"—this is the meaning. "Clad in red garments" means adorned with the saffron robes (kāṣāya) which are the conventional attire for that period; this is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) of other ascetic emblems such as the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). "Seated" means sitting upon seats appropriate for a teacher and a disciple. The use of the present tense in "they enter" is because they are present in the form of a continuous stream of actors. These two should be understood as the middle and low-ranking characters (viṣkambhaka-pātra) [of the play].
As it is said: "At the beginning, one should perform a *viṣkambhaka* or an act (*aṅka*) according to the requirements of the plot."
Having abandoned the irrelevant and the tedious expansion of subject matter.
As it is said: "When one should reveal what remains, then one should perform the *viṣkambhaka*";
[it is] "the indicator of those portions of the story that have already occurred and those yet to occur."
In brief, however, the *viṣkambha* is performed by a character of middle status.

As it is said: "It is produced as single, manifold, pure, mixed, or by the low and the middling," this [work] is therefore mixed (*saṅkīrṇa*). For this very reason, there is a mixture of *Saṃskṛta* and *Prākṛta*. Furthermore: "The recitation (*pāṭhya*) should be in *Saṃskṛta* for men who are not low-born and who have cultivated their souls."
"Among *liṅginīs*, a great queen, a minister’s daughter, and a courtesan [the latter two] may occasionally [use Sanskrit].

Because of this statement, the former woman (the great queen) employs Sanskrit because she is a *liṅginī*; however, the other (the minister’s daughter), although she is a *liṅginī*, employs Prakrit because she is a disciple (*śiṣyā*). Furthermore, it should be understood that the initial entry of the female renunciant (*pravrājikā*) marks the commencement of the purpose of the *Kāmasūtra*.
"The wife of a perfumer, a garland-maker, or a washerman; a female renunciant (*pravrājikā*); and a female seller..."
"A nurse, a neighbor, and a woman of steady character—these may serve as female messengers," according to the *Kāmasūtra*. Furthermore, the address "Bhagavatī" (O Blessed One) is used;
for it is said: "Those who are learned, divine sages, or ascetics are to be addressed as 'Bhagavantaḥ' by those of lower status."
Because of this statement, and because of the term "vatsa" (child):

"A charioteer [is addressed] by his driver as 'long-lived one' (āyuṣman); disciples, sons, and younger brothers [address] their superiors as 'dear child' (vatsa), 'father' (tāta), or by a name that is auspiciously invoked. Even those who are worthy of honor may be so addressed by them.
Because of this statement, one should likewise act according to propriety in other instances as well.
"May the Blessed Lady command"—by this, he indicates an excess of great respect for the words she is about to speak.
"Perhaps," and so forth; the reason for this is that the task at hand is connected to dharma and artha, yet consists of the nature of kāma.

For it is said: "The task is the triple aggregate (trivarga), which is pure, and is connected to both the one and the many. To explain: for him who has completed his student life (brahmacarya) and whose time has arrived to enter the second stage of life (āśrama)—which is capable of benefiting all—attaining a wife is the root of the triple aggregate, because she is the means for accomplishing the five sacrifices, because she is a cause of happiness, and because she brings about the acquisition of kinsmen in the form of kings and ministers. "When both husband and wife are mutually submissive to one another..."

"For then there is the convergence of all three—dharma, artha, and kāma"—so it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*. Therefore, he introduces the seed of that [plot], which is the cause for its accomplishment, through the mouth of Kāmandakī, who stands in the position of a minister; for the success of the leader depends upon her. As it is said: "That which is briefly indicated as the cause is the 'seed' (*bīja*), which is expanded in many ways."

This is because of the aforementioned statement. Furthermore, *api nāma* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) used to indicate possibility or hope. *Kalyāṇinī* means "possessing auspiciousness," where "auspiciousness" (*kalyāṇa*) refers to meritorious action (*puṇyakarma*); thus, one who possesses it is *kalyāṇinī*, and one who possesses it is *kalyāṇī*. The suffix *-in* is applied here. [The phrase] *tayoḥ kalyāṇinoḥ* means "of those two auspicious ones. [The rule] *pumān striyā* [applies].

(1-2-67) Thus, there is an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one term). By this, it is indicated that because they are endowed with divine fortune (*daiva-sampannatva*), their success is unfailing; furthermore, it is suggested that our intense affection for them causes us agitation. The use of the proximate demonstrative "of these two" (*anayoḥ*) is due to their being constantly present in the mind. [The compound] "the offspring of Bhūrivasu and Devarāta" means: by respective order (*yathāsaṅkhyena*), Mālatī is the offspring of Bhūrivasu, and Mādhava is the offspring of Devarāta; [the phrase refers to] those two. By this, the praiseworthiness of their shared relationship is manifested. "Desired" (*abhimata*) means most beloved to us.
"Taking of the hand" (*pāṇigraha*) means marriage. "May it be" (*syāt*) is used in the sense of a formal inquiry (*saṃpraśna*) in the optative (*liṅ*).
Joy (*harṣa*) is the clarity of mind produced by auspicious omens indicating the accomplishment of a desired object;
as it is said: "Joy [arises] from festivals and the like, manifesting as clarity of mind, tears, perspiration, and faltering speech."

"Vivṛṇvatā iva," and so forth. By the word *vivṛṇvatā* ("by one revealing"), it is as if he is being shown: "Let this auspicious object, which is of the nature of your desired goal and exists right here in your presence, be beheld"—it does not mean that he is merely describing it. By this, the manifestation of its infallibility (*avyabhicāritva*) is revealed, as in the expression: "He announced Rāma standing before him. *Antarajñena* means by one who knows the [proper] occasion, because [the omen] flashes forth at a time of doubt, as in: "In the meantime, news of Sarasvatī’s descent... [The suffix -ka is applied] according to the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*.

(3-2-3) "By the throbbing," meaning by the quivering; "by the left," meaning by the left-hand one—the suffix *ka* is used here either in its own sense or to denote compassion. Regarding compassion, it is said: "They call courtesy that disposition which acts in accordance [with others], such that even for one who is taking away one's very life-breaths, there is no power to remain [unyielding]."

Thus it is defined. Here, however, only favorability (*ānukūlya*) will be discussed. The word *vāma* also denotes the unfavorable, as seen in such usages as "one who is perverse by the nature of desire" (*kāmasvabhāvavāma*). Here, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the throbbing [of the left arm] as being a manifestation [of favor], with "knowledge of the inner state" (*antarajñatva*) serving as the cause; thus, in the first half-verse, there is the figure of speech *utprekṣā*. In the second half-verse, moreover, there is a contradiction (*virodha*): the left side assumes the status of the right, and the unfavorable becomes favorable. Since the contradiction between two qualities manifests in both ways, the favorability of destiny (*daivānukūlya*), which brings about the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), is also suggested by this.

And herein, there are five junctures (*sandhi*)—namely, the *mukha*, *pratimukha*, *garbha*, *avamarśa*, and *nirvahaṇa*—which correspond respectively to the five stages consisting of commencement, effort, attainment, hope, and the arrival of the fruit through certain acquisition; these stages are characterized by the five types of plot-essentials (*arthaprakṛti*), namely the seed (*bīja*), the drop (*bindu*), the banner (*patākā*), the secondary banner (*prakarī*), and the business (*kārya*).
Regarding this, it is said: "The *mukha* is the emergence of the seed, from which various purposes and aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) arise.
In that context, there are twelve constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the *mukha*-juncture, beginning with the introduction (*upakṣepa*).
"The *pratimukha* (intermediate juncture) should be the emergence of that [seed] as if barely visible or invisible.
Its thirteen components are *vilāsa* (amorous play) and so forth.
"The *garbha* (developmental juncture), however, is the repeated searching for the seed that was seen and then lost."
And its twelve components include the "false accusation" (*abhūtāharaṇa*) and others.

Regarding the "dénouement" (*avamarsa*): "Where one should be struck down by anger, or due to calamity or seduction, for the sake of revealing the seed (*bīja*) hidden within the womb—that is known as the *avamarsa*."
And its thirteen constituent parts begin with the *apavāda* (denouement):

"Where the elements beginning with the *mukha* (opening), which possess seeds and are scattered according to their respective purposes, are brought together toward a single goal— that indeed is the *nirvahaṇa* (conclusion)."

The junctures (*sandhi*) have fourteen constituent parts (*aṅga*). Thus, the five junctures are explained as having sixty-four parts. Among these, the six functional parts are: the binding of the intended meaning, the concealment of what is to be concealed, the revelation of what is to be revealed, the increase of fresh passion, the production of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), and the expansion of the narrative of the plot. We shall apply the constituent parts of the junctures in their respective places. For example, "api nāma" and so forth is the *ākṣepa* (suggestion). "By unfolding through the planting of the seed (*bīja*)" and so forth is the *parinyāsa* (resolution), because it determines the accomplishment of one's own activity through favorable destiny.

Great indeed is this agitation of the Blessed Lady’s mind—an agitation meaning both distress and wonder—that now the noble Bhūrivasu should employ the Blessed Lady, who has taken up the wearing of tattered rags and whose livelihood consists of mere alms-food, in such labors as these; and that even you yourselves, having severed the obstruction of saṃsāra, should likewise cast yourselves into it. "Tattered rags" (*cīracīvara*) refers to the saffron garments made of scraps of cloth worn by those under vows; according to the *Vaijayantī*, "tattered rags" specifically refers to the *saṅghāṭī* robe of a monk.

"Parigraha" refers to the accumulation of wealth. "Piṇḍapāta" is the designation for the fixed meal of Buddhists and others, as the author himself will state later: "except at the time of the alms-round (piṇḍapāta). And as stated in the *Harṣacarita*: "The one named Divākaramitra was a piṇḍapātī. "Prāṇayātrā" means the maintenance of the body. In such endeavors—consisting of the employment of means to bring about the union of bride and groom; in these labors that produce exhaustion of speech, mind, and body—he "niyojayati," meaning he directs them like servants and so forth, thereby intimating an excellence of affection.
"On this earth bounded by the oceans, there are only two lowest of men:
the householder who makes no effort, and the mendicant who makes effort."

Because it has been thus censured; by the word "in that" (tasmin), the subject under discussion is referred to. Worldly activity (*laukika-pravṛtti*), which is dependent on ignorance, desire, and action, and is defiled by pleasure, pain, and so forth—that is *saṃsāra*. That itself is an obstruction (*avagraha*) or bondage. Alternatively, it is an obstruction to rain, because it prevents the rain of the experience of supreme bliss. That [obstruction] is "uprooted" or shattered by whom. The plural form "by you" (*yuṣmābhiḥ*) is used with respect to the gurus. "Self" (*ātmā*) refers to one's own true nature (*svarūpa*).

Alternatively, [the word "manas"] refers to the mind, because all activities are preceded by it. It is "deposited," meaning it is entrusted through a state of dependence; it is not merely inserted at some random time. "Bhāvaī ṇiodi" (O lady, she is being appointed) refers to the stage of undertaking the task. "Mā maivam" means "do not speak thus. The repetition (*vīpsā*) indicates haste. The deficiency of words (*nyūnapadatvam*) indicates affection and agitation. "Yanmām" and so forth: regarding the object to be enjoined, that is, in a situation where something must be done. "Sa bhavān" means "that venerable one," similar to the expression *tatra bhavān*. "Niyuṅkte" (he appoints): this is a reference to the act of making someone a servant, which was previously expressed as "niyojayati" (he employs).

"Regarding that which is established by its own nature, they speak of a transformation of the self called 'affection' (sneha), which arises through its own causes and brings pleasure to the mind"—so says Divākara. Its fruit or purpose is [the affection] residing in the heart, because it is to be inferred from its effects; for one employs such expressions as "he is he," "this is he," and "that is he. [This refers to] *praṇaya*, which is long-standing intimacy.
"Pranaya may mean acquaintance, a request, or even friendship," according to the Vaijayantī lexicon. Sāra means a firm part; [it is derived from] the root sṛ in the sense of "to be firm."

(3-3-17) Thus, the suffix *ghañ* is applied; the meaning is "having mortified. Regarding "with the vital breaths" (*prāṇaiḥ*): the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the wind that sustains the body; the plural number is used due to the different functions such as moving upward and downward. The mention of "vital breaths" first follows worldly convention, because for ordinary people, these [austerities] are the most beloved. The word "or" (*atha vā*) serves to set aside the previous position. "Desired" (*abhimataiḥ*) is an adjective qualifying austerity (*tapas*). Since the vital breaths themselves are afflicted by means of fasting and so forth, and thereby acquired through those [austerities], it is shown that austerities are objects of one's own desire even more than the vital breaths.

The suffix *liṅ* in the word *ghaṭeta* expresses possibility (*sambhāvanā*). The meaning is: "If it were possible to accomplish the task for our friends by these means alone, in the absence of any other method, then that would have been done; however, you must understand that what is being done or will be done cannot possibly achieve that result. This is intended to ensure that no doubt remains in you regarding this matter. By this, the eagerness for the success of the friends' mission is suggested (*dhvanyate*). In the first half of this verse, the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).

In the second half [of the verse], because the gravity of the friend's duty is described as surpassing both life-breaths and ascetic penances, there is the suggestion (dhvani) of the figure of speech *vyatireka* (contrast). Furthermore, the commencement of the action is indicated here by the expression "pleasing through friendship" (*sauhārdahṛdyāni*).

"Do you not know?"—the word "this" (idam) is to be supplied as the object. The meaning is that even previously, when it was being told by us in the course of conversation, it was already known by you. "At which very time" (yadaiva)—this refers to the time [when we were together]. "Of us" (naḥ) is a reference to herself, to Bhūrivasu, and to Devarāta. "Vidyā"—those which make known dharma and so forth, namely the Vedas and other scriptures; the suffix *kyap* is applied here according to the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ samajaniṣadādi*.

(3-3-99) / *Parigrahaḥ* means acceptance. By the phrase "from various quarters," it is indicated that because the teachers of those respective sciences reside in different regions, they are difficult to find in one place; furthermore, this highlights the necessity of wandering about in order to follow them with faith. *Sāhacaryam* refers to the state of being a fellow student (*satīrthya*), which implies brotherhood by virtue of dharma and being bound by unbreakable affection. By the particle *eva* in the phrase "only then" (*tadaiva*), it is revealed that this objective was a long-cherished desire.
"In the presence of our Saudāminī"—that is, in the vicinity of her who is related to us by name, Saudāminī, and who is [my] disciple—"according to the rule *pratiparasamanubhyo 'kṣṇaḥ*."

By this [rule], *ṭac* is applied. Through this restatement, there is an indirect indication (*sūcana*) of the character Saudāminī, who is a constituent part of the conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*). This is what is about to be stated. A "proposition" (*pratijñā*) is the statement of a matter to be established with the desire to communicate it. "Necessarily" (*avaśyam*) means certainly. "By us two" (*āvābhyām*) means by you and by me. "Connection through offspring" (*apatyasaṃbandhaḥ*) refers to a bond mediated by progeny. By using the word "offspring" (*apatya*), which is common to both male and female, it is suggested that, by the power of fate, one who possesses a son should give his daughter to the son of one who possesses a daughter.

The word *iti* denotes a manner of assertion. This assertion is the primary seed (*bīja*) of the plot, because the marriage is the effect of that [assertion]. That [marriage], in turn, should be understood as the seed because it is the cause of the three aims of life (*trivarga*).

The section beginning with "Since you have commanded me" and ending with "a connection through offspring must be made by us both" constitutes the *parikara* (elaboration), because it serves to expand upon the seed. The word *tat* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetu*). By "the virtuous one," it means by you who exist.

"Ānvīkṣikī is the science of the self, so called because of the investigation (*vīkṣaṇa*) of pleasure and pain; by means of that [science], one who perceives reality casts off joy and sorrow"—thus says Kāmandaka. For the purpose of studying that [science], [I shall go to] Kuṇḍina, the city of the King of Vidarbha, according to such statements as "I will not enter Kuṇḍina"; and Padmāvatī, the city which is the residence of Bhūrivasu, that [city I shall go to].
It falls into [the category of] *pratītya* because of the statement "send [it]"; as in the verse:
"The self-controlled Vasiṣṭha sent that couple back to their own capital city.
*Suvihitam* means "well-done" or "beautifully performed."

He establishes the very fact of being well-arranged [in the verse] with the words "apatya" (offspring). The word "priyasya" (of the beloved) implies that he must necessarily be remembered; the sense is that his relationship [to the parents] is most venerable. "Smṛtim" means the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). "Loka" refers to ordinary people, as in the saying, "The world follows what has gone before. He is one whose qualities—such as modesty and sweetness of form—are not shared by other people. "Sāmānya" is formed by adding a taddhita suffix in its own sense (*svārthika*); this is like the expression, "the common duty (*sāmānyadharma*) of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. "Tanūja" means born from the body;
[this is according to the rule] "it is seen in other cases as well."

(3-2-101) Thus, the suffix *ḍa* is applied. "For the sake of incitement" means for the purpose of generating intense desire in the girl and others. "Manifested" means made perceptible; for if it were indirect (*pārokṣya*), there would be the possibility of doubt regarding her form and other qualities. The reasoning beginning with "that now," etc., is employed because of the deliberation on matters conducive to the task at hand. //13//

"Then what? [The question implies: Why does the minister not himself bestow Mālatī upon Mādhava, such that he urges the Holy Lady toward a clandestine marriage? "Therefore" means: because his noble lineage and other qualities have been personally recognized by the other; therefore, "himself," meaning by his own hand. This is an indeclinable used as a substitute for a case ending, as in the verse:
"Even by the command of the Ruler, or by yourself, you have come from the forest to honor me.
"Bestows" means he gives her away.

"Viśrāṇanam, vitaraṇam, sparśanam, pratipādanam"—thus says Amara. *Caurikā* is the state of being a thief (*cora*); the suffix *vuñ* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.133 (*dvandvamanojñādibhyaśca*). A marriage performed by that [stealth] is a *caurikā-vivāha*; the meaning is "one unknown to the world."

He states the reason for this: "He asked her," and so forth. A *narmasuhṛt* is a friend in play; the meaning is a *vidūṣaka*.
