For this very reason, his being characterized by defects such as old age, deformity, and dullness is established. The term *narmasuhṛt* highlights an excellence of affection. [The request was made] through the mouth of the king, but not through his own mouth; thus, by means of the king's mouth, it becomes impossible to refuse. A direct refusal would be an explicit rejection, saying "I will not give her," which leads to anger and agitation on the part of the lord of men (the king).

The word "tu" (but) is displaced in its position. This means: "But this means is auspicious," being pure through the avoidance of misfortunes such as royal wrath; "this" refers to the form of the marriage involving theft that has been commenced by way of the mouth.

"It is a marvel! Indeed, it appears that the minister is indifferent [to Mādhava], for he does not even know his name. The word "even" (*api*) implies a contradiction: although he knows everything, such as his lineage and so forth, the contradiction lies in the fact that he does not even know his name. This is resolved by his indifference, which avoids the consequence of such knowledge. It is said "it appears" because the heart is not directly perceptible;
this indicates that it must be inferred from one's conduct—that concealment is the secrecy of counsel. The meaning is that his outward appearance and gestures are hidden.
For it is said: "One should protect the seed of counsel, for that is the very seed of kings."
As Kāmandaka has stated: "When that [counsel] is disclosed, there is certain disclosure; when it is kept secret, it is the highest secrecy.

It is not only for worldly reasons that the protection of counsel must be maintained, but for this further reason as well; thus he says, "especially" (*viśeṣatastu*). By the words "due to childhood" and "out of innocence," his lack of discernment regarding future merits and defects is implied. "Of those whose feelings are revealed" (*vivṛtabhāvayoḥ*) means those whose intentions, in the form of mutual longing, have been made manifest. "By him" refers to Bhūrivasu. "Should be done" (*kāryaḥ*) means fit to be performed; the suffix *ṇyat* is used here in the sense of fitness (*arhe*). "Concealment of one's own mind" (*svamatinihnavaḥ*) means the hiding of one's own intellect.
Otherwise, there would arise the suspicion based on common rumor that this matter exists solely in accordance with the minister's own understanding. //15//

Nevertheless, fearing that there might be public rumor even regarding their mutual passion, he says: "anurāga" [and so forth]. "Anurāga" refers to the object of mutual love; "pravāda" means public gossip. The word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction: the meaning is that this is not merely a fault, but on the contrary, it is indeed a merit for us. "Vatsayoḥ" refers to Mālatī and Mādhava. "Sārvalaukikaḥ" means known by all people. Regarding the sense of "known therein," the rule "lokasarvalokābhyāṃ ṭhañ" (Pāṇini 5.1.44) applies, as well as "anuśatikādīnāṃ ca."

(7-3-20) Thus, there is a vṛddhi of both members [of the compound]. The phrase "if there should be a rumor" is the ellipsis. This is because Mādhava had not seen Mālatī prior to this. "Our welfare" means more praiseworthy. For (*hi*)—that is, because—in this manner (*evam tu*), meaning in such a state; that is to say, when there is public gossip that they two, deluded by the intoxication of youth, have proceeded independently out of mutual passion, disregarding once again the minister’s counsel. They can be deceived (*pratārayitum śakyau*) because it is perceived by them that the minister is innocent. //16//

He says, "Behold," meaning: one should carefully examine with the intellect how, for a person whose mind is determined by the treatises on political ethics (*nītiśāstra*), there exists in such applications both an unfailing result and a conduct of unsurpassed profundity that cannot be understood by others; this is what must be discerned by the skillful in the world. Thus is the meaning.

"Externally," and so forth. "Externally" means in a place outside the heart, within the range of direct perception. "In every way charmingly inclined" means being modest in all respects, such as dress and speech; it is "beautiful" because it is perceived as unartificial. "Acting" means proceeding without doubt in one's affairs. Regarding the term *vyavahāra*: "The prefix *vi-* signifies variety (*nānā*), and *ava* signifies doubt (*saṃdeha*). *Hāra* is said to mean 'removal' (*harana*). Because it removes various doubts, it is traditionally known as *vyavahāra*."

Thus says the Smṛti. "Tanutarāṇi" means even extremely subtle; "parābhyūhasthānāni" refers to vulnerabilities that give rise to the suspicion in enemies—that is, opponents—that "this person has acted otherwise [than he claims]"; "sthagayati" means he conceals them. The meaning is that he rectifies them instantly. "Vidvān" means one who is skilled in the application of the principles of the science of polity (*nītiśāstra*). By the word "eka" (alone), his peerless heroism is implied. "Atisandhāya" means having deceived; as it is said: "Deceit (*vañcanam*), however, is *atisandhānam*, *vyalīkam*, and *pratāraṇam*."

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*. "By guiles" means by the employment of *māyā* (deceitful stratagems). "Standing on the bank" (*taṭasthaḥ*)—the figurative usage (*lākṣaṇikaḥ prayogaḥ*) implies that he remains merely situated on the shore and does not descend into the water. Just as a crane standing on the bank pursues a fish and, having swallowed it, remains silent, so too [the king] stays at a distance himself and has not entered [the enemy's domain]; this is the meaning. "His own" (*svān*) refers to his intended purposes (*arthān*). By the use of the plural number, it is indicated that a single objective once undertaken may involve multiple subsequent aims.

He brings about [the task] and accomplishes it without obstacle. Anticipating the thought that "while a task is being accomplished, one may indeed remain silent, but once it is achieved, even boasting is fitting," he says: "silence" means the state of remaining quiet. The meaning is that even when the fruit is attained, he does not engage in boasting precisely because there would be no purpose for it.
As it is said: "When a wise man exerts himself like a lion at the proper time, his own kin recognize the deed as it is being done, while others recognize it as already accomplished."

Thus it is stated by Kāmandaka. Here, by means of the two *ca* (and) particles, the transition between the two mental states of *mati* (resolve) and *dhṛti* (fortitude) is revealed. The poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) employed are *svabhāvokti* (description of nature) and *sūkṣma* (the subtle). //17//

"By me," and so forth. By me also, according to your word, Mādhava is being led along the royal road near Bhūrivasu’s residence by various pretexts (*upanyāsa*). The repetition "by this and that" suggests that these were devised on the spot due to his presence of mind (*pratyutpannamati*). Amara states: "A *upanyāsa* is the opening of speech.

*Dhātreyī* means the daughter of a foster-mother; [the suffix] *ḍhak* is applied after feminine stems. And the mention of *dhātreyikā* is because she too is reckoned among the ranks of female messengers (*dūtī*).

"Again and again," and so forth—meaning repeatedly. "By the street of the nearby city" means by the royal road (*rājamārga*) situated close by; according to Amara, "rathyā," "pratolī," and "viśikhā" all mean a street. "Wandering" means moving about; this is derived from the root *aṭ* (to wander) with the suffix *śatṛ*. "Having seen, having seen"—this indicates the result of his repeated wandering. "The palace turret" (*bhavanavalabhī*) refers to the upper chamber of one's own house; as stated by Māgha, "the young men [met] the turrets along with their brides," and according to Vaijayantī, "kūṭāgāra" is indeed a turret (*valabhī*).

"Vātāyanam" and "gavākṣaḥ" (masculine/neuter) mean a window—so says Amara. She was situated within that [window]. By this, her invisibility to Mādhava is indicated, as well as the fact that she could be won over merely through his pursuit. As Vātsyāyana says: "Gazing upon the royal highway from a palace. "New," meaning manifested after transcending the ill-fated curse of Viriñca (Brahmā). By the word "sākṣāt" (directly), she is suggested to be the very repository of the entire essence of the qualities of Smara (the God of Love), such as the sweetness of form. Through this poetic fancy (utprekṣā), she is illuminated as an unsurpassed excitant (uddīpana-vibhāva).

By the phrase "like love" (*ratir iva*), he indicates the future occurrence of the fruit of love, which is unfailing. She is one for whom there has grown deep within her the state known as longing (*utkaṇṭhā*).
Poets define longing as: "The mental activity wherein there is the relishing of the pleasure of all the senses; the desire for its attainment accompanied by volition—this they know as longing."

Thus ends the *Bhāvaprakāśa*. With limbs that are exceedingly delicate and therefore pitiable—limbs such as hands and feet that are utterly withered like jasmine garlands crushed by the palms, having been repeatedly and gently pressed—[she is] in a state of compassion.

(5-3-76) Thus, the suffix *kan* is applied. This instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*upalakṣaṇe*). The root *tam* is used in the sense of exhaustion (*glānau*); Dhanika states: "In this context, exhaustion (*glāni*) consists of the loss of vitality due to passion, fatigue, thirst, and hunger. The syntactical connection is: "That which [she] suffers (*tāmyati*) has already been described. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) here is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because both her directness and her novelty are being fancied. From "by me" (*mae vi*) up to "suffers" (*tāmyati*) constitutes the *karaṇa* (the means of accomplishment), as it initiates the subject matter at hand. //18//

"Certainly, it is true. For instance—in that very way—I had a likeness of Mādhava painted on a picture-board to dispel her distress, and placed it in Lavaṅgikā’s hand; she, in turn, has today entrusted it to Mandārikā’s hand. 'Dispelling distress' means the passing of time during the suffering of separation."

"In separation and in absence, the experience of those who resemble the beloved, the sight [of them] for a long time during the time of viewing paintings or sleeping, and the touch of objects that have come into contact with their limbs—this is said to be a certain remedy for those whose minds are tormented by desire," according to the statement of Guṇapatañjali. Halāyudha states: "Pratirūpa, pratikṛti, and praticchanda [mean] a likeness."

"Having reflected"—the meaning is, having considered the reason for placing [the letter] in Mandārikā’s hand. "Mādhava’s attendant" means Mādhava’s servant. "Vihāradāsī" means a female servant of a Buddhist monastery (*bauddhāyatana*); Amarasimha states, "The term *vihāra* may refer to the monasteries of Buddhists and others. Likewise, in the *Daśakumāracarita*: "Of a great circle of Buddhist monasteries (*kṣapaṇakavihāramaṇḍala*). "Desires" means he longs for. "By this Kalahaṃsa"—by him as a "tīrtha," that is, as a means;
for it is said: "The word *tīrtha* refers to mantras, teachers, scriptures, and sacred water;
it also refers to a worthy recipient, a means, a descent-place, the menses of a woman, the womb, and sacrifice."

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*: "An introduction (*upodghāta*) is a prelude, an introductory statement, a preliminary remark, a prologue, or even a restatement. [The word] *upeyāt* is used in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*), employing the optative suffix (*liṅ*). By implication, this refers to the intention of Lavaṅgikā.

Mādhava, too—having aroused curiosity, I sent him to Makaranda’s garden at dawn, where the great festival of Madana was underway; there Mālatī will go, and from that, their mutual sight will come to pass. Makaranda’s garden is the name of a grove.
"In which the great festival of Madana has commenced" means: that in which the great festival of the Blessed One Madana, who is present in the form of an image, has begun or been set in motion.

"Excellent"—the word "this" is to be supplied as the object. "By my dear one's insistence" means by her persistence in following my will. "The former disciple" means the principal disciple, or the one who was a disciple during the earlier period of acquiring knowledge. "Saudāminī" refers to her as previously introduced in our presence. "You remind me" means you bring her to the range of my memory. By this, her departure for another country with permission obtained is indicated; for when one perceives someone of similar character, the recollection of such a person is inevitable.

The poet indicates the narrative relevant to the conclusion through the mouth of Avalokitā: "Friend, the venerable Saudāminī has now attained the power of the accomplishment of a mantra of wondrous form on Śrīparvata and observes the vow of a Kāpālika. *Samāsādita* means obtained; she is one by whom a marvelous, astonishing majesty produced by the practice of mantras such as that of Mahābhairavī has been attained.

In the land of Āndhra, there is a preeminent mountain named Śrīparvata, a field for the attainment of all branches of knowledge, where even today the luminous *jyotirliṅga* of the Lord Parameśvara manifests every year. The vow of the Kāpālikas is a discipline established by the Somasiddhānta, described in sequence as: "one who has made beautiful ornaments from a garland of human bones, who dwells in cremation grounds, and who eats from a human skull," and so forth.
From whom? From which person was this heard? This is the ellipsis. According to Amarasimha, "news" (*vārtā*), "occurrence" (*pravṛtti*), and "event" (*vṛttānta*) are synonyms.

Then, by means of a question and answer, the poet indicates the presence of the character Prakari: "There is; there is in this city, in the region of the great cremation ground, a Cāmuṇḍā named Karālā. Cāmuṇḍā is Bhadrakālī. As the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "Caṇḍamuṇḍā, Cāmuṇḍā, Carcā, and Mārjārakarṇikā [are synonyms]."

"It exists" is a restatement; the meaning is that "I indeed know its existence. "Kila" (it is said) implies that this is not the ultimate truth (*aparamārtha*). "Jīvas" are living beings (*prāṇins*); she for whom their sacrifice—that is, an offering in their form—is dear. "Sāhasikānām" refers to those who act according to their own impulses, whose nature consists of *rajas* and *tamas*. "Pravādaḥ" is a discourse that does not correspond to reality.

By the use of both "kila" and "pravādaḥ," it is suggested (*dhvanyate*) that, in reality, only activity arising from *sattva* truly pleases the deity, whereas the other two [types of activity] produce little pleasure because they are merely imagined by the conceptualizations of deluded people.

Indeed, that highly powerful disciple of the practitioner named Aghoraghaṇṭa—who wears a skull, has come from Śrīparvata, and resides at a place neither too far nor too near here—namely Kapālakuṇḍalā, arrives every evening. From this comes the following report: she does not reside in a place that is either too far or too near from this city; one whose habit is to dwell in such a location is described as "residing at a place neither too far nor too near. The practitioner is one engaged in the performance of mantra-siddhi.

"Indeed, this [form] is remembered as distinct for the sake of protecting the practitioner," according to the scripture. [He is] one who wears a shaven head and observes the vow of wearing ornaments made of human skulls;
the suffix *ṇini* is applied here by the rule *vrate* (Pāṇini 3.2.80). "At every junction" means at each and every *saṃdhyā*. "From her" means from her presence.

For everything—such as the power of having attained the marvelous perfection of mantras—is [attained]. By the term "Saudāminī," through a *dhvani* (suggestive power) wherein the literal meaning is transferred to another sense, her fitness as a vessel for the abundance of all virtues is revealed. "Is considered" (*sambhāvyate*) means it is deemed appropriate or is inferred.

Enough now—enough of this. Revered lady, if that companion of Mādhava, his childhood friend Makaranda, were to marry Nandana’s sister Madayantī, it would indeed be exceedingly pleasing to Mādhava. [The word] *alaṃ* is used here in the sense of prohibition; the meaning is that this matter is irrelevant to the present context. *Sahacaraḥ* means one who constantly stays by one's side. *Bālamitraṃ* means a friend from the very time of childhood.

The word *mitra* is always neuter in gender and denotes a friend. "He carries off" means he marries. That object [is] "excessive," because for one who has already achieved his purpose through the acquisition of Mālatī, there arises an even greater degree of pleasure through the prosperity of his friend beyond that point. In that regard, concerning the task consisting of their union, "she" refers to the recollection of her previously experienced cleverness. By the address "dear friend," respect for the command is conveyed. "It was well-arranged by the Venerable Lady."
By the restrictive particle *eva* in "Mālatī alone," the fact that she was previously encouraged is illuminated.

She is of an exceedingly noble nature (*atyudāraprakṛti*) and an extremely modest disposition (*atipraśritasvabhāvā*); as Dhanika says, "Nobility and modesty are always [found together]. By this, her difficulty of attainment due to her lack of impetuosity (*acāpalya*) is suggested. "Skillfully" (*nipuṇam*) means that the application [of the stratagem] was not perceived because of her cleverness (*vaidagdhya*).

The ritual procedure for the envoy with full discretionary power (*nisṛṣṭārthadūtīkalpa*): the method of employing an envoy with full discretionary power as set forth by Vātsyāyana is presented in the section beginning with "She, however, should enter [her confidence] through her character. This is because of the statement in the *Ratirahasya*: "Having understood his intention, she who undertakes the task solely through her own intellect is indeed called an envoy with full discretionary power. It should be "employed" (*tantrayitavyaḥ*), meaning it should be put into practice. Regarding the word *tantra*: "Tantra refers to the administration of one's own kingdom, weaving, clothing, a treatise, medicine, a preeminent horse, the employment [of means], and the performance of sacrificial rites."

"In the case of one thing serving both purposes," so says the *Vaijayantī*. And here, the application of the usage mentioned regarding an adulterer should be understood as referring to the maiden, because it is proclaimed that Mālatī was bestowed upon Nandana. Now, at the conclusion of the display of the portions of the story already occurred and those yet to come, she prays to Fate out of being overcome by affection for the fulfillment of her long-cherished desire: "In every way" (*sarvathā*). This means: by her own exertion and by the favor of Fate.

Regarding the phrase *śarajjyotsnā* ("autumnal moonlight"): the mention of "autumn" (*śarat*) is intended to indicate its intense purity by virtue of being free from the veil of clouds. *Jyotsnā* means the moonlight. *Kāntam* means lovely or desirable. *Tam mādhavam* refers to that Mādhava. *Nandayatu* means "may she cause him to rejoice" or "may she make him prosper"; the verb is used in the imperative mood (*loṭ*) to express a prayer or wish. She is Mālatī. Just as autumnal moonlight [delights] the night-lotus (*kumuda*), this comparison is intended to reveal their genuine mutual passion; therefore, there is no fault of dissimilarity (*asādṛśya-doṣa*). Furthermore, the hero is not made the object of comparison (*upamāna*) here, but rather the night-lotus is employed [as the standard of comparison].

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a discrepancy in grammatical gender (*liṅgabhedadoṣaprasaṅga*), because the connection [of the two words] would occur only between those whose difference is not perceived due to both ending in the accusative case. This is established by common usage in constructions such as *candra iva mukham* ("the face is like the moon"), and also by the rule: "The word *kalyāṇī* is generally desired [to be used] in both the masculine and neuter genders. [The term] *sujātam* means "of beautiful birth," owing to the complete collection of all qualities such as noble lineage (*abhijana*) and so forth. [The term] *kalyāṇī* means "possessing auspicious qualities," as seen in the usage *upasthiteyaṃ kalyāṇī* ("this auspicious woman has arrived"), and by the rule *kalyāṇyādīnāminaṅ*.

"One who has performed meritorious deeds" (*kṛtapuṇya*) means one whose good karma was practiced in a previous birth; this is the sense to be inferred. By the word "youthful" (*yuva*), the cause for his youth being fruitful is established. "Barīyān" means more extensive or greater. According to the rule *priyasthirādi*, the word *uru* undergoes the substitution *bara*, followed by the suffix *īyasun*. "Skilled in the creation of mutually excellent qualities" (*anyonyapraguṇaguṇanirmāṇanipuṇaḥ*): *praguṇa* means straight or excellent. Since it is said, "By a composition of excellent [qualities], I shall summarize the characteristics," similarity is thereby indicated. Thus, he is clever in the fashioning of qualities such as form that are mutually similar to one another.

May the activity of the Creator—the effort of Brahmā—bear fruit; may it become purposeful through the union of two beings with mutually corresponding qualities, for otherwise, being useless, it would fall within the scope of reproach from those of refined taste. And may there be a virtuous connection characterized by a beautiful continuity of affection and the birth of a worthy son. Herein, the ornament (alaṅkāra) in the first half-verse is *upamā* (simile), and in the second half-verse, it is *sama* (parity). 19.
"Both have exited" means they have gone off the stage.
This is a *miśraviṣkambha* (mixed interlude) because it is composed of a mixture of Sanskrit and Prakrit.

Now, as the poet begins the act, he first sets forth the entrance of Kalahaṃsa and Makaranda—this being a part of the hero's entrance previously indicated as the occasion for their entry—with the words "Then enters... [The phrase] "holding painting materials" (*gṛhītacitropakaraṇaḥ*) means one by whom the painting materials—the portrait of Mādhava painted by Mālatī—as well as the implements for drawing such as brushes and pigments, are held in his own hand.

Where now—where shall I look for my lord Mādhava, whose greatness of soul has captivated the heart of Mālatī through his form and graceful charms, which have surpassed the pride of the god of love (Makaradhvaja) by their beauty? His "greatness of soul" refers to his noble character, he by whom Mālatī’s mind was carried away through a form and gestures that eclipsed the arrogance of the fish-bannered god due to their shared excellence of loveliness. I call him "lord" as a figurative expression of his mastery over her. I am utterly exhausted.
"Until I have rested for a moment here in this garden and beheld my lord Mādhava, who is accompanied by Makaranda. The word "until" (*yāvat*) serves as a rhetorical ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*).
From the context, it follows that she has entered the garden.

He recalls what was previously said by Avalokitā: "Makaranda has been sent to the Makaranda Garden, which is like a festival for those who have arrived. It is called the Manmatha Garden because it is presided over by the God of Love in the form of a statue; however, by name, it is the Makaranda Garden. "Let it be so"—the sense is that this is also my own approval. "By good fortune" (diṣṭyā) means by the power of fate; thus, his joy is manifested at the sudden sight of him, who had been suffering from the pain of a moment's separation. "Vayasya" means a friend. "From this very place" means in this very spot.
"Having observed" means having mentally reflected upon the condition of him as he approaches.

"Going," and so forth: "going" (gamana) means moving about; "indolent" (alasa) means unskillful, meaning devoid of pride and haughtiness. "Empty" (śūnyā) means lacking focus due to being heartless; "gaze" (dṛṣṭi) refers to the act of seeing. By the phrase "devoid of excellence" (asauṣṭhava), which means lacking the charm of graceful movement (vilāsa), it is indicated that both her gait and her gaze are bereft of the grace defined as "speech accompanied by a smile in moments of charm" (vilāse sasmitaṃ vacaḥ).

(ca) This is indicated: "breathing" (*śvasitam*) means breath (*śvāsa*). "Excessive" (*adhikam*) means exceeding the measure of the previous state. "What indeed could this be?"—this is the reflection (*vitarka*) as to what its cause might be. "Or rather" (*athavā*) indicates a shift in position; it is the thought: "What else could it be than this? The word "from this" (*ataḥ*) refers back to that which is about to be described. To the question "What is that?", he says: "it wanders" (*bhramati*). It proceeds without coming to rest. "In the world" (*bhuvi*) is used in the singular to denote the class; the meaning is "in the worlds."

The command of Kāma is of such a nature that "one must remain immersed in the essence of the objects of sense through the instruction of Kandarpa. By the word *bhramati* ("wanders"), its omnipresence (*sārvakālikatvam*) is indicated; by *bhuvane* ("in the world"), its all-pervasiveness (*sarvapathīnatvam*); and by *ājñā* ("command"), its inviolability like a royal decree (*durlaṅghyatvam*) is illuminated. "Vikārin" means having the nature of agitating the mind. "Lalita-madhurāḥ" means delicate and beautiful. "Te te" (those various) refers to both the objective supports (*ālambana-rūpāḥ*) and the excitants (*uddīpana-rūpāḥ*). By the repetition (*vīpsā*), it is indicated that even a slight thing may be the cause of someone's transformation. "Bhāvāḥ" refers to entities or objects.

They "cast away" or "reject"; the verbal root is *kṣip* in the sense of "casting out. The phrase "iti yat" (that which... refers back to the meaning of the entire sentence, as it is followed by the question "what else [could it be]? The meaning is: "this is indeed the cause of that. This should be understood as the *narmasphoṭa* (the disclosure of jest) limb of the *kaiśikī-vṛtti*, which consists of the gentle and graceful activities of the hero, such as singing, dancing, and the enjoyment of desires. Because Mālatī’s passion is inferred through slight gestures such as her movements, the poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) here are *anumāna* (inference) and *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic indication). //20//
"Niśvasya" (having sighed): by implication, "having sighed excessively," which is an *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) of anxiety (*cintā*).

Regarding "tām" and so forth: the word "tām" (her) refers back to her as being distinguished by all qualities such as sweetness and delicacy; because it is a demonstrative pronoun (*tacchabda*), a relative pronoun (*yacchabda*) is not explicitly supplied. She has a face beautiful as the moon.
As for the phrase "the face is half of the body, or the whole body is said to be the face": [this is the traditional definition].

Thus, the description of the face, by virtue of its preeminence, serves as an indicator of the beauty of the remaining limbs. This is an "obscured simile" (*luptopamā*) intended to illuminate that her face is distinguished by qualities such as loveliness (*lāvaṇya*), like the moon. By contemplating [her] and experiencing [it] through the gateway of the eyes, the second stage of love—consisting of attachment of the mind—is indicated. As it is said: "First is the delight of the eyes, then the attachment of the mind, then the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*), followed by loss of sleep, emaciation, withdrawal from sense objects, and the destruction of shame."

"Insanity, fainting, and death—these alone are the ten stages of love," as stated in the *Kāmaśāstra*. "With great difficulty, by some means or other" (*kathaṃ kathamapi*); for Bhaṭṭabāṇa uses the expressions "he brought [her] by some means or other" (*kathaṃ kathamapyanaiṣīt*) and "that night passed away by some means or other" (*kathaṃ kathamapi sā kṣapā kṣayamagamat*). And Murāri uses the expression "the jewels which were being carried on his shoulder with great difficulty due to the fear of excessive punishment" (*daṇḍādhikyabhayāt kathaṃ kathamapi skandhopaneyān maṇīn*). "It turns back" (*vyapavartate*) means it returns toward this direction; however, by the word "not turned back" (*na tu vyapavṛttam*), the impossibility of its being turned back is suggested (*dhvanyate*).

The word "ma" (do not) indicates that because the self is distinguished by qualities such as modesty (*lajjā*), it is incapable of undergoing transformation even in a dream. He demonstrates this very point by way of negation with the words beginning with "lajjām" (modesty). Since a negation is only appropriate for that which has already been attained: *lajjām* refers to shame, which is the fear of having done what should not be done; *vijitya* means having thoroughly overcome it. *Vinayaḥ* is the removal of joy and sorrow from the mind through the study of the scriptures, such as the science of logic (*ānvīkṣikī*); *tam* refers to that discipline. *Vinivārya* means having warded it off and cast it far away. *Dhairya* is the state of remaining unaltered even when faced with causes of transformation.

"Unmathya" means having stirred excessively. "Viveka" is the capacity for discerning what is appropriate and inappropriate; that [mind] whose "manthara" is slow or dull is so described. "Akāṇḍe" means at an improper time; the meaning is that it is an unsuitable occasion because of the absence of prior acquaintance and because [the person] is difficult to approach. The suffix *lyap* is to be connected with the word "mantharaviveka. Because of his mastery over the senses, one should understand that the steadiness of his mind is the cause of his modesty (*vinaya*), and that modesty and other qualities are the cause of the excellence of his virtues.

The transitory mental state (vyabhicāribhāva) called *cintā* (reflection) is manifested by the thought, "What should be done regarding the unrestrained nature of the mind? *Pratyasūyā* (resentment) is directed toward the mind by the phrase "precisely at an improper time. Here, the permanent mental state (*sthāyibhāva*) known as *rati* (love) toward Mālatī—manifested through the objective determinant (*ālambanavibhāva*) "her," the consequents (*anubhāvas*) such as sighing, and the transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) such as reflection—is perceived as having transformed into the essence of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*).

In the phrase "her whose face is as beautiful as the moon," because the excellence of her beauty capable of agitating the mind is expressed, the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction) is suggested by way of her being superior to other women. //21//
It is wonderful and causes amazement;
that which begins with "yadvismaya" [is explained as follows]:
"When there is the perception of something contradictory for men by means of a prior mental construction..."
"That state which is 'Oh, indeed this! is precisely wonder."
Thus says Divākara: "Stimitta" means motionless and fixed due to the wonder produced by beholding the excellence of his physical beauty;
that which cannot be moved from its own range is called "stimitta."

Thus ends the *Bhāvaprakāśa*. [The state is] one in which all other states have set, and in which activities such as the recollection of other objects have utterly vanished, because [the mind] has dissolved right there along with the functions of all the senses. It is "dull with bliss" (*ānandamanda*), languid like one intoxicated by drinking honey-wine due to the experience of supreme happiness. Its dullness with bliss is the cause for the setting of all other states. This is due to "bathing in nectar," that is, plunging into a lake of ambrosia.

The supramundane nature of her presence is revealed through the perception of unsurpassed bliss and so forth; just as [the world is seen] when the six waves have been uprooted, so too is there the contemplation that the joy of seeing her is exceedingly gentle. By the use of the word "abhūt" (it was), because it must be remembered as something past, the wretchedness of that state is suggested. "In her presence" (*tasyāḥ sannidhau*) indicates direct perception. "Now, in her absence" (*adhunā tadasannidhau*) is the meaning. "My own" (*madīyam*) means related to me. Because it belongs to the *tyad*-class, it receives the designation *vṛddha*, and by the rule "vṛddhācchaḥ," the suffix *cha* is applied.

He reflects with wonder, thinking, "That was mine," "I too am that very person," and "This too is that very thing. "Touched by embers" (*aṅgāracumbitam*): according to the *Vaijayantī*, "ember" (*aṅgāra*) is a term for a fire whose flames have been extinguished; thus it means touched by an ember. The verbal root *cubi* signifies the act of touching with the mouth. By the specific mention of "embers" (*aṅgāra*), it is suggested that while contact with a flame results in instantaneous incineration and thus its pain is momentary and perhaps bearable, the touch of an ember produces continuous suffering. "Boiling" (*kvathat*) means being cooked. "Remains" (*āste*) means persists.

Because it is present, the impetus (*āvega*) is suggested. Since the immersion in nectar and the touching of the charcoal are the objects of comparison, and because the contradiction between the preceding and succeeding states flashes forth, as well as the avoidance of their proximity and non-proximity, the figure of speech here is "apparent contradiction" (*virodhābhāsa*). Furthermore, this is a statement of injunction—*yadvismayastimitam*—because it establishes both pleasure and pain. //22//

*Lalāṭantapaḥ*: Because it is exceedingly fierce, it "scorches the forehead" (*lalāṭaṃ tāpayati*); thus, by the rule *asūryalalāṭayordṛśitapoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.36), the suffix *khaś* is applied. It "shines" or "illuminates.

*Kahaṃ*—How is it that the Lord Mādhava, the companion of Makaranda, adorns this very grove of young trees? Therefore, I shall show him my own likeness, which brings delight to the eyes of Mālatī as she suffers from the pangs of love. Or rather, let him first experience the pleasure of rest. The word "this one" (*ayam*) is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence.

*Ucchvasita* means blossomed. *Kesara* refers to the filaments (*kiñjalka*). *Kaṣāya* means colored or dyed, as in the expression "her breasts were dyed by that very [color]. *Śītala* means cool or refreshing. *Āmoda* means a beautiful fragrance; Amara states: "*Āmoda* is that which is exceedingly pervasive. *Vāsita* means perfumed or made fragrant. Regarding the *Kovidāra*: "The *camarika*, the red-flowered tree, and the *yugacchada* are synonyms for *kāñcanāra*."

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*. "Returned from the procession" means having come back. Because the festival of Kāmadeva is primarily presided over by women, there is the mention of it being set in motion by the city's young ladies. "Of a different sort" means changed from its previous state. "I perceive" (*avadhārayāmi*) means "I ascertain"; by this, she indicates her own infallible power of reasoning through the excellence of characteristics such as her languid gait. According to Amara, "api" is used in the sense of a question or with a conciliatory nuance.

"Rati-rāmaṇaḥ" means Kāma. "Bāṇa-gocaram" means the range of his arrows, the sphere of their falling. "Avatīrṇaḥ" means you have arrived or entered. "Vihasya" means having smiled; the sense is that he smiled after observing her effort to conceal her facial expression out of shame. "Tat kim iti" (Why is this?)—having attributed silence to him as a form of speech, he says: "If it is true that you have descended [into my heart], then why do you remain with this charming and beautiful lotus-face bent down, revealing your internal bashfulness? Otherwise, if you have not descended, then what is the point of standing thus?"

By this very posture, he indicates that his intention has been understood as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand; furthermore, the lowering of the face is a physical manifestation (*anubhāva*) of shame.

Now, in order to clarify the specific nature of an attachment to sense objects that was previously known only in general terms, he dispels her shame through reasoning while inspiring confidence in her, beginning with the words "among the lowest creatures" (*antyeṣu jantuṣu*). "Among the lowest" means among those existences at the end of all wombs; the meaning is, among those born in extremely low births. "Creatures" (*jantuṣu*) means living beings; the meaning is, among worms, insects, and so forth. The word "and" (*ca*) is used here in the sense of "even" or "furthermore," implying a contrast. "Enveloped in darkness" (*tamasāvṛteṣu*) means those whose knowledge is obscured by ignorance.

"Knowledge is enveloped by ignorance; by that, living beings are deluded"—from this word of the Blessed One. By the unrestricted pronoun *viśvasya* (of the universe), the world consisting of the moving and the non-moving is referred to. In the *dhātṛ* (the Sustainer), who is the substratum like a piece of mother-of-pearl is for silver; by this, its status as the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) is stated. And this is also a distinction from being the ultimate [cause]. In the *parameśvara* (Supreme Lord), the place of rest for sovereignty, the power of knowledge, and so forth, which is Śiva; "No one equal to Him or superior to Him is seen"—from this Vedic scripture. By this, His status as the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) is stated.

This is because of the traditional teaching (smṛti): "And [He is] the material cause, so that there may be no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples. This is also the removal of the state of being enveloped by darkness. *Sama* means equal activity. For even the Supreme Lord—who assumes a playful form (*līlā-vigraha*) out of grace toward His devotees—is well-known for such acts as marrying Pārvatī and dividing His body into two halves. By the two uses of the word *api*, the wonderful nature of the equality of activity across these two utterly contradictory poles is revealed. *Saḥ* refers to Him who was previously heard as being such; *ayam* refers to this one.

The meaning is: "now possessing the power being experienced by you. *Prasiddhavibhavaḥ* means one whose majesty or power is renowned. The particle *khalu* indicates agreement or confirmation. *Cittajanmā* refers to that which has its birth (*janma*) from the mind (*citta*); this suggests its inherent difficulty to restrain. *Kathaṃcit* means "by some means whatsoever. The sense is that whether in engagement or withdrawal, manifestation in every way is indeed better. *Apahnutiḥ* means concealment. *Mā bhūt* means "let it not be. [This is according to the rule] *na māṅyoge*.

(6-4-74) Thus, there is a prohibition of the augment *aṭ* for the *luṅ* [aorist] tense; this is because the sense is "pertaining to me. Here, in the first half [of the verse], the figure of speech is *viṣama* (the incongruous), because of the extreme disparity and the lack of a logical connection between the elements. Alternatively, it is the figure *virodha* (contradiction), as it possesses the appearance of contradiction. In the second half, however, the figure is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise). As for the question "What is the fault in *apahnuti* (concealment)?"—it is because, by establishing the causality of the great power residing in Love (*manmatha*) in the context of its effect, it indicates the apprehension of an undesirable consequence. Furthermore, the figure *vyatireka* (distinction) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*) through the statement of Love’s distinction from other heroes. //23//

With his heart steadied by the demonstration of that [truth], he says: "Why shall I not speak?"—meaning, "For what reason shall I not speak? I shall indeed speak. This is a rhetorical objection to the prohibition of speaking, because he had previously resolved not to speak out of shame. "Listen!"—this marks the commencement of the detailed narration. "Curiosity was aroused in Avalokitā"—this connects with the words of Avalokitā beginning with, "Even Mādhava has aroused curiosity," and so forth. *Āyatana* means a temple or shrine.

By the phrase "wandering here and there," the extent of the sanctuary and the abundance of objects to be seen are illuminated. "Wandering" (parikramaṇa) means moving about; "from exhaustion" (pariśramāt) refers to the fatigue of roaming. "The fragrance of wine" (madirāmodaḥ) is the scent of honey. "Perfume" (parimalaḥ) is the blending of the scents of many flowers. "Drawn" (ākṛṣṭam) means brought forcibly into one's vicinity. "All-voiced" (sakalakalam) means accompanied by a tumultuous noise. "Mingling" (milat) means becoming a mass. "Confused" (saṅkulam) means agitation; "disturbed" (ākulitam) means agitated by that [confusion].

The word *mukula* indicates a flower in its unopened state. Consequently, because of the surging fragrance of wine, the bees’ greed for tasting a flavor that has not yet faded is revealed. This refers to a young *bakula* tree—a tree with fresh filaments—growing in the courtyard of a temple; [the action occurs] by chance, without prior intention, near the base where it is rooted.

By the terms "blown open without interval" (*nirantaravikasitāni*) and "blown open without gaps" (*nirvivarāṇi vikasitāni*), the abundance of flowers on the young *bakula* tree and its accessibility from below are revealed. "Artful arrangement" (*vidagdhaviracanā*) refers to a refined construction resulting from a particular artistic conception; thus, the creation is free from vulgarity. A "garland" (*srajam*) is a wreath (*mālām*). "Moving about" (*sañcāriṇī*) means having the habit of wandering; that is, it is mobile. This distinguishes it from other banners. It is a "victory-banner of world-conquest" (*jagadvijayavaijayantikā*), a standard raised by the conquest of the three worlds.

Because the banner is a sign of victory (*jayalakṣaṇa*), there is the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that it is like a moving *vaijayantī* (victory banner). From this, the possibility of agitation even in one whose nature is exceedingly steadfast is illuminated. According to Amara, "a *patākā* is a *vaijayantikā*. The phrase "having emerged from the inner chamber"—meaning from the interior of the temple of the God of Love—is the cause for the poetic fancy. It is "resplendent" (*ujjvala*), meaning brilliant, because it is composed of precious gems; it is "refined" (*vidagdha*), meaning non-vulgar, because it is not ostentatious (*anulbaṇatvāt*).

*Mugdham* means tender; *bālanepathyam* refers to ornaments suitable for wearing by those distinguished by the stage of childhood, since the science of ornaments (*ābharaṇa-śāstra*) prescribes the wearing of specific decorations according to caste, stage of life, and the appropriateness of each particular state. *Vibhāvitakumārībhāvā* means one whose maidenhood has been made manifest; as the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "A *kumārī*, a *kanyakā*, and a *kanyā* [are synonyms]. The *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) is a particular sovereignty unimpaired by fickleness and the like, as it is said: "But from a particular *anubhāva*, she is as if surrounded by an army. And: "He in whom emotions are always observed to exist solely for the sake of helping others..."

"And that is called majesty (*anubhāva*), for which people yearn"—thus says the *Bhāvaprakāśa*. "Of a nature possessing great majesty" means having an inherent and great power. "Having an exceedingly noble retinue" means having a retinue that is not mean. At the time of seeing her, because her lineage and name were unknown, she is referred to as "some woman" (*kāpi*). "Right there" means in that very place. And immediately thereafter, the contemplation begins with "of the Lord" (*devasya*) and so forth. [She is described] due to the immersion in the sentiment of the marvelous (*adbhuta-rasa*). "She" and so forth. "Ramaṇīyakam" is the state of being beautiful (*ramaṇīya*). It is called "beautiful" (*ramaṇīya*) because it delights both the eye and the heart. [This is formed according to the rule: "The kṛtya and lyuṭ suffixes are used diversely."

(3-3-113) Thus, the *kṛtya* suffix is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). By the rule "vuñ after a word having *y* as a penultimate letter and a heavy penultimate syllable" (5-1-132), the suffix *vuñ* is applied to denote its state (*bhāva*). Its "treasure" (*nidhi*) is an imperishable heap; just as a heap of gold and so forth is designated by terms such as "conch-treasure" (*śaṅkhanidhi*) and the like. The "presiding deity" (*adhidevatā*) is the deity who possesses the conceit [of being that object]. The sense is that the presiding deity must indeed correspond to the object of the conceit. For instance, in that context, the presiding deities of the conch-treasures and so forth are described as raining down streams of the nine gems:
"Wearing divine garlands and garments, adorned with divine ornaments and ointments..."

"The treasures with divine limbs are to be meditated upon as filling the earth with wealth"—this is the meaning of "or" (*vā*), which indicates an alternative. Anticipating a doubt regarding the difference between the presiding deity (*īśitavya*) and the presiding divinity (*adhidevatā*), he again offers another alternative: "Or [as] the abode of the collection of the essence of beauty.
This refers to that excellence of major and minor limbs which is neither deficient nor redundant.

"That whose joints and connections are perfectly harmonized is declared to be beauty"—thus says the *Bhāvaprakāśa*. Just as butter is extracted as the essence of luster by churning objects such as peacock plumages, lotuses, and water-lilies, this [essence] is the place where that collection [of beauties] is deposited according to its fitness for the mass of hair, face, eyes, and so forth. Because of the statement that "or" (*vā*) refers to a collection of the essence of beauty, a superiority over the previous alternative should be understood. And therefore, by the reason of being the locus of unsurpassed beauty, its production from a unique cause is inferred. Regarding the word "tasyāḥ" (of her):

The meaning is "of her who is indeed of such a kind. "Friend" (*sakha*) indicates that I have certainly not spoken a falsehood in the presence of my dear companion. "Niyatam" (certainly) is an indicator of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). "Indukalā-mṛṇāla-jyotsnādi" refers to the crescent moon for the face, lotus stalks for the hands and feet, and moonlight for the beauty pervading all her limbs; the word "ādi" (etcetera) expresses a variety of types. For the eyes and other features, the corresponding objects are the blue water-lily (*kuvalaya*) and so forth. "Cause" (*kāraṇa*) here means, by implication, the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).

He intoxicates, thus he is Madana; Kāma, who has assumed a form that deludes the three worlds. The word *ca* is used in the sense of "but. Vedhas is Brahmā; it means the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Here, in the first half-verse, there is doubt [as to the identity of the cause]. However, in the second half-verse, by excluding well-known causes and describing a transcendent cause, the figure of speech is *asaṃbandhātiśayokti* (hyperbole of non-connection) regarding the relationship. //24//

Regarding "atha": by the word *praṇayinībhiḥ* ("by those who are affectionate"), it is suggested that their words are not to be disregarded. By the word *anucarībhiḥ* ("by the female attendants"), it is meant "by her friends"; the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied because the root *cara* is listed among the *pacādi* group. *Abhyarthyamānā* means being entreated—that is, being urged with the plea, "This place is delightful; please honor it with your presence. *Alaṅkṛtavatī* means she adorned [herself]. This is because, through her proximity, that place attains a state of exceptional beauty. *Kasminn api puruṣaviṣaye* means "toward some particular person."

In him whose birth was of great fortune and immeasurable merit—since being the object of such love is the result of extraordinary spiritual merit—the particular state [of her condition] increased over many days; the word "iva" (as if) is used because it was as if being carried away. This refers to a specific state resulting from the torment of passion, the effect of the heat of desire.

He describes the manner of transformation observed through the words beginning with *parimṛdita* (crushed): it is withered and exhausted like a lotus stalk distressed by contact with the palm of the hand. From the mention of the lotus stalk (*mṛṇālī*), its softness, glossiness, charm, and whiteness are also understood, according to the rule: "When one of two properties is mentioned, the other is cognized through association. *Aṅga* refers to the limbs such as hands and feet. *Kriyāsu* refers to activities such as viewing beautiful objects. *Pravṛttiḥ* is exertion; [it occurs] through the entreaties of attendants, and not of her own accord.

By the use of the plural number, the repetition of the prayer at every action is understood. Furthermore, by the phrase "somehow with difficulty," the two transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāva) known as exhaustion (glāni) and laziness (ālasya) are revealed in the two sentences respectively, as well as the two stages of love (madanāvasthā) known as attenuation (tanutā) and withdrawal from objects (viṣayanivṛtti). "Kalayati" means he binds or fixes. "Of the stainless"—that is, of that which has its blemish removed. "Whose luster is like the luster of a fresh elephant-tusk fragment. By proximity, the word "fragment" (cheda) indicates the substance [the tusk] itself.

The word *abhinava* (fresh) indicates the absence of such things as being greyed by dust. Regarding the phrase *niṣkalaṅkasya* (of the stainless one): since he will become stainless [only later], the use of the genitive *tasya* (his) is an instance of *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole). In the expression *himāṃśor lakṣmīm* (the beauty of the moon), there is the figure of speech *nidarśanā* (illustration), meaning "beauty similar to that of the moon. Furthermore, the paleness of the cheeks is a transformation caused by love (*smaravikāra*), as seen in the usage: "a face pale and emaciated" (*pāṇḍukṣāmaṃ vadanam*). [This is illustrated by the verse: "In that city, the splendor of jeweled mirrors was found upon the golden pillars of the temples, reflected in the cheeks of women who shared the same hue [as gold] and were pale with love; these cheeks served as the visible counterparts [to the mirrors]. (Note: This passage describes a city where the golden pillars of the temples reflect the faces of women who are themselves golden-hued and pale from passion, thus creating the illusion that the mirrors are actually their own reflections.)
And because of this statement by Māgha. //25//

The "ambrosia-collyrium" (*amṛtavartikā*) is a medicinal probe made from a stream of nectar; for Vāhaṭa states: "Collyrium applied by a skilled eye-doctor [removes] all eye-diseases. It is called *atiśaya* because it surpasses (*atiśete*) everything else without exception—that is, that by which all other forms of bliss are cast aside as inferior. They "provide" means they offer. The "iron-stone probe" (*ayaskāntamaṇiśalākā*) refers to a specific kind of stone possessing the power to attract iron, known as the magnet; the term "probe" (*śalākā*) is used here because the object of comparison is feminine.

"Lohadhātum" (iron ore): according to the lexicon, "ore is [the substance] of mountains such as realgar (*manaśśilā*)"; because ores are of many kinds, "iron ore" means an ore in the form of iron. "Antaḥkaraṇam" is the mind (*manas*). "Upasaṃhṛtavatī" means she brought it near to herself. Here, by the words "of the eyes," two states are indicated: the delight of the eyes and the internal organ, which is the attachment of the heart (*cittāsaṅga*). In the passage beginning with "She is mine," there is either the figure of speech *upamā* (simile), or *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the qualities of being a brush and being a stick are objects of imaginative identification (*adhyavasāya*).

"In every way" (*sarvathā*) and "in every manner" (*sarvaprakāreṇa*) suggest that [the state] is difficult to ward off. Furthermore, one should not suspect redundancy here between the lines beginning with "her whose face is as beautiful as the moon" (*tāmindusundaramukhīm*) and those beginning with "from the moment of seeing her" (*sā mama darśanāt prabhṛti*), because the former expresses his own experience at the time [of meeting], while the latter describes what he has experienced now. Regarding the passage beginning with "fever" (*santāpa*): "a succession of fevers" (*santāpasantatiḥ*) is a stream of pain from the arrows of Love; for that great calamity (*mahāvyasanāya*), meaning to undergo a great misfortune (*mahatīm āpadam*). [This is according to the rule: *kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi sthāninaḥ*.

(2-3-14) Thus ends the fourth [section]. "Attached" (*āsakta*) means bound on all sides; by this, attachment to every single limb is revealed. "This"—this is a reproach directed at such a person who lacks discrimination (*avivekī*). "Disregarding causes" means not taking into account motives such as ease of access or proximity. Now, since the production of an effect is impossible without a cause, and because no external cause can be identified while the production of the effect is nonetheless observed, one infers some unseen cause—namely, "fate" (*prāya*).

"Grāmaḥ bāhulyena" (the village, by way of abundance) is an indicator of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). She ordains—that is, she performs—the auspicious and the inauspicious, as well as pleasure and pain. Alternatively, she is "all-consuming" (*sarvaṃkaṣā*) because she pervades the entire world or because she repels everything by her own power; the suffix *khac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.42: "The root *kaṣ* [takes *khac*] when preceded by *sarva*, *kūla*, *abhra*, or *karīra*. She is called "Bhagavatī" (the Blessed One) by metaphorical usage because she is the power of the Supreme Lord and because her capacity is insurmountable. "Necessity" (*bhavitavyatā*) is the power of destiny (*niyati*), which is the cause for the non-confusion of the respective attributes of each and every object.
As it is said in the *Mahābhārata*: "By whomsoever and wherever pleasure or even pain is to be experienced, he is led there by destiny, as if bound by a rope with force."

And as stated by Māgha: "Then the chariot toward Śauri, its horses urged on, set forth under the compulsion of destiny in the form of a charioteer. Here, in the first half-verse, there is the poetic figure *vibhāvanā* (the description of an effect despite the absence of its cause), and envy (*abhyasūyā*) toward the mind is suggested. In the second half-verse, however, there is *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle), and the mental states (*bhāva*) of deliberation (*vitarka*) and dejection (*dainya*) are suggested. //26//

Then Makaranda establishes that very same reflection of his by means of an illustration: "Friend," he says. That affection arises spontaneously, yet it is dependent upon and expectant of an external cause—this statement is contradictory, being mutually opposed. Contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*) is a conflict between two propositions of equal force.
He shows the illustration preceded by the apprehension of a pervasion (*vyāpti*): "Behold! he says.

"Vyatiṣajati" means he binds in various ways with great intensity; from the root *ṣañj*, meaning "to attach. By saying "objects" (*padārthān*), it is indicated that this rule applies not only to sentient beings but even to insentient ones as well. "Internal" (*āntara*) means existing within; by the word "internal," its imperceptibility is characterized. It is some [power] of inconceivable influence. "Cause" (*hetu*) means destiny (*niyati*). "External adjuncts" (*bahirupādhīn*) refers to perceptible causes.

[An adjunct is defined as: "When two things, which are mutually devoid of connection, are invariably concomitant with the same probandum, that which is invariably concomitant with the absence of the probandum is the adjunct (*upādhi*); its exclusion [is required]."

Thus, although defined in this manner, "limiting condition" (*upādhi*) here is synonymous with "cause" (*kāraṇa*), as Murāri has stated: "In that context, this limiting condition prevails as the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the agent of birth. "Delights" (*prītayaḥ*) refers to pleasures based on mutual affection; by the use of the plural number, the abundance of objects is indicated. "For" (*hi*) is used in the sense of what is well-known. "At the rising of the sun" (*pataṅgasyodaye*) means at the appearance of the sun from the eastern mountain; by this, its great distance is revealed.

In the phrase "of the moth," qualities such as being difficult to touch or difficult to look upon are revealed through a suggestion (*dhvani*) wherein the literal meaning is transferred to another sense, just as in the case of "I am Rāma, I endure everything. Similarly, in the word "lotus" (*puṇḍarīka*), qualities such as being pleasant to the touch and beautiful to behold are suggested. It "melts" (*dravati*), that is, it becomes moistened.

In the sun's rays there is coolness, tenderness, and so forth; in the moonstone, on the other hand, there is hardness, insipidity, and so forth. Thus, even though these two possess mutually opposing qualities and lack any mutual assistance, this mutual affection is observed between them despite their being situated in distant places. The meaning is that this is indeed the power of destiny (*bhavitavyatā*). The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle). //27//
"Then what? After that, please tell us more"—by this repetition, according to the dramatic convention (*nāṭakanyāya*), the listener's curiosity is expressed.

"Accompanied by a play of the eyebrows," and so forth. *Pratyabhijñā* (recognition) is the reflective awareness of a previous experience upon seeing an object again, in the form "this is that very thing. "With recognition" means accompanied by such recognition. The word *iva* ("as if") indicates a state of doubt (*vitarka*), because there is no definitive determination of its being exactly as it was before. "Having looked at me" means having gazed upon me. "Then" (*atha*) means immediately thereafter. By the phrase "by the clever one" (*catureṇa*), meaning by the artful one, the capacity for interpreting gestures and nuances that are imperceptible to ordinary people is revealed. "By the circle of friends" (*sakhījanena*) means by the group of female companions.

"With playful arching of the eyebrows" means accompanied by the movement of the brows. "As if it were he indeed" (*so'yamitīva*): the particle *iva* here indicates a conjecture (*vitarka*), while *nāma* is used either to indicate manifestation or possibility. By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "only toward one another," the skill in concealing [their feelings] from others is suggested. "Sweet with the nectar of smiles": the smile is metaphorically identified as nectar through the scattering of the rays from their exceedingly white teeth; they are captivating because of this nectar-like smile. "Glances were cast forth" (*muktāḥ*) means they were directed.
Here, the figure of speech is *sūkṣma* (the subtle). //28//

Then Makaranda, unaware that Mādhava had been seen by them before, asks: "How?"—the word *katham* expressing wonder—and "How indeed could there even be recognition?"—the word *nāma* here indicating possibility. "Playfully" means with grace. "Uttering" (*uttālā*) means raised; because their lotus-like hands were joined together in a cluster, there was the clashing of palms against one another. [The suffix] *-vuñ* is applied to the root *tala* in the sense of "striking. That [cluster] in which the row of bracelets—the series of jeweled bangles—is "tremulous" (*taralā*), meaning moving restlessly.

With a charming and graceful movement of the feet—the gait of a *kalahaṃsa* (a species of grey-winged swan) that is exceedingly terrified and intoxicated by drinking the honey of lotuses; with a sound imitating the word "raṇaraṇā," [expressing] a tinkling or jingling, formed according to Pāṇini 5.4.57 (*avyaktānukaraṇe ḍāc*) and 3.1.13 (*lohitādiḍājbhyaḥ kyaṣ*), and optionally following 1.3.90 (*vā kyaṣaḥ*).

(1-3-90) Thus, the *ātmanepada* suffix *śānac* [is applied]. "Mañjīra" means an anklet; it is "mixed" (*anuviddhena*) with its "sweet" (*mañjunā*) or melodious "resonance" (*rasitena*), that is, sound. And likewise, it is "chattering" (*mukharam*)—meaning talkative—with the "jingling" (*raṇatkāreṇa*), a specific kind of sound, of the "cluster of girdles" (*mekhalākalāpasya*), which is an ornament in the form of a waist-belt, consisting of "little golden bells" (*kiṅkiṇīnām*). These three words are adverbs qualifying the action of "returning. Having "returned," meaning having gone back. Regarding the term "Bhartṛdārike":
"The king is the lord (*bhaṭṭāraka*), the god (*deva*); his daughter is the 'Bhartṛdārikā' (the princess)."

Thus says Amara. He addresses her in this manner because she is the daughter of the minister Rājasena. "By good fortune we prosper" means we become filled with luck. The use of the plural "we prosper" (*vardhāmahe*) rather than the singular "you prosper" (*vardhase*) is intended to avoid her embarrassment, and to indicate that your success is the success of us all. The word "some one" (*ko'pi*) suggests that he cannot be described due to his unsurpassed qualities. "Of some one" (*kasyā api*) implies that such a state belongs to a certain woman. "Vallabha" means a most beloved one.

The sense that "someone is dear to someone" is suggested through a resonance (*anuraṇana*) rooted in the power of meaning; because the statement "your beloved" is thus lacking in cleverness, a joke is implied by means of this suggestion which is intent on concealment. They "announced"—that is, they spoke—by means of the playful gesture of pointing with their fingers, specifically the graceful movement of indicating [him] with the index finger. The grammatical connection is: "they announced that he was standing there," preceded by the pointing of their fingers.

"Hanta" expresses joy, because her speech accords with Mādhava’s desire; "hanta" is used for joy and dejection, according to the *Vaijayantī*. "Prāganurāgasya" refers to the love previously arisen. "Udbhedaḥ" means its manifestation.

"Sarasaramaṇīyānubandhinī strīkathā" means a discourse concerning women that is connected with and characterized by aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); it is a discourse or utterance regarding women that follows upon a subject matter which is both flavorful and thus delightful.
Now, at the time of her [own] sight—

He describes the quality known as *vilāsa* (grace), which is defined as: "Grace is a momentary distinction in the movements of the limbs and so forth. He says this with the words beginning "atrantare" and so on. "At this interval" means at this juncture; that is to say, immediately after that narration and upon my looking [at her]. "Something" (*kimapi*) is that which can be understood only through personal experience. "Whose variety transcends the power of speech" (*vāgvibhavātivṛttavaicitryam*) means whose diversity exceeds the capacity of the organ of speech. "With manifest coquetry" (*ullasitabibhramam*) means in which specific gestures such as side-glances and the movement of the arms have arisen.

By the phrase "lotus-eyed" (*utpalākṣyā*), it is suggested that her eyes, resembling blossoming blue water-lilies (*kuvalaya*), were also clearly manifest at that time. The word "that" (*tat*) refers to what is well-known from the treatises of Bharata, Vātsyāyana, and others. "Abounding in *sāttvika* transformations" means that the *sattva*—the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—is characterized by a profusion of *sāttvika* changes born from its agitation; these are numerous *sāttvika* transformations such as trembling, perspiration, and so forth. As it is said: "Trembling, perspiration, horripilation, loss of voice, shaking, change of color, tears, and fainting—these eight are known as the *sāttvika* [transformations]."

Thus says Bharata. *Apāstadhairya* means that by which the state of the mind characterized by fickleness has been cast away—that is, discarded far off. *Ācāryakam* is the function (*karma*) of a teacher (*ācārya*). [The suffix] *vuñ* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.132: "After a word ending in *ya* as an upadhā and having a heavy penultimate syllable.
It means "instruction. As it is said:
"To approach one who is lower than the lowest—this is the nature of water; what kind of teaching is this?"

Thus it was said by Murāri. "Vijayi" means one whose nature (*śīla*) is victory—that is, subjugation through overpowering—thereby manifesting the capacity for forceful action. "Mānmatha" means pertaining to the God of Love (*manmatha*). By this, the skill in the various amorous graces (*vilāsa*) unfolding at that moment even among the innocent (*mugdhāḥ*) through the instruction of the Teacher, the God of Love, is revealed. As it is said: "It is the intoxication of youth alone that teaches graceful charms to passionate women."

Because of this statement, the word *āvirāsīt* (appeared) signifies that [the state] manifested spontaneously through the intensity of love, rather than being produced by the lotus-eyed girl; thus, its manifestation is revealed as occurring entirely by its own natural impulse. The indeclinable *āviḥ* is a synonym for "manifestation. Here, the poetic figures are *parikara* (periphrasis) and *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because the epithets possess intentional significance (*sābhiprāya*) and because the playful gesture is identified with the role of a teacher (*ācāryatva*). //29//

Now, he describes the specific glances of hers which are the *anubhāvas* (consequent manifestations) of the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) known as *rati* (love). The word “then” (*tataḥ*) is used; the particle “ca” (and) serves to carry over the term “of the lotus-eyed one” (*utpalākṣyāḥ*).

Regarding the passage beginning with “stimita” (steady): among the one hundred and four glances mentioned by Bharata that are applicable to the nine rasas, sixty-four are applicable to the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa; some of these are now being revealed. “Steady” (*stimita*) means motionless: “That which does not move from its own range is called steady.”

Thus ends the *Bhāvaprakāśa*. All treatises concerning the characteristics of the *dṛṣṭis* (gazes) should be understood from the *Bhāvaprakāśa* (as indicated by the *ṛ*). And this is a manifestation of wonder (*vismaya*), as stated in his own words: "that which is motionless with wonder. It penetrates the specific objects such as the blossoming [flowers], by means of plunging into the beauty of the facial features and other limbs that have opened and become fully bloomed. And this is a manifestation of joy (*harṣa*), belonging to those whose creeper-like eyebrows are quivering, indicating their inner intention through the rising creepers of their eyes.
"Where the intention shines forth, that is called 'radiant' (ullāsī).
This is the gaze known as "upturned" (udvartita). "That should be understood as 'upturned,' which is the upward trembling of the eyebrows."

Thus [it is said]. This is a manifestation of wonder; or rather, it is a manifestation of the thought of attainment, as in the verse: "Her face with one creeper-like eyebrow raised. Regarding the term *masṛṇa-mukulitānām*:
"That which is known as *masṛṇa* is that which is reddened by passion (*anurāga-kaṣāyita*).

The meaning is that they are *masṛṇa*, being gentle due to the power of passion. By the word *mukulitānām*, because of the propriety of the context, the state of being half-closed is expressed. They are half-closed due to the experience of bliss.
"Half-opened like a star, with lids half-closed and moist,
it is known as the 'half-closed' gaze.
And this is an external manifestation (*anubhāva*) of delusion (*moha*).

As Māgha has said: "She quickly crossed the tips of her beloved's hands with a gaze half-closed like a bud. [The phrase] *prāntavistārabhājām* means those that possess expansion at the end—that is, at the conclusion of the sight of him.
As it is said: "That by which an object is embraced is called its expansion (*vistārin*)."

This means devouring the visible world with their tips directed downwards; or else, it refers to those [glances] that are expansive at the corners—that is, at the outer edges—as they spread out. This is an indicative mark (*anubhāva*) of awakening as the opposite of delusion. "Upon the falling of each eye" means when my two eyes are turned in the opposite direction. "Slightly contracted" means slightly withdrawn. A contraction is a withdrawal back to the way it was; the mention of "slightly" reveals a slowness in that withdrawal. And this is an indicative mark of bashfulness (*lajjā*):
"In their union, [the eyes] were timid, fixed for a moment, and then withdrawn."

"...the charming eyes, glancing at one another, underwent a bashful restraint," as it is said; and likewise in the *Śākuntala*: "When I was facing her, her gaze was withdrawn. By the word "various" (*vividha*), there is an inclusion of other modes not explicitly mentioned, since they are impossible to describe in full. This is an adjective qualifying "glance" (*ālokita*). "Vessel" (*pātra*) means a container; as it is said: "The word *pātra* refers to a worthy vessel, wealth, or the space between the two banks."

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*. Because the word *pātra* (vessel/receptacle) is invariably neuter, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "I" (*aham*). [The term] *ālokitānām* refers to the acts of looking; here the suffix *-ta* denotes the abstract state (*bhāve*). By the statement "I have become a vessel," it is suggested: "Oh, how fortunate I am! Previously, such a mass of merit was not even conceivable in me. Since this describes the natural disposition of her passionate glances, the figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) here is *svabhāvokti* (description of nature). Furthermore, one should consider the application of what was previously promised: "The compositions of the Rasas are profound due to their abundance. //30//

Now, he describes the unsurpassed power of such glances to agitate the mind, beginning with the words "alasā" and so forth. The word "alasā" (sluggish) is a restatement of the phrase "slightly contracted," because it has been said:
"Sluggishness (*ālasya*) is that turning away from a desired object due to shame and the like. The word "valita" (turned) and so forth is an explanation of the adverb "vividham" (in various ways).

"It is the side-long glance of one who has turned back, characterized by a triangular look. Here, "triangular" (tryaśra) means cast obliquely upward. "Innocent" (mugdha) means unartificial; as it is said:
"The innocent glance is natural, though it may conceal inner emotion through artifice."
Thus [it is said]: "It is glossy (*snigdha*), thick with a mass of non-dry radiance;
that which is the object of the 'glossy' [vision] becomes permeated by that radiance.
It is motionless (*niṣpanda*), in that it does not flicker anywhere when one looks elsewhere."

Thus: "Niṣpandatva" (immobility) is defined as not moving from one's own object by oneself; "stimitatva" (stillness), on the other hand, is not moving even when impelled by another—this is the distinction. "Manda" means one who is unskilled in perceiving even when another object is present nearby. According to the *Vaijayantī*: "The words mūḍha, alpa, apaṭu, nirbhāgya, and manda [are synonyms]. [The eyes were] with glances that were languid, rolling, charming, affectionate, motionless, and slow.

"Those whose pupils (*tārā*) are smiling with wonder—having the quality of being smiling (*smera*) because of the internal wonder intensely expanding within, which causes the pupils to expand further with an inner astonishment. [The suffix] *ra* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.167: "The suffix *ra* is added after the roots *nam*, *kamp*, *smi*, *jas*, *kam*, *hiṃs*, and *dīp*.
It is said: "That in which the eyebrows, eyelashes, and pupils quiver is called *smera* (smiling)."
(Thus:

"The heart" means the mind (*manas*). "Without refuge" (*aśaraṇam*) means devoid of a protector; the sense is that qualities such as discipline (*vinaya*), which ought to be protected, have been cast far away. According to Amara, "refuge" (*śaraṇa*) refers to both a house and a protector. "Of the long-lashed one" (*pakṣmalākṣyāḥ*) means of her whose eyes are distinguished by excellent eyelashes; the suffix *lac* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*). Alternatively, it is derived from the root *lā* with the suffix *ke*.
As it is said: "A casting of the pupil toward the outer corner of the eye is called a sidelong glance (*kaṭākṣa*)."

Thus: *apahṛtam* means taken possession of, as in "she carried away her beloved even as he was striving"; *apaviddham* means cast down, as in "the arm that had been cast down"; the meaning is that [the object] has been submerged within its own domain. *Pītam* means swallowed whole; the meaning is that it has been ingested within by means of its own form. *Unmūlitam* means completely dissolved into itself; the meaning is that it has been destroyed without remainder because not even the slightest trace remains visible within the lotus of the heart.

Through the words "stolen" (*apahṛtam*) and so forth, the progressive intensification of the affliction is revealed; since there is no other mode beyond that, the rest comes to repose in its full manifestation. By the phrase "my heart," its weakness is suggested because it belongs to me; by the phrase "with the side-glances of the long-lashed-eyed one," their strength is suggested through the power of their source, as they belong to her.

"The heart is defenseless against side-glances"—this expresses compassion for the heart, indignation toward the side-glances, and a sense of wretchedness due to one's own inability to protect it, given that this single, helpless person is being oppressed by many who possess superior strength. Here, the figure of speech is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because the specific manner in which the heart is rendered helpless by the side-glances is superimposed through terms such as "stolen" (*apahṛta*). Furthermore, there is *dīpaka* (illumination), as a single agent [the heart] is connected with multiple actions such as being stolen and so forth. //31//

Now he speaks of his own conduct: "Ah, me! The particle *tu* indicates a distinction; it highlights that even in this state, which cannot be denied, something difficult has been done by me. [She was] one who enters the heart—that is, the mind—in every way, being charming through all her aspects such as beauty, character, and so forth. [The suffix] *khac* is added according to the rule *gamessupyupasaṅkhyānam*. [She was] one whose essence of affection was being inferred—that is, for whom a certain intensity of love was being conjectured in me by the inferred essence of her affection.

"By being in close proximity," that is, by standing before him; "even though brought under control," meaning even though made subject to his will; "restlessness" means fickleness; "desirous of concealing," meaning wishing to hide it—the elision of the letter *m* [in *apahnotukāmaḥ*] occurs according to the rule "the suffix *tumun* is used with *kāma* and *manas*" (*tuṃ kāmamanasorapi*). By the phrase "somehow," it is revealed that the undertaking of the clever composition was abandoned with great difficulty. "Thus" (*evam*) conveys the sense: "Oh, what fortitude I possess! "Thereupon" (*tataḥ*)... [text continues].

"Staff-bearers" refers to the doorkeepers (*pratīhāra*); since they have a staff (*vetra*) in their hands, the word *vetrapāṇayaḥ* has its locative-ending member placed last according to the rule: "It should be stated that the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) and the locative case follow words used in the sense of weapons. "Eunuchs" (*varṣadhara*) means impotent men; those men who are numerous among them and act as attendants are called *parivāra*, and she is one whose retinue (*parikara*) consists of such people. The term "female elephant" (*gajavadhū*) refers to a female elephant (*kariṇī*), used here for the sake of auspiciousness. "Going toward the city" means having the habit of traveling toward the city; the meaning is that it is favorable for proceeding to the city.
[As the saying goes: "This path leads to Vidarbha; this one will go to Kosala."

As in the expression "moon-faced" (*induvadanā*), by this term the perfection of her face’s resemblance to the orb of the moon situated on the mountain of sunrise (*udayagiri*)—while she rests upon the shoulder of an elephant—is illuminated.

Now, he describes her behavior at the time of departure with the words beginning "yāntyā" (as she goes): "muhur" means many times. "Valitakandharam" refers to that whose neck-stalk (*kaṇṭhanāla*) is turned sideways. "Ānanam" means the face. By the word "tat" (that), the beauty experienced by herself is illuminated. "Āvṛttavṛntaśatapatranibham": "āvṛtta" means turned; "vṛnta" is the stalk or peduncle; "śatapatra" is a lotus. Thus, it resembles a lotus whose stalk has been turned.

(Yathā): When the neck is turned, then the face resembles a lotus with its stalk bent back; this is the figure of speech *upamā* (simile), because the relationship between the neck and the stalk, and between the face and the lotus, is established through the relation of prototype and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba*). As for the qualities of "being turned" (*valita*) and "being bent back" (*āvṛtta*), they are distinct only due to the difference in their respective substrates (*sambandhi-bheda*), but not in meaning, as they are synonyms. *Digdha* means smeared or anointed; the root is *diha*, meaning "to smear. [The word is used here] with *amṛta* (nectar) because it signifies favorability.

But [it is called] "poison" because of the suspicion that it is difficult to obtain for oneself; or else, the ornament *virodha* (contradiction) is present here, because it brings pleasure at the time of experience and brings pain at the time of separation. *Gāḍham* means firmly. *Nikhātaḥ* means fixed like a stake. *Iva* is an indicator of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). This is because it does not depart from his heart. From the passage beginning with "In the meantime, something... up to "...the side-long glance in the heart," the *kaiśikī* style (*vṛtti*) is to be understood. In other instances as well, one should follow this same principle.
"The *vṛtti*, which consists of those activities, is fourfold; among them is the *kaiśikī*."
