"O Noble One, desist from this; I am not able to endure anything further," according to the usage of this very poet [in the verse beginning with] "pañcamī vibhakte."

(2-3-42) Thus [the word "mama"] is in the fifth case. If it is argued that this entire misfortune is easily remedied by relying on some degree of independence, he says in response: "But for me" (*mama tu*). The particle *tu* indicates a distinction; the meaning is: "Let such a thought be yours, but mine is not so. "Beloved" (*dayita*) means one who is to be protected because of being most dear. "Praiseworthy" (*ślāghya*) means worthy of honor due to learning, character, and so forth. "Of pure lineage" (*amalānvayāḥ*) means previously free from any connection with impurity or defect. "Mother" (*jananī*) means the mother.

The word *dayita* (beloved) undergoes a grammatical transformation [to *dayitā*]. Even though both possess virtues, he says that some degree of impurity (*malinimā*) may exist among their descendants; thus he uses the word *kulam*, meaning lineage or family. This applies without distinction to both the mother’s and the father’s line. "Immaculate" (*amalinam*) means renowned for being free from defects in conduct (*vṛtta*). As stated in the Mahābhārata: "In my opinion, lineage is no authority for one who is devoid of good conduct. The word *dayitam* undergoes a transformation [to *dayitā*]. Being praiseworthy and so forth are the causes for being beloved.

"The unchaste maiden brings three families into jeopardy: her mother’s family, her father’s family, and that family to which she is given"—this is the observation of Vyāsa, and my meaning is that I am not the fit ground for such a thing. If it is argued that, in that case, you are the cause of his [the bridegroom's] misfortune and that, because of you, there will undoubtedly be a loss of life for you as well, he replies: "But certainly not" (na tv eva). This person refers to Mādhava; because he is present in the heart and because he is the subject at hand, he is referred to by the pronoun *idam*. However, this person is indeed beloved; the meaning is that there is no doubt about that.

If it is asked, "In that case, how can this be a supermundane passion for her?", he says in response: "Nor is my dear life to be protected. The intention is that since its purpose is fulfilled only through the sacrifice of my life, I owe her nothing even for that passion. Therefore, by this [statement], he shows that independence is not being maintained and his life is being surrendered:
"It is the vow of the virtuous to gratify the world for any cause whatsoever;
indeed, that has been fulfilled by my father, who has released both me and his own life-breaths."

According to the sequence thus stated, the Supreme Lord has revealed—and this should be understood—that Mālatī’s status as an *uttama-nāyikā* (the highest type of heroine), which causes aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) in connoisseurs, is characterized by the thought: "For those intent on preserving their family lineage, the lineage itself must be protected even at the cost of life; and when love is firmly rooted in someone, it cannot be shaken even by the sacrifice of one's own life. Furthermore, the emotional state (*bhāva*) of fortitude (*dhairya*) is manifested here.

In this passage, because excellence (*atiśaya*) is conveyed by words such as "let it blaze," and because the effect—the performance of a rash act—is revealed by way of its cause, the poetic figures *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) and *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) are present. Furthermore, two varieties of the figure *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) should be seen here in part: first, the negation of what is desired, expressed in the words "but this person shall not [die], nor shall my life"; and second, the prescription of what is undesired, expressed in "or rather, what is beyond death?"—both of which ultimately result in the communication of a specific restriction regarding the search for means other than rashness. //2//

"What is the means now?"—the meaning is: "In such a calamity, what is the remedial measure? "Partially entered from the tiring-room" (*naipathyārdhapraviṣṭā*) means having entered slightly from the tiring-room; this reveals her state of apprehension due to not knowing the [current] situation. "The female door-keeper" (*pratīhārī*) is the female gatekeeper. "This venerable lady" refers to the holy Kāmandakī. The word "means" (*upāya*) is connected [to the previous context] by way of divine intervention. Both Mālatī and Lavaṅgikā [speak]. "With curiosity" means accompanied by a desire to hear. "What is the venerable lady doing?"—this is a general question.

"By saying 'the Blessed Lady has arrived,' she sent her disciple; thus she spoke"—since such a connection with a general action is possible, the intended connection is that [the disciple] has come desiring to see the young lady of the house. And this is the introductory element (*prastāvanāṅga*) called *gandha*. It should be understood as having been composed by the poet through his ingenuity, characterized by the definition: "A *gaṇḍa* is that which is suddenly uttered, having a meaning different from the subject at hand. Why is there a delay? The word "by her" is to be supplied as the remainder. The meaning is: "Indeed, even for us, there is no certainty as to when the Blessed Lady will arrive."
"She covers the painting" is said for the purpose of concealing her fickleness;

"she has indeed become well-composed" refers to her arrival at the moment when the means [of concealment] were being sought. Thus, through the mouth of Lavaṅgikā, the poet reminds us of his own skill in dramatic arrangement.

"‘May he prosper for his own kinsmen’—thus [the author] connects the matter introduced in the *praveśaka* with the words ‘Well said, friend! He addresses him directly into the air, saying ‘Friend,’ because they share the status of fellow religious students (*sabrahmacārin*). ‘Well said’ means excellent. The repetition (*vīpsā*) reveals an extraordinary degree of wonder. It is ‘not opposed to either world,’ meaning it is not contrary to both this world and the next, because it conveys what is both pleasant and true through both the expressed (*vācya*) and the implied (*vyaṅgya*) meanings. ‘Reply’ refers to the response."

"By the king's command"—this is the implied meaning. "By means of the account," that is, by their mutual sightings and so forth. "Something wonderful" refers to an indescribable marvel. The "interwoven narrative" (*vyatikara-saṃvidhānaka*) concerning Bakulāvalī and the picture-board consists of the following sequence of events: the arrival of the garland woven by Mādhava into Mālatī’s hands; the portrait of her drawn by Mālatī coming within Mādhava’s sight; his subsequent drawing of her; and her seeing that [portrait]. This is a composition of the story characterized by such an intermingling.

It causes supreme joy (*pramoda*) to blossom and unfold. Mutual affection (*itaretarānurāga*), that is, love for one another, exists at the time of marriage (*dārakarma*). "Most excellent" (*parārdhya*) means praiseworthy. "Auspicious" (*maṅgala*) means a means for prosperity (*abhyudaya*). By the phrase "most excellent auspiciousness," he indicates that this very [marriage] is the foremost among all auspicious things, such as the counting of days, the *māhendra* rite, and so forth. To establish this point, he cites the authoritative statement (*vacana*) of the venerable Āpastamba: "It has been sung," meaning it has been declared.

"In her there is prosperity" means that upon which the binding of the eye and mind rests. Just as when a bridegroom's eye—and through it, his mind—is attached to a maiden, everything [his success] is established by the increase of wealth and so forth in her; "in her there is prosperity" is a metaphorical usage for the sake of indicating the cause.
This is Mālatī.
Having gazed upon her, that is, having scrutinized her form.

"Excessively" (*nikāmam*) and so forth—"excessively" means intensely. "With emaciated limbs" (*kṣāmāṅgī*) refers to her body having become thin; this is a statement regarding her entry into the fifth stage [of love]. "Charming like the core of a fresh plantain tree" (*sarasakadalīgarbhasubhagā*) means she is beautiful with a whiteness of loveliness (*lāvaṇya*) like that of a fresh plantain stalk; these three adjectives constitute the common attribute. "Remaining as a mere digit" (*kalāśeṣā*) means that of which only a digit remains—other than those consumed by the gods through drinking. Her "form" (*mūrtiḥ*) is her body, for at that time it consists of nothing more than a single digit.

The expression "the form of the moon" (*śaśino mūrttiḥ*) is a metaphorical usage, like the phrase "the head of Rāhu. Alternatively, it refers to the immutable substratum (*kūṭastham adhiṣṭhānam*) of the digits (*kalāḥ*), which by nature undergo waning and waxing; this is called the "form" (*mūrttiḥ*) as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of consciousness. The term "festival" (*utsava*) in the phrase "causing a festival for the eyes" (*netrotsavakarī*) indicates joy (*pramoda*); thus, she is the cause of delight for the eyes. [This is formed] according to Pāṇini 3.2.20: *kṛño hetutācchīlyānulomyeṣu*.

(3-2-2) Thus, the suffix *ṭa* is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). By the phrase "causing a festival for the eyes," her state as the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*) is revealed; according to Amara, "a particular state [of time] is *kālika*. She has reached a condition distressed by the intense burning of the fire of passion—that state of being overwhelmed by the excessive heat of Love, which is as unbearable as fire. She is auspicious (*kalyāṇī*), meaning possessed of excellent qualities. She delights (*ramayati*), that is, she brings happiness, because she causes a festival for the eyes and because she is favorable to one's own desires. She makes one tremble (*kampayati*), both because she overpowers one with affection and because she agitates one with the fear of evil.

Due to the distress caused by the burning of passion and because of her extreme delicacy; here, in the former half [of the verse], there is the figure of speech *upamā* (simile), while in the latter half, there is *virodha* (contradiction). Furthermore, the transition (*sandhi*) between the two emotional states of joy and agitation is manifested. //3//

Since she herself will effectively provide for the alleviation of the pain of love, he casts aside his agitation and again marvels at her extraordinary beauty, beginning with the words "paripāṇḍu" (extremely pale), and so forth. "Pāṃsulakapolaṃ" means having cheeks marked by the dust of the sandalwood paste from the forehead-mark (*lalāṭikā*); there is also a reading "durbalakapolaṃ," which means that due to emaciation, the cheeks have become exceedingly delicate. "Manoharataratvaṃ" means being more beautiful even than her previous state. [This is according to the rule: "The suffixes *tarap* and *īyasun* are used when a comparison or a division is expressed."

(5-3-57) Thus, by analysis, when there is an *upapada*, the suffix *tarap* is applied. According to the statement, "The superlative (*atiśāyinika*) [suffix] is used even when the correlative (*pratiyogin*) is conceptual (*bauddha*)," the usage of the superlative here refers to that which has its correlative in a prior state existing within the mind. In the phrase *ramaṇīyajanmani*: "of beautiful birth" means having a lovely, natural form. *Paribhraman* means moving about, with all limbs throbbing. *Lalitaḥ* means beautiful. *Vidhiḥ*: that which is ordained or performed is a *saṃskāra* (refinement). *Mānmathaḥ*: because it is produced by Manmatha, or belongs to him, or has come from him; hence the suffix *aṇ*.
*Vijayate*: it stands above everything. The word *hi* indicates well-known fact (*prasiddhi*).

The meaning is that this principle is well known: according to the maxim, "An action indeed becomes clear when applied to a substance," just as a gem polished on a whetstone, so too does the specific craftsmanship fashioned by Kandarpa (the God of Love) enter the path of conceptualization for one who is naturally beautiful and a creator of loveliness. Thus it is said in the *Kādambarī*: "In whatever measure this [body] is kindled by the fire of love, in that same measure its beauty (*lāvaṇya*) becomes utterly stainless, like a silken garment purified by fire. This is also the ornament (*alaṅkāra*) called *kānti* (loveliness), defined as:
"Loveliness is known as that splendor whose radiance is nourished by the God of Love."
Because of this statement, the figure of speech *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) is employed here. //4//

Then, observing his appearance, she infers that he possesses the state of longing—the mental resolve for union—based on the saying: "The mental resolve for union is the gazing with hope along the path [of the beloved]. She concludes this with certainty (*niyatam*).

"Created by imagination" means fashioned by thought. "Union with the beloved" refers to the enjoyment of one's lover. The phrase "for instance" (*tathāhi*) marks the beginning of an explanatory demonstration.
"The loosening of the knot of the lower garment" (*nīvībandhocchvasanam*), and so forth; [it is said: "The *nīvī* is the binding of the cloth worn upon the hips of a woman."

Thus says Amara. The "unfastening of the knot" (nīvībandhasya ucchvasanam) refers to its loosening; for it is stated in the *Ratirahasya*: "The knot of the women's lower garment, though firmly tied, slips away—this is a sign of love. "Trembling of the lower lip" (adharaspandanam) is the quivering of the lips; by this, the commencement of a kiss is indicated. "Sinking of the arms" (dorniṣādaḥ) is the complete exhaustion of the two arms due to being overcome by fatigue. "Perspiration" (svedaḥ) is the state of the body being moist with sweat. [And her gaze was] smooth, sweet, sidelong, tender, and charming.

"It is known as *masṛṇa* (smooth) when it is colored by passion (*anurāga-kaṣāyita*). This means sweet and not agitated. Dhanika states: "Sweetness (*mādhurya*) is the absence of excess. "With the corners of her eyes slightly contracted, full of joy, and half-closing her lids..."
"The gaze with pupils repeatedly rolling is known as *ākekarā*," so says the *Bhāvaprakāśa*. "Lubricated" (*snigdha*) means not dry;
"that [gaze] is lubricated whose object is mingled with its radiance."

Thus it was said; "innocent [expression] observed by its own nature" was also stated. Stiffness of the limbs (*gātrastambha*) is the state of the body being devoid of activity. An intense flow (*utprabandha*) is a continuous succession. Upon the expanse of the cheeks (*gaṇḍābhoga*), that is, the broadness of the temples, there is a mass of horripilation (*pulakapaṭala*). Fainting (*mūrcchanā*) is a delusion arising from the excellence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). And consciousness (*cetanā*)—the remainder of the sentence being that this occurs upon the cessation of delusion—is the state of awakening for her. Here, the *sūkṣma* (subtle) figure of speech is the ornament. //5//
"She moves Mālatī" means she urges her by the touch of her hand; this indicates that [Mālatī] has her mind fixed elsewhere.
"O Blessed One, I bow to you.

With the intention that the attainment of a virtuous husband is the fruit [of her devotion], a benediction is employed: "May it be so. The optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of a blessing (*āśis*).
"The seat is pure"—the word "this" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].

"Is the Blessed Lady well?"—he asks this while sighing in order to dispel the suspicion that his words were not preceded by affection. The word "as it were" (iva) indicates that this is not the ultimate truth; he conducts himself outwardly as if he were composed.
The meaning is that there is no longer any composure of mind.

"Internal" (svagatam) refers to her thorough understanding of the actual state of affairs. This is indeed the prologue to this deceptive drama—a performance consisting of trickery—and serves as the preliminary ritual (*pūrvaraṅga*), for from this point onward its enactment will begin. By saying "aloud" (*prakāśam*), she, through her cleverness, provides an opening for what she intends to say. The speech of the Venerable Lady is of a different kind altogether; with her heart heavy, obstructed by tears, and sluggish, it lingers within and fails to emerge. With the flow of her words faltering due to a heart dulled by the suppression of thick tears, it is of an unprecedented manner.

So, what will now be the cause for agitation? Agitation (*udvega*) is a particular modification of the mind resulting from hearing something undesirable and so forth. [Objection: But surely it is in the context of the conversation. The word "this" (*ayam*) is spoken with a gesture indicating Mālatī as the object. A *cīra* is a piece of cloth; a *cīvara* is a garment made from that, the clothing of Buddhist renunciants—as in the *Harṣacarita*: "His high, fierce loincloth was bound by a strip of coarse woolen cloth. That which is contrary or adverse to this is meant.

"From the Vedic scripture: 'On the very day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce,' for the stage of liberation is rooted in dispassion. Likewise, in the Mahābhārata: 'Let whatever time it may be, and let the supreme reality be as it is;
he in whom dispassion exists—for him there is liberation; such is my conviction.'"

Thus: *paricaya* means familiarity; and that [familiarity] is used here figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*). Here, it refers to the affection (*sneha*) which is its effect. "How indeed?"—the meaning is: in what manner does this [affection] become a cause for agitation?

*Ayī* is an indeclinable used in address. "You too"—the meaning is: since you are constantly present at the minister’s house, you too are fully aware of all the events there. "This matter" is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*).

"This here," and so forth. "This" (*idam*) is a gesture toward what is present before one. "In this world" (*iha loke*) means in the entire world; the meaning is that there is no other means for victory. "Victorious" (*jaitram*) means a means of victory. The body, which is the basis of innate grace—meaning it was created having taken as its very cause those very unartificial amorous gestures—is [the means].

"Lamentable through union with an unsuitable husband" means lamentable through the union or meeting with a husband who is utterly unfit due to deformity, old age, and so on; it is an object of pity for connoisseurs. [The suffix] *ṇyat* is applied according to the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*.

(3.1.124) *Viphala*: "one whose excellence of qualities (*guṇātiśaya*)—namely, the superhuman nature of his beauty, character, and other virtues—is fruitless. This is because its fruit is union with a suitable bridegroom; it will come to pass, but it has not yet occurred, and even now it does not transcend the present. By stating that its avoidance is indeed possible through taking action, he dispels Mālatī’s distress caused by the cutting off of her hope. The word *iti* indicates a manner. The connection is as follows: "Do you not also know that, in this manner of apprehension, intimacy is a cause of agitation? //6//

"He shows feigned anxiety" means that she acts out a state of dejection of mind. This demonstrates the result of the role of the female messenger (*dūtī*) as described in the *Ratirahasya*—beginning with "Even a slave has been released by him; alas, this man is her husband! and so forth—which consists of causing her to attain detachment (*vairāgya*) through words enumerating the faults of the husband, and which was introduced [in the previous verse] as being directed toward an unsuitable suitor.

He elaborates upon her statement: "All the people despise the minister because Mālatī was promised to Nandana in accordance with the King’s command. This refers to the matter mentioned by the Bhagavatī [Mālatī] herself; "in accordance with the King’s request" means for the sake of complying with his words. "To Nandana" means for the purpose of Nandana. "Was promised" (*pratipannā*) means she was accepted (*abhyupagatā*); or else, it means she was "bestowed" (*pratipāditā*), i.e., given, since she had already been verbally betrothed. The causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is implied here, because the act of bestowing (*pratipādana*) carries the meaning of giving. Thus, the sense is that she was given by him.
"Sakala" (all) refers to that which is well-known to the entire world; this indicates that Mālatī alone does not know [this].

Then, as if by the falling of a thunderbolt of a bride-price, she reveals her father’s alienation from her, being filled with agitation: "How have I been made into an offering for the king by my father? The word "how" (*katham*) expresses astonishment; the meaning is that even in a dream this matter had never been imagined by her. "Offering" (*upahāra*) means a gift. She says, "I have been made into an offering like fruit, flowers, or sprouts. By the suffix *cvī*, which denotes the state of something previously non-existent now becoming so, the fact that this is the first occurrence of such a thing is revealed, thereby manifesting the cessation of affection. By saying "for the king," an extreme impropriety is suggested.

The meaning is that it has never been heard before that, at any time or place, a daughter was ever given away by the king's command. By the address "O Father," which suggests a state of being melted by such affection, the cause for the wonder— namely, how this could have happened—
is established.

Having recognized that state of mind, he intensifies his hatred toward the father with the words "devoid of regard for virtues," and so forth. "Devoid of longing for excellent qualities"—such as beauty, youth, virtuous character, sweetness, and cleverness—is an adverbial modifier of the action of "undertaking. "This matter" refers to the act of giving a daughter in marriage to an unworthy person. "How was it undertaken? means in what manner was it begun? The sense is that this objective is difficult to accomplish for any conscious being whatsoever. Alternatively, the phrase "or rather" sets aside the point he had previously considered.

From where, for what reason? *Apattyasneha* is affection (*vātsalya*) toward sons or daughters. [This refers to those] whose minds are expert in crooked policy—those whose hearts have been trained in the treatises of Kauṭilya and others, which teach deception even toward one's own kin through a method characterized by lack of integrity. The suffix *ṣa* is applied according to Pāṇini 8.3.89: *ninadībhyāṃ snāteḥ kauśale*. Likewise, in the *Kādambarī*:

"What is improper for those for whom the *Kauṭilya-śāstra*—which is merciless and consists primarily of instructions on extreme cruelty—is an authority? This reflection of ours is appropriate only when there is affection for one's offspring; the point is that such affection does not exist here. Having stated that their minds are "skilled in crooked policy" (*kuṭilanayaniṣṇāta*), he anticipates the question, "What then is this 'policy' (*naya*)? and says: "But this... The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction. By the phrase "this [is] the non-deluded intent," the task (*kārya*) is referred to in general terms.

"One for whom the task alone is the supreme goal" is *idaṃparaḥ*; the state of being such is *aidaṃparyam*. That is to say: the reason for making him a friend is that he is the king’s court jester (*narmasaciva*), and thus capable of assisting both through the king and by himself; [the thought is] "let him be a friend. That is to say, this is *aidaṃparyam* (purposefulness), and not affection—this is the meaning. //7//

He states the fruit of encouragement: "Service to the King is indeed a great matter for my father, but Mālatī is not. Service to the King means performing what is pleasing to the King. "Great" (*guru*) means significant; the ellipsis implies that it is an object worthy of great respect. But Mālatī, on the other hand, is not great—meaning she is as light as a blade of grass. This is because of the saying: "One should cause even that very fault from which one fears to sprout further."

He proclaims the fault of the antagonist: "Just as it was commanded by the Blessed One, so it is"—this is the ellipsis. He establishes that very state [of things] by way of contrast: otherwise, why did the minister not deliberate upon that bridegroom who is difficult to behold and whose youth has passed? "Otherwise" means: if he were merely devoted to policy (*naya*) and not characterized by affection (*sneha*). By the word "that" (*tasmin*), he refers to him—either through personal experience or common renown—as being devoid of virtues. "Bridegroom" (*vara*) refers to the son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*).

The term "excellent" (*vara*) is used because of the minister’s own imposition of the intention that he was excellent. Regarding "hard to behold" (*durdarśana*): his sight is a source of suffering due to an extreme degree of deformity. To the objection that even deformity might be tolerated if youth were conducive to enjoyment, he says: "an old woman whose youth has passed away. This illuminates both her detachment from sense-objects and her incapacity [for them]. "In him" refers to that object. "By the minister" implies the capacity for deliberation through the role of counselor. "Why? means for what purpose;
"not considered" means not ascertained that "he is such a person. The underlying sense is that, therefore, there is not even a fraction of affection [toward him].

In the *Nandana* commentary, he describes her detachment rooted in those words: "Alas! I am ruined! She is one for whom the fall of the thunderbolt of misfortune has arrived; she is ill-fated (*mandabhāginī*). *Ha* is an indeclinable expressing despondency. *Hatā* means "I am destroyed" or "I am ruined," [caused] by fate or by my father. By implication, the misfortune (*anartha*)—the calamity consisting of union with an unsuitable husband—is like the falling of a thunderbolt (*vajrapatana*) upon her. She is *mandabhāginī*, meaning "one whose portion (*bhāga*), that is, fortune (*bhāgya*), is small (*manda*). Although the word "I" (*aham*) is not explicitly used, it is understood through the use of the first person.

Having understood Mālatī’s heart, Lavaṅgikā entreats her: "Therefore, be gracious, O Blessed One; save this dear friend from this living death. She is as much your own daughter as [Mādhava's]. 'Living death' (jīvanmaraṇa) refers to the abandonment of life while one is still alive—death that is no different from being alive. It is a metaphorical expression because, like one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta), there is an absence of the experience of pleasure which is the fruit of living, and because such a person resembles a corpse (kuṇapa). Regarding the phrase 'as much yours': just as she is Bhūrivasu's, so by law is she your own daughter, since she is your sister's child. And this is the reason why she must be saved.
O simple one! O you of straightforward intellect!"

5. By the phrase "one who perceives exactly as she has seen," it is suggested that you observe only the minister’s outward conduct toward us with respect; you do not know his self-serving intent, which persists even through his transgression against me. Regarding the word "Bhagavatī"—by saying "not mine," she implies: "One such as I is merely a fit object for their salutation, 'Bhagavatī,' but is certainly not empowered to engage in such matters."

Regarding the word "generally" (*prāya*): because of the Smṛti text beginning with "the father, the grandfather, the brother," and so forth, the term "generally" is used because even the grandfather and others have the authority to give the girl away only in the absence of the father. "The progenitor" refers to the father. And the phrase "and the divine [offering]" (*daivam*) indicates that she cannot be turned back due to her independence. Now, "first, through the practice of extreme affection, one should distinguish her by means of stories and the like."

Having thus stated the means, he employs it by way of negation with the words "yatkila" (it is said that). "Kila" is used here in the sense of tradition (*aitihya*). Kauśika is Viśvāmitra; because she was born of Menakā, his daughter, she is called Kauśikī. The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after the *aṇ* suffix in the sense of offspring. [He approaches] King Duṣyanta, the descendant of Puru; [and] the celestial nymph (*apsaras*) Urvaśī. Although the word *apsaras* is recorded in the *Liṅgānuśāsana* as being plural in the feminine (*striyāṃ bahuṣvapsarasaḥ*), its use in the singular is correct due to the usage of the great poets.

Likewise, in the *Śākuntala*, it is stated according to the definition: "The Apsaras named Sānumatī. Because of the strength of the usage [of the verb], she "desired" (*cakame*) King Purūravas, the son of Budha and known as Aila; thus, by the force of her love, she indicates her own approach to him. Those who know the narratives (*ākhyāna*) such as the *Mahābhārata* and others are called "knowers of narratives" (*ākhyānavidaḥ*), meaning those who are conversant with ancient history. Vāsavadattā was the daughter of Pradyota, the lord of Ujjayinī. "Pratta" means that which has been commenced to be given because it has already been verbally betrothed (*vāgdattatayā*). [This is derived from the rule: *aca upasargāt taḥ*.

(7.4.47) "She gave herself, bestowed by her father"—by these two preceding [verses], she demonstrates her extraordinary independence. To him, Udayana, the King of Vatsa, she gave; she bestowed [herself]. This is the *laṅ* [aorist] of the root *dāṇ* (to give), with the substitution of *yaccha* according to the rule beginning with *pā-ghrā-* (Pāṇini 7.3.78). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the conduct of Ahalyā and others is indicated. That which is indeed [described] is a matter that is almost like a rash act (*sāhasakalpa*), the behavior of foolish people; it is slightly incomplete (*īṣadasamāptam*).

The inclusion of the word *kalpa* (in the sense of "method") indicates an exclusion of other rash acts (*sāhasa*), because of the reason that [the father] has accepted [her] by falling upon a suitable spot. The underlying intention is that we need not provide further instruction, as our task is solely to prevent rashness. Now, he terrifies her by demonstrating the absence of all other means: "in every way" (*sarvathā*). This means "by every possible manner," since there is no other recourse.

Regarding the passage beginning with *rājñaḥ priyāyai* (to the king’s beloved): it is due to the motive (*nimitta*) of a purpose consisting of the acquisition of wealth and so forth. By the phrase *ātmajām* (his own daughter), it is suggested that since the object is under his own control, who could possibly restrain his will?
"That state which, through its solitude, is not afflicted by the sufferings of embodied beings, and which kindles both resolve and the intellect—that indeed is true bliss (*nirvṛti*)."

Thus says Divākara. "Possessing nirvṛti" means being happy by virtue of having accomplished what was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatayā*). "Let it be" (*bhavatu*) is used here in the *loṭ* (imperative) mood in the sense of granting permission (*kāmacārakaraṇe*). "By this minister"—let it be joined (*ghaṭatām*), let it be applied; this is the *loṭ* used in the sense of *vidhi* (injunction). "This" is a gesture indicating its delightful nature through all its qualities. "By this" is a gesture indicating its contrary state. "By the smoke-grasper" (*dhūmagraheṇa*) means by a specific deity in the form of smoke; that is to say, by the one well-known as Dhūmaketu.

Because she is stainless due to her youth, being like a fawn that has not yet sprouted [antlers], she is presented as being free from blemish on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*); thus, there is the figure of speech *upamā* (simile). Alternatively, by imagining her stainlessness as distinct from the well-known digit of the moon’s blemish, there is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). Furthermore, here the figure of speech *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis) is perceived, because—through the semblance of an undesirable injunction that leads to the performance of a rash act—he teaches the means for achieving the desired goal, thereby establishing the specific excellence of making one's birth fruitful. //8//

Now he shows the fruit of what was said: "Alas, father! Even you, indeed, have become thus for me"—in every way, the thirst for enjoyment has triumphed. The particle *api* is used in the sense of contradiction; the meaning is: "even you, who were experienced [by me] as being helpless through such affection. "For me" (*mama*) means: "I am that very Mālatī. *Nāma* is used in the sense of censure; it means "fie, fie upon this! "Thus" (*evam*) is a dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) of the cruelty committed through obsession with one's own purpose; the meaning is: "you have become like this. "By the thirst for enjoyment" (*bhogatṛṣṇayā*) means: by the desire for the experience of sense objects.

The meaning is that it stands having conquered and surpassed the entire world. The point is that through the favor of a king or a royal favorite, one obtains sovereignty and the means of enjoyment even greater than before, but not dharma or liberation.
Now, "one should indeed describe the multitude of the hero's qualities in this manner according to the context."

Having spoken thus, in order to introduce the qualities of the hero (*nāyaka*), she provides the opportunity [for his entrance] through the device of a clever pupil, by means of *nisṛṣṭārthatva* (the entrustment of the matter): "The venerable lady has delayed for too long! Indeed, I say that the noble Mādhava is unwell. "Delayed for too long" (*cirāyitam*) means that she has tarried for a great length of time. By saying "Indeed, I say," the impropriety of the delay is suggested. "Unwell in body" (*asvasthaśarīraḥ*) means one whose body is not in its natural state; the meaning is that he is afflicted by fever or some such ailment. This is the reason for the impropriety of the delay.
It is understood that this is an expression of agreement with those words. Because of her haste, the speech remains incomplete.

It is like saying, "Enter the ball of rice," and so forth. This exists; it has been remembered by me as well; the ellipsis is "it is gone today. Grant permission—consent—to my departure; this is the ellipsis.
Lavaṅgikā, having found an opportunity for questioning through her observations, addresses Mālatī in accordance with her inner thoughts, using the *janāntika* (aside) convention:
"With the hand formed into the *tripatāka* gesture, excluding others from the conversation..."

"That which is a mutual address in the presence of people is *janāntika*," says Dhanika. "Friend Mālatī! Now we learn of the origin of that noble-souled one from the presence of the Holy Lady—'from the presence' meaning from near, that is, from her mouth; 'origin' meaning birth, since his form and other qualities have been seen.
Friend, I have a curiosity"—this implies that due to bashfulness, she is not able to ask [the question] herself.

"O Blessed One! Who is this person named Mādhava, for whom you, O Blessed One, sustain yourself with such heavy affection, and who carries a heart overwhelmed by the weight of your love? To generate an excess of respect, she negates even her own intended meaning through a clever turn of phrase—[saying it is] 'inopportune' (*aprastāvikī*). That in which something is introduced is an *upodghāta* (an introduction); the time for narration is the *prastāva*. Since that does not exist for him, it is *aprastāvikī*. The meaning is: at present, the time for that occasion is not sufficient. The reason for this is: 'great,' meaning possessing no small subject matter; this story is a discourse concerning Mādhava."

Out of an excess of newly arisen respect, he requests: "Nevertheless, may the Blessed Lady explain; may she show her favor. By the word "nevertheless" (tathāpi), he indicates that it should be told even in brief. "Favor" (prasādam) means grace or kindness.

"Listen"—this serves as an introductory prologue (*pīṭhikābandha*) to what is about to be said. By using the present tense in "there exists," he indicates its current reality. By describing him as "the minister of the Lord of Vidarbha," even though he is a Brāhmaṇa, his possession of unsurpassed sovereignty—like that of Droṇa and others—is revealed. By calling him "the crest-jewel of all preeminent men" (*samagrapuruṣaprakāṇḍacūḍāmaṇi*), the excellence of his venerability is indicated through metaphorical usage (*lakṣaṇā*). As it is said: "The words *matallikā*, *macarcikā*, *prakāṇḍa*, *udgha*, *tallaja*, and so forth, are synonyms for 'praiseworthy'."

Thus says Amara; *nāma* is used here in the sense of renown. [Regarding the phrase "whose greatness of merit is to be honored by the entire world"]: his greatness (*mahimā*)—consisting of the excellence of conduct and study—is a merit that removes sin and is worthy of honor (*mahanīya*) by the whole world (*aśeṣabhuvana*). He determines that it is the father alone, and no one else, who possesses such capacity, because he himself is distinguished by qualities similar to those [of the father]. This is according to the maxim: "One without virtue does not know the virtuous," and as stated in the Mahābhārata: "A Brahmin knows a Brahmin, and likewise a husband knows his wife."

Because it has been said, "Marriage and debate are both desired by the wise only with equals," the fact of an equal relationship is also indicated. The word "they" (te) refers to [Mādhava] even though the question was posed by Lavaṅgikā, because in effect it was prompted by Mālatī; thus, the statement is made directed toward him. "He who" (yo'sau) refers to one born of such a lineage, since birth provides the standard of proof. "Of what kind" (yādṛśa) means endowed with such qualities; for an entity that has attained existence is distinguished by its qualities. "He" (sa) means "one such as that," the sense being that he knows [this].
Because the word *yat* (which) is employed in the subsequent sentence, the word *tat* (that), occurring in the preceding sentence, is implied by the force of that context.
Furthermore, he praises its great majesty for the sake of inciting enthusiasm toward it, saying "Moreover" (*apica*).

"Whose horizons have become intermingled": *vyatikara* means mixing; those whose horizons have come into contact with one another. "By whitening," that is, by becoming bright white. The whiteness of fame is due to its being produced from a substance as pure as crystal, or according to poetic convention (*kavisamaya*). The verbal root *śvit* (to be white) is conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). By the use of the present tense, its continued existence even now is indicated. "By glories" refers to the renown produced by one's own heroic deeds.
As it is said: "If that [fame] has come down through family lineage, it shines under the name of *kīrti*; if it is born from one's own heroic deeds, it is designated as *yaśas*."

Thus ends the *Bhāvaprakāśa*. It is the locus, the substratum, of the manifestations of well-performed deeds—the transformations of merit consisting of birth, lifespan, and experience—of those things that are "ūrjasvalānām," meaning characterized by excellence. As it is said: "The words *jyotsnā*, *tamisrā*, *śṛṅgin*, *ūrjasvin*, *ūrjasvala*, *gomin*, *malina*, and *malīmasa* [are used in the sense of being possessed of]."

[The word *akalitamahimānaḥ*] is correct by virtue of this grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) [Pāṇini 5.2.114]. [Those whose greatness is unmeasured: those whose greatness—their capacity consisting of brilliance, power, and so forth—is *akalita*, meaning uncounted or beyond limitation in its extent. The verbal root is *kala* in the sense of "counting. The distinction is that previously the greatness was described as meritorious, whereas now its indefinability is established. *Ketana* means a banner; for it indicates an auspicious arrival due to its attainment by the family and its observers. Alternatively, *ketana* is simply *niketana*, meaning a house.
Or again, *ketana* means an invitation.

"Likewise, a *devalaka* (one who lives off temple offerings) does not deserve an invitation to a *śrāddha*, according to the Smṛti. 'You are worthy recipients for us' means you are surrounded by auspiciousness; that is, by prosperity (*abhyudaya*). In this world—that is, on the terrestrial plane (*bhūloka*) suitable for human habitation; the implication is that such things might be possible in the heavenly realms (*svarloka*) and so forth. 'Such as those' means equal to them. By the use of the plural number, he says this: that one [son] was born to us through our merits, and even if another person like him, such as Bhūrivasu, were to be found somewhere at some time through diligent searching, he might indeed be obtained."

Therefore, it is indicated that only two such [beings] can possibly exist, and not a third besides them. How so? The meaning is that for many [such beings], rebirth is simply impossible. Here, even though no explicit standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is mentioned, this constitutes the figure of speech *upamā* (simile) residing within the sentence. //9//

She demonstrates the correspondence between that meaning expressed as "only your father knows" and the heart of Mālatī: "Indeed, my lord, my father remembers him by his name at all times. He says "by his name" because he was taken [as a son] due to his being a friend of her father and because of the intention that he would become her husband; thus, she does not state the name herself. "At all times" means on every occasion—on every occasion such as, "Devarāta spoke thus," "it was done thus," "he laughed thus," or "he sighed thus"—the sense is that he dwells upon these things constantly.

"Friends, it is said by those who know that time that the acquisition of knowledge was indeed made together with the lady from the presence of their preceptor. [Regarding *vidyādhigama*: the acquisition (*adhigama*), that is, the attainment (*prāpti*), of sciences (*vidyā*) such as the Vedas and so forth, was accomplished; "by the two of them" is the ellipsis. This shows that the lady and the two ministers possess unsurpassed friendship due to being fellow-students (*satīrthya*). [Regarding *tatkālavedinaḥ*: elderly people who know that time. [Regarding *mantrayante*: the meaning is that they speak.]

Regarding the passage beginning with "tataḥ": "tataḥ" means from that Devarāta; by the phrase "like the mountain of sunrise, as from the eastern mountain," qualities such as loftiness, stability, greatness, and the capacity to bear the burden of the earth are demonstrated. The expression "only one, without a brother" illuminates his being the sole recipient of his father’s entire affection, as well as his sovereignty over complete dominion.

Beautiful with the radiance of manifest virtues: either "radiances" (*dyutayaḥ*) refers to the splendors that are his very virtues—beauty, character, and so forth—which had manifested even in childhood; or he is beautiful by means of a splendor (*dyuti*) in which his virtues are manifest. Possessed of arts (*kalāvān*): at that very stage, the entire collection of the sixty-four arts had manifested through his prior impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*), and he was distinguished by two or three arts as his own special portions. Of the great festival: by metonymy, this refers to the activity of the festival, namely, the great gladdening of the heart.

This indicates that there is a consensus among all those with eyes—not only those who possess specialized knowledge—regarding this matter. The verb *udiyāya* (he rose) is used in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the intention of expressing mere factuality, as in the phrase "he made the Mandara trees devoid of fire."

It is like [the compound] *bālacandraḥ*, which means "this is both a child and the moon. Although one could have used the term *mādhavenduḥ* (the moon that is Mādhava) in place of *bālacandraḥ*, the name was not explicitly stated for the sake of producing an excellence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Here, the figures of speech—simile (*upamā*), metaphor (*rūpaka*), semantic pun (*arthaśleṣa*), verbal pun (*śabdaśleṣa*), and hyperbole (*atiśayokti*)—exist in mutual dependence; thus, there is the figure of speech known as "Commixture" (*saṅkara*). //10//
With the hope that "perhaps he might be Mādhava," she demonstrates the fruit of her speech.

Then, having revealed his extraordinary modesty and his praiseworthy youth, she entices him with the words beginning with "asau" (he). The subject at hand is Bālacandra. By the word "vidyāśābhiḥ"—meaning by the desires for the eighteen branches of knowledge such as the Vedas and so forth—the plural number (*bahuvacana*) is used because of the great abundance of things to be heard. By the word "śiśuḥ" (a child), it is suggested that although he is a boy, he is endowed with innate goodness (*sattva*).

By the words "having gone out from the palace" and "departing from his own home," it is suggested that staying at home and indulging in the company of kinsmen is an obstacle to the acquisition of knowledge.
As it is said: "One who seeks pleasure should abandon knowledge, or one who seeks knowledge should abandon pleasure;
for how can there be knowledge for one who seeks pleasure, and how can there be pleasure for one who seeks knowledge?"

Thus, according to the statement of Vyāsa: "here in Padmāvatī," the phrase "has arrived" (*āyāta*)—meaning he has come—suggests that there was no great effort on the part of his father in sending him forth. "Now" (*saṃprati*) refers to this present time. "Sweet as the full autumn moon" means that, due to having ascended to youth, he is as sweet and beautiful to behold as the moon intensified by the fullness of the autumn season. He shows the fruit of this sweetness: "in whose place of vision" (*yadālokasthāne*), meaning in the range of whose sight; "the city" (*puram*) is Padmāvatī.

"Tremulous with madness" means unsteady due to the helplessness of the heart produced by the strikes of Cupid’s arrows. By the mention of "madness," it is suggested that the sight [of her] acts as the cause for entering the eighth stage [of love] almost instantaneously. "The window is turned into a blue lotus" means that a garland of blue water-lilies has formed there; "window" refers to the lattice. This is because it is covered by a mass of dark, thick, and cool radiance. Furthermore, according to the maxim "women are the objects of desire for those who desire," it should be understood that her extraordinary beauty is revealed here for the sake of arousing interest.
In this verse, the poetic figures (alaṅkāras) are Simile (upamā) and Poetic Fancy (utprekṣā). //11//

Even though he has reached the bloom of youth, the author describes his habit of acquiring knowledge as if he were still in childhood: "here, in this city," by means of a "childhood friend"—that is, one with whom he shared play in the dust during his early years and whose friendship was firmly established—his status as a ground for supreme trust is revealed. He studies—that is, practices—the science of *ānvīkṣikī*, which is devoted to determining the true nature of the Self; the meaning is that it is the Vedānta scripture. The mention of *ānvīkṣikī* is intended to indicate that for one who is wise and tranquil, that [scripture] is of primary importance.

Having aroused full curiosity by describing his multitude of virtues, such as noble lineage and so forth, she reveals the hero’s name at the end for the sake of his delight: "He is this very one named Mādhava. The meaning is: "He is the one thus described by me; he is now the one introduced by Avalokitā. The word *nāma* is used in the sense of renown; the meaning is: "Who in the world does not know him? The passage beginning with "There is a minister of the Lord of Vidarbha" and ending with "he is this very one named Mādhava" constitutes the *vilobhana* (enticement), because it entices Mālatī.

The meaning is that it is an experience of supreme bliss manifested through the emergence of sensations such as horripilation accompanied by joy upon hearing his name. "Friend Lavaṅgikā! Have you heard?"—the word "this" is to be supplied. By saying "have you heard," she suggests that it is indeed pleasing to you that the object of her passion has fallen within your own sphere of influence. "How is it that he, though born of a great family, is so fortunate?"—"Born of a great family" means one for whom a great lineage is the source or place of origin.
The particle *api* (even/though) conjoins this quality with other virtues.

He says, "O friend! From where else could the Pārijāta tree have emerged, were it not from the great ocean?"—meaning, from what source? He means the great ocean, the Ocean of Milk, which is distinguished from all other oceans as the place of origin for nectar and other such things. By the expression "of the Pārijāta," with its literal meaning transferred to another sense, its renown throughout the entire world is implied. "From where" (*kutaḥ*) implies "from what cause. "Having excluded the great ocean" (*varjayitvā*) indicates that there is no other possible source. "I had already inferred this matter precisely because I perceived his virtues even before the words of the Blessed Lady. Thus he speaks.

Indeed, just as other trees do not arise from just anywhere without the ocean-jar [as their source], the jewel-like *pārijāta* tree does not come into being from some random location; therefore, the sense is that this matter regarding the waters is also necessarily inferable. Furthermore, in these two statements—"How could that illustrious one, though born of a great lineage, [be here]? and "From where else could the *pārijāta* emerge, were it not from the great ocean?"—there occurs the figure of speech *prativastūpamā* (parallelism) by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*), because a single common attribute is established through different words.
[The phrase] "I have heard from my dear friend" and so forth refers to the "attainment," due to Mālatī’s happy arrival.
"Aho" signifies an interruption in the flow of conversation. "Kālātipātaḥ" means the passing of time.

Regarding the phrase beginning with "kṣipan": "kṣipan" means casting off; the verbal root is "kṣipa," meaning to cast away. "Nidrāmudrām" refers to the state of numbness produced by sleep. "Madanakalahacchedasulabhām" means that which is easily attained at the conclusion of sexual union.
As it is said: "In the first battle of passion, women are possessed of little self-control."

Thus, by the expression "having drunk the sweat-water, its power spent in the battle of love," sexual union is described using the term "Madana’s war. From the very beginning—that is, from the start—those birds whose trembling was suddenly assumed through the force of fear upon hearing the great roar without any suspicion; such is the state of the pairs of birds (*vihagamithuna*). Of the palaces (*saudha*), that is, the mansions; in the large, expansive bowers (*nikuñja*), namely the recesses of the attic chambers (*candraśālā*).

According to Amarasimha’s statement, "The words *nikuñja* and *kuñja* are used in the neuter for the interior of a place covered by creepers and the like," the word "and the like" (*ādi*) includes areas enclosed by walls and so forth. *Ghanatām* means density or compactness. *Sandhyā-śaṅkha-dhvaniḥ* is the sound of a auspicious conch blown at the time of the evening twilight (*sāyaṃ-sandhyā*). *Anibhṛtaḥ* means not contained; the sense is that it cannot be restrained because there is insufficient space. Due to the impressions (*saṃskāra*) formed over a long period, it moves and wanders in the sky (*khe*). Here, the poetic figure is *svabhāvokti* (description of nature), along with other ornaments.
Because of the description of the nature and color of an extremely subtle bird, and because of the statement regarding the vastness of the sound that depends on the sky as its support. //12//
"At the time of departure, he utters the blessing 'May you remain in happiness' because of his [the other's] importance.
'Aside' means that, having feigned not hearing what was said due to being overcome by anxiety, he speaks to himself."

From the words "Where? up to "the rising of the Pārijāta," [the poet] demonstrates that the mission of the female messenger has borne fruit by showing her renewed detachment from the Nandana grove, her reproach toward her father, and her great esteem for the hero. By manifesting an eager longing with the thought, "Might I see him once again?", the master of poets concludes this act while maintaining the primary sentiment of love-in-union (abhilāṣa-śṛṅgāra) and introduces the transition to the subject matter of the subsequent act; thus it should be understood.
"Let us descend here by this *sañjavana*. According to Amara, "a *sañjavana* is a quadrangular courtyard (*catuḥśāla*)."

Now, having followed the meaning of the *Kāmasūtra* as it has been practiced, he considers the portion that remains to be performed. "Well done"—this is an adverbial modifier for the act of making [the matter] light. "As if standing apart" (*taṭasthayā eva*) means: without resorting to any particular side in order to avoid a lack of confidence; for if it were known that she was either a partisan of Mādhava or instigated by Bhūrivasu, her heart would not be revealed due to the resulting suspicion. "Toward Mālatī" (*mālatīm prati*)—meaning with Mālatī as the objective; the accusative case is used here according to the rule: "It is also seen in connection with *prati*."

The *nisṛṣṭārthadūtīkalpa*—the procedure for a female messenger with full authority—is to be applied to one who has been accepted [as a messenger]. "Burden" (*bhāra*) refers to the gravity of the duty to be performed. The use of the word "burden" is intended to indicate that proceeding according to the scriptures is difficult to bear. "Lightened" means made easy to carry; the sense is that what remains to be accomplished is minimal.
To introduce the answer in the form of a challenge—"Why is this?"—it follows: "If you ask for what reason it was lightened, it is because of this."

He states that very reason: "In another suitor," and so forth. "In another suitor" refers to Nandana, who has become a rival; "hatred" means displeasure. Regarding the father Bhūrivasu, "doubt" (*vicikitsā*) is the uncertainty as to whether he is affectionate toward his own [daughter] or not, due to his performing what ought not to be done. As the *Vaijayantī* states: "Doubt (*vicikitsā*), however, is uncertainty. And: "Appointed for her destruction, he wavers out of concern for women."

*Itivat* means "like this. *Janitā* means "produced" or "generated. In the phrase *dveṣo janitaḥ*, there is a change of gender (from masculine to neuter). By means of "allusions to past events"—that is, by introducing historical narratives such as those of Śakuntalā and others—the meaning is that she has indicated: "Just as in the case of Śakuntalā and others, when you act in the same manner regarding the course of duty (*kāryapadavī*), there will be no fault whatsoever. *Stutam* means "praised. *Māhābhāgyam* means "greatness of fortune"; it follows that this refers to being endowed with extraordinary merit.

That which [is obtained] by lineage—that is, by birth—and that which is obtained by virtue—such as good fortune and so forth; because the fruit of meritorious deeds consists of birth, lifespan, enjoyment, and physical form; and that which occurs by chance through incidental connection—not, however, through insistence on this matter—this explains the cause for the doubt. Thus, "because" (*iti hetau*) means "for this reason," providing the answer to the question "from where? "Now" (*atha*) means immediately following; "indeed" (*khalu*) is used for emphasis; "to be performed" (*vidheyaḥ*) means to be practiced.

The meaning is that the very impression (*vāsanā*) of mutual passion must be nourished through repeated sightings, exclusive association, conversation, and so forth; for familiarity is what sustains it.
[As it is said: "Having engendered a sense of well-being, one should say: 'O fortunate one, listen to this:
there is a certain extraordinary circumstance regarding that youth, who is as delicate as a flower.'"
"O friend, bitten by the serpent of false views, you have fallen into doubt.
When this is said, if he endures it, one should meet him again on the following day and bring about a reconciliation.
Thus, with well-established expectations amidst circumstances consisting mostly of calamities, quarrels, and festivals—
during garden parties, drinking excursions, processions, descents into water, and even the outbreak of fire.
"Or he should unite with her in his own house, which has been prepared to ensure there is no mishap.

The meaning is that after this, one must carry out the performance according to the sequence thus described. However, one who intends to make an advance himself should first establish a familiarity. Beginning with the words, "The external and internal causes for establishing familiarity are now stated," [it continues]:
"One should first establish familiarity, and thereafter engage in conversation."
"Followed by the perception of outward signs mixed with reproaches"—
since the cause for becoming acquainted [with the beloved] has been stated by this statement of Vātsyāyana, all is entirely auspicious.
Thus concludes the examination of the meaning of the second act of the *Mālatīmādhava*.
By the grace of Pūrṇajyotis, she became Pūrṇasarasvatī.
Thus ends the second act.
Now begins the third act.

Then he commences the introductory scene (*praveśaka*)—entering as Buddharakṣitā. Buddharakṣitā was previously indicated by the statement, "A friend, Buddharakṣitā, has indeed been appointed there. By the manner of addressing her as "O Avalokitā," he introduces another character. The repetition [of the name] indicates the urgency of the summons. "Do you know where the Blessed Lady is?"—the particle *api* is used here in the sense of a question.

Buddharakṣitā: Buddharakṣitā, have you forgotten? What a long time has passed while the Blessed One was neglecting the time for alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*) to follow after Mālatī! The word *prasmṛtā* is a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) used in the active sense (*kartari*), meaning "she has forgotten" (*vismṛtavatī*). The root *smṛ* with the prefix *pra-* signifies forgetting. The phrase *imam artham* ("this matter") is to be supplied as the object. [*Piṇḍapātavelām*]: *Piṇḍapāta* is the term used by the followers of the Sugata (Buddhists) for a meal; it refers to the time for that meal. *Visṛjya* means having let pass or having neglected. The sense is: immediately after the meal. *Anuvartamānāyāḥ* means attending upon or serving.
*Ko'pi kālaḥ* means a great length of time. The ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*) is "has elapsed."

*Huṃ* is an indeclinable used here as a particle of address. "But where are you going?"—the word *punaḥ* is used for emphasis. The meaning is: having abandoned the companionship of the Blessed Lady, which has never been forsaken before, where have you gone?

The meaning is that since I have indeed been sent by the Blessed Lady to the presence of Mādhava, I am merely carrying out her command. And she instructed him: "Go to the Kusumākarodyāna garden connected to Śaṅkarapura and stay within the dense thicket of red aśoka trees at the edge of the groves and bowers. Mādhava has gone there. In the phrase "tassa," the dative case is replaced by the genitive in Prākṛit according to the rule "caturthyāḥ ṣaṣṭhī" (the sixth [case] is used for the fourth). Śaṅkarapura is the name of a particular sanctuary of Śiva.

*Kusumākarodyānam* refers to the pleasure garden known as Kusumākara. *Kuñjanikuñjaparyantaraktaśokagahane*: a *kuñja* is a bower of creepers; by metaphorical extension (*lakṣaṇayā*), a *nikuñja* refers to the interior of that.
"To give to one prostrate with devotion those [bees] hidden within the hollows of the small huts formed by the folds of flower-buds..."

"Like that" (itivat). "Paryantaḥ" means the vicinity. "Tadgate" refers to the red Aśoka—a specific variety of Aśoka with crimson blossoms—located there; "gahane" means dense, crowded with rows of branches. "Stay," and [the words] "and thus instructed by the Blessed One" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. By saying "he went," since he has spoken of his own desire, it is indicated that he acted immediately.
"Avalokite! For what reason? means: what is the cause for this message and for the journey?

Observing this motive, Avalokitā reveals: "Today is the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight; Mālatī will go to the temple of Śaṅkara together with her friend Ananyā. For it is said that by doing so, one's good fortune increases. With this as a pretext, Mālatī, accompanied by Lavaṅgikā, will be led to that very Kusumākarodyāna garden under the guise of gathering flowers with her own hands; thus, their mutual sight shall come to pass. By the phrase "the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight," it is indicated that because the fourteenth day of the waning moon is a day sacred to spirits (*bhūta*), it serves as a means for the propitiation of the Supreme Lord.

Then, immediately after her departure; "thus indeed" (*evaṃ kila*) means when it has been done in this manner. The particle *kila* indicates tradition (*aitihya*), meaning that this matter is well-known from the Āgamas, Purāṇas, and so forth, as evidenced by the Purāṇic statement: "One's own worship with devotion. Her good fortune (*saubhāgya*) increases—that is, she gains the affection of her beloved—because beauty is the fruit thereof, according to the saying:
"For loveliness bears the fruit of good fortune among those who are dear.
[This follows the rule: *hṛdbhagasindhvante pūrvapadasya*.

(7-3-19) Thus, there is *vṛddhi* in both parts of the compound. The meaning is that although he does not "become" [newly], because he has already been perfected by his very form, character, and so forth, he attains a state of ever-increasing excellence through the grace of the Supreme Lord. By the phrase "by this reason," he describes the manner of his own presentation. He speaks thus because picking flowers with one's own hand—even when there is a multitude of servants—indicates a particular intensity of devotion, as expressed by the rule: *hastādāne cerasteye* ("the affix *ka* is used after a verb meaning 'to take' when it refers to taking with the hand, provided it is not theft").

(3-3-40) Thus, the suffix *ghañ* [is applied]. "Having aimed at" means having made it the object. "That very same" means that which was already presided over by Mādhava, as previously stated. "Will be brought" means will be caused to arrive; this is understood from the context as being "by the Blessed One. "Mutual sight" refers to the seeing of one another between Mālatī and Mādhava. "It happens" means that this is the cause for it. "But where are you setting out?"—the reason for my departure has indeed been explained to you; now let the reason for your own departure also be told—this is the sense.

"I was indeed invited by my dear friend Madayantika, who has set out for Śaṅkarapura itself. Therefore, having performed obeisance at the feet of the Blessed Lady, I shall go there. By the phrase "to Śaṅkarapura itself," her eagerness to see the Lord (Īśvara) on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight is revealed, just as it was in Mālatī's case. Madayantika was previously indicated to be the sister of Nandana. She was "invited" (*āmantritā*), meaning summoned to accompany her; and "having performed obeisance at the feet" is mentioned because the failure to worship those worthy of honor acts as an obstacle to spiritual welfare (*śreyas*).

"Regarding the matter for which you were indeed appointed by the Blessed Lady, what is the news?"—by this it is indicated: "I have indeed appointed my dear friend Buddharakṣitā there. What is meant is the courting of Madayantika for the sake of Makaranda; "what is the news" means "what is the report."

By me also, at the command of the Blessed Lady, during various confidential conversations, such-and-such reports regarding Makaranda were conveyed to my dear friend Madayantika in her absence, so as to elevate her secret passion to such a height that even her desire was: "O, would that I might see him! The repetition in the phrase "in those various [conversations]" indicates frequency. By the mention of "confidential conversations," it is implied that a firm sense of trust has been established between her and herself.

In confidential conversations—those dialogues employed without hesitation due to trust—the summary of his own descriptions of him in the form of elaborate discourse, such as "he is like this" or "he is like that," refers to Makaranda as the object; the meaning is that he was, as stated in the *Kādambarī*, "as if possessed of a hatred for the pleasure of love. [Parokṣānurāga: Love or the bond of affection produced by mere hearing even in the absence of sight—that is, while out of one's view. In what manner?

"Far" means brought to the highest point. "In such a way" (yathā) refers to the manner by which. "Desire" (manoratha) is the thirst of the mind; here, the emergence of the state known as eagerness (*autsukya*) is perceived, thus it is the figure of speech called *bhāvodaya* (the emergence of a state).
"Well done, Buddharakṣitā! Well done!"—this repetition expresses the wonder of her cleverness. "It is done"—this is an ellipsis used out of the force of joy.
"Come, let us go. [The plural number is used for the singular] "self," or it may refer to two people.
Thus ends the introductory scene (*praveśaka*).

Now, following the entry of Kāmandakī—who was previously indicated by the phrase "following after Mālatī" and described as specified—the author states her entrance as a prologue (*pūrvaraṅga*) to the heroine's own entrance with the words, "Then she enters. She marvels at the unfailing efficacy of the principles of the science of love (*kāmaśāstra*) that she herself has practiced, which leads inevitably toward her desired goal, with the word "thus" (*tathā*). The word "thus" refers to her personal experience. Although she is humble through modesty, she is nevertheless characterized by a devotion directed toward her elders.

"May I" expresses her own application to the science [of love]; "Mālatī" indicates that she is difficult to win over due to her exceedingly noble nature. "By means of a stratagem" refers to the performance of the duties of a messenger as prescribed for those who approach another's wife. "In a few days" means within a limited number of days. "The state of being fit for the confidence of friends" means being worthy of cultivation through the trust placed in friends such as Lavaṅgikā and others. As it is said: "Whatever flashes forth in one's own mind, making it known in its entirety to those with whom one is familiar—that disposition is celebrated as 'confidence' (visrambha)."
Thus says Divākara. Here, the poetic figures (alaṃkāra) are Contradiction (virodha) and Illustration (nidarśanā). //1//
Then, through her facial expressions and gestures, he establishes confidence in her with the words "Now indeed" (*saṃprati hi*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "she goes" (*vrajati*): *virahe* means in separation, in the absence [of him]. *Vaicittyam* means a state of despondency in the heart. *Naḥ* (of us) is used in the plural for the singular, referring to himself. *Prasīdati* means she rejoices. *Sannidhau* means in his presence, in his direct sight. *Rahasi* means in a place devoid of other people; the meaning is "with me as her companion. *Ramate* means she finds pleasure; the meaning is that she gains an opportunity to reveal her own heart. *Dāyam* refers to what is given, namely a reward such as clothing, flowers, unguents, camphor, and so forth.

She attends upon him by massaging his limbs and so forth, doing what is pleasing. At the time of departure—that is, at the moment of setting out elsewhere due to some business—she clings to his neck, embracing his neck and not letting go. By repeatedly saying "niṣidhya" (having restrained), she indicates: "You have only just arrived; for what purpose are you departing this very day? Through this repetition (*vīpsā*), her skill in employing numerous methods of dissuasion is revealed.

"Since you must certainly go, [I entreat you] with many means of convincing her, such as oaths: 'I adjure you by my own life, and by my father and mother,' and so forth; [and I request] an immediate return—that is, a return without delay. The phrase "having prostrated" implies that, fearing that the oaths were insufficient, she resorted to grasping his feet, joining her palms in *añjali*, and other such acts. The construction is transitive (*dvikarmaka*) because the root *yāc* (to beg) belongs to the class beginning with *duh*. Here, the specific intention residing in the heroine is revealed through its effect, and thus the figure of speech is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description). And here—
"When he is thus engaged, his disposition should be observed;
seeing it, she speaks with a smile and seats him very close to her."
She asks about his food and bed, speaks to him in private, or meets with him in secret; she sighs or yawns, and gives him some sign from her own heart.
"She says, 'He is going, you will go again,' yet how can she be a speaker of truth?
Having said something inconsistent, she then resorts to that very story.
Having reflected on such manifestations of her character, one should offer a gift.
Thus, it should be understood that the application of the meaning of the *Kāmatantra* has been completed. //2//

Furthermore, he describes her action which manifests its conformity with his own desired object, saying "And this" (*idaṃ ca*). "This" refers to what is about to be said. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate what was previously mentioned. "Therein" (*tatra*) refers to the matter at hand, being ever present in her own heart; it means "with regard to that object. "More firmly" (*sādhīyaḥ*) means more strongly. "The basis for hope" (*pratyāśānibandhanaṃ*) is the cause for the persistence of the desire that she might become favorable even in time. As it is said: "Even when opposition is manifest, that which consists in the inability of men to disregard [a thing], thinking 'this may happen to me in time,' they call that 'hope' (*āśā*)."
Thus says Divākara.

Regarding "the *Śākuntala* and so forth": *Śākuntala* is that which was composed concerning Śakuntalā; the suffix *aṇ* is applied here, and [the term refers to] those works beginning with that. "Itihāsa discourses" refers to the utterances spoken in the *Mahābhārata*. "By means of words" means by means of speech. "With others having different purposes" means by those whose primary intent is directed toward another matter—namely, those devoted to the meritorious stories of Kaṇva and others intended for passing the time. "Introduced" means brought forward through a sequence of related topics, such as: "O Blessed One, how did Śakuntalā become the daughter of Kaṇva, who is eternally celibate? and so on.

The word "herself" (*svayā*) is understood through the force of the context, for otherwise it would give rise to doubt. "Having heard" means having heard from my presence. "With her limbs placed upon my lap" means she whose body was freely laid upon my lap; by this, the state (*bhāva*) called languor (*glāni*), produced by love, is revealed. "For a long time" means for a great duration. "Stupefaction due to anxiety" refers to the immobility resulting from meditation on whether, in this situation, I should treat her like Śakuntalā or not.

By this statement, "My father is indeed my beloved and praiseworthy," the loosening of her previously manifested fortitude is revealed, as well as her entry into the seventh stage of love known as the "shedding of shame. Here, the figure of speech is *sūkṣma* (the subtle), because a subtle meaning, perceived through gestures and facial expressions, is made manifest. //3//

"Today, in the presence of Mādhava"—that is, in the immediate vicinity of Mādhava—because [the words] are heard while remaining invisible. The subsequent response, "Now indeed, an introduction must be made," refers to the task previously indicated that is to be performed immediately. The reading "upakramiṣye" means "I shall begin"; this is because the Ātmanepada ending is prescribed by the rule *propābhyāṃ samarthābhyām* (Pāṇini 1.3.42). By saying "Child! This way, this way," he reveals the departure for Śaṅkara’s hermitage that was previously indicated.

Now, the connection of the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa—which consists of the lover’s longing and separation—is established for the purpose of avoiding faults in the aesthetic sentiment (*rasadoṣa*), since it has been stated that "the non-connection of the principal [sentiment]" and so forth constitute such faults. It should be understood that by avoiding other modes of expression—such as "How have I become a mere offering?"—and instead employing the very mode of speech previously mentioned, the firmness of the rival hero's hatred, the father's doubt, and the hero's passion is manifested through their respective intensities.
For a speaker characterized by states such as sorrow, envy, or joy, the repetition of words already spoken is not a defect; on the contrary, it is indeed a merit.
As it is said: "If that which was previously stated is taken up again without distinction, that is not a fault for those whose minds are captivated by rasa, as it serves a single purpose."
Thus says Bhoja.

This [wind] embraces you—this wind which is delightful with the fragrance of *campaka* flowers, slightly opened and formidable, as they are torn apart by the swarms of restless bees flying up from the tops of mango trees agitated by the clamorous warbling of cuckoos sporting in the act of devouring clusters of most sweet and glistening blossoms; a wind whose cool touch acts like sandalwood upon your lovely moon-like face, which is illuminated by drops of nectar-like sweat brought forth by the movement of your feet as they falter under the weight of thighs made slow by the fullness of a swan’s hips.

The breeze from the Kusumākarodyāna garden! Let us enter it. It carries the fragrance of the Campaka flower—slightly broad and distorted due to its petals being loosened by the friction of a swarm of restless bees that have flown up from the tips of the most fragrant mango trees, agitated by a battle of "first-me, first-me" among the cuckoos distinguished by their sweet, indistinct warbling as they sport in tearing apart flower buds that have been heavily drenched with delicious nectar.

It is made fragrant; by that, it is heart-pleasing. "Marāla" is defined as a symmetrical meter (*samavṛtta*); or else, it is slightly yellowish-red in color. According to the *Vaijayantī*, "marāla is slightly yellowish-red."

The circumference—that is, the width—of his hips and the front part of his waist is even and yellowish-red; by the weight of his thighs, which are slow-moving and unsteady due to bearing that [weight], his feet stumble and rise, and the drops of perspiration accumulated through the exertion of setting them down are like sprays of nectar. His touch, acting like liquid sandalwood paste, cools the delicate moon of his face as it is adorned by those [drops]. Here, the aesthetic state (*bhāva*) known as *lalita* (grace) is manifested: "Grace (*lalita*) is a smooth and delicate movement of the limbs."

From this statement, because the face is metaphorically represented as the moon, it is logically consistent to represent the droplets of sweat as drops of nectar (*sudhā*). By the word *pariṣvajati* ("embraces"), there is a *bandhu-samādhi* (a poetic figure based on a verbal root). Here, the figures of speech are *udātta* (the noble) and *svabhāvokti* (description of nature).

Then, "Mādhava enters"—since his dwelling in the thicket of red *aśoka* trees has been indicated, the meaning is that he enters in that very state. *Hanta* expresses joy. She has arrived (*parāgatā*). He establishes why her arrival is a cause for joy with the words, "For this [is] mine," where the particle *hi* indicates a corroboration.

"Appearing," and so forth. "Appearing" means coming within the range of vision. "First" means at the very beginning. "With a sigh" (sochvāsam) means that the mind, which had been breathless due to the delusion born from the continuous experience of suffering, is now being restored to life; this is the meaning. The statement that it is "with a sigh" is made because the sight of the beloved alone is the cause of complete relief, as the appearance of the Blessed One merely indicates the reunion with the beloved. As it is said: "The mind of Kāma, who was afraid of his previous transgression, has now sighed with relief."

And from the usage: "As if having suddenly heaved a sigh that bore the weight of the pride of the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa) disregarded. The common attribute here belongs both to himself and to the young peacock (*śikhaṇḍiyūna*): being scorched by the heat of separation, afflicted by the fever of the arrows of Love, and tormented by the rays of the sun fierce with summer heat. By the term *śikhaṇḍiyūna*—meaning a young peacock—the fact that [the peacock] is undeserving of such suffering is suggested. *Aciraprabhā* means lightning.

Because the throbbing of that [heart] is indicative of the immediate falling of a stream of water, the simile reveals that the torment can be remedied by no other means, that upon its attainment there is the acquisition of unsurpassed bliss, and that it constitutes a bond of unfeigned love. The poetic figure is Upamā (Simile). //4//

"By good fortune" (*diṣṭyā*) means through the favor of fate. The particle *api* is used for the purpose of drawing in the word "gone away" (*parāgata*) from the preceding context. Then, reflecting upon the highly distinct difference in state between the moments immediately before and after seeing his beloved, he says: "A marvel, [is] the lotus-eyed one," and so forth. Because of the proximity of the stainless moon of her face—wherein the face itself is the spotless moon—the term *sānnidhya* (proximity) refers to its very presence, that is, its being directly perceived. The secondary suffix (*taddhita-pratyaya*) is used here in its own primary sense, as in the case of words like *cāturvarṇya*. This is according to the rule: *pañcamyāstasil*.

(5-3-7) *Muhuḥ* means "from a moment" (*kṣaṇāt*). According to the *Vaijayantī*, "muhuḥ" [is used] in the sense of a moment (*kṣaṇa*) and at every moment (*anukṣaṇa*). *Jaḍimānam* refers to coolness resulting from the cessation of the heat of passion; its meaning is "inertness" (*apratipatti*), which is not appropriate here.
