This is because it is more fitting to establish the alleviation of the very heat previously introduced as being "burnt by the heat," and because fluidity (*dravatva*) is mentioned immediately thereafter. *Jātyena* means "by that which is of pure birth" (*viśuddhasvajātibhava*), that is, free from blemishes and the like, since such [a substance] produces its own effect instantly.

By "moonstone" (*candramaṇi*), meaning the gem known as *candrakānta*; for the *candrakānta* is a specific kind of crystal, as it is stated in the treatises on gems (*ratnaśāstra*) that it is one among the various gems. By the comparison to a mountain (*mahīdhara*), such as Kailāsa or other peaks, it is revealed that even for that which is by nature extremely stable, the occurrence of dullness (*jaḍatva*) and liquefaction (*dravatva*) is established solely through the power of the intrinsic nature of the object being perceived. It is "sustained," meaning it is properly held. "Consisting of fluidity" (*dravamaya*) means having the essential nature of moisture.
"Agitation" (*kṣobha*) is a modification in the form of a particular favorableness that generates the thought, "What can I do to please her?"

"Whatever one knows to be dear to another, performing that very thing quickly— this they call 'fitness' (yogyatā) and 'tenderness' (ārdratā), which destroys the turbidity of the mind," so says Divākara. Or rather, it is simply being under the sway of aesthetic sentiment (rasa).

"Just as [it is said]: 'When they do not exist, there is no melting of the heart, nor the shedding of tears of love, nor the rising of horripilation,'" so too, by the phrase "by my mind," it is meant that this state of supreme bliss is being experienced; thus the sense is: "May we prosper by good fortune. In the case of the moonstone (*candramaṇi*), however, "insensibility" refers to the manifestation of its natural coolness through the subsiding of the heat of the day; "melting" refers to the trickling forth of drops of water. By means of this simile, it is illuminated that in her presence, there is the experience of insensibility and melting, while in her absence, the persistence of distress continues as before. Here, one should understand the subsiding and arising of the two emotional states (*bhāva*) of agitation and joy.
The figure of speech here is *saṅkara* (commixture), because *rūpaka* (metaphor), *upamā* (simile), and *śleṣa* (paronomasia) exist in a relationship of mutual support. //5//

"More delightful than her previous state"—meaning she is even more endowed with beauty than before. The sense is that she is being intensely heated by Hiraṇyaretas, that is, Kandarpa (the god of love), like gold of sixteen-fold purity.
This is in accordance with the statement in the *Śākuntala*: "But the summer has not committed such a beautiful offense against young women."

"Jvalayati" (he inflames), and so forth. Because of the momentary pacification [of passion] through the delight of seeing her, he rekindles the fire of love—which had reached the state of glowing embers—by means of separation, which creates a longing for a firm embrace that has been obstructed. It "intoxicates," meaning it renders even a mind held by fortitude subject to another's power; or else, because that particular state of affairs accords with his own desires, it means it makes him full of pride.

The meaning is that the eye fulfills its purpose by making the object to be seen one whose desires are complete, because it has beheld the extreme sweetness of the object and because seeing alone is the means [to that end]. "By those possessing a grace—that is, a beauty—like that of a *campakāvalī* (a garland of *campaka* flowers) that has been crushed and worn out by contact with the palms of the hands. It should be understood that the mention of the *campakāvalī* is intended to convey the similarity of the complexion and the extreme softness of the loveliness (*lāvaṇya*).
As it is said: "A certain woman, with the luster of blue lotus petals, was as fair as a *campaka* flower."

This is because it is stated as a praise in the *Madanatantra*. The reason for this is: "with limbs such as hands and feet that are disheveled and languid, and rendered unskilled in actions due to the exhaustion of passion. Here, the figure of speech is *dīpaka* (the illuminator), because a single agent in the form of Mālatī is connected with many actions such as "she causes to blaze" and so forth. //6//
"Friend! Friend! Let us gather flowers in this bower of creepers," and so forth.

[With his hair standing on end] by the hearing of the words of his first beloved—that is, by hearing the speech of his own beloved for the first time previously—[he was one] whose horripilation (pulaka), the bristling of the hair, was quivering and emerging. Of the dense mass of clouds—that is, of the cloud-line—at the beginning of the fresh rainy season, by that very first sprinkling of water—that is, by the downpour of rain.

The "splendor" (*ḍambara*)—meaning the intense manifestation or, by figurative extension, the beauty—of the *kadamba* tree, which in an instant has its buds bound [together] on all its limbs; that is, the *nīpa* tree whose every limb is covered with fully developed buds.

According to the *Vaijayantī*: "The word *āḍambara* refers to intensity, a drum, or the trumpeting of an elephant. Here, the poetic ornaments are simile (*upamā*), "correspondence" (*yathāsaṃkhya*), and "illustration" (*nidarśanā*), because the beloved and the others are compared to the mass of clouds and so forth, because of their sequential connection, and because the splendor resembling the [tree's] splendor is conceived as a simile. //7//
"Friend! Let us do so. (The reading is *puṣpāpacāyam*).

Mādhava marvels at Kāmandakī’s strategic maneuver—which consists of bringing Mālatī and gathering flowers with her own hands, and so forth—being in accordance with his own heart's desire: "Of immeasurable wonder," meaning a marvelous application that cannot be fully delimited; "the teacher's role," meaning skill in instructing on the proper means. "Let us gather others from here as well. The phrase "here and there" indicates a gesture toward other locations. By the word "api" (also/even), an excess of zeal is revealed even in the face of difficulty.

Perceiving the fatigue caused by the excessive delicacy [of her body] resulting from the gathering of flowers, he spoke with conciliation: "Having embraced... This means that, having performed the honor of an embrace through the wonder of an excess of devotion in propitiating the deity. "Cease," meaning "desist"; the word "from this activity" is to be supplied as the object. The *parasmaipada* ending is used according to Pāṇini 1.3.83 (*vyāṅparibhyo ramaḥ*). "Unable to endure" means incapable of bearing; as Murāri has stated: "Incapable of enduring the assault of Love for very long periods."

By establishing her very state of helplessness through a parallel descriptive epithet (*tulyaviśeṣaṇa*), she indicates the imminent sight of her beloved by means of the *patākāsthānaka* (the dramatic device of the "banner"), as seen in the passage beginning with "she falters in her speech.
"The indication of a matter currently unfolding through the mention of another thing,
characterized by a parallel arrangement of descriptive epithets, is the *patākāsthānaka*."

Thus, according to the statement of Dhanika: "It causes speech to falter" means it obstructs the flow of words. "Each limb"—meaning each individual part such as the hands and feet—"makes them droop" means it renders them incapable of their own functions. However, if the reading is *saṃśrayati*, the causative sense (*ṇij-artha*) should be understood as "it causes [them] to rest upon one another. "Shining from the moon of the face" refers to those [drops] whose nature is to shine upon the moon that is the face; the mention of the drops being connected to the face is due to the appropriateness of the trickling of drops of nectar from it.

First, because they appear upon the surface of the forehead and the regions of the cheeks; "mukulayati" means it causes them to form buds—by a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the meaning is that they close. "In every way" (*sarvathā*) means in every manner. By the address "O fair-browed one" (*subhru*), he indicates the particular loveliness of her creeper-like eyebrows at that time due to their drooping. "Fatigue" (*kheda*) means exhaustion. "Shines forth" (*vilasati*) means it is perceived with intensity. "Equally" (*tulyam*) means similarly; this is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). "By the sight of her beloved" (*vallabhālokanena*) means by the seeing of her most cherished one.

The compound is formed with the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*), and not with the genitive case in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). For if it were explained thus [as an agentive genitive], it would be illogical for a heroine who is being watched by an invisible hero to experience such things as a faltering of speech. [This is based on the rule: *tulyārthair atulopamābhyāṃ tṛtīyā 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.72).

(2-3-72) Thus, the third case ending [is used]. Here, the figure of speech is *arthaśleṣa* (semantic pun), because a comparison is perceived through the medium of the meaning. Although there is in reality a difference between the stammering of words and other such symptoms produced by exhaustion and those produced by the sight of a beloved, they are identified as non-different through *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole). This should be understood as *vacas*, *hāsya*, and *narman* (jesting), which are constituent parts of the *kaiśikī* style (*vṛtti*), according to the statement: "Jesting (*narman*) consists of playful wit and the act of coaxing a beloved. Furthermore, this jesting is a constituent part of the *mukha* (opening) [of the drama], because it consists of the employment of humorous speech. //8//
"He displays shame" means:
"One should infer the absence of boldness due to shame caused by misconduct and the like from such signs as turning the body aside,
covering the limbs, change of color, looking downward, and so forth."
By this statement, the meaning is that she is enacting gestures such as turning her body sideways (*sācīkṛtāṅgatva*).
"The Blessed Lady’s command is excellent" means it is very well said; "this [act] is indeed quite perspiring" is the sense.
"Heart-captivating" means charming. The intention is that it is a "jest" because of the manner in which her own appearance, which was about to occur during play, is revealed.

"Tad" (therefore)—because distress is manifest in you, therefore; "āsyatām" (please sit down). "Kiñcit" (something) is used because the *Kāmasūtra* states: "When [the woman's] affection has been extended, one should speak thus regarding the remainder of the task. This marks the commencement of speaking about the remainder of the task toward the heroine whose affection has been made manifest by such statements as "she falls into a state of agitation during separation. "Kiñcit" is a general expression;
it should be understood that this is for the purpose of testing whether she, through her knowledge of his heart, will agree with what he intends to say or not.

He shows their conversation with the words "they sit down. By avoiding forms of refusal such as "the propitiation of the deity must now be performed; Mother cannot endure any delay," he indicates her consent. This refers to all of them: Kāmandakī, Mālatī, and Lavaṅgikā.

"The chin" refers to the lower part of the face; "having raised it" means having lifted and caressed it with the hand to dispel her bashful modesty. The words beginning with "Listen" remind one of the *Kāmasūtra* itself. Having ascertained that this does not contradict [the treatise], the manner of stating the matter is: "O fortunate one! This is an encouragement, meaning: "By good fortune you prosper," because she is worthy of being sought after by a husband suited to her. "Wondrous" means marvelous; the sense is that this inconceivable thing has come to pass through fate.

He shows the fruit of encouragement: by saying "I am attentive; I stand here with one-pointed concentration," an excess of respect is revealed. Incidentally, he reminds [the audience] of the context of Avalokitā’s statement, "Mādhava’s body is unwell," and Lavaṅgikā’s question, "Noble lady, who is this Mādhava? [by saying] "It has already been told. This means that his noble lineage and virtues have already been announced; however, his actual existence and so forth need not be explained now. For that which has not yet been heard is what must be explained because of the desire to know it. [The word] *māmakīya* means "belonging to me" (*matsambandhin*).

"Secondness" (*dvitīyatva*) refers first to a bond or fetter, because [the child] is held firmly by being prevented from wandering among other objects. "Second" (*dvitīya*), however, means "other than you. Even though the word "second" is employed, the expression "like you" (*tvam iva*) is used to reveal that there is not even the slightest deficiency [in him]. The grammatical connection is: "The boy indeed exists."

"We remember, but not now" indicates that it is being constantly recollected. When Mālatī gives her attention by saying "I am attentive," Lavaṅgikā’s reply, "We remember," is because she is constrained by bashfulness; thus, the friend, remaining in that state [of bashfulness], speaks in response—this is what the author suggests.

The word *khalu* denotes well-known fact (*prasiddhi*). The meaning is: "It was told by me and understood by you both. *Durmanāyamānaḥ* means "becoming one whose heart is pained"; [this is derived from the rule] *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca*.

(3-1-11) Thus, the suffix *ky-aṅ* is applied. "As if under another's power" (*paravāniva*) means as if dependent on another. "By bodily affliction" (*śarīropatāpena*) refers to the cause, namely a physical fever. Here, by the phrase "being dejected" (*durmanāyamāna*), the existence of mental suffering is stated; and by "by bodily affliction," the existence of physical suffering is stated. He establishes this through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the verse beginning "When the moon... (*yadindau*). [The word] *indau* means in the moon. The word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) is to be supplied.
[The verse continues: "By cold for fire, by thirst for water, and by hunger for food..."

"By others, the state of being a cause of happiness is produced for that which is its opposite"—according to this principle. Suspecting that the moon's quality of bringing pleasure might be non-conclusive due to specific variations in place, time, and circumstance, he says "or" (*vā*) to exclude what was stated previously. He illuminates the fact that its status as a cause of bliss is absolute (*aikāntika*) in the case of a beloved person—that is, one who is the object of intense affection such as Makaranda—by saying "it does not fail" (*na bhajate*), meaning it does not cease to do so. By stating "it does not fail, nor did it ever fail," he demonstrates a distinction from its former state. "Since" (*yat*) means because; "therefore" (*tat*) means for that reason; "it manifests" (*vyanakti*) means it makes clear.
Inner heat refers to mental suffering. "Exceedingly steadfast" means extremely profound.
As it is said: "That man who is able to restrain even abundant sensations through his own intelligence alone, provided he is diligent, is considered steadfast."

Thus says Divākara. The particle *api* is used here in the sense of contradiction (*virodhe*). If it were possible to conceal [the truth], he would indeed have concealed it; rather, by manifesting it through his inability [to do so], he indicates that the state [of his condition] has reached an extreme limit. It is "uneven" (*viṣama*) because it produces various effects such as delusion and the like from moment to moment, and is thus manifold. His "limb-nature" (*aṅgaprakṛti*) is dark and glossy like a *phalinī* creeper, meaning his bodily constitution is naturally dark and lustrous. Here too, *api* is used in the sense of contradiction, because it contradicts the presence of paleness (*āpāṇḍutva*) in him. The particle *ca* (and) is displaced in its position [within the compound].

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "and she bears a body... [The phrase] *āpāṇḍumadhuram* means: *āpāṇḍu*, having become slightly pale in color; *madhuram*, gentle, because it is devoid of arrogance (*auddhatya*); *kṣāmakṣāmam*, having become exceedingly emaciated. Because of the use of the present tense in the word "bears" (*vahati*), there is also a figure of contrast (*vyatireka*) here. By stating the sequence, the fact that the other [the body's state] is caused by the torment of the mind is revealed: "The torment of the mind and the body mutually affect one another through the relationship of support and supported, like a heated vessel and the clarified butter within it."

Thus, in order to dispel the doubt—namely, "Could mental distress not also have fever and the like as its cause, since medical authorities state this?"—he says, "And it becomes delightful. Let it be granted that another [type of] mental distress may indeed have fever as its cause; however, he dispels the further doubt—"Could this [distress] not rather be rooted in the longing to see one's father and so forth? by stating, "And it becomes delightful. For if internal distress were produced by other causes, pallor and similar symptoms would necessarily occur. But this [distress] possesses a stainless radiance that arises moment by moment; therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), he establishes through reasoning that it has exclusively the intoxication of love (*manmathonmāda*) as its cause.

"His eyes are exhausted from wakefulness due to anxiety; though diminished like a great gem polished by its own quality of brilliance, it is not perceived [as such]," as is well known from the *Śākuntala* and other works. Furthermore, regarding the cause consisting of grief born from separation from parents and others, there is: "Tears fall, the mouth becomes parched, the voice is broken, and the complexion turns pale."

Because loveliness is perceived through such *anubhāvas* (consequent emotions) as these, the poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāras*) here are hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), inference (*anumāna*), and parallelism (*tulyayogitā*). //9//

This too was spoken at that moment by Avalokitā, who was urging the Blessed Lady to hurry; it concerns this matter of Mādhava’s ill health. "At that moment" means at the time when the conversation began incidentally. "Urging" means impelling her toward a swift departure. "Spoken" means said. This connects with the statement: "It has been a long time since your ladyship [last saw him]; Mādhava’s body is unwell. Now, she identifies the general state of intoxication caused by love with its specific cause—beginning with the word "yāvat. The word *yāvat* is used here for emphasis.

"Yāvat-tāvat [is used] in the senses of totality, limit, measure, and restriction," according to the *Vaijayantī*. "Manmathonmādaḥ" means the mind's wandering onto a wrong path produced by passion (*kāma*); or there is the reading "unmāthaḥ," which means an arisen agitation. By the restrictive particle "eva" in the phrase "I heard that Mālatī alone was the cause of his passion for love," it is indicated that many speakers are in agreement. "The world follows what has come before; it is not a world of ultimate truth."

According to this principle: having raised the objection that if the speakers are untrustworthy, there is the possibility that [the woman's behavior] was caused by another woman, and thus the restriction [in the verse] would be redundant, he says, "It is mine too. Determination does not arise solely from the conviction of the people who speak; what then?
"It is mine too. The word *api* is used in the sense of conjunction. The meaning is: that very same determination which belongs to those speakers is the very same determination for me as well.

To the question, "Whence does this restriction [of the definition] arise? he introduces the reason preceded by a proposition: "anubhavam" and so forth. Here, by the word *anubhava*, what is intended is the sub-class of experience (*anubhūtitva*) known as immediacy (*aparokṣatva*), which is synonymous with directness (*sākṣāttva*). "The moon-like face" (*vadaneṇduḥ*) means a face that is like the moon; according to the rule: "That which is compared [to something else] is compounded with words such as *vyāghra* when a common property is not expressed."

(2-1-56) Thus ends the compound of comparison (*upamā-samāsa*). "Like milk" (*paya iva*) is used for the sake of conformity with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). "Fixedly" (*niyatam*) and "certainly" (*niścitam*) are adverbs (*kriyā-viśeṣaṇa*). By the gesture (*abhinaya*) that indicates the direct experience of the moon-like face of Mālatī standing before him, there is a reference to its being indescribable. "He attained a fixed experience"—this is the proposition (*pratijñā*). "Of this" refers to Mādhava. "Noble-souled" (*mahātman*): one whose soul—that is, whose mind—is great and unshakable by such and similar objects. "Agitated" (*kṣubhitam*): [a state] characterized by overflowing emotional transformation.

"Tremulous with longing, it has been made to abandon its own steadfastness by great waves and is restless; '... *utkaṇṭhā* and *utkalikā* are synonyms,' and 'a wave (*ūrmi*), a large surge (*kallola*), a towering billow (*ullola*), a cresting wave (*laharī*), and a surge (*utkalikā*) are [synonyms]. "

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*. "Stimite" means previously motionless due to being windless. Here, the figure of speech is *saṅkara* (commixture), because the mind of this great-souled one is described as the prototype (*bimba*)—like the waters of the great ocean when still—and because it is supported by the simile (*upamā*) of the "moon-like face," while "tremulous with longing" (*utkalikā-taralam*) is a punned (*śliṣṭa*) common attribute (*sādhāraṇa-viśeṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the figure of speech is *anumāna* (inference), since there is the presentation of the relationship between the probandum and the probans.

Just as the ocean-king undergoes transformation merely at the sight of the moon, and not from the sight of stars and such, so too did his heart become agitated only upon seeing your face, and not that of any other woman; for no one else possesses the power to cause such agitation. Thus, the unsurpassed nature of the heroine’s face-moon as an excitant (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) is revealed, as well as the hero’s extraordinary fortitude that transcends the world. //10//

"Aho" expresses wonder; the sense is that no one else possesses such cleverness (*vaidagdhī*). According to Amara, "an *upanyāsa* is the opening of speech. The purity of this *upanyāsa*—the opening of the speech intended to request favor for a union with the hero—is its state of being unrefutable by subsequent [objections], due to the removal of defects such as non-establishment (*asiddhatva*). Regarding the attribution of greatness: "That embodied being who has either attained or not attained all things that are to be attained, yet is devoted to the service of others, is called great."

By stating, "Thus, there is an inclination toward accomplishing within ourselves that greatness which has been characterized and which wins over Mālatī’s heart," he causes one to believe that even his own natural qualities are being attributed [to him] by her; through this, his lack of boastfulness and lack of egoism are revealed, owing to his status as a noble hero (*uttamanāyaka*).

The words "or rather" (*athavā*) and "oh! (*aho*) set aside the sense of wonder previously expressed. Regarding the term "in the treatises" (*śāstreṣu*): a *śāstra* is a work that establishes multiple meanings connected to a single purpose. The use of the plural number indicates its manifold variety; the meaning is: in the *Nīti-śāstras* of Bharata, Vātsyāyana, and others. "Finality" (*niṣṭhā*) means an unsurpassed state; the meaning is "the ultimate extraction. "Innate understanding" (*sahajo bodhaḥ*) is the discernment produced by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of merit from previous births, which serves to refine one's "tendency toward the treatises" (*śāstravāsanā*).

*Prāgalbhya* (boldness) is the state of being free from timidity. She is one by whom the *guṇas* (qualities) have been practiced—those qualities described as: "Sweetness, clarity of syllables, logical reasoning, boldness, and relevance to the subject;
these are the five qualities for one who speaks. Her speech (*vāṇī*) is her voice, because the excellence of speaking is produced through association with a praiseworthy mouth.

"Truth, beauty, learning, knowledge, lineage, character, strength, wealth, valor, and eloquent speech—these ten are the sources of social connection," according to the statement of Vyāsa. "Adaptation to time" means following the appropriate opportunity; it is the possession of presence of mind.

"Pratibhā is considered to be wisdom (prajñā) characterized by ever-new flashes of insight"—this *pratibhā* itself is what is meant by *pratibhāna*. The suffix *-lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). The possessive suffix *-matup* indicates a constant connection with that quality. The reading is *caitaḥ*. Here, among the six qualities mentioned, their mutual relationship as benefactor and beneficiary is revealed in pairs by means of three *ca*-conjunctions.

For it is well known that innate awakening, in the absence of mastery of the scriptures, is like the cognition of infants or the mute; even eloquence, when devoid of the excellence of speech, produces only a sense of detachment like the grunting of an old elephant; and even inspired intuition, without regard for the proper time, is useless as it causes the neglect of sowing rice seeds in autumn.

Therefore, it should be understood that the employment of the three *cakāra*s (the particle "and") is due to the two acting together to produce an effect, like fire and wind. These enumerated qualities (*guṇas*) are specific attributes of the self (*ātman*); they are called "wish-fulfilling cows" (*kāmadughāḥ*) because they milk out—that is, they yield—the desired objects for those who employ them. [This is according to the rule: *duhaḥ kabghaśca*.

(3-2-60) Thus, the suffix *kap* and *gha* [are applied]. Regarding "in actions" (*kriyāsu*), which refers to activities that ought to be performed: by this general statement, it is indicated that this rule does not apply solely to the subject at hand—the union with the beloved—but rather that wherever one is engaged in any task, this is universally the means for achieving the goal. Therefore, the intended meaning is: "What can we possibly describe of the Blessed Lady who is distinguished by such a collection of qualities?
Here, because the cleverness residing in the female messenger is revealed through the medium of its cause, there is the figure of speech *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Praise of the Irrelevant). //11//

It has been stated that his mind is agitated; how is this known? To this he says: "Since" (*yataḥ*), meaning from which cause. By that Mādhava, who was trembling—meaning fearing—for his life, that is, for the maintenance of his vital breaths, because of his inability to endure the sensation. [This is according to the rule: *bhītrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ*.

(1-4-25) Thus [the word] "pañcamī" [is used]. "Difficult" (*duṣkara*)—by implication, [difficult] for those separated from their beloveds; the meaning is that even what is impossible to do. "Something" (*kiñcit*) means "anything whatsoever. "Is not not done" (*na na kriyate*) means that everything is indeed done. This is because, according to the rule "two negatives indicate the original sense," the two negatives function as an affirmation. Since it is said "it is not not done," the ellipsis is: "therefore, mental agitation is inferred from the resulting action."

He states what that task is with the words "tathāhi" (for instance): "dhatte" and so forth. "Dhatte" means he holds [it], but not that he sends it; the meaning is that he causes it to remain for a long time. The word "cakṣuḥ" (eye) is used in the singular to indicate its nature as a sense organ (*indriya*). "Mukulini" means abounding in buds, and not merely blossomed; by this, the excellence of its status as an *uddīpana-vibhāva* (an excitant factor) is proclaimed through the state of flowers blooming higher and higher. "Raṇatkokile" means where the cuckoos (*parabhṛta*) are warbling.

Here too, by the use of the present tense, the uninterrupted flow of the warbling of the sweet-voiced cuckoos—whose throats are parched by tasting the new sprouts—is revealed. Through the two adjectives, the beauty produced by the presence of the spring season is manifested. By the term *bālacūte* (on the young mango tree), it is suggested that the mango tree, with its lush, charming, and thick foliage shining forth due to its youthfulness, is difficult to endure at other times as well, let alone at this particular moment. *Bālacūte* signifies the locative case of proximity (*aupaśleṣike'dhikaraṇe*).

Having anticipated that he would travel along this path, she obstructed that very road beforehand—not merely at the time of his arrival—as is indicated by her intense agitation [expressed in the thought]: "Without killing him, do not permit him to move even a single step. *Gātra* refers to the body; she casts it away, mercilessly discarding it like an unbearable burden.

By the word *garbha* (interior/womb), it is suggested that [the breeze] has come having drunk in the fragrance of the *kesara* flowers which contain the scent of *bakula*, yet has not touched them again. By this qualification, it is implied that the breeze belongs to the "Spring-kinsman," the wind from the sandalwood mountain, moving with very slow and gentle motion. Regarding *dāvapremṇā*: according to the *Vaijayantī*, "dava" and "dāva" both mean the fires of a forest or jungle (*vanāraṇyavahnī*).

In the forest fire (*dāva*), there is a love (*prema*) or affection (*sneha*) [for it] on the part of those wishing to die, because of the absence of any other kinsman like it; the meaning is that they are bound to it by that love. "Having only the lotus leaf of the lake as an interval" means that the fresh lotus leaves, recently brought and moist with liquid camphor and sandalwood, which were placed upon them by friends as cooling treatments, served as the only interval—that is, the only obstacle—against their immediate death.

"With a languid form" (*tāmyanmūrtiḥ*) means that his body collapsed due to being afflicted by fever; this indicates stumbling, falling, and so forth as he goes to take refuge (*śrayaṇāya*). "He takes refuge" (*śrayati*) means he approaches. "Many times" (*bahuśaḥ*) means repeatedly. By this, the repeated turning back of Makaranda and the others against their will, their going again, and their returning again are illuminated. "For death" (*mṛtyave*): by the word *mṛtyu*, death (*maraṇa*) is indicated; the meaning is "for the abandonment of life. "Moonbeams" (*candrapādān*) refers to the rays of the moon. The term "for death" is connected to all three clauses.
Here, the poetic figure is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), as in "it bears an eye" and so forth, due to the employment of a specific type of sentence (*vākya-viśeṣa*). //12//
"He performs what is exceedingly difficult" shows the corroboration by his own experience.

"Therefore" (*tat*): for that reason. "Thus" (*evam*) refers back to the manner previously described. "Naturally delicate" (*prakṛtyā sukumāraḥ*): soft by nature. "A youth" (*kumāraḥ*): this expresses the state of being in the bloom of fresh youth. "Once" (*kadācit*): at one time. The sense of "even" (*api*) should be understood here. "In another matter" (*anyatra*): in some other circumstance serving as a cause. "Never before afflicted" (*aparikliṣṭapūrvaḥ*): one who has not previously experienced suffering. The point is that if suffering had been experienced before, it would be endurable due to the force of its latent impressions (*vāsanā*). "Pitiable" (*tapasvī*): an object of compassion. Thus is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*).

"Being thus" means "because [he] is in such a state. "That" (tat) is the correlative of the pronoun "which" (yat). "Now" means at this time. "By this Mādhava"—since the attainment of the goal is certain through the completeness of the means, even death might be experienced or reached by performing reckless acts such as plunging into moonlight in the absence of friends and others; this is "possible," meaning easily accomplished. As for the passage beginning with "by him" and so forth, and likewise that beginning with "thus having set out," one should understand that the *Kāmasūtra* itself has been directly applied in its appropriate place by the lord of poets through his ingenuity.

Regarding the term *janāntika* (aside): because Kāmandakī has avoided being overheard, Mālatī—unaware that Mādhava is concealed and thus listening exactly as she speaks—says: "Friend, for my sake, fearing some misfortune regarding him who is the ornament of the mortal world, I am afraid and do not know what I shall do. "For my sake" means on account of me.

He who was the ornament of the mortal world, being a jewel among men, had become the very adornment of the circle of the human realm by generating an excellence of beauty; "something" (*kimapi*) is not explicitly stated because it is inauspicious, meaning the destruction of his body. Though terrified—that is, with a trembling heart—she thinks, "What shall I do? Having summoned her courage, she wonders whether she should protect him even through a rash act, or, being unsteady due to affection for her father, perish along with him; thus, the meaning is that she does not know which of these two courses she should adopt.
By this statement, he demonstrates compassion toward the subject of the messenger's task.

He says that very thing: having heard her words, Mādhava thinks, "By *diṣṭyā*—by the favor of fate—I have been accepted as an object of compassion. By the word *diṣṭyā*, joy is expressed upon reflecting on the success of the messenger's efforts.

Following this, the master poet proceeds to present one part of the duties of a messenger—which were intended as the "instruction" (*vidheya*) in the words "Now indeed, the instruction must be given," and which were commenced with the thought "I shall begin the reply in Mādhava’s presence"—consisting of the manifestation of mutual passion and so forth, and residing in both parties. Having, through the mouth of Kāmandakī, established the first part as the elixir for Mālatī’s heart, he now begins to reveal the second part, the nectar for Mādhava’s ears, through the mouth of Lavaṅgikā.

"By the words *bhāvadī* and so forth: the Blessed Lady (*bhagavatī*) is described as speaking thus. The word *evam* (thus) refers back to the manner in which she spoke, beginning with "Listen to the wonderful... and so on; that is, in this way. By the term *bhagavatī*, the meaning is: previously, because we did not know Mādhava’s heart and because of our shame before the Blessed Lady, this matter was not disclosed by us. Now, since she herself has reported his condition, we too speak with confidence."

"Our mistress as well—having frequently beheld him, who for a moment adorns the street near our residence—though her passion is made lovely by the intensity of the pangs of love manifested through the beauty of her limbs, which are as charming as the root of a lotus touched by the rays of the sun, yet she causes distress even to her attendants. Regarding the phrase "our mistress as well": you have already described and reported the condition of your own prince.

The particle *api* suggests that our master’s daughter has likewise been experienced by us as not lacking even slightly [in her qualities], and this is being reported. By the word *tasyaiva*—referring to him who is indeed such on account of her—the restrictive particle *eva* implies the meaning: "Congratulations, for you have attained your desired object. By the phrase beginning with *bhavanāsannā*, he connects [the present situation] with the passage beginning with *bhūyo bhūyaḥ savidhanagarīrathyayā* (1.18, p. 45). The compound *tasyānubhūtadarśanā* is formed because the sense is already clear (*gamakatvāt*).

Just as in the verse, "He beheld the world-protectors among men, who had been drawn away from their playful ease like the gods of the celestial chariots," [the face] was somewhat withered by being touched by the rays of the sun; "āladdhi" means touched.
As in: "The sun's rays, turned back by the dense clouds, have touched [it]."

Thus it was said by Setu: "She is beautiful even though her limbs—the lovely parts such as hands and feet—are like the tender, unripened lotus-root or a lotus-fiber, and are illuminated by their own splendor and luster; yet she is distressed by the surge of the pain of the bodiless god (Kāma), that is, the manifestation of the fever of love, or the agitation and turmoil of the heart produced thereby. It has been established previously that the torment of passion can produce beauty. She causes distress—that is, she torments—her attendants, such as her friends and those nearby, out of fear for her own misfortune; this is the underlying sense.

She does not take delight in artistic pastimes such as painting and the like, nor does she attend to diversions such as gambling; by the use of the plural number, her detachment from all such activities without exception is indicated. If so, how is time passed? To this he says: she passes her days with her cheeks resting upon her sprout-like hands, which resemble fading lotuses.

"Acting like a withering lotus"—the meaning is that she was exhausted; "she whose round cheeks were cast down," meaning they were placed there helplessly; "having become thus" is an adverbial phrase qualifying that moment. This is a manifestation of her anxiety. She "passes them somehow," meaning she endures them; the sense is not that, due to a lack of diversion, the moments themselves lengthen and pass by of their own accord.

Moreover, wishing to pass her days with her mind distracted by thoughts of her beloved, she finds that even the intervals between them cannot endure such great distress; thus he says: "She languishes because of the breeze from the edge of the palace garden, which is beautiful with the trickling nectar of full-blown lotuses and carries a multitude of droplets of honey from the blossomed *kunda* and mango trees. *Mākanda* means mango tree; *sandoha* means a multitude or collection. By mentioning "the wind from near the house-grove," the inevitability of its arrival is illuminated.

It is set aside by the expression of discontent through such passages as "by the beautiful abundance of the nectar of blooming lotuses," and so forth. These twelve elements of the *mukha* (opening) are employed to illuminate the seed (*bīja*) and the undertaking (*ārambha*). There is a discrepancy between their enumeration and their detailed description because the specific sequence of actions is not intended to be emphasized.

Furthermore, on that day, there was the joy of mutual glances between him—who, having assumed a form for his own great festival, was like the divine Madana adorning the grove of desire—and her, whose youth had been rendered precious by the persistence of various amorous dalliances and passion; a joy in which curiosity arose from hearts tormented by the intervals of deception during their exchange of looks, while trembling and fear surged forth, and which delighted her friends with limbs slowed by paralysis, accompanied by perspiration, horripilation, and quivering.

It has been attained. In that [attainment], "constant experience" or "renown" is being referred to. By the word *nija* ("one's own"), Madana (the God of Love) is referred to. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the prosperity and splendor of his own festival procession"—there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) suggesting that it is like Kāma himself, who, having abandoned his unpraiseworthy state of bodilessness (*anaṅgatva*), has assumed a physical form. The reason for this is given as: "adorning the grove of Kāma," meaning he embellishes Madana’s garden. The reading is *tassa sea*.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: from that time onward, whatever happiness was attained by this Mādhava and this Mālatī through their mutual gazing—that is, the pleasure obtained by seeing one another.

He describes what kind of happiness it was: it is a state in which the onset of youth—the arrival of adolescence for both—has been rendered highly precious (*mahārghīkṛta*) by the bond of affection consisting of various amorous sports and the attachment of mutual love; it is such that it cannot be purchased even at a price as great as the three worlds, or rather, it has been made worthy of worship by all people. According to the *Vaijayantī*, the term *aghag* signifies "worship" or "reciprocal service."

The moment of deception through the casting of mutual glances—the occasion for avoiding the convergence of one another's gazes; the time of sudden turning away out of shame; and, due to the absence of even that much looking, the agitation arising in the hearts already scorched by her presence, which was then intensified by the burgeoning curiosity to see her; and the paralysis born of that agitation, causing the limbs to become sluggish and motionless as they were individually pervaded by it.

With perspiration, horripilation, and trembling—wherein "trembling" (*utkampa*) refers to an intense shaking of the body—and wherein the circle of her friends is delighted (*ānandita*), exulting at the mutual passion between the two suitable lovers, thinking, "Oh, I am fulfilled!"—the meaning is that it was such as that. From that moment onward, experiencing a transformation of her state that is especially difficult to bear, fierce, and intensified by the unfolding of love, she withers away for a moment like a young lotus-plant that has encountered the rising of the full moon. "She withers, [like] a fresh lotus-leaf in the heat."

"Like that" (itivat). "From then on" means starting from the time of experiencing that pleasure. "With a particularly unbearable unfolding of love" means with an expansion of passion so excessive that it was more than could be endured, due to its surpassing the state of looking through the window, and because it manifested the very essence of its own effects; "fierce and cruel" means unrestrained and harsh; "as if wishing to devour even her life-breaths" is the meaning; "the transformation of her condition" means the ripening of her state, that is to say, the highest pitch.

"She experiences [this] herself" means she consumes it alone because it cannot be shared; "we, however, merely assume the role of witnesses. The phrase "Alas, what misery! suggests the sentiment of compassion (*karuṇarasa*). Through the simile, "like a young lotus-plant at the rising of the full moon," it is illuminated that just as the rising of the full moon, though a source of joy for all people, torments the lotus-plant, so too does the sight of Mādhava [torment her]. The word "young" (*bālā*) reveals her susceptibility to withering. The statement "she withers for a moment" is made because a change in her condition will be described after a short interval.

And likewise, I know that for a mere moment, with the union with her beloved being fashioned within her heart, she becomes cool, as if the earth were being drenched by a heavy downpour of water. The phrase "and likewise" (*tathā ca*) implies that there is something else to be heard similar to this. Alternatively, by stating that she "becomes cool" (*śītalāyate*) just as she was "withering away" (*śuṣyati*), he demonstrates the sudden interchange of these two contradictory states.

She is one for whom the enjoyment of her most beloved lover is being performed—presented by her imagination and held within her heart. By the simile "the earth being drenched by a heavy, full shower of water," it is suggested that just as the earth, parched and weary from the length of the summer heat, becomes cool through a momentary downpour, so too does she, tormented by separation, become refreshed by this union brought about by her imagination. "I know thus" means that I infer this from her particular gestures.

He establishes that very same sign: she who bears a charming lotus-face, beautiful with a crescent-moon forehead made lovely by incessantly breaking drops of perspiration; her cheeks bristling with dense, quivering horripilation, exquisitely adorned by the radiance of rows of pearl-teeth emerging from throbbing lips; her eyes like blue lotuses, slightly uneven, motionless, languid, wide, smooth, fleshy, and half-closed; and her face graced by a continuous stream of tears of bliss welling up from within.

She has manifested the state of maidenhood through the mental perception of her clever companion. Her lower lip—the lip—is quivering due to the intention to kiss; from it emerge the teeth themselves as pearls, jewels, whose rows and lines [are visible]. With its luster and radiance, upon her cheek—which is thick with horripilation (pulaka) like a fringe of eyelashes—it flows and spreads, wherein there is a continuous, unbroken stream of tears of joy. As it is said: "The streams of tears flowed like a torrential downpour; the maiden was indeed overwhelmed."

Thus, from the application of the prefix *sa-*: "slightly uneven" means somewhat askew; "motionless" means steady within its own range; "slow" means either moving according to the sequence described as "moving slowly with pupils flickering in turn," or else unskilled in perceiving objects; "whose pupil (*tārā*) is upturned" refers to that which is turned upward; "smooth" means reddened by passion (*anurāga*); "full" means possessing a thick mass of radiance; and "becoming like a bud" refers to the lily-like eye that is closing. This describes the state [of the eyes].

By these adjectives, the state of joy at the conclusion of sexual union—intensified by shame, wonder, longing, passion, and affection—is revealed. "Charming with a new crescent-moon" refers to the forehead, which is delightful due to the incessantly emerging drops of perspiration; this is a description of the fatigue from lovemaking. The comparison of the face to a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) should be understood as being caused by its paleness from passion (*smara*), for the lexicon states: "A *puṇḍarīka* is a white water-lily."

This indicates that even though her companions—who were clever and capable of perceiving the emotional transformations resulting from the experience of the pleasure of union with their beloveds—were constantly in her immediate presence, they nonetheless knew perfectly well that her conduct remained unbroken. Her maidenhood (*kumārībhāva*), that is, her state as a virgin, was doubted by their minds—that is, suspected of being broken.

"Furthermore"—the meaning is that while the events of the day have thus been related, let the events of the night also be heard. She passes her nights wide awake, wearing a necklace of moonstones from which flows a continuous stream kissed by the mass of the unbridled rays of the moon; her bed consists of young plantain leaves bristling with a spray of droplets from a shower of the essence of sandalwood paste, exceptionally cool and infused with abundant camphor; and she is attended by a throng of female companions who hasten in the service of massaging her and bringing her lotus petals moistened with water.

By the mass—that is, the collection—of the moonbeams, which are unrestrained and unbridled due to the absence of obstructions such as clouds, [her face] is kissed, that is, touched; for this very reason, it has begun to flow, meaning the emission of drops of water has commenced. By this, it is suggested that because she cannot bear the sight of the moon, her friends have placed her in the moonlight and brought back that [moonlight] once it had begun to flow. She is one whose nature it is to wear a necklace of moonstones—a string of beads made of *candrakānta* gems.

Because it is mixed with abundant and copious camphor, the mass (*chaṭā*)—that is, the collection—of sandalwood paste, which is exceptionally cool due to its natural coldness, forms a shower (*āsāra*) or sprinkling; by the droplets (*śīkara*) produced from that, [the bed] is made uneven (*danturita*), meaning its surface is made jagged or irregular. A bed (*śayana*) is prepared—that is, a couch is fashioned—with young, tender plantain leaves. *Saṃvāhana* refers to the massaging of the hands, feet, and other limbs.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), offerings such as bracelets of lotus stalks are included. By whom was she attended with such care—that is, fashioned and prepared by the circle of her friends who were diligently striving with various activities and tasks to determine what might pacify her distress and bring on sleep? She was brought near and applied [to her] with a lotus-leaf fan moistened with water; a "wet cloth" (*jalārdra*) refers to a piece of garment sprinkled with cold water for the purpose of fanning.
As it is said: "Her body did not find relief from the wet-cloth breezes, though they were soft with drops of sandalwood-scented water."

Thus [it is said] in the *Māgha*. "Unnidrā" (awakened), meaning having emerged from sleep; by this it is understood that she has not obtained even a moment's sleep. Since the union through mental construction (*saṅkalpa*)—expressed as "the meeting with the beloved being fashioned by the power of longing"—has already been presented, he now describes the union in a dream, beginning with "kathamapi" and so forth.

Having somehow obtained sleep—with the juice of *piṇḍālaktaka* oozing from her sprout-like feet, with the knot of her lower garment loosened by the broadness of her thighs which acted as a supporting ground for her lips, and with her heart agitated—she suddenly awakens, her downy breasts heaving unevenly with sighs like surging waves from within her chest, while the encircling embrace of her trembling vine-like arms remains pressed upon them. "Somehow" means by the nature of time and through the efforts of her friends.

From her sprout-like feet, which were perspiring and from which [the moisture] was oozing due to being moistened, there issued forth a mass of liquid lac—a specific kind of lac-dye—from which it flowed. (The verb *udvam* is used even when it lacks an object; for instance, in the *Kādambarī*: "as if vomiting the pure stream of the Gaṅgā, like Jahnu," and in the *Kirātārjunīya*: "vomit[ing], he shone on all sides"). The phrase *dharādharāyāmāṇā* is an imitation of the indistinct throbbing produced by love. [The suffixes] *ḍāci*, *vīpsā*, and *śānac* [are employed here].

On one side of her broad and fleshy hip-region, which acted as a support for the earth—meaning not at the navel region, which is its proper place—the binding of the lower garment (nīvībandhana), that is, the knotting of the cloth, had become loosened and thus altered from its former state due to its slackness.

With a heart agitated by intense passion, trembling with joy, or stirred by the force of sexual union; breathing unevenly—high and low—with surging breaths that rose one after another; quivering; and with her arms—thick and downy with horripilation—wrapped around and encircled upon her breasts which were trembling from the fear of their first bold act or from the physical transformation caused by the pleasure of her lover’s embrace.
By means of the adverbial expression, it is understood that the awakening of one whose thirst remains unquenched occurs while still immersed in the pleasure of mutual embrace;
as it has been said: "O blue-throated one, where are you going?"—thus she spoke with indistinct words, her arms still entwined around his neck.

By the phrase "she awakens instantly," the sudden breaking of sleep due to the force of restlessness is revealed. He states that such an awakening is the cause of terrible suffering in the verse beginning with *paḍivoha* (awakening).

At the moment of awakening, her eyes—half-closed in a faint born from the realization that her empty bed was deserted by the sidelong glances cast during the hours of consciousness—suddenly regain the hope of life through long sighs emitted at the very instant her swoon is broken by the anxious inquiries of her friends; thus she brings her circle of companions, who were previously bewildered as to what should be done, into a state where their only activity is to reproach the uncontrollable and wicked play of fate, for they had first prayed for the end of her own life.

At the time of awakening, by means of a sidelong glance—a look sent forth or dispatched toward Priyadarśanā (as implied by the context)—she understood from the empty bed that, according to the maxim "prohibitions and injunctions involving a qualified subject apply to the qualification," the bed was devoid of her beloved; thus she realized the bed was empty of her lover. Due to delusion—that is, fainting—the mind, along with the senses, was dissolved because of the impact of grief; thus she had closed eyes, meaning her eyes were becoming like buds.

Therefore, by the efforts of her friends—who were agitated with haste and distracted by their affection for her—consisting of sprinkling cold water, fanning, massaging, and so forth, she attained the cessation or subsiding of her fainting fit; at that time, she was one whose hope or confidence in sustaining her own life—that is, in maintaining her vital breaths—was produced or generated by the long sighs that issued forth in a continuous stream. [The phrase "of the friends" is understood.]

Because the previously arisen delusion of death, caused by his lack of movement, had not yet been dispelled by the sign of life—the exhalation of breath—he was rendered helpless by indecision, wondering, "What should we do? He was one who had previously prayed for, or desired, the separation from his own life before the collapse of Mālatī’s life, for the purpose of avoiding the sight of such unbearable suffering.

The reason for this is as follows: "durvārasya" means of that which is difficult to ward off; "daivadurvilasitasya" means of the wicked conduct performed by Fate (the Creator); "upālambhaḥ" means reproach or censure; and "tanmātravyāpāraḥ" means one whose sole activity or effort consists of that [reproach] alone. The underlying sense is: "May we not even become mere witnesses to such an event," since it is unavoidable and certain to occur.

Now, under the guise of a terrifying threat, she urges Mālatī to act with immediate daring: "Behold, O Blessed One! How long can the skillful termination of this Love-god’s cruel manifestation last, directed toward these limbs so exceedingly delicate in their construction and abounding in loveliness? By saying "Behold," she indicates that you yourself must investigate; by saying "this burden belongs to you alone," she highlights her own role. By using the word "these" (*eṣu*) with a gesture, she expresses their pitiable state. The reason for this is given: "in these limbs... exceedingly delicate in their construction and abounding in loveliness."

Because it was fashioned by a creation consisting predominantly of *lāvaṇya* (beauty), having mixed only a trace of other elements and taken up mostly *tejas* (light/heat) from all sides, the sense is that the solidity of the earth-element and the strength of the wind-element are minimal.
As it is said: "That which consists mostly of *tejas*, softened by abundant water, and which produces delight for the eyes, is called *lāvaṇya*."

Thus says Divākara: "In a manner that is harsh (*dāruṇa*) and even more cruel (*krūra-tara*). [The word] *vijṛmbhitasya* means "of one who has manifested," that is, one who has become prominent through the disclosure of the fullness of his own activity. By the mutual contradiction between "frivolity" (*paripelavatva*) and "harshness" (*dāruṇatva*), the ease with which danger may arise is suggested. "For how long?"—the remainder of the sense is "for what measure of a long time. Alternatively, since the word *cira* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the meaning is "after how much time" (*kiyatā cireṇa*). The inclusion of the word *kiyat* is due to the fact that the pair *cira* (long) and *acira* (short) require a correlative for their meaning.

"Having a virtuous conclusion" means the state of that whose end, result, or transformation is auspicious and virtuous through mutual union. Now, he describes the irresistible power of passion (*madana*) because it is inflamed by the specific qualities of the season and the night: "And how are these faces of the night, where the veil of darkness has been violently shattered by the intense moonlight of the pure, overflowing moon—[a light] as soft as the cheeks of a Kerala woman blossoming with the flush of anger during a lovers' quarrel in amorous play?"

The expressions "these" and "these here" indicate the modest gesture [of the women] because spring is currently present. The "sportive quarrel" (*kelikalaha*) is a battle consisting of play with beloveds, rooted in such things as calling each other by the wrong name; the "passion of anger" (*kopoparāga*) arising from that is the intoxication of wrath, and from that, being "sprouted" (*pallavita*)—meaning having put forth new shoots—the quality of redness is indicated.

The moonlight, reddened by the flush of dawn, is eclipsed by the Kerala women of noble lineage—women of golden complexion—whose cheeks, pale with passion, are adorned by the glow of anger; for they attain an unbroken resemblance to it. And it will be said: "By the leaves as pale as the cheeks of the Keralan brides, hardened by intense longing" (Raghuvamśa 19.46).

Thus: "Soft as the cheek of a Kerala woman" means tender and beautiful; "overflowing" means existing beyond its bounds—that is, it is all-pervading. "Whose veils of darkness have been violently shattered" refers to those whose concealment in the form of gloom has been unrestrainedly destroyed by the moonlight of the stainless, clear moon due to the departure of the snow (winter). "The faces of the nights" refers to the beginnings of the nights.

"How is it that they do not act for the sake of my dear friend?"—here, the connection is made with the modified gender found in the subsequent sentence. In this context, the resolution (*samādhi*) is to be understood as the heroine’s state when her blue veil has been suddenly removed by the hero’s friend.

O dear friend, these transitions of night—bright with moonlight as white as a mass of overflowing, thickened milk, washing the vault of heaven and mingling with the dense, surging fragrance emanating from the *pāṭala* and *bakula* trees; and with the ten directions’ faces turned greyish-white by the soft Malaya breeze, which seems to grow more substantial through the convergence of all those scents—these become the bringers of misfortune.

The flood or current of the mass of milk—that is, the ocean of milk—which is "ullasita" (exultant) or agitated by the rising of the moon; and [the sky] which has been washed or bathed by the intensely white and brilliant moonlight. Because it has completely abandoned its own blackness and assumed a white color, there is a *śūnyotprekṣā* (a poetic fancy devoid of a verbal indicator), suggesting that it is as if it has been bathed. In the phrase "in that courtyard of the sky" (*abhoṅkaṇe*), the contraction of the "courtyard"—that is, the expanse—of the sky is expressed.

The vastness of that which is rubbed together, gathered, and relied upon is being elucidated. The mention of the *pāṭala* flower is used because it blooms even in spring, apart from the summer season.

Or rather, the faces of the ten directions have been rendered greyish—thickly dusted with the pollen of flowers—by the Malaya breeze, which is smooth and gentle, and which acts as if it possesses a fleshy body through its entire, complete, and dense union with the mass of fragrance issuing from the Bakula trees, those Pāṭala-colored Keśara blossoms that are full of sweetness.

In which [conditions] do those things that cause harm—namely, the causes of calamities such as the loss of life—not occur? "The transformations of the night" refers to the ripenings of the nights in the form of their third watch. The mention of the "transformation of the face" (or the end of the night) reveals that: first, because of the efforts of her companions and the coolness of the time, she obtains some sleep during the first watch when her restlessness is increasing; second, because it becomes unbearable in the second watch, she wakes up suddenly thereafter; and finally, in the third watch, her condition surges once more.
By saying, "How can they not become doers of harm? she indicates a request that a remedy be considered immediately.

Then Kāmandakī, having heard the account of those events, confirms the firmness of his bond of passion through a clever turn of phrase, beginning with "If" (*yadi*). The word "if" is spoken while acting out the pretense of not having previously known [the situation]. Its object is Mādhava, upon whom [Makaranda's] affection has been directed. "Bond of passion" (*anurāgabandha*) means a bond consisting of passion—that is, a fetter—or else it is the "bonding" of passion, its strengthening.
[As it is said: "One regards that which is to be experienced as consisting of pleasure and pain as being of the nature of pleasure."
"That by which passion (rāga) arises is called such because of the coloring of both the object and the self;
passion that persists without interruption is declared to be attachment (anurāga)."

Thus ends the *Bhāvaprakāśa*. "Clearly" means with certainty. "Fruit" means the purpose. "Knowledge of qualities" (*guṇajñatā*) refers to the specific knowledge of an individual distinguished by qualities such as lineage, physical form, character, sweetness, and skill in the arts. "This" refers to that which consists of the bond of passion directed toward him. The particle "hi" indicates what is well-known; the meaning is that this matter is agreed upon by all the world. Otherwise, how could it be consistent to say that one knows someone distinguished by qualities yet feels passion for another? This is the sense in which the wise cast [this view] into the category of madness.

"By this reason," it is said; "rejoiced" means delighted. By the use of the word "api" (even), she implies that since even her own father-like [relative] was not welcomed by her, there should be no suspicion regarding her father and others, because partiality toward virtue is praiseworthy for all people. "It is rent asunder" means it is split apart. The reason for the word "dāruṇayā" (by the cruel one) is that it cannot endure any further delay, meaning it gives rise to the apprehension of calamity. "My heart" reveals that it is bound by sincere affection.

In this verse, the poetic ornament (*alaṃkāra*) in the first half is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), while in the second half it is the conjunction of emotions (*bhāvasaṃdhi*). This is because there is a conceptualization based on the word *yadi* (if), and because the two emotions—joy and impetuosity—are presented as existing in a state of rivalry with one another. //13//

"At the proper place" means at the appropriate occasion; the sense is that the intention he wished to know has been understood in its entirety. "Hi" is used for emphasis, meaning "only at the proper place. "Ullāsa" means joy. It should be understood that this is an expression of joy alone, because joy is a *sāttvika* emotion, whereas agitation (*āvega*) is merely simulated. However, if the reading is *hṛllāsa*, it refers to a specific heart ailment; as it is said: "Hṛllāsa is a distress of the heart accompanied by excessive salivation."

Because this is defined thus in medical science (*vaidyaka*), here, however, by means of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), "heart-sorrow" is expressed, as it is said that "the heart is being torn asunder. Now, hearing of that condition and being struck with fear, suspecting some misfortune, he says: "Alas! (*aho*). This expresses astonishment because it was not anticipated. By his own state, which has now come within the range of his experience, he previously imagined it to be extremely terrible; now, reflecting upon how even more terrible than that this condition is, he manifests a sense of wonder, thinking: "How has this matter, so unthought of, been brought down by fate? Negligence (*pramāda*) is an evil that ought to be avoided through careful attention.

He establishes the very nature of negligence with the words beginning "prakṛtilalitam" and so forth. "Prakṛtyā" means by its own nature, and not by the arrangement of dress; "lalitam" means beautiful. "Etat" (this) is a demonstrative gesture toward the experience before one's eyes. "Saukumāryaikasāram" means that for which tenderness alone is the essence—essence being either strength or the stable constituent part. It is like the bark of bamboos or the fragrance of sandalwood trees, since they are called "tvaksāra" (having bark as their essence) and "gandhasāra" (having fragrance as their essence).

"This" (*ayam*) is a gesture indicating that he is being experienced as constantly present nearby, like an arrow with its feathers fixed. "Truly" (*satyam*) expresses the absence of doubt because it is established by direct experience. "Having a beautiful moon as his crest-ornament" (*cārucandrāvataṃsaḥ*): one whose ear-ornament (*avataṃsaḥ*), consisting of jasmine clusters and the like, is a beautiful and serene moon. By the word "this," there is a reference to Spring (*vasanta*) because of its current presence. Through the two particles *api*, cruelty is conjoined.

"This five-arrowed one (Kāma) is cruel, and this season (Spring) is also cruel"—from such a reflection within her own heart, she thinks: "This body is naturally graceful and its sole essence is tenderness, yet these two are cruel;

therefore, because of the extreme disparity between the tender and the cruel, what manner of thing will come to pass? This is the implied meaning. Here, the emotion (*bhāva*) called anxiety (*cintā*) is manifested, and the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is the Incongruous (*viṣama*). //14//
Furthermore, let something else known be understood by the Blessed Lady; let some other matter besides what has been mentioned be known by the Blessed Lady.
[The suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied here] according to the rule: *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.188).

The genitive case in *kta* is used in the sense of the agent according to Pāṇini 2.3.67 (*ktasya ca vartamāne*). This picture-board is adorned with a portrait of Mādhava. By saying "this" (*etad*), it is revealed that he was always held in her own hand. The intention is that by removing the cloth from her breast, she reveals the Bakula garland—which had been hidden out of modesty—and thereby brings about the sovereign joy of Mādhava’s eyes through the sight of her budding breasts.

"This too was fashioned by his own hand"—thus [she speaks of] the bakula garland hanging from her neck, which is the very life-restorer for her dear friend. "Life-restorer" (*sañjīvanam*) means the means for sustaining life. She states the result of the removal of the cloth from her breast with the word "longingly" (*saspṛham*): "Oh, how blessed she is! Such is the ripening of our merit!"—the meaning is that she herself feels a sense of longing toward that person's birth.

"Victory," and so forth. Here, "in this world," and not merely in this particular place; "conquered" means standing having overcome everything—this is the past participle used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve niṣṭhā*). Of this Mālatī. "A friend" (*sakhī*), and not "a daughter" (*vatsā*); for the status of a friend is even more significant than that of a daughter. This expresses a request: "Since she is the ground of your confidence, you should remind this person [of her] at the proper time. "Beloved" means most desired. Therefore, the meaning is: "You have become one whose birth is fruitful."

Otherwise, because of the use of the word "asi" (you are), there would be the undesirable consequence of the word "jātā" (born) being redundant. He establishes her status as a beloved (*vallabhā*) as follows: "ripened" means somewhat withered; "lotus-stalk" refers to the stalk of a lotus-fiber (*mṛṇāla*); and "like that" refers to the breasts, which have a pale-white color at their tips, are charming, and are not yet mature due to being newly sprouted. The mention of a "ripened lotus-stalk" is intended to reveal the reddish-brown beauty of the breasts—which have the color of *campaka* petals—by showing that the paleness caused by love (*smarapāṇḍima*), though present, is not yet distinct.
"With her foremost fingers, pale and radiant like firm stalks of lotus fiber, she first reveals the foot of Viṣṇu as a reflection."

Because it has been so stated. "Pariṇāha" means width; its "vilāsa" is its splendor. For that purpose, the Vaijayantī [banner]—the flag and banner raised by the conquest of the three worlds—having become [that], is the sense. Here, since it is impossible to address an insentient object as if it were sentient, even though the literal meaning (vācya) is unattainable, there is a perception of superimposition (āropa) through the intended sense (tātparya). Thus, by way of contrast (vaidharmyeṇa), this is the figure of speech Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description). Furthermore, because the subject at hand (prastuta)—namely, "we have not been conquered"—is perceived through contrast, there is also an inference (anumāna).

In the phrase "vaijayantī," there is a metaphor (*rūpaka*) due to the indication of the goal and the means. From the passage beginning with "Then, let us sit; something must be told" up to the end of "the banner of amorous sport" (*vilāsavaijayantī*), there is a progressive unfolding (*pragama*) because of the successive narration.

Now, having thus manifested their mutual passion through the mouth of the messenger, [the author] introduces a calamity in the form of an attack by a tiger as a stratagem for the two protagonists to see one another—specifically, as a means for the banner-hero Makaranda to behold Madayantika.

Since it is certain that affection for a hero will become firm through gratitude even in one who was rescued by him at the risk of her own life and is already enamored of his virtues, the story of Śārdūlaka is now told to strengthen the bond of love between Madayantikā and Makaranda. The story of the Kāpālika will be told regarding Mālatī and Mādhava. Thus, for those two who have mutually accepted each other, their union occurs through the mediation of a messenger; and that—

"According to the words of Vātsyāyana: 'In the case of visiting deities, on a journey, going to a garden, at play, descending into water, at a wedding, at a sacrifice, during calamities or festivals, in the event of a fire, during a disturbance caused by thieves, when the people are mobilized for a military expedition, or at a spectacle—at these various activities,' so says the school of Bābhravya.

*Kalakala* means a tumultuous noise; it refers to a great sound from many people whose individual distinctions are not discerned. "They listen" (*ākarṇayanti*) means they turn their ears toward that [sound] from all sides; it means they hear it with focused attention. [This is according to the rule: "After a nominal stem, [the suffix *ṇic* is added] in the sense of the verbal root's meaning."
(ga. Thus ends the section on the causative suffix *ṇic* //15//

"Are! Are! and so forth. "O people dwelling in the city of Śaṅkara! This one, indeed—his bodily form formidable and terrifying due to the uneven banner-tassels of his beloved’s high tail which quivers with playful grace; having burst through the iron cage by the force of an unbearable outburst of indignation and rage intensified by the onset of youth; and now standing amidst the limbs of many living beings being greedily devoured at that very moment after emerging from the monastery—"

His cavernous mouth was made formidable by sharp fangs that acted like saws, creaking with a harsh *kaṭakaṭā* sound as they gnawed through cruel pieces of bone; the interior of his throat-cavern was filled with the marrow of many horses violently crushed by the force of his manifest, gaping, and fierce slaps, while the expanse of the sky was filled with a continuous roar of deep gurgling and the resounding *ralliṅgallaraṇa* sounds arising from within him, which terrified and caused the entire multitude of people to flee and scatter.

"The wicked tiger—whose path of movement is mired in the mud of blood from the bodies of creatures hurriedly dragged mercilessly by his claws, which are like hard, jagged vajra-stones—is acting out the sport of Death (Kṛtānta). Therefore, protect your own lives to the best of your ability! *Are are* is an indeclinable used to call someone toward oneself; through its repetition (*vīpsā*), urgency is expressed. *Janapadāḥ* means people. According to the *Vaijayantī*, "janapada" refers to both a country and the people thereof.

Having previously been confined in a cage even during childhood, he is now at the onset of youth; full of unbearable indignation and unable to endure the constraints of captivity, the wrath he feels toward those who restrain him—a fury born of the desire to strike—is such that it results in compulsion and impetuous action. The sense is that when one who is naturally strong becomes angry, his strength is doubled:
"For generally, a person attains his own greatness through anger."

Thus, according to the statement in the *Śākuntala*: "By that [act], the iron cage—the metal binding-mechanism—having its joints disarticulated and loosened, and for that very reason having its parts broken off on its own, was 'saṅgalitaḥ' (emerged) by means of 'pratibhaṅga' (the breaking apart), that is, by the crushing of each limb, and thus emerged without obstruction."

By means of his playful grace—the movement employed for sport—his tail, which was tossing upward, moving, most beloved, lofty, and naturally elevated, served as a vast and formidable banner-cloth (*vaijayantikā*). Because it was visible from afar due to its flickering height, his bodily configuration (*śarīrasanniveśa*)—the arrangement of his body—was uneven, characterized by depressions and elevations, and terrifyingly majestic (*ḍāmara*).

From the *maṭha*, that is, from the dwelling place of students and others situated near a temple, or from the location where [the bird] was kept in a cage. Amara states: "A *maṭha* is the abode of students and others."

Having stepped forward and leaped up, at that very moment—immediately upon his departure—he greedily devoured, as he had long desired, numerous embodied beings; and as he chewed and crushed their bodily parts, such as the head and other limbs, along with the cruel, hard bones situated within them, such as skulls and the like, there arose the sound *yaṣṭaṅkāraḥ*, an imitation of the sound produced by the crushing of hard substances.

As stated in the *Mahāvīracarita*: "The sound of the *ṭaṅkāra* [crackling noise] produced by the effort to break the staff-like bow of Candraśekhara, which was bent by his staff-like arms, is the drum signaling the beginning of the noble youth’s deeds. By this, they are making the sound *kaṭakaṭa* due to their mutual clashing, as in:
"Having pressed hand against hand and ground one's teeth with a *kaṭakaṭa* sound..."

Thus it is stated in the *Rāmāyaṇa*. Like a saw (*karapatra*), his mountain cave—the form of his mouth—is made formidable and distorted by large, jagged fangs and teeth. Through a manifest, clear, and wide-yawning gape—extremely fierce and cruel—he forcibly strikes with the palm of his hand (*capeṭa*), which, when not [in use], has its claws retracted into its sheath due to the contraction of his hands and feet. As it is said: "The words *capeṭa*, *pratala*, and *prahasta* refer to a hand with fingers spread out."

Thus says Amara. By means of the *avagāra*—that is, the eating—of the *jāṅgala* meat of many slaughtered horses (*turaṅga*, *aśva*). The form is derived from the root *gṛ* (to swallow) with the prefix *ava* and the suffix *ghañ*; [as per the rule] "ādavāpayoḥ."

(The vowel *o* [is used] according to Prākṛtaprakāśa 4.110. "Filled" means completely filled. In the hollow of the throat-cavity (*galaguhāgarbhe*), that is, within the cavity of the throat-pit, there is a roaring (*garjitam*) caused by the excess of joy in tigers and other beasts; this is the sound-complex of *ralli-gallūraṇa*, characterized by a deep, weighty, faltering, and surging resonance. This is a regional (*deśī*) word. "Complex" (*sandarbhaḥ*) means a weaving together (*grathanam*), in the sense of a continuous succession occurring one after another. By this, the portion of space (*nabhobhāgaḥ*) is filled.

The meaning is that the multitudes of people were terrified and frightened, and for that very reason they perished, having been driven out of sight and hidden within vine-bowers and the like; they were scattered to the ends of the earth and fled in all directions by him. [This was done] by means of "thunderbolt-like claws"—that is, by means of claws consisting of hard, bowl-shaped fragments—following behind those who had been mercilessly dragged away (this is the implied sense). Alternatively, there is the reading *ṇahakaḍamba*, which means "by a multitude of claws. *Urappha* is a regional (deśī) designation for a thunderbolt (*vajra*).

The path of movement of the creatures rushing to enter the city in haste, their bodies bent forward as they ran, was made muddy with blood that splashed upward from the dragging of one body-part over another, causing them to fall face-down; by the term "path of movement" (gatipatha), it is implied that the path is precisely where they go.

Although the meaning is already conveyed by the word *śārdūla* (tiger), the use of the word *duṣṭa* (wicked) is not faulty because it expresses the speech of frightened people. "The very sport (*līlā*) of Kṛtānta" means the playful activity of Yama; he performs that [sport], which signifies his intense zeal for the destruction of all living beings.

And here, one should not suspect redundancy in the phrases "having swallowed many [elephants]," "having crushed many horses," "having terrified, destroyed, and put to flight [the enemy]," and "having mercilessly dragged the bodies of people fleeing from the camp. For although the result is the same in each case, the presentation of the different modes of destruction produces aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*); thus, the Furious Sentiment (*raudrarasa*) is suggested (*dhvanyate*). Furthermore, the *ārabhaṭī* style of composition should be recognized here, as it is in other similar instances. As it is said: "The *ārabhaṭī* style, moreover, is employed in the Furious Sentiment and in the Odious (*bībhatsa*)."

Because of this statement, you must protect [it]. "According to your ability" means without exceeding each person's own capacity; that is to say, by such means as entering inner sanctuaries, climbing trees, or running long distances.
