By this, the external manifestation of fear (*bhayānubhāva*) is revealed through her prior sight of the tiger and her subsequent anxiety regarding her own destruction. The phrases "as if infused with nectar" and "as if immersed in a pool of nectar" illuminate how the pain of the wound was pacified by the mere touch of that [hand]. The grammatical construction is: "That she embraced—that is, that she clung to—disturbs my mind. //8//

She consoles her with a logical justification: "Buddharakṣitā is your dear friend. By the name "Buddharakṣitā," her status as a ground of Madayantika’s own confidence is understood; by the term "dear friend" (*priyasakhī*), Madayantika’s trust in her is likewise recognized. Therefore, she is not difficult to obtain. He states that there is yet another justification as well, beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*).

"Having crushed the flesh-eater"—that is, having killed him. "The flesh-eater" is a statement emphasizing his cruelty. "At the time of death," meaning at the moment of relinquishing life; this indicates the greatness of the favor rendered. "Embrace" means a hug. "Of you"—this reveals your supreme excellence. "Elsewhere," that is, with another person. "How indeed might she take delight?"—in what manner might she sport? This connects to the previous sentence: "Buddharakṣitā’s dear friend."

Since "being the dear friend of Buddharakṣitā" is one reason for her accessibility, "having been given life by you" is another, and "having obtained your touch, which is like nectar," is yet another—these three reasons serve as inferential marks (*anumāpaka*) for her accessibility. He states that for this accessibility, there is not only inference, but also direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is the foremost among the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, "just as [there is] inference, so too" refers to the operation of the eyes, the manner of gazing; "manifest affection" means clear affection.

"Stimitaramaṇīyaḥ" means beautiful through being "stimita," that is, fixed motionlessly upon you; it was "tarangita" by waves of gestures such as languid glances and the like. It was not for a moment, but for a long time—"it was so"—he says this to indicate that it was seen by us beyond all doubt. Here, a state of mind (*bhāva*) directed toward a friend is revealed. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is inference (*anumāna*). //9//

"Pārāsindhusambheda" refers to the confluence of the two great rivers named Pārā and Sindhu. "Having bathed" (avagāhya) means for the purpose of refreshing us, who are exhausted by the wounds inflicted by the tiger, and for the purpose of performing the sun-worship (sūryopasthāna). By saying "the city itself," he dispels the suspicion that they might be going elsewhere.
"Walking around" (parikrāmataḥ) means enacting the act of proceeding toward that [city].

Regarding the phrase "this is that" (*ayamasau asau*), he explains the meaning of the word *tat*: by virtue of its association with *idam* (this), the meaning is "that which was previously introduced is this. Because of the purifying nature of two great rivers and because they flow as far as the ocean, [the text refers to] two great rivers, Pārā and Sindhu. *Vyatikara* means their confluence.

He says that this [river] is enjoyed by young women who are eager for water-sports to alleviate the heat of midday: "This one whose... and so forth. Those women whose deep (nibhna) and profound (gambhīra) places, such as the hollows of the navel, and whose elevated (unnata) and lofty places, such as the hips, are clearly seen and distinctly visible through their garments—which, though soaked with water, are tight against the body and, by implication, transparent—and whose banks are surrounded, meaning whose shores are reached on all sides.

"By those who had just arisen from their bath" (*snātamātrotthitābhiḥ*) means by those who had just emerged from the water at the very moment they had finished bathing; this implies that because their garments had not yet been wrung out, their clothes remained saturated with water.

Regarding the fruit of the bath—the alleviation of heat—it says: "In their breasts, which were beautiful and possessed a magnificent expanse and height like golden jars (*kanakakumbha*)—those gold pitchers which are faultless due to being fashioned by skillful artisans—they placed their hands in the form of a *svastika*, meaning their hands were bound together in the shape of a *svastika* crosswise."

The meaning is: by means of women (*vadhūbhiḥ*)—as Amara states, "A woman is called *yoṣā*, *sīmantinī*, or *vadhū*"; they have formed the *svastika* gesture with their hands for the purpose of warding off the excessive coldness of the touch of the very cool waves of the wind due to their moist bodies. The syntactical connection is: "This is that confluence of two great rivers whose banks are completely surrounded. Here, the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state). Thus [ends] the entirely auspicious [section]. 10.
Thus, by the grace of Pūrṇajyotis, Pūrṇasarasvatī has composed this exposition of the meaning of the fourth act of the *Mālatīmādhava*.
Thus ends the fourth act.

Now begins the fifth act. Next, in order to introduce the subsequent act by indicating the portions of the story already occurred and those yet to happen, he commences the *viṣkambha* (interlude). By means of "ākāśayāna"—that is, the mimetic representation of traveling through the sky—she appears with a "terrifying and radiant costume" (*bhīṣaṇojjvalaveṣā*). It is terrifying because it is distinguished by such items as a trident and a skull-bowl; it is radiant and glowing because of the combination of her mass of tawny matted hair, golden bells, and other ornaments; such is the arrangement of her attire and decoration.

In the first act, the character Kapālakuṇḍalā—a female Kāpālika who is a disciple of Aghoraghaṇṭa—is indicated by the passage beginning with "That one, indeed, who has come from Śrīparvata" and ending with "arrives at every twilight. This refers to the Prakarī character.

In accordance with the Soma-siddhānta which he himself has accepted, he refers to the Supreme Lord, who is the object of his own experience, as the Self—beginning with the words "six plus ten," etc. [The Self situated in the center of the wheel of sixteen channels: He is one whose Self—the reality whose nature is radiant vibration—is eternally present within the pericarp-like centers (karṇikā) in the midst of the wheels of channels characterized by the number sixteen (six added to ten). Here, by the word "channel" (nāḍī), the central channel of the body known as Suṣumṇā or Brahmanāḍī is intended;
its specific joints are the wheels (cakras) and supports (ādhāras).

And thus they are described in the Āgamas. Those wheels are enumerated in the Āgamas as sixteen, namely: the station of the Mahābindu-pīṭha, the station of the Transcendent (Atīta), the station of the Arrived (Āgata), the Tranquil-Transcendent (Śāntātīta), the Solar Wheel (Sūryacakra), the Sky-Lotus (Vyomāmbhoja), the Preta-bhūmi, the Half-Moon (Ardhacandra), the Beginning (Ārambha), the Setubandha, the Command (Ājñā), the Viśuddhi, the Anāhata, the Maṇipūraka, the Svādhiṣṭhāna, and the Mūlādhāra.

Among these, the first is the partless space (*niṣkalākāśa*) whose nature is the state of the form of the void; the second is the pervasive state (*vyāpinyavasthā*); the third is the state beyond the mind (*unmanāvasthā*); the fourth is the state of equilibrium (*samāvasthā*); the fifth is the station of the supreme power (*parāśakti*) known as emission (*visarga*); the sixth is the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) known as Peace (*śāntā*), situated in emission; the seventh is the station of Sadāśiva known as Power (*śakti*), located in the pericarp situated within the aperture of Brahmā; the eighth is the station of the filaments consisting of sixteen digits (*kalā*) of the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrārapadma*); and the ninth is...

The division [of the locations] is as follows: the ninth is the place of the thousand-petalled lotus consisting of *nāda*; the tenth is the void in the middle of the forehead consisting of *bindu*; the eleventh is the middle of the eyebrows; the twelfth is the station of Īśvara, the throat; the thirteenth is the abode of Rudra, the heart; the fourteenth is the station of Viṣṇu, the navel cavity; the fifteenth is the station of Brahmā, the base of the *liṅga*; and the sixteenth is Kuṇḍalinī, the middle of the body. The meaning is that the Self resides in the center of these foundational lotuses. Alternatively:
"Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā, Gāndhārī, and Hastijihnikā..."
Suyaśas, Lambusā, Pūṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī.

"The Vimalā, Ghoṣiṇī, Pṛthvī, and Āpyāyanī, as well as Tejovatī and Vāyavī—these sixteen channels (nāḍīs) are proclaimed. This refers to the heart-lotus (*hṛdayakamala*) within the central wheel (*madhyacakra*) among the collections of channels mentioned in the *Yogaśāstra*. "Having his form specially placed in the heart" (*hṛdi vinihitarūpaḥ*): by the word "specially placed" (*vinihita*), it is implied that [the form] is not merely being placed, but has been directly realized; thus, the state of one who has achieved perfected concentration (*viniṣpannasamādhi*) is expressed. "Bestower of success" (*siddhidaḥ*): the giver of liberation (*mukti*). Alternatively, the giver of the eight supernatural powers (*aṣṭasiddhi*) beginning with *aṇimā*.

Alternatively, it is said that [this practice] bestows the fivefold accomplishment (*pañcasiddhi*), namely those known as the subterranean pill (*pātālagulikā*), collyrium (*añjana*), sword (*khaḍga*), and mudrā, or those known as sovereign power (*adhikāra*), mantra, yoga, and self-knowledge (*ātma-jñāna*). For those who know this—that is, for those who have learned or attained, through the mouth of a guru, that the Self resides within the center of the wheel of the ten-and-six channels (*nāḍīcakra*)—the word "knowing" (*vid*) is derived either from the sense of knowledge or from the sense of attainment, by means of a *kvip*-suffix derivation. With minds unshaken by such obstacles as:
"Laziness, violent diseases, negligence, misplaced doubt, instability of mind, lack of faith, and deluded vision..."
"Suffering, mental distress, and longing for sense objects—these ten are proclaimed as obstacles for men who are practicing yoga. And:
"Six divine portents arise, indicating the [attainment of] the perfections."

"Insight, hearing, report, vision, tasting, and feeling"—by these obstacles (*antarāya*) and afflictions (*upasarga*) mentioned in the *Yogaśāstra*, the one-pointedness of mind of those practitioners (*sādhaka*) engaged in the practice of mantra-yoga remains unimpeded; it is rightly revealed that this refers to practitioners, not to those who have already attained perfection (*siddha*). "Being sought" means being pursued; the meaning is that it is investigated by those desiring to know reality through long-term, uninterrupted, and respectful application.

Enveloped by powers (*śakti*) through the specific functions of creation, maintenance, dissolution, and so forth—which are the various operations of the Root Power (*mūla-śakti*)—wherever the rays converge, there the All-pervasive One (*vibhu*) alone unfolds. As stated by the learned, he pervades the universe with a network of rays like the sun; for Amarasimha says, "expansion" (*pariṇāha*) means "vastness.
And: "In reality, the single principle known as Śiva is inlaid with hundreds of diverse powers;
these perceived distinctions are imagined due to the different operations of those powers."

Thus it is said by Bhoja. Alternatively, he is "Śaktinātha," meaning he is bound on all sides—that is, served—by the nine Śaktis established in the Śrutis and Āgamas, as stated: "Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Śivā, Raudrī, Cittonmādakarī, Sukhā, Kālī, Kalebarā, and Bhūtadamanī are the powers of Īśa."
"The first unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of Him who desires to create, for the sake of favoring both consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*),
is designated as His *Śakti-tattva*, which has attained a state of non-differentiation from Him alone.

Thus, the Lord of the thirty-fifth *tattva*— this *Śakti* who is defined by the above, who is non-distinct from Himself, who is the agent of all, and who serves as the locus for the emergence and dissolution of the thirty-four *tattvas* beginning with Earth and ending with Sadāśiva— is Śiva, the thirty-sixth.
"Akula is said to be Śiva, while Kula is proclaimed to be Śakti;
Kaular is the transformation of their radiant energy—such is the determination of the triad."

Thus, according to the *Śrīrudratantrokti*, because all principles (*tattva*)—namely Śiva, Śakti, and the collection of their effects—are subsumed under three categories in the Śiva-āgama, He is of such a nature. "He triumphs" means that He exists in a state of supreme excellence; thus, one contemplates how the bliss of His self-awareness (*vimarśa*) surpasses all other forms of happiness. Here, although the channels (*nāḍī*), wheels (*cakra*), and so forth are not perceived through mere scriptural application, there is no fault, because those who know them possess direct personal realization (*svayaṃparāmarśa*). In this verse, the aesthetic emotion (*bhāva*) directed toward the Supreme Lord is manifested.
The figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) is the *bhāvika*. //1//

Having contemplated the majesty of the Supreme Lord from a detached perspective, he now reveals his own experience regarding Him and its fruit, the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth: "I am this very one who, through the grace of the Guru, now knows the Lord to be of such a nature. The meaning is: "I am such as this. The word "now" (*idānīm*) is to be connected with the phrase "has arrived" (*abhyāgatā*) found in the following verse.

"Perpetually deposited," and so forth. "Perpetually deposited" means always established in their respective locations; by the inclusion of the word "perpetual," one-pointedness (*aikāgrya*) is indicated. It is "placed" in the six-limbed wheel (*ṣaḍaṅgacakra*), that is, in the wheel of the six limbs beginning with the heart, because it is the cause of the presence (*sānnidhya*) of that [deity] through the ritual deposition (*nyāsa*). "The omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, eternal unimpaired power, and infinite power—those who know the ritual say these are the eight limbs of the Great Lord (*maheśvara*). Thus they speak of the eight limbs of the pervasive Lord.

The meaning is that [the deity] flashes forth in the aggregate of the six limbs—heart, head, crest, armor, eyes, and weapon—which have been described as belonging to their respective classes and are placed in their locations.

Alternatively, the meaning is that [the deity] is present within the six bodily wheels of the limbs, which are the support-lotuses known as Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūraka, Anāhata, Viśuddhi, and Ājñā; these are eternally established in their respective four, six, ten, twelve, sixteen, and two-petalled lotuses, where the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) has been constantly performed with the consonants from *va* to *sa*, from *ba* to *la*, from *ḍa* to *pha*, from *ka* to *ṭha*, from *a* to the visarga, and with *ha* and *kṣa*. Because [the Self] is accessible through instruction, whereas the throbbing of the heart-lotus is within the range of everyone’s experience, the meaning is that it is "risen" and especially manifest in the center of the heart-lotus. Indeed, no one thinks, "My knowledge is in my head, hand, or foot"; rather, everyone thinks, "It appears thus within my heart. Thus, consciousness is established as being reflected in the mirror of the heart. "The Self" refers to the individual soul (jīvātman), which is the size of a thumb and composed of light.

By virtue of absorption (*laya*), one perceives that which has the form of Śiva—having become one with the Supreme Śiva residing at the *dvādaśānta* through the contemplation of identity with one's own radiance, which, rising through the aperture of the *suṣumnā*, is as slender as a grain of wild rice (*nīvāraśūka*)—because it has been dissolved and liquefied like a bracelet [is merged] into a mass of gold. "Perceiving, not thinking" indicates direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). And this is the formless meditation (*nirākāra-dhyāna*) among the two types, with and without form. As the venerable Guru said: "Meditation with form has been described; now the formless is being told."
Either in the heart-lotus, or between the eyebrows, or in the point (bindu) at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths].
One should meditate on the supreme light, inferable by its nature, which is the size of a thumb;
from that, a light resembling the awn of a grain of nīvāra rises upward through the *suṣumnā*.
Having emerged and attained oneness with Śiva who resides at the *dvādaśānta*,
one should meditate with an unwavering mind upon that which pervades and encompasses the entire universe.
This, however, is the highest of meditations, and this yoga is considered supreme;
thus, the yogi whose self is constantly disciplined shakes off all bonds.

"Having attained the sovereign power (*aiśvarya*) of the qualities such as *aṇimā* and so forth, one reaches liberation (*nirvāṇa*). Here, "dissolution" (*laya*) means the non-perception of a difference in essential nature due to entering into another; this is evident from the usage of the teachers: "I dissolve into the Supreme Brahman," "whose mind is dissolved in the Supreme Brahman," and "this is established: for that which has no origin from something else, its function within that [source] is dissolution, not the dissolution of its own essential nature. Regarding the phrase "of the channels" (*nāḍīnām*), such as *iḍā* and so forth, there is a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the support and the supported, and the plural number is used.

The meaning is: of the great elements (mahābhūta) manifested even in the two nostrils, which serve as the gateway for the two channels (nāḍī). "Udaya" means manifestation. [As it is said: "In both nostrils, the earth is in the form of a staff, water is below, fire is above, wind is across, and in the middle of the nose is the eightfold ether; such is the movement of the elements at the emergence of the body."

The meaning is that by the method of manifestation taught by the Teacher (*ācārya*), there is the arising of each respective element, which facilitates the easy acceptance of each of them. [This occurs] for the world or for living beings, because of the extraction of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*)—that is, through the attainment of the essence of sound, touch, taste, form, and smell, which is called "nectar" (*amṛta*) because it is life-sustaining—and because [the practitioner] has been nourished by drawing it forth with the *vidyā* known as *Amṛtākarṣiṇī*.
Alternatively, according to the technical terminology of the Kaulika Tantras: "Feces, urine, blood, marrow, and semen are known as the five nectars."

Thus, regarding the five nectars (*amṛta-pañcaka*), the term "nectar" is used because they consist of the states of the body. In this context, the meaning is "in the order of the arising of the respective channels (*nāḍī*) that carry them," since the *vidyās* such as Amṛtākarṣiṇī and others are established in scripture by such passages as: "Amṛtākarṣiṇī indeed, and she whose form is the attraction of sound. She had not yet reached the exhaustion of flying upward; she had not encountered the fatigue of soaring to the peaks of the sky. She was dispersing [the clouds] like a mass of cotton-wool scattered in all directions by the wind of her combined momentum, shattering them as she went. "In front of the sky" (*agre nabhaḥ*) means in the upper part of the firmament.

"By the analysis of grammatical rules (*yogavibhāga*), all compounds may remain unelided (*aluk*). Thus, there is no elision [of the case-ending] in *ambhomucaḥ*, meaning "clouds. Alternatively, it means "in front," in the fore-part; thus, *nabhombhomucaḥ* means "clouds stretching across the sky. "Now I have arrived" refers to her having just departed from Śrīparvata, based on the previous context that she was arriving "toward evening. By stating she has "just now arrived," she expresses the wonder of her speed. Through the swift attainment of her desired destination, joy is manifested. The poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) here are Hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) and Natural Description (*svabhāvokti*). //2//

Now, he expresses wonder at the speed of her movement as a source of assistance, beginning with the words "udvṛttā" and so forth: where there are small bells (*kiṅkiṇyaḥ*)—which, being of various kinds, are formidable (*karālāḥ*) and distorted—that ring out (*kvaṇitāḥ*) due to the clashing and striking of the garland of skulls (*kapālakaṇṭhamālā*), a necklace for the purpose of adorning the neck consisting of severed head-bowls, which has become upturned (*udvṛttā*) by the force of leaping and thus moved upward from its place, and which then falters and returns back down. These small bells, by implication, exist as part of that very garland of skulls.

"Sufficient" means complete: namely, the state of being delightful, formidable, and terrifying. As Murāri stated: "Indra, whose power is fierce in the spreading battle... He "unites" (sandhatte) means he joins me together. [The speed of the journey through the vault of the sky: the speed or velocity of that journey which takes place in the vault of the sky. //3//

He establishes that very connection [between the two verses] with the words "moving in all directions" (*viṣvagvṛtti*), and so forth. That which has a movement (*vṛtti*) in every direction (*sarvataḥ*) is a qualification of that time. "It moves" (*pracalati*) means it trembles intensely. "A binding with dense knots" (*nibiḍagranthibandhaḥ*): he whose binding—meaning the means of binding such as cloth-bands—is a binding with firm knots (*dṛḍhagrathana*). "Burden" (*bhāraḥ*) means a collection (*samūhaḥ*). According to the *Vaijayantī*: "The words *nibiḍa*, *nibirīsa*, *dṛḍha*, *sāndra*, and *nirantara* [all mean 'firm' or 'dense']. [This is derived from the rule: "After the prefix *ni*, the suffixes *biḍac* and *birīsac* [are applied]."

(5-2-32) Thus, there is the *biḍac* suffix. The meaning is: "in such a way that it persists for a long time," like the process of ripples and waves produced by the first sound through a series of sounds (*śabda-santāna*)—which is synonymous with resonance (*anuraṇana*)—and which is refined by the lengthening [of the vowel] in the *saṃskāraka* [rule]. "Clearly" (*paṭu*) means manifest by its own nature; "it resounds" (*raṭati*) means it makes a sound. "Having performed repetition" (*kṛtāvṛtti*) means having performed a repetition—that is, a recurrence—by repeatedly striking the tongue; these three are adjectives qualifying the act of resounding. A "khaṭvāṅga-bell" refers to a specific weapon called a *khaṭvāṅga*, which resembles the leg of a bedstead.

Based on the words of the Teacher, "The great bull, the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), the axe, the deerskin, ashes, and serpents," a bell is tied to his head. He shakes or causes to tremble it upward, above; for the roots *dhuñ* and *dhūñ* signify trembling, and this form belongs to the root *dhūñ*. Resounding—that is, making a sound—by entering through the apertures of the garland, which is a series of skulls with gaping mouths, arranged like a thicket among rows of exposed corpses; for there is a root *guñj* meaning "an indistinct sound. It is *uttāla*, meaning arrogant or haughty, and because it rests upon his own shoulders.

Of the *kiṅkiṇīs*—small bells fixed as ornaments; according to Amara, "the *kiṅkiṇīs* are small bells. It is the cause of the incessant tinkling sound (*anavarataraṇatkārahetuḥ*), meaning the cause of an unceasing, uninterrupted jingling. Regarding the banner (*patākā*) or the cloth of the flag (*dhvajāṃśuka*), [it refers to] that of the *khaṭvāṅga*, as is evident from the context. Because its nature is to hang downward, it shakes upward. The meaning is that it moves so as to remain level both at the end of the *khaṭvāṅga* itself and at its own edge, as in: "The flag-cloth stands level on the tip of the staff and at its edge due to the force of the wind."

Thus it was said. Here, the poetic figure is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause), because the cause—the conjunction of loveliness and ferocity—is presented as the meaning of the sentence; and there is also *svabhāvokti* (description of nature). //4//

"Having looked down"—that is, toward the ground. By saying "with old," meaning that which has stood for a long time, he indicates its extremely pungent odor. "With neem oil"—that is, with the oil of the *picumanda* tree.
[As the lexicon states: "Ariṣṭa, sarvatobhadra, hiṅguniryāsa, mālakā, picumanda, and nimba [are synonyms]."

Thus says Amara: "The juice is the liquid of garlic (*rasona* or *laśuna*), which has been smeared with oil, sprinkled with water, and roasted—that is, cooked thoroughly on all sides—possessing the scent of that juice. [Amara-kośa states: "For garlic: *gṛñjana*, *ariṣṭa*, *mahākanda*, *rasonaka*."

Thus says Amara. In the section on foul odors, the *Vaijayantī* states: "The nimba tree is called *tiktaka*. Therefore, because of the bitter odor of nimba oil, and because garlic possesses a similar odor, when it is being fried with that [oil], its smell becomes disagreeably bitter and pungent; likewise, it should be understood that the smoke from funeral pyres also possesses a similar odor, as it contains the scent of the hair, body hair, and other parts of hundreds of corpses being burned. A *citā* is a heap of wood for the purpose of cremating a corpse.

"Citā, cityā, and citi are feminine," according to the *Vaijayantī*. By means of the smoke associated with that [funeral pyre], which spreads through the sky and serves as a sign (*liṅga*), it is revealed—that is, made manifest—that [the pyre] exists below. By the word "great" (*mahataḥ*), meaning extensive due to its connection with a great city, the abundance of corpses is indicated, arising from the multitude of people; for even among those dying, they are innumerable, and thus the corpses are likewise numerous. And he will say later: "from many more funeral pyres."

"la. 17)" [Thus: "The cremation ground enclosure (*śmaśānavāṭa*) is the region of the cemetery; *nedīyaḥ* means nearest; *karālāyatanaṃ* is the abode of the goddess Cāmuṇḍā known by the name Karālā. He connects this with what was previously introduced: 'There is a woman here,' and so forth. For one who has completed the mantra-sādhana—that is, for one whose mastery of the *mahābhairava-vidyā* and other mantras is finished—*sādhanaṃ* refers to the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) prescribed in the ritual manuals (*kalpa*). By the word *samavasita*, it is indicated that an inauspicious event is about to occur."

To this extent alone is his mantra-attainment complete; beyond this, it is indicated that [the practice] is for others. By "command" (*ājñayā*) is meant by injunction. "Today especially" means from the day of beginning the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) until that very day, because ordinary worship has ceased; for the meaning has already been indicated previously by the phrase "he comes at the time of the atom" (*aṇusaṃjhaṃ āacchaï*). "The equipment for worship" (*pūjāsambhāraḥ*) refers to the collection of materials such as honey, meat, and so forth, for the purpose of worship; it must be "placed nearby," meaning it should be kept close at hand.

Wherein there is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of "this very thing" (*tad idam*). He reveals by way of a stylistic turn (*bhaṅgyā*) the specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) indicated by the term "with its particulars" (*saviśeṣam*): "For it was said" (*kathitaṃ hi*), meaning because it was stated; "by my teacher" (*me guruṇā*)—thereby his confidence in her and her satisfaction with his words are revealed. "Previously," on the day of beginning the mantra-practice (*mantra-sādhana*), he had made a vow (*upayācitam*), promising, "I shall give. [As in: "That which was previously vowed by you... (*tvayā purastādupayācito yaḥ*).

This is according to the statement in the *Raghuvamśa*. The term "jewel among women" (*strīratna*) indicates the manner of his request; it means he promised that at the conclusion of the mantra-sādhana, he would offer as the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) a maiden who is the best of her kind due to the purity of both her lineages and her perfection in beauty, auspicious marks, and so forth. The word "jewel" (*ratna*) denotes the most excellent of its own class, as seen in such usages as "jewel among horses," "jewel among elephants," and "jewel among gems. The suffix of necessity (*kṛtya-pratyaya*) in "to be offered" (*upahartavya*) implies an obligation. "Right here" (*atraiva*) refers specifically to Padmāvatī, which is presided over by Karālā.

This indicates the ease with which [the person] may be drawn forth. "Known" means that it has already been discovered through prior investigation that "[he] is present in this house"; this is stated by the words "he sits" or "he is present. Therefore, "with distinction" means that his drawing forth must also be performed.

The phrase "there is indeed no other means than the sale of human flesh" introduces the sale of human flesh; this indicates the entrance of the hero (nāyaka) as he enters the cremation ground by himself after deceiving Makaranda. The word *tat* (that) means: "Since this [sight] produces curiosity even in me, therefore it must certainly be examined. *Atigambhīramadhurākṛtiḥ* refers to one whose physical form (*ākṛti*)—the configuration of the body—is exceedingly profound, sweet, and either entirely indefinable, captivating, or not coarse.
By this, it is demonstrated that it is impossible to know [another's mind] through either facial expression or gesture, in the form of thinking, "This motive is the cause of his activity.
As it is said: "That state wherein anger, joy, fear, and the like—though present—are not perceived through one's manner or facial expression, is called profundity (gāmbhīrya)."

Thus [describes] Divākara: "With his curly locks bristling" (*uttambhitakuṭilakuntalaḥ*) means one whose curled hair is tied upward. By this, his fearlessness is indicated, and in another sense, his readiness for battle even against *vetālas* and the like. "With a sword in hand" (*kṛpāṇapāṇiḥ*) means one who has a scimitar in his hand—specifically, in his right hand. [This follows the rule: "The past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) and the locative case (*saptamī*) follow words used in the sense of weapons."

(vā. 2-2-37) The compound is formed by the rule stating that "bhavataḥ" [is used] when it ought to be so stated. By this, the poet indicates that for one intent on selling human flesh with the thought of providing a remedy against the great calamity of separation from his beloved, wielding a weapon is not a fault, just as it was for Droṇa and others; for in times of distress, the taking up of arms and other duties of a Kṣatriya are not forbidden for a Brāhmaṇa.
As it is said: "But a Brāhmaṇa who cannot subsist by his own prescribed occupation may live by the dharma of a Kṣatriya, for that is next to him."
This is according to the statement of Manu.

"Like the petal of a blue lotus" (*kuvalayadala*) and so forth: he is glossy and dark like the leaf of a blue water-lily. By nature, his complexion is pale-grey and entirely lacking in gloss due to his lack of grooming. His gait is both graceful and imposing; by nature it is charming due to his inherent pride, yet it is imposing due to his haste, being more striking than the former. According to the *Vaijayantī*, "imposing" (*vikaṭa*) means "deformed" (*virūpa*); "gait" (*nyāsa*) refers to the placement of the feet. He is "glorious" (*śrīmān*), meaning that even though he is alone, he appears as if surrounded by many people, his majesty inferred from his extraordinary splendor.

"His face resembles the moon; his countenance is as serene as the moon. By the term "mṛgāṅka" (the moon), it is suggested that even a slight trace of the gloom of despondency exists. Through both [epithets], he foreshadows the future victory. Otherwise, it would contradict the saying: "For those who have set out for battle, if their face becomes lusterless, their life comes to an end."

This is according to the statement in the *Rāmāyaṇa*. "Who is this? is the phrase to which [the following] is connected. "He carries away" means he obscures. He carries away "discipline"—that maturation of the mind produced by the certainty derived from the scriptures. By saying "he carries away," he indicates that it exists in reality, for it is impossible to carry away what does not exist. The reason for this is: "one who has displayed violence"; "violence" (*sāhasa*) means lack of discernment (*avivekitva*), and it is that which has been displayed by him. "With mud of blood flowing profusely": because of the cutting at that very moment, there is a mire of blood flowing copiously from the flesh in which [the action occurs]. "With dangling human carcasses": human flesh is sporting about; the verbal root is *lala* (to sport/dangle).

"Either with milk, mung-bean soup, or the broth of wild game," according to Vāhaṭa’s statement. Here, by the mention of "man" (nara), it is intended that even above [the neck] there shall be the offering of human flesh; thus, because of the mention of "man," one should not entertain the thought of selling one's own flesh. This is because it is described as a specific variety of "great meat" (mahāmāṃsa) sale, referring specifically to the sacrifice of a person, and because it will be stated later that it is "prepared from the limbs of a man. Otherwise, it would have been said, "sporting with his own wild game," or "wandering about for the sale of his own flesh."

By the mention of "jungle" (*jāṅgala*), it is shown that the meat—fit for an offering as prescribed in the ritual manuals—is taken from a human body severed by a sword, just like the omentum (*vapā*) and other such parts. This indeed constitutes its distinction from the sacrifice of a human being (*puruṣopahāra*). Here, the sentiment of horror (*raudrarasa*) is manifested. The poetic figure is *bhāvika*, because the state of being [the emotion] is clearly perceived. There is also *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), since the cause, namely agitation (*udvega*), is conveyed by means of its effect. //5//

"Having scrutinized" means having investigated carefully; that is to say, having recognized her by her physical characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). [He is] the son of Devarāta, the friend of Kāmandakī. By this, his status as an object of her affection is illuminated. Furthermore, the mention of her knowledge of his relationship [to Kāmandakī] is for the purpose of facilitating the protection of Mālatī, which is to be described later through the agency of Saudāminī. "A hawker of human flesh" means a seller; according to the rule *vyavahṛ-paṇoḥ samarthayoḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.11], the term *paṇitṛ* denotes a seller.

(2-3-57) Thus, when the word *paṇi* is used in the sense of "selling," the genitive case is employed for the object. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "This Mādhava has been staked. The meaning is: "What then is the use of this? Since he was seen before, why is such curiosity now being shown toward him as if he were something unprecedented? "I shall accomplish the task without overstepping what has been undertaken according to the intended plan" (*yathāsamīhitam*). Alternatively, *yathā* and *yathāvat* are separate words; the meaning is "the desired object" (*samīhitam iṣṭārtham*). "Almost vanished" (*vigalitaprāyaḥ*) means that it has mostly departed, leaving only a small remainder. The explanation of that is introduced with "for instance" (*tathāhi*).

"Of the sky," and so forth—of the sky (*vyoman*), that is, of space (*ākāśa*). "By rows of *tāpiñcha* clusters" means by series of bunches of *kākatuṇḍikā* flowers. Halāyudha states: "The *tāpiñcha* is the *kākatuṇḍikā*. The *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "A *guccha*, *guluccha*, or *stabaka* [is a cluster]. Alternatively, it refers to the *tamāla* tree; Amara states: "The *kālaskandha* is the *tamāla*, and the *tāpiñcha* is also [so called]. The expression "by creepers of darkness" (*tamovallarībhiḥ*) is used because they emerge here and there, overwhelming [the light], as if they were blossoms of gloom (*timiramañjarībhiḥ*).
Amara states: "The words *vallarī* and *mañjarī* are feminine. Alternatively, [it may be interpreted differently].

By such usages as "the creeper of long matted locks" (*dīrghajaṭāvallarī*) and "the creeper for falling upon what has been broken by an elephant," the meaning is: because of the spreading and extending of the creepers of darkness. They are "covered" (*vriyante*), that is, concealed. "The borders" (*paryantāḥ*) refers to the adjacent regions, meaning the faces of the directions. Above it is thus; but below, however, it is by means of the "enclosure" (*vṛtiḥ*)—that is, the surrounding, the covering—of the borders, namely the coastal regions of the ocean, which is caused by and has as its basis the darkness. Alternatively, *vṛtti* means sequence; thus, it means "by way of the sequence of the borders. "In the water" (*payasi*) means in the liquid; "fresh" (*nūtane*) means new.
The meaning is that the flood of rainwater is dark blue and reddish-pink due to its turbidity from mud, as stated in the verse:
"The fresh waters are as if completely turbid.

By this, the mottled nature of the darkness, resulting from its connection with the twilight, is revealed; for it is said in the *Harṣacarita*: "When the earth sinks into the darkness of fresh water—darkness copper-colored from the lingering twilight and possessing the luster of a ripe palmyra fruit. *Vasumatī* means the earth. *Majjati* means she becomes submerged or deeply immersed. By the use of the present tense, the progressive nature of the submergence is indicated.

Furthermore, in its center, it possessed a splendor like the beauty of a dense, thick mass of smoke (*dhūmyā*)—a collection of smoke—that was spread in all directions, diffused everywhere, whirled into a circle, expanded, and intensified by the great force and velocity of a whirlwind (*vātyā*). According to the *Vaijayantī* lexicon: "A *vātyā* is a circular wind," "a *dhūmyā* is a whirlwind or a forest fire," and "the term *sarva* applies to a multitude of such things."

The comparison to a bracelet (*valayita*) is employed because the orb of the sky is perceived as having a circular shape contracted by darkness. "At the beginning" means at the mere moment of its own manifestation. The particle *api* indicates a contradiction. "Triyāmā" means night. "Tarūṇayati" means it makes [the world] young; that is, it makes it youthful. The suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule "that which causes something to become so. "Nija" refers to its own inherent blackness, the quality of being dark-colored. This is derived from the rule "from *pṛthu* and others, the suffix *imanij* may be added optionally."

(5-1-122) Thus, the suffix *iman* is applied. By the phrase "in the forests," the state of being especially darkened is revealed through the density of leaves and shoots which prevents the sun's rays from entering even during the day, as well as by the presence of herds of boars emerging from the ponds at that time. Here, a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is suggested based on the cause of the creepers of darkness: it is as if the horizons of the sky are being enveloped by rows of *tāpiñcha* clusters acting as long pendants, and as if the earth, by its very edge, is sinking into fresh water.

For that very reason, it is said that the night makes the forests young with their own natural blackness even at the beginning [of the day]. Since the manifestation of a complete form occurs only in youth and not in childhood, the phrase "makes them young even in childhood" is a *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) devoid of a formal indicator (*dyotaka*), as it suggests they are being made young despite being in childhood. Alternatively, because intentional youth is impossible, this is an *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), since it describes a relationship where no such relationship exists.

In these three statements, there is revealed, respectively: the exceptional beauty of the celestial chariot in the sky through its suspension and support; the gradual disappearance of the entire earth in reverse order from the penultimate to the final [verse]; and the dense blackness of the forest interior even compared to other large expanses. Furthermore, the figure of speech *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description) is suggested here. //6//

Because the world above, below, and in between is shrouded in darkness, we shall now proceed without restraint for the sake of accomplishing our intended purpose at this opportune moment; having thus revealed through the means of its cause the meaning of the verse, which demonstrates both the already occurred descent of Mādhava into the cremation ground and the yet-to-be-occurring sacrifice of Mālatī, he concludes the *viṣkambhaka* with the words: "Exeunt.
(The *Viṣkambhaka*).

Now, by means of the entrance of the hero who has been previously indicated, he begins the act for the performance of the dramatic matter with interest, starting with the words "Then enters": "as described" means characterized by the manner in which he was spoken of by Kapālakuṇḍalā;

"with a sword grasped in his right hand," "with human flesh dangling from the lotus of his left hand," "with his curly locks firmly bound by a creeper-like girdle," and "wearing a very firm loincloth fastened at the waist"—the meaning is that he walks about with a graceful yet formidable gait, possessing a form both fierce and charming that captivates the three worlds.

"I truly see no other means than the sale of human flesh"—with these words, the crest-jewel of the community of poets and connoisseurs provides a thematic connection (*anusandhāna*) for the principal sentiment (*aṅgin*), which is the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) consisting of longing-in-separation (*abhilāṣa-vipralambha*). This sentiment serves as the motivator for the protagonist’s selfless exertion, which was introduced at the conclusion of the previous act. The phrase "with hope" (*sāśaṃsam*) signifies that it is accompanied by *āśaṃsā*, meaning prayer or aspiration; this illuminates the essential nature of longing. For it is defined as follows: "Longing is proclaimed to be that means of union with the beloved which is preceded by a resolve born from desire and imagination."

"Moist with love," and so forth. "Moist with love" means [moistened] by affection. "That bond of feeling which is established through mutual dependence, such that it would not exist if even one of the two were removed—that is called 'love' (prema)."
"That moisture and softness of the mind arising from a sense of 'mine' toward objects, whose essence consists of fear and apprehension—that alone is called affection (sneha). And:
"That which is moisture and coolness of the mind in all states..."
And thus says the Bhāvaprakāśa:
"Affection (sneha), however, being induced by an object through accumulation, casts a man helplessly and constantly toward its vicinity; it is thus designated as love (prema)."
Thus it is said:
"Whatever is dear to him, by that very thing one should quickly bring about his readiness,
receptivity, and clarity of mind that destroys mental turbidity."

Thus says Divākara: "By means of love, which consists of an excellence of affection (*sneha*), they are cool and entirely favorable"—this is the meaning. It is as stated in the *Raghuvamśa*: "The bond of feeling between the two named 'Chariot-Wheels' became a mutual dependence of love. Love is mentioned first because it alone is the substratum of sexual passion (*rati*).

"Where Madana, denoted by the word *ī*, is perceived in its highest degree—that is *prema* (love), which is the substratum for the mutual passion (*rati*) of the two youths. This is according to that statement. For, following the maxim "there can be no painting on a wall if the wall does not exist," the establishment of that which is supported occurs only when there is a supporting substratum. [The term] *praṇayaspṛśaḥ* means those who touch upon affection (*praṇaya*).
"When the love between two youths has been brought to its highest pitch through mutual outward and inward attentions, that is known as *praṇaya*.
(Thus it is said.)

The external [pleasures] consist of embracing, kissing, and so forth; the internal are the specific varieties of sexual union (*rativiśeṣa*). Through familiarity—that is, through long-term practice free from obstacles—the arising of intense passion occurs for those [pleasures]. Regarding this, it is said: "If that very [object] is colored by qualities, substances, place, time, and so on within the heart, and if it shines forth in the mind, it is called *rāga* (passion)."
(Thus. "That very [nature] is called affection (*sneha*):
'That which, through time, remains as the essence of affection once the veil has been removed by its maturation.'"

Thus it is said in the *Uttararāmacarita*. By the repetition of the word "those various" (*tāstā*), the fact that [the states of love] cannot be described—due to their variegated nature consisting of jealousy, pride, affection, and so forth—and that they are accessible only through direct experience (*anubhava*) is revealed: "Love may sprout through affection; it may put forth leaves through pride;
it may form buds through endearment; and it may blossom through deep attachment."

For it is said: "And this [love] becomes fruitful when it is enjoyed with passion. By the phrase "of the lovely-eyed one" (*mugdhadṛśaḥ*), the natural beauty of her gaze is revealed; her "actions" (*ceṣṭāḥ*)—specific movements consisting of speech, limbs, and disposition—are "naturally sweet," meaning they are inherently charming. The term "naturally sweet" (*nisargamadhurāḥ*) serves as a restatement (*anuvāda*). There is a prayer that these naturally sweet actions, distinguished by qualities such as being moistened with love, might exist in me; the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of a prayer (*prārthana*).

"In me," that is, within my own sphere; because it is inferred by the mark (liṅga) of the non-simultaneous production of cognitions, and because it resides within the body and serves as the instrument of cognition, [I refer to] the internal organ, which is the mind (manas). The external organs are so called because they obstruct the functioning of the external instruments; for although the eyes and other senses are "internal" in relation to the gross body, they are "external" in relation to the mind, as they abide outside it. Furthermore, they are called "instruments" (karaṇa) because they are the means for accomplishing knowledge and action.
As the Blessed One has said: "They say the senses are superior, but the mind is superior to the senses."

"External [organs] belong to the present time, while internal organs belong to the three times," according to the Sāṅkhya teaching. Their functions consist of grasping objects such as the visible and pervading [the domain of] the speakable and so forth; his nature is to restrain or ward off these. By this, it is revealed that because the mind is the charioteer of all the senses, when the mind is dissolved, all the senses are dissolved. By the word "in an instant" (kṣaṇāt), he expresses the capacity of activities to be performed with speed. "In those imagined through longing" means in those constructed on all sides by mental desires—like the father of Somaśarman—as if they were being experienced or contemplated.

By the word *api* (even), it is suggested: "how much more so when [the objects] are directly attained. By the phrase "dense with bliss" (*ānandasāndra*)—meaning abundant with happiness—the exclusion of the delusion (*moha*) produced by intense suffering is indicated, as it is said: "When the functions of the senses are paralyzed by a delusion arising from an intense affliction... *Laya* (absorption) is a state of rest like being devoid of one's own nature due to the cessation of one's own activity. Here, the emotional state (*bhāva*) of longing (*autsukya*) is suggested. Furthermore, the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), because the excellence is manifested by both the word *ati* and the word *kṣaṇa*. //7//
He states the prayer again by way of another method with the words "api ca" (and also).

Regarding "avimuktā" and so forth: "unreleased" means never abandoned at any time. The reason for this is "strung by me," meaning woven together by me, and not because of the weight of the material. Therefore he says: "a garland of filaments (*kesarāvalī*), and not a necklace of pearls. By that [garland], "constantly" means without interruption. It is "perfumed" (*adhivāsaḥ*), meaning made fragrant; and that which is "naturally beautiful" (*prakṛtyā subhagaḥ*); and to whom the breast has been "offered," meaning given without restraint for kissing, embracing, and so forth.

"Having placed his face at the root of [her] ear" (*karṇajāhaviniveśitānanaḥ*): this refers to one whose mouth (*mukha*) is specifically set or placed (*viniveśita*) at the side of her ear (*karṇapārśve*), that is, at the base of her own ear (*svasya karṇamūle*). By this, the intensity of his passion for kissing her cheek (*tatkapolacumbanasaṃrambha*) is suggested. [The formation follows: *pākamūle pīlvādikarṇādibhyaḥ kuṇabjāhacau*.

(5.2.24) Thus, the suffix *jāhac* is applied. The agentive word "by the beloved" (*priyayā*) is directly connected with the action of "placing," while it is connected with the action of "offering" by implication. The word "api" has the sense of "and" (*cārthe*), conjoining the two qualifiers. "Even though being thus and so" (*evamevamapi bhavan*) is a temporal qualifier for that moment. "The exchange of her limbs" (*tadaṅgaparivṛttim*) means the substitution of her limbs—the arms, hands, thighs, and so on—with my own limbs; that is, the placement of my limbs in the positions of her limbs, and her limbs in the positions of my limbs.

The meaning is that at the time of union, one should employ the specific form of embrace known as *tilataṇḍula* (sesame and rice). Vātsyāyana states: "When two people on the bed have crossed their thighs and arms, and embrace firmly as if with friction, that is *tilataṇḍula*. The singular number indicates that it occurs only once. The optative suffix (*liṅ*) in *āpnuyām* ("may I obtain") expresses a prayer. Here too, in the forthcoming phrase *tat paśyeyam* ("may I see that"), it is precisely this eagerness (*autsukya*) that is manifested, despite the difference in object.

Here, the figure of speech is Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description), as mutual passion is revealed by means of its effect. Here, by the words "moist with love" (*premārdrāḥ*) and so forth, the happiness of union with the beloved—arisen from a sentiment that has flourished continuously over a long period—is expressed as a hope. However, by the words "in Avimukta" (*avimukte*) and so forth, it is illuminated that even in the absence of such [union], it would be better to experience the desired embrace at some point and die immediately thereafter. //8//

Now, having set aside both of those, he establishes his hope for a festival occurring prior to that—“*athavā*” (or rather) serves to exclude what was previously stated. The sense is: “far indeed,” for such a mass of merit does not even exist within the range of one’s desires (*manoratha*).

According to the *Vaijayantī*: “*yāvat* and *tāvat* [are used] in the senses of totality, limit, measure, and restriction. This refers to the pair immediately mentioned; “this” refers to what is about to be said; “*tāvat*” means first.

He describes the manner of the prayer with the words beginning "sambhūyaiva" (having come together). "Sambhūya" means having become assembled or united; this is a form derived from the root *bhū* in the sense of "attaining," with the prefix *sam-* and the suffix *lyap*. He will also say later, "sambhūya kāntaiḥ pibanti" (having come together with their beloveds, they drink). The word "eva" (indeed) means that there is no doubt in this matter. Or, the reading may be "iva" (as if). "Sukha" (happiness) is defined as: "that for the sake of which everything exists, and which is not for the sake of anything else—that is happiness."

The word "pleasures" (*sukhāni*) is expressed in the plural to indicate those pleasures of whatever kind and however many they may be, arising from any source whatsoever. "Supreme abundance" (*bhūmānam*) refers to unsurpassed expansion; for contraction is of the nature of suffering. By this, the poet also calls to mind the statement from another Vedic scripture: "That which is abundance is indeed happiness. "Wherein"—that is, in that face—descending into the path of light, entering the range of vision, but not merely clearly visible nearby.

By this, it is illuminated that he appears from afar as if barely discernible; by this very [phrase], it is also made clear that he has entered the path of sight, smell, taste, and so forth. "Rati" means sexual pleasure, dalliance, or sport. "In the mind"—this is all that is intended. "Prasnauti" means to pour forth or rain down, as in:
"He pours forth [the essence of] the highest good and extends his fame."

It is like the word *itivat*. Or rather, it means "he introduces" (*prastauti*), that is, he begins. "A festival for the eyes" (*netrotsavaḥ*) means a festival for the two eyes. The meaning is that it performs a play consisting of dancing and so forth, born of pride in the mind—which is satisfied by seeing from afar—through the clear observation [of the performance] nearby. This is because the meaning of the verbal root is taken as "to sport" (*ramu krīḍāyām*), and not because the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of love (*rati*) is being expressed here.
For it is said: "The transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*), the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), and the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) are [only] denotable by words [in such cases]."

This is because the teachers have stated that [these qualities] constitute the excellence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). He describes the extraordinary beauty that serves as the cause for this reality: "from the collection of the crescents of the young moon"—that is, from the gathering together in one place of the lunar digits, which possess a charming loveliness due to their being still immature; "by means of those gathered"—meaning accepted or taken up. The word *apacita* (gathered) suggests through a poetic suggestion (*dhvani*) whose literal meaning is not intended, the sense of "as if by flowers gathered from creepers," as in the verse:
"Three kinds of men gather the gold-flowered earth."

It is as if [the body] were produced or created from essences—the fresh butter of loveliness—as its constituent materials; it is not, however, merely smeared with liquid camphor. It is the auspicious house (*maṅgalagṛha*) of Anaṅga (the Bodiless One), the abode that serves as the means for the prosperity of Madana. The meaning is that just as people constantly attend with reverence to sacred places such as temples for the sake of their own well-being, so too do they attend to this body. By this, it is revealed that the irresistible power of Anaṅga arises by virtue of having that [body] as his locus.

The phrase "bhūyo'pi punarapi" (again and yet again) establishes that the thirst [for her] was not pacified by the previous sight. The suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of a prayer, as in "may I see her. The word "tasyāḥ" means "of her," referring to her who was experienced through such a state of being overwhelmed by passion. Here, if the reading is "eveti" (as if), there is the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (hyperbole); if the reading is "iveti" (like), however, it is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). Furthermore, in the second half-verse, there is both *utprekṣā* and *rūpaka* (metaphor). The example beginning with "sambhūya" is cited because it expresses excellence (*utkarṣa*).
Therefore, it should be understood that these three prayers are appropriately offered to the deities as the price for the sale of his own flesh. //9//

As if casting aside the hope for a vision formed by the thought "perhaps I might see him," he describes the mind's exclusive focus on that [object] through a stylistic turn, saying "Or rather" (*athavā*). That which is true is indeed true. "Sight" (*sandarśanam*) means making something an object of the eyes; "no" (*na*) expresses its absence, as in:
"virility or impotence, knowledge or ignorance, life or death."

Thus it has been stated by Vāhaṭa. "In these two modes, there is but a slight difference" (*svalpa-viśeṣaḥ*) means a very minor distinction (*laghīyān bhedaḥ*). The use of the term "slight" (*svalpa*) suggests that the absence of perception when the mind is unsettled is a source of suffering. He establishes this very point with the words: "For my [perception] now... (*mama hi samprati*). The particle *hi* indicates a reason. "Intellection" (*buddhi*), "apprehension" (*upalabdhi*), "knowledge" (*jñāna*), and "cognition" (*pratyaya*) are synonyms. This [intellection] is one whose nature is made possible by previous perceptions characterized by excellence (*sātiśaya*).

Of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—whose nature has been properly produced and confirmed by a previous, superior, and distinct perception concerning the beloved (i.e., a cognition)—there is a quality that is dissimilar to it yet produces another impression of the same class as its own producer; because of the constant awakening of that [quality], which consists of *bhāvanā*, there is a perpetual expansion due to the absence of obstacles. Thus, it is "extending," meaning it is spreading out.

By the word "dissimilar" (*avisadṛśaiḥ*), the continuum (*santāna*) is referred to by means of that same term; [these are] "contradictory" (*viruddhaiḥ*) because they possess a different nature from it. By other conditions (*pratyayāntaraiḥ*), such as specific cognitions like "I am this," [the continuum is interrupted], just as the continuum of the cognition of a jar is [interrupted] by cognitions of a jar, a cloth, and so forth. "With its flow unobstructed" (*atiraskṛtapravāhaḥ*) means with its progression uninterrupted, because those [other cognitions] have not entered between the preceding and succeeding flows.

The "stream of the arising of the cognition consisting in the recollection of the beloved" refers to the continuous succession of the emergence of that very cognition—which takes the form of remembering the object dear as one's own life—produced by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). The phrase "of the nature of that" means having the very form of the beloved. The word "as if" (*iva*) is used because, in reality, the mind does not actually possess that nature. "Through conformity with the mental modification" (*vṛttisārūpyataḥ*) means through having an identical form or a single aspect with the mental modification, that is, with the cognition in the form of a *buddhi*-modification.

Consciousness (*caitanya*) is knowledge that constitutes the very nature of the Self. This is the meaning: when the stream of cognitions consisting of the mental modifications (*buddhivṛtti*)—such as those of "dear" or "I remember"—which arise in the form of a single aspect of consciousness and are synonymous with meditative reflection (*adhyāna*), dissolves by attaining identity with the consciousness of the Self, there occurs a state known as *samādhi*. This state is a mere experience of bliss, devoid of differentiation, as if empty of any distinct nature. Thus have the learned said: "He who is not interrupted by states, whether contradictory or non-contradictory, and who leads other things to his own being, is the permanent [sentiment], like a salt-mine."* *The reference is likely to Bharata’s *Nāṭyaśāstra* 6.32.*

Thus it is said. And here, it should be understood that the meaning of that [text] is revealed with poetic elegance by the poet, who is thoroughly conversant with all the paths of the Yoga and Vedānta scriptures. For instance: by the words "unsurpassed" (*niratiśaya*) and so forth, the perfection of the five limbs beginning with *yama* (restraint) is expressed; by the word "of the impression" (*saṃskārasya*), *dhāraṇā* (concentration) is indicated; by the word "extending" (*pratāyamāna*), the possession of the six limbs beginning with *dhāraṇā* is shown; and by the words "by those dissimilar" (*tadvisadṛśaiḥ*) and so forth, *dhyāna* (meditation) is indicated, because it is defined in the Yogaśāstra as "the practice of a continuous flow of homogeneous cognitions uninterrupted by heterogeneous cognitions," which is *nididhyāsana*.
"O King, that meditation, which is a continuous stream of cognition focused exclusively on that form and free from desire for anything else, is accomplished through the first six factors."

This is also evident from the statement in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*: "By means of [the phrase] 'he makes it as if consisting of that' and so forth, *samādhi* is described. For that which is the apprehension of the essential nature of that very [object], devoid of conceptual construction, accomplished by the mind through meditation—that is designated as *samādhi*."

"And as it is stated in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa: 'O Sage, that [meditation] leads the meditator on Brahman to his own essential nature (ātmabhāva) by means of its own power, just as a magnet attracts iron that is susceptible to transformation.'"
``The continuous and uninterrupted contemplation of Śiva— the all-pervading pure consciousness— as one's own identity is considered the supreme samādhi.''

Thus says the venerable Guru. Regarding the phrase "by means of the conformity of the mental state" (*vṛttisārūpyataḥ*): just as one extracts the blade of *iṣīkā* grass from the *muñja* reed, one extracts the aspect of consciousness (*caitanya*)—which is not of the nature of "this"—from the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), which consists of both "this" and "not-this. Then, through the knowledge called *vidyā*, which takes the form of a modification of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*) and has been repeatedly practiced, and by virtue of the Śruti and the grace of the teacher, there arises the experience of being Brahman—the Self (*brahmātmatvānubhūti*)—known as awakening (*prabodha*). This occurs because, through its uniformity, all distinctions are sublated. Thus, while propounding the Advaita Siddhānta, he indicates the soul's inclination toward that [realization].

Here, the poetic figure is *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation), because the unmentioned subject is understood through the similarity of attributes (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*). This occurs because the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), though unmentioned, is perceived as that which delimits the mentioned object, namely the beloved. Furthermore, this very figure establishes the process of identification (*tanmayīkaraṇa*), which consists in superimposing the conventional usage of a scriptural reality upon a worldly object—just as it is said: "As if merged," and so forth. "As if merged" means having entered and become closely united within the mind, which stands in place of the inner chamber, out of fear or shame from some source or other—as in the phrase, "merged among clusters of white lotuses."

For in such passages as "He who protects [the sun] hidden in caves" and "He surpassed the two [eyes] absorbed by bees," it is understood that the word *līna* denotes merely a relationship of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Alternatively, having raised the objection—"How can an external object, which is all-pervading, enter into something as small as an atom?"—he says: "As if reflected, as if entered in the form of a shadow into that [heart] which acts like a mirror. Even though the entry of a reflection is not real, [it is used figuratively].
"Like a shadow entered into the surface of a mirror," "The moon entered the faces of the fair-eyed women through the guise of a reflection, their cheeks radiant";
"A mass of white clouds clinging to the reflections of the laughing [faces]."

In such passages, this description is used because of the well-known entry [of the reflection] into that [mirror]. Fearing that the reflection might vanish upon the removal of either the original object (*bimba*) or the mirror, he says: "as if painted with colors using a brush upon that which has become like a wooden board. Fearing its destruction due to the encounter with opposing elements such as water, he says: "as if carved out of that which has become like a pillar, fashioned by the sharpened chisel of asceticism," just as Murāri said: "He who, having whetted the body of a Kṣatriya with his ascetic chisels, raised him up to the status of a Brāhmaṇa."

Anticipating that even there, due to the power of time, there might be discoloration and the like according to the principle stated—"the female figures on the pillars, whose sequence of colors has faded"—he says: "as if inlaid" (*pratyupteva*) in that [pillar] which resembles the luster of gold, or as if actually placed there by being set in, like rubies and other gems, as in the description:
"a woman with hips adorned with a girdle inlaid with priceless jewels."

For in such usages as "by the luster of the emerald gems set in the tips of his shimmering golden earrings" and "set with rubies that cast a halo of light," *prativāpa* is seen to refer to the inlaying of gems; even there, fearing that the view might be incomplete due to the nature of the inlaying process, he says: "as if firmly joined by the medicinal paste called *vajralepa*, like a divine image on a pedestal. This means it is as if firmly adhered by the substance known as *vajralepa*.

"Resin of lac, śarjarasa, conch-shell, sand, the juice of the three myrobalans (triphalā), and kunduruṣka—these, when ground together, are declared to be this 'adamantine ointment' (vajralepa)," according to the *Siddhāntasāra*. Even there, fearing movement due to the loosening of the bond over time, he says: "as if buried within," meaning as if it were placed inside after being dug out from the surface of the earth, like a treasure (nidhāna). The word *antaḥ* ("within") is to be connected individually with each of the phrases beginning with *līnā* ("merged").

By this chain of poetic conceits (*utprekṣā*), in which each preceding desire is set aside by the succeeding one, the beloved is presented as having entered within the mind, yet remaining unperceived, indestructible, possessing unfading beauty, visible in its entirety, and not wavering for even a moment; thus, an extraordinary meaning that captivates the hearts of the connoisseurs is offered.

What aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) is there in an interpretation that treats [the elements] as mutually independent? Furthermore, an abundance of poetic conceits (*utprekṣā*) would result in being purposeless, since the mere perception of attachment is established by any one [conceit] alone. Moreover, this is a conceit of action (*kriyotprekṣā*), because the act of attaching is imagined as being the acts of merging and so forth.

In the phrase "utkīrṇarūpā" (as if carved), although the relation [of the compound] is subordinate because a compound functions as a connector of related elements and relations possess the status of established attributes, it must be understood that this is indeed a *kriyotprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on action), since the act of carving is intended here as the primary element. Now, if a cause is fancied here, it is that [act] which was the object of an extraordinary previous perception; the meaning is: "for us who desire her even more than our own lives."

"Kīlitā" means "fastened with a pin" (*kīla*); it is as if a golden plate were made to have a pin fixed upon it, like a door-panel. The suffix *ṇic* is used in the sense of "that which causes [something] to do" (*tat karoti*). According to the *Vaijayantī*: "A *dhruva*, a *kīla*, and also an *aṇi*—these six [are synonyms]. By means of the "viśikhas"—arrows—of the "Cetobhū," the mind-born one; for Kāma has his origin in mental conception (*saṅkalpa-yoni*). The mention of the number "five," though already well-known, reveals the pinning down by means of those five arrows acting as pins (*aṇi-bhūta*) against the five-limbed body.

Because their [thoughts] fall without interruption, there is such a visualization: the "stream of thought" (*cintāsantati*) is a continuous flow of reflection (*anudhyāna*); that itself is a "web of threads" (*tantujāla*), a collection of fibers, because it is subtle and extensive. Just as something is "densely sewn"—meaning well-fastened—by a web of threads inserted through the eye of a needle, so too is it as if sewn by the stream of thought, like one cloth being attached to another. According to the *Vaijayantī*, "threads are the warp and weft."

The word *syūtā* is a form of the root *sīv* (to sew), meaning "binding," ending in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). Here, the word *iva* everywhere indicates a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). The *ca*s are for the purpose of completing the meter, according to the rule: "The particles *tu*, *hi*, *ca*, *smaha*, and *vai* are used for filling the meter. Indeed, it is better that a word be meaningless than that it convey a false sense; for this very reason she is attached, she therefore makes [him] as if composed of her. Thus, because there is only a slight difference between seeing her and not seeing her, each preceding state is presented as the cause for each succeeding one.
And thus, through a union of imagination that serves as a substitute for actual sight, a slight subsiding of agitation is revealed; this is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). //10//

"Aho saṃprati!"—the word "aho" indicates wonder. It reveals the acquisition of power by the *tāmasa* beings on account of a particular time; that very point is expressed by the word "saṃprati. The meaning is: because the evening of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇacaturdaśī*) is currently present. This is because it was said, "Today is the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight," and because it will be stated later, "In the great cemetery on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight. Furthermore, night provides strength to those who are *tāmasa*; how much more so does the night belonging to the day of spirits (*bhūta*), the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight? For it is said: "Therefore, the Asuras are strong at night, while the gods are strong by day."

Thus, according to the statement in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*: "With his strength increasing, being unrestrained, proceeding, and beginning to roam—in this cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) where there is a multitude (*nikara*), that is, a collection, of *kauṇapas*—meaning flesh-eating *rakṣasas* and *piśācas*—there is ferocity (*raudratā*), that is, a state of terror."

"Limiting," and so forth. "Limiting" means obstructing the surrounding space; "thick and dense" (*medura-dhana-styānam*) means massed together like a cloud that is heavy with water, dense, glossy, and dark. Amara states: "The word *medura* means dense and glossy. [The term] *styāna* is derived from the root *styai* or *ṣṭyai*, meaning "to collect" or "to sound. "Of the funeral pyre flames" (*citājyotiṣām*) refers to the fires attached to the piles of wood used for cremating the corpses. "Brilliance" (*aujjvalyam*) refers to the manifestation of their radiance.

[The *parabhāga*: excellence of qualities; according to the *Vaijayantī*, "the *parabhāga* is the excellence of qualities. By means of that, he makes manifest—that is, he renders clear—because, due to the opposition between the black and tawny colors, they bring about the manifestation of one another. [The suffix] *kaṭac* is applied after the prefix *sampra-* (or *samproda-*)... [as per Pāṇini 5.2.29].

(5-2-29) *Ābhogabhīmam*: terrifying due to its vast extent. *Tamaḥ* (darkness) functions as the agent. By the employment of the word *tamas*, its quality of delighting those characterized by *tamas* (the ignorant) is illuminated. Therefore, he says: *saṃsaktākulakelayaḥ*. "Saṃsaktāḥ" means engaged; "ākulāḥ" means characterized by agitation. The meaning is that they are crowded with such activities as one person running toward another, another pulling someone else away, and another falling upon yet another.

Those by whom there are playful sports (*kalayaḥ krīḍāḥ*); through tumultuous shouts of "kilikila"—for "kilikila" is an imitation of the sound of joy among low-born folk, as it is stated in the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa* regarding the monkeys that "then they shouted 'kilikila'"—through such clamorous noises (*kolāhalaiḥ kalakalaiḥ*) [out of] *samād*. *Samād* is joy, according to the rule "the forms *pramada* and *samād* are used for joy" (Pāṇini 3.3.68). For that reason, they are *uttālāḥ*, meaning unrestrained. The *kaṭapūtanās* and others: the *kaṭapūtanās* are specific types of female *piśācas* covered with old rags (*jaraṭha-kaṭa-prāvṛtāḥ*), or else they are a particular class of *piśācas*.

"Having smelled the fragrance of the smoke from a straw mat, the inhabitants of Vraja [departed]," as it is said in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam. Since the word *kaṭa* itself denotes a *piśācī*, [it is said]:
"A fallen Brahmin becomes a *preta* with a mouth like a vomited firebrand."
But a Kṣatriya who eats impure matter and corpses becomes a Kaṭapūtana.

And because of this statement of Manu: "The use of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* [in *piśācī*] denotes a female Piśāca, since the masculine form *pūtanacakra* is to be mentioned later. For this very reason, the word *prabhṛti* ("and so forth") is included to encompass other species:
'The Ḍākinīs, the Yātudhānīs, the Kūśmāṇḍas, those who are child-seizing spirits (*arbhakagraha*), the Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, and Vināyakas.'"

These and others are recited in the Purāṇas. *Sāṃrāviṇam* means a pervasive clamor (*saṃrāva*). [The suffix] *inuṇ* is applied in the sense of "pervasion" according to Pāṇini 3.3.44, and [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to 5.4.18. Since there are other types of *sāṃrāviṇa*, the term *kilikilā-kolāhala* (the tumultuous sound of shouting "kili-kili") is included here for the purpose of excluding those other forms; otherwise, the meaning would already be conveyed by the word *sāṃrāviṇa* alone. Here, the Furious sentiment (*raudrarasa*) is manifested. In the first half of the verse, there is the composure (*samādhi*) of the heroes, whose facial expressions remain serene even while surrounded by the ocean-like opposing forces. The figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) is the Marvellous (*vicitra*). In the second half, there is the Description of Nature (*svabhāvokti*). //11//
Then, facing toward them, he makes the proclamation as stated in the ritual manual: "O, O! You venerable ones whose abode is the cremation ground, whose dwelling is the charnel house!
[You who are] 'purified by your own weapon,' and so forth; because you have been severed by a sword held in your own hand, you are purified—that is, cleansed.
For it is said: 'A Kṣatriya whose inner self has been purified by a weapon for the sake of cows or Brahmins, having been slain in battle, goes to heaven.'"

In such statements from the *Mahābhārata* and other texts as, "I tell you that he has departed to the realm of Yama, purified by the weapon," it is understood that the falling of the weapon removes sin; thus, there is the mention of being "purified" (*pūta*). For that very reason, there is the mention of "holding a sword in hand" (*kṛpāṇapāṇi*), since there would otherwise be no occasion for holding a weapon either before or after that event. However, if the reading were *aśastrapūta* ("not purified by the weapon"), the contradiction would be manifest, as it would involve the negation of purity while simultaneously enjoining impurity.

It has been prepared for your sake from the limb—a pure part—of a man who is free from defects such as being eunuch, diseased, burnt, or wounded; it is being offered for exchange at the price desired by us. Please accept it; take possession of it. The repetition [of the word] suggests respect. 12.

It was agitated, thrown into turmoil, and shaken from its place—as if uprooted—by a tumultuous, confused, and therefore indistinct clamor of voices rising up on all sides immediately after the loud proclamation. The cause of this was the density of the host of *pramatha* spirits appearing before one's eyes, resulting in an earthquake rooted in that very presence. Or rather: "The world, with its pillars of water trembling and its trees swaying..."
"The sky appears as if it were falling— whirling in confusion, displaced from its station, and loosened. (Ratnāvalī 1.54)

Thus, according to the logic stated by Setu, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that [the city] seems to be in motion due to its nature as being both perceptible and imperceptible amidst the agitation of the elements and the clamor of sounds. By saying "it is a marvel," he expresses astonishment at seeing what has never been seen before.

Regarding the passage beginning with *karṇābhyarṇa*: "near the ears" means close to the two ear-lobes (*śravaṇapālī*). As for the synonyms for proximity: "samīpa, nikaṭa, abhyarṇa, abhyagra, abhyāsa, antika, and bhuva."

"These words beginning with *samīpa* [proximity] are neuter when denoting a property (*dharma*), and [of all three genders] when denoting that which possesses it (*tadvat*)," according to the *Vaijayantī*. Also, "after *abhya*, [the suffix *cha* occurs] in the sense of proximity (*avidūrya*)."

(7-2-25) Thus, there is the absence of the augment *iṭ* after the root *abh*. "Torn apart" (*vidīrṇābhyām*) means for that very reason specifically split; this is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) derived from the root *dṛ*, meaning "to tear. "From the corners of the mouth" (*sṛkvabhyām*); Amara states: "The two edges of the lips are called *sṛkvaṇī*. "With a hideous" (*vikaṭena*) means with a deformed [face], by means of the gaping open of the mouth (*vyādānena*). Vaijayantī states: "And *vikaṭa* may mean deformed (*virūpa*). "With blazing fires" (*dīptāgnibhiḥ*) means with flaming fires; because of the natural disposition of that species, they are therefore known by the name "Meteor-mouthed" (*ulkāmukha*).

"With fangs formidable from their tips" means with large fangs that are broad at their points; "viśaṅkaṭa-daṃṣṭraiḥ" is the meaning. Alternatively, there is the reading "visaṅkaṭaiḥ," which means especially dense.
[As it is said: "The two central teeth are the *rājadanta*s (king-teeth), and the two on either side of them are the *daṃṣṭrā*s (fangs)."

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*. The expression "from here and there" (*ita itaḥ*) illuminates the state of being agitated by the search for prey. The description of the [beasts] as "running" (*dhāvadbhiḥ*) is stated as an epithet of their mouths; even though their bodies might be stationary at some point, because their necks (*kaṃdharā*) are long, this serves to reveal their wandering toward the ends of the quarters.
