Thus says Amara:
"Harṣa (joy) is clarity of mind; it arises for men at all times from the attainment of a desired object or from the acquisition of an inconceivable and wished-for thing."
Thus, by Harṣa as so characterized, [the king] was like a lotus blossomed by the morning sun, its contraction dispelled;
[he was recognized] by horripilation, embraces, perspiration,
graceful clapping of hands, the clarity of eyes and face, and also by sweet speech.

"The manifestations born of joy arise from a continuous stream of renunciations and gifts"—this is the meaning of the statement that the effects of joy are complete. Here, one should understand that the causes for the various rasas are presented: for *bhayānaka* (terror), by the phrase "like Rāhu seizing a digit of the moon" (*dasyor ānanacarīm*); for *karuṇa* (pathos), by "his beloved" (*preyasīm*); for *vismaya* (wonder), by "having encountered him by fate" (*daivāt samāsādya*); for *raudra* (wrath), by "of him" (*asya*)—implying he still lives and stands before us; and for *hāsya* (mirth), by "snatching [her] away from the reach of the sword's fall" (*kṛpāṇapātaviṣayād ācchindataḥ*). This is because even when words are syntactically consistent, the fitness of conveying a specific meaning depends solely upon expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*).

Otherwise, even in cases such as "Know Rāma to be Daśaratha," the fault of expressing a non-connection would ensue; for in that instance, Rāma, Janaka’s daughter, and the forest are the subjects (*uddeśya*), while the knowledge of Daśaratha, Sumitrā, and Ayodhyā are respectively the predicates (*vidheya*). Furthermore, within the composition of the text, because the two sentences would otherwise be inconsistent, it is proper to establish the syntactic connection by following the sense. This should be understood everywhere. *Katham* means "in what manner"; *vartatām* means "let it remain."

The meaning is this: while it is possible for a single object to exist in only one mode, the mind—being constantly tormented in a thousand ways by various modes such as dejection and the like that manifest in a variegated manner—is unable to remain stable in any single mode whatsoever. In this regard, there is the principle: "There is no fault in the mention of a transitory emotion (sañcārī-bhāva) by its own name in certain cases."

Because of this statement, since it is difficult to describe things established by one's own experience without such a reflection (*parāmarśa*), there is no fault even in expressing them by their own names; it is "implied" (*ārtha*) in the same way as in the verse beginning with *autsukyena kṛtatvarā*. Here, the figure of speech is *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence), for although the connection of the whole is expressed by direct hearing (*śrauta*), the sequential relationship of the parts is perceived through the pursuit of the logical sequence of the meanings, based on the relation of cause and effect.

And there is also simile (*upamā*). Emotional complexity (*bhāva-śabalatva*), however, is quite evident. Furthermore, the performance here possesses general representation (*sāmānyābhinaya*), because the four types of representation—bodily (*āṅgika*), vocal (*vācika*), internal (*sāttvika*), and external (*āhārya*)—are present. //28//

"Are! is an address with reproach; the repetition [of the word] reveals the speaker's haste. By the terms "O Brahmin child! and "O infant of a Brahmin!", he indicates that a Brahmin is naturally devoid of the strength of arms, let alone in his childhood. Furthermore, because he has repeatedly and deliberately sought out the murder of a Brahmin, this suggests: "By good fortune, we are now prospering through the arrival of that very act."

"Smelled by a tiger," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "smelled by a tiger" (*vyāghreṇa śārdūlena āghrātāyām*): the expression "smelled" (*āghrātā*) is used because of the saying, "Beasts see with their sense of smell. This implies that she was pursued by one who smelled her with intent and seized her out of a desire to devour her. Regarding the "deer" (*mṛgī*), meaning a female deer (*hariṇī*): "by the logic" (*nyāyena*) refers to the sequence of events for the male deer (*hariṇa*), whose mind was bewildered and agitated by compassion (*kāruṇya*). The "logic" here is that even though he could do nothing [to help her], he himself made an effort to perish along with her. This is exactly what happened.

The meaning is that even for you, there is an assault upon me due to compassion regarding your beloved. "One who delights in violence" refers to one whose taste and excessive passion lie in the slaughter of living beings. "O sinner," because you create obstacles to the worship of the Goddess, you are a doer of evil deeds. "Of him who possesses the banner of animal sacrifice"—that is, he who has obtained a banner marked by the victory over merciless people through the offering of embodied beings made a thousand times for the sake of worship; or alternatively, "ketana" means an invitation or initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the act of sacrificing living beings.

Because of the traditional legal text (*smṛti*) stating, "They do not deserve an invitation to a *śrāddha* feast," [the word] "attained" implies that you have arrived by the impulsion of destiny (*niyati*), and not that you were brought here by my effort. The use of the word "me" expresses the excellence [of the sacrifice] through the powers of body, vital breath, mind, mantra, and tantra. "Within range" means a place reachable by hand. "I, who was thus provoked by you of your own accord"—this is the meaning of "so'ham. "Previously" means before this maiden; for it is intended that she herself shall later be offered as a sacrifice.

"By you alone"—let it be that she was to be protected; the meaning is: "by you alone," who have arrived with the thought that she is already protected. Or, because the Brahmin is primary, the meaning may be: "by you alone," as the principal sacrificial offering (*pradhānahaviṣā*) from the Brahmin woman. She is the "mother of beings" (*bhūtajananī*), for she is the source of the creation of all beings—both moving and unmoving—who are the objects of the notion of existence (*asti-pratyaya*), since she is the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*). This is in accordance with the statement: "Among beings, living creatures are the best. "I satisfy" (*ṛdhnomi*) means I please her.
"By the blow of the sword" (*khaḍgāhatyā*) means by the stroke of the sword; "of one whose shoulders are severed" (*vyastaskandhasya*) means of one whose base of the neck has been separated.

"Skandha, bhujaśiras, and aṃsa are masculine," according to the *Vaijayantī*. For this very reason, regarding the lower body of a headless trunk (*kabandha*)—"A *kabandha* is a headless torso endowed with action," according to the *Amara-kośa*—its "opening" (*randhra*) is the cavity of the throat-tube, which has the nature of "flowing forth" (*niṣyandituṃ śīlam*) a "mass of blood" (*rudhiraprāgbhāram*), that is, a burden of gore. The use of the term *prāgbhāra* (mass/burden) reveals that, due to its youthfulness and splendor, it possesses fresh and complete bodily constituents (*dhātu*). Here, the Furious Sentiment (*raudrarasa*) is manifested. The poetic figure is either *nidarśanā* (illustration) or *dṛṣṭānta* (simile). //29//

Then, reflecting upon its cruelty regardless of any specific qualities it might possess, he spoke with indignation: "It is essence-less," and so forth. "Essence" (*sāra*) refers to that portion which is worthy of being adopted; that which is devoid of this is "essence-less. Since this [world] alone possesses such essence, he describes the ocean of worldly activity (*lokavyavahāra-sāgara*)—the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) agitated by the waves of birth, death, and so on, and rendered unstable by the blows of the submarine fire of the three types of suffering.

With its supreme treasure stolen away, meaning all its most excellent things have been carried off by thieves, for she alone is that treasure; the three worlds—consisting of heaven, the earth, and the netherworld (pātāla)—which comprise seven and fourteen divisions respectively due to their internal subdivisions; deprived of light, meaning it is overcome by darkness because it is devoid of illumination, for she alone is that light;

with death as its refuge, meaning for whom the abandonment of life itself is the protector from the pain of grief; the circle of kinsmen, where "kinsmen" (bāndhava) refers to relatives such as fathers and so forth—the suffix being used in its own sense (*svārthe*)—and their entire assembly; and devoid of pride.
"That disposition which causes men to engage even in objects free from passion, being subject to pleasure and tranquility, is called pride."

Thus, [he thought: "The one devoid of pride" (lakṣitadarparahitam) refers to Kandarpa, Kāma, because she alone is the cause of his pride. "The creation of the eyes of people"—the creation of the sense-organ of sight for the world of beings by the Creator (Brahmā)—is "fruitless," being without purpose, since the very sight of her constitutes its fruit. "The entire world" is like a "worn-out forest," a forest long abandoned and burnt by fire, devoid of fruits, flowers, and shoots; for in her absence, the world is unfit for enjoyment.
"To create" means to bring into being; he has "resolved," having made a firm determination. The suffix *niṣṭhā* is used here in the active sense (*kartari*).
"An effort arises to perform some task;
he for whom that effort remains unfulfilled until the completion of the task is also called by that name," says Divākara. How have you resolved?

By the phrase "in what manner have you resolved [to do this]?", it is illuminated that even the mere resolution to perform such an act—which is far removed from being a means—is difficult for a conscious being; here, through this [resolution], there arises the perception of happiness within this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) which is essentially suffering.

In sequence, it is suggested that she is the very essence of spring; that she is the ornament of the three worlds; that she is more alluring than moonlight and the like due to her preeminent loveliness; that she has bound her kinsmen with the fetters of her manifold virtues; that she has instilled in the God of Love the hope of victory even without cause; that she delights the eyes of people with the beauty of her form; and that she renders the world a source of enjoyment for the amorous, just as a flowering creeper adorns a garden.

Although the subjects (uddeśya), such as *saṃsāra* and so forth, and the predicates (vidheya), such as their worthlessness and so forth, are generally synonymous, it should be understood that when they are stated again by a speaker whose mind is overwhelmed by affection for a beloved or by hatred toward an enemy, this is not merely a fault but is indeed a merit. This is because of the statement in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*: "Sometimes even a fault becomes a merit; sometimes neither. And: "If what was previously stated is repeated again without distinction, that is called 'redundancy' (*ekārtha*); however, it is not a fault for those whose minds are captivated by aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)."

And because of these words of the illustrious Bhoja: "In this context, since the killing of the jewel-like maiden—which you have undertaken—is impossible as a literal connection of objects due to its effecting the worthlessness of worldly existence and the like, a simile is constructed. This is the ornament of *mālā-nidarśanā* (the garland-simile). Alternatively, because the attempt to kill Mālatī is identified with the effecting of the worthlessness of worldly existence and so forth, it is the ornament of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole)."

In this context, the notion that "kinsmen are a refuge at the time of death" has entered [the mind] as a point of contention, even though it contradicts the [actual] companion [of the dying person]. Since this lacks the status of a formal simile (*upamā*), that too is a defect already answered by the previous resolution. Here, the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇa-rasa*) is suggested (*dhvanyate*), as well as indignation toward the enemy. Through the mutually incensed words beginning with "O wretched Brahmin boy" and "O evil-souled, heretical outcaste," the *toṭaka* meter is employed. (30)

Reflecting again upon those offenses, his anger intensified, and he said: "praṇayisakhī... and so forth. By the word *praṇayinīnām* (of the affectionate ones), his compassion is illuminated through his being overwhelmed by love for them even more than for his own body; by *sakhīnām* (of the friends), their status as objects of affection and confidence is shown. In their playful passion for joking, accompanied by the imitation of their beloved, there is a delight in play. As it is said: "Līlā is that imitation of the beloved by both women and men, joined with affection, through sweet words, gestures, and movements of the limbs."

Thus was *līlā* defined; according to Amara, it refers to "fluid play and jesting. By "attained" (*adhigataiḥ*), it means obtained. "By blows with lovely *śirīṣa* flowers" refers to those strikes made with *śirīṣa* blossoms that are tender due to their lack of wilting. Alternatively, "lovely" (*lalitaiḥ*) may qualify the "blows," meaning they are produced by charming [actions]. It "faints" (*tāmyati*), becoming withered like a fresh sprout touched by fire. "Therein," in that body—that is, regarding that physical form—"of one who hurls," meaning one who projects [the flowers] nearby.

Alternatively, he speaks of his lack of discrimination by comparing him to one who hurls a weapon for the slaughter of a victim about to perform a sacrifice; due to the extreme disparity between them, he says that Yama’s punishment is like a sudden thunderbolt—meaning it falls unexpectedly and without warning, striking instantly like a bolt from the blue, being the staff of Yama, the Time-Spirit.
As it is said: "Now, Vaivasvata Yama is the punisher of those whose sins are concealed."

From this statement, the grasping of Yama’s staff is indicated; furthermore, the sufficiency of the arm for taking a life is illuminated here. The poetic figures (alaṅkāras) are the incongruous *kāvyaliṅga* and *upamā*. The passage beginning with "praṇayisakhī" constitutes a *saṃpheṭa*, due to the speech of anger. //31//

He speaks with derision: "Strike! Strike!"—the meaning is, "What power do you have to strike me? He explains that very point: "This is not you. This water is such [as it appears], while you are merely approaching; this is because of the use of the middle voice (*madhyama-puruṣa*). "It is not" means "you will perish instantly"; the present tense (*laṭ*) is used here to denote proximity to the present (*vartamāna-sāmīpye*).

Out of affection, fearing his impending downfall, she says: "Be gracious, O rash Lord! Truly, this cursed one is cruel. Save me by turning back from this perilous uncertainty. Be gracious—grant me your favor. The reason for this is: "cruel" means harsh; "truly" (*khalu*) indicates a well-known fact; "cursed" (*hatāśa*) refers to one whose hope or intention (*āśā*) is ruined or corrupted by its focus on unrighteousness. Alternatively, it refers to one by whom the directions have been defiled through his own wicked deeds.

He states the manner of his confidence: "from this form of the body," meaning from the uncertainty of misfortune—that is, from the doubt regarding calamity—because there is no certainty of victory in either case; "having desisted" means having ceased [the fight]. "Protect me" means that since my own ruin is inseparable from your ruin, protecting you alone is protecting me. In the reading *ṇivvattīadu*, the ellipsis is "let it be turned back by you.
The ablative case is used because the sense is "cessation" (virāma), according to the rule *jugupsā-virāma-pramādārthānām upasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini 1.4.25).
"Be vigilant and attentive! Strike!

Kill!"—the connection [of these commands] with Mālatī and Kapālakuṇḍalā is respectively according to their order; that is to say, Aghoraghaṇṭa aims at Mālatī, while [Mādhava] aims at Kapālakuṇḍalā. This unification of speech, according to the dramatic convention, serves as the basis for the representation of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

"Exercise fortitude," and so forth—"exercise" means establish it, because it has wavered. The use of the past tense in "was killed" (*hata*) is intended to show that there is no doubt in this matter. In Mādhava's speech, "this one" (*eṣa*) refers to the Kāpālika; in his [the Kāpālika's] speech, it refers to Mādhava. "Wicked" (*pāpa*) is used because he is clothed in a mass of great sins and because he destroys worship. "What" (*kim*) is used as an interrogative particle. "Or" (*vā*) is used as a particle of option. The meaning is: "Has it ever been experienced by anyone, or has it been witnessed directly?"

In the act of combat with the *sāraṅga* deer—that is, in engaging in battle with the deer—the thunderbolt-like hands of [the Lord], which are accustomed to cleaving the mountain peaks in the form of the elephant’s frontal globes (*kumbha*), possess the quality of shattering the mountain summits that are the elephant’s head-masses. As Amara states: "The two *kumbhas* are the two globes of the head," and "A *kūṭa* is a peak, a summit, or a horn. By metaphorically describing the two *kumbhas* as *kūṭas*, the metaphorical representation of the elephant as a mountain is established. [The suffix] *ṣākan* is applied after the roots *jalpa*, *bhikṣa*, *kuṭṭa*, *luṇṭa*, and *vṛṅ*.

(3-2-155) Thus, the suffix *ṣākan* is applied. By the word *pāṇikuliśa*, the nails situated on the hand are identified through poetic hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). The propriety of calling them a *kuliśa* (thunderbolt) follows from the mention of their "peak-like" nature (*kūṭatva*), for the thunderbolt is well-known for its power to split the peaks of mountains. [The words] "of Hari" and "of Indra" flash forth [in the mind], referring respectively to the lion and the god Śakra. "Pramāda" (heedlessness) means, by indication (*lakṣaṇā*), a lapse of attention or addiction to improper activity. Here, the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is suggested (*dhvani*).
The poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) are: *prativastūpamā* based on contrast (*vaidharmya*), *ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka* (partial metaphor), and *atiśayokti*. //32//

"Seekers of Mālatī" means those whose nature it is to search for Mālatī; that is to say, those whose habit is to wander here and there for the purpose of finding her. "Consoling" means making [her] free from grief by recounting auspicious omens and the like. "Of unimpeded movement" (*apratihatagati*) refers to one possessing the power of knowledge extending to all paths. According to the rule, "verbs meaning 'to go' have the sense of 'to know'," the word *gati* denotes knowledge. This is based on the rule: "The root *gam* is used with the suffix *ṇic* except in the sense of cognition."

This is because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the root *gam* also possesses the meaning of "making known," as in [the rule] 2-4-46. Let it be completely surrounded—that is, let it be attacked from all sides. From the statement "this," the proximity of the speaker to the abode of Karālā is to be understood.

He states the reason for her persistence with the words beginning "not from Aghoraghaṇṭa," and so forth. "Elsewhere" means in another person. It is "terrible and wonderful" (*dāruṇādbhutam*): terrible because it takes the form of the murder of an innocent woman; wonderful because she was drawn away at midnight from the midst of her circle of friends who were staying on the upper veranda. "From the offering to Karālā" means giving [the victim] as a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to Karālā. "Another fruit" refers to some other purpose. "Is perceived" (*vibhāvyate*) means it is discerned. This connects with the phrase "she thus commanded. [This is according to the rule] *anyārād...* [Pāṇini 2.3.29].

By the rule beginning with "itthambhūtalakṣaṇe" (Pāṇini 2.3.21), the fifth case is used in connection with the word *anya*. Here, the figure of speech is *anumāna* (inference); furthermore, this constitutes the internal limb (*garbhāṅga*) called *anumāna*, because there is an inferential deduction (*abhyūhana*) from a mark (*liṅga*). //33//
The Kāpālika’s female companion said fearfully to the Kāpālika, “We are hemmed in; we are besieged,” meaning by the minister’s soldiers.

The Kāpālika replied with composure, “Now, amidst this great pressure from many people, especially and to an extraordinary degree, this is the occasion, the time for manly valor. For while such fame as that could not have arisen from one person defeating a single opponent, when one defeats many, it is praiseworthy in every respect; therefore, one must exert oneself and display prowess.”

Regarding the phrase "the speed of their journey through the expanse of the sky," it should be understood that although these two possess the power to travel through the heavens, their progress has been obstructed because they are bound by the noose of demerit (*adharma*).

Having heard the words of her own kinsmen from outside, Mālatī says with longing, "Alas, Father! and "Alas, Blessed One! The meaning is that, because both Bhūrivasu and Kāmandakī have been called to mind, she weeps while uttering their names, recollecting their sorrow.

"Well-situated among the circle of kinsmen" means standing fearlessly within the assembly of relatives. The passage beginning with "Let it be so" refers to the panic, arising from the mention of the execution of the Kāpālika.

Moving from another previous location toward his kinsmen and directing them to another place, they—having their anger inflamed by the recollection of the insults suffered from their beloved and by the obstruction of their worship—spoke these words beginning with "kaṭhorāsthi" (hard bones). [The corpse] is talkative, making a loud noise through the clashing together of hard bone-joints and the articulations of the skeletal connections, a specific sound resembling the noise produced when striking black stone with a mason's chisel.

For whom the cessation of the momentum of the fall was effected for a brief moment by the cutting of the rough, hard tendons, joints, and veins—just as the descent of an axe engaged in splitting hard wood is slightly delayed by being caught in the coils of a matured creeper; who is "free from fear" (nirātaṅka), meaning devoid of apprehension, which here figuratively denotes the absence of any obstruction; [moving] "as if in mud," because there is no solid substance in the way.

In the "masses of flesh" (*piśitapiṇḍeṣu*), meaning the thick flesh in regions such as the shoulders and buttocks; "sword" (*asi*) refers to a scimitar; "limb by limb" (*gātraṃ gātram*) means each individual member; "instantly" (*sapadi*) reveals that wrath cannot endure for any interval of time; "in pieces" (*lavaśaḥ*) means having made it into bits like sesame seeds; "let him scatter" (*vikiratu*) means let him throw [them] about in all directions. The verb form is the imperative (*loṭ*) in the sense of a command (*vidhi*). Here, the Furious (*raudra*) sentiment is manifested. The figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) is *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state). The "firm bones" (*kaṭhorāsthi*) and so forth constitute "resolve" (*vyavasāya*), because one's own power is expressed. This is also the dramatic element (*ārabhaṭyaṅga*) called *sampheṭa*:
"A *sampheṭa* is a violent clash between two persons who are enraged and agitated."
Because of this statement. //34//
"All have departed"—[referring to]:
"A long journey, execution, battle, the ruin of a kingdom, country, or the like;
imprisonment, eating, bathing, sexual intercourse, and the application of unguents."

"Because of the scriptural injunction, 'One should not point out directly such things as the seizing of garments,' he concludes the act with the exit of the characters, intending to indicate the battle and the slaying of the Kāpālika through the *viṣkambhaka* (interlude) that follows; thus all is entirely auspicious."
Thus, by the grace of Pūrṇajyotis, Pūrṇasarasvatī has composed this exposition of the meaning of the fifth act of the *Mālatīmādhava*.
Thus ends the fifth act.
Now begins the sixth act.

Now he begins the *viṣkambhaka* with the words "entering" (*praviśya*). [The word] *āḥ* is defined in the *Vaijayantī* as being used in the senses of anger and pain. "On account of Mālatī" (*mālatīnimittam*)—that is, for the sake of Mālatī—is an adverbial modifier of the action of "overthrowing. The expression "on account of Mālatī" highlights the persistence of enmity toward her as the cause. "Our teacher has been overthrown" (*vinipātitāsmadguruḥ*) means he has been killed; the use of the plural number in "our" (*asmākam*) indicates one's own power to subdue him. By the explanatory phrase "by whom our teacher [was slain]," it is made known that he was killed by Mādhava on the field of battle.

"O wretched Mādhava! O you whose character is ruined by the name of Mādhava!"—this is an address directed toward the air. At that moment, by the statement "she was struck down," the meaning is the time of her falling; "striking mercilessly" means striking cruelly. The word "even" (*api*) reveals her own inviolability: she is one who has been disregarded and treated with contempt because she is a woman, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*): "Brahmins, cows, women, children, and kinsmen are not to be slain.
By this low compassion, the hero's *sāttvika* quality known as "splendor" (*śobhā*) is revealed.
"Compassion toward the inferior and rivalry toward the superior [are appropriate]; in beauty, there is heroism and skill.

According to this saying. "With anger"—the meaning is that he enacts the transformation of anger by reflecting upon her injury. "That"—meaning, because of that, since I am alive. "Inevitably" (*avaśyam*) means unfailingly. By the name "Kapālakuṇḍalā," and not by "I," she indicates her well-known power. "Vilasitam" (sport) refers to its ripening.

He establishes the stated point through an illustration with the verse beginning "Whence peace? and so forth. Whence, from what cause, can there be peace—that is, the tranquility of the mind—for one who has always been agitated by being a source of suspicion toward the enemy of serpents (the peacock), having killed the male of a serpent pair? Regarding that object, they have not abandoned their lingering resentment—that is, they have not relinquished long-standing hatred.
As it is said: "Lingering resentment (*anuśaya*) refers to remorse, as well as to long-standing hatred and its persistence."

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*. The word "always" (*sadā*) means eternally; the particle "even" (*eva*) is displaced in its order [to be read after *jāgarti*]. She "is ever awake" (*jāgartyeva*), meaning she never sleeps; the verbal root *jāgṛ* signifies "the cessation of sleep. She exists as one who is "ever vigilant," that is to say, constantly seeking out vulnerabilities. "For the sake of stinging" (*daṃśāya*) means for the purpose of biting. "With the tips of her fangs sharpened" (*niśātadaṃṣṭrākoṭiḥ*) means having the points of her fangs made keen. "Heavy with the emission of venom" (*viṣodgāraguruḥ*) means heavy due to the spitting of poison, possessing unimpeded power. A "female serpent" (*bhujaṅgī*) is a female nāga, the companion of a slain male nāga, distressed by separation from him.

Here, the figure of speech is the *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration) by way of contrast (*vaidharmya*). This is because the statement regarding the lotus (*padma*) serves as a clear reflection (*pratibimba*) of the "originals" (*bimba*) mentioned in the sentence "That must necessarily [be done]"—namely, the Kāpālika, his slayer Mādhava, and herself who desires to retaliate against him; this is reflected respectively by the "serpent" (*bhujaṅga*), the enemy of that serpent, and the female serpent (*bhujaṅgī*). Furthermore, it constitutes an illustration by contrast because the reason for what was stated—"you shall experience"—is established through a contrasting argument.

Alternatively, disregarding the preceding sentence, upon close consideration, there is either *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), because the subject matter at hand is understood by means of what is not the subject matter, or *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because the subject matter at hand is apprehended through the suppression [of its own nature] by means of a similar thing. The phrase "you will necessarily experience" and so forth constitutes a contradiction, because it is spoken with vehemence. //1//

Now, for the sake of the hero's objective, the poet establishes a connection with the previously introduced festival of Mālatī’s marriage—specifically that she "was bestowed upon Nandana by the king"—by means of the following: [Offstage: "O Kings," and so forth. This connects with what is to be said later, namely, "he issues this command. The manner of the command is: "O Kings," and so on.

The mention of "Rājagṛha" is for the purpose of indicating that, because the festival was inaugurated by the universal monarch Padmāvatīśvara, the subordinate rulers—who were bowed down by his majesty and devotion—performed the duties of servants. "Those of the final age" refers to those whose life-stage is the final or last, meaning those who have passed ninety years and are in their tenth decade; by the mention of their old age, their knowledge of the Dharma is implied, for otherwise, like animals and the like, they would be unfit even for the designation of being "old."

"According to the saying, 'That is no assembly where there are no elders; nor are they elders who do not speak of dharma,' [the word] *teṣām* refers to those who are experts in Vedic and worldly conduct. By their *ājñayā*, that is, by their command or appointment, proceed (*sañcaradhvam*)—that is, engage—in the duties to be performed (*kartavyeṣu*), such as the erection of arches, the setting up of pillars, the hanging of canopies, the decoration of the pavilion, and so forth. Regarding the expression *ājñayā sañcaradhvam*, [the rule] applies: 'after the prefix *sam-* joined with the third case...'"

(1-3-54) Thus, the *ātmanepada* [ending is used]. The meaning is: that which is pleasant to hear even when heard without reflecting on its meaning—a means of auspiciousness such as the recitation of the *puṇyāha-svasti-vācana* and so forth, and the *sahasranāma* and so forth; "the gods of the earth" refers to the Brāhmaṇas, for they alone have the authority to officiate at sacrifices (*yājana*); "let them recite" means let them study.

Let there be performed—that is, let it be set in motion—a spectacle distinguished by various modes such as singing, instrumental music, and dancing, by means of multitudes of diverse utterances; that is to say, by actors, dancers, cymbal-players, wandering bards, and others, whose collections of words are devoted to the praise of various specific deities such as Hari, Hara, Pitāmaha, Skanda, Kandarpa, Rudrāṇī, Indrāṇī, and so forth. The plural number is used for "auspicious rites" (*maṅgalebhyaḥ*) because they differ according to their function as means for achieving results such as longevity, health, sovereignty, good fortune, and the prosperity of sons, all for the sake of worldly advancement (*abhyudaya*).

"Proximate" means separated by only three or four *nāḍikās* (periods of twenty-four minutes). "He urges us on excessively" means he strongly encourages us toward such activities—this is the ellipsis. "The entry into the wedding procession" (*janyayātrāpraveśaḥ*): the procession (*yātrā*) of the *janyas*, that is, the kinsmen of the bridegroom; their arrival for the sake of a festival or for the purpose of choosing the bride.
As it is said: "The *janyas* are the relatives and servants of the newlywed, or the affectionate friends of the bridegroom."

Thus [it is said], and the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "The *śāntiyātrā* is the invitation of the bridegroom. The non-use of the word *śānti* here is due to common usage. Alternatively, the *janyayātrā* is the bridegroom’s procession (*varayātrā*) as indicated by the term *janya*; the *Vaijayantī* states: "The *daundubhī* [musical instrument] is used in the bridegroom’s procession (*varayātrā*). And it should be understood that this is for the purpose of concealing what has been done. Its "entry" (*praveśa*): the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*) associated with that [procession] is called "entry," because one enters into it. The phrase "he hastens exceedingly" is a statement regarding the performance of actions conducive to that [entry].

Here, the figure of speech is *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth), because the effect—the movement about [the stage] and so forth—is supported by its cause—haste for entering. Alternatively, it is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description), because through the effect—the movement and so forth—the cause, namely the festival of Mālatī’s wedding, is indicated. //2//

"Until"—that is, during that period of time—the word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the sense of the sentence; meanwhile, the relatives (*bandhavaḥ*), desiring a connection through the daughter as the medium of relation—just as Murāri stated, "Pulastya, Pulaha, and others are the relatives"—do not arrive, do not come. During that very period of time, she is called the "city deity" (*nagaradevatā*); this indicates her necessity for being approached because she is both the presiding deity of the region and the family deity (*kuladevatā*).
[This is done] for unimpeded auspiciousness—that is, for welfare free from obstacles—for otherwise, "the neglect of honoring those worthy of honor obstructs one's prosperity."

This is because obstacles arise according to this principle (*nyāya*). The word "and" (*anyacca*) serves to draw in the verb "commands" (*ādiśati*). "Having assumed special ornaments" (*gṛhītasaviśeṣamaṇḍana*) means that since she was already adorned previously by the expansion of her divine powers (*vibhūti*), she has now accepted even more exquisite decorations for the sake of the festival. "Let him wait" (*pratīkṣatām*) means let him await her as she goes out. "An attendant" (*ānuyātrika*) refers to one whose purpose is following and service; the meaning is "retinue.
The words "O King," and so forth, constitute an incitement (*prarocanā*), because they present a future event as if it were already accomplished.

"Let it be so"—this signifies a partial acceptance; "let it be performed in vain, for I shall uproot you from your very foundation"—this is the underlying sense. *Itaḥ* means from this [place]. *Parikarma* refers to the preparation consisting of the settling of people in the service-quarters and the employment of various individuals in their respective tasks; in that regard, there were doorkeepers (*pratīhāra*) with cane-staves in their hands, who were hurried and agitated—a hundred of them, from whom the place was crowded and congested. (The *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "The two door-keepers at the gate are called *pratīhāra*"). *Saṅkulāt* means from the congestion.
"Regarding the injury to Mādhava"—that is, aiming for something unpleasant toward Mādhava—"intent," meaning persistent, or rather, seeking out a vulnerability.
She exits, having indicated the past event of the killing of the Kāpālika, the future calamity caused by Kapālakuṇḍalā, and the departure of Mālatī; thus he concludes the *viṣkambhaka*.
[End of the *viṣkambhaka*]
Now he begins the act for the purpose of representing the actual events: "Then enters Kalahaṃsa.

Kalahaṃsa says: "I have been commanded," and so forth. "I have been commanded by my lord, who is staying in the inner sanctum of the city deity's temple, together with Makaranda. By saying "with Makaranda," he indicates that Makaranda is present with him. "By my lord" means by the master Mādhava. "Find out first whether Mālatī has set out in this direction or not. "In this direction" (*itomu-kham*) is an adverbial phrase meaning "with her face turned toward this region. "Set out" (*pravṛttā*) means she has departed.

Alternatively, the word "no" (na) indicates apprehension regarding misfortune, according to the maxim that "prosperities are beset by many obstacles. By this turn of speech, it is revealed—preceded by the intentional hint from Kāmandakī—that these two were already staying within the inner sanctum of the city deity's shrine, and that Mālatī’s approach to them occurred by her command. Furthermore, this connects with the statement, "One must depart for the sake of unimpeded auspiciousness. The meaning is: "I shall gladden [her] with pleasant words.
The word *yāvat* is used either as a poetic embellishment (*vākyālaṅkāra*) or for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
Now, because their presence in the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) has been indicated, he states the entrance of the hero and the supporting hero (*upanāyaka*): "Then they enter.

Having determined one of the two outcomes—success or failure—and having extracted either life or death [from that certainty], the bold Dhṛṣṭa says, "Of Mālatī," and so forth. Starting from the day of the first sight—that is, taking as the beginning the day of her departure for the Madana garden marked by that initial vision—he describes [the love] which is "expanding" (*vistāriṇaḥ*), meaning increasing of its own accord merely by the sight of the sweetness of her form. "Expanding" (*vistāribhiḥ*) is a corrupt reading, because it would render words such as *bhūyaḥ* (again) redundant.

Furthermore, later on, by means of affectionate gestures—meaning acts of love, specific modes of conduct, such as drawing portraits, wearing or giving jasmine garlands, listening [to her voice], turning pale, fainting, and speaking incoherently during moments of death—the deer-eyed Mālatī brought him to the highest pinnacle, having raised him to the ultimate limit.

"They experienced the supreme limit of bliss," as stated in the *Kādambarī*. "Now" (*adya*) means at this present time; for there is no possibility of another time to be awaited, such as "from now on" (as previously mentioned), "tomorrow," or "the day after tomorrow. "End" (*antaḥ*) means the conclusion. "Indeed" (*khalu*) is used for emphasis. "In every way" (*sarvathā*) means by every possible manner, that is to say, whether in success or in failure.

The word *asya* ("of this") is a gesture indicating that which is being experienced; it refers to the "toil of love," meaning the suffering produced by Kāma, which is intensified on all sides by factors such as internal and external circumstances, place, time, and condition. "Welfare" (*kalyāṇam*) means the auspicious attainment of the beloved. "The policy of the Illustrious Lady" refers to the strategy and application of means employed by Kāmandakī. Let it "go astray" (*viparyetu*), meaning let it undergo reversal or change due to the occurrence of obstacles to that attainment. Here, the two mental states (*bhāva*) known as joy (*harṣa*) and fortitude (*dhṛti*) are manifested.
Paralelism (vikalpa) is an ornament, because it is composed through the state of rivalry between two [alternatives] of equal strength regarding their establishment or non-establishment. //3//

Then, perceiving his intention—which was intent on the effort of giving up his life in the event that he could not obtain her—[the author] dispels the suspicion of any other alternative by means of a logical argument: by the phrase "of the Blessed One," he indicates the fulfillment of her resolve because her power is well-known; and the blessing "samedhā" (may she be endowed with wisdom), for the *Vaijayantī* states: "wisdom (*medhā*) is intelligence (*dhī*) possessed of retentive power (*dhāraṇā*)."

By the word *medhā* (wisdom), its effect—the application of political strategy—is meant; *āśāsti* (blessing) is that which is accompanied by this [strategy], namely a benediction preceded by affection, such as "May it be well with him. Regarding the objection "How so?", [the answer is] "In what manner will it be reversed?"—that is, how could it become the opposite? By the maxim "Even from a curse, even from an arrow," the meaning is that when these two, each capable on its own, are combined, there may never be a failure of the result, just as in the case of fire and wind together.

The passage beginning with "Of Mālatī, first... and ending with "...how could the blessing of her intellect fail? constitutes an *ākṣepa* (anticipation), because it sets forth the seed of the plot (*garbhabīja*) in the form of the Blessed Lady’s plan. "Nātha" and so forth: "O Lord, congratulations! Mālatī has indeed set out toward this very goal.
The particle *api* is used here in the sense of a question; not believing that such a fortune could truly belong to himself, he asks, "Is it really so? (satyaṃ kim?).

"Aśraddadhānaḥ" means not trusting. Halāyudha states: "Faith (*śraddhā*) is the conviction that 'it is so'. It is not merely that she has set out or departed; rather, she is *pratyāsannā*, meaning she has become close at hand. He establishes this proximity as follows: "Of us," and so forth. "In one step" (*ekapade*) means at the very moment of placing the first foot, without even the opportunity for the second foot to move; by this, it is said to be within a single instant (*kṣaṇa*). This is based on the usage: "This separation from her occurred in one step. [The word] *pada* is used in the senses of place, arrow, protection, footprint, and footprints.

"Regarding sound, a ray, a thing, a sentence, determination, and designation"—thus says the *Vaijayantī*. "Scattered by the wind," meaning dispersed by the breeze; this suggests its being characteristic of the rainy season (*prāvṛṣeṇya*). "In which there is a resemblance (*anukṛti*) to the thundering (*rasita*), the rumbling, of the mass of clouds (*jīmūtajāla*). "From whose birth (*janma*)—that is, origin—there is a thousandfold [sound] from auspicious *mṛdaṅga* drums, deep-sounding and bottomless, upon hearing the sound of which [the rain] becomes a cause of welfare. "The *mṛdaṅgas* are *murajas*," according to Amara.

The compound *maṅgalamṛdaṅga* is formed according to the rule for compounds such as *śākapārthiva*. It "removes" or sets aside that capacity—the proficiency of the sense of hearing—which consists in the grasping or hearing of other sounds, that is, sounds distinct from itself. Here, the poetic figures are *udātta* (the sublime) and *atiśayokti* (hyperbole). //4//
"Come, come! Through the lattice-path—that is, through the opening of the window in the inner chamber; for the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: 'Lattice (*jāla*) means a window or a net.
In that manner, as described, they act—they perform [the rite]; the meaning is that they look on.

'O Lord! and so forth: O Lord! Behold, behold! Here, first of all, are the masses of auspicious umbrellas, which bear the likeness of broad-tipped white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*) in a lake upon the surface of the sky-court, where waves are stirred by rows of plantain trees swaying under the impulse of the breeze from chowries as beautiful as the grace of soaring royal swans."

[Of those] delightful [and] captivating white yak-tail fly-whisks, which possess a grace and movement like that of soaring royal swans; and of the plantain-tree banners on the elephants' standards, fluttering through the impulsion of the wind—[as described in the verse]:
"High above, a row of forest-like plantain trees was shimmering."

Thus it is as stated by Māgha. According to the *Vaijayantī*, "the plantain tree (*kadalī*) is the emblem (*ketu*) of elephants. By means of these [plantain trees], which form rows (*paṅkti*), the lake was made wavy—having acquired surging waves—and for that very reason, it became shallow, having lost its depth, because its upper portion was demarcated by them. As it is said: "The word *nimna* means deep (*gabhīra*); *uttāna* is the opposite of that."

Thus says Amara. Alternatively, as in the expression "lying on one's back" (*uttānaśaya*), the meaning is that they possess an expansive form above due to the density of their lower parts. They bear the grace—the playful charm—of white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*) whose stalks have emerged, which are dense with one another and joined together, belonging to a lake in the form of the courtyard of the sky. These are collections of umbrellas intended for auspiciousness; by the mention of "auspicious umbrellas," their whiteness is implied.

The meaning is that, due to their swaying motion in the vast sky-lake of their own will, the chowries assume the state of royal swans, the plantain trees the state of waves, and the auspicious parasols the state of white lotuses. Here, the poetic figure is *udātta* (the exalted) combined with *rūpaka* (metaphor).

They are seen—female elephants occupied by throngs of courtesans, who fill the expanse of their cheeks with playful mouthfuls of betel-leaf and raise a sweet, auspicious clamor of singing; who scatter the sky with fragments of Indra’s bow imitated by the radiance of various jeweled ornaments; and whose tinkling jingling resounds with the chiming of shimmering golden bells.

The phrase "savilāsakabalita" (swallowed with grace) indicates that even the manner of chewing betel-leaf brings beauty to the face through its artistry. Because their mouths were filled with betel, [the sounds] were "pratiskhalita"—meaning they stumbled or were obstructed from emerging—as the cheeks expanded; they were "madhura" (sweet) due to the smoothness and redness of their throats and their skill in performance, thus being "hṛdayagrāhin" (heart-captivating); and because they consisted of hymns to deities appropriate for the occasion, they were "maṅgalārtha" (auspicious), while the "udgītakolāhala" refers to the loud, resonant clamor of singing at a high pitch.

By means of the clusters of rays—the masses of light—from various ornaments made of great gems such as rubies and others, which were of diverse colors—red, white, blue, yellow, and dark—the meaning being that these rays fell upon the bodies of the female elephants which were blue in color; by these rays acting as the cause, the surface of the sky was "mocked," that is, imitated, by the fragments or shards of Indra’s bow (the rainbow), since that possesses many colors; [this was done] by the throngs of courtesans, that is, by groups of principal prostitutes.

"...a courtesan (veśyā) who lives by her beauty (rūpājīvā), when honored by people, is called a vāramukhyā"—thus says Amara. "Adhyāsitāḥ" means occupied or presided over. "Kanantīnām" means shining or radiant; the root is "kana," meaning to shine, to be beautiful, or to move. Those [elephants] which possess a jhaṇajhaṇa-jhaṅkāra sound in the form of the tinkling of golden bells (kanaka-kiṅkiṇī). "Jhaṇajhaṇa" is an imitation of the sound, while "jhaṅkāra" refers to the collective resonance. Thus, female elephants (kariṇyaḥ), that is, female elephants (gajavadhvaḥ), are seen.

"Desirable" means that they arouse the longing: "What indeed is that penance which is the cause of such splendors? If it were known, we all would have practiced it. Here, the *kṛtya* suffix is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). The particle *khalu* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). "Splendors" (*vibhūtayaḥ*) refers to riches; by the use of the plural number, their manifold nature is indicated.

He supports that [point] as follows: "For thus," beginning with *preṅkhabhūri* and so forth. *Preṅkhatām* means "of those moving" [peacocks]; *mecakāḥ* refers to their eyes. According to Amara: "The peacock is called *barhiṇa*, *barhī*; *maucandra* and *mecaka* are synonyms. *Tannibhaiḥ* means "resembling those.
[The suffixes] *pratima*, *prabhā*, and so on, follow words [meaning] "equal" (*tulya*) or "of the same color" (*savarṇa*).
"Ābhā, prakhya, upamā, abhikhyā, and prakāra; likewise sannibha and nibha; and words such as nikāśa and others have the meaning of similarity."

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*: "Interspersed with the luster of the wings of opening blue jays (*cāṣa*). By "opening" (*unmeṣa*), a throbbing motion is indicated; [the phrase means] mixed with the beauty of the luster of the throbbing wings of the *cāṣa* birds. The word "as it were" (*iva*) is displaced in its order; it means "as if interspersed. "Whirling" (*vivartin*) means proceeding with various colors. The *Vaijayantī* states: "The *rājavihaṅgama* is the *cāṣa*; it has a jeweled neck and variegated wings"; "wing" (*chada*) is synonymous with "feather" (*pakṣa*) and "pinion" (*garut*); and "luster" (*chāyā*) refers to both shade and beauty.

The quarters of the sky are imagined as being covered on all sides—horizontally and upwards—even in their upper portions, because these too constitute directions, being surrounded at their edges and nearby by the expansions of upward-radiating jewel-lights from the crowns of those facing upward, and by the splendor of the fresh gems set in the ornaments of parasols, chowries, elephants, and the women of the harem. Thus, they appear as if possessing clearly visible, unbroken rainbows stretching horizontally.

They appear as if covered by a profusion of Chinese silks (*cīnāṃśuka*)—fine cloths manufactured in China such as *devāṅga* and others—which are distinguished by raised patterns of various colors, as if spread out upon a carpet.

[The word *prastāra* is formed with the suffix *ghañ* according to Pāṇini 3.3.32, "prestro 'yajñe," as seen in the expression "lying on a bed of flower-spreads" (*puṣpaprastāraśāyinā*) in Bhartṛhari’s poetry. Here, the poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) are *udātta* (the sublime) and *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). //5//

"Agitated," and so forth. The retinue stood at a distance, having formed a circle demarcated by lines traced with cane-staves variegated with panels of shining gold and silver, which were held down and bent by the circle of door-keepers (*pratihāramaṇḍala*). [The cane-staves] were radiant and shimmering.

The reason for this is as follows: on the ground encircled by cane-staffs of various colors—with leaf-patterns made of molten gold and silver for the sake of contrast—he has formed a circular enclosure (*maṇḍala*) by means of a line established in a circle, which serves as a royal command stating, "One must remain strictly outside this line. Thus, he has created a circular arrangement.

And here comes Mālatī, having advanced a short distance; she adorns a female elephant that is like a night whose face is reddened by the twilight glow of a thick mass of vermilion and who wears a girdle of stars swaying about; she is being watched by all the people with faces blossoming in curiosity, and her beautiful, pale, and emaciated bodily splendor reveals the pangs of love, bearing the likeness of the first crescent of the moon.

Sindūra is a specific mineral; because it is red in color, the rising twilight is superposed upon it. By that [twilight], her face—her countenance—is "uparakta," meaning stained or colored, as if suffused by the deep red glow of the twilight resembling a mass of abundant sindūra. Furthermore, she possesses the habit of wearing an ornament in the form of a garland of stars (*nakṣatramālā*) which is swaying or moving.
As it is said: "The *nakṣatramālā* is declared to be a necklace consisting of twenty-seven pearls."

Thus says Halāyudha; and "Tārakāvalī" is also expressed through *śleṣa* (paronomasia). She is a "female elephant" (*kareṇu*)—that is, the night in the form of a female elephant—and she is like a female elephant because the night possesses a large dark form due to its being the cause of her exaltation. This is because it is well known that all people feel curiosity upon seeing maidens whose marriages have commenced, and because she has newly arisen.

She is one in whom the "anguish of the bodiless god" (*anaṅgavedanā*)—the pain born of love—is manifested or revealed by the beauty of her body, which is charming, not pale, yet slightly emaciated; and she is one by whom the future torment of love for the world is indicated by the beauty of her body acting as a sprout of moonlight.

For this very reason, Mālatī—possessing the likeness of the first crescent of the moon, bearing the grace of the digit of the moon that has risen on the first day of the bright fortnight, with her commencement reddened by the twilight, resembling the night which is beautiful with its clusters of stars while its beginning is colored by the twilight, her face crimson with vermilion and wearing pearl ornaments called *nakṣatramālā*, mounted upon a female elephant and distinguished by common epithets such as "eyes wide with curiosity"—is like the crescent of the moon on the first day of the lunar month. This is the meaning.

"Having extended a little distance," meaning she reached a small space between us and herself; or alternatively, the compound "kiñcidantaram" means "a slight interval. "In such a way as to be a slight interval" (*svalpāntarālam*) functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) for the verb "extended" (*prasṛtā*). Here, the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is *saṅkara* (commixture).

"‘This one,’ and so forth. ‘With limbs’ means with the parts [of the body] and the branches [of the hair]. ‘Adorned with ornaments’ (*alaṅkṛtamaṇḍanā*) means she by whom the ornaments have been adorned—that is, embellished—since through their contact with those limbs an extraordinary beauty arises, as it is said: ‘the ornament of ornaments. By the term ‘adorned with ornaments,’ he shows that although they were placed there with indifference, they are nevertheless desirable; thus he expresses a bodily state called *vicchitti* (graceful charm):
‘Even a slight placement of garlands and the like upon one’s own adornment, which produces supreme beauty, is declared to be *vicchitti*.’"

According to this statement: "kalitakusumā" means having blossoms attached; "bālā" means immature; "antaḥpariśoṣiṇī" means withering within due to the absence of timely watering and other such care, resulting in internal desiccation. At that time, she was adorned with ornaments consisting of limbs that were pale and emaciated by the fever of love, yet she was withering within. Therefore, the figure of speech here is a simile (dṛṣṭānta) supported by paronomasia (śleṣa), wherein she is compared to a young creeper that has blossomed but is standing with branches that are pale and thin while withering within.

Nor should one suspect an excess of poetic figures (*dharmādhikya*) on the grounds that she is a girl who withers from within; for the comparison is valid only for a creeper characterized by such qualities. Regarding *varārohā*, Amara states: "A woman of beautiful hips (*varārohā*), a spirited woman (*mattakāśinī*), an excellent woman (*uttamā*), and a woman of excellent complexion (*varavarṇinī*). [She was] lovely (*ramyā*), meaning beautiful to behold. Regarding [the phrase] *vivāhamahotsavaśriyam*: "The marriage rite for women is traditionally considered equivalent to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*)."

According to this statement of Manu, [she attained] that splendor or beauty (*śrī*) which arises from the great auspicious rite called *pāṇigrahaṇa* (taking of the hand), which takes the form of a sacrament (*saṃskāra*) that is the cause of being twice-born (*dvijatva*). The suffix *-ṇini* in *udayinīm* is used in the sense of habit; the meaning is that she was manifesting it herself as an indicator of future prosperity. [She also attained] the mental affliction (*manorujaḥ*), the disease of the mind. In the second half of the verse, the figure of speech is *samuccaya* (accumulation), because the two actions—carrying and expressing—are presented simultaneously.

In this context, the charge of tautology should not be suspected regarding the fact that the very same meaning previously stated by Kalahaṃsa in the words "pāṇḍaraparikkhāma" (pale and emaciated) is again set forth by Makaranda in the words "pāṇḍukṣāmaiḥ" (pale and wasted), and so on; for both speakers are merely reinforcing a single point in order to reassure the hero. On the contrary, this should be understood as a merit [of the composition]. //6//

"Niṣāditā" means seated for the purpose of descending. "How so?"—thus, having observed that her own fortune is on the verge of fruition, her astonishment is revealed. "Having descended" (*avatīrya*) means having alighted from the female elephant.
"With joy" (*saharṣam*) means with delight, signifying that she perceives the proximity of the success resulting from her own efforts. "Aside" (*apavārya*) means [speaking] to herself.

By invoking the chosen deity appropriate to the occasion, he prays for his desired object: "May the Creator grant us prosperity," and so forth. The Creator (vidhātā) is the Lord Prajāpati, the creator of the entire world; may He grant (vitaratu)—that is, bestow—upon us (naḥ) prosperity (bhadram), meaning freedom from obstacles and auspiciousness.

According to Amarasimha: "Viśrāṇanam, vitaranam, sparśanam, and pratipādanam [are synonyms for giving]. The mention of the Creator highlights the suitability of the World-Sustainer as the means to achieve this, since the purpose of marriage for those of great character is the acquisition of virtuous progeny.

As stated in the *Raghuvamśa*: "Then, with self-restraint and desiring a son, they worshipped the Creator," and from such usages as "for the sake of progeny for householders" and "a wife for the sake of offspring"; [the phrase] "for a pleasing rite" means for a beautiful performance, and "for the sake of an auspicious alliance" means for the purpose of a praiseworthy union between the daughter of a friend and one who is equal in character, age, beauty, and noble lineage. "May the gods"—Hari, Hara, and others—"desire to perform"—that is, may they wish to bring about—the "supremely delightful," that is, the most desirable, "conclusion"—meaning the fruition of the result or subsequent abundance of wealth and so forth.

"Having accomplished its purpose" means having fulfilled its objective. "Regarding Bhūrivasu and Devarāta, who are dear friends and beloved allies," means concerning those two. "By efforts" means by exertions; "by desired ones" because they lead toward the objects one wishes for. "Entirely" refers to this present effort, including that which was employed by Avalokitā, Buddharakṣitā, and others. "May it now bear fruit" means may it now succeed without obstacle. "May it be auspicious" (śivatātiḥ) means that it shall bring welfare hereafter and result in a continuous succession of blessings. [The suffix *tāt* is used after *śiva*, *śam*, and *ariṣṭa* when followed by *kara*.]

(4-4-143) Thus, the suffix *tāti* is applied. Halāyudha states: "Śivatāti means one who brings about auspiciousness. Here, the optative (*liṅ*) and imperative (*loṭ*) moods are used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). This is the poetic figure known as *āśīr* (benediction). The passage beginning with "May the Creator grant us prosperity" and so forth constitutes a *vicalana* (a shifting of the subject), because Kāmandakī thereby indicates her own efforts. //7//

Now, the heroine reflects upon the firmness of her love for the hero and her aversion toward the rival hero—by what means, indeed, shall I now experience the extinction of death? Or there is another reading: "I shall bring about an interval [between myself and] the extinction of death. [The term *maraṇanirvāṇa*] refers to the bliss consisting of death, because at that moment the suffering being experienced is severed:
"That state in which the embodied soul remains isolated from destroyed afflictions, which kindles both resolve and the intellect—that indeed is *nirvṛti* (extinction/bliss)."

Because it has been characterized in this way, "its interval" means its opportunity; "I shall bring about" means "I shall attain. Even death is desired by me, an unfortunate woman; thus, it becomes difficult to obtain. By the phrase "even death," it is suggested that the abandonment of life is achievable for everyone through mere resolve, as opposed to living. "Unfortunate" means one of little merit (*alpapuṇya*); "desired" means wished for (*iṣṭa*). For this reason, it becomes difficult to obtain—that is, impossible to attain.

In this context, there is no fault in the mention of death, which is inauspicious, because it is spoken by one who is despondent and hopeless regarding her own desires; furthermore, the phrase "of me, the unfortunate" suggests self-reproach, while the words beginning with "by what means" express agitation (*udvega*).

Having understood her intention through her gestures and facial expressions due to her detachment from her father and others, he said: "Indeed, my dear friend has been greatly distressed by this favorable deception (*anukūla-vipralambha*). She has been excessively tormented by this present 'favorable deception'—that is, by a deception that is favorable (*anukūla*) in being consistent with her own desires, yet deceptive (*vipralambha*) because it conceals the ultimate truth and speaks otherwise; or rather, by the deluding of us who are ourselves so devoted. [She is] "holding a casket in her hand," meaning she has a box of ornaments in her hand.
"Paṭala refers to a film over the eye or a roof; it is neuter, and masculine in the sense of a boil or a multitude," according to the Vaijayantī lexicon. *Pratīhārī* means a female doorkeeper.

The minister says to the Blessed One: "Mālatī must be adorned with special splendor before the deity with this bridal attire sent by the lord of men. By the phrase "sent by the lord of men" (*narendrānupreṣitena*), meaning "dispatched by the sovereign of Padmāvatī," he indicates the exceptional favor shown toward Mālatī by the one who gave her [the attire] himself. "Before the deity" (*devatāpurataḥ*) means "in the presence of the city goddess"; thus, while expressing auspiciousness, he implies that it should take place right there in the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), unknown to others.
"With special splendor" (*saviśeṣam*) means "more than before," because the royal decree is to be honored; such is the explicit meaning (*vācyo 'rthaḥ*).

The distinction (*viśeṣa*) is the exclusion (*vyatireka*), suggested by the fact that the manhood of the person is concealed. "To be adorned" (*alaṅkartavyā*) means to be decorated; "alaṃ" signifies sufficiency, meaning "without doubt"; "to be made" (*kartavyā*) means to be created—this is the suggested sense. One who understands what is thus revealed says: "It is fitting" (*yuktam*), meaning it is logical, as he speaks, [referring to] the minister according to the context. "Auspicious" (*māṅgalika*) means having the purpose of auspiciousness; "hi" indicates a well-known fact; "this place" refers to a site in the form of a temple, because it is a ground free from suspicion—this is the intended meaning. "From here" is said with a gesture, meaning "in front of us."

He displays the wedding attire after dividing it: "First, this pair of silk garments; these are the sets of ornaments for all parts of the body; these are pearl necklaces; this is sandalwood paste; and this is the crest of white flowers. Because clothing is the primary form of ornamentation, it is mentioned first: "A pair of silk garments" means a set of two linen cloths, consisting of an undergarment and an upper garment. The mention of "silk" (*paṭṭāṃśuka*) is because of its auspicious nature:
"A certain youth has revealed as an auspicious sign a linen cloth as white as the moon."

Thus it is said in the *Śākuntala*. "The collections (*saṃyoga*) of ornaments covering all limbs" means the assemblages of ornaments extending over every part of the body, from the toe-rings up to the crest-jewel (*cūḍāmaṇi*). The suffix *kha* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.7: "The word *vyāpin* is added after *sarva* and so forth, when combined with *pathin*, *aṅga*, *karman*, *patra*, or *pātra*. Because pearl necklaces produce an excellence of beauty, are auspicious, and are of great value, they are mentioned separately as the primary items. An *āpīḍa* is a crest-jewel; white flowers are specified because of their excellence.

"Whatever flower is pale, whatever unguent [is white]," according to this saying. The minister himself reveals the meaning previously signaled through his own internal reflection by the phrase "for it is delightful," because [the girl] is adorned with these [white items]. By the word "child" (*vatsa*), he expresses Mālatī’s fitness for that designation due to her tenderness, beauty, and so forth. By the word "people" (*jana*), he states that other people perceive things exactly as they see them. "In this way" (*evam*) means "this is how we shall act."

Likewise: Out of cleverness, she causes the heroine—who is accompanied by her friend—to enter the interior [of the temple] so that she may engage in casual conversation and the like with the hero who is staying inside; "the interior" refers to the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) of the deity.
Although the friend knows the truth, she asks, "How is the Blessed Lady? in order to dispel any suspicion on that account.
"How? [The answer is: he will act," is the ellipsis.

He states the appropriate reason: "In a secluded and solitary place, for the sake of one-pointedness of mind, according to the treatise"—that is, according to the *Ratna-śāstra* (Treatise on Gems), because it has been established by Buddhabhaṭa and others that "prosperity comes from wearing faultless and quality gems such as diamonds in accordance with one's caste, age, and condition; otherwise, there is calamity"; thus, the meaning is that he will examine and determine the qualities and defects based precisely on that treatise.

She demonstrates the fruit of Kāmandakī’s clever application of strategy: "By good fortune, I have come to have Lavaṅgikā as my sole attendant. The word "by good fortune" (*diṣṭyā*) is spoken out of joy at having obtained the opportunity desired by herself. "[Having Lavaṅgikā as her sole attendant]" (*lavaṅgikāmātraparijanā*): this is the third separation, meaning she whose attendants or retinue consists of Lavaṅgikā alone. "This is the door of the temple of the deity. "Let my dear friend enter"—this indicates the performance of a secret location.
"Concealed by a pillar" (*stambhāpavāritau*): covered by a pillar.
"Friend! Here is body-unguent; here are these flower-garlands. "Body-unguent" means an ointment.

"Then what?"—this is a statement of indignation regarding what should be done with those objects. "Friend! You have been sent by my mother to worship the deities for the sake of securing auspiciousness at the commencement of this auspicious marriage ceremony"—the meaning is: for the purpose of bringing about prosperity at the onset of the beautiful rite that is the wedding. By the use of the plural "deities," she indicates a multiplicity of deities to be worshipped according to her desire. "Sent" means you were dispatched. The sense is: "Have you forgotten that?"

With agitation she said: "Why now, having had my mind brought to its final conclusion—filled with the suffering that is the result of the cruel onset of fate's wicked play—must I, unfortunate as I am, be tormented again and again by this unbearable cutting of my vital organs?"

The "wicked play" (durvilāsa) of fate is its extremely cruel onset; by its "consequence" (pariṇāmena), that is, its ripening—since there is nothing further for it to do—her mind has been rendered full of sorrow, filled with anguish, brought to an end, destroyed, or, in other words, made desolate. Furthermore, the phrase "again and again" refers to the recollection of the offenses committed by her father at one time, by her mother at another, and by her friend at yet another.

"Unbearable due to the piercing of the vital points (*marmāṇi*)," meaning the locations where the life-breaths reside; it is unbearable because of their being pierced. Why [is this said]? There is expressed both indignation and agitation: "In causing such a succession of torments, what fruit do you have? A clever female friend, perceiving her intention, provides an introduction for mentioning that very matter in the presence of Mādhava: "O, you appear as if desiring to say something"—the word *ayi* is used in an affectionate inquiry. "Something [you desire to say]" means you seem to be wishing to speak; therefore, the sense is: "Tell me specifically and without hesitation what you wish to say."

Having found the opportunity, he raises an objection with the desire to state a distinction: "Now, what is this person saying, whose fortune contradicts the desires of one who is intent upon an unattainable object? The word "now" (*idānīm*) indicates that the [proper] time has passed. "One whose fortune contradicts"—that is, opposes—the "desire," meaning the mental longing, of one who is "intent," meaning persistent, upon an "unattainable thing"; the sense is that his aspiration is directed elsewhere while his fate is ordained otherwise.

"What is he deliberating? means there is no opportunity at all to speak. The sequence beginning with "What now... and so forth arises from the narration of attaining the state of Mālatī while she was being contemplated.

The friend gladdens him, saying, "It has been heard. Because that state was not yet clear by that much alone, he says, dissatisfied: "It has been heard"—that is, it has indeed been perceived; the word "this" refers to the speech [of the messenger]. The particle *tu* indicates a distinction. There is dissatisfaction of the heart (*hṛdayasya*), meaning the state of non-contentment does not cease. By saying "It has been heard / But there is dissatisfaction of the heart," he takes up [the matter] because of the inclusion of the accomplishment of his own desired purpose.

"Having embraced"—this is a manner of consoling for the sake of securing her own desired favor. "O my true sister! Dear friend Lavaṅgikā! This dear friend of yours, now helpless and on the verge of death, embraces you in a manner consistent with the confidence that has grown continuously since her birth from the womb, and thus entreats you. Therefore—since the opportunity for speech has thus passed—it means that an entreaty directed toward anyone other than you will not bear fruit. O true sister (*paramārthabhagini*)! One who is a sister in the non-figurative sense."

"By me" means because you alone have nourished me as well. "Dear friend" (priyasakhī) means you are the object of my affection even more than my own life; such is the meaning. "This one" (eṣā) implies that even though she is seen, my condition is known [by her]. "Now" means at this final hour. By saying "dear friend," he expresses the bond of mutual love: not only are you mine, but I too am your dear friend.

"Helpless" means being abandoned by protectors such as parents; "with death present" means having no other recourse, they take refuge in death alone. "From the womb" (*āgarbhataḥ*) refers to the emergence from the mother's belly; starting from that point—where *āṅ* is used in the sense of inclusion—they act in a manner similar to the confidence that has grown continuously and deeply without obstruction.

"She entreats, she begs"—the very expression "I do not entreat further" indicates that such a breaking of her request must not be committed even in a dream. Forcibly making her speak, she reveals the object of her petition: "If I am to be followed by you, then, holding me in your heart, gaze with joy upon the lotus-face of Mādhava, which is the singular auspiciousness for the possession of the entire splendor of fortune and is softened by bliss."

"Anuvartanīyā" means they should be followed with compliance and satisfied. In the word "te," the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) due to its connection with the suffix of the gerundive (*kṛtyapratyaya*). [The thought is: "Your compliance is indeed required; nevertheless, my fear of separation from you does not allow me to comply. To this she says, "holding me in your heart"; the meaning is that when she is present within the heart, what room is there for any suspicion of separation?

For the sake of embracing the singular and peerless auspiciousness—the glory of the fortune of good fortune (*saubhāgyalakṣmī*), which consists of being desired by all people—there is the lotus-face of Mādhava, the beautiful lotus-like face of Mādhava. The word *śrī* here is used in a figurative sense (*upacāra*). It is "smooth with bliss," meaning gentle through the experience of happiness; that is to say, for the purpose of reminding me of him. The statement "he weeps" is an expression made because his remembrance has renewed my grief.

His heart satisfied by the manifestation of those words, he said: "Of the withered," and so forth. "Of the withered" means of that which is exhausted by contact with the forest fire of despair. "Of the flower of life"—that is, of the flower whose nature is the consciousness of the self—these [words] are "causing it to bloom," meaning they produce joy. They are "satisfying," meaning they provide nourishment, because they instantly nourish the emaciated body; for in medical science, a medicine that replenishes an emaciated body is designated as "satisfying" (*santarpaṇa*).

They are enchanters of all the senses, bringing the external organs such as the ears and others under their sway; they are sources of bliss, generating immediate and supreme happiness; they are the sole elixirs for the heart, serving as the primary restoratives for the mind even in the future. An *rasāyana* is a specific medicine that removes old age, death, and other ailments; the meaning here is that [these words] cause the heart to remain steadfast by cutting away every doubt and distress. "By me also"—that is, by one whose own life was certain to perish once all the bonds of hope were severed—[it was said]:
"May I behold once more her face, the auspicious abode of the bodiless god of love."

The meaning is: "even by me, desiring only this much. The phrase "attained" (*adhigatāni*)—meaning obtained rather than merely heard—indicates that they were preserved like a treasure. "Nectar-words" (*vacomṛtāni*) means nectars in the form of speech. Because those very words possess sweetness, they have the power to revive the dead; and since they manifest favor toward oneself, the superimposition of "nectar-ness" is expressed by asking, "What more need be said? Here, the mental state (*bhāva*) called joy (*harṣa*) is revealed. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is a complete metaphorical identification (*mālārūpaka*). //8//

Act in such a way that, upon hearing that I am perishing, he who granted me my life does not suffer so much that his precious body wastes away; and act so that even when I have gone to another world, that person, by merely maintaining the practice of remembrance and conversation concerning me, does not let his worldly course slacken over time. By the term "one who granted me my life," he expresses the successful application of the method for encountering misfortune as described in the *Kāmasūtra*.

By describing [the body] as "most helpful for reclaiming the life-sustaining breath swallowed by the Kāpālika," he demonstrates the firmness of his affection out of gratitude. The phrase "now sinking" means that it is perishing in the course of time due to the opportunity afforded for death. The expression "of such a kind"—referring to the manner or state of its experience—indicates that although this jewel of a body is itself subject to the emaciation of torment, it possesses ever-new loveliness.

"It does not perish; it does not become exhausted"—the logical connection is "act thus," meaning by means of consolation. "Even though I have gone to another world"—that is, even if, by the power of fortune, I have found an opportunity this very day and, having abandoned life, have gone to the next world—nevertheless, [he will come] for my sake. The word *api* (even) serves to draw in the sense of *yathā* (as if). "Aiming at" means making me the object. "That person" refers to the most beloved one.

"By the mere acceptance of remembrance and conversation"—that is, by the acceptance and adoption of the mere conversation engaged in through recollection, consisting of such talk as "she did this," "she laughed thus," "she looked at me," or "she spoke in such a manner. The word *api* (even) suggests that other forms of connection have been shattered by fate. By "after some time" (*kālāntareṇa*), meaning through the separation of time—the sense being that according to the maxim "affection [is severed] due to the influence of travel," the severance of affection is possible through the interruption of time.

"Lokayātrā" means the worldly course of life; the meaning is the maxim that "when one of two people who love each other has passed away, the survivor remembers [the deceased]. "Does not slacken" means she does not diminish it. "Act accordingly" means by going to her side every moment and causing me to be remembered. In this very way, your dear friend Mālatī becomes well-supported and her desire fulfilled. By acting in the manner thus described—"evam"—it is implied that if there were any deviation from this, she would act as an enemy.

By the term "dear friend" (*priyasakhī*), it is suggested that the fact of her being the ground of your love will become clear through this very address. By saying "you have a protector" (*sanāthā*), my state of being helpless (*anāthatva*) is dispelled, for I am now protected by you. By saying "she has had her desire fulfilled" (*sakāmā kṛtā*), it should be understood that you have also rendered fruitful the prayer I offered to you; thus, both what was said [by me] as "I am helpless" (*aṇāhā*) and "she entreats" (*abbhatthedi*) will be resolved. The word *hanta* expresses despondency; "what has been commenced" (*prastutam*) refers to that which has begun, which is exceedingly piteous and brings about extreme sorrow—this is the ellipsis to be supplied with "by her" (*anayā*).

Then, due to the fear of her passing away and the hearing of words expressive of her passion, he remained in a state between despondency and joy, thinking: "The lamentation born of affectionate delusion"—"affection" (*vātsalya*) here signifies *sneha* (love) by way of secondary indication; the "delusion" (*moha*) caused by it is the failure to discern what ought to be done; and the "lamentation" (*paridevita*) produced by that. [This refers to the lamentation of the fawn-eyed one,] whose mind was distressed by despair—her heart being timid through hopelessness regarding union with me—and which was exceedingly piteous because of her exertion to give up her life, and captivating because it indicated her firm passion.

Having heard her lamentation, and [perceiving] the calamity of anxiety and despondency—the calamity produced by the dejection of the mind (the state of being overwhelmed by mental suffering) arising from the thought, "What will happen?"—as well as the physical exhaustion and other misfortunes, and the great festival—the supreme joy [expressed by] "Oh, how fortunate I am! For she who is equal to my own life-breath has such affection for me"—by which, through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), her resulting happiness is meant; here, the two emotions of despondency and joy are manifested in a state of rivalry. This is the figure of speech known as *bhāvasandhi* (the conjunction of emotions). //9//
