Then a female friend, fearing ill omen, says: "Friend! May this inauspicious word of yours regarding death now be averted—that is, may it be warded off by the remembrance of the Lord and other such means; [may there be peace]. This is understood from common usage such as "May evil be stilled" (*śāntaṃ pāpam*) and "May ill omen be averted" (*pratihatamamaṅgalam*). "I shall not hear any further words from you. She says this with indignation, meaning: "Beyond what has been said, I will not listen, because it is painful to the ear."

Attributing a figurative character to those words because they were not preceded by affection, she spoke with indignation: "Friend, Mālatī’s life is indeed dear to you, but not Mālatī herself. The particle *khalu* is used here in the sense of inquiry (*jijñāsā*), according to the rule: "The particle *khalu* is used in prohibition, as an ornament for a sentence, in inquiry, and in conciliation."

Thus says Amara. By the plural "yuṣmākam" (of you all), the inclusion of father and others is intended. By the statement, "Mālatī’s life is dear to you, but Mālatī herself is not," he intends to express this: "By whatever means possible, let her—who is tormented by suffering like a *śakuntikā* bird impaled on a stake, with nothing remaining but her breath—experience a state that is living death. This is the meaning of the phrase "Mālatī’s life is dear to you."

However, by means of the "transferred denotation" (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*) of the word *mālatī*, she is not regarded as such because she is characterized by being raised in luxury, being undeserving of suffering, being worthy of fondling, being worthy of compliance, and so forth;
not understanding this intended meaning, she asks: "Why was it said by you?"

He explains his own intended meaning: "By which arrangements of words, serving as bonds of hope, I have sustained this most loathsome undertaking. The phrase "by bonds of hope" means by causes that are like snares of expectation, such as: "We shall thus win over my father," "We shall employ such another stratagem toward my mother," "This will be done today," "This tomorrow," or "This the day after tomorrow."

The meaning is that [he restored her] by means of verbal arrangements—consisting merely of words—and not by the actual performance of remedial measures. By saying "having brought her back to life," the sense is that otherwise, had this matter not been resolved, she would have abandoned her life even earlier due to the severance of all hope.

Now, this present undertaking—which, being devoid of any quality other than extreme loathsomeness, has been set in motion solely for the sake of the task and is thus an object of universal loathing—and which consists of an enterprise that results in an undesirable outcome: by using the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the phrase "I have been made to experience" (*anubhāvitā*), the author indicates the element of compulsion. The word *yena* is an indeclinable (an avyaya) that functions as a synonym for the relative pronoun *yat*, acting as a substitute for a case ending. The connection of the sense is as follows: because I have been made to experience this, my beloved is Mālatī’s life, and not Mālatī herself.

Anticipating the objection that "since this misfortune has thus been brought about by fate, what can be done now? It should simply be endured in silence," he says: "But now, my resolve is only this: having abandoned myself—who have offended because of belonging to another—to him who gave me life, I shall find peace. The word *punaḥ* (but) indicates a reversal; the meaning is that your intention is not to be followed at all. *Manorathaḥ* means resolve (*saṅkalpa*). *Etāvān* means of such a measure. *Eva* (only).
By the maxim, "Who can turn back the mind that is fixed on its desired object, just as water flowing toward a low ground cannot be turned back?

[the verse] suggests that even Brahmā could not prevent this. By the phrase "those who granted life," she reveals the firmness of her remembrance of their kindness; she indicates, "Since my life was given by them, it must be sacrificed for their sake alone—what effort is required of me in this? Regarding the fact that they belong to others:
"The father protects in childhood, the husband protects in youth..."

For it is stated in the *Smṛti*: "But in old age, a son does not deserve independence from his mother. Thus, she was dependent upon her father. Regarding the offense consisting of the touch of another's hand—an act that causes supreme misfortune—there is the reading *anaparāddham* ("one who has not offended"). Since the offense was unintentional, there is no fault whatsoever in one who, being bound and led away like a beast due to lack of autonomy, is full of remorse. For if the act were intentional, there would be no expiation even for crimes such as the killing of a Brahmin; however, expiation is prescribed specifically for one who is remorseful.
"According to the statement of Manu, 'The wise know that expiation is for a sin committed unintentionally,' [it follows that] those men who are devoted to sins and do not perform expiation..."
The meaning is that this is because of the statement of Yājñavalkya: "Those who feel no remorse go to terrible and dreadful hells. Here, "self" (ātman) refers to the body;
as it is said: "Ātman [is used] for the body, for fortitude, for the living soul (jīva), for one's own nature, and for the Supreme Self."
Thus says the Vaijayantī: "Having abandoned oneself" refers to the following:
"Having carefully considered the place, the time, the age, the capacity, and the sin, an expiation (prāyaścitta) should be prescribed where no specific atonement has been mentioned."

Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Yājñavalkya, she herself reflects and determines an expiation (prāyaścitta) appropriate to her sin. The meaning is that when a husband—who has been chosen by her own will, who is of suitable lineage and other qualities, who is full of affection, and who gives her life—is involved, there is no other expiation possible for the offense and transgression arising from her dependence on him, nor is any such expiation sufficient, except for the sacrifice of one's own life. She is "tranquil" (nirvṛtā), meaning made happy by the removal of the fear of hell; for it is said:
"A doer of evil goes to hell if he turns his back on expiation."

The sense is that this is because of such a traditional authority (smaraṇa) and because the expiation has been performed. The thought is: "Let this world indeed be useless; but let not that other world be so. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Such is the object [of my concern], and this alone is my desire. By this statement, one should understand that the stability of what was said in the verse, "Neither this person nor life itself," is being reaffirmed.

When this purpose, which consists of the fruit in the form of supreme bliss, has been indicated as pertaining to the next world, the phrase "my dear friend" (me priyasakhī) suggests that it is entirely improper for you—who have until now sought my beloved’s welfare—to act contrary to him now. The term *aparipanthinī* means "not being an obstacle" or "not opposed"; the use of the *loṭ* (imperative) mood in *bhavatu* expresses a prayer. By saying "she falls at her feet," he indicates that the mistress's request is not to be transgressed, as she performs the duty of a servant (*ceṭī*) toward her, since the matter is one that requires persistence.

That behavior causes wonder—the reading is *saiṣā*. According to Amara, "both *sīmā* and *sīmā* [are used] for the feminine. That which is well-known in the world, this which is now being experienced—namely, the mistress’s prostration at the feet regarding the maidservant—is the *sīmā*, the ultimate limit. If the reading were *sa eṣaḥ*, one would have to supply the word *vidhiḥ* (ordinance). [This refers to] the affection, the passion directed toward you.

The poet arranges the meeting with the hero through the mouth of a confidante who knows the right moment: "By a sign with the hand" means by a gesture of the hand as a form of secret summons intended so that the heroine does not recognize [the speaker]; "summons" (āhvayati) means he calls out with the intention, "Come and stay here in this place. It is a bold act to summon Mādhava by a sign with the hand, because it deceives Mālatī.
He explains her gesture: "Having approached," meaning having gone near; "in the place of Lavaṅgikā," meaning at that spot where Lavaṅgikā was previously standing; "stay."
Gesticulating with a tremor of joy, he said: "Paravān" means dependent on another, that is, one whose body is not under one's own control; "sādhvasena" means with a trembling of the heart.

He establishes this very point: "This very state"—characterized by being distinguished by present apprehension and so forth—belongs to those who are *nedīyasām*, meaning closest at hand. When one is far away, there is longing, with the prayer, "When will it happen?"; but when [the object] has come into one's hands, for those longed-for things that were previously unthought of, there occurs, due to being overwhelmed by joy, a multitude of symptoms such as paralysis and trembling of the mind. This alone is the *prakṛtiḥ*, the inherent nature, like heat in fire; therefore, it is not within the scope of logical reasoning (*vitarka*). [This applies to] *abhyudayānām*, i.e., prosperities. *Svairam* means gradually, so that the sound of footsteps is not heard.

Falling at her feet, she said: "Friend, show favor through your kindness. By "kindness" (*anukūlatayā*) is meant compliance with her wishes; by "favor" (*prasādam*) is meant a gracious act of grace. Then, standing in the place of Lavaṅgikā and mimicking her speech out of cleverness, he speaks—beginning with "O simple one," etc.—in order to dispel that suspicion. "O simple one" (*sarale*) means "O you who are not crooked"; this is the vocative. As it is said: "O girl, shame has been cast away! No, no, O simple one! Is a bodice a cause for shame?"

...as in that [expression]. By this, it is suggested: "Oh, how great is this straightforwardness of yours, in that you do not accomplish your own desire, regarding your father and others as mere blades of grass! Alternatively, it means "not vulgar" (*agrāmya*). According to the *Vaijayantī*: "Not vulgar, straightforward, noble, clever, witty, and courteous. [The phrase] "attachment to rash passion" refers to an inclination toward acting without deliberation in the form of self-sacrifice, since even suicide is counted among the great sins (*mahāpātaka*).
"Those who drink liquor and those who commit suicide are not entitled to the period of impurity nor to the water-offering," according to the legal tradition of Yājñavalkya;
likewise: "And for those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) as well as for those who have committed suicide..."

And from the *Saṃvarta-smṛti*: "One should not offer water, nor food-balls (*piṇḍa*), nor even perform religious duties. Therefore, avoid it; abandon it. [O lady with thighs like plantain stalks (*rambhā*): she whose thighs possess the roundness, tapering shape, smoothness, coolness, and fair color of the trunk of a plantain tree. He states the reason for avoiding such rashness: "Abandon your agitation—that persistent insistence born of resentment toward your father and others.
An 'obsession' (*āveśa*) is simply a state of being full of wrath toward an object that opposes one."

"And even more so, it returns again to a state of agitation," says Divākara. "Virasam" means devoid of pleasure. "Tava virahāyāsam" means the distress of separation from you. "Cittam me soḍhum asaham" means my mind is unable, or incapable, to endure it. [This is based on the rule: "The suffix *tumun* is used after the roots *śak*, *dhṛṣ*, *jñā*, *glā*, *ghaṭ*, *rabh*, *labh*, *kram*, *sah*, and *arh* in the sense of 'to be able' (*asti-artha*)."

(3-4-65) By this statement, she indicates: "If you perish, I too shall not live; therefore, for the sake of protecting both of us, do not act with such rash passion. Here, the emotions (*bhāva*) of *mati* (resolve) and *āvega* (agitation) are manifested. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is *bhāṣāśleṣa* (blending of dialects), because it is employed by a superior character (*uttamapātra*) occupying the role of a middle character (*madhyamapātra*), and thus belongs to the class common to both Sanskrit and Prākṛit.

This is an example of *tatsama* (Sanskrit identical to the vernacular), as defined by Daṇḍin and others: "The *tatsama*, *tadbhava*, and *deśī* [terms] constitute the various varieties of Prākṛit usage. //10//

Perceiving Lavaṅgikā’s lack of consent, he again requests her with a different artifice: "Friend Lavaṅgikā! Mālatī’s salutation must not be disregarded by you. The phrase "Friend Lavaṅgikā" is a strategic address intended to create a sense of distinction. "Not to be disregarded" (*alaṅghanīya*) means it is not fit to be treated with disrespect by stepping over it. By saying "Mālatī," he indicates that she is moistened by the fluid of natural affection. "Salutation" (*praṇāma*) implies a humble act. "By you" (*te*) is the genitive case used for the agent.

Under the pretext of seeking her consent, he reveals his own intention with the words "What shall I say," and so forth. The meaning is: when you speak thus, what can I possibly say to you without your permission? Regarding the phrase "causing the pain of separation," this is further explained: she whose nature it is to inflict (*kāriṇī*) cruel (*dāruṇa*), that is, unbearable (*dussaha*), distress (*āyāsa*) or suffering (*duḥkha*) during separation (*vicchede*) or absence (*virahe*)—that you are! The underlying sense is: disregarding the torment of your kinsmen, you desire only your own pleasure; oh, how heartless you are!

"Do as you wish; do what you desire. Grant me at least an embrace, a close hug; even by this much, please me. This is to be understood as the speech of a female friend (*sakhī*), yet it is suggested (*vyaṅgya*) as the speech of the hero (*nāyaka*). "How can the pain of separation from you be described by me? Therefore, fulfill my longing. If you ask what that is: grant me an embrace. By that alone, my purpose will be fulfilled"—this is the underlying sense. Here, *autsukya* (eagerness or longing) is suggested. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is simply *bhāṣāśleṣa* (punning ambiguity of language). //11//

Having imagined her consent—out of joy and because it would be easy for her own desires—the poet says: "How am I permitted? This means she consents to death. "I embrace this [person]" means "I do what is dear to you. By this artifice, the poet avoids the fault of the innocent girl embracing her beloved in the presence of her friends; for [the poet implies] that a final sight of her dear friend cannot be obtained again due to the pressure of tears.

By the pressure of tears—that is, by a flood of tears arising from either the joy of granting permission due to feminine nature, or from the recollection of kinsmen—he is not obtained, meaning he is not reached; the sense is that because the range of vision is obstructed, he cannot be seen. This is because it is the "final" (apaścima)—meaning there is no other after it—and thus, being produced at the very moment of his passing, it is the last [glimpse]. The meaning is that he is not attained due to the cessation of the expansion of sight.

Even in the absence of visual perception, one concludes from the nature of things that the touch of a most beloved person bestows a particular kind of pleasure compared to other touches; as Rāma says in the *Uttararāmacarita* regarding the touch of Queen Sītā when she was concealed by the boon of Bhāgīrathī: "This is she! She is being grasped! And likewise in the *Raghuvamśa*:
"Though her lips were not clearly seen because her eyes were blinded by tears, they were recognized through the experience of the pleasure of her son's touch."

Friend! Today the touch of your body soothes me in a way entirely different from before; it is as dense and thick as the interior of a hard lotus that has opened yesterday and reached its full bloom. Because of his delicate nature and because his body is both soft and firm due to manly exertion and the like, he is compared to a hard lotus. "Entirely different" means distinguished by a quality other than what was previously experienced.

"Thus" means that there is no delusion whatsoever in this matter. By the word "now," her perception—arising from the innocence [of youth] as to how she might appear in such a state due to being in her final condition—is illuminated. "She extinguishes" means she brings about the happiness of liberation (*nirvṛti*). "O friend! Furthermore, with palms joined upon your head, inform that person on my behalf. "Furthermore" implies something else that I must say.

She concludes the message intended for the hero with the words "Do so," following up on what has been presented; otherwise, there would be an interruption in the middle due to the introduction of other clusters of sentences by way of digression or incidental elaboration. [With palms joined upon her head: She is one by whom the *añjali*—the form of two hands joined together—is placed upon the head, as a mark of respect.
Regarding this, it is said: "The topknot (*cūḍā*), the crown (*kirīṭa*), and the hair bound together (*saṃhata-keśa*)—these three are called *mauli*."

"A man with his two hands joined in *añjali*," so says Amara. "In such a manner" (*yathā*) means by whatever way it is requested; thus, "it is told" follows by implication. He describes the manner of the request: "By me, of little fortune, the great festival for the eyes was not long enjoyed through the free sight of that orb of the moon-like face, which steals away the playful splendor of the blooming hundred-petaled lotus (*śatapatra*).
[Note: *Sahasrapatraṃ kamalaṃ śatapatraṃ kuśeśayam*—"The thousand-petaled is the lotus, the hundred-petaled is the *kuśeśaya*"]."]

Thus says Amara: *vilāsa* means expansion. Because the face is superimposed as the moon, its appropriateness for stealing the beauty of the lotus is established. "By a glance at will" (*svacchandadarśanena*) means by a look performed according to one's own desire, without being obstructed by the window. "Honored" (*sambhāvitaḥ*) means respectfully treated. It was a great festival for the eyes, a joy for the sight. If one asks, "In that case, how was life sustained? he replies: "The heart was maintained by mere vain desires, while its bonds were being loosened by the onset of an irresistible agitation expanding through the pangs of separation."

By means of futile desires—that is, by false imaginings that bear no fruit—the bonds [of her heart] were loosened, causing them to slacken from their natural state. Her friends were repeatedly tormented by the particularly unbearable distress of her suffering, and the physical fevers of her body were brought about. "Howsoever" she managed to pass through a succession of calamities, such as the Malaya breezes, the moonlight, and so forth (the word *prabhṛti* including the warbling of cuckoos, the fragrance of bakula flowers, and the like). "Passed" (*ativāhitāḥ*) means brought to an end. The word *prabhṛti* implies the inclusion of the calls of cuckoos, the scent of bakula blossoms, and other such things.

Successive calamities, arising one after another in an uninterrupted stream, bring about suffering; thus, in all three sentences, they are connected with the phrase "by vain desires. "But now I have become hopeless"—the word "now" refers to the effort made to give [myself] to another; "hopeless" means devoid of hope for attaining you, and therefore the meaning is that I am indifferent even to life. The particle *iti* marks the conclusion of the manner of this communication.

"O dear friend! I am to be remembered by you at all times. Here, the genitive case (*tava*) is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). The statement "I am to be remembered" (*smartavyāsmi*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) revealed through *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification), and not an injunction (*vidhi*), because that would be improper. The meaning is: "There is never anything other than me to be remembered by you. Even though it is not explicitly stated, she is always to be remembered; therefore, the intention is that you need not be specifically entreated for this purpose. This is like the word "to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) in the passage, "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen" (*ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ*). For: "Since a restrictive rule (*niyama*) or an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*) may also occur even when there is an injunctive sense."

"By the very perception of non-self, we worship the Supreme Self"—so says the Teacher. And this beautiful *vakula* garland, fashioned with her own hands by Mādhavaśrī, should be regarded by my dear friend as no different from Mālatī herself; it should always be worn upon the heart. The injunction "it should be seen" and "it should be worn" is established because its nature is already proven.

As the Teacher has stated: "An injunction (*vidhi*) applies when something is absolutely unestablished; a restrictive rule (*niyama*) applies when there is an optionality; and an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*) is proclaimed when [an action] is established both there and elsewhere. "Having released" means having lifted upwards; "placing upon the neck" indicates that at that moment, a close observation is necessary for the purpose of positioning [the garland]. "Suddenly withdrawing" means going quickly away; the meaning is that she withdrew out of shame upon realizing, "This is the hero. "With a tremor born of agitation" refers to the shaking of the body produced by mental disturbance; "embracing" is the subject at hand.

Continuing with the very joy of the embrace of his beloved, which had come upon him unexpectedly, he says: "ekīkṛta" and so forth. "Ekīkṛtaḥ" means mixed together. "Tvacī" refers to the sense organ of touch; "niṣiktaḥ" means showered, as in the phrase, "showering nectar-like joys upon the skin. The meaning is that she has extracted her own essence by pressing [him] like a mechanical press, or else by crushing his chest with a firm embrace.

Or rather, by the pressure of her chest—she whose budding breasts are full and curved—she has made him small, for those breasts are large because they have newly emerged, or because they resemble the calyx of a lotus.

"Her breasts were compressed by a firm embrace, causing a thrill of horripilation to break forth," so it was said. From the root *bhuja* meaning "crookedness" (*kauṭilye*), when combined with the prefix *nir-* and followed by the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*), the form *nirbhugna* is derived. By the phrase "by her standing before [him]," the ripening of her own good fortune is indicated. A *hāra* is a string of pearls. Regarding sandalwood: "The *tāmrasāra* is indeed sandalwood";
"The yellow sandalwood (*pītacandana*) is desired by the sun; it is called *gośīrṣa* and *haricandana*."

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*. Regarding "the exudation of the moonstone" (*candrakāntaniṣyanda*): since the moonstone is a particular kind of gemstone, the term "exudation" (*niṣyanda*) is used specifically for the liquid water produced upon its contact with the moon, because of its coolness; it should be understood that other substances are not included here because they are naturally cool [without such a process]. "Water-moss" (*śaivala*) is "water-needle" (*jalaśūka*), according to the *Vaijayantī*. "Lotus-fiber" (*mṛṇāla*) is "lotus-stalk" (*bisa*). "Frost" (*hima*) is "cold water. The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) expresses a category; thus, this is a class or collection of such types.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the moon’s rays, frost, water-lilies, plantain shoots, lotuses, blue water-lilies, and so forth. Because of the rule stating that "there is no fixed order when many [words] are involved," the placement of words at the beginning is not restricted by their brevity or their relative importance. Here, the poetic figures are *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) and *atiśayokti* (hyperbole). //12//

Out of embarrassment, he says: "Aha! Lavaṅgikā has employed a stratagem to separate Mālatī [from her lover]. By the exclamation "Aha!", it is indicated that this was something he had not even suspected in his dreams.

By means of the pretext of reporting her own condition, Mālatī avoids his embarrassment by deceiving him: "O you who know only the sensation within your own heart!"—that is, one whose nature it is to know only the suffering of her own heart. "O you who are ignorant of the pain of another!"—meaning, one who does not recognize the agony or distress of another, namely, my own (the opponent). You, being such as this, are "reproached"—you are addressed with harsh words accompanied by irony (*utprāśa*). According to the *Vaijayantī*, "irony" (*utprāśa*) is a form of reproach (*upālambha*).
Since she knows only the sensation of her own torment, the very statement that she is ignorant of the pain of another constitutes the reproach actually employed.

He states the reason for this with the words beginning "uddāma": [The hells are those] in which there are great fevers—great torments characterized by "unrestrained bodily conflagrations," that is, the unimpeded act of burning the entire body; [those] in which the sensations—the experiences of suffering—are "allayed" or relieved by "associations of imagination," that is, by enjoyments fashioned through thought; and [those] in which life, though intent on departing, is "supported"—forcibly restrained—by the "consciousness of affection for you," the recognition that "you are kind toward me. As it is said: "Even when the god of love has failed in his purpose, the longing of both parties creates delight."

This is according to the maxim [of the *Nyāya*]. "By me too" means "just as by you. The statement is phrased as a question—"Have the days not been passed?"—though it is well known to all the world; you too have surely heard this through the mouths of Kāmandakī and others. Therefore, the meaning is that because of your own experience of suffering, you indeed deserve reproach. Here, indignation (*asūyā*) toward the heroine is suggested. The poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) is *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Praise), because by means of the effect, the cause—the extraordinary nature of his own passion—is revealed.
Or it is *Paryāyokta* (Periphrasis), because the passion, which is to be understood through implication, is expressed by way of a synonym. //13//

He reinforces that statement: "O friend! You have been reproached for what deserves reproach. The word "what deserves reproach" (upālambhanīyam) refers to a matter worthy of censure; this is the implied sense. Through the mouth of Kalahaṃsa, the poet reminds connoisseurs of his skill in composition: "Oh, how full of aesthetic flavor is this arrangement! By its "flavoriness"—that is, by its being inflamed with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*)—the power of wonder produced by this construction, whether by the author of the plot or by the poet, becomes manifest.

Then, strengthening the meaning spoken by the hero through his own experience, he prays for favor: "O Mahābhāgā!"—this indicates that among women you alone are the most fortunate, for this jewel of a man has such affection for you.
"You are *vatsalā*," etc.; *vatsalā* means affectionate toward her own object. By this reason—"your consciousness of [his] affection"—[the phrase] *tvatsnehasaṃvit* [is established].

This is a paraphrase of *Ṛgveda* 1.3 and so forth. There too, "somehow" (*kathamapi*) means with great difficulty; "one who has supported the self" (*avalambitātmā*) means one who has sustained the body. According to the *Vaijayantī*, "self" (*ātman*) refers to the vital breath (*jīva*), fortitude (*dhṛti*), and the body. The phrase beginning with "somehow" leads up to "the union of resolve" (*saṅkalpasaṅgama*).

This is a restatement of *Ṛgveda* 1.34.1 and other passages. The meaning is that "truth" (*satyam*) signifies "that which is unfailing," implying that even such things as the testimony of a balance-scale can be employed by me for this purpose. The phrase "this person" indicates the demonstration of emaciation, discoloration, and so forth through the touch of the hand. "Of this much" (*iyataḥ*) means "of this extent," which is a gestural indication of length. "He has led away" (*anaiṣīt*) means "he has taken away"; he uses the past tense rather than the present (*nayati*) or future (*neṣyati*) to suggest, like you, a state of despair, indicating that this man likewise will not live beyond this point. Thus, he employs a specific verbal form to highlight this distinction.

Therefore, having obtained your favor—which is a grace consisting of friendship or intimacy between the two hands that have bound bracelets upon them (for the *Vaijayantī* states, "A bracelet is also [called] a hand-thread")—[he says this]. By the expression "in the joining of the hands," he indicates that because they share a common relationship, it is worthy of praise by all people; for it is taught that "the sacrament of taking the hand is prescribed for women of the same caste."

This is according to the traditional rule (*smaraṇāt*). "May he rejoice" means "may he prosper"; "this person"—that is the sense. "For a long time" means for a great duration. "May [his] desires bear fruit" is like the expression "may the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpataru*) bear fruit"; that is, may his longings—such as the thought, "When indeed will this man have accomplished his purpose?"—be fulfilled. Since no distinction is specified, it is established that this applies to all of us. Here, the emotion (*bhāva*) directed toward a friend is revealed. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is Hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). The phrase beginning with "O affectionate one" (*tvaṃ vatsale*) constitutes a formal service (*paryupāsti*), due to the heroine’s entreaty through the mouth of Makaranda. //14//

"Even if the grasping of the hand is performed by force, there is no fault whatsoever; therefore, let it be accepted of your own accord. In this manner, the friend conveys her point through a clever turn of phrase: "O noble one! This person possesses an unimpeded audacity for self-seizure even within the heart. Why then is deliberation made regarding the hand adorned with the marriage bracelet? By saying "even within the heart," she reveals a paradox: because the heart is internal, it ought to be most carefully guarded.

"Unobstructed" means unimpeded; "rashness of self-choice" refers to that rash act of seizing [the hand] by one's own will even without the leader’s (Mādhava’s) consent. "This person" refers to Mālatī. "The ornament of the bracelet" is a restatement of her words, "with the bracelet bound. "The hand" is mentioned because its being outside makes the consent for self-choice easy to obtain. "What is there to deliberate?"—the word "what" is used in a sense of censure, meaning that she has no doubt at all regarding this.

Understanding his intention, Mālatī says to herself: "Alas, woe! Alas, woe! She is proposing something quite contrary to the conduct of a woman of noble family. The phrase "something" (kimapi) means something unthinkable due to its impropriety.

In order to accomplish the task by removing all doubt, he introduces Kāmandakī at the appropriate time with the stage direction "entering. Having observed her apprehension through her outward demeanor, he says: "Daughter! O timid one! What is this? By addressing her as "daughter," he dispels the suspicion that she might be acting without the consent of her father and others, implying: "Surely, while your father, mother, and I are present, such a rash act would not be possible. By calling her "timid," he means that even regarding a desired object, fearfulness arises due to innocence and the very nature of women.
Nevertheless, lest there be such excessive timidity, he says: "What is this?"—the meaning is, what is this extreme timidity that is being observed?
"Trembling" means quivering with the fear of a rash act; she embraces her mother like a child, out of a sense of seeking refuge.
"The chin" refers to the lower part of the lip. "Having raised it up" is because her face was bowed down by modesty. And this is the manner of her conciliation.

He steadies her by manifesting their mutual passion and by recollecting the suffering of their separation, beginning with the words "At first, the attraction of the eye" (*puraścakṣūrāga*). "At first" (*puraḥ*) means initially. "Attraction of the eye" (*cakṣūrāgaḥ*) is the affection arising from the conceit that [the beloved] is beautiful to the sight. "Thereafter" (*tadanu*) means immediately following that. "Devotion to no other" (*ananyaparatā*): that which has no other object as its primary or principal focus is *ananya-param*; the state of being such is *ananyaparatā*.

"Absence of devotion to anything other than [him] in the mind" indicates, through the attachment of the heart, the cutting off of the sleep of volition, the cessation of objects, the destruction of shame, and madness and fainting, since these are rooted in the attachment of the mind. "Wasting of the body" is emaciation of the frame; as Māgha said, "The rise of oneself is the wasting of another. The root *jyā* means "to decline in age. The mention of "wasting of the body" separately is because it is perceptible, whereas the other states are to be inferred from their effects. Death is not mentioned because it is not applicable here. "In you" means regarding you.

In this regard—that is, concerning this youth who is fit for enjoyment, who has been described by me as being complete in all qualities such as noble birth and so forth, and who was heard of by you; "this one" means he is fortunately present here, and "dearest" (preyān) means the most beloved, implying that he was sought after by you because of your desire to obtain him—here, in the matter of this youth.

"O fair-faced one"—this is a sarcastic address meaning "you of beautiful countenance. The implication is: "The favorability of your heart is being expressed by your serene face even as you depart; why then do you distress us? "Stupefaction" (jaḍatā) refers to a lack of resolve regarding what ought to be done, according to the definition: "stupidity is a lack of comprehension.
[Therefore,] release [us].

May your cleverness—the skill consisting in the synthesis of the totality of qualities required for the creation of the beauty of your forms—shine forth and manifest in the presence of virtuous people. May Madana, the god of love, who inspires mutual passion, also have his desires fulfilled through this union. By the use of the words "this very one" and "here," he suggests that even the remorse felt for neglecting what is present nearby will afflict you. The poetic figures employed here are Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description) and Atiśayokti (Hyperbole). //15//

The friend said with apprehension: "O Blessed One! This man is indeed a reckless adventurer, whose perilous undertaking is unique for wandering through the great cremation ground on the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kṛṣṇa; he possesses the audacity of mighty, staff-like arms that have utterly destroyed fierce heretics. For this reason, my dear friend has become trembling. By specifying 'on the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight' and 'in the great cremation ground,' he highlights the terrifying nature of the place due to ghosts, vampires, jackals, and the like.
His 'wandering' is for the purpose of selling human flesh, and it is 'distinct'—that is, clearly set apart from others."

From such usages in the *Setubandha* as "whose vision of happiness was overflowing" (*ṇivbaḍiasuhāloaṃ*) and "whose splendor was overflowing because the task was accomplished" (*ṇivvattiakajjaṇivbaḍattacchāaṃ*), [the meaning is clear]. "Viṣama" refers to one whose resolve—the firmness of undertaking—is contrary to [what would be expected from] his own nature, condition, lack of knowledge, delicacy, and so forth. By this, the extreme gravity of his passion is indicated.
[As it is said: "But regarding tasks that are flawed, having reflected upon them, [one should choose] that which is more meritorious."
"He who resolves to act is called one who possesses perseverance.
And:
"But he who, regarding deliberation over tasks as procrastination,"

"He who decides quickly is considered impetuous," so says Divākara. "Niṣṭhāpitaḥ" means completed; "caṇḍaḥ" means cruel, which suggests that his sword-blade was fashioned from the stalks of *kaṇṭaka* (thorny) plants—this being a delicate [iron]. "Pāṣaṇḍaḥ" refers to one by whom [the world] is confounded; therefore, it highlights the gravity of the service consisting of saving his life, namely his impetuous valor (*sāhasa*) in his arms, which is extraordinary (*uddaṇḍa*). "Ut kampitā" means terrified by the sight of him, that is, trembling; for trembling is common to both joy and fear.

This is the figure of speech *vyājokti* (concealment under a pretext), because the trembling that has manifested is hidden under the pretext of fear; or it is *mīlita* (the concealment of one thing by another).

He expresses this with charm, as the occasion for such a statement has arrived—[speaking] to himself: "Excellent," meaning "praiseworthy," [referring to] "this matter"—the word "this" being understood. By repetition (*vīpsā*), he indicates respect. "In the proper place" means at a suitable opportunity. Regarding "of affection and assistance," the phrasing follows the sequence of his previous statement. "Of the two weightier ones" means of those that are exceedingly great. "Proposal" (*upanyāsa*) refers to the statement made as a means to what he intends to say.

Then, he describes the state of the heroine’s heart being overwhelmed by his words: "Alas, father! Alas, mother! The exclamation "Ha" expresses despair; the meaning is that at this moment you two were not present. Alternatively, it implies: "By overstepping you both, I have resolved upon this.
Having observed her state of agitation through her outward appearance, he says: "Dear Mādhava! This indicates that because of my presence, your proximity to Devarāta and the others was not required.
By saying "Command me," he expresses his respectful attention upon hearing her words.

Now, he says "this [land]," and so forth, to show that since a previous gift made by one who lacked authority was as if not made at all, we—being currently authorized to give—bestow it now according to the path prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti. "Sāmantas" are kings existing on all sides; because Padmāvatī’s lord is a universal monarch (cakravartin) and this king is his very self, and because of his Brahminhood, they bow before him. On their heads, which are thus bowed, are the *uttaṃsas*—the crest-garlands—and by their *parāgas*, that is, their pollen-dust.

"Vataṃsa, uttaṃsa, and śekhara" are synonyms according to the *Vaijayantī*. "Parāga is the pollen of flowers," according to the *Amara-kośa*. He is one whose toes are colored or stained [by the pollen]. "The jewel of a single offspring"—this indicates that, due to the absence of any other children, he is the sole object of the totality of his affection. According to the *Amara-kośa*, "apatya, toka, and taya" are all terms for offspring. By describing him as the "best of offspring," it suggests that he is worthy of being cherished even by virtue of his own qualities, owing to his possession of every excellence.

By the phrase "by the Creator," who delights in the union of the similar and is intent upon the conjunction of those with equal virtues, [the author] demonstrates that even when obstacles are numerous, the accomplishment of one's resolve cannot occur without the favor of destiny (*daiva*). By the phrase "by Love" (*manmathena*), he indicates the future prosperity resulting from the mutual passion existing in this marriage ceremony, which is the most excellent of auspicious rites. By the word "mine" (*mama*), referring to her who stands as both Bhūrivasu’s daughter and Devarāta’s daughter—[as it is said]: "In this case, the giver and the receiver are both the son of Kuśika himself"—he [establishes her noble lineage].

The phrase "itivat" (as it were) indicates that the acts of giving and receiving are independent of anything else. By the particle "ca" (and), which serves as an unexpressed conjunction with "by the father," it is implied—according to the understanding of the recipient—that the gift is being made by her own hand for the sake of avoiding falsehood. Furthermore, the use of the form "tubhyam" (to you) rather than "tava" (your) reveals that she is the recipient (*sampradāna*) because of her possession of complete virtues and her status as a common kinswoman.

It is given preceded by water; the meaning is that [the ownership] is made subject to you by the cessation of one's own right, since the marriage rite witnessed by fire will be described later. This is the context beginning with "this [kingdom] among all the vassals," and so forth, because of the glorification of the Guru.

Remaining silent due to joy and bashfulness, the hero speaks his reply through the mouth of his friend: "It has borne fruit" means it has become purposeful; "it has come to pass" refers to the culmination of the emotion (*bhāva*). "No" is used here to include those connected to both families. "Therefore," meaning from that service to the feet of the Blessed Lady, "by their grace" means by their favor. The phrase "for then it has indeed borne fruit for us" and so forth indicates power (*śakti*), because of the pacification of conflict.

Observing that an unexpected sorrow has arisen at a time of joy, he says "tat" (that). The meaning is: since this is now the occasion for joy because the long-continued effort of the Blessed One has borne fruit, for what reason [is this]? Why? "Bāṣpāyitam" means characterized by the shedding of tears; it is formed with the suffix *kyap* according to the rule "bāṣpoṣmabhyām udvamane" (Pāṇini 3.1.16).

"With the hem of her garment" means with the edge of her saffron robe; the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states, "the edge of a garment is called *añcala*. She states the cause of her tears: "O child!"—this is a mere indication intended to generate respect. By addressing him as "virtuous," meaning one who will possess future prosperity due to his great fortune, she indicates both the natural steadfastness of her own intellect and her effort to speak out of the power of her affection. She reveals her desire to speak immediately after he has approached her by saying, "I wish to say something, yet I do not speak."
He dispels that apprehension: the particle *nanu* is used for emphasis; the sense is that the Goddess must surely command it, for even that which is difficult will be performed.

Having set aside his doubt, he states what he intends to say, beginning with "pariṇati... and so forth. "Pariṇati" refers to the ripening of time; the meaning is long-standing acquaintance. "Manoharāḥ" means captivating. "Prītayaḥ" means affections or attachments; by the use of the plural, their manifold nature is suggested. Regarding those like you, there is the saying: "The world hates long acquaintance and desires ever-new things."
For such great beings as yourself, who have transcended the world as described above, it is said in the Mahābhārata: "Friendship with them does not grow old through cohabitation... and so forth.
"Just as there is a gradual excellence of flavor at every joint from the tip of a sugar-cane, so too is the friendship of the virtuous; but for the contrary, it is the opposite.

From this saying, the phrase "of those like you" states the reason for the permanence of the association. He also combines another reason with that: "I too... [is] "honored by you," meaning worshiped; and "by those various [reasons]" implies their innumerability—the reasons being: [her status as] a paternal relative, nourishment, protection, instruction in knowledge, her taking up of the wandering life (pravrajyā), her engagement out of affection in whatever she desired, and so forth—meaning by these and other limitless causes.

The phrase *tat tasmāt* means "therefore," because while I am alive, there is not even the slightest suspicion of a breach in our affection, even in a dream. Here, the term *suvadanāyām* ("of the fair-faced one") is an elliptical expression; it implies that for this woman, who is endowed with all the auspicious marks of every limb, any calamity is at no time to be suspected. Nevertheless, it is understood that I speak out of affection, saying, "I must tell you. The address *tāta* is used because of the scriptural injunction, "But the son, O child, [should address his father as] 'Tāta'. The word *mattaḥ* means "from me" (*mat*), according to the rule *pañcamyāstasil*.

(5-3-7) "In the future" (*parastāt*), meaning in a subsequent time; the suffix *-astāti* is used here in the sense of time, signifying "after the release from my body. Whether love born of intimacy arises by fate or not, let there be no suffering for her who has long relied upon me due to the compassion that is synonymous with courtesy—the desire that she not suffer because of this long-standing acquaintance. In every way and by all means, having considered the noble birth and other qualities of both, as well as our own affection, [consider] her visible form, her status as a lawful wife, her reliance on us, and her womanhood.

The meaning is "in an unseen form. This is because of the statement of Manu, "A virtuous wife and an infant son [must be protected]," and because of what is said in the Rāmāyaṇa: "I have heard from you yourself that compassion is the supreme dharma."

"Women are said to be the glories of the home; therefore, they must be protected with special care," according to the Mahābhārata. "Do not desist"—do not turn back. The fifth case ending is used here by the rule *jugupsā-virāma-pramādārthānām upasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 2.3.28), as in the rule *vyāṅparibhyo ramaḥ*.

(1-3-83) Thus, the *parasmaipada* ending is used. Here, the figure of speech is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description), because the cause—affection—is revealed by means of its effect. In such instances, one should keep in mind what was said [previously]: "The actions [of the virtuous] are pleasing due to their friendliness. //16//

And his affection is marvelous: through affection—that is, through love—he transcends, meaning he goes beyond all bounds. The sense is that there is no occasion for me to speak thus regarding this matter; such is the implication.

He states the infallibility of her observance of his command by means of an argument, beginning with "ślāghyānvayā" (of noble lineage), and so forth: "Ślāghyānvayā" means born of a venerable family; "nayanotsavakāriṇī" means causing a festival for the eyes due to her possession of unsurpassed loveliness; "nirvyūḍhasauhṛdabharā" means she by whom the weight of friendship—the excess of affection—was brought to its ultimate fruition, having been carried through to its conclusion by her steadfast resolve to renounce her life as soon as she was seen at the window; and "guṇojjvalā" means radiant with virtues, both innate ones such as good character and sweetness, and those acquired through refinement.

"And [the world] is set ablaze by immodesty and the like. The word *iti* everywhere denotes a manner; the ellipsis is "an object of such a kind. "Each one" means individually, without depending on a second. As stated in the *Kādambarī*: "Being a lord in the womb, being in the bloom of youth, possessing incomparable beauty, and having superhuman power—this is indeed a great succession of calamities. Each one of these is a locus for all forms of immodesty; how much more so their combination?"

*Vaśīkaraṇam* refers to a medicinal herb or a mantra-word that brings about subjection; here the suffix *lyuṭ* has an instrumental sense (*karaṇasādhana*) and not a verbal-nominal sense (*bhāvasādhana*). *Garīyaḥ* means "greater," because it effects a state from which there is no returning. By the statement "each one alone," it is suggested: "how much more so their combination? The word *yuṣmākam* (of you) uses the plural form because [the Lord] is among many gurus. *Evam* is a gesture indicating that he is the object of His affection, which is the cause for the statement "after Me" (*mattaḥ parastāt*). *Iti* indicates the manner.

The word *atha* (now/then) signifies a transition; it means: "In this manner, what more need I say? Her perfection of fortune is beyond the reach of speech and mind. Here, the poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) are *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause) and *atiśayokti* (hyperbole). //17//

Now, since the householder’s stage of life— which is capable of benefiting all and is praised over the other three stages by such Smṛti texts as "The remaining three stages of life depend especially upon the householder"— is the means for accomplishing the entirety of dharma only when husband and wife act in mutual harmony, [the author] establishes the presence of both to instruct them in the practice of dharma together, addressing him as "Dear Mādhava."
"Command me" expresses respect;
"O child Mālatī" [is used];
"Let the venerable lady command" indicates attentiveness.

He teaches: "The beloved" (*preyas*) means that which is most dear; "friend" (*mitra*) means a companion; "kinship" (*bandhutā*) refers to the group consisting of maternal and paternal relatives, brothers, uncles, and so forth—according to the rule: *grāma-jana-bandhu-sahāyebhyas tal*.

This is because the suffix *tal* is prescribed in the sense of a collection [by Pāṇini 4.2.43]. *Samagrā* means "entire" or "complete. The word *vā* is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*). As the *Vaijayantī* states: "The word *vā* is used in the senses of option (*vikalpa*), comparison (*upamāna*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*). *Kāmāḥ* are the objects of desire, namely the sensory objects such as sound and so forth; *sampadaḥ* are the prosperities consisting of wealth, grain, and the like, which serve as the means for attaining those desires; and *jīvitam* is the maintenance of life, which is the root of everything for all beings.
As it is said: "The body is indeed the primary instrument for the practice of *dharma*."

Because of this statement. Here too, the word *vā* (or) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Since there are two groups based on the distinction between external and internal, one group is conjoined with one [word] and the other with the other by means of the two *vā*s. The "supporter" (*bhartṛ*) is designated as such by the Creator (*dhātṛ*) because he is charged with maintaining and nourishing [them], according to Manu: "When parents have grown old, a virtuous wife, and an infant son—even if they have committed a hundred wrongs, they must be supported."

According to this statement, "the lawful wife" (*dharmadārāḥ*) means a wife wedded according to the law—one of the same caste (*savarṇā*), given by her father, and married in the presence of the sacred fire (*agnisākṣika*) through the *śrauta* and *smārta* rites; for she is a companion in dharma, whereas others are for the sake of pleasure. As it is said: "The service of the husband's body and the daily performance of religious duties must be performed by one's own wife alone among all [wives]; never by one of a different caste."

This is because of the statement of Manu: the word *dāra*—which is a synonym for *bhāryā* (wife)—is used both in the masculine and in the plural, as seen in such usage as "we here" and "these wives. "Thus" (*iti*) refers to this state of affairs. The word *iti* is displaced [in its logical position]; the connection is: "let it be known thus. "Mutually" (*anyonyam*) means one another. By saying "of the two children," even though they already know what ought to be known, he indicates that because of their youth, they must be awakened again and again for the sake of strengthening their understanding.

The injunction is: "Let it be known"—just like a royal command—let the words of the Śruti and Smṛti be accepted; one must not entertain doubt in this matter. The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "Let it be known that for both women and men, the husband and the lawful wife are, respectively, each other's category of friends and so forth, and the category of objects of desire and so forth."

A beloved friend is to be cherished because he is a ground of supreme trust; kinship is to be cherished because they constantly seek one's pleasure and welfare, and because one experiences joy and sorrow without distinction from them; sensual desires are to be cherished because they are the causes of happiness; prosperity is to be cherished because it provides the collection of objects for enjoyment; and life itself is to be cherished because, in the event of mutual separation, even that [life] becomes something to be abandoned due to its bringing about suffering.
As it is said: "A father gives in limited measure, a brother gives in limited measure, and a son gives in limited measure; who would not honor a husband, the giver of the unlimited?"
"There is no separate sacrifice for women, nor a vow, nor even a fast; yet by serving her husband, she is exalted in heaven.
Through such statements, because he benefits her in both worlds, the husband is like a friend and so forth to women.

"In matters of dharma, artha, and kāma, the wife is the man's companion"; "and when he travels to foreign lands, she alone is his source of trust"; "offspring, religious duties, service, and supreme pleasure [depend on her]."

It should be understood that through such Smṛti statements as, "For heaven for one's ancestors and for oneself likewise depends upon one's wife," the wife, friends, and so forth are described as the religious duty (*dharma*) of men. By the phrase "let this be known," the instruction is illuminated that since knowledges other than the knowledge of the Self from the Upaniṣads are useful for engagement in action and withdrawal from it, one should practice the common religious duties together with mutual non-deviation after having understood this:
"There shall be mutual non-deviation until the end of life."

"This is the excellent dharma for men and women, to be known in brief," according to the words of Manu. By this mode of expression, it is indicated that this is a *prājāpatya* marriage and not a *gāndharva* one, as [it says]:
"Having addressed them with the words, 'May you both practice dharma together'..."
"Having honored the giving away of the daughter, this is remembered as the Prājāpatya rite," according to the words of Manu; and:
"The mutual union of the girl and the groom through their own desire... [is the Āsura rite].

Because it has been stated, "That Gāndharva rite is to be known as that which arises from desire through sexual union," and because a voluntary union is not mentioned here, and because mutual affection is a factor beneficial to all forms of marriage, yet by that alone the status of a Gāndharva marriage is not established; furthermore, the figure of speech here is *ullekha* (multiple description), since one thing is apprehended in many ways due to various causes, and because the cognition that they are "mutual friends" and so forth is described as being common to both. //18//
Then, because the two leaders were sealed with the threefold seal [of secrecy], the male and female companions repeat their words, saying: "Atha kim?
(Indeed, so be it). This means: "Just as you command, so shall it be, for this does not transgress the meaning of the scripture."

Now, since the bestowal of Mālatī—which he himself had desired—has been accomplished, he instructs him in a single means that is both beyond suspicion and refined, intended for the purpose of concluding the current matter of Nandana’s marriage under a pretext and for the abduction of Madayantikā: "[My dear Makaranda... By this [phrase], the command sent by the king is indicated; "with the attire of Mālatī" means with the collection of ornaments intended for Mālatī; "conceal" means hide [yourself].

By the statement "with the dress of Mālatī," it is established by implication that [she should act] "in the character of Mālatī. "For her own marriage" means for her own wedding with Madayantikā. Regarding the reading "apavāritam vartayasva," the meaning is "send yourself away concealed.
"Paṭalaka" refers to a casket for ornaments.

Out of friendship and apprehension for some misfortune, he says: "Though easy to obtain"—meaning easily attainable through the power of skillful means—"it is fraught with many calamities," being perilous due to numerous misfortunes; that is to say, it is "unending" (*duranta*), because it would cause agitation to the king and his two ministers. The particle *hi* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*); as the *Vaijayantī* states: "The word *hi* is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*) and emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). This matter refers both to the deception of Nandana and the abduction of Madayantika. By the phrase "of my friend," his timidity born of affection is illuminated. The expression "though easy to obtain" and so forth expresses hope for its attainment.

He establishes him through the fear of both means and failure, by way of well-considered security: "Who are you?"—in this kind of deliberation regarding the task, who are you? The word *kaḥ* (who) is used in a sense of negation; it means "no one. What connection do you have with the deliberation of the task? The authority lies with us, while for you there is only the status of being the enjoyer of the fruit; such is the meaning.

He follows that intention: "Thus"—"only in the Blessed One," meaning that just as previously here, so too from now on, only the Blessed One is the authority in this matter; our deliberation, however, is merely restlessness—this is the sense.

It should be understood that here, the *garbhasandhi* (the "embryo" juncture), which consists of the search for the *bīja* (seed) that was first seen in the passage beginning with "Who are you?", then lost through the calamity of the army sent by the king's wrath, and finally seen again through the favor of the monarch and other means, is now being commenced.

The phrase "having laughed" (*vihasya*) is used because these words were spoken in the very presence of Mālatī. The meaning is: "If anyone dares to reveal [our secret] by saying 'I am Mālatī,' then we shall know [his identity]."
"With curiosity" because of the charm arising from the perfect fit of her attire; "with a smile" because it manifests the sentiment of humor (hāsya-rasa) in a man assuming the role of a woman.

"Having embraced"—the meaning is that she embraces out of joy, having considered both her inclination toward performing her own task and her perfectly fitting attire for the purpose of accomplishing it. "Adorned in such a manner" means dressed in Mālatī’s costume; "even for a moment" is said because the deception would become evident thereafter. She "will desire," meaning she will regard him with the sentiment of a lover. The phrase "if" refers to this false attribution made during the praise of one adorned in Mālatī’s costume as "Blessed Nandana," due to the employment of a disguise.

Having departed from this place, go to the garden grove—the garden area—behind our monastery, behind our vihāra; that is, to the western part, so that you may remain in seclusion and remain unrecognized by people. To the question, "What is to be done there? he says: "Suvihitam" means well-prepared or properly accomplished; "vaivāhikam" means that which has marriage as its purpose (*prayojanam*), according to Pāṇini 5.1.109, with the suffix *ṭha* (ika).

*Dravyajātam* refers to the collection of materials such as clarified butter (*ājya*), *kuśa* grass, sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), *śamī* leaves, parched grain (*lāja*), and so forth. By the word "well-prepared" (*suvihitam*), it is indicated that these were provided at the command of the family priest and that they were present nearby. The phrase "and furthermore" (*bhūyaśca*) means that it is stated once again.

He describes how the garden enclosure acts as an excitant (*uddīpana*) through the abundance of materials for enjoyment, beginning with the words "intense longing" (*gāḍhotkaṇṭhā*). "Intense" (*gāḍhā*) means deeply rooted within due to long separation; "longing" (*utkaṇṭhā*) is the yearning for union with the beloved; those [women] whose [longing] is "hard" (*kaṭhorāḥ*) are mature (*prauḍhāḥ*).

"A girl is [called] *bālā* (a child) up to sixteen years; beyond that, she is *taruṇī* (a young woman) until thirty; thereafter she becomes *prauḍhā* (mature) until fifty-five; and after that, a woman reaches the state of being *vṛddhā* (old)."

Thus, according to the *Ratirahasya*, there are the women of Kerala who possess intense longing and are robust; their cheeks have petals that are slightly pale, meaning their leaves are somewhat white. Two adjectives are employed because of their slight pallor and their lack of [ordinary] luster. The mention of "Kerala women" is due to their natural golden complexion. Since the leaves on the branches serve as the objects of comparison (*upamāna*), and it is well known that leaves harvested and processed [as betel] possess an excellence of whiteness and luster—[as in the verse]:
"Or the betel leaf, pale as the cheek of a Śaka maiden, torn by the tips of the reddened nails of young brides..."—[the comparison is established].

From such usage [as this]: "In which [forests] the betel-nut trees (*pūgadruma*)—those whose fruits have been embraced by clusters of *tāmbūlī* (betel vines), that is, by masses of *nāgavallī*—are bent down by that very weight of their fruit; and in which the calls, that is, the sounds, of birds (*vikira*) are charmingly soft due to their having eaten the fruit of the *takkolī*, a specific fragrant vine.
"......... *ṭakkola* is another name for *kolaka*; it is also called *kośaphala* and *phāla*........."

Thus, the *Vaijayantī* states: "The *śalaka*, *vikira*, *tuṇḍī*, *nīḍaja*, and *vātagāmī* [are synonyms for parrot]. By the word *vikira*, birds such as parrots that have been reared [by humans] are meant. "Its grounds" refers to the portions or regions of the garden land. "Having fences of swaying *mātuluṅga* creepers" means those [grounds] which have a fence—a boundary enclosure—consisting of *mātuluṅga* vines gently shaken by the breeze.
"Phalapūra, bījapūra, rucaka, and mātuluṅgaka; ... [the] enclosure at the edge is called prācīna."

Thus says Amara: *preyas* means a most beloved object; by this, through its cleverness (*vaidagdhyāt*), it indicates the sovereignty of sexual enjoyment (*sambhoga*). They will provide (*vidhāsyanti*)—that is, they will create—for you two (*vām*); here, the form *vām* is the substitute for the word *yuṣmad* in the dual genitive case. Here, the restoration of lost passion is established, as well as the abundance of substances suitable for mouth-perfuming (*mukhavāsa*), and the presence of the clamor of flocks of birds such as parrots and starlings, which serve as excitants (*uddīpana*). "The rind of the citron (*mātuluṅga*), betel, and mouth-perfumers should be present."

"Outside of that [house] are cages for pet birds," according to Vātsyāyana’s description of the layout of the pleasure-chamber (*ratibhavana*). The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) here is *udātta* (the sublime), because it describes an object of great prosperity. //19//

Therefore, because this location is so enchanting, it is stated that there is no need to go elsewhere—namely, for the arrival of Madayantikā and Makaranda, for as long as the time required for their arrival may last. By this, he confirms the meaning previously expressed by the words "for the sake of my own marriage."

Out of joy, he marvels at his own good fortune: "For those possessed of auspiciousness—that is, for the meritorious—the attainment of auspiciousness, the abundance of blessings, [occurs] above, that is, higher and higher. The repetition (*vīpsā*) should also be understood from the sense of the word; the meaning is 'higher and higher,' because what is intended is that 'success follows upon success. Even so, it will be for us—this manner of events, namely Makaranda’s marriage. The particle *api* includes Mādhava’s marriage as well. By the use of the interrogative intonation (*kāku*) in the phrase 'it will be for us' (*naḥ bhaviṣyati*), it culminates in the question: 'What indeed will happen?'"

He states the answer to the question: "How? In what manner?"—that is, regarding this matter. The meaning is that since the attainment of the result has been determined by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no possibility for doubt whatsoever.

She gladdens Mālatī: "It has been heard by my dear friend. The words "these [words]" are to be supplied. "From here" means "by this path," which is a gestural indication of the way to the wedding place; or else, "from this region. "We set forth" means we go. [This is according to the rule: *samavapravibhyaḥ sthaḥ*.
(1-3-22) Thus, the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] ending is used.

Because she cannot endure the separation from her friend, she says: "O friend! You too must go. By the interrogative intonation (*kāku*), a question is implied. Through the word "api" (also/even), it is suggested that while the departure of the other two may indeed take place, your departure is improper.

"Having smiled"—referring to her indication, by the words "you too must go," that she cannot endure separation from him, he says with a touch of irony: "Now indeed we long for this. By "now" (*sāmpratam*), he means: now that you are satisfied by the union with your beloved, which was sought for so long; "for this"—regarding the matter of non-separation—we "long," meaning we become desirous. The present tense (*laṭ*) is used here to indicate immediate proximity to the future. The sense is: "Upon seeing you, we alone shall be longing, because, being constantly intent on the flavor of sexual enjoyment, there will be no opportunity for us even to look [at you]."
"Today, indeed, for me, this entire exhaustion caused by love has reached its end.
(Laṭakamela-rakṣita,
Act 3)

Thus, reflecting on the imminent pacification of the long-endured torment of love that was so favorable to his own desires, he spoke joyfully: "I am this very one"—meaning, "I am this very person who has been scorched by the flames of the submarine fire of such intense passion"—"now," that is, at this very moment.

"From the root to the neck," and so forth: his arm is "thorny," meaning it is covered with horripilation (pulaka) from the base up to the shoulder region. The "arm" (*bāhu*) is the area between the shoulder and the wrist; as the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "The words *bāhā*, *bāhu*, and *bhuja* do not take the feminine suffix *ṣaṇ*. His fingers are "moist," meaning perspiring like petals. By resorting to a simile-based compound (*upamā-samāsa*), the term "hand-wing" (*karapakṣa*) is formed. By this, a natural emotional transformation (*sāttvika-vikāra*) is expressed. "Lovely" (*kānta*) means beautiful due to its association with qualities such as ruddiness and softness.

Regarding the lotus (*paṅkaja*): its stalk is like an arm, thorny from the root down to the bulb; its petals are like fingers, moistened by the water of a lake or sprinkled with honey—this application to the side of the lotus is achieved by resorting to a *madhyamapadalopa* (elliptical) compound. "Lovely" (*kānta*) is a common adjective. "Hand" (*kara*) refers to the palm;
as it is said: "The *maṇibandha* is at the base of the hand, while *maṇi*, *pāṇi*, *kara*, and *śaya* all denote the hand."

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*. "Tormented by the heat of the bodiless one": in the context of the hero (*nāyaka*), this means tormented by Kāma, who is like the summer heat (*nidāgha*); in the context of the elephant, it means tormented by a summer heat resembling the bodiless one. "With the trunk" (*kareṇa*) refers to his own hand, and [in the other case] to the tip of the trunk (*puṣkareṇa*). "I grasp" (*ākalayāmi*) means I take hold of; the verbal root is *kala* in the sense of "binding. "A reddish lotus" (*āraktapaṅkaja*) is a crimson lotus. "The elephant" (*dvirada*) is a tusker. "Of the lotus-stalk" (*nalinyāḥ*) refers to the stalk of a lotus or the lake itself. As it is said: "... *nalinī*, furthermore, *bisinī*, *padminī*, and so forth, denote both the lotus-stalk and the lake."

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*: when the lotus-stalk (*padmastamba*) serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), qualities such as coolness and delicacy [of the stalk] are understood to correspond to the coolness and delicacy [of the heroine], while qualities such as clarity, freshness, and depth [of the lotus-stalk] are understood to correspond to the heroine. By the mention of the "elephant" (*dvirada*), he indicates an excess of intensity, since the intent lies merely in its being grasped. One should not suspect a fault in employing a subverting (*bādhaka*) standard of comparison; for if every instance of similarity were rejected, it would result in the collapse of all illustrative examples.

Here, the poetic figure is *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration), because the hero and the heroine, the hand and the elephant, and the lotus and the red lotus are presented through the relationship of prototype (*bimba*) and reflection (*pratibimba*). Furthermore, the relationship of prototype and reflection among the adjectives is already demonstrated by virtue of the two compounds. By the statement "I grasp the hand," it is implied that "the sacrament of taking the hand is prescribed for women of the same caste."

Thus, by indicating that the auspicious rite of taking the hand, as traditionally remembered, shall be performed according to rule, Kavikulamukunda causes to blossom the performance of the complete meaning of the scriptures, which benefits both worlds; may all be most auspicious. //20//
Thus, Pūrṇasarasvatī has composed this analysis of the meaning of the sixth act of the *Mālatīmādhava* through the grace of Pūrṇajyotiḥ.
Thus ends the sixth act.
Now begins the seventh act.

Now, in order to present the narrative of the hero of the *patākā* (the secondary plot) separately, he begins the *praveśaka* with the words "Then enters... The entrance of Buddharakṣitā occurs because she was previously appointed by him [Makaranda] for the purpose of bringing about Madayantika’s union, as indicated by the statement: "Indeed, my friend Buddharakṣitā has already been commissioned by me for that task."

"Suśilaṭṭhietyādi" and so forth. Makaranda has been safely protected by the arrangements of the Blessed Lady in the house of Bhūrivasu; there, his marriage to Nandana was deceived by the splendor of Mālatī’s attire, which was so well-constructed that its true nature remained unrecognized. "Suśliṣṭayā" means "by that which is well-fitted," which is the reason for the failure to discern the difference. "Mālatīnaipathyalakṣmyā" means by the beauty of assuming Mālatī’s costume; "vipralabdhaḥ" means deceived; "[Nandanakaragrahaḥ]" refers to Nandana’s taking of her hand in marriage.

By the arrangements of the Blessed Lady—through such means as the clearing away of outsiders, being surrounded by her own circle of female friends, and the use of veils and curtains—he was protected and concealed with safety. Today he has arrived at the residence of Nandana. The word "by us" includes Lavaṅgikā and the others; it means "together with us. Then the Blessed Lady, having taken leave of Nandana, went to her own dwelling.
That is, immediately after the departure for the son-in-law's house, or from that house, having taken leave—that is, having obtained permission—she went to her own abode, her own vihāra.

Moreover, this evening—during which the entire retinue is occupied solely with the great festival of the "Unseasonable Moonlight" (akālakaumudī) prepared for the entrance of the bride and groom—will favor our undertaking today. The word "ca" (moreover) serves to conjoin the sense of the sentence.

In this newly arranged "untimely Kaumudī festival" (*akālakaumudī-mahotsava*) for the bride and groom—the newly wedded couple and their son-in-law—occasioned by their entrance [into the city], the term "untimely" (*akāla*) is used merely out of joy, since the Kaumudī festival, which consists of the Indra-sacrifice, is traditionally performed during the first fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, the first month of the autumn season; it is called the "Kaumudī festival" because it was celebrated during the bright fortnight characterized by moonlight, as in the phrase:
"the Kaumudī festival for the gaze of my friends."
This is according to the statement in the *Raghuvamśa*, and he will later say, "the festival of the moonlight (kaumudī-maha) which brings joy to kinsmen.

Furthermore, there is the statement of Vātsyāyana: "even during the Kaumudī festival on the eighth lunar day of the month of Āśvayuja. The word *mātra* is used for emphasis. By the phrase "in which the attendants were entirely agitated and bewildered," he indicates the lack of vigilance even among the guards. Amara states: "Pradoṣa is the beginning of the night. "He will make favorable" means he will make it propitious or successful. With the word "no," she indicates her own and Lavaṅgikā’s resolve through the instruction of the Blessed One (the Goddess).

It is resolved, it is firmly determined—the task consisting of the abduction of Madayantika. To further reinforce the suitability of his own resolve, he adds another reason: "And now, the son-in-law, having hastened with lustful desire and entreated her with prostrations at her feet, was again assailed by Makaranda with violence and struck harshly."

The phrase "now, with eager desire" indicates that once confidence has been gradually established, it would be improper to initiate the pursuit of one's objective prematurely; for such an action would contradict the injunctions of the *Kāmasūtra*, which state: "For the two who have come together, there shall be sleeping on the ground and celibacy for three nights."

Again, because he did not obtain the fruit of his entreaty, he ran toward her—that is, approached her with desire to sport—and was struck mercilessly; just as the pain from a blow to the body persists for many nights, so was he struck heartlessly, beaten by feet that were hardened by physical exercise, like a donkey.

And he, filled with both embarrassment and anger—being either deceived or agitated—the word *ḍhulukkhido* being a regional term (*deśīpada*) meaning "deceived"—with his face weeping and quivering, made a vow with an oath, saying, "I have no further need for this harlot from my youth," and departed from the bedchamber.

According to the statement, "That which acts with a distracted mind is called *vailakṣya* (embarrassment)," he was [filled] (*nirbharaḥ*) or full of the embarrassment and anger born from the frustration of his own intentions; for that very reason, he was agitated (*kṣubhitaḥ*).

"Whose face has tearful eyes, quivering, and a lower lip throbbing for harsh words"—this is said with the rumor of his passion for the unchaste woman of youth (kaumārabandhakī)—that is, a wanton woman of low character who was a maiden in her youth—held in mind. "With an oath" means accompanied by a solemn declaration, such as: "If she is ever touched by me, I shall become a transgressor of the commands of my chosen deity and my preceptor, and a perpetrator of a great sin. This is the meaning.

He reflects upon how the circumstances of that event have been brought about by fate in a manner favorable to his own desires: "By this very occasion, I shall bring Madayantika and unite her with Makaranda. The sense is that through this pretext, there will be an opportunity for the rebuke and consolation of Mālatī; thus, because it is appropriate to bring in Madayantika—the sister of her husband—there is no room for suspicion.

He concludes the interlude (*praveśaka*) by stating "she has exited," since the events already occurred—the arrival at Nandana’s house and her departure in anger—and the event yet to occur—the bringing of Madayantika—have both been indicated.
Thus ends the introductory interlude.

Then he begins the *aṅka* (act) for the purpose of narrating the episode of the *patākā* (the secondary plot), according to the statement that "the *patākā* should have a continuous connection"—hence the stage direction: "Then enters [he]... The expression "lying on the bed" (*śayyāgata*) means "resting upon the surface of the couch," which is stated as an indication of his role as a newlywed bridegroom.

"Transferred to Buddharakṣitā, entered into Buddharakṣitā"—by this [phrase], he indicates that the "method of Kāmandakī," which is the strategy of the Blessed Lady, consists solely in the performance of the aforementioned manner [of acting] like a puppet or the like; however, the agency of the operation belongs to her alone. "It will be victorious" means that, having warded off obstacles, it will become fruitful. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to Pāṇini 1.3.19: *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ*.
How can there be doubt on the part of the Illustrious One?

"What more need be said?"—desiring to state the justification for the absence of doubt, she anticipates her intended meaning by inferring a causal proximity: "Just as this sound of anklets is heard"—the word "is heard" being understood from the context—"so do I know that Madayantikā has been brought here by Buddharakṣitā under that designation. The word "by him" (*tena*) refers back to the subject at hand, because it was previously established as a conventional sign.

Under the pretext of this instruction: "Your brother, provoked by Mālatī, has departed after making a solemn oath; therefore, you must bring him under your brother's control through both reproaches and conciliations. By this, [Makaranda] brings together the words of Buddharakṣitā: "So, on this occasion, I shall bring Madayantikā and unite her with Māraṇda. "Concealed by her upper garment" means covered by the upper cloth; *supta* is the state of sleeping (*supti*), formed with the past passive participle suffix in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), and it is by way of that pretext.
"‘Lakṣaṃ’ is neuter when it means a target; it is not feminine. It is not masculine when it means a pretext or a hundred thousand.
Thus says the Vaijayantī.
Buddharakṣitā related the account of Nandana for her own concealment and to incite him to speak with confidence."
He reveals this through the manner of his speech: "It is true indeed that my brother has been deeply provoked by Mālatī;
what else could it be?"

"Alas! What a great calamity, what a terrible misfortune! The meaning is that when one of a couple is overcome by passion while the other remains indifferent, it becomes a cause of unsurpassed suffering for both. Therefore, come; let us go after rebuking the perverse-natured Mālatī. For this reason—that since this misfortune must be averted by us through our friendship—come, you too must provide assistance; this is my request. 'Perverse-natured' (vāmaśīlām) means one whose disposition is contrary [to her husband's], referring here to the husband."
