By this, he implies the innocence of his own brother; the meaning is that she has been disciplined by being rebuked with harsh words. "Afterwards we shall go to our own quarters"—by this, he indicates that the employment of this pretext is now tending toward its fruition. This is the *vāsabhavana*, the bed-chamber.

Having inferred [her state] from her being covered by an upper garment and her lack of movement, he says: "Friend Lavaṅgikā! It is known that your dear friend is fast asleep. By saying "your dear friend," he suggests: "Is even you encouraging her wicked conduct?"

"Friend! Awaken her. The reason for this is: "She has been despondent for a long time; now I think she is slightly asleep. "Despondent" (*durmanāyamānā*) means experiencing mental anguish, which indicates her offense against Nandana. "Now I think she is slightly asleep"—this is the connection. Therefore, sit down very gently right here at the edge of the bed. "Right here" (*ita eva*) is indicated by the pointing of a finger to ensure she is not awakened; it refers to one part of the bed, as seen in the usage of the phrase "the edge of the ground" (*mahialaddhantā*).
Having acted thus and having sat down, she becomes dejected; or, in this alternative, she herself behaves contrary to her husband's wishes and becomes dejected—what is the reproach [in such a case]?

Perceiving her effort at reproach, [the messenger] himself reproaches her so as to leave her no further opening: "How indeed could my dear friend become dejected after having obtained for a husband such a brother—skilled in the means of winning the confidence of a new bride, charming, clever, sweet-spoken, free from anger, and not timid? As for the means of winning the confidence of a new bride: 'Therefore, one should treat her with conciliation and with tact; one should find an opening through tact.'"

One should know him as described in the *Kāmasūtra*: "He should enter after her" and so forth; he who is charming (*laṭaha*), handsome, whose speech is clever, sweet, refined, and full of flavor—by this, the skill in conversational artifice taught in the *Kāmasūtra* is indicated, such as: "There, one should speak with a successful woman for the sake of hearing her words; one should ask about something of little meaning, as if not knowing.
Furthermore, he is "not prone to anger," meaning that because she is exceedingly shy and of a contrary nature, he does not become angry;
as it is said: "But he who neglects a maiden simply because she is possessed of great shyness..."

Because of the statement, "One who does not understand the intention is treated like a beast," it indicates that one should act with courage and free from timidity; having understood his intention, even a slight use of force may be employed.

"Success with young women is achieved neither through excessive conformity nor through contrariety; therefore, one should proceed with moderation. From this statement of Vātsyāyana, by means of *viparīta-lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication), there is revealed a lack of knowledge regarding the proper means, ugliness, the use of vulgar and harsh speech, irritability, and cowardice. As for the phrase "your brother," everyone considers their own kin to be virtuous and does not perceive their faults.

This indicates the maxim stated as: "O Bhārata, all auspicious things [occur] for the beloved, while evil things [occur] for the one who is hated. By the word *bhartāram* (the husband), the lifelong nature of this thorn in her heart is revealed. The phrase "how will she be distressed? and "in what manner will she be agitated? employs *viparītalakṣaṇā* (contrary indication). Through this *dhvani* (suggestion) wherein the literal meaning is completely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*), it is suggested that there is always only room for despondency and never even a trace of happiness.

Having understood the intention behind those words, he says: "Look, Buddharakṣitā! We are being reproached for our contrary behavior. The word "look" means: let this profound censure be examined. "Contrary behavior" (*vipratīpa*) means adverse or hostile.

Alternatively, by means of a conceptual distinction, he establishes the propriety of Lavaṅgikā’s reproach through a rhetorical turn: "Is it contrary, or is it not contrary? In both ways, it can be joined by the clever; however, in reality, only one alternative remains—this is the meaning.
[As the saying goes: "To turn even faults into virtues, and to turn even virtues into faults..."
One who is capable and eloquent may speak that which is not true; faults are [regarded as] faults, and virtues are [regarded as] virtues.
Because of this statement, she asks out of a desire to know that: "How indeed?"—the meaning being, in what manner is there the application of both [conditions] to a single person?
She demonstrates that manner: "Insofar as my husband, though bowed at his feet, was not honored..."

The phrase "first of all" (*la tāvadādau*) indicates the state of non-investigation; "great respect" (*bahumānaḥ*) means honor, which was not obtained when complying with her affection. The meaning of "that" (*yat*) is that this very thing is suspected by you to be the cause for reproaching her. To this, he states the rebuttal: "In this matter, this person is not to be reproached on account of the fault of bashfulness. Here, "in this matter" (*atra*) refers to this point; "on account of the fault of bashfulness" (*lajjādoṣeṇa*) means due to the fault consisting of bashfulness, caused by such factors as unrefined innocence, or rather, due to the transgression of bashfulness—[a fault] arising from the thought, "May they perceive my lapse."

"Shame is a mental transformation that opposes all [other] functions," says Divākara; "this person" is Mālatī’s dramatic gesture. "He is not to be censured"—meaning he does not deserve reproach—is the reply to what was said [by her]: "I am censuring you for your contrary behavior. Furthermore, as for that indescribable, unseemly thing uttered by your brother—whose high-mindedness was shattered by the embarrassment of stumbling through an impetuous advance contrary to the decorum of a new bride—it is being considered: "Who are we? [to judge such things].

A "new bride" (*navavadhū*) is a girl recently married; [the text refers to] that which is contrary to her, or opposed to her, because such [conduct] is forbidden in the *Kāmaśāstra*: namely, a "rash commencement," an initiation of sexual union accompanied by impetuosity. As it is said: "One who disregards all limits, acting with haste and overstepping the proper sequence..."

"Such impetuous activity is considered impossible for others to endure," says Divākara. The sense is that "stumbling" refers to an obstruction, because transgressing the meaning of the scriptures results in contrary consequences. [The opponent is one] by whom the "greatness of high-mindedness"—the majesty born from lineage, sovereignty, learning, and the maturity of age—has been "vomited out" or cast away through the "embarrassment" caused by that [transgression], which is to say, an excess of shame; for there is the saying, "The virtuous have forgiveness as their essence."

The phrase "of her brother" indicates that because he is related to all of us, his offense produces shame in us. The expression "consisting of words" implies that physical punishment, such as beating, would have been appropriate—since it serves as a form of discipline and its pain is relieved at that very moment—but verbal abuse, by striking at one's vital points, never subsides. As it is said: "Arrows of speech fly from the mouth; struck by them, one suffers through nights and days. They fall upon the vital spots of another; therefore, a wise man should not discharge them at others."

Thus, he indicates this by the words "according to the statement of Vyāsa. By the phrase "something [unknown]," he expresses its difficulty of being spoken due to its extreme harshness. *Appaḍiṭṭhāṇakaṃ*—or alternatively, the reading is *appaḍiṭṭhāṇaṃ*—means *apratiṣṭhānakaṃ*, which refers to an action that transgresses a suitable place; the meaning is "improper speech. For that reason, it is investigated and examined.

Alternatively, there is the reading "keṇa jāṇīadi" (by whom is it known?), meaning "by whom is it known? The word "we" refers to those residing in Nandana's house. As for the word "who"—since Mālatī has placed them in the category of those not to be reproached by saying "this person is not to be blamed"—it is not known in which category we ourselves should be placed: in the category of those to be reproached or in the category of those who reproach; this is the meaning.

The statement "incompatible with a new bride," "in which great nobility has been scattered," and "which is without foundation" constitutes a clear proclamation of faults; however, it should be understood that by saying, "I do not know [the answer], but you alone, being possessed of intelligence, are the authority for its determination," she is indirectly reproaching us herself while establishing her own position. The use of the interrogative pronoun *ke* in the masculine plural indicates that Mandana is primarily being referred to, as he is the one under consideration; otherwise, she would have had to say, "What are we? (using the feminine).

Having already stated that [the conduct] is contrary to the nature of a new bride, he establishes this for the purpose of censuring the [opposing view of] Nandana by citing the *Kāmasūtra*, beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). Furthermore, I shall say something else; you should not think, "This is merely my own invention. The meaning is that I am demonstrating the very meaning of the authoritative treatise (*śāstra*). He cites that very treatise, starting with "Those who share the nature of flowers," and so forth.

They have a nature similar to flowers: just as flowers, when gathered with care and placed upon the head, produce supreme happiness and an excellence of beauty, yet cannot endure being squeezed in the palm of the hand or subjected to excessive force; so too women are to be cherished and not to be tormented—this is the meaning.

As it is said: "The natural state of a fragrant flower is established upon its head; it is not achieved by blows from pestles. Here, *hi* signifies a well-known fact. This is a characteristic of women in general (*yoṣit*), let alone of maidens (*kanyā*), since this is read in the section concerning the winning over of maidens. They are "approached with gentle means," meaning their sexual union is to be accomplished through soft methods; the verb "they become" (*bhavanti*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Those women, in particular, when being approached by force—that is, being forcibly initiated into sexual enjoyment—by men who have not attained their confidence or gained their trust, immediately at that very moment become hostile to union, meaning they develop a disposition of aversion toward contact with men. Furthermore, he describes their state of repulsion: "or else, they become haters of men. This means those whose nature is to hate even mere men, even without sexual union, including in matters such as seeing or touching them. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the aphorism.

"Thus, indeed" (*evvaṃ kila*): "thus" (*evaṃ*) refers to the manner [of expression], because there is a multiplicity of such statements. "Thus, indeed, the authors of the *Kāmasūtra* maintain" means that the authors of the *Kāmasūtra*—namely Nandīśvara, Śvetaketu, Bābhravya, Vātsyāyana, and others—maintain (*āmananti*) or study [this]. "Indeed" (*kila*) indicates renown; the sense is that this matter is already known to you as well, since you have studied it. The particle "iti," like the word "śruti" (Vedic revelation), indicates that the *Smṛti* concerning women which follows it possesses unfailing results, that it is not to be questioned, and that if one acts otherwise, the result will be contrary.

It should be understood that the portion of the sūtra beginning with "kusumaiḥ" and ending with "puruṣadveṣiṇyo vā" is in Sanskrit because it is an imitation (anukaraṇa), and by the rule "anukaraṇe tu sarveṣām," such imitations are grammatically correct; whereas the portion beginning with "evaṃ kila" is in Prakrit because it constitutes his own speech. It is not, however, [the case] that the former relies upon Sanskrit, for that [Sanskrit] falls within the scope of his own utterance.

The phrase "with tears" expresses his skill in cultivating the conviction of truth. In every house, men marry women; yet no one, even among the best, the middling, or the lowly, ignites with the fire of their words that innocent young maiden of noble family—whose very ornament is modesty and whose nature is guileless—saying, "I am the master. They marry, that is, they wed her. "No one at all" means whether he be superior, mediocre, or inferior. Modesty itself is her ornament and adornment, according to the saying: "Modesty alone clearly adorns women."

"Anaparāddhaḥ" means one who has never committed an offense, being free from transgression at any time; the reason for this is that he is "mugdhaḥ," possessing a natural disposition as unartificial as that of a young fawn. The sense is: what man indeed, unless he were insane, would harbor a base resentment even toward children, animals, or maidens when they act unwisely out of innocence? [He regards] the "kulakumārījanaḥ" as those born of a praiseworthy lineage, and the "kanyājanam" as those who are the protectors of their family.

By this, it is illuminated that since the three aims of life (trivarga) depend upon him, she may be accepted when he is favorable—like a courtesan—and abandoned when he is adverse; and whether this is possible or appropriate is thereby shown. "I am capable" means "I am the master, I am the lord. The particle *iti* indicates a reason; for this reason, and not on account of some slight transgression committed by him, who indeed could prevent the caressing or fondling of the entire remainder of the world? Nevertheless, the sense is that the second alternative is improper.
By the fire of speech—that is, by the fire in the form of words—it is metaphorically described as fire because it produces unsurpassed pain and because there is no rejoining [of the wound].
As it is said: "A wound caused by speech, consisting of a loathsome ill-spoken word, does not heal."

Thus it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*. "He kindles" means he makes [the fire] blaze; the expression "he kindles, but does not burn" is used because, like a *puṭapāka* (herbal steaming), it constantly generates a seething heat in the mind without reducing it to ashes. Indeed, these are the thrusting of darts into the heart—difficult to endure as long as one lives, causing detachment from dwelling in another's house, and constituting great humiliations. The word "indeed" (*khalu*) is used for emphasis.

These, being seen by the world for as long as one lives—that is, throughout one's life—are like the implanting of a thorn in the heart; they take the form of burying a thorn, namely an arrowhead, within the mind because they cause internal anguish. They are unbearable when remembered, piercing the vital organs at every recollection even more so than during the time of the actual experience. By the word "para," a place other than one's father’s house is meant. Those whose nature it is to feel despondency due to detachment while dwelling in the houses of others are called *mahāparibhavāḥ*—insults that are greater even than beatings and the like.

"For whose sake their kinsmen loathe the birth of a female child"—that is to say, for the sake of which reason, out of apprehension regarding future humiliations, their kinsmen, such as fathers and others, loathe and despise the birth of females within their own lineage. As it is said: "Fie indeed upon the birth of a daughter in the family of men who are of noble character, exalted, illustrious, and of pure essence!"

Thus it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "In this situation, upon the birth [of a daughter], the kinsmen offer water for the girls with tears from their eyes," and so forth. Having ascertained that she is truly suffering on account of her weeping and other such signs, she says: "Friend Buddharakṣitā! My dear friend Lavaṅgikā is greatly tormented. Has some great offense been committed by my brother against her? The particle *api* is used here in the sense of a question. She uses the word "great" because weeping and the like would not be appropriate if the offense were merely trivial.

He brings forward precisely the offense: "What then? Having made a solemn vow with oaths, saying, 'I have no need for this unchaste woman from my youth,' he departed from the bedchamber"—thus he connects what was already stated in the *praveśaka*.
Covering his ears with both hands, [he says]:
"Wherever the censure or even the reproach of one's teacher occurs..."

The meaning is that, having prescribed an expiation for hearing the censure of a virtuous person based on such traditional law (*smṛti*) as, "The ears should be covered there, or one should depart elsewhere," [the friend] says: "Oh, what a transgression! Oh, what a lapse! A transgression (*atikrama*) is the overstepping of proper bounds; it is improper to speak thus regarding a maiden of noble family. The cause of this is a lapse (*pramāda*), meaning a lack of attention. "Oh" (*aho*) expresses astonishment; the sense is: how could such a disturbance of the intellect have arisen in that person of great majesty? Ashamed because of his offense, she says: "Friend Lavaṅgikā!"

"I am unable to look upon your face. "Unable" means powerless; the word "out of shame" is to be understood as the ellipsis. She begins to justify her brother's lack of fault by way of a clever turn of phrase: "Nevertheless, being empowered, I shall say something. "Nevertheless" means: let it be that an offense has indeed been committed by him. "Being empowered" means: because of our friendship, I am authorized to restrain you and speak; this is the meaning. "Something" means: whatever occurs to my mind; the request is that this must be endured.

Then, as if consenting to that, she cleverly provides an opportunity for confidential conversation in order to descend [to the earth] according to her own desire: "This person is at your disposal. This means she is under your control; "this person" refers both to Mālatī and myself. By this, she indicates that there shall never be any jealousy on our part regarding your words.

Then he begins to address him with the intent of a friend: "Let be for now my brother's ill-conduct and his instability. Ill-conduct means a corrupt nature; instability means fickleness. Let these not be mentioned now, because they are already well known—this is the meaning. Even such a person as this must currently be followed according to your own wishes by you all, on the grounds that he is your master.

The word "api" (also/even) conjoins that you yourselves also possess guilt, not only he; it signifies opposition, meaning that although he is of such a nature—characterized by bad conduct and so forth—and thus unfit to be served by others, he must nevertheless be followed and attended to now that the taking of her hand has been accomplished, according to one's heart—that is, without transgressing one's own mind, in accordance with one's desire. To the question, "Is this a royal decree that even one devoid of virtue must be followed? he says: "By whom [the husband]... [is meant].

The word *yena* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that functions as a substitute for a case ending; its meaning is "because" or "therefore. By this, it is suggested that the Vedas (*śruti*) and the Smṛtis are not to be questioned, just like the command of a king: "Whether he be lacking in character, acting according to his whims, or devoid of virtues, a husband must always be served by a virtuous wife like a god."

This is because of the statement of Manu. He says that the root of her offense is not merely bad character, but something else as well: "And you do not know the root of this reproach and censure consisting of insults in vulgar words. Vulgar words (*anabhijātākṣara*) are the speech of those of low birth (*akulīna*); an insult (*adhikṣepa*) is harsh language, and by means of that comes the censure (*upālambha*), which is blame; the "root" (*mūla*) of that is its cause.

Although Lavaṅgikā knew the intention behind those words, she spoke as if she did not know: "How can we know what is 'internal' (ātmagata)?"—meaning, how can we know what resides within the mind? The sense is: according to the maxim that "the intentions of a speaker are known through the signs of their speech," your intention is understood once you have spoken; therefore, let it be told. In the reading *asantam*, the meaning is "unreal" or "false," the implication being that such [an internal state] lacks any basis in reality.

In the reading *ṇa vāāgāṃ*, the statement "How could we not know even what has gone forth from their speech? is an intentional remark intended to refute the meaning he wishes to convey; the sense is that there is no basis for it other than the wicked character of your brother, and that this is made manifest by his own words.

He explains the basis for the censure: "That which was merely a word from Mālatī regarding that noble Mādhava has now become a rumor that has reached the highest pitch among all people; indeed, this is what is unfolding. The word "in him" (*tasmin*) refers to the representation of the experience of Mādhava, because he was seen at the time of the Śārdūla encounter. Alternatively, "in him" refers to the representation of his entry into the city of Śaṅkara.

"In regard to Mādhava, 'something' [is the case]"—this is a concealment of the fact that he is an object of her affection, because it would be improper to speak of affection for another man when she has been given to someone else. "Kila" indicates tradition; the sense is: "I am merely repeating what I have heard, so you should not be angry with me. "Mere words" refers only to the mutual conversation between the friends and others, since the marriage ceremony was completed elsewhere. Or alternatively: "By good fortune you are here, having regained consciousness, O noble one! and:
"Therefore, by the rite of the *pūrṇapātra* (the vessel of abundance), he has full power to accept my heart and my life."
the vowel ṛ (ṛ.

There was merely a matter of words, such as "this favor has indeed been accepted," regarding which there arose a public rumor—an ill-repute—reaching the highest pitch, the ultimate limit, for all people from children to the elderly, because it was proclaimed everywhere at all times. The grammatical connection is: "now that the rumor has reached its highest pitch. By this, he connects with what was previously stated: "But the rumor of affection between the two children is universal," and so forth.

That very thing—indeed, the word "khalu" serves as an emphasis—having become these harsh words of Nandana, unfolds and transforms; the meaning is that, having taken that to heart, he uttered that wicked speech which defiles her character by calling her a "whore from her youth."

Therefore, dear friend! Act in such a way that her husband’s partiality for the opposing side is extracted from her heart without remainder; know that otherwise there will be great trouble. "Her husband’s heart" refers to Mālatī's own heart; "partiality for the opposing side" means an attachment to the contrary position, a stubborn insistence—by implication, the apprehension of that [attachment]—should be removed and eliminated entirely, without exception. Act so that it is so; thus, she must be won over with all your soul.

By using the plural form "kuruta" (you all must do), he indicates that even though Mālatī may not understand due to her innocence, she must be instructed and protected by you who have become one with her. He states the negative consequence of failing to act: "Otherwise"—that is, if you do not act accordingly—there will be a great fault or calamity, because if there is mutual discord between husband and wife, the destruction of the household itself is likely. He suggests this indirectly, implying that it might happen that a wicked wife could not be abandoned or that she might be superseded [by another]:
"Even after accepting a wife according to the prescribed rites, one may abandon a wife who is censurable."
"One who is diseased, or corrupted, or approached through deception," and "She who is a drinker of liquor, untruthful in conduct, and hostile."

For it is said in the words of Manu: "A wife who is diseased, cruel, or constantly wasteful of wealth should indeed be superseded," and "One who speaks unpleasantly [should be superseded] immediately. By means of *dhvani* (suggestive power), in which the literal meaning is transmuted into another sense, this is manifested as an instruction, with the intended meaning being: "Let this be understood; let it be accepted as a teaching."

He provides the justification for the probable cause of her renunciation and so forth: "Women are indeed unshakable and cruel; they torment the hearts of men through such a wicked assault. "Unshakable" means firm in their resolve regarding desired objects; "cruel" means pitiless even toward a person who is under the sway of passion. The particle *khalu* indicates a well-known fact. The meaning is that this point has been established by sensitive critics through such sayings as, "Women are indeed hard and do not break," and "What is more cruel than a woman's heart? and so on.

From such a wicked attachment—one resembling the pursuit of Mālatī, which is evil and opposed to both worlds, and which consists of an affection directed toward anyone whatsoever apart from her husband—the word *iti* indicates the cause. By the phrase "of men," the instability of their love is suggested, according to the saying: "The love of men for women is indeed unstable, but not so for friends," and also according to the words of Vātsyāyana: "Because the minds of the human race are inconstant. Since those who are thus tormented proceed even to acts of abandonment and the like, the connection [of the sentence] is: "Therefore, let it be understood that otherwise there would be a great fault."
"By seizing him by the hair, one should turn a friend away from an improper act;
having exerted effort to the best of one's ability, one becomes beyond reproach by anyone.

Following this saying, she says—"Do not say it! Do not say that Madayantika did not tell me"—in order to prove her own innocence. By the mention of "Madayantika," the intimacy and confidence born of playing together as children (*pāṃsukrīḍā*) is implied. The meaning is: "Alas! Even though Madayantika knew this matter, she did not tell us"; do not speak thus later, for the fact was already pointed out by me beforehand.

She said, provoked by love: "O you, deluded by the incoherent rumors of the world! Begone! I will not converse with you. The meaning is: O you whose heart is deluded—that is, distracted—by the incoherent (*asambaddha*), that is, false and inconsistent (*asatya-viṣaya*) rumors (*pravāda*) of the world, that is, of other people; *apehi*, move away from my presence. I shall not engage in conversation with you, because it is improper to hold discourse with those who are like madmen. This is the intended sense.

Then, seeking to appease her by establishing the ultimate truth of her own words, she refutes her statement—"deluded by irrelevant worldly rumors"—as follows: "Friend! Be gracious; do not be angry. Or rather, you were not spoken of first. The word "or rather" (*athavā*) serves to set aside what was previously stated. "You"—referring to Mālatī and the others—"were spoken of first," meaning they were mentioned by me as having fallen under the sway of worldly rumors; or else, the ellipsis is to be supplied: "you were informed by me beforehand that such future calamity would occur."

The meaning here is that there is a doubt among you. "Wait for a moment and remain silent"—the intention is that I shall then corroborate the matter I have stated. He begins the corroboration: "Furthermore, we know Mālatī to be truly one whose life consists of Mādhava. By "we," Buddharakṣitā is included. "Truly" means not merely by popular rumor; she is one whose life is identical with Mādhava, having Mādhava as her very soul.

By this, he indicates that even death and the like are possible if that [state] is not attained. In the reading "we do not know," the interrogative intonation (*kāku*) suggests: "How could we not know?"

Anticipating the question, "How is this known by you?", he says that this matter is known even to children and cowherds: "By whom has the body of Mālatī and Mādhava—not been perceived? [A body] whose exquisite beauty was manifested through the frailty of limbs resembling the interior of a hard *ketakī* flower; [a body] whose life was sustained solely by the *bakula* garland fashioned with his own hands by Mādhava and worn around the neck; [a body] whose appearance was lovely yet emaciated and pale like the orb of the morning moon."

The body of Mālatī—and by extension, the body of Mādhava—is described as follows: it possesses a *vibhrama* (graceful charm) like that of the interior petal of a mature, full-blown *ketakī* flower, owing to its slightly pale, delicate, and lovely nature; its inherent beauty has become distinct and set apart from the ordinary through the languor of physical weakness; its sole means of sustenance and life-sustaining medicine is the necklace hanging from her neck; and thus her body is fully manifested and discerned.

Moreover, on that day, at the meeting point of the street bordering the Kusumākarodyāna garden, as they both displayed curiosity with playful grace, I too observed the glances exchanged between them—glances made radiant by the playfulness of their pupils moving with graceful and smooth gait, and charmingly beguiling through the innate cleverness fashioned by the most diligent instruction of the Master of Love’s own musical school.

In that [state] there is a constant reflection upon the experience; in their meeting, which was produced by the agitation of the tiger’s assault, there arose a flurry of excitement and a mutual longing to see one another. *Vibhrama* is the disarray of ornaments and so forth caused by haste.
As Dhanika says: "Vibhrama is the displacement of ornaments from their proper places due to haste."

They were beautiful and radiant with glances characterized by playful charm, smoothness, grace, and lack of vulgarity in their movement; for the beauty of the graceful movements of the hands, feet, and other limbs has its root in the playfulness of the eyes, according to the maxim: "All states of being are manifested in the eye."

"By the instruction of the dance teacher Anaṅgarūpa, who is skilled in music, with every mark of respect—that is, with all his respectful teaching—[these women], having manifested their own cleverness through the imparting of training born from the partiality felt toward gaining good disciples, are themselves charming and therefore captivating. 'By me too' means that my conviction does not arise from another's word; they were also personally observed and seen by me. 'Nanu' is used here for confirmation, meaning 'together with you two. Or, there is a reading 'na' (not)."

At that time, in the phrase "and moreover" (*kiṃ ca*), the connection is with *kim* (meaning "why"), the sense being: why were they not observed? The word *ca* (and) serves to conjoin another reason. "The collisions of their glances" (*dṛṣṭisaṃbhedāḥ*) refers to the mutual intermingling of the eyes of these two, Mālatī and Mādhava. He states another reason: furthermore, having heard the news regarding my brother, was their heart not perceived—its physical luster fading due to the immediate onset of a surge of agitation, its very root-attachment as if about to unravel?

Having heard from the mouth of a man that "Mālatī has been bestowed by the Supreme Lord himself upon my brother Nandana," at that very moment, his bodily splendor and luster—withered like a flower touched by fire due to the impact of a surging, overflowing agitation; for the heat of the mind is invariably accompanied by the heat of the body, as the venerable Vāhaṭa has said: "The heat of the mind and the body shall mutually affect one another."

For this very reason, the mind—whose root-bonds are being loosened—is as if its joint-bonds have been severed from its own support, which is called the "heart-knot" (*hṛdayagranthi*); for, like the eyes and other senses, the mind also possesses a sense-organ nature, and thus its stability within its substratum [the heart] is lost. "Heart" (*hṛdaya*) here refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Why was it not noticed? It was indeed seen, because the mental state is to be inferred by signs (*liṅga*), and the sign in the form of pallor manifested instantaneously; such is the meaning. Furthermore, something else has also occurred to my memory.

Furthermore, another thing—this is the ellipsis for "I say"—is that there is yet another matter; the meaning is that something previously remembered has now been forgotten and then [re]appeared. In the expression *me smṛtam* ("it is remembered by me"), the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the present tense because it belongs to the class of roots meaning "cognition" (*mati*) according to Pāṇini 3.2.18 (*matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca*), as indicated by the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne*.
Thus, the genitive case [is used].
Desiring to explain that [point], she introduces it by means of a question, in accordance with her own intention: "O friend! What else has now been forgotten? Her silence indicates haste.

He reveals the matter he has remembered: that for Mālatī—who announced the acquisition of consciousness to that noble one who restored my life—the heart and life of Mādhava were offered as a reward by the Blessed Lady, prompted by her skillful speech, to be accepted at his own discretion. By the word "his" (*tasya*), his experience is manifested as being distinguished by sweetness of nature, heroism, courtesy, and so forth. By the phrase "who restored my life," it is implied that there is no greater favor than the gift of life. As it is said: "On one side are all the sacrifices completed with the bestowal of desired gifts..."

By performing the gift of life for one who was terrified on all sides—thus praised by Vyāsa as the "gift of breath"—the poet demonstrates his supreme beneficence toward him, as well as his own gratitude in seeking out his beloved and his eagerness upon seeing her. Through this, the poet reveals the fulfillment of both the meeting in calamity and the principles of the *Kāmasūtra*. Furthermore, the marvelous intellect of the hero is manifested in his prowess, characterized by such unsurpassed power as to be capable of slaying a beast of prey of that magnitude.

By the words beginning with "cetanā," he recalls what was said [by Mādhava]: "O noble one, by good fortune you remain conscious and have regained your senses. This is due to the introduction of speech by the venerable Kāmandakī, consisting of clever and refined expressions, such as: "Dear child Mādhava! By good fortune you are prospering; this is the moment for the gift of affection from Mālatī."

The meaning is that the statement "she, who is as dear to you as life, must be cherished by you" was vulgar in the presence of many people, because its suggestive power (*vyañjana*) produces aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) through poetic refinement (*vicchitti*). Being urged—that is, impelled—by Mādhava, [the messenger] was appointed to seize her by force herself; she was entrusted [to him] with the words beginning, "She who is bewildered and deluded by the fainting of her friend wounded by the serpent," and so forth.

Now, Lavangikā! You yourself said, "This favor has indeed been accepted by my dear friend. By saying "you yourself," she implies: "Oh, what a deceit you have practiced!"—referring to you who now reproach me as one "deluded by the nonsensical rumors of the world," who are angry, whose cheeks are drenched by the shimmering flow of no small amount of tears, and who weep, crying "this is false! (Note: The term *kaitavam* here refers to the artifice or hypocrisy of her earlier acceptance of the gift, which contradicts her current behavior.)

Now, reflecting upon the bond of love that has grown for her toward Makaranda, he diverts her attention with a different subject in order to cause her to forget the matter at hand: "But who is that noble-souled one? [She replies:

"I have forgotten him. The word *punaḥ* (but/however) indicates a turning away; the meaning is: "Let this matter be for now. "Who is he? refers to the one indicated by you as "the giver of life to me. "Which one?"—among those many who were present there, which one?

"Friend! Remember, remember him!"—thus she speaks as he approaches. By the word *upari* (above), it is implied that on that day, when I had fallen within the range of a fierce and wicked tiger and was without refuge, I was protected by one who stood nearby for a moment, supported by the pillar of his stout arms; he, my disinterested kinsman, performed the audacious act of offering his own body—the sole essence of the entire world—as a sacrifice. The repetition "remember, remember" (*smara smara*) suggests great urgency and importance regarding that matter. On "that day" refers to the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇacaturdaśī*).

The "vast and formidable precipice of the wicked tiger" refers to the range and domain of its leap. "Without refuge" indicates her lack of protection because her attendants have been killed or scattered, thus highlighting her state of helplessness. By the phrase "present at that very moment," the absence of any prior acquaintance is made known.

"Somewhere, fashioned on the tip of a scale, it is pure according to the scriptures"—thus [it is said] in the *Setu*. And he is the cause of being a kinsman without motive. By his two thick, stout, pillar-like arms—due to their being round, elevated, firm, and long—he was favored: having been received with respect, embraced tenderly after entering between them, and supported by being placed behind him. "By one who is a kinsman without motive" means by one who has adopted the state of kinship without any prior cause, such as a previous favor.

"Because it is defined as: 'He who becomes a refuge without being asked for anything is a true kinsman,'" [the author] states that his own body is the object of supreme love, since it is the singular essence of the entire world—the unified excellence of all realms—and because it is the locus of the totality of all virtues; the meaning is: "having performed the rash act of offering, which consists of surrendering himself to the tiger, acting without hesitation."

"First my body was offered to a beast of prey for my sake, and I experienced a blow; afterwards, by fate, I was restored to life while he was killed"—this expresses his own obstruction of compassion. "I have been protected"—that is, I myself have been saved.

"By me, however, unfortunate as I am, nothing pleasing was performed regarding him"—thus her wretchedness is revealed. And for my sake, the Wealth of Compassion—resplendent with a broad, muscular, high, and expansive chest, and wearing a heavy, aged, and tattered string of pearls—endured the blows of the thunderbolt-cages of all his falling nails. "Endured" (*vidhṛta*) means "obtained" (*viḍhatta*); as Murāri says: "The mass of *kalaṅga* flowers was obtained. *Vikaṭa* means hard and uneven;
the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "*Vikaṭa* may mean deformed."

As it is said in the *Harṣacarita*: "A complex arrangement of syllables is difficult to find in its entirety in one place. Upon that chest—which was fleshy (*māṃsala*), plump (*pīna*), prominent (*uttāna*), elevated (*unnata*), expansive (*pariṇāhi*), and vast (*viśāla*)—there shone a radiant, throbbing, mature (*jaraṭha*) [garland], which had reached the state of ripeness at the appropriate time and was shattered by the force of the blow; this was a crest of pearl-strings (*muktālatāpīḍa*), a garland in the form of a string of pearls. By means of that [garland], which was captivating (*hārin*) because it had the nature of holding [the pearls] or because it was beautiful, and which was rich in compassion (*karuṇā*), where compassion is indeed pity for living beings.

"Whose wealth is his entire being. By the phrase "with the wealth of compassion," the lack of expectation for any recompense is suggested. "For my sake" means for the purpose of my task; as seen in the usage of Bhartṛhari: "The son of the eldest wife was exiled for the sake of the son of the youngest. From the force of the blows, the wounds from the strikes of the entire collection of sharp, hard nails—which, like a cage of thunderbolts (*vajra*), penetrate deep into the chest and sink within—are being submerged; as in the expression "sinking into the mud... (*paṅkakhuppantavaga*).

"Ṛ) *ailakkai seṇṇaṃ* (O, army of elephants!)"—so it is said in the *Setu*. And that wicked beast-of-prey, the great rākṣasa, was slain. The attribution of "great rākṣasa" to the beast-of-prey is for the purpose of demonstrating his extreme cruelty. The syntactic connection is: "He by whom I was protected, by whom the blows of the thunderbolt-cage were warded off, and by whom the beast-rākṣasa was slain—remember him! She speaks with a gesture of remembrance: *huṃ*. According to the *Vaijayantī*, "huṃ" is used in addressing or in reproaching: "huṃ [is used] in addressing or in reproaching."* Makaranda:
Ṛ. *The *Vaijayantī* states: "huṃ [is used] in addressing or in reproaching."*
Acting as if she had not heard what was previously said, out of a desire to hear it again, she says: "Friend, what do you say?
Knowing her intention, she replies: "Indeed, I am saying 'Makaranda'. The word "nanu" (indeed) implies: "Have you not heard this?"

Now, in order to reveal the heart of her who has entered the path desired by herself, he explains the particular physical expression he observed: "With a smile" (*sasmitam*) indicates the knowledge of her inner state. By saying "touching her body," it is understood that she has suddenly become horripilated upon hearing the name of her beloved. The use of the refined language (*saṃskṛta*) is for the purpose of making an unrestrained reproach. "We are likewise," and so forth: "we" (*vayam*) is a collective reference to Mālatī and the others; "likewise" (*tathā*) means characterized by that same nature; "namely" (*nāma*) is used here either to indicate manifestation or contempt—the meaning being that they are well-known in that way, or indeed contemptible.

"In whatever manner" (*yathā*) means by which specific quality; "you say" (*yatprakāraviśiṣṭatayā āttha*)—this is the form of the second person singular present indicative of the root *brū* (to speak), with *āha* as the substitute and *thas* as the ending. The meaning is that those who, without the taking of hands in marriage, transgress the bounds of propriety due to being overcome by passion for another man are indeed contemptible. "What shall I say? means: when a matter has been established by you as authoritative, how can its contrary nature be asserted?

Alternatively, this is an introductory framework (*pīṭhikābandha*) for the matter about to be stated: "Everyone is clever at observing the faults of others, but they do not recognize their own faults; regarding this matter, what shall I say? Alternatively, *kim* is used in the sense of a question: "I am stating the matter perceived by me; why should you harbor resentment toward me? The word *tu* indicates a distinction. "Suddenly" means without cause.
[This occurs] while the unimpeded and clear cognition of [him who is] dark as a *tamāla* tree remains awake.

This is because of the syllogism of the teacher Citsukha: "Why is darkness perceived as a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) without cause? and because of other syllogisms such as "the consequence of being causeless" (*ākasmikatvaprasaṅga*). "Vikala" means dependent on another. By the phrase "in the midst of the conversation"—referring to the discourse initiated for the purpose of reproaching Mālatī—he indicates: "In this incidental context, what can we say regarding the fact that this is your primary state?"

It has the shape of a *kadamba* bud and the form of a *nīpa* tree blossom; for, due to its dense horripilation (*pulaka*), it is well known that such bristling hairs resemble *kadamba* buds. Although the word *gola* (ball) denotes merely a spherical mass, by its proximity to *kadamba*, it here indicates a bud. "How? expresses wonder. "Pure and innocent" (*viśuddhamugdha*): because passion does not arise in an inappropriate place, he is pure (*viśuddha*)—meaning faultless—and innocent (*mugdha*)—meaning untrained in deceit. By this, he suggests a contrast (*vyatireka*), implying: "In comparison to him, we are impure and deceitful."

The "group of noble maidens" refers to the class of young women whose sole vow is the preservation of their family lineage. The inclusion of the word *jana* (people) is intended to distinguish them from one's own circle; the meaning is that "this person is one [of them], while we are others. In this matter, you too, being tormented by some passion, falsely desire to seize Mālatī;
for as the saying goes: "When a fault is equal for both parties, or the remedy is likewise equal, one should not be the sole object of reproach in such an inquiry into the matter."

By the phrase "according to this logic," it is suggested through *viparīta-lakṣaṇā* (contrary indication). Here, a specific emotional state (*bhāva*) called *moṭṭāyita* is revealed. Dhanika states: "But *moṭṭāyita* is that [state] occurring when one contemplates the feelings of another during desired stories and the like. This is the *sūkṣma* (the subtle) ornament, because it reveals a subtle meaning that was previously unperceived; and it is also *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), because the cause—the passion of Makaranda—is understood by means of its effect.
And there is *nidarśanā*, because it involves the conceptualization of a comparison, [stating] that "a form is similar to a form. //1//

Then, out of shame, she conceals her own intention: "Friend! Why do you mock me? For what reason do you reproach me by imagining me to be otherwise? Indeed, the matter I have been thinking of is not the cause of the horripilation, perspiration, trembling, and so forth, by which I might be an object of ridicule. This is the meaning.

To the question "Who then is this other person?", he says: "Indeed, I say that even the mention of the name of such a person—who is a great benefactor for bringing back by force the life of one who is being devoured by Death (Kṛtānta) through a selfless resolve—is enough to cause agitation. It causes agitation, that is, it terrifies; the root *āvij* is used in the sense of "fear and trembling. Because fear is mentioned, the occurrence of physical effects such as horripilation (*pulaka*) is also logically established as resulting from that fear.

Regarding the phrase "of such a one," it expresses that he has treated the prowess of a tiger as if it were mere straw—meaning one whose resolve is indifferent to his own self and who is free from any apprehension regarding the loss of his body. By the term *kṛtānta*, Yama (the God of Death) is intended; the tiger is determined to be *kṛtānta* because of its nature as a destroyer. Alternatively, since Yama himself is the destroyer even through the agency of the tiger, it is Yama who is being referred to. The phrase "being swallowed" (*kabalikriyamāṇasya*) means being currently devoured, rather than merely about to be devoured; this highlights the proximity of the moment of death. [This is achieved] by forcibly restoring his life.
"Action performed in other births is *daiva* (fate), while action in this life is *pauruṣa* (human effort).
When action is divided into three parts according to its quality—superior, middling, and inferior—it is said:
'Indeed, *daiva* is overcome by *puruṣakāra* (human exertion) when it is weak.'"
As it is stated in the *Saṅgraha*: "Likewise, human effort is rendered weak by powerful destiny," and from the saying:

"Indeed, powerful human exertion (*puruṣakāra*) even overcomes destiny," the meaning is that even certain death was averted through the power of human exertion. The phrase "of the person" refers to one who has been a benefactor and whose nature is supreme kindness; this is spoken with a degree of detachment for the purpose of concealing one's own affection. "Conversation" means the narration of events, and "mentioning the name" means the proclamation of the syllables of the name.

The phrase "even the utterance of the name" is mentioned later in order to indicate that even the mere syllables of the name, when heard, cause agitation; let the conversation for now be set aside. Here, the poetic figure is *vyājokti* (concealment under a pretext), because of the hiding of a matter that has already been revealed.

He confirms this very quality of your selfless resolve: "Likewise, O noble one, you too have personally witnessed that illustrious man, for whose sake the entire world of living beings—so precious and vast—was sacrificed; he who, having forgotten his attachment to the body upon experiencing the pain of a deep wound from a claw, held his vital strength with the steady firmness of a staff-like sword planted in the earth, while his pair of blue-lotus eyes closed in a swoon as delusion overwhelmed him."

Thus, by the stroke—the impact—of the nails deeply sunk into his chest according to the manner described by me, he experienced a sensation, an intense pain; through the attainment of that, his attachment to the body and his sense of "I" were forgotten and lost. Due to the delusion born of that pain and the resulting fainting fit, his two blue-lotus eyes were closed.

He whose bodily strength—the physical vigor or the excellence of the body—is firmly and immovably supported by the brace, that is, the support of the sword-blade (asiyaṣṭi), the edge of which plays upon the ground and whose tip is sunk into the surface of the earth; [this he does] for the sake of Madayantika, which highlights his gratitude as well as his own lightness of heart.

"By whom the great and most precious life-essence has been scattered": *vicchardita* means abandoned; *mahārgha* means exceedingly costly, because it is the means for experiencing the fruits of merit characterized by an excellent birth, long life, and enjoyments. The compound with the word *mahā-* is formed because the word *mahārgha* is conventionally established in that very sense. Alternatively, *argha* refers to that in which there is a *maha*—a festival—and *artha*—worship; for Amara states, "A *maha*, *uddhava*, and *utsava* [are synonyms]," and Vaijayantī states, "*Argha* and *pratikriyā* mean worship."
The "world of the living" (*jīvaloka*) refers to the world of living beings, namely human beings; the meaning is the land of Bhārata, because it is more esteemed than heaven.

As it is said: "The gods indeed sing these songs: 'Blessed are those men who, on the portion of the land of Bhārata—which serves as the path to the abodes of heaven and liberation—return again from the state of being gods.'"

By such statements as these, [the author] illuminates the gravity of the favor shown: even though that Brahmin—who is preeminent among those possessing a multitude of virtues such as supramundane knowledge, sovereignty, beauty, and good fortune—is born from a specific merit accumulated over countless previous births, he did not consider even a blade of grass sufficient for the protection of my life, which was as dear to me as grass.
As it is said: "For a Brahmin, upon being born, is truly born upon the earth as a lord of all beings for the protection of the treasury of Dharma."
This is because of such statements from Manu.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the *sāttvika* emotions such as paralysis (*stambha*) and others are included. The phrase "he acts out" (*nāṭayati*) means that he performs the representation without hesitation, since it is designated as a cause for fear.

Then, in order to ascertain her intention, he urges her toward a means [of inquiry] out of friendship: "O dear friend, we are distressed by our co-resident Mālatī! By this address—'O you whose body is unwell,' meaning one whose body is currently not abiding in its natural state due to the presence of emaciation, paleness, and so forth—the entire situation is revealed by her physical condition alone; it indicates why she should no longer endure the affliction of futile concealment."

"Udbhinnāḥ" means we have become those whose secrets have been revealed—by such verbal formulations as "this [happened] all of a sudden," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "sahavāsinyā" (with her who dwells together): it refers to one whose nature is to dwell together [with Mālatī]. By the expression "Mālatyāḥ sahavāsinyā" (with Mālatī’s co-resident), it is revealed that since she has been instructed in the various modes of the torment of love by Mālatī herself, she possesses the capacity to infer those same signs in others as well.

Having gained the opportunity through the statement, "We have been revealed," she employs a form of self-consolation: "Friend Madayantikā! We too know what ought to be known. By saying "we too," she means that just as Buddharakṣitā does, we also—because you are a ground of affection and confidence—certainly know your story, especially since it is already known in general. Therefore, be gracious; desist from this pretext. For that reason, since we are desirous of knowing, grant us the favor of speaking.

"From the pretext"—that is, from the expression of a disguise such as fear—"cease," meaning "turn back. "Come"—meaning "approach"—this follows common worldly usage; that is to say, come from the contrary path and so forth onto the favorable path. "Conversations filled with confidence": we remain in a state of exceptional happiness. By means of conversation—that is, discourse—filled with confidence, meaning containing internal trust, we remain in a state of exceptional happiness; for since happiness already exists simply from seeing you, we remain in such a way that there is even greater happiness than that. The underlying sense is based on the saying: "The essence [of friendship] is not deceiving one's friend."
He confirms her statement: "Friend! Lavaṅgikā has spoken well.

Out of innocence, falling in with her intention, she says: "I am now at the disposal of my two dear friends. "At their disposal" means submissive to their will, as in the expression: "The conqueror of cities, whose mind was made submissive by compassion."

Then, she prepares to open the door in order to delight Makaranda—the blue lotus—by means of the nectar of affectionate words flowing from her lotus-like mouth: "If it is so, then tell me, how indeed does your time pass? The phrase "if it is so" (yadyevam) means "if you are subject to my will. "Therefore" (tat) means for that reason; the sense is: "Tell me, do not deceive me. *Nu* is an indeclinable used to indicate a question, as the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "In a question or in an alternative, *nu* and *svid* [are used]."
"How," that is, "in what manner," do those nights and days pass for you? You are being asked this because your mind is shrouded by the pain of longing.

Now, he describes the manner of passing the time by way of a stylistic turn: "Listen, dear friend!"—the meaning is "hear. For, due to my conviction in Buddharakṣitā’s partiality toward him, from the very beginning my heart was filled with constant longing and desire for that person.

By means of the conviction—which is trust in her virtues—born of partiality and affection for Buddharakṣitā; and by means of a mental longing, a continuous stream of thoughts characterized by the hope of attainment through an unceasing and uninterrupted yearning even before the first sight [of Mādhava]; it should be understood that by this [description], the principle stated by Vātsyāyana—"between two persons who have not seen each other's forms and whose dispositions are unknown, [love arises] from the conviction based on a messenger"—is illustrated.

Then, due to the sight of those acting wickedly under the command of fate, my heart was scorched by the continuous suffering of an irrepressible and terrible distress; my hope for life shattered, I became overwhelmed by an unbearable agony from the fierce burning of the fire of passion, which had been previously concentrated throughout all my limbs. With my attendants despondent, and with my body disordered by the inevitable calamity intensified by the words of Buddhārakṣitā—which were contrary to the peace of death that would have been easily attained through the abandonment of hope—I now experience this reversal of the world of the living.

She whose vision was accomplished by the decree of fate—that is, by the command of the Lord—since it occurred spontaneously at the moment of the tiger’s pounce; she whose heart was being consumed by the fever of the pain of affection, with her body struck by an irresistible and cruel affliction that could not be remedied, and who, as her heart was being torn asunder, made a prayer to sustain her life; by the phrase "the pain of separation," the excellence of the objective excitant (*ālambanavibhāva*) is stated.

By the phrase "expanded beyond its former state," the intensification of the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāva) such as languor (glāni), along with the consequent physical symptoms (anubhāva) like paralysis and trembling, is expressed. By the word "unprecedented" (*apūrveṇa*), meaning never experienced before, the unbearable intensity [of the passion] due to a lack of practice is revealed.

She is one whose attendants are despondent because of the distress caused by the unbearable exhaustion—the bodily affliction arising moment by moment from tossing about on the bed of flowers, rising, wandering, sitting, and so forth—produced by the fierce burning of the fire of love that pervades her entire body.

"Hope" refers to the thought that [the goal] will be attained in time; its refutation is easily achieved—that is, obtained without effort—merely by [pointing out] liberation. This is because life itself is sustained only by hope. By the words of Buddharakṣitā, which were contrary to—and opposed against—the bliss of death (the nirvāṇa of dying), meaning by those words which generate hope such as "if this is done, it will happen thus," "it will happen today," or "it will happen tomorrow," there was a mingling or mixture with the intensification of the obsession—that is, the persistence regarding that object. La... [text fragment]
"There is nothing else beyond this for me"— with such a sense of urgency,
the one-pointed mental state is proclaimed as *āveśa* (possession).
Thus says Divākara.

The meaning is that she is disordered, fickle, and incapable of adhering to either alternative. Now, even this very cycle of the world of living beings—the transformation of the mortal world from its former state—is being experienced:
"Those things which were delightful for me when I was with her, those very same things become un-delightful for me when I am without her."

The meaning is: "I experience [this] in the manner described in the *Rāmāyaṇa*. Furthermore, regarding intention (*saṅkalpa*) and dreams: "Deluded by longing and madness, I see that person. In intention—that is, in meditation—and in the state of dreaming, being deluded by longing and madness, I think: "In this way I embrace him; in this way I kiss him; with him I shall behave thus when offended in love," and so forth. This very thought, which is a form of madness or delusion, has rendered me distracted because it lacks ultimate reality; this is the reason for saying "I see. The expression "I see" is used specifically to indicate a cognition of direct perception.

He explains the manner of his vision: "In that way, dear friend! For a moment, I shall gaze upon him—whose pride in the Maireya liquor has grown fierce and intense, whose agitation is manifested by his wide-open, red lotus-eyes that are rolling and expanding, unrestrained by the astonishment he has momentarily assumed. "In that way" (*tathā*) means "in such a state; listen to it."

For a moment—that is, for some time—he was filled with wonder; by this, his stillness is expressed. His lotus-like eyes were red and expanding, spreading wide as they blossomed, surging unrestrainedly and restlessly; the state of being such is "the condition of having lotus-like eyes of that kind. By this, his state of being rippled by the waves of manifold emotional nuances is suggested.

Therefore, he says: "By him, agitation was manifested and revealed; the surge of intoxication arose. By that, he became *ḍāmara*—frightening. Fully developed and complete, he became hardened through the performance of his own [intoxicating] effects. *Maireyadarpa* is a specific kind of transformation produced by drinking liquor, belonging to one for whom there is pride (*darpa*). As it is said: 'That state of being which causes men to engage in activity even toward objects that are not normally objects of passion, being dependent upon pleasure and satisfaction—that is called *darpa*.'"
Thus says Divākara: the mention of "intoxication with liquor" (*maireya-darpa*) is because seeing the drinking of liquor in a dream is an omen indicating future auspiciousness:
"Eating rice-pudding with ghee from a lotus-leaf or a golden vessel, or consuming curd and milk, or drinking liquor or nectar."

Thus says the venerable teacher in the section on auspicious dreams: "Due to the mental construction (saṅkalpa) of a passionate woman who is deluded regarding the consideration of virtues and faults, and acting in accordance with her own desire for sexual union—even in that mental construction, the consumption of liquor is possible; however, it is not possible for that best of the twice-born by his very nature, for it is said:
'Liquor is indeed the dregs of food, and evil is called the dreg;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink liquor.'"
Thus, because of the prohibition against brahmins and others [performing such acts]; "I contemplate" means "I behold," for the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "Contemplation (*nidhyāna*) is looking."

Furthermore, he speaks, filling the cavities of my ears with a deep and resonant *bhāratī* voice, faltering and gurgling like the cry of a swan whose throat has been reddened by swallowing the filaments of lotuses: "My dear Madayantikā! For his throat-organ is purified by the excellent flavor [of the pollen], as his throat has been made astringent by tasting the filaments of the lotus; this is because the filaments of the lotus possess an astringent taste (*kaṣāya-rasa*). Likewise, they are enumerated in the *Saṅgraha* among the category of astringent substances (*kaṣāya-dravya-skandha*) in the passage beginning: "The *padmā*, *padmaka*, the lotus flower, and *nāgakesara*... and so forth.

Regarding this, it is said: "Among those, the first [bitter, pungent, and astringent tastes] destroy wind (māruta), while the three beginning with bitter [bitter, pungent, and astringent] destroy phlegm (kapha). This is because medical treatises state that bitter, pungent, and astringent tastes remove phlegm, and because of the usage in the *Kumārasambhava*: "His throat was parched from tasting the mango sprouts. The voice of the *kalahaṃsa*—a specific kind of swan—is resonant yet rattling (*gharghara*), indistinct, faltering, and intermittently obstructed in its passage. This rattling and faltering are due to the effects of intoxication (*maireya*).

With his voice—deep and resonant due to its connection with a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa), according to the statement of the *Sāmudrika* science that "he is deep in three places and elevated in six"—he speaks, filling and saturating the cavities of the ears, the openings of the hearing, so that they are completely full. Now, as he speaks, she terrifies him, her heart sighing heavily (*dhamadhamāyamāna*) with surging breaths caused by the humiliation of clutching the hem of her upper garment (*uttarīya*) which had been pulled away in anger.

She was agitated and turned away by anger—either born from the commencement of her violation as a maiden or caused by the delay in his arrival; at that moment, she was humiliated by the hem of her upper garment being caught [by him], for it is improper to pull at the breast-cloth of a girl of noble family; she possessed a heart that was "dhamadhamāyamānam"—an onomatopoeic imitation of the manner of trembling, meaning "dham-dham"ing—due to sighs that were surging and proceeding one after another.

The meaning is that she terrifies her by threatening her with the thought: "If you act contrary to my wishes, then I shall defile you with nail-scratches, tooth-marks, and so forth, and show you to my friends. This is because of the words of Vātsyāyana: "And one should threaten her if she does not comply, saying: 'I shall make a tooth-mark on your lower lip, or a nail-mark upon the surface of your breast,'" and so on.

Having laughed at her—who had suddenly retreated from the pleasure she had just released; whose swelling breasts were concealed by the embrace of his arms, which became both harsh and soft and moist in that very instant; whose forward movement was blocked by her thighs, which were occupied in fastening the loosening girdle and its rings; whose heart was made harsh by the pain of a momentary eclipse of anger brought about by every kind of contrary effort; and who revealed the entirety of her inner essence through her affectionate, repeatedly-blinking, long-lashed eyes.

O dear friend! Having rendered him motionless by the embrace of his double-stemmed arms, and having made him unable to endure the harsh pressure of his chest—which was laid bare as an ornament for the rows of fierce, diamond-like claws of a full-grown tiger—the one whose lotus-face is cleverly playful with the features of his face held steady and slightly raised, while his hands grasp and toss back his disheveled tresses from his head which is shaken in agitation; [He is] thus [described].

Her body was beautiful with horripilation arising from the intense touch of his lower lip, which had long rested upon the root of her left cheek and was now quivering and pressed together; her consciousness was reeling, sluggish with the delusion of uneven agitation caused by surging fear and joy, as he—engaged in some inexplicable, audacious effort suited to his ill-bred boldness—seemed to be entreating me.

"Suddenly" (*sahasā*) means "lest there be excessive obstruction"; "released" (*visṛṣṭām*) means "dismissed," that is to say, with her upper garment loosened; "having moved away quickly and easily" means having run away from him; "at that very moment," i.e., at the time of his touch—[he embraced her] with a binding of the arms in the *svastika* posture, [arms that were] hard and bristling with horripilation, thus rough, yet tender and yielding due to their softness, becoming moist and perspiring—like the word *taṇṇāā*, meaning "moist," as in the phrase *mahutaṇṇāpasarantaṇavakusumarāa*.

She whose budding breasts were concealed and covered for fear of a forceful embrace; she whose backward movement—her turning away—was forbidden and checked by her thighs, which were being bound and restrained by the circular girdle-string as it slipped and loosened, or else which were throbbing with the signs of her inner emotion, and which were thus occupied and intent upon proceeding toward him.

"Placed in opposition" means it was made so because it was contrary to what she desired, rather than because it remained inherently hostile; thus, by the force of that state, her feigning of such a condition is suggested. Her heart was "made harsh with sorrow," meaning it was rendered distorted with great difficulty due to a momentary coloring of anger—a brief flash of wrath manifested through the knitting of brows and other signs produced by every kind of effort.

He was revealed—that is, made manifest—to him by her eyes, which were moist and distinguished by the quality of unctuousness, repeatedly long-lashed, and previously thick; which, out of curiosity for his gaze, had become doubly long-lashed; and by which eyes the entire essence of her heart—the core of the mind in the form of passion—was disclosed.

Alternatively, "the essence of the heart" may be understood through *viparītalakṣaṇā* (indirect indication) as "the strength of the heart"; thus the meaning is that her ears-whispering eyes declared: "This is the extent of the strength of her heart—it is nothing at all."

Or rather, the anger displayed externally is merely feigned and not from the heart; therefore, the meaning is that she is as if prompted by the thought, "Let him approach at his own will. Here, the emotional state (*bhāva*) known as *kuṭṭamita* (feigned anger) is indicated.

"From the joy of rasa, one may react with a *kuṭṭamita* when the hair or the lip is seized," says Dhanika. "Having laughed at me" means having laughed because of his complete knowledge of my inner state. Upon that broad expanse of the chest—which has for its ornament and decoration a wide and extensive pattern of scars (*prarūḍha-kiṇī-bhūtā*) formed by the thunderbolt-like claws of tigers (*śārdūla-kararuha-vajrāṇām*), specifically a particular arrangement of wound-lines—he, through a cruel placement—that is, a merciless pressing—rendered me helpless.

Having rendered [him] motionless, with her head shaken violently and with anger, as her braid—its binding having loosened—fell away, she seized the hand placed within the mass of her hair with a firm grip; and upon his face being overcome and raised up—[the term] *āaggia* meaning "overcome," according to the usage of the word *āaggaituhmajaso* mentioned by her—in its parts, that is, in certain portions such as the forehead, eyes, cheeks, lips, and the interior of the mouth, she displayed her unrestrained dalliance.

"Employed according to his own will" means he acted without any restrainer. "Clever" means trained in the kisses of maidens—namely, the *nimitaka*, *sphuritaka*, and *ghaṭṭitaka* types. "[Whose] lotus-face": one whose face is like a lotus.

The application of the sequence from the *Kāmasūtra*—beginning with "When constrained by force, she places her mouth against his mouth and does not struggle because of that"—should be understood here. Her bodily splendor was thrilled (*pulakitā*), meaning her body was covered in horripilation due to the charming touch of the bud-like, swelling, and throbbing mass of flesh at the base of her left cheek, which was like a casket of lips;
for it is said: "A swelling [mark], a coral jewel on the cheek, a kiss like an ear-ornament, and a bite from the teeth—these are the ornaments for the left cheek."
The grasping of the left cheek of women is also due to the fact that the left side is the locus of the erotic arts (*kāmakalā*).

Furthermore, the expression "with lips quivering and gathered" is stated for that purpose, based on the saying: "Through the practice of joining the teeth and lips, the perfection of the coral-gem [lip] is achieved; by pressing it, that very gem becomes swollen."

With her consciousness (buddhi) reeling—slow and dull due to a delusion caused by a manifold and uneven agitation (sambhrama), which consists of a tremor born of maidenhood arising from intense fear, and a supreme bliss consisting of joy caused by the union with her beloved; and the word "kimapī" (something indescribable) indicates that it cannot be defined because it is unfamiliar, while the repetition [of the suffix -api] suggests its manifold nature.

The meaning is: "the specific types of embracing and kissing, as well as the specific modes of sexual enjoyment, that correspond to his own desires. He states the reason for this: "one whose resolve is consistent with the reckless audacity of the ill-behaved. This indicates that his determination is similar to—that is, like—the reckless, unreflective actions of the undisciplined; it shows that even without my consent, he proceeds by himself toward what he desires.
The word *nāma* (indeed) in the phrase "he indeed requests" (*abhyarthayate nāma*) suggests either the onset of anger or contempt, because the act of requesting is a mere mockery.

"Having experienced everything in the presence of my dear friend, this unfortunate woman suddenly perceives the world of the living once again as resembling a desolate forest. [The particle] *iti* indicates manner; thus, one manner has been described, while other varieties of manner are experienced moment by moment—this is the meaning.

"In the presence of her dear friends," that is, in the vicinity of Buddharakṣitā and the others—this indicates that dreams and mental constructs occur at indefinite times. "Having experienced" means having directly perceived "the entire account. "Suddenly" (jhaṭiti) reveals a sense of dissatisfaction, because within that state there is the possibility of awakening and distraction. "Resembling a desolate forest" means it is as distressing as a deserted woodland due to its likeness to a lonely forest. "Once again" implies that because that very state was a cause of suffering during the previous waking condition, that same state is being experienced once more.

"It is perceived"—this expresses resentment toward her own ill fortune by the thought, "I am unfortunate. "I discern" (vibhāvayāmi) means "I see," which manifests dejection regarding the world of the living (jīvaloka), that is, the mortal world.

Then, in order to make her firm in that matter, he asks her a question—even though it is vulgar—by way of a non-vulgar jest: "Friend Madayantika! Tell me clearly: on that occasion, was your seat—the *āsūraka* cushion or the bed-covering—which ought to have been hidden even from the attendants, being observed by Buddharakṣitā’s eyes as they opened slightly with a playful smile, was it so or not?"

The word *api* is used here in the sense of a question. At that moment, during the time of their union in dream and imagination, she looked with a playful grace—a deliberate artifice to avoid being recognized by her attendants—with the eyes of Buddharakṣitā blossoming with a slight smile; she was observed in this way because she must be protected even from her own attendants for fear of the disclosure of the secret. She sat upon a cushion shaped like a lentil seed (*masūraka*), which is half the size of a seat, round, elevated, smooth, and made of silk (*paṭṭa*). It was not very far from the ground.

Based on Vātsyāyana’s statement, “the round rug (*masūraka*), the board for drawing lines (*ākarṣaphalaka*), and the gaming board (*dyūtaphalaka*”), and Harṣacarita’s mention of “pillows with *masūraka* covers,” the term refers to the bedsheet—the cloth covering the mattress and bedding—or rather, it is used as an alternative option because there is no fixed rule regarding seating and reclining. The syntactical connection is: “Tell me whether this is so or not.
She replied with indignation: “O you whose habit of joking is ill-placed! Begone, you who are fond of inappropriate jesting! Move aside!”

She removes her embarrassment: "Friend Madayantika! This very person, Mālatī’s dear friend, knows such things. Because she has been a witness to Mālatī’s pangs of love, this Lavaṅgikā is the one; by the use of the word "this very" (*eva*), the contrast is implied that it is not we who know them. The meaning is that such matters are vulgar. Fearing that Mālatī might overhear, she says: "Do not indeed mock Mālatī in this way. By the phrase "in this way," which highlights her lack of decorum, the sense is expressed: "Such mockery of her is not pleasing to me."

Out of friendship, she employs a stratagem to lead her toward her desired object in the presence of Lavaṅgikā: "Friend Madayantikā! I shall now ask you something, provided that you do not break my confidence—that is, provided you do not cause the destruction or violation of my trust by failing to tell the truth."

He strengthens the sense of confidence by means of a negative argument (*vyatireka*): "Was this person already guilty of an offense before, by the rejection of his request, such that you speak thus? The word *puraḥ* means "previously"; "guilty of an offense by the rejection of his request" means by the refusal of his entreaty. "That you speak thus" means that you say it as if implying "if [he were guilty]"; therefore, the connection is: "Is this person guilty of an offense? because you speak in this manner.

He states the justification for this confidence: "O dear friend! You and Lavaṅgikā are now my heart. The word "now" (sāmpratam) means at this present time; the intended meaning is that since the moment you and Lavaṅgikā entered our house through your connection with Mālatī, Lavaṅgikā, like you, has become as trustworthy as my own heart. This is because, according to the maxim of the "unburnt fire," Buddharakṣitā’s trustworthiness was already established previously, whereas Lavaṅgikā’s trustworthiness is what is now being predicated; for only that which has not yet been reached [as a known fact] is what remains to be established.

Reinforcing her previous statement, she indicates her own intention through a change of phrasing and reveals her heart: "If that is so, then tell me: if Makaranda should somehow again come within the range of your sight, what would you do? The meaning of "somehow" is "through our efforts. The meaning of "what is to be done" is "you will act accordingly."

He states what must be done: "I shall for a long time cause my eyes to find rest, made motionless by being fixed upon each individual limb. The meaning is: by fixing them intensely upon each part of his body, such as the face and so forth, making them motionless and unable to reach any other object, I shall cool them—having been heated by the sight of burning substances like the moon—by immersing them, as it were, in a lake of nectar.

Now, as she proceeds according to the sequence of the festival, she makes herself agreeable to him by offering herself, so that he may not be disturbed—[she says]: "Now, compelled by the power of Love, he shall take you, the mother of Kandarpa, as his wife through self-choice (*svayaṃgrāha*), just as Puruṣottama took Rukmiṇī; what will be your response to this? Here, *atha* marks the exclusion of other alternatives. Let your inclination toward seeing him be set aside for a moment; he, moreover, is "compelled by the power of Love," meaning he is forcibly impelled by Kāma.

The reason for this is as follows: "She is the mother of Kandarpa, the cause of desire"—with such flatteries he seeks to subdue her, implying that in the sight of you, whose vision is such, whose mind would not instantly be enveloped by the flames of the fever of Love’s arrows? Thus he wins her over with coaxing words.
