And [he married] Rukmiṇī-devī, the mother of Kandarpa Pradyumna and daughter of Bhīṣmaka, the King of Vidarbha; by this comparison—due to the totality of her qualities such as noble lineage and their mutual suitability—the Blessed Vāsudeva, the Supreme Person, illuminates the fact that their union is worthy of praise throughout the entire world. By means of "self-choice" (*svayaṅgrāha*)—that is, through the audacity of taking her hand himself without the consent of her father and others—even the Blessed One [was won] by Rukmiṇī.

Since she was married by means of the Rākṣasa form of marriage favored by the Gandharvas, the meaning "he makes her his partner in dharma, his lawful wife" is obtained through the force of intonation (kāku); from that, what subsequent action or engagement would there be for you?—this is the implied sense.

Having considered the impossibility of such a great merit existing within herself, she says: "Sighing," which means having let out a long sigh indicative of the agitation born from the suspicion that she lacks good fortune. "Why have you expected so much of me?"—why, for what reason? "So much" refers to that which was taken up by her own hand; the ellipsis is to be supplied as "merit of this magnitude. She has been "expected" (āśāsitā), meaning she has been honored. To converse with her using only common speech, he says: "Friend, tell [me]."

What will words accomplish? The state of affairs has already been fully understood. Thus, he says by way of a different turn of phrase: "Friend! It has already been told by the long sighs that indicate the agitation of my heart. The meaning is: the agitation is such that [I think], "This is not my good fortune"; therefore, what is the point of deliberating upon its restatement?

He dispels her doubt with a direct statement: "O friend! What am I to him—[to that very person] who, having been drawn from the jaws of death by staking himself on me, is my own? The word *keraka* (belonging to) is used in Prākṛt both in its full form and in an abbreviated form; this is seen from usages such as *parakeraehiṃ tassa keraeā*. Thus, it refers to his own little body (*ātmanaḥ śarīrakasya*). The interrogative particle *kā* expresses a relationship; the meaning is: 'What kind of relationship does she possess? "

By the gesture "of this one" (*asya*), he indicates the state of being a servant (*kṣullakatva*). Anticipating the objection that a relationship of master and servant exists here, he refutes it: the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "by that very [act]" (*tenaiva*) excludes the possibility of such a relationship. By stating that he has made his own self—his own body—the price, he expresses its high value.

"From being devoured by Death"—that is, from being forcibly seized and swallowed by Yama in the form of a tiger; "of that very thing which belongs to oneself" means that, indeed, in this world, even with excellent objects such as jewels, a pot, a cloth, or the like, once it has been purchased by someone, it never becomes the property of the seller. The sense is: [this refers to] my own body—a wretched, small, and pitiable physical frame.

He expresses wonder at her statement for the sake of its stability: "It is worthy of your noble nature"—that is to say, it is consistent with your excellence in qualities such as lineage; the meaning is that this speech is such that it illuminates both your partiality toward virtue and your gratitude.
He confirms what was said at the opportune moment in the presence of witnesses, lest there be a possibility of contradiction later due to shame: "Friend! Remember this which you have now spoken."

Now, in order to arrange what he intends to say, the poet indicates the commencement of that [narrative] by interrupting the story: "How is the sharp drum beaten at the interval of the second *nāḍikā*? A sharp drum—that is, a *paṭaha* or *ānaka* with a clear sound—is being struck to signal the cessation of the second *nāḍikā* of the night; this is understood to be done by its player, for such a practice is followed in royal palaces to determine the lapse of time-measures.

Therefore, now I shall either rebuke Nandana or entreat him with prostrations so that he will become favorable toward Mālatī. Since it is already deep night, I shall either threaten him, saying, "My dear friend Mālatī has been tormented by you because you did not understand her intentions," or else, overcome by shame, I shall appease him with a prostration, saying, "Forgive the offense she committed for my sake. Thus, I shall make him well-disposed toward Mālatī—that is, I shall win him over regarding Mālatī.

"Having uncovered the face" means having revealed it by removing the veil; even with the reading "having opened," the meaning is the same. She takes it by the hand—that is, she takes it playfully by the palm—meaning Madayantika.
She asks out of the belief that it is Mālatī: "Friend Mālatī! Are you awake? Are you free from sleep?"

"Having beheld" means having looked clearly; "with joy" because of seeing her beloved; "with trepidation" because she had not expected it and due to her innocence. "Of the day"—this expresses wonder: "something else entirely is happening here. "Something else" means other than the matter at hand, the story of Mālatī; "something indescribable" refers to this object currently being experienced.

He dispels her trepidation with the words beginning "O lady with thighs like plantain stalks" (*rambhoru*). O *rambhoru*—one whose thighs (*ūru*) resemble the trunk of a plantain tree (*kadalīkāṇḍa*)—cast away, abandon this fear, this sudden trepidation arising from the mere sight [of me], which is natural to the female disposition. He states the negative consequence of not doing so: the agitation produced by labored breathing, belonging to that mass of breasts (*stanabhara*), heavy and difficult to bear due to their fullness and height, which are prone to trembling because of the internal fear.

The middle part is the region of the waist; the sense is that it is extremely slender. Nevertheless, suspecting that fear might arise at the sight of one who is unfamiliar, he says: "In this manner"—that is, by the method just described, beginning with "by the conviction of Buddharakṣitā’s partiality" and ending with "I experience a transformation of the world of the living"—the *praṇaya* (intense affection) has been expressed by you yourself, and not through the mouth of a friend; [this refers to] the favor or grace consisting of that very affection.

In the phrase "in the satisfactions of intention" (*saṅkalpanirvṛtiṣu*), the word "intention" (*saṅkalpa*) also indicates "dream," since that too is a property of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Thus, [the phrase refers to] "the pleasures of the union of intention and dream. These have been elaborated upon in the passage beginning with "I see that person in my intentions and dreams" (*saṅkappasiviṇaesu a pekkhāmi taṃ jaṇaṃ*) and ending with "I perceive the world of living beings" (*vibhāvem i jīvaloaṃ*). The meaning is: "This servant is refined and well-acquainted [with these states]; therefore, there is no room for fear. Here, in the first half-verse, the poetic figure is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole); in the second half-verse, it is either *vibhāvanā* (causation by an unusual cause) or *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation).

Because of the assertion of non-connection where there is a connection; because the effect, fear, is produced even in the absence of a cause characterized by being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); or because, despite the existence of its own causes due to being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), there is the non-arising of the effect characterized by the absence of fear. //2//
Then Buddharakṣitā, whose heart was no different from her own, consoles her by reminding her of former favors, beginning the consolation with the words, "Lift up your face.

Regarding the verse beginning with *preyān*: "cherished" (*preyān*) means sought after by thousands of desires—that is, longed for by many aspirations; by the word "he," it is suggested that he is the object of unsurpassed love; "he, the beloved, stands here before you."

He says that even the fear of the guards no longer exists for you: "The people are asleep and intoxicated"—some are asleep, while others are intoxicated, being distracted by the preparations for a festival and thus inattentive to the protection of the inner apartments; he indicates this state by gesturing with the word "this" (*etad*). It is the minister’s house, the Nandana palace. He further states that the time is also favorable: "The darkness is matured," meaning it is dense.
By this, the state prior to the rising of the moon is described, since the rising of the moon will be mentioned immediately thereafter.
"The rising lunar light [is] the first illumination [that dispels] the mass of darkness. (La-Ṛ)
"Ṛ ṛ.

1)"—this means that out of gratitude and by remembering the supreme favor she has done for you, she too must be protected by you; this is the intended meaning. The particle *eva* (only/indeed) is placed out of its natural order. "Bhadram" means welfare or auspiciousness; the sense is, "I shall surely bring about [welfare] for all of us, so do it without doubt. Fearing that the sound of her anklets at the time of departure might awaken people, he says: "utkṣiptamūkamaṇinūpuraṃ" means with the jeweled anklets removed and the jeweled anklets displaced from the base of the shanks; "yāmaḥ" means we go; "ehi" means come, implying "be favorable for that purpose."
Here, the figure of speech is *parikara* (poetic elaboration). //3//

By saying "let us go" (*yāma*), he indicates the place to which they must travel; he then asks for its specific location: "Buddharakṣitā! Where should we go now? The word "by us" includes Makaranda and the others.
To encourage them by pointing out the elephant’s mate, he says: "Where Mālatī is. The connection is that "one should go there."

Since it could also be said that she was in the monastery garden (*vihārikodyāna*), he speaks by means of inference based on that statement: "Has Mālatī accomplished her daring? This means: has she gone to meet Mādhava by transgressing against her father and others? Or rather, "Is it so?"—meaning, is it exactly as expected? Furthermore, [he says] "the beloved one, encompassed by a thousand desires... (*preyān manoratha-sahasra-vṛtaḥ*).

By means of the reasons subsumed in the phrase "ṛ ṛ 3. and so forth, which are presented as a collection, the sense is that there is another reason for doing what is auspicious, because [the matter] intervenes in the course of the discussion with the statement "we must go" and so on. The application of dissension (*bheda-prayoga*) is as follows: you have said, "Who am I to offer myself to him? and so forth; if you do not carry out this speech—which is backed by witnesses and functions like a formal pledge—there will be the fault of untruthfulness on your part, which will contradict both worlds (this world and the next).
The mention of "shedding tears" is because the falling of tears is a sign of favor.

"An affected laugh was given by me, but tears that rob one of composure were shed by her. From such usage, it should be understood that the tears are born from the recollection of kinsmen. By the phrase "she causes [them] to fall," the subsiding of her agitation is indicated. Her friend, perceiving her intention, says: "Indeed, accept yourself as given by your dear friend. The word *khalu* is used for emphasis. Because a gift is traditionally preceded by water, the meaning is that she has been given with tears themselves serving as the ritual water.

By saying "your own dear friend" (*svāṃ priyasakhī*), he indicates that she was given by him himself, independent of any other kinsmen; and by this, he shows that she must be constantly cherished by you even more than your own life, due to such causes as natural affection, partiality for her exceptional virtues, and gratitude. *Pratipadyasva* means "accept" or "regard with high esteem. Keśavasvāmin states: "The word *pratipatti*, however, [is used] in the sense of respect or attainment."

He accepts those words with great respect, saying "Today," and so forth. "Ūrjitam" (exalted) means "in an exceeding manner"—this is an adverbial modifier. "By me [it] has been conquered" means it stands preeminent above all; the ellipsis is "what else need be said? The "festival" of youth—that is, of adolescence—is "fruitful" because of the attainment of a beloved wife worthy of one's lineage and other qualities, and it is "auspicious" through the fulfillment of the enjoyment desired by oneself.

He states the cause for the two festivals of victory: by the phrase "by the Lord, whose face is bright with favor" (*prasādasumukhena*), meaning through the power of grace, the wonder is raised as to what indeed might be impossible for him who possesses such "greatly marvelous majesty" (*mahādbhutaprabhāvena*). He is one "whose yoke of kinship" (*bāndhavadhurā*)—that is, the burden or responsibility toward his father and others who are authorized to bestow gifts—is upon him. Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the rule for compound suffixes, there is an absence of the suffix *ap* prescribed by the rule "ṛkpūrabdhūḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.74).

"Because she was surrendered—that is, given—to me by Makaradhvaja, [that is] Kāma; therefore, victory has been won by me. This is because such good fortune is impossible for anyone else, as it is said: "My dear friend has given herself. The use of the term "Makaradhvaja" implies that the matter is rooted in desire (*kāma*). By the demonstrative pronoun "this one" (*iyam*), through the dramatic representation of her excellence in beauty, character, sweetness, and so forth, the justification for her victory over youth is made manifest.

The coexistence of mutual affection and qualities such as beauty and so forth is extremely rare. Having obtained this through the power of my fortune, she dispels her friend's doubt by asking, "What room, then, is there for hesitation in cherishing this? The poetic figure (alaṅkāra) here is Hyperbole (atiśayokti). //4//

Since this residence in the Nandana grove was obtained as a limit for our gains, and since this [opportunity] has been secured, therefore—by this means, that is, by way of the side-door of the bedroom (as opposed to the main gate)—it might be recognized by some upon exiting through the great gate; thus, the sense is that it is for the sake of avoiding that.

According to the *Vaijayantī*: "The word *dvāḥ* is feminine, while *dvāraṃ* is neuter; *pakṣakaḥ*, however, refers to a side-door (*pakṣadvāraṃ*). "We shall accomplish" means we shall fulfill our own desire; this is an expression of "we go" in a refined manner.
*Nibhṛtam* means silently or quietly.

*Niśīthinīsañcāraramaṇīyatā* refers to the charm of wandering at night; there is also a reading, *niśīthanissambādharamaṇīyatā*. According to Amara, "midnight and *niśītha* are two [synonyms]. The meaning is that due to the depth of the night and the absence of crowds of people, it is captivating to the hearts of those filled with desire. *Rājamārgasya* refers to the great central thoroughfare of the city; by this, even the arrival at the royal road is indicated.

He establishes its loveliness—now, with the words beginning "of the palaces" (*prāsādānām*) and so forth: "of the palaces" refers to royal residences and mansions (*saudha*), according to Amara’s definition, "a palace belongs to gods and kings. "On top" means in the upper part, specifically in the *valabhī-jāla-vātāyanas* (latticed windows on the roof-ridges) and the *kūṭāgāra* (pinnacles) windows; as the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states, "a *kūṭāgāra* is a *valabhī*. These are mentioned because they serve as instruments for enjoyment, as seen in Māgha’s verse: "The youths [enjoyed] the *valabhīs* together with their brides," and so forth.

"Having attained fragrance" means having obtained joy, due to the perfection of the refined scent; he supports this very point: "that which has within its womb—the interior—of it the perfuming of the scent of *pariṇata-surā*, that is, ancient wine; which possesses the fragrance of a garland (*mālyāmodī*), meaning a scent belonging to flowers that is exceedingly intense for those who are skilled in garlands; and which repeatedly bears the pervasive scent of camphor (*upahitasphārakarpūravāsaḥ*), meaning the impression of the fragrance of abundant camphor intended for purposes such as mouth-perfumes and cloth-perfumes."

That [fire] has been placed and established upon which the wind—meaning the breeze—manifests or reveals the presence of the beloved bride, that is, her staying there; this is the usage [of the word *vāta*] because it performs an action conducive to that end. This is a case of *dhvani* (suggestive poetry) based on *lakṣaṇā* (indication), where the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is not hidden. Thus, through the attainment of the most beloved at a delightful time, joy is manifested, as in the thought: "By good fortune, we are prospering. Here, the figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) is *udātta*, because it describes an object characterized by prosperity (*samṛddhimad-vastu-varṇanāt*).

And there is inference (*anumāna*), because the presence of the bride is inferred from the signs of the wind. Here, the resolution is to be sought either in the case of a virtuous person who, having eaten delicacies near certain wealthy men and being adorned with garlands and unguents given by them, goes outside delighted and describes their generosity, enjoyment, and so forth; or else, in the case of a wicked person who slanders their lack of decorum. Thus, everything is most auspicious. //5//
Thus, by the grace of Pūrṇajyotis, Pūrṇasarasvatī has composed this analysis of the contents of the seventh act of the *Mālatīmādhava*. [End of] the Seventh Act.

The Eighth Act. Now the introductory scene (praveśaka) begins: "Then enters Avalokitā. "I have paid my respects to the Holy Lady who has returned from the residence of Nandana. Therefore, I shall now go to Mālatī and Mādhava. "She has been saluted" (*vanditā*) means she has been greeted; this is said because paying respects to one's elders is a vow to be performed daily. "From the residence of Nandana" (*nandanāvāsāt*) means from his house; this connects with what was previously stated: "Having taken leave of Nandana, she went to her own quarters. (Act 5).

The word *yāvat* is used here as a rhetorical ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*) or for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). The meaning is: "I shall go right into the presence, that is, the vicinity, of Mālatī and Mādhava, who are staying in the pleasure garden. It should be understood that the poet here relates the events of the day preceding the night of Madayantikā’s abduction in their proper sequence, leading up to the occurrence of that night. Indeed, these two, Mālatī and Mādhava, having completed their bathing at the end of the summer day, are now gracing the stone slab on the bank of the long pond.

Therefore, I shall approach them. They have completed their evening bath—the head-bath—at the close of the summer day; for, with the departure of the spring previously described, it is now summer. They are adorning the crystal-paved terrace on the bank of the pleasure-pond to obtain coolness, for the stone surface acquires an excellence of beauty through that very fragrance.
[As it is said: "Gardens, water-sports, shade, sprouts, and carpets;
fountain-houses, jeweled chambers, lotus-stalks, and crystal pavements."

"...these and others, when combined in summer, are inflammers of passion," according to the statement; and also from such descriptions as "possessing delightful immersion in water" and "delightful in their transformation. The mention of bathing at evening during the summer season and the stone slab is due to their excellence as excitants (*uddīpana*), as in: "Rivers, sandbanks, the shore, forests, gardens, and mountains..."
By the statement, "The places for recreation should be during the day," the banks of the long pond are included.
//Interlude//
The phrase "they have sat down" connects with what was previously stated, "adorning the surface of the stone slab. And by the mention of Avalokitā, her approach is also indicated.

"With joy" refers to the arrival of a favorable moment. "Is occurring" (*vartate*) uses the present tense (*laṭ*) to indicate immediate proximity to the present; the meaning is that it "will occur" (*vartiṣyate*). "Friend of the maturity of Love" means one who has become a companion in the accomplishment of the power of Madana. Regarding the word *niśītha*: although it is said that "the *niśītha* is midnight," here the word *niśītha* denotes the night in general, because midnight alone constitutes its "youthful prime."

The "glory of youth" is the splendor of the middle watch; at that time, because the world was illuminated by the mass of rays from the moon—the lord of the cool season—situated at the peak of the sky, it was considered to be day, and thus the meaning is that the night provided assistance for extraordinary enjoyment.

He establishes the future glory [of the moon] through inference, beginning with the words "dalayati" (shatters) and so forth. "Pariśuṣyat-prauḍha-tālī-vipāṇḍuḥ": the term *pariśuṣyat* (drying up) is used rather than *pariśuṣka* (completely dried) to express a slight paleness; *prauḍhā* means matured; *tālī* refers to the leaf of the silver palm (*rājatālī*), which is pale-white due to its discolored whiteness, as it is touched by the glow of sunrise. It "shatters," that is, breaks into pieces, the mass of darkness (*timira-nikara*). "Udyann" means rising. The reason for its paleness is that it did not shatter [the darkness] nor has it fully risen.
"Aindavaḥ" means belonging to the moon (*indu-sambandhi*), according to the rule "tasyedam" (this belongs to that).

(4-3-120) The suffix *aṇ* [is applied here]. "Light" (*prakāśa*) in the eastern direction (*prāk*) means mere illumination, and not a mass of rays, since that too has already been mentioned, as stated in the *Kādambarī*: "Immediately thereafter, the eastern quarter (*vāsavī dig*) assumed a greyish hue from the thin and sparse light produced by the approaching moonrise, like a row of forest groves in spring from the pollen of flowers."

"Upward-facing" means ready to ascend; "fresh" means clearly white due to its novelty at the time of blooming; "dense" means continuous; and "red with nectar" (*mākaranda*) means colored by *makaranda*, which is the juice of the flower. The suffix *aṇ* is applied here according to the rule *tena raktaṃ rāgāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.1), and not according to *tasyedaṃ* (4.3.120), because, according to the lexicon—"*Makaranda* is the juice of the flower, while *parāga* is the pollen of the flower"—the two are distinct substances.

"In 'Move away, O bee! Even though the ketakī flower is thick with fragrance, there is no gain of honey-drops here; rather, your face will become grey with pollen,' and so forth, the absence of honey in the ketakī flower is established. How, then, can there be the expression *mākaraṇda* (honey) used here?"

It is said in reply: because there is no difference in its being a flower, honey certainly exists in this one as well; however, it does not exist in abundance like that of the *kunda* or *mākanda*, due to the predominance of pollen (*parāga*). Even in the verse "Move away, O bee," the absence of honey is not what is being asserted, for it is the acquisition of it that is being prohibited. The reason for this is that her face is greyed by a mass of pollen. Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

The mention here of "makaranda" (honey-nectar) is for the purpose of establishing that the pollen (*parāga*), which is naturally white, is permeated by color; otherwise, it would be impossible for the lunar light, which is stained by the rising glow [of dawn], to serve as a point of comparison. Therefore, the meaning is that, just as the abundance of grain is inferred from the sight of beautiful sprouts, the glory of her approaching youth is thus inferred. Here, the poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) is *upamā* (simile). //1//

[To himself: Since this [affair] will turn out to be a great calamity unless it proceeds favorably, therefore I shall win over—that is, bring under my control—the one of perverse character who, due to her being newly married and her innocence, acts contrary [to my wishes] out of modesty even while she is actually overwhelmed by love; for such is the well-known definition in the *Kāmasūtra*: "the winning over of the object of desire. Very well, let her behave in that manner; even so, if I act in this way, the accomplishment of my goal will come to pass—such is my own firm resolve.

"Thus" (*evam*) refers to the manner that will be described. "First" (*tāvat*) indicates priority; the sense is that if even this should turn out otherwise, we shall employ another means. "Aloud. [She was] exceptionally cool from her recent evening bath—her body more chilled than before due to the immersion at the close of day which had not yet lost its potency—and naturally so, for even before [the bath], her own limbs were sufficiently cooling to dispel the heat of passion, surpassing even moonlight or sandalwood paste.

The meaning is: "For the sake of allaying the heat of the summer season—that is, for the purpose of dispelling the exhaustion caused by the warmth of the summer days—I request something, that is, I speak with a plea regarding a certain matter about to be described."

Therefore, the meaning is: "for that reason," because it is fitting to protect one who is tormented. "Why? means for what purpose? "Always" means at all times; or perhaps shame may arise two or three times, the sense being, "we too might sometimes be objects of pity. Otherwise, by treating me with hostility—that is, by acting contrary to my desired object—you honor me; thus he illuminates that even your opposition is an elixir for his heart. Or rather, the meaning is: "why do you regard me otherwise—as some other person who is an object of shame, and not as your own servant?"

He describes the very manner of his communication with the words "niścyotante" and so forth. "Niścyotante" means they drip down excessively. By the address "sutanu," meaning "O fair-bodied one," he reveals that you yourself are capable of reviving me with the nectar of touch; how much more so now, when you are cooled by a recent bath! "Kabarībindavaḥ" refers to the droplets of water from the mass of hair that remains damp from bathing—the sprays of water—for as long as, that is, during which period of time.

The space between the two breasts, which are like fresh buds just sprouted—the region of their middle—does not abandon its moist state because it does not dry up quickly due to being slightly depressed; thus the poet indicates this as a supreme mark signifying long life. Possessing a dense, continuous, and very fine eruption of horripilation (a growth of bristling hair) due to contact with the cool breeze, her slender frame—the arrangement of hands, feet, and so forth—is characterized by that [state].

For that duration of time, my sole desire is for you to embrace me firmly and tightly—even just once; the sense is: "If even that cannot be granted, then let it not be. By using the word *vitara* ("grant"), he indicates: "This will cause you no effort at all, but for us, it would be like the discovery of a great treasure."

"Embracing (āliṅgana), taking to one's bosom (kroḍīkaraṇa), and holding on the lap (aṅkapālī)"—so says the *Vaijayantī*. "Be gracious; show compassion," for the sense is that the complete alleviation of the heat of the summer-torment, which is desired in the very next moment, would otherwise be impossible. Here, longing (*autsukya*) is suggested. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is Hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). //2//
"Niranukrośe" means devoid of compassion;
"karuṇā, however, is dayā, kṛpā, ghṛṇā, anukampā, anukrośa, and kāruṇya... [as defined in the lexicon].
Thus says the *Vaijayantī*.

Anticipating the objection that what was previously stated is impossible, he expresses his prayer regarding a somewhat nearer stage: "jīvayan iva" (as if reviving), and so forth. The suffix *śatṛ* in "jīvayan" (reviving) denotes intention, meaning "desiring to give life. The word "iva" (as if) indicates a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*); the sense is: "as if desiring to revive me, who am utterly bewildered by being scorched with the heat of separation. He states the cause for this conceit: "samūḍhasādhvasasvedabinduḥ"—one by whom drops of perspiration produced by the fatigue born of "sādhvasa," the fear of a first union, have been "samantāt ūḍhaḥ," i.e., borne all over.

Because a sprinkling of water-drops serves as a means of consolation, the phrase "as if giving life" implies that it does not actually restore life; thus, even though you are merciless, it is shown that at least some compassion for me is seen in your arm. "Adhikaṇṭham" means upon the neck—that is, on the neck itself—because the vital breaths residing there must be restrained. "Arpyatām" means let it be given; "by you" is the ellipsis. "Bāhuḥ" refers to the vine-like arm; by using the singular number, it is revealed that for the sake of restoring life, that single arm alone is sufficient, independent of a second.

At the stage when drops of perspiration are visible, he employs a simile: "Possessing the charm of a necklace of moonstones dripping [with water] when kissed by the rays of the moon. This means that because it is touched by the rays belonging to the moon, its charm is like that of a necklace fashioned from moonstone beads which have the nature of trickling drops of water. Here, the word *hāra* (necklace) indicates the mere string itself through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

"Because of the usage by the Teacher [Vāmana] in the passage, 'It shines like a necklace (hārāvalī) made of emeralds,' and because the word *hāra*—as in 'A *sūtrikā* is made of pearls' and 'A *hāra* is a string of pearls (*muktāvalī*) for a woman'—functions primarily in the sense of a pearl necklace; there is thus a statement of similarity with a necklace of moonstones (*candramaṇi*) based on qualities such as being smooth, glossy, white, cool, thin, round, and long. Here, the figures of speech are *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) and *upamā* (simile). //3//

There too, despairing due to impossibility, he seeks another object—by saying "or rather" (*athavā*), he sets aside what was previously stated. The reason for this is: "this [request] made by us is far away"; that is to say, it is at a remote distance because its object is difficult to attain. "How? expresses astonishment.

The phrase "merely sharing conversation" refers to a situation where one may speak without hesitation; by adding "even," it reveals the ease with which this can be done even from a distance without physical contact. "This person is an unfit vessel" means that he is renowned in the world as a fit recipient for your affection and confidence. [This belongs] to you, your ladyship.

He establishes that even the sharing of conversation is of supreme benefit, stating "dagdhaṃ cirāya" and so forth. For a long time (*cirāya*), meaning for many moments, [it was] by the Malaya breezes and the rays of the moon—that is, by the southern winds and the lunar beams. The statement that it was "burned" (*dagdha*) suggests, through the propriety of its immediate extinguishing, the impropriety of neglecting it. It was "extinguished" (*nirvāpita*), meaning cooled. The particle *tu* is placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakrama*) for the sake of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). The connection is with the word "body" (*vapuḥ*).

"Indeed not" means certainly not; for it is impossible to extinguish [the fire of passion] without an embrace, and since that [embrace] is hindered by shame, let it not happen there—this is the sense, meaning that such a thing is quite possible. The word *nāma* is used here in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*). She was "distressed by the cries of intoxicated cuckoos," meaning she was tormented by the sounds of cuckoos who were intoxicated by drinking the nectar of their incessant warbling on all sides.

"Because the spring season has not long passed, and the suffering of separation has been experienced, [the voice] captures the scent of the Malaya breeze and the song of the cuckoo. 'Hṛdyām' means charming or captivating. 'Śrutiḥ' refers to the sense of hearing. 'Kinnarakaṇṭhi' means one whose throat is like the throat of the Kinnaras—the horse-faced celestial singers; the meaning is that your throat is smooth and red, free from defects such as being muffled by phlegm or being harsh and cracked, as in the expression, 'O Kinnarakaṇṭhi! Why are you sleeping?'"

This is the reason for its being heart-pleasing: the word *śruti* (the ear) takes the imperative (*loṭ*) in the sense of a prayer—"may it drink," that is, may it taste, the heart-pleasing speech. The use of the particle *tu* in the phrase "but the ear" (*śrutistu*) serves as a distinction: even if one fails to perform the greater service of an embrace which delights all the senses, one must still show favor by delighting the ear alone; for if one fails to perform even a minor service that is possible, there is the risk of being called cruel. Here, the emotion (*bhāva*) of longing (*autsukya*) is manifested. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). //4//

Then her friend, through her cleverness, employs a stratagem to converse with her by means of a false statement: "O you who are never satisfied! Since even now, though Mādhava has been separated from you for but a moment, you speak before me with a troubled mind, saying: 'My noble son-in-law is delaying; perhaps I shall see him soon, so that, having cast off all fear and forgotten obstacles, I may look upon him and say this, and say that, and honor him with a double-folded embrace'—this is the result [of your behavior]. (Addressing her: "O, my friend!"

5. She whose nature is *anirvahaṇa*, meaning she does not bring to completion what has been begun. He supports that very state: "Now," that is, in the time immediately past, and not in another age; "Mādhava," meaning Kṛṣṇa, was separated from her for a mere moment because he had departed for the purpose of performing his twilight devotions (*sandhyopāsana*) and so forth—meaning, his sight was lost to her. The word "api" (even) suggests: "If this is so when he was separated by only a single watch (*yāma*), what need is there to speak of longer intervals?"

When she speaks—that is, tells—while being dejected and grieving in my presence and not in the presence of another man, that speech indicates her state of concealment at those very times. He describes the manner of her speaking: "He delays," meaning he lingers for a long time. "Noble son" (*āryaputra*) is a conventional term used by virtuous women regarding their husbands; the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "Husband, noble one, and noble son. "Perhaps" (*api nāma*) expresses a possibility.

Because excessive affection is suspected of being sinful, he says here what you will do upon seeing him after so long: "By which" (*yena*), that is, because all fear has been cast off, every trembling abandoned, and obstacles forgotten; "in such a way" (*yathā*) is an adverbial phrase meaning with such a manner that the obstacle to seeing—namely, shame—is not perceived due to the agitation of longing from not having seen him for so long. "Beholding" (*avalokayantī*) means looking with straightforwardness. "I shall speak thus" (*evaṃ bhaṇiṣyāmi*) means "I shall speak in this way," used to indicate the impossibility of describing the various modes of speech already mentioned.

This is a summary: by saying "I shall speak," because of her inability to endure long delays and her state of jealousy, when she asks, "Where have you gone now?", if he replies, "I went to see Makaranda," and so forth, then even the exchange of words such as "In that case, you have gone elsewhere to some place for diversion" is implied.

"Twice-wrapped" means an embrace with her two arms doubled around me, like a binding all over with a chain; by that embrace, I shall honor him—that lover who is afraid of my affection—by manifesting favor, since he has been subjected to the punishment of long delay; the meaning is: "I shall cause him joy by showing his gratification. This is the construction: "Thus you speak before me. The result, conclusion, or end of those words is this present state consisting of silence, avoidance of looking at me, and so forth.
"With resentment" (sāsūyam) means with anger; the word "as it were" (iva) expresses that this was not done intentionally.

Aside (to herself): "Aho! expresses joy. By the phrase "from the quality of the genius of the venerable Kāmandakī, her chief disciple who has acquired [learning]," she illuminates what indeed cannot be accomplished when there is the combination of the instruction of a true guru and the quality of genius; "sarvatomukha" means that which has its face—that is, its orientation—toward all branches of knowledge and all arts; "vaidagdhyam" means urbanity or refinement.

"An inexhaustible," meaning without end, "treasury of well-spoken jewels"—that is, a treasury (a storehouse) consisting of the very jewels that are "well-spoken" (*subhāṣita*), which, because they are employed at the appropriate occasion and are flavorful, are endowed with the status of jewels due to their priceless nature and their capacity to bring forth splendor. As if not knowing [the answer], he asks: "Does he speak the truth, the ultimate reality?"—this is indicated by the interrogative intonation, implying "or does he speak what is untrue?
He shakes his head—the top of the head—with the gesture of negating its truthfulness; the meaning is that he moves his head sideways.

Having gained some ground by the fact that her nodding of the head was interpreted as an affirmative response to his own words, he said: "You have been sworn—that is, you have been made to give your solemn pledge—by my life, by my vital breaths, and by the lives of Avalokitā and Lavaṅgikā; the connection is with 'by [their] life. Since there is no one else besides these three who has become a vessel for your affection and confidence, if you do not speak with your voice—meaning if you do not speak whether this which has been said by her is true or false—not even by gestures."

The meaning is: "Then you will have committed a transgression against the curse upon our lives. The use of the instrumental case in *jīvitena śāpitāsi* ("you are sworn by life") is intended merely to express an oath. The dative case prescribed by the rule *ślāghanuṅsthāśapāṃ jñīpsyamānaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.34) is not employed here because there is no intention to address someone as the object of an entreaty (*jñīpsyamānatva*). "And by Dardara, O Goddess, I swear to you, and by roots and fruits!"

And from the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*: "By Malay, Vindhya, Meru, and Mandara," as well as from the observation of such usages as: "I swear by my own study, I swear by my axe, and I swear by the lord of beasts."

He demonstrates the result of employing that means: "I have not said anything at all. By this [statement], she implies: "Regarding what has been presented as my own speech, I have not said even a single word; she has spoken falsely. Since the intended meaning remains unspoken—meaning that when a portion of the statement has been made, such as when it is half-uttered—she "enacts bashfulness. This means that although she had previously begun to speak immediately out of straightforwardness and an inability to tolerate her false words, in the midst of it, natural bashfulness firmly overcame her. And this is the emotion (bhāva) known as *vihṛta* (the playful or affected).
For according to the saying: "That which one does not speak when the time has come is indeed rendered futile by shame."

"Aho" expresses joy. It refers to the sweetness of speech that is "anavasitārthamanthara"—that is, not abrupt because its meaning is not yet fully concluded. This should be understood from the passage beginning with, "How is this person of yours unworthy even of a share in conversation? and ending with, "O, the loveliness of speech that is slow because its meaning is not yet concluded!"—namely: "Having touched [the hand] and stood for a long time, if she is pressed further, she should shake her head."

"If she is a well-known friend who is favorable and trusted by both parties, one should initiate the conversation by interposing her; then, looking down, she should smile at him. If she does not speak, one should prompt her and engage her in conversation. She, for the sake of jest, should say, 'This was said by her,' even if it was not actually spoken. Then, having dismissed her, he should say to her with indistinct syllables and unfinished meaning, 'I do not speak thus. This is cited as the application of conversation (*ālāpayojana*) as described in the *Kāmasūtra*.

Then, perceiving a change in her expression, he said with fear—"Suddenly!"—this being the manifestation of his alarm; "having observed," meaning having looked closely: "What is this? What is the cause of this?"

He shows her what was pointed out: "with the water of tears," and so forth. By using the form *mṛgadṛśaḥ* (genitive) rather than *mṛgadṛśā* (instrumental), it is illuminated that due to the melting of the mind, the flow of tears occurs spontaneously and instantaneously. "Pure" means naturally stainless. By stating "is washed" (*prakṣālyate*) rather than "is being washed" (*dhāvyate*), the futility of the act of washing is revealed due to the absence of any need for effort. The word *sapadi* (immediately) indicates that because she was occupied in the midst of jesting, the cause [of her weeping] was not perceived.

This [nectar] is rising; it is "drinkable by a mouthful" (*gaṇḍūṣapeya*), meaning it can be drunk by filling the cavity of the mouth with a single mouthful; that is to say, due to its extreme abundance, it is sufficient to fill the hollow of the cheeks upon drinking—just as in expressions such as "honey to be licked from the hollow of the ear" (*śruticulukalehya*) or "drinkable from the cupped palms of the ears" (*śravaṇāñjalipuṭapeya*). [This usage follows the rule: "With gerundive participles (*kṛtya*), when expressing an excessive degree."

Thus is the compound. "Desirous of drinking the nectar of beauty" means wishing to drink the ambrosia consisting of an excellence of loveliness (*lāvaṇya*). "In which [cheek] the lotus-stalk of rays is placed" means that upon which cheek the rays—those very rays which are like a round, long, pure, and tender lotus-stalk—are placed or inserted within. At the time of its rising, the moon is poetically imagined as being positioned directly facing [the cheek], with its rays like a lotus-stalk placed therein.

"Just as one emaciated by disease and other afflictions might consume an elixir (*rasāyana*) for nourishment, desiring to drink the nectar of beauty (*kāntyamṛta*) as if it were a mouthful of water—so too, the moon, its qualities diminished, seems to thirst for the nectar of beauty in order to increase itself. Through this poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), the cheek's superior loveliness compared to the moon is illuminated. One should understand that the superimposition of the "lotus-fiber" (*mṛṇāla*) upon the ray of light is because the lotus-fiber is one of the means for drinking water mentioned in medical treatises, and because of its excellence; as stated by Amaru: "Beloveds drink the essence brought by the stalks of their lotus-eyes. (5)
"Friend! Why now do you weep so slowly, with a heavy surge of rising tears? For what reason do you weep so silently and gently, with a flow of tears set in motion?"

In this regard, she states the cause: "How long shall I experience the sorrow of the absence of my dear friend Lavaṅgikā? Of what measure is this long duration of the pain of non-proximity—the distress born of not seeing her due to her being far away? Even obtaining news of her is difficult; even the acquisition of knowledge regarding her form—what she is doing—is hard to attain. (The word "exists" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. Out of modesty, she asks for clarification so that what was softly spoken into her ear may become manifest: "What indeed [is] the cause? (The word "stated" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense).

He explains: "By your very mention [of her], she remembers Lavaṅgikā and, for the sake of obtaining news of her, she becomes distressed—that is, she suffers. By the words "by your very mention" and "of Avalokitā and Lavaṅgikā," he says that one should not feel grief here. "Indeed, in our agreement, you too have surely known that I sent him"—the meaning is that while being sent, he was indeed seen.

To the question, "I have understood why he was sent; is it not so? he replies: "In secret," meaning in such a way as to remain unknown to those on the spot, "to the abode of Nandana," that is, to Nandana’s house. Since "news" (pravṛtti) is mentioned without qualification, it is established that this refers to the deceptions of Makaranda, Lavaṅgikā, and Buddharakṣitā, which were practiced upon the deceived Nandana. The phrase "iti" implies "having spoken thus. "Sāśaṃsam" means with hope or prayer. "Api nāma" is an indeclinable used to indicate possibility.
"Phalodarkam" means that which has its fruit or purpose in the "udarka," that is, in the future.
"Whatever subsequent fruit there may be at a later time in the future," so says the *Vaijayantī*. Addressing Madayantika, the optative "syāt" (it might be) is used in the sense of possibility.

Now, by means of the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikayā*), he dispels her doubt through his wit: "At the very first touch of the tiger’s claws, you—commissioned by the Goddess to announce the breaking of Makaranda’s swoon—granted Malati’s heart along with her life. *Ālukkhiaṃ* means "touched."

"From such usage as stated in the *Setu*: 'One whose sleep has long been honored [by rest], yet who feels longing bestowed by the ocean of separation parched by parting'... Now, if some person increases the joy of that very Makaranda by the acquisition of Madayantika, what reward will there be for him now? "Some person"—meaning someone among us—will increase his joy and announce the pleasant news, saying, "Congratulations, you are prospering! The use of the present tense (*laṭ*) indicates proximity to the present moment. "Reward" (*pāritoṣika*) refers to a gift given out of affection. By the expression "some person," she (Mālatī) incites Mādhava.

The *udghaṭṭitajña* (one who understands by a hint) says: "It is fit to be pursued; it is worthy to be asked; I have been pursued, I have been asked. [He points to] his heart, his own chest. [He refers to himself as] a witness to the affliction (*abhiṣaṅga*) at the first sight of Mālatī—that affliction, the suffering of love, which occurred during her previous meeting with him in the Madana garden. By indicating that since this was produced while standing near the basin surrounding the Bakula tree, if anyone should dispute this matter, then the Bakula tree itself should be questioned, he reveals his meaning.

At that time, being alone, he reflects upon a particular state of being accessible only through his own personal experience: the flower-garland of the *kesara* tree—the *bakula* tree—which adorns the forest of desire (*kāmakānana*), which produces an excellence of beauty for the garden of passion (*madanodyāna*) because its qualities are superior to those of other trees, and which is possessed of fortune (*lakṣmīvat*), being endowed with divine grace.

He establishes her very possession of fortune (lakṣmīvattva) with the verse beginning "With love" (premṇā), and so forth. "With love" means with affection. The reason for this is given by the phrase "composed by me" (madgrathita), meaning "woven by me"; through that love, she was brought near—brought by the hand of a dear friend, namely, by the hand of Lavaṅgikā. The word "by her" (anayā) is an indication made through a dramatic gesture (abhinaya) referring to Mālatī.

By the phrase "with the burden of the buds of the jars of her expansive breasts" (*vistāristanakumbhakuḍmalabharotsaṅgena*), it refers to those two forms of breasts which have the nature (*śīla*) of expanding—that is, becoming increasingly vast—moment by moment. This is a metaphorical usage (*lākṣaṇika-prayoga*), similar to the expression used by Māgha: *stanakalaśakiśorakau kathañcit* ("the jar-babies of her breasts"). Likewise, Murāri says: *tārakeśvarakiśoraśekharaḥ* ("the crest-jewel of the young son of the Lord of the Stars").

"Bhara" means a burden; "sambhāvitā" means cherished through the constant carrying of it by its middle (utsaṅga). The sense is: who could have any doubt regarding the auspiciousness of her, who is the source [of such excellence]? Not only that, but there is a further reason for her praise; thus he says—using "tu" as a particle of distinction—in "pāṇipīḍanavidhau," that is, in the performance of the marriage ceremony for the sake of Nandana's wedding. "Pāṇipīḍana" is marriage, as in:
"After the rite of pāṇipīḍana, [she was given] to Hara, the daughter of the King of Mountains."

This is according to the statement in the *Kumārasambhava*. "Toward me" means with reference to me; "with her hope departed" means with her hope for union shattered; "having realized [it] in this manner" means having understood that "this is Lavaṅgikā"; and the meaning is that when she had prostrated at my feet to seek permission for death, and I was standing in the place of Lavaṅgikā.

The "gift of all one's possessions" (*sarvasvadāya*) is the giving away of all one's own wealth; just as someone on the verge of death might personally entrust his entire accumulated wealth—however it was acquired—to his sons and others, saying, "This must be guarded with vigilance," so too [is she]. The meaning is that she has been respectfully entrusted [with the words]: "This Mālatī also must be regarded as no different from yourself; she is to be held in your heart at all times."

The reading ends in the feminine because "done" (*kṛtā*) is the subject (*uddeśya*), and the predicate (*vidheya*), namely "always dependent," finds its resolution therein. Here, in the first half, the emotion (*bhāva*) called affection (*sneha*) is manifested, while in the second half, the emotion called dejection (*dainya*) is revealed. This is the figure of speech *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), as it reveals a transcendent passion by means of its effect. //6//

"Friend! This Bakula garland is indeed dear to you, since you gaze at it so intently. [Commentary: "Dear" means very beloved; "indeed" (*khalu*) is used for emphasis; "since" (*yataḥ*) means because you gaze—looking with intense focus—at this [garland], as the sense implies. By this turn of phrase, she suggests: "Out of a longing for a firm embrace, you are looking at the breast of your lover under the pretext of the garland, while feigning bashfulness before me. Oh, what a secret lover you are! Thus it is implied.

Perceiving the nuance of her words, she says: "Friend, you are mocking me! She mocks by concealing something within her heart; she ridicules with an intonation that suggests, "Why is this? Under the pretext of hearing the sound of footsteps approaching, she says: "How is it the sound of feet?—the noise produced by the placing of feet upon the surface of the earth. The word *iva* indicates a conjecture.

Having observed signs such as the brightness of her face which indicate the success of his mission, she says joyfully: "Aye!"—an indeclinable expressing joy—"He has arrived; he has come from the abode of Nandana."

Having ascertained the success of the task through the words of her most beloved elder, and having cast aside the constraints of shame under the influence of joy, she—having already perceived in her mind the auspicious increase of fortune through the words of Avalokitā—expresses that very blessing: "By good fortune you prosper through the acquisition of Madayantika; by luck, may you have your desires fulfilled through the attainment of your friend Madayantika. This is the meaning.

With the word "joyfully" (*saharṣam*), she expresses the propriety of the embrace even in the presence of her friends, as its cause is joy and the like. By the statement, "She embraces and then gives [herself], but having given, she does not embrace again," she reveals that—just as a thief might plunder another's wealth while in a state of negligence—the long-desired embrace, though hindered by shame, was executed instantly through skill upon finding the opportune moment. "Dear to us" means it is our desire; the word "accomplished" (*siddham*) is to be supplied. She expresses her joy through the repetition (*vīpsā*).
"Because she had already been designated as her reward with the words 'the Bakula-garland'.

He causes Buddharakṣitā to marvel: "Buddharakṣitā has indeed fulfilled the burden of the venerable lady's expectations (*sambhāvanā*). The venerable lady Kāmandakī’s *sambhāvanā* refers to the thought, "She is capable of accomplishing this task," as in the expression, "A wise man [acts] by the very expectation of his sovereign";
or else, it refers to honor (*satkāra*), as in the phrase, "He honored them in due order."

"A burden of such a kind" refers to a heavy object that must be carried; "borne" means brought to the stage of completion, which, by figurative extension, signifies having been led to the culmination of the fruit.

*Ahnāya* is an indeclinable expressing wonder (*āścarya*). Thus, there is a sense of wonder because such a meeting was considered improbable in so short a time. "He rises" means he moves from his seat to honor [him] by rising to meet him.

"Agitated" (*sambhrānta*) means possessed of agitation (*sambhrama*), which is a state of being overwhelmed; this is to be construed with the word "agitated" (*sambhrāntāḥ*) modified by the particle *ca*.

"Save me, save me, O illustrious one! The repetition [of the verb] expresses the intensity of his fear and agitation. To the question "From what? Who is to be saved? he replies: "On the very way—meaning at the midpoint of the path—Makaranda was attacked by the city guards. "On the way" (*ardhamārge*) means in the middle portion of the road.

The city guards—the men appointed to protect the city—having intercepted him and questioned him, "Who is this? Who is she? From where? Where is he going? and having thus investigated, they came to know the truth: that this Makaranda, having deceived Nandana by assuming the guise of Mālatī, entered his mansion, abducted his sister, and was departing from there toward Mādhava in the night. Crying out "Thief! and pursuing him, Makaranda was being overwhelmed by them; therefore, he must be protected from them.

[The phrase] "by you" is understood from the context. To the question, "In that case, how did you ladies come here, having escaped from the crush? she replies: "We were sent along with Kalahaṃsaka, who joined us at that time. This means that at that time, during the moment of the attack, Makaranda came from here, met us, and sent us—Madayantikā and the others—along; that is to say, he dispatched us.

She reinforces Lavaṅgikā’s statement for the sake of urging haste in providing assistance: "Just as a clamor has been heard by those who have set out toward this direction, so we know that another infantry force has also arrived. "Toward this direction" means having set out or departed with this region as their destination; this is established by the word "by us" (asmābhiḥ), which follows immediately after the previous mention of "ahmehi" (by us). The masculine gender is used because the speaker is Kalahaṃsa. By the word "api" (also/even), she indicates that some infantry force had previously been seen.

"In what manner" (*yathā*) means by whatever mode; since the distinction between the density and sparseness of the preceding and succeeding moments is easily understood, we know—that is, we infer—in that very manner. "Another" (*anyat*) refers to what has been encountered other than what was previously attained, having been acquired by the king's command. The word *pāikka* denotes a foot-soldier. As in: "The army advances, its horses stumbling over the ground due to the dense throngs of cavalry, while the ranks of foot-soldiers press upon the flanks, crowded with the noise of the rear guard."
Thus, from the application of this device:

"Alas! Alas! A simultaneous mingling of joy and agitation has occurred. Joy arises from the acquisition of Madayantika; agitation arises from hearing of the attack by the guards. Their "mingling" (*sambheda*) is their mixture, which has now "occurred," meaning it has arrived.
Free from confusion through her composure, she honors the new bride out of propriety; she addresses her as "friend" because she is the wife of a close friend.

This is based on the statement in the *Mahābhārata*: "O Kṛṣṇa, you are my dear friend. "Welcome" means a beautiful arrival; the phrase "it was yours" is the ellipsis. "Favored" means beautified by your entry, for you possess a praiseworthy kinship. The expression "our home" refers to our own residence; this is said to demonstrate that for Makaranda—his friend who is no different from his own life—his own parents are indeed his parents and his own house is indeed his home, and likewise, for her [Mālatī], his parents are her own parents and his house is her own home.

Now, he pacifies their agitation by means of reasoning: the word *nanu* is used for emphasis. "Ladies"—Madayantika and the others—"are you well, with your minds free from disturbance? Having raised the doubt regarding the cause of their ill health, he dispels it: the meaning is that this situation—namely, the assault by many hostile men upon one who is alone and without assistance, resulting in being completely besieged—is indeed a source of apprehension for you. This is the matter at hand.

By the term "of the friend" (*vayasyasya*), which functions as a suggestion (*dhvani*) where the literal meaning is transferred to another sense, his strength, diligence, and fortitude are suggested. The phrase "whatever it may be" (*yatkiñcit*) is a ground for contempt due to its insignificance; therefore, the intended meaning is that this apprehension should not be entertained.

He supports the stated point with an illustration, beginning with "Of Hari" (*hareḥ*), and so forth. Of *hari*—that is, the lion—who is eager for the display of incomparable valor; "of that which lacks comparison" (*atulavikrama*) refers, by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), to being devoid of similarity. Regarding the "display of valor" (*vikramapraṇaya*), the meaning is its application, specifically the act of humbling others. He who is "eager" (*lālasa*)—meaning curious—for this, in battle (*āhave*), as an ally, is none other than he who is renowned; no one else. He is "fierce with his ringing claws" (*kvaṇatkararuhapracaṇḍaḥ*).

His companion, [the elephant], becomes terrifying with his bellowing claws, which produce a sound causing apprehension like the resonance of a multitude of sharp chisels engaged in splitting black rocks. He states the cause for the ringing of his claws: "In the *karaṭa*—that is, the hollow of the temple (*kapola*)—which is throbbing and shining.

According to the *Vaijayantī*: "The word *karaṭa* may refer to a rogue, a wood-apple tree, a crow, or the temple of an elephant. With ichor (*dāna*), which is flowing without ceasing due to its hardness, unevenness, and vastness—like a mountain torrent tumbling down a cliff—"ichor" (*dāna*) also refers to the rutting-fluid of an elephant, according to the *Vaijayantī*. His friend is thus formidable.

He is a peerless hero, possessing valor such that he alone is capable of splitting—that is, tearing apart—the hard bone situated upon the heads of lordly elephants, the leaders of elephant herds, whose faces have been drenched by the pouring rain; for there is no second person to perform this task, his hand alone suffices, and he has no need for any other instrument. Furthermore, the meaning is that he regards even many [enemies] as if they were blades of grass.

Here, the poetic figure is *vyatireka-mukha-dṛṣṭānta* (an illustrative simile expressed through contrast), because all elements are presented in the relationship of the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*). //7//

Since there is no dependence on companions for that [task], the word "also" (*api*) indicates that there is no room for assistance even from me. "Purified by valor" means cleansed by heroic prowess due to its sincerity; "of one sporting" means of one who plays. By saying "dear friend," he indicates: "Nevertheless, because of my agitation born of affection and my curiosity to behold his valor, I shall stand as his immediate neighbor"—that is, I shall remain close at hand. "Vikaṭam" means distorted, through the abandonment of one's natural course.

"Perhaps these two noble souls, Mādhava and Makaranda, will return unharmed. "Unharmed" (*anagha*) means free from *agha*, which is calamity (*vyasana*); as the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "In the sense of suffering, distress, and calamity, [the word] *agha* [is used]. This conjecture arises because battle is fraught with danger and because affection is characterized by apprehension regarding misfortune.

Distressed by those words, she said: "Friends, Buddharakṣitā and Avalokitā! Go quickly and report this news to the Holy Lady—this matter concerning the assault by the guards. This statement is made because she has determined that Kāmandakī is capable of providing a remedy even against a curse or an arrow. And you too, dear friend Lavaṅgikā! Quickly inform the Noble Son: "If we are indeed to be pitied by you, then exert yourselves with vigilance."

The plural form "yuṣmākam" (of you) is used out of respect for her husband. "If [you] are to be pitied," meaning if [you] are to be protected. By the plural "vayam" (we), she indicates: "In the event of your departure, I shall not live; upon the death of both of us, two families and their dependents will perish. Regarding "yuṣmākam," the rule "kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā" (the agent may optionally be expressed with gerunds and similar forms) applies.

(2-3-71) Thus, the genitive case [is used]. Therefore, for that reason, "exert yourselves with vigilance," meaning remain attentive and display your valor in the midst of the enemy; the implication is that otherwise there would be the danger of being struck by the weapons of the foe. Here, the emotion known as *śaṅkā* (suspicion/anxiety) and the *bhayānaka-rasa* (the sentiment of terror) are manifested.
"All" refers to Avalokitā, Buddharakṣitā, and Lavaṅgikā.
"They have exited" means that Madayantikā and Mālatī remain behind.

Agitated by the intense anxiety born of fear, she cries out: "Alas! Alas! It is not known how the time may pass; by what means can this moment be spent? Let it be so—she reflects upon some method for passing the time. She says that very thing: "I shall remain here, watching the path by which my dear friend Lavaṅgikā returns. She mentions Lavaṅgikā specifically because she was sent to her beloved and there is a haste to hear news of her.

By casting her gaze toward the path of retreat from afar, she indicates a slight subsiding of her distress through fixing her mind upon that very spot. "Wandering" means going elsewhere away from Madayantika; here, it should be understood that the poet has established the heroine’s solitude—due to the departure of Buddharakṣita and others, as well as her distance from Madayantika—in order to provide an opportunity for Kapālakuṇḍalā, who is seeking a vulnerability. Now...

Since the hero of this dramatic work has been defined as "steadfast, tranquil, and an achiever of dharma, kama, and artha despite their attendant dangers," Bhavabhūti—whose intellectual power surpasses that of Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods—introduces a cause of unsurpassed suffering for Mādhava, who is currently immersed in the bliss of attaining his beloved, in order to demonstrate his attainment of a pleasure intermingled with pain.

"Full of apprehension" means accompanied by the fear, "Will some inauspicious event surely befall?"—for the fear of the loss of her beloved was already present in her mind. "How indeed has it throbbed? refers to the throbbing, the vibration, or the twitching of my right eye, which possesses beautiful pupils.

The suffix *niṣṭhā* is used in the sense of state (*bhāve*). How so? He reflects upon the wonder of the sudden adversity of fate. Since the throbbing of the left and right eyes and so forth in women and men respectively indicates auspiciousness, whereas their reversal indicates inauspiciousness, he uses the term "not-left" (*avāma*) [to refer to the right eye]. "He sits down" (*upaviśati*) means that he sinks down upon the ground, overcome by despondency.

The statement "having entered, she does not enter" indicates that upon finding an opening, she has instantly entered. By this, the previously mentioned [statement], "I am intent upon doing harm to Mādhava," is brought into connection. *Ā* expresses anger. *Pāpe* ("O sinner") is used because her conduct is rooted in the sin of murdering her own guru.

By saying "Stay! Stay!", the effort to withdraw in fear is revealed upon seeing the wicked woman who was previously seen by Karālā; otherwise, since she was already seated, the command "stay" would be inappropriate, and one would have had to say "rise."

"Alas, noble son! Noble son!"—this is the commencement of a cry for protection. "Stuttering of speech" (*vākstambha*) means the non-functioning of speech, caused either by its [the curse's] power or by terror. "With a wrathful laugh" means accompanied by a laugh born of anger; it is a derisive laugh because of the futility of his actions. The particle *nanu* is used in an interrogative sense, meaning "why do you cry out? Since it will be said later, "Cry out, cry out, O husband," the word "husband" (*pati*) is established by implication. "Call out, call out" (*āhvayāhvaya*) is a repetition (*vīpsā*) used in derision. The sense is: "My speech has indeed been paralyzed by me; how then can you cry out now?"

In order to demonstrate that his own action has a cause, he revives their former enmity with the words "one who is devoted to you," and so forth. By saying "devoted to you" (tvadvatsala), meaning "affectionate toward you," he indicates that because my teacher’s murder was rooted in you, his removal will be accomplished simply by your dismissal. By the phrase "of the ascetic folk"—meaning a person distinguished by praiseworthy austerity—he suggests through implication that he is exempt from being killed on account of his status as a *liṅgin* (one wearing the sectarian marks).

If it is argued, "What offense has been committed if he is killed during the attempt to kill me, a maiden of a Brāhmaṇa woman?", to that he replies: "Alas! (hanta). Even so, it is proper to protect you, and not to kill him who is intent upon his own duty in the form of an offering to the deity; this is the sense. He states another fault as a reason for his deserving punishment: "A seducer of a maiden" (kanyāviṭaḥ), meaning one who enjoys a young girl who has not yet been given away by her father.

By the word *viṭa* (libertine), he indicates his exclusive devotion to aesthetic sentiment (*rasa*) and his disregard for dharma. "Husband" (*pati*) means that he was later made a supporter through force and the efforts of Kāmandakī and others. "Where indeed is the husband?"—the ellipsis being "in what place does he reside?"—"May he protect you. The verb is in the imperative mood (*loṭ*), used either to grant permission to act according to one's desire or to pose a question. This speech is also sarcastic (*sotprāśa*). The sense is: "I have come here only after ascertaining his absence; so where are you, and where is he?"

He clarifies this very point: "Nanu" is used here as an address. The meaning is that such an opportunity has been awaited for a long time (*cirāt*), through constant vigilance, thinking, "When will such a chance arise? You have been "made into a morsel" (*kabalīkṛtāsi*)—a morsel (*kabala*) being a mouthful; the sense is that you are not merely being made so now, nor will you be, but rather that there is no longer any doubt regarding the abandonment of your life. Therefore, she is "terrified by the swoop of the hawk" (*śyenāvapātacakitā*), trembling at the attack of the *suparṇa* bird.
As it is said: "The *vyāghrāṭa*, the *bharadvāja*, the *kṣipra*, the *śyena*, and the *suparṇaka* [are names for the hawk]."
In the female hawk, the female cricket... [and so forth].

Thus says the Vaijayantī. "Navavartikā" means a young quail (*bālavartikā*). The inclusion of the word "new" (*nava*) indicates an extreme state of timidity and weakness. In the *Saṅgraha*, it is mentioned as a specific species of bird called "scattered-feeders" (*viṣkira*), alongside the statement: "The quail (*vartikā*) and the francolin (*varāṭa*) are indeed *viṣkiras*. This is also illustrated in the *Vṛtti*: "The hawk (*śyena*) makes the quail cry out. Furthermore, what do you intend? For what purpose do you exert yourself? By way of comparison, even the quail flutters for a moment, yet it is not released from the hawk because there is no remedy.
This indicates that you, too, are likewise [the Tathāgata]. Here, the poetic figures (alaṃkāra) are *parikara* and *upamā*. //8//

The particle *yāvat* is used here as a sentence ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*) or for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). The statement "having brought her to Śrīparvata" is spoken because Kāmandakī and the others are unable to prevent her from leaving due to their distance; this is also indicated by the earlier mention of Śrīparvata as her fixed place of residence in the words, "of one who has come from Śrīparvata. Furthermore, as stated in the first act, "Now that Saudāminī, having attained the power of the accomplishment of extraordinary mantras, maintains the form of a Kāpālika on Śrīparvata," [the author] thus arranges what is necessary for Mālatī’s protection.

"Piece by piece" (*tilaśaḥ*) means having cut and severed it into parts as minute as sesame seeds. "One whose nature is to die with difficulty" (*duḥkhamāriṇī*) refers to one whose character is to die through the experience of extreme agony; the implication is that she was fit for a varied execution because she was the cause of her elder's death. "Together with Mālatī" means she departed after lifting up Mālatī and acting out the gesture of flying into the expanse of the sky.

"I too shall follow Mālatī. "I too [was] followed by Lavaṅgikā until Mālatī. By saying "I too shall follow Mālatī," he suggests that the circumstances of Mālatī's abduction were unknown [to him]. "Friend, O Mālatī!"—this is an address intended to indicate her presence nearby. "Madayantikā! I am indeed Lavaṅgikā. "Have you honored the noble one? The word *api* is used in the sense of a question. "Honored" means treated with respect according to Mālatī’s words. "The noble one" refers to Mādhava.

No, no; it is connected with the word "sambhāvita" (feared). Through the repetition (*vīpsā*), despondency is suggested. Indeed, having heard the clamor immediately upon descending from the garden, he rushed forward with great force—his formidable thighs like pillars cast wide and with a sudden, forceful stride—and entered the enemy army. The connection is as follows: "descending from the garden" refers to the descent or going down due to the garden's elevated ground; "exit" refers to the departure onto the path; and "having rushed forth" means having fled from that very spot.

The cause for this is: "having heard the clamor"—that is, having heard the tumultuous noise of the army. With "impetuous strides," meaning with steps taken at a great distance accompanied by mental agitation; with "thigh-staffs" that are tossed, trembling, formidable, vast in nature, and exceedingly heavy—this last being an adverbial modifier for the action of rushing—the enemy force, i.e., the hostile army. By this, the state of being overcome by affection for a friend and the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) are suggested.

Then I returned, unfortunate as I am; that is, because it was impossible to reach them. "Unfortunate"—this expresses my despondency. And I hear in every house the lamentations of the city folk, who are overflowing with affection for their virtues: "Alas, Mādhava! Makaranda! O rash one!"—that is, of the citizens, the people born in the city, who were filled with love for the qualities such as integrity found in Mādhava and Makaranda, due to their long residence there.

*He* [expresses] sorrow (*viṣāda*). The meaning is: having determined that disaster (*vyasana*) will result from an attack by many upon the two [of them]. By the word *sāhasika* (rash/violent), there is an indication of the cause for the arrival of this disaster. The sense is that because such reckless action—consisting of the forcible abduction of Mālatī and Madayantikā—is the cause of the king and minister’s wrath, the resulting calamity is unavoidable. The word *iti* indicates manner; the meaning is "of such a kind. *Paridevanā* refers to words of lamentation.

"I hear this in every house," and so forth, is a summary of the castes (*varṇasaṃhāra*), because the virtues of the hero are praised through the words of all the castes. It is further suggested that even the Great King, having heard the account of the separation of his two daughters-in-law, was overcome by a surge of indignation; he instantly dispatched a multitude of foot soldiers and was seen standing upon the roof-terrace of the palace in the moonlight. "The Great King" refers to the lord of Padmāvatī. By the use of the word "even" (*api*), it is indicated that this matter has been learned by the King himself, and thus it highlights that it will lead to disastrous consequences.

*Kile* means "reportedly. Regarding the account of the separation (*vipralambha*) between Vadhū—the two maidens Mālatī and Madayantikā—it refers to the occurrence in the form of a deception, since Makaranda, disguised in the attire of Mālatī, acted as the instrument for the abduction of both girls. Consequently, he became possessed by an outburst of indignation (*matsarāvega*), an agitation of intolerance arising from the fact that his own act of giving [the girls] had been rendered void. He dispatched numerous throngs of foot-soldiers, having repeatedly sent forth countless groups of infantry with the command: "Go! Go! You two ill-behaved wretches of Brahmins, kill them!"

The sense is that, according to the scriptural statement, "One may slay even an assailant who approaches with intent to kill, even if he is a master of the Vedānta; by so doing, one does not become a killer of a Brāhmaṇa," these two are assailants (*ātatāyin*) because they have abducted his wife. [This is said] by means of the moonlight acting as the instrument of observation, because, like midday, all events are clearly visible. It is "counseled" (or discussed), with the words "by the citizens" being understood to complete the sense.

Having ascertained that her calamity was inevitable because it had been recognized by the king, she said: "Alas, I am destroyed, unfortunate as I am! She asks out of a desire to see her: "Friend! Where is Mālatī again? The word "again" (*punaḥ*) implies a reversal; the meaning is: "Let this matter rest for now, but tell me this instead."

She indeed set out first to look for your path, and afterwards I [set out], yet I do not see her. By saying "first, right before me," he expresses that there was no interval [between their departures]. The phrase "afterwards, I set out following in her footsteps" is thus connected. The word "and" (ca) highlights the wonderfulness of not seeing her, given that their departures occurred at the same time. [One wonders] perhaps she has entered the thicket of the garden.

"Into the thicket of the garden"—a region rendered dark by the density of trees and creepers; the sense is that this is because she does not know the path for following you. The phrase "she might have entered" implies a question through the use of *kāku* (intonation). The suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*). The word *nāma* also indicates possibility. [As stated: "The particle *mā* is used with *na* in the sense of prohibition."

She said with fear: "Friend, let us search quickly. She refutes the possibility of her being there by providing a reason: "My dear friend is extremely timid; she would not stay in the garden at this moment. "Extremely timid" (*atikātarā*) means one who is exceedingly fearful. By saying "my dear friend," she indicates that her character is known only to herself through long association, and not by you. "At this moment" means at this time of night when the attendants have departed.
"Staying in the garden" implies that the place is a source of fear due to the abundance of darkness.

"Friend Mālatī! Indeed we say, 'Friend Mālatī!'—by saying 'Indeed we say,' we call out with a loud voice from the previous [distance]; yet you give no reply," this is a speech full of jealousy. "Delighted"—meaning, acting out joy. "By good fortune (diṣṭyā), safely (kuśalena), I have emerged from the difficult passage of the crush. "By good fortune" (diṣṭyā) means by the favor of fate; the third case ending is used here in the sense of cause. "Safely" (kuśalena) refers to well-being, such as having one's body unharmed, and so forth. "From the difficult passage of the crush" (saṅghaṭṭadurgamāt) means from that place where it is impossible to move due to the thronging of people. "Hīmāṇahe! (Ah, what joy!)

The word *ṅa* is a regional term used by those of inferior capacity to express joy and wonder. I seem to behold [the army] appearing as if turned tawny by the mass of moonbeams reflected in the edges of the swords, which are brandished continuously and without interruption with pure, upward-tossing waves; resembling the stream of the Daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā) when its waves are stirred and tossed upward by the playful, effortless pulling of the plow wielded by the mighty arm-staffs of Kāmapāla, who is moved by the playfulness of intoxication; and agitated by the turbulence caused by the contact with the honey [of battle], which has fallen unrestrainedly and mercilessly upon them.

"I seem to see, as if it were present before me, the multitude of foot-soldiers who have turned back and whose tumultuous clamor spreads through the entire expanse of the sky; I seem to experience it"—the word "as if" (*iva*) is used because [the event] has already passed.

It was such that its appearance was characterized by being turned tawny by the mass of moonbeams reflected upon the edges—the sharpness of the blades—of the swords; for these swords were stainless, polished on whetstones until they were free of blemish, and were being incessantly and closely brandished and brandished upward in great numbers, creating surging waves as they rose. This was because their rippling folds quivered with the force of their trembling, and thus the sight of them appeared tawny in color.
The description of a tawny (piñjara) color arises from the blending of the blue hue of a sword’s edge with the white rays of the moon;
