as Divākara states: "From the union of white and blue, that which is called kaḍāra is born," and the *Vaijayantī* lexicon defines: "Piñjara is yellowish-red; babhru, kaḍāra, and kapila [are synonyms]. [This refers to] Kāmapāla, that is, Balabhadra, who is possessed of the playful grace of intoxication produced by the wine of Vāruṇī.

"Revatīramaṇa, Rāma, Kāmapāla, and Halāyudha"—thus says Amara. By that which is "vikaṭa," meaning broad, the *bhuja-daṇḍa* (staff-like arm) is meant; by the *hala* (plow) held therein, the *sīra* (plowshare), the effortless *karṣaṇa* (dragging or pulling) is performed. By that, the stream of the Kalinda-kanyā—the flow of the Yamunā—is *taralita*, meaning agitated; hence it is "like the one with upsurging waves. Through this comparison, the agitation of even a powerful being, his fleeing in many directions, and his shining from afar at night due to his deep blue color are illuminated. And here, the ancient legend is called to mind, as follows: [The text continues with the narrative of the Yamunā being dragged by Balarāma.]
"O Yamunā, come to bathe! he said, overwhelmed by intoxication, shining with pearls that were drops of the water of his own dharma as he stepped upon her.
But that river, regarding his speech as the talk of a madman, did not come;
thereupon the wielder of the plow, becoming enraged, seized his plow.
Seizing her on the bank, he dragged her along, overwhelmed by intoxication:
"O wicked woman! You will not come? You will not come? Go elsewhere as you please!"

"Having been suddenly dragged by him, that river abandoned its course and flooded that forest where Baladeva was staying," according to the statement in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*. Because there is no other way for one who has fallen into an unbridled state, he attacks while free from the bodily constraints of self-preservation; for this very reason, he is "cruel" (*nirdayaḥ*), meaning devoid of compassion, and his "crushing" (*avamardaḥ*) refers to the trampling of enemy forces.
"Even five hundred heroes can crush a vast army,
or even just five, six, or seven who are determined to die."

Thus it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*. "Vihvalam" means overwhelmed and rendered helpless by the agitation caused by the disturbance of Makaranda's situation. By this, it is implied that even one who has been defeated may return once more, either through renewed efforts such as regaining the command of the army or out of shame. "I see, as it were, a host of foot-soldiers," [referring to] one in whom there is a clamor—a tumultuous roar of lion-like shouts indicative of enthusiasm—that has arisen (*udgata*) and emerged (*udbhūta*) upon the retreat, spreading and pervading the entire expanse of the sky.

And I remember Lord Mādhava, who performed a perilous feat of daring by providing a passage for the army’s retreat through a path cleared amidst the chaotic flight of the troops, as they were overwhelmed by the impact of various weapons cast off by the multitude of great warriors scattered and crushed within the cage-like thunderbolt of his terrifying arms.

By means of a terrifying arm-form, which is a vajra-cage and a nest constructed of vajra-jewels; by means of this vajra-cage form, because it cannot be pierced by the weapons of others and because it itself shatters the forces of the enemy; with the hosts of excellent warriors—the multitudes of heroes—shattered, split asunder by hundreds of blows, overturned, and cast down; with the various weapons such as swords and spears released [by those warriors] crushed and crowded together; and with the troops and soldiers who have retreated far away, having fled in a formidable retreat.

The construction is as follows: "I remember and contemplate Nāthamādhava"—that is, I keep him in mind—on a wide, open, and secluded path where movement is unrestricted, because previously, due to the crowding of people, there was no opportunity for free movement; he is one by whom a difficult and daring feat, impossible for others, has been accomplished—a courageous stride devoid of regard for his own body. Here, the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is suggested (*dhvani*), and the *sātvatī* style (*vṛtti*) should be understood, according to the rule:
"In the heroic [sentiment], the *sātvatī* [style]," and "The *sātvatī* is free from sorrow, characterized by courage, heroism, renunciation, compassion, and uprightness."
And because of such a statement, it should be understood in the same way elsewhere as well.

Oh! What devotion to virtue the King possesses! For now, standing upon the roof-terrace of his palace, having observed [the situation] and pacified the conflict by offering respectful greetings through the chamberlain, he became entirely gentle in disposition. Having brought forth Nāthamādhava and the lotus-faced Makaranda, and having repeatedly silenced the clamor of his own attendants, he recognized their noble lineage and felt a deep sense of satisfaction. Then, with sweet words, he addressed Bhūrivasu and Nandana, whose faces were stained by the soot of shame and throbbing envy.

"Is there now any dissatisfaction with you two sons-in-law—who are ornaments to the expanse of the world, possessed of great majesty, and delightful due to the qualities of your recent appearance? Having thus consoled them, the king went inside. "Aha! How wonderful is this devotion to virtue, this partiality toward qualities such as heroism and the like, shown by honoring these two even though they have committed a great offense"—this is the underlying sentiment. He describes that very honor with the words beginning "That... [yad...]: "By the humble submission of the doorkeeper (pratihāra) whom we had sent, [the king explained]: 'These two of ours are of noble birth; they have offended out of ignorance.'"

"May that be forgiven by you"—in these words, he instructs his own people: "Whatever harm has been done to you out of ignorance and the like, it should be endured by you both. By such humble speech, beginning with the address "O Lords," the conflict—the mutual quarrel—between them was pacified. Being of a single gentle essence, he was characterized solely by serenity, having abandoned the impulse of resentment born from hearing the news of their separation. Having brought them near, he led them into his presence.

By the phrase "the lotus-faced one," which serves as an indicator of her tenderness and beauty, he suggests that his passion would be doubled upon seeing them. "Again and again" means repeatedly. "Whose clamor was warded off"—that is, whose tumultuous outcry, such as "Let them be slain! Let them be slain! born from the indignation at the slaughter of many kinsmen by his own people (his own army), had been suppressed.

The poet indicates Bhūrivasu’s employment of a stratagem by stating that he learned of [Bhānumatī’s] noble lineage from an attendant at court, having discovered that she was the sole daughter of Devarāta, the minister of the illustrious King of Vidarbha, and that she was born of the same family line as his own.

The meaning is that their faces have been turned pale by the application of collyrium (kajjala), which acts as a pigment of discoloration due to the following: on the part of Bhūrivasu, because his great respect [for the bridegroom] has vanished and his wonder has arisen, his face is stained with the soot of manifest envy and embarrassment; and on the part of Nandana, because he has deceived me with a false marriage that makes him a laughingstock to the world, his face is discolored by shame at the thought, "My sister has been taken away without my consent. Thus, they are both stained by the soot of their respective emotions.

Alternatively, since embarrassment due to stinginess is common to both, the fact that they have been deceived by the abduction of their respective daughters is equal for them both. By this, the poet reveals the minister Bhūrivasu’s skill in acting out the absence of agreement within his own heart. According to the *Bhāvaprakāśa*: "That state in which the mind acts with embarrassment is called *vailakṣya*. Through the introduction of speech intended to appease the heart by means of the employment of sweet words, he describes the manner of that speech, beginning with: "What now? and so forth.

Why is there dissatisfaction—that is, a lack of satiety—regarding these two sons-in-law, the suitors for Mālatī and Madayantikā, who are the ornaments of the entire expanse of the world (*bhuvanābhoga*), possessed of great majesty (*mahānubhāva*) such as noble lineage and greatness, and who are delightful through their qualities that are seen for the first time by those of us who have not previously beheld such virtues, or alternatively, who are delightful through their qualities and possess a fresh appearance characterized by youth, as in the expression "fresh women are delightful through their qualities"?
Why this lack of contentment?

The word *ṛ* means "in this manner. Even though it has been stated that "the son-in-law (*jāmātā*) is the husband of the daughter," the description of Nandana as the son-in-law should be understood as being due to the fact that, according to the saying "the eldest brother is equal to a father," there is no distinction between a younger sister's son and [one's own] daughter. Because he went inside, to the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*), having made [Nandana] possessed of the knowledge that pacifies agitation while being thus enlightened—that is, for which reason—oh, how great is the King's affection for virtue! This is also the dramatic element (*vṛttyaṅga*) called *sampāta*: "Sampāta is the breaking of a joint [of a plot] by means of the power of counsel, purpose, fate, and so forth."

Because of this statement, it is said that by divine power the King has been separated from Nandana; furthermore, Mādhava and Makaranda have arrived here. "I shall report this news to the Blessed Lady," [he says], with the underlying sense that it is solely through her grace that their prosperity has come to pass.

Because it was indicated by the words "these two," there is an entrance. [The word] "of the beloved" means of Mādhava, the most dear one. "Of one whose nature is to surpass and exceed all men. "Without guile" means free from the employment of deceit, because he acts without transgressing righteousness (*dharma*). The meaning is that he has engaged [in battle] excluding those who have laid down their weapons, those with disheveled garments, those with loose hair, those who have abandoned their mounts, those who are under attack by enemies, and so forth. "Majestic" means distinguished by energy. "Splendor" (*tejas*) is the prowess that is incapable of being overcome by others.
He confirms this state of affairs: "For instance."

Regarding "dorniṣpeṣa" and so forth: by means of the crushing of arms—that is, the pulverization resulting from striking with the form of an arm as a weapon due to emerging swiftly and being unarmed—he [the demon] has his mass shattered, his cohesion broken, and his skeletal frame crushed such that the bones of his body are snapping.

"Previously," that is, at the start of the battle, "of him who was crushing the heroes"—meaning those who were agitating the brave—"having pursued them from behind," by which it is understood that their flight had begun; "seizing their weapons," that is, forcibly taking their arms, "of him who displays valor," meaning one who exerts prowess against those facing him; the word "dearest" (*preyasaḥ*) is supplied from the preceding sentence.

In front, in the space ahead, was a wide and expansive path formed by the ranks of foot soldiers who stood motionless like pillars out of fear on both sides; this path led through a vast ocean-like mass of battle, strewn with many headless trunks (*ruṇḍas*), dancing corpses (*kabandhas*), and numerous fragments such as heads, hands, and feet, which were tossing and writhing—this attribution of "ocean-ness" is due to its immense terror and its vast expanse.

By the word "purastāt" (in front), it is suggested that wherever [the army] goes, there is such a state [of the path]; whereas by "pṛṣṭhataḥ" (from behind), their turning back and the resulting state of being completely filled with noise, as well as their fleeing upon looking back again, are illuminated. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "In front of the beloved, the path became a mass of hosts. By the term "saṅghodadheḥ" (of the ocean-like host), the composure of the *timiṅgila* fish and others sporting unrestrainedly in the *taraṅgamālinī* river—which is crowded with the breaking of towering waves—is indicated.
Here, the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is perceived. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). //9//

In response to this objection: "Alas! This place of latent resentment (anuśaya) is a ground for remorse, thinking, 'I have not acted with such courage. According to the *Vaijayantī*: 'Anuśaya refers to remorse, as well as to long-standing enmity and persistence. This is my own conduct; behold it—examine it."

Regarding the passage beginning with "this very day" (*adyaiva*): because the moonbeams, reflected in the wine contained within jeweled goblets due to the [hero's] position atop the palace roof, appear to break into fragments and be drunk themselves as that wine is being consumed, there is the poetic expression that [the palace] is "inlaid" (*khacita*)—that is, connected—with fragments of the moonbeams.

As Bhartṛhari stated in his poetry: "He partook of the moon reflected in the cup as if it were nectar. This refers to the occasion of the *niśīthotsava*, the festival of love to be performed at midnight; for the drinking of honey-wine (*madhu*) serves to kindle passion. [The grammatical rule is: "The locative case is to be used when a word expressing a cause is connected with an action."

The locative case [is used] according to [Pāṇini] 2.3.36. "By whom" refers to those who have drunk today itself—that is, at this very moment—the remainder of what was left over from the mouthfuls used for filling the mouths of their beloveds, those lovers whose nature it is to grant playful embraces and who occasionally offer amorous caresses; the word "even" (*eva*) serves to indicate the simultaneity of these two actions. "Of your arm-gates" means of your gate-like arms.

"Kavāṭa and arara are synonyms; its bolt (viṣkambha) is called argala," according to Amara. With limbs—that is, bodies—whose bones were shattered by heavy operations such as crushing and other such actions, [they were] "devoid of essence" (asāravidhurān); since essence means strength, they were devoid of it and thus perpetually suffering. Alternatively, there is the reading *sāravidhurān*, which likewise means "devoid of essence."

"Generally" (*prāyeṇa*) means "for the most part"; this indicates that it is uncertain whether anyone, anywhere, or at any time, will ever become one who possesses essence. [The phrase] "those wandering in the path of worldly existence" refers to those situated on the path of active involvement, which is rippled by the continuous waves of birth, death, and so forth. "They speak" is used in the sense of performing actions conducive to that [goal]. Here too, the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is suggested.

In this case, the poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) are Contradiction (*virodha*) and Illustration (*nidarśanā*), because of the presentation of two contradictory emotions—joy and dejection—and because the connection between each emotion and its respective cause is expressed through the action itself. //10//

"Smartavyam" means it is to be remembered; the sense is that it should be kept in mind by the intellect for as long as one lives. The particle "tu" indicates a contrast: although we have undoubtedly committed a great offense, he has nevertheless concealed it out of his benevolence (*saujanya*). Benevolence is the disposition of a respected person; it consists of being devoted to virtues without envy. Regarding the word "aparāddhayoḥ": it is the form of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the active sense derived from the root *rādha* (meaning "to accomplish") preceded by the prefix *apa*, with the sense of "those who have committed an offense," that is, those who have performed an undesirable act.

The phrase "of the two who have not offended" does not convey the mere absence of offense; rather, by implication, it conveys the sense "as if they were benefactors," because a greater act of requital would be inappropriate toward the mere absence of offense. The meaning "within our domain" is established by the context.

"Having performed the formal approach (*upasadana*) and having manifested his devotion (*prāvaṇya*)"—for in passages such as "to a disciple who has approached according to rule," the term *upasadana* is seen to signify devotion—and "he has acted" or "he has practiced"—this recalls what was stated previously, "having recognized his noble birth, he has produced great respect. Therefore, the meaning is: "since our desires are thus free from obstacles, therefore [let us go]. The word "come" (*ehi*) indicates haste.

"In the very presence of Mālatī—that is, in her immediate vicinity—we experience—meaning we understand perfectly—the account of Madayantikā’s abduction or seizure, which consists of the detailed execution of the plan, as it is being related at length through a proliferation of words; the word 'by you' is to be supplied [as the agent]. By the use of the plural number, the speaker refers to himself along with Mālatī, Avalokitā, and others."

He states that the statement "in the presence of Mālatī" is purposeful because it conveys unsurpassed aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), beginning with the words "while he speaks," and so forth. The meaning is: while he was speaking, she was distinguished by a gentle smile; just as joy arises in a thief upon seeing another thief due to the perception of shared security and fate, she was likewise gladdened by his audacity being equal to her own, and thus possessed of a soft laugh. She was struck by Mālatī’s side-long glances—curved, tremulous, and darting.

With pride mixed with reproach, as if struck by blows from falling staffs, his gaze was motionless due to a sudden flash of shame; for after first observing Mālatī’s fickleness through his own cultivation of self-control, he subsequently experienced a lack of steadiness—that is, a flickering gaze—due to the shame arising from his own rash action. This is because fickleness is well-known as an outward manifestation (*anubhāva*) of shame in such passages as "for a moment, with eyes turned toward her, trembling with bashfulness. Alternatively, "motionless" (*stimita*) means fixed without movement due to resentment toward Mālatī.

The address "friend" (*sakhī*) is used because she is the wife of a friend. "She will bow her head" (*namayiṣyati*) means she will keep her face cast down; this is an *anubhāva* (consequent emotion), as stated in such passages as: "While the divine sage was speaking thus, she stood by her father's side with her face turned downward. Here, the sentiment of humor (*hāsya-rasa*) is suggested. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is inference (*anumāna*). //11//

"This one standing before us" means "that one where Mālatī is located. "They enter" means they perform the act of entering. She continues to pursue the current subject, which is the search for Mālatī:

"Friend, Mālatī!"—the word "let her be seen" is to be supplied. "By good fortune, those two noble ones are seen once again"—"by good fortune" (diṣṭyā) means by luck; otherwise, there would be joy because she had been searching for them out of affection.
"Where is that Mālatī?"—meaning, she who is being sought by you two; or rather, the sense is that she is desired to be seen by us two, who are like those parched with thirst.

By the word "pada" (footstep), we have been deceived regarding our ill fortune; that is, we have been deluded by the thought that Mālatī was approaching based on the sound of the footsteps of you two, since you both called out, "Mālatī!"—this is the intended meaning.

Having said, "O unfortunate one," he spoke with apprehension: "O ladies, by some means or other—through great effort—it seems to be falling apart or being shattered due to the agitation of manifold and multifaceted anxieties. Or there is the reading *eva*; or the reading *na vidhvaṃsate*. The sense is that it is maintained with extreme effort; otherwise, it would surely fall apart.
Since this is so, therefore let that account be told clearly and explicitly—that is to say, let it be narrated for the sake of determining one side of the matter.

Now, since an ill omen has already indicated this misfortune, he asks, "What is the use of repeating your names? and says, "For me," and so forth. Regarding Kuvalayākṣī—that is, with reference to Mālatī—for one whose mind is incessantly fixed on her alone as the sole object of desire, the acquisition of such a jewel of the three worlds—endowed with noble lineage, beauty, character, sweetness, and unsurpassed affection—as if obtained in a dream, shall not endure for us for long; for such merit is impossible to conceive. Thus, regarding this impending calamity, by whatever means...

Because of this cause, even though there is absolute destruction [of the body], he whose intellect and mind are eternally fixed on one [object], perceives that very thing as a trembling of the inner self—the heart—a continuous and surging agitation that produces the cognition, "It will fall today, it will fall today," and thus determines the infallibility of its result, which is inauspiciousness.
For, "In matters where doubt arises for the virtuous, the inclinations of the internal organ are the authority."

Thus, according to the words of great poets, the throbbing of the left eye for a man is an omen of inauspiciousness; by this, it is stated that there is also a physical ill omen. Furthermore, these words of yours—"O unfortunate one, you have been deceived"—are painful and difficult to hear.

In this matter, in every way and by all means—meaning by your words, both mental and physical, which are causeless and yet consistent with that [state]—I am destroyed, I am lost; the sense is that I am ruined by the loss of such a jewel. This is the *avamarśa* juncture (the point of falling into calamity), characterized by the reflection on the seed-meaning already introduced, arising from the calamity consisting of separation from the beloved; for it is said, "Let it be clearly stated. (12)

She states this clearly: "When that noble lady had departed from here, she sent Lavaṅgikā with Avalokitā and Buddharakṣitā to the presence of the venerable lady, instructing her: 'Inform the noble son [Makaranda] to be vigilant. Then, becoming anxious, she went forward to look for her path; I followed behind, but I did not see her. Thereafter, we both searched among the thickets of branches until you were seen.
This refers to that specific period of time, as it is stated explicitly.
Having ascertained her loss, he laments: "Alas, my beloved Mālatī!"—this is an utterance addressed to the empty air, fixing his gaze upon it.

"Something or other" (*kimapi kimapi*) and so forth: I suspect, that is, I am reflecting upon, that object which is "something or other," meaning it is inexpressible. By means of this repetition (*vīpsā*), he expresses the necessity of suspecting divine and human calamities as the causes of this misfortune. Why is it inexpressible? He says: "Other than auspicious things" (*maṅgalebhyo 'nyat*); for it is improper to speak immediately without knowing the true nature of an inauspicious or evil event. [This follows the rule] *anyārāt*.

(2-1-21) By the phrase beginning with "ityādinā," the fifth case [is indicated]. Since the word *yat* is employed in the subsequent sentence, the word *tat* follows by implication in the preceding one as "that something or other" (*tatkimapi kimapīti*). "I fear" (*śaṅke*) means this is merely a suspicion arising from my affection for you; however, it is suggested that such a thing is impossible for you, a virtuous woman (*kalyāṇī*). If it is asked, "In that case, how is there no sight of her? he says in response: "Let the jest—the play consisting of making oneself invisible—cease"; the verb form is used in the sense of a request (*prārthana*).
The sense is: "You mock me by suggesting that only what is already established can be negated; however, this is no occasion for deception. [This refers to the rule: *vyāṅparibhyo ramaḥ*.

(1-3-83) Thus, the *parasmaipada* ending is used. "O Caṇḍī, O wrathful one!"—by this, the cause for her jesting is suggested: "It appears that you harbor jealousy toward me because I have been delayed. Amara states: "Caṇḍī, however, means a wrathful woman. Then he states the reason for desisting: "I am *paryutsuka*, I am eager for a sight of you separated by even a moment; therefore, let her desist"—this is the meaning. Again, he speculates in another manner: "Do you consider what he will do upon seeing me? You wish to know."

By means of an interrogative intonation (*kāku*), the question "What? is implied. He says that even such a calculation need not be made now: "I am known by you exactly as I am—both who I am and how much I am. By using the past tense (*bhūta-nirdeśa*), he reveals the meaning: "Previously, when I was engaged in selling my own flesh and so forth, you already discerned me as one who disregards his own life and for whom the sole wealth is the sight of you; therefore, what is the point of this 'grinding of what is already ground' (*piṣṭapeṣaṇa*) now?"

"Give me a word—even before granting me your sight—a shower of nectar that extinguishes all suffering, saying: 'I am here; do not fear. Grant me this speech. Because she does not grant even this speech, he reproaches her with agitation: "Within the interior of my body, my heart wanders, agitated and helpless, moving about bewildered as to what should be done. Even knowing this state of mine, you do not acknowledge me with even a mere word. What else can there be?"

"You are merciless; you are devoid of compassion toward one who is distressed and in peril"—here, the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇarasa*) is manifested. This is the figure of speech *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), because the effect—namely, the abandonment of her own life—is indicated by way of the cause, which is the state of being unseen. //13//
Alas, dear friend! Where have you gone?
Why—on what account—do you, without understanding the truth (the word "truth" being understood), assume this state of agitation, the condition of one who is distressed and lacking composure?

"How can I not succumb to despondency? he asks. "You too"—the meaning is: you who have witnessed these things firsthand within the inner sanctum of the city goddess's temple. "Of her who is distressed by love for Mādhava"—that is, of one whose heart was rendered helpless by affection toward me on the occasion of the proposal of Nandana’s marriage. "The acts of despondency" refers to those deeds born of the fear of not attaining him, such as the resolve to die, lamentation, and prostrating before Lavaṅgikā. Therefore, the sense is: how can there be peace for me as I remember them?

This is so; everything you have described as a fact has been personally witnessed by me. However, there is also a specific detail: it is suspected that there will be a visit to the feet of the Goddess. This means that a journey to the feet of the venerable Kāmandakī is suspected for the purpose of seeking her blessing for victory over our enemies, as such an occurrence is possible. Even in this matter, there is no certainty; nevertheless, the sense is that it must be investigated in every respect.

Because the Blessed Lady’s monastery is situated near the monastery located in the garden, the suspicion regarding her is plausible. Therefore, "come"—that is, come without agitation. "There," at the feet of the Blessed Lady; "first" (*tāvat*) is used for emphasis; the ellipsis is "we shall surely see her. The emphasis is for the purpose of consolation.
This too is possible: this matter spoken by Makaranda is possible—that is, it is conjectured. The sense is that no other alternative is conceivable.
Because he has become somewhat reassured, anticipating that possibility, he says: "Let it be so."
"Having reflected" (*vicintya*) means having contemplated a sign that causes agitation of the mind.

"She has gone," etc.—*yātā* means she has departed; the suffix *-liṅ* is used here in the sense of possibility. "Our friend Mālatī. Now, the word *atha* serves to exclude other alternatives: whether she has gone or not, even if she has gone, will she return alive or not? In this regard, there are three possibilities: has she perhaps gone to the house of the Venerable Lady (Kāmandakī)? Or, being alive, will she come here, or not? Regarding this matter, I am apprehensive; my heart is utterly agitated by doubt.

The meaning is that my mind has no certainty as to whether she has already gone there or whether she will arrive safely. The phrase "will she come? or "will she not come?"—in every instance, a doubt is raised through the use of an interrogative intonation (*kāku*).

Having determined some ill omen from the very agitation of his mind, he imagines the adverse turn of fate, saying "generally" (*prāyeṇa*); the sense is that while happiness is experienced for the most part, it is possible only rarely, for someone alone, and only as a result of an infinite heap of merit.

"Meeting with kinsmen, friends, and loved ones," and so forth: "kinsmen" refers to those related through one's mother and father; "friends" are companions; "loved ones" are husbands, wives, and the like. "Meeting" with them means dwelling together. This is a case of designating the effect by the name of its cause—the meaning being that it is the result [of such association]. This is the primary mode [of happiness], or rather, the cause. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), houses, fields, wealth, and the like are included. "Saukhya" means happiness (*sukha*); here, a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita-pratyaya*) is used in the sense of the base word itself.

"Unsteady like the flashing of lightning"—lightning (*saudāminī*) means "electricity"; thus, by describing the nature of the world as being as unstable as its flickering, the thought is revealed: "If even this condition of ours is subject to such instability, how can it be averted? Here, the figure of speech is *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle), because a particular instance is supported by a general statement.

By the phrase "as flickering as a flash of lightning," the poet—the Brahmā of literature, whose skill is intent upon unfolding the elaborate arrangement of aesthetic flavor (rasa)—also indicates the entrance of the yoginī named Saudāminī, who was previously introduced and enters as a character in the *viṣkambha* (interlude) of the following act according to the maxim that "one who has not been indicated [previously] may not enter. Thus, all is most auspicious. //14//
By the grace of Pūrṇajyotis, Pūrṇasarasvatī has thus composed this exposition of the contents of the eighth act of the *Mālatīmādhava*.
//The Eighth Act//
//Now begins the ninth act.//
Now, he introduces the Yoginī, who is instrumental for the *nirvahaṇa* juncture, as a supporting character (*viṣkambha-pātra*),

[according to the definition]: "That is the *nirvahaṇa* where the elements beginning with the *mukha*, containing the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and scattered according to their respective places, are brought together toward the final purpose."

Thus [ends the previous section]. Its fourteen constituent parts (aṅgas) are the twilight rites (saṃdhyā) and so forth. Then enters Saudāminī. "I am this Saudāminī. Here, *asmi* is an indeclinable synonymous with the word *aham* (I), as seen in such usages as "I speak to you, O learned ones" (*tvāmasmi vacmi viduṣām*). The mention of her name, Saudāminī, is intended to indicate that, by virtue of her connection to Kāmandakī, she must necessarily perform the act of favoring Mālatī and Mādhava. The term *bhagavataḥ* is used as a respectful designation because he is a follower of the Supreme Lord and because the place is a field of spiritual attainment (*siddhikṣetra*). Alternatively, the genitive case in *bhagavataḥ* expresses the relationship with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).

From Śrīparvata, previously mentioned, [the statement] "Śrīparvata holds Kāpālikas" connects [to this context]. Therein, the sense is that Padmāvatī is unable to endure the sight of the familiar places—such as Madanodyāna and others—which were experienced in the company of her beloved; for the sight of them is as painful as salt rubbed upon a wound. [This is said] by the circle of friends, the group of kinsmen beginning with Makaranda.

*Bṛhaddroṇī* is the name of a certain region near Padmāvatī; the mountain situated there is *Bṛhaddroṇīśaila*. Its *kāntāra*—meaning a difficult forest, as Amarasimha states, "a *kāntāra* is a path that is hard to traverse"—is its entryway. The meaning is: having heard from the people about the entry into that place for the purpose of abandoning the body by means of leaping from a precipice (*bhṛgupatana*) and so forth, I am going toward the vicinity of Mādhava; that is, I am proceeding with him as my destination.

This establishes his singular preoccupation with beholding her. "Bho" follows common worldly usage and indicates astonishment. "Tathā" means in that manner; "utpatitā" means flown up to the very peak of the sky. "Yathā" means in such a way. "Eṣa" is used in its full sense as a demonstrative pronoun to indicate the act of pointing toward the specific location he intends to reach, and not merely toward the earth's surface, as that would exclude the possibility of reaching oceans, islands, and so forth.

A mountain (*giri*) refers to a great valley (*bṛhaddroṇī*), a rock (*śaila*), and so forth; a city (*nagara*) is Padmāvatī; a village (*grāma*) is a tax-exempt estate (*agrahāra*) situated near that [city]; rivers (*saritaḥ*) include the Pārā, Sindhu, Lavaṇā, and others; a forest (*araṇya*) refers to a great valley-forest (*bṛhaddroṇīvana*) and the like; "the account" (*vyatikara*) refers to the events concerning these. It is "encircled" (*parikṣipyate*), meaning it is swallowed up or encompassed like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand, as seen in such usage as "encircled by the stream of the Gaṅgā. By this, he indicates that because the desired account of Mādhava is included within that [vast expanse], its easy comprehension follows by the logic of *kaimutika* (how much more so).
He states the result of the circumambulation: "having looked behind. The word "behind" (*paścāt*) is used because he was moving forward with speed; it means having turned around and looked back.

Regarding "Padmāvatī," etc.: Padmāvatī is the city; *parikara* refers to the waist-band formed by the two rivers, Sindhu and Pārā, which have pure waters (*vimalavāryoh*), are vast (*viśālayoḥ*), and are wide-spreading (*vistṛtayoh*).
[The term *parikara*] may mean discernment (*vivekaḥ*), a waist-band (*paryasti*), or a retinue (*parivāra*).
"Even in the case of a firm binding of the limbs and at the commencement of a multitude," so says the *Vaijayantī*.

Under that pretext, [he beheld] the lofty, well-erected mansions; the rows of white palaces; the temples of the gods—shrines of deities such as Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha; the gate-towers (*gopura*) and city gates; the watchtowers known as *aṭṭālaka*; and various types of platforms (*mañca*).

According to the *Vaijayantī* lexicon: "A *saudha* is a white building made of lime (*sudhā*)," "a *gopura* is a city gate," and "an *aṭṭālaka*, *aṭṭa*, or *kṣoma* is a watchtower. Through their collision—that is, by being struck together with a firm impact—they were split and shattered; thus, having been released from their original positions and cast down on all sides, they reached the atmosphere, the sky.

Although space (*ākāśa*) is an all-pervading substance and is thus in contact with every material object, here the word "intermediate space" (*antarikṣa*) refers to the sky visible from afar above, which is perceived by the ignorant through the superimposition of qualities such as surface-dirtiness. Otherwise, the mention of its height would be redundant and the description would be purposeless, as in:
"And Raghu spoke to him—who was touching the sky, radiant, and of noble complexion—with words that touched the heavens."

This is because of such usage [in literature]. Purity (*vimalavāritva*) and vastness (*viśālatva*) are the grounds for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), as seen in usages such as "because of the sky's clarity and expansiveness" and "like the autumnal vault of heaven dissolved. Furthermore, the non-perception of the upper atmosphere within the interior of the palace is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*). Here, the figure of speech is *sāpahnavotprekṣā* (fancy with concealment), since concealment is conveyed by the word *chala* ("under the guise of") and the fancy by the word *iva*. This is like the verse: "Where the Siprā shines as if laughing loudly with pearls lost under the guise of a mass of shimmering foam. //1//

Looking elsewhere, he says: "This very one," and so forth. The word *sā* (she) refers to what is well-known; *eṣā* (this) indicates its presence before him. *Lavaṇā* is a certain river, whose *lalitāḥ*—meaning beautiful—are the rows of waves (*ūrmipaṅkti*), that is, garlands of ripples. By this, the state of its waters being tossed by the onset of a gale is illuminated. The reason for this is: *abhrāgame*, at the time of the arrival of clouds (*abhrāṇi*), meaning at the commencement of the rainy season (*prāvṛṭ*). By this, the commencement of the rainy season immediately following what was previously introduced is indicated, as in: "The quarters of the sky become dark with banks of clouds (*kādambinī*)."

This is for the purpose of connecting what is about to be said. It is to produce joy for the *janapada*—the people of the realm; for the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "The word *janapada* refers to a country or its people. The form *pramadāya* is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) according to Pāṇini 3.3.68: "*pramada-sammadau harṣe*" (the words *pramada* and *sammada* are used in the sense of joy).

The dative case is used according to Pāṇini 2.3.14: "*kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi sthāninaḥ*" (the fourth case is used for the object of a verb whose subordinate word [upapada] expresses purpose). He states the reason for this: "The surrounding forest circles near which are frequented by those carrying offerings of fresh *ulapa* grass, dear to pregnant cows. "Pregnant cows" (*gavāṃ garbhiṇyaḥ*) means those possessing embryos; according to the rule "*catuṣpādo garbhiṇyā*" (Pāṇini 2.1.71), the compound is formed with the word *garbhiṇī*.

(2-1-71) Thus, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. For them, the fresh *ulapa* grasses—meaning young blades of *darbha* grass—are dear because they serve as the longings of pregnancy (*garbhadauhṛda*). According to the *Vaijayantī*, "the *ulūka* grass is the *tūlaba* [variant: *ulapa*] *darbha*. The mention of "fresh *ulapa*" is due to their being succulent and tender. Their "garland" is the line of growth that has sprouted along the two marshy banks; those [women] whose nature it is to bear that [line] are referred to. [This is according to the rule: "In the case of *iṣṭakā*, *iṣīkā*, and *mālā*, [the final vowel is short] before *cita*, *tūla*, and *bhārin* respectively."

(6-3-65) Thus, there is a short vowel [by rule]. Because they are associated with the proper seasons (*ṛtu*), the surrounding forest groves—the lines of woods in the vicinity—are to be resorted to by the playful; for, due to the absence of agitation caused by the falling of rain during the summer heat, and because they are neither too cold nor too hot, they are to be attended by those seeking pleasure. By the phrase "surrounding forest groves" (*upakaṇṭhavipināvalayaḥ*), which refers to the rows of nearby forests, their status as a cause of delight for the people is indicated: because they suggest future abundance through the nourishing of pregnant cows, and because they are pleasant to enjoy at that very time. Here, the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state), or perhaps *udātta* (the description of a magnificent object). //2//

He is renowned for his purifying nature; the word "Bhagavatī" is used as a term of reverence because she is a great river. "Of the Sindhu" refers to the one currently under discussion, the Sindhu-pārā. "Having rent the subterranean realm" means having playfully shattered the surface of the earth upon her descent. A "prapāta" is a place of falling, specifically the lower region where a mountain from which she originates descends, as in the expression "the young grass grown at the edge of the Ganges' waterfall."

He describes the world-terrifying nature of the sound of the falling water’s velocity with the verse beginning "yatratya" and so forth: *yatratyaḥ* means "arising in which region"; [the suffix] *tyap* is used here according to the rule *amehakvatāsitrebhya eva*. *Tumuladhvaniḥ* means a tumultuous, confused noise; *ambugarbhatayā* means because of containing water within; *gambhīram* means deep or more weighty; *nūtanasya* means of a new; *ghanasya* means of a cloud; *stanitam* means its thundering or roar; like that, it is *pracaṇḍaḥ*, meaning fierce or cruel.

Because it is pervaded by the form of echoes within the caves of the nearby mountains due to the expansion [of sound] from the mountain thickets at the horizon, and because of the throat-thundering—the roar from the throat—of Heramba, the elephant-faced one; of that throat-thundering...

Or rather, *pratimānam* means similarity (*sāmyam*). Halāyudha states: "A *pratimāna* is a likeness (*pratikṛti*) or a reflection (*praticchāya*). Here, by taking the throat-thunders of the Lord Gaṇapati as he engages in the fury of battle with the Asuras and other such activities as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), it is suggested that even the sound of the falls of great rivers fills the cavities of the three worlds and serves as the means for accomplishing all auspiciousness. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is Simile (*upamā*). //3//

"Śarja is the aśvakarṇa tree," and "śarala is pūtikāṣṭha," according to the *Vaijayantī*. These forest lands—dense and thick with these many trees and other wild ones, fragrant with ripe *mālūra* fruits (or perhaps with blooming *bilva* flowers), and scented by the ripe *bilva* fruits—are reminiscent of [those pastures], bringing them to mind. "In the case of *bilva*, the terms *śāṇḍilya*, *śailūṣa*, *mālūra*, and *śrīphala* are used," says Amara. These forest regions evoke memories.

[He saw] those [mountains] whose broad and extensive slopes were made resonant by the Godāvarī river—a river whose flow of sound was deep, heavy, and faltering, its roar thickened by echoes as it resounded within the dense, great, and weighty bower-thickets where the darkness was enveloped and the gloom had vanished; and whose current was obstructed in its exit by the impact against the massive rocks on its rugged banks.

The Southern Forest (Dakṣiṇāraṇya) refers to the Daṇḍaka forest because it is situated in the southern region of the Vindhya mountains; for it is well known from works such as the *Kādambarī* that the Daṇḍaka forest is connected to the Vindhya wilderness, as in the passage:
"The rows of cranes on the Godāvarī and Oṣṭha rivers seem to rise up into the sky to meet you."

Because the Godāvarī is established as being connected to the Daṇḍaka forest by such phrases as "here along the Godāvarī" (*atrānugodam*), [the poet] refers to the mountains associated with it: Vindhya, Mālyavān, and Ṛśyamūka. [He also mentions] "purified by the confluence of the Madhumatī and the Sindhu": the Madhumatī is a certain river, while the Sindhu is the one under discussion; their "confluence" (*sambheda*) is the place where they meet, like Prayāga, and [the location] is "purified" (*pāvana*), meaning it is a cause of sanctity.

By the phrase "the husband of Bhavānī, the beloved of Pārvatī," the fact that this sacred field bestows both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*) is illuminated through its association with the Goddess, the mother of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*). As for what has been stated by some—that in the term *bhavānīpati* there is the implication of another husband—that is an unconsidered assertion;
for [the scripture states]: "Śivā, Bhavānī, Rudrāṇī, Śarvāṇī, Sarvamaṅgalā."

Thus, because [the term] is listed by the lexicographers (*naighaṇṭukas*) as a proper name (*saṃjñā*) through a combination of etymological derivation and conventional usage—just like words such as *Umā* and *Gaurī*; because it has been employed hundreds of times in various places by great poets; and because there would otherwise be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), as in the verse: "At the commencement of the dance, Bhavānī, her devotion witnessed, [looked on] with eyes stilled and free from agitation, as she desired the wet elephant-hide for Hara, the Lord of Creatures. For indeed, [it is derived as] "the wife of Bhava," according to the rule: "Indra, Varuṇa, Bhava, Śarva... [etc.].

By the rule *ityādi-sūtreṇa* (Pāṇini 4.1.49), the suffix *ānuk* is applied, and by the rule *puṃyogādākhyāyām* (5.1.48), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added, thereby establishing the word *bhavānī*. Consequently, even in the expression *bhavānyā dṛṣṭabhaktiḥ paśupateḥ*, because the perception of another husband is unavoidable, one would have to say *bhavasya* [instead of *paśupateḥ*]; thus, there follows an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), as it would lead to the breakdown of such usages as *bhaginīpatiḥ* ("sister's husband") and *duhituḥ patiḥ* ("daughter's husband").

In the expression "the husband of Bhavānī," since the understanding that "Bhava himself is the husband of Bhava’s wife" is unimpeded through its natural consistency, the specific recollection of meaning based on *saṃyoga* (association) and other factors—which you yourself have asserted—would result in futility. For if one were to say "the lover of Bhavānī," there would indeed be the perception of another husband; however, enough of this excessive elaboration. Regarding the *liṅga* (phallic emblem) which, being non-human (*apauruṣeya*) and having manifested itself spontaneously for the sake of favoring devotees, possesses installation and presence:
"Even those located in forests, mountains, rivers, oceans, sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*), and holy fields..."
"Those for whom supreme perfection is attained through sight, touch, and worship—know them to be self-manifested *liṅgas* (*svayambhuliṅga*), in which Śiva is eternally present.
Thus it is stated in the *Siddhāntasāra*. It is called "Suvarṇabindu" (The Golden Drop) because of its golden color and its subtlety.
"Furthermore, the self-manifested lingas (svayambhuliṅga) are dilapidated, emaciated,
short, or exceedingly long, and they possess various colors and forms."
Since it is stated right there [in that very work]: "It is narrated" (*ākhyāyate*) means it is proclaimed by those who know the ancient lore.
In order to ensure the completion of the task at hand—the duty toward his kinsmen—without obstacles, he praises the Supreme Lord with a salutation in an Āryā verse:
"For the neglect of honoring those worthy of honor obstructs one's spiritual welfare."
Because of this statement: "having prostrated" means having become humble through speech, mind, and body.

"Victory! and so forth—O Lord, O locus of the collection of activities such as playing (*krīḍā*) and others whose meaning is "to sport"! He explains that very point: "O Creator of the Worlds! (meaning, O bestower of existence upon the worlds); for the implication is that what is non-existent is merely imagined within the nature of the Existent. "O Blessed One!"—by this phrase, "possessing qualities such as unsurpassed knowledge and sovereignty," the cause for being the Creator of the Worlds is stated, namely, omniscience and the like.

O Bestower of all boons (*akhilavarada*)! "Boons" (*varāḥ*) are those things which are chosen or prayed for, namely the human goals (*puruṣārthas*). He whose nature it is to grant all—that is, the entirety of *dharma*, *artha*, *kāma*, and *mokṣa*—is so described. By this, it is stated that he is the benefactor of all through his two forms, both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*). The reason for this is: "O Treasure of the Vedas" (*nigamanidhe*). O You who are the repository of the Vedas (*nigamas*), the meaning of the Vedas being Your own command! For the grace of the Supreme Lord and His state as the bestower of boons arise from the performance of the meaning of the Vedas, which constitute His own command. As it is said: "By a person possessing the conduct of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, is propitiated."

"There is no other path that brings him satisfaction," and from such Smṛti texts as, "The Veda alone is the supreme means for attaining the highest good for the twice-born. O Rucira! O you who are captivating with your playful form! O Candraśekhara!—he whose crest-jewel (śekhara) or garland (āpīḍa) is the moon (candra).

"O Madanāntaka! and "O destroyer of Kāma with the fire of Your eye"—by these two [epithets], the fact that You are the cause of the nourishment and drying up of the world through the fire and moon, which are Your own abodes, is illuminated, as well as Your intentness upon favoring and restraining those who are devoted and non-devoted respectively. "O Ādiguru! O Teacher of all sciences even to Brahmā and the others"—by this, the Śruti passage beginning with "He who first creates Brahmā," as well as [the verse]:
"Of these eighteen sciences, whose paths are diverse... [is cited].
"He is the primordial creator, the poet, the manifest wielder of the trident"—thus says the Śruti;

and he [the author] reflects upon this Smṛti as well. By this, he suggests that [Śiva] is the cause of all worldly activity through his role as the proclaimer of the scriptures that set forth the two paths consisting of engagement and renunciation, and that he is worthy of worship by all the world. The use of the imperative mood (*loṭ*) in the prayer "Be victorious" (*jaya*) illuminates his state of being subservient to devotion; otherwise, it would be inappropriate and ineffective toward the Supreme Lord, who exists in a state of supreme excellence by his own nature. //4//

"This one is new," and so forth. According to Amara, "sānu, prastha, taṭa, and bhṛgu" all mean a mountain slope. In this place, the *kekā*—the cries of peacocks—which are emitted, set in motion, continuous, and uninterrupted by peahens (*mayūrī*), the females of the *śikhins*, who are made vocal (*mukharābhiḥ*) by the joy (*mada*) produced by the sight of the new clouds; according to Amara, "*kekā* is the voice of the peacock."

[The forest] is variegated with various colors by means of birds (śakuni); because birds possess various colors and because of their eager activity in building nests at the onset of the rains, it is characterized by trees (anokaha) which possess nests (nīḍa)—that is, bird-dwellings—wherein [the birds reside]; [and the mountain] whose body (varṣman) is glossy. "Varṣman" is not feminine; it refers to a beautiful form, a gentle being, or the measurement of the body.

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*: "The mountain Bṛhadoḍḍroṇī" is the hill situated in the region of Bṛhaddroṇī, which was previously introduced. It "bestows joy" (prītiṃ vitarati), meaning it grants it because it is suitable for beholding Mādhava when he is being sought after, and because of its loveliness. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state). //5//

He describes further with the words beginning "dadhati" and so on: "In this mountain, the roars of young bears—those who frequent the hollows (*kuhara*) of caves and are arrogant due to their youth—become heavy with resonance, amplified by echoes. *Styānam* means density or thickness; [this is derived] from the root *styai* (or *ṣṭyai*), meaning 'to congeal' or 'to sound,' with the suffix *lyuṭ*. *Ambūkṛtāni* means accompanied by sputtering (or, according to some, dug out due to the nature of that species)."

"The forest edges, where the weapons of the Kirātas have fallen in terror at the roars of full-grown bears dwelling in the caves," as Murāri has described. "Ambūkṛtam" means accompanied by spitting; thus says the *Vaijayantī*. "Śiśirakaṭukaṣāyaḥ": *śiśira* means cool; *anugra* means pungent (*kaṭu*); and *surabhi* indicates astringent (*kaṣāya*), which denotes a tannic taste. *Styāyate* means it becomes thick or dense. "Sallakī" refers to a particular kind of creeper; "the *sallakī*, however, is dear to elephants," according to Amara.

The fragrance of the exudation from the joints of the sprouts and shoots—broken by elephants for the sake of fodder and subsequently half-chewed and spat out in their midst due to their abundance—is [the scent] of the trickling sap. (Note: "Paruḥ," "parvaḥ," and "granthiḥ" are masculine terms for a joint. By means of these two sentences, he expresses both cruelty and loveliness. Here, the poetic figure is *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state). //6//

"How is it midday?"—this question, by expressing the sense of wonder that the passage of time was not noticed due to being preoccupied with the means of proof and the distraction of seeing various objects encountered on the road, highlights the state of astonishment. He establishes the fact that it is indeed midday: "For instance, now—" [beginning with] "the *kārṣmarya* tree," and so forth.
Regarding the term *kārṣmarya*: "The *gopabhadrā* is the *kārṣmarya*; the *kārṣmarī* is the *kṛṣṇavṛntikā*."

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*. From the *kārṣmarya* tree, which was resorted to in the forenoon, there is a thinning of its foliage during the rainy season because it is accustomed to the heat of summer; the sense is that its shade is sparse due to this. *Kṛtamāla* is the *āragvadha* tree: "The *āragvadha*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *śamyāka*, *caturaṅgula*, *ārevata*, *vyādhighāta*, *kṛtamāla*, and *suparṇaka* [are synonyms]."

Thus says Amara. The reason for this is: "with petals risen and sprouted on all sides. The *koyaṣṭika* is a bird called *śikhari*, which is a water-dweller; according to the *Vaijayantī*, "the *koyaṣṭi* and *śikhari* are synonyms. It "walks" (*ṭīkate*), meaning it goes there to alleviate the heat of the sun's rays, as it is said: "In the rainy season, the day heats intensely when the arrival of clouds is imminent. The root is *ṭīkṛ* (to go). [The phrase] "whose faces kiss the pods of the *aśmantaka* on the bank" refers to the waters, since a reservoir will be described later; thus, it refers to the *aśmantakas*, a specific type of tree known as *āmroṭa*, located on the shore.

"...*ślakṣṇapatraka* in the *śapharī* [fish]; *śikhī*, *indrāśmantaka*, *āmroṭā*..."—so says the *Vaijayantī*. *Śimbi* is a pod; those whose beaks hold (*cumbati*) it—that is, grasp it—subsequently for the purpose of eating.

"Śimbikā, mudga, maṅgalya, vanamudga, and kuṣṭhaka," so says Vāhaṭa. They run swiftly, they go; *apaḥ* refers to the waters of rivers and the like; *pūrṇikās* are a species of bird. With *dātyūhas*, i.e., *kālakaṇṭhas*; for "the *dātyūha* is the *kālakaṇṭhaka*," according to the *Vaijayantī*. Of the *timiśa*: "... ... ... *atimuktaka* is [another name] for *nemīya*."

"Citrakṛt, timiśa, and nemī... [so states] the *Vaijayantī*. "Koṭaravat" means characterized by a large cavity; "niṣkuṭa" and "koṭara" are not feminine, according to the *Vaijayantī*. "Skandha" refers to the place where branches grow;
"prakāṇḍa" and "skandha" are not feminine, and denote the part of a tree from the root up to the branches.

Thus says Amara. "Having settled" (*nilīya*) means having embraced, that is, having hidden oneself from the rays of the sun. The word "sthitam" is used in the sense of a state (*bhāve*), meaning a cessation of movement has been effected. "Of the pigeon whose nest is in the creeper"—after its cooing (*kūjitam anu*), either following the sound or making it its object; for it is their nature to coo at midday. They "cry out," that is, they coo or make noise, situated below in the lower part.
"A *pratāninī* is a creeper (*latā*); it is also called *vīrut*, *gulminī*, or *ulapa*."
Thus says Amara: "The *pārāvata*, the *kalarava*, and the *kapota* are its varieties. "...
... ... In the category of *hārīta* are the *madgu*, the *kāraṇḍava*, the *plava*, the *tittiri*, the *kukkuṭa*, the *lāva*... [and so forth].
And thus says Amara. //7//

"Let it be so"—the *loṭ* suffix here denotes permission (*kāmacārakaraṇe*). The sense is: "What does it matter to us regarding the wretchedness of the times? He states the reason for this: "yathā," meaning "properly" or "well," refers to the subject at hand (*prakṛtam artham*), namely, that which consists of consolation and so forth through the narration of Mālatī’s story. The transition is: "So be it;

having searched for Mādhava and Makaranda, I shall accomplish what has been proposed. Because the purpose of the interlude (*viṣkambhaka*)—the arrival of the seeds of the resumed plot—is accomplished, he concludes it with the stage direction "she exits," thus ending the interlude.
[Thus ends the Interlude.]

Now, beginning the *aṅka*, he describes the entrance of Mādhava, who was previously indicated by the *viṣkambhaka* as having entered the Bṛhaddroṇī mountain forest together with Makaranda: "Then," and so forth. "With compassion" means with sorrow.

Having reflected upon the particular state being experienced due to seeing the condition of his friend, he says: "Not where," and so forth. "Wherein" means in which [state] one does not experience the hope regarding Mālatī—thinking, "She will be seen today, tomorrow, or the day after"—[the word *na* functions here like *naśabda* and so on]. I obtain... [the rest of the sentence follows].

The sense is that this is because no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established for anyone. "Or does not abandon" (*rahayati na vā*) means that it does not let go; this is a certain conclusion regarding the opposite case. The meaning of "in the remainder" (*śeṣe*) is that this alone is the point of rest here. [He] enters—that is, plunges into—the dense darkness of the form of a swoon, a blinding gloom of delusion; as Amarasimha states: "In deep darkness, there is *andhatamasa*. Not performing—not employing—even some single [means], whether great or small, because it is beyond their reach.
As it is said: "Even without doing anything at all, one dispels sufferings through happiness."

Thus it is as stated in the *Uttararāmacarita*. This is a compound word (*samastapada*). The meaning is: "Just as animals, such as cows and the like, having fallen into a well or similar pit, revolve there experiencing suffering because they do not know the means of escape; so too [is this].
As it is said: "Others, such as beasts and the like, are renowned for being primarily composed of darkness (*tamaḥ*) and lacking knowledge."

"And they follow a wrong path, considering themselves wise despite being ignorant"—so says the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*. Furthermore, the Teacher [Vātsyāyana] has established in the *Nyāya-sūtra* (1.1.2) that "there is no distinction from beasts and the like" regarding the desire for pleasure, the wish to avoid pain, and the ignorance of the means thereto, as these are found even among beasts. The word "aho" expresses astonishment at the occurrence of something that was not even thought of, even in a dream.

The cause for this is the capriciousness of the Creator and the adversity of fate, and not due to any fault of human effort; we revolve in calamity and misfortune, turning in every direction, or rather, we remain in a state of whirling. With the word "these," the speaker clearly indicates the visible discoloration and other symptoms to the onlookers. Here, the poetic figures are *virodha* (contradiction) and *upamātiśayokti* (hyperbole by comparison). //8//
Turning toward his beloved in the sky, he said: "Alas, my dear! Where are you? In what place do you dwell?"

"Since the true nature [of the matter] was unknown—that is, since the ultimate reason for her departure was not understood—it was, for that very reason, most wonderful and exceedingly marvelous; such is the adverbial phrase *yathā tathā*. 'Suddenly' (*jhaṭiti*) means quickly, without time being allowed for a remedy. 'She has departed from this place' (*apasṛtā*) means she has fled immediately. 'In what manner? (*katham*). 'Nanu' is used as an interrogative particle. 'O merciless one! (*akarune*), meaning devoid of compassion! 'Be gracious' (*prasīda*) means show mercy; 'show honor' (*sambhāvaya*) means treat her with respect, because the mere sight of you constitutes the highest form of honor."

Now he establishes his own status as an object of compassion with the words "priyamādhave" and so forth. By saying "Mādhava is dear to her," he highlights that your love for me is indeed well-known to the world. Why? For what purpose? [The word] "mayi" (in me) is revealed through a suggestion (*dhvani*) in which the literal meaning is transferred to another sense, implying: "in me, who have you as my sole refuge and am innocent. "Avatsalā" means one who lacks affection; this is an inference-based statement regarding her failure to grant an audience. He further substantiates the fact that Mādhava is indeed dear to her with the words "nanu saṃvāde" (surely in their conversation).

The particle *eva* is displaced [in the sentence]. The connection is "I am that very same person. "Anandayat" means he made [it] prosperous. "Purā" means in former times; by saying "himself," independent of father and others, he suggests the quality of unfeigned affection. "Āgṛhītakamanīyakaṅkaṇaḥ" means one by whom a beautiful, lovely bracelet—the marriage token—has been accepted; the meaning is: in the garden of Kāmandakī’s vihāra. "Mūrtimān mahotsavaḥ" means a great festival, a supreme celebration, in embodied form.

By the word "great festival" (mahotsava), its effect—happiness—is indicated through metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā). Through the poetic fancy (utprekṣā), it is revealed that the hand is the object of long-cherished desire and the cause of supreme bliss. This is the figure of speech known as utprekṣā. //9//

He says that it is not only passion, but gratitude as well that agitates him: "Of such an extent" (*tāvataḥ*), meaning of that same measure as the [love] of Mālatī. By the word "that" (*tat-*) in the phrase "gone to me" (*mad-gata*), the emotional state (*anubhāva*) is revealed. "Possibility" (*sambhava*) means arising or origin.

It has been said; now [the author] establishes her affection [for him] with the verse beginning "sarasam," etc. "Sarasam" means fresh and unfading; "like that" refers to [her] emaciated [limbs], by which emaciation weakness is indicated. "The great fever of the bodiless one" (anaṅga-mahājvara) is the great torment produced by desire (kāma). "Uninterruptedly distressing" (aviratonmāthī) means having the nature of incessantly agitating. "Terrible at every moment" (pratikṣaṇadāruṇaḥ) means cruel because it increases moment by moment and because it generates delusion and other such states. "Endured" (soḍhaḥ) means experienced; the meaning is: "by the hope of attaining me."

The meaning is that, consequently, the shattering of her hopes occurred in the context of the granting of the Nandana grove. Regarding the phrase "his very life-breaths": since everything is dearer than one's own life-breaths, he gave even those; by saying "like a blade of grass," he indicates the total absence of compassion even for them. "His mind was restrained" means it was fixed within his heart, rather than being merely feigned through a display of words. Let all that which has been said rest; what else could there be beyond this that would be more significant than this task?

The construction of the sentence is as follows: "What more [can be said] than this fact—that the audacity of offering tribute was carried out and executed while great kinsmen such as his father were present nearby, without their consent? The word *yat* (that) refers back to the entire meaning of the preceding clause. //10//

Again, he establishes her extreme passion for him by means of another method, beginning with the words "mayi" and so forth: "In me," that is, regarding me; "because her hope was especially destroyed" means because her hope had utterly perished due to the absence of any expectation toward me; "in the rite of marriage," that is, on the occasion of Nandana’s wedding proposal; "with impaired faculties" means those whose external and internal senses (indriyas) were impaired and rendered subject to another's will; "distressed by the pain of the severing of the vital points" (*marmaccheda*): the vital points (*marmas*) are the specific locations where the life-breath (*prāṇavāyu*) pulsates most intensely; the pain arising from their being split asunder—by that [she was distressed].

The word *vyathā* (distress) signifies *vedanā* (sensation/pain), and through the phrase "as if by those who are helpless," the internal nature and the absolute character of suffering are revealed. By "wailings" (*ākrandaiḥ*), which are accompanied by the shedding of tears, the state of having impaired faculties (*vikalakaraṇatva*)—which is a property of the agent—is expressed as the effect, just as in the expression "milk burns. Alternatively, the word *vidhura* here denotes the state of being distressed (*vaidhurya*); since words such as *dhīra*, *gabhīra*, and *vidhura* function to denote both the quality and the possessor of the quality, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).

The phrase "as if by the causes consisting of the distress of her agitation" is a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*). In the word *ruditaiḥ* ("by weeping"), the instrumental case is used in the sense of an instrument. She "displayed"—that is, she spread throughout the world—her "intent of death," which was prompted by affection and performed out of love.

"I too"—the word "too" (*api*) here implies a contradiction—was one who, by the thought that I had fulfilled my purpose through the sight of you, was worthy of joy alone; yet I became one whose joy was rippled with pain, meaning that waves of suffering arose within it, making it variegated at intervals. Joy (*sammada*) is happiness; the distinction is that there was pain due to his compassion and the apprehension of some misfortune, while there was joy because he complied with my own desire.

"Indeed, do you remember?"—this indicates that this entire sequence of events took place with you as the witness within the inner sanctum of the city deity's temple. In these two verses, there is the figure of speech *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), because through the description of the effect, the cause—the intensity of affection—is revealed. //11//

Reflecting upon this state that exists in contradiction [to his previous condition], he says: "Aho" expresses wonder; "nu" introduces a question; "bho," having addressed the world in the sky, he speaks. "The heart breaks," and so forth: it "breaks" (dalati), meaning it shatters due to intense inner agitation and the excess of profound suffering. The particle "tu" indicates a distinction; it does not split into two parts—that is, though torn asunder in both ways, it does not fall apart. "Vikala" means helpless, like one belonging to another; "kāya" means the body; "moha" means a swoon characterized by the inability to discern what ought and ought not to be done; "vrajati" means it goes toward that state. The particle "tu" is to be carried over into all three clauses.

By stating that she does not abandon the experience of painful sensation (*vedanā*), he indicates a certain degree of heightened awareness; otherwise, since delusion (*moha*) consists in the obstruction of the functions of all the sense organs, it would necessarily exclude the experience of pleasure and pain. As it is said: "With her senses' activity paralyzed by a delusion born of intense affliction, Rati—for a moment—seemed as if she had received a favor, for she remained unaware of her husband’s calamity."

Because of this statement: the saying "the body does not release delusion" is due to the manifestation of the fruit of delusion—namely, physical emaciation—upon the body, which serves as the immediate substratum for the mind; for the Veda establishes that delusion belongs to the mind in the passage, "Sorrow and delusion are of the mind. It "kindles," meaning it makes radiant, the *tanūm*, i.e., the body (this word *tanū* ends in the vowel *ū*); "internal burning" refers to an internal fever. "Reduced to ashes" means entirely turned to ash, according to the rule *vibhāṣā sāti kārtsnye*.

(5-4-52) Thus, the suffix *sāti* is used here, but not the root *kṛ*. He states the reason for all this: "It strikes" (*praharati*) means it afflicts; "it cuts the vital points" (*marmacchedī*) means it destroys life and the breaths, but it does not "cut" (*kṛntati*) or sever them. Even though [the thunderbolt] possesses the power to assist by tearing the heart asunder, releasing the body's pain, reducing the heat to ashes, and severing life according to destiny, there is no actual assistance rendered; thus, envy toward those [functions] is expressed. Here, the figure of speech is *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation) with an unstated cause, because even when the full collection of causes such as splitting and so forth is present, the effects such as being torn asunder do not occur.
Because it is stated in the *Ṛtupāda*. //12//

With the intention of offering consolation and diversion, he says: "Unrestrained" means without obstruction, the sense being that there is no remedy; the expression "as if fate" is a *sahokti* (simultaneous comparison), meaning that just as fate burns us, so too does the sun, Vivasvat, burn along with it. The word "dāruṇaḥ" (fierce) is used because it occurs at midday during the onset of the rainy season. By this, he connects with the midday indicated by the *viṣkambhaka*. With the gesture "this," he indicates the inability to endure any other time.

"Padmasarasaḥ" refers to a reservoir of water distinguished by its lotuses; this is a compound formed according to the principle of "Śākapārthiva" (where the middle term is omitted). "Parisare" means, by implication, in the shade of the trees on the bank. The word "hi" indicates a reason. Regarding the phrase beginning with "unnāla": because the water has been dried up by the summer heat, the stalks have emerged above the water—as in the expression "the lotus with its stalk raised high in the palace pond. "Bālakamalākarasya" refers to a cluster of lotuses that is tender and not yet matured. Although the word *ākara* denotes a place of origin, here it figuratively signifies a multitude.

"Victorious is the Sun, who causes the laughter of the lotus-ponds by awakening their fragrance with the Maruts!"—from such usage as this, [it follows that] he is a friend (*bandhu*) to the thick (*māṃsala*, i.e., abundant) scent due to its *saṃvalana* (mingling), which is a mixing caused by the flow (*niṣyanda*) or stream belonging to the nectar (*makaranda*). He will cause [me], who am seized by delusion—the word "me" being understood—to breathe, that is, to take heart.

[The phrase] "puraḥ agre parivartamānaiḥ paritaḥ prasaradbhiḥ" means "moving in front and spreading all around"; alternatively, the analysis of the reading as "puraḥ prācyāṃ diśi parivartamānaḥ—parito vījamānaḥ" (moving in the eastern direction in front and fanning [the air] all around) signifies that which comes from the east, indicating the onset of the rainy season. "Kallola" refers to great waves. "Śīkara" denotes droplets of water; as Amara states: "śīkaro'mbukaṇāḥ smṛtāḥ" (śīkara is known as droplets of water). The word "tuṣāra" also denotes droplets, as seen in such usage as "vṛttastuṣārairgirinirjharāṇām" (surrounded by the droplets of mountain torrents).

In this context, the distinction is that large droplets are *śīkara*s, while fine ones are *tuṣāra*s. It is dull and cold. Here, the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic causality), because the smelling of the cool fragrance and the touch of the water droplets—which are the causes of life—are presented as the actual entities [of the cause]. The *svabhāvokti* (description of nature) is, however, quite evident. //13//
"Let it be"—this much has been done as a means of consolation. "In this manner," that is, first of all; "I shall distract," meaning I shall cause [her] mind to turn elsewhere.
"In this," and so forth—in this lotus-lake.
"And this royal swan, subsisting on milk, with its red feet and beak..."
"Those Dhārtarāṣṭra geese have dark eyes like jasmine; [the others] are those with eyes other than white," according to the *Vaijayantī*.
[The compound describes] those [lakes] in which there are white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*)—white water-lilies—with their broad stalks quivering and trembling, shaken by the wings of the Mallikākṣa geese.

The meaning is as follows: "In the interval between the falling and the rising of the tears"—that is, between the falling (the trickling down) of the tear-water that first appeared in the eyes and the subsequent rising (the future emergence) of that which is about to appear; at that intermediate time, because the eyes possess the power of vision, whereas in the preceding and succeeding moments they are obscured by the vapor. The phrase "possessing unseparated splendor" (*avirahitaśriyaḥ*)—meaning their beauty is not distinct [from one another]—is the reason for this observation. "Divisions" (*vibhāgāḥ*) refers to specific regions.
This is the *udātta* (magnificent) ornament, due to the description of a thing endowed with prosperity. //14//
Because that statement is intended to point out the object of stimulation (*uddīpanavastu*), on the contrary, it means "with agitation," that is, accompanied by mental disturbance.

"Non-comprehension" (*apratipatti*) means either not esteeming the meaning spoken by me or failing to follow it up. "Empty-hearted" (*śūnyamahṛdayam*) means not having any intention whatsoever. "Elsewhere" (*anyataḥ*) means in another place. "Sighing" (*niśvasya*) is an expression of the outward manifestation (*anubhāva*) of compassion. Desiring to distract him again, he says: "With the *vānīra*... and so forth. "With *vānīra* blossoms" means with the flowers of the reed-plant (*vetasa*).

"Śīta, abhrapuṣpa, vānīra, vañcula, vetasa, and ratha [are synonyms for the cane tree]," according to the *Vaijayantī*. Because the groves (*nikuñja*) and rivers are wild, the water—their streams being concealed by forest-creeper arbors—has a "clinging scent," meaning it is infused with fragrance; this is the sense. The water exists [thus], as is understood from the context. On the peripheries—that is, on those riverbanks—are *yūthikā* flowers, which are specific varieties of jasmine blossoms.

"Revatī is the species [of jasmine] among *mālatī*s, and *manojjvalā* is that of *yūthikā*"—thus says the *Vaijayantī*. "In the feminine, *sumanasaḥ* means flower"—thus says Amara. *Ujjṛmbhita* means blossomed; here the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used in the sense of the action itself. *Jālakaiḥ* means by clusters or by buds. "A *jāla* is a *jālaka*; a *kalikā* and a *koraka* [are synonyms]"—thus says the *Vaijayantī*. *Unmīlat-kuṭaca-prahāsiṣu*: in those [trees] possessing the nature of laughing intensely through whiteness, due to their blossoming *kuṭaca* flowers. "The *kuṭaca* is the *girimallikā*"—thus says Amara.

"In the regions to the east of here," that is, resting upon and relying on the ridges—the peaks—of this mountain; according to Amarasimha, "snu, prastha, and snu are masculine or neuter. The meaning is: scattered upon the slopes for the sake of rest, due to the exhaustion from carrying an excessive burden of water.

The mention of the *śikhaṇḍins* (peacocks) is for the purpose of describing their extreme beauty through the mass of their circular tail-feathers during the performance of their dance (*tāṇḍava*). The specific term "peacock" (*mayūra*) is not used because of the rule: "When the qualifier alone is employed, the qualified object is understood. When the peacocks begin their wild dance out of joy—like actors who have entered the stage—they are further "canopied" (*vitānāyyate*) by means of canopies (*vitāna*) being tied above them, as if by various garments called "compassion" (*dayā*). [Note: The suffix *kyaṣ* is used here, resulting in the form *vitānāyyate*.
Here, the poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāras*) are *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state), *upamopakrama* (simile-based suggestion), and *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). //15//

"Jṛmbhājarjara," and so forth—*jṛmbhā* means yawning or blossoming; by that [blossoming], the *jarjarāṇām* (withered) *ḍimbānām* (buds), which have their petals falling away, possess a *ḍambareṇa* (excess of splendor). According to the *Vaijayantī*, "ḍimba" refers to the spleen or the egg of a bird (*khagāṇḍa*). Here, due to the similarity with the egg of a bird, the term is used metaphorically for a bud, just as the word *gola* is used in expressions such as "having the shape of a kadamba-bud. Alternatively, the reading may be *ḍimbha*.

By the word *ḍimbha*, which denotes a child, the flower bud (*mukula*) is indicated. The quarters—the directions—are the expanses of the mountain ranges, characterized by dense beauty (*ghanaśrīmantaḥ*), meaning distinguished by thick splendor, wherein the *kadamba* flowers abound. They are dark-hued like a bank of clouds (*kādambinīśyāmalāḥ*), for Amara states that "a *kādambinī* is a mass of clouds. They possess lovely *ketaka* flowers and sprouting *kandala* shoots; that is, they have the nature of bearing lovely *ketaka* blossoms and *kandala* buds that are breaking forth.

"Anūpa is that which abounds in water; kaccha is a similar term," according to Amara. *Kacchas* are the lands adjacent to the banks. "Smiling with the blossoms of *silindhra* and *lodhra* flowers whose fragrance has become manifest": they are characterized by the laughter (the blossoming) of the flowers of *silindhra* and *lodhra*, which have appeared with their full perfume. Because these flowers are naturally pale-red and white, there is a resemblance to the mingling radiance of lips and teeth. *Silindhra* and *lodhra* are specific types of trees; however, the word *silindhra* does not refer here to the tuberous root of the earth (*bhūkanda*). As it is said: "The *alinī* [forest] delighted in the *silindhra* trees, which were as beautiful as evening lamps glowing with a pale-red hue."

This is because the *pāṭala* flower is established as having a pale-red color (*pāṭalavarṇa*) and an abundance of fragrance (*parimalatva-bahulatva*) in the usages of great poets, such as in the passage beginning with "adhipurandhri silindhrasugandhibhiḥ. Furthermore, in the *Vaijayantī* lexicon, that very same [flower] is called *silindhra* in the entry "chatrākaśca silindhraśca," since words may have multiple meanings.
