According to the *Vaijayantī*, "the white *lodhra* is the *mahālodhra* and the *śambara*. The word *tati* means expansion (*vistāra*). The verb "it exists" (*bhavati*) should be supplied to each sentence. Here, the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is *svabhāvokti* (description of nature), because the natural state of the *vānīra* shoots and other things during the rainy season is described. //16//

Then, having entered another state that is beyond the scope of being interrupted by his intended purpose, he says: "Friend, I see. The meaning is that the perception of things present before one is necessarily inevitable. But—"the word *kintu* serves to exclude the previous position"—they are difficult to behold (*durālokāḥ*), meaning impossible to look upon. The reason for this is: "delightful" (*ramaṇīyāḥ*), meaning more beautiful than their former state, because of the excellence of beauty accumulated at the onset of the rainy season. The implication is: "Is it then a fault in these delightful things, or rather a lack of knowledge regarding their virtues? as in: "Those very things which were delightful when I was with her, become un-delightful to me when I am without her."

Thus it is as stated in the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*. Therefore, the following is a reflection (*vitarka*): "I do not know what this thing is—the fact that those who are now beautiful are difficult to behold—and what its cause is. Having determined the matter he was considering, he says: "What else?"—meaning, what other cause could there be besides that which is about to be described?
He states that very cause: "With blossoming *arjuna* trees," and so forth; [that is,] with blooming *arjuna* (*kakubha*) and *sarja* (*aśvakarṇa*) trees.

"nadīsarjo vīrataruḥ indradruḥ kakubho'rjunaḥ" (Amara), "sarjo'śvakarṇaḥ" (Vaijayantī). Of the easternly gale—meaning a wind blowing from the east, the direction in front—that has been scented (made fragrant) and is blowing (fanning); of the gale (jhaṃjhāvāta)—defined by the Vaijayantī as "a gale accompanied by rain"—by its swaying (preṅkhola), that is, its shaking; [the trees] stumbled, because the activity of the clouds is dependent upon the winds.

"Agitated" and "smooth like fragments of sapphire"—by this simile, their quality of being distinguished by a non-rough, deep blue color is revealed; [the season] in which there are rows of clouds, that is, garlands of clouds. [The air is] fragrant, distinguished by scents that satisfy the sense of smell, because of the earth—the ground—sprinkled with showers, washed by the downpours of rain; for it is well known that when the earth, scorched by the heat of summer, is first moistened by the droplets from the clouds, it emits a fragrance, as in the verse: "And the scent of ponds struck by showers..."

By such expressions as "fragrant from the immediate turning up of the furrows," they have arrived; that is, they have come. They are well known for being the snatchers of the lives of those separated from their lovers. These [days], now being manifested by their own specific characteristics, are spoken of as parts because time—which is an all-pervading, eternal substance and the unique cause of notions such as "long ago" and so forth—is stable as a whole, whereas its parts, namely the specific days, are subject to coming and going.

"Carrying the splendor resulting from the transition between the departure and arrival of heat and water": that is, the departure (*vigama*) of "heat" (*gharma*), meaning the summer season (*grīṣmakāla*), and the arrival or descent (*avatāra*) of "water" (*ambhas*), meaning the rainy season; the "transition" (*vyatikara*) is the junction (*sandhi*) between these two, and they possess the beauty (*śrī*) or splendor arising from that. Alternatively, because the unbearable state produced by the junction of the seasons consists of cold and heat occurring alternately as rain and sun, there is a beauty characterized by enjoyability through the transition between the departure and arrival of "heat-water," which is sweat-water.
The meaning is "carrying that. Here, the poetic figures (alaṅkāras) are *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state) and *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence). //17//

Her fortitude being clouded by the intensification of the excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*), she remembers and says, beginning with "taruṇa... and so forth. A *tamāla* tree that is very young (*taruṇatamāla*) is a *tamāla* tree with a glossy color due to its youth; like that, [the clouds] are blue, dense, and continuous, rising up but not [excessively] high. By this, the commencement of various activities and their persistence for a long time over the surface are illuminated—[this refers to] those in which the water-bearing clouds (*ambudhara*) reside.

Shaken—that is, stirred and scattered—by the cool breeze released from the belly of the clouds in the winter season; [I would see] those [clouds] in which there are dense droplets of fresh water recently rained down. "I might behold" (avalokayeyaṃ) expresses a wish or possibility (liṅ in the sense of *anavaklṛpti*).

The reason for this is: now, at this time made bitter by separation from you, [I would see] those possessing the "weapon of Hari"—Hari being Indra, his weapon (*heti*) being his bolt; that is, the rainbow—or else the thunderbolt (*vajra*), because even its glare is as difficult for one separated from their beloved to bear as the pain of separation itself.

The quarters (the directions) are resonant—that is, clamorous—with the tumultuous cries of peacocks (*kekā-kolāhala*), which are characterized by the quarrels—meaning the battles—of beautiful peacocks intoxicated with passion due to their pride; by the use of the plural number, the all-pervasive nature of this calamity is revealed, according to the maxim: "Where can a traveler cast his gaze? (Note: *mukharā* means "talkative" or "clamorous"; *kakubhaḥ* refers to the "quarters" or directions; *bahuvacanena* indicates that the plural form emphasizes the extent of the distress.)

By describing how [the clouds] "cause the eyes to burn" through the phrases *unnamad-ambudharāḥ* ("with rising clouds") and *hari-hetimatyāḥ* ("possessing Indra's weapons"), how they "torment the sense of touch" through the phrase *ghananūtanavārikaṇāḥ* ("with thick, fresh drops of water"), and how they "are the cause of fever in the ears" through the phrase *nīlakaṇṭha-kalahaḥ* ("with the cries of peacocks"), the poet—by means of the words "how could I look upon them?"—illuminates that merely looking at these [clouds], which inflict pain upon all the senses, is as terrifying as falling into the Raurava hell; how much more so their actual experience! Here, the poetic figures of *vitarka* (deliberation) and *dainya* (dejection) are suggested (*dhvani*), and the ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state). //18//

Regarding the affliction of grief: "Sorrow is defined as the distress of all the sense faculties arising from separation from what is desired, from a curse, or from the loss of children, wealth, and so forth."
Thus ends the *Bhāvaprakāśa* [section on the manifestation of emotions], concerning the suffering rooted therein:
"Tearful weeping, dryness of the mouth, change of voice, discoloration,
sighing, loss of memory, lamentation, and stiffness of the limbs."
The meaning is that there is a proliferation of effects such as the onset of delusion, distress, falling to the ground, and lamentation, as previously described.

Having observed that state, he says: "some indescribable ripening of the condition" refers to the ultimate limit of the state. The word "again" (punaḥ) indicates a distinction. By one who was "unaware"—meaning not reflecting on the full extent of this condition—and who was "adamantine," because there was no melting away even upon seeing this [suffering], due to extreme hardness; the phrase "constructed by Kuśīla" is a hyperbolic expression (*atiśayokti*). The particle "kila" implies unreality. "Distraction" (*vinoda*) means diversion; the sense is: "it is called distraction, but it is not truly a distraction—it is merely a pushing away (*noda*)."

"Commenced" means begun with the words "I shall reproach—in this moment of intoxication," and so forth. "In this manner" refers to the current state of affairs. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "but. Our hope for Mādhava, shared by all of us who are partial toward him, is almost exhausted, or nearly at its end.
[As it is said: "Among women, low-born persons, and the like, this grief leads to the resolve for death;
among those of middle character, it results in grief, or the desire to die, or even death itself."

"By the principle stated thus—'The intense [sorrow] of the highest-natured person is pacified by discernment alone'—the grief of this noble-souled one will be extinguished through discernment over time. The meaning is that there remains for us the hope that even if Mādhava does not obtain Mālatī due to his past misdeeds, he himself survives. Furthermore, even for one of the highest nature, grief and the like are unbearable due to the gravity of the cause: 'Whom else could these emotions not overpower, since they touch even him who is the Lord of all?'"

The meaning is that this is because of the statement of authoritative persons and because such is observed in the case of goats and other animals. "With fear" means characterized by fear due to the apprehension of sin. Addressing Mālatī—who is utterly bewildered and the very root [of the matter]—as if facing her in the air, he would reproach her: "What else? What more shall we say? (the word *iti* is understood); you are merciless, having cast away all compassion.

Regarding the passage beginning with *apahastitabāndhavā*: *apahasta* refers to the back of the hand; a blow struck with that is commonly known as an *apahasta*. By means of the figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) "one struck with an *apahasta* is *apahastita*," the term is used here in the sense of being treated with contempt. Thus, she is one by whom her kinsmen—her father and others—are disregarded.

The reason for this is as follows: by stating "done today," the absence of any lapse due to the freshness of the act is revealed. He expresses that very point: "Therefore (tat), in this state (iha)," which is a gesture toward her current condition; "toward the beloved (priye)" who is innocent (anaparādhini) and free from any breach of affection; "chosen by herself" (svayaṃvṛtavallabheti). By addressing her as "friend" (sakhī), he reveals her role as his disciple because she is the ground of his confidence. The word "what" (kiṃ) is used in a sense of reproach.

The word "this" (*ayam*) indicates that [the speaker] was previously [connected to him]; "abandoned by compassion" (*karuṇojjhitaḥ*) means devoid of pity. By this, it is understood: "Since he is your dearest, there ought to have been affection; yet that was not seen in you.

Let that be as it may, but even pity is not felt for one who is suffering—oh, what cruelty is yours! Here, the figure of speech is *viṣama* (incongruity), because of the conjunction in a single locus of two things that are incompatible: the performance of a rash act and the absence of compassion.

And there is the refutation [of the opponent's position], because it is demonstrated that the effect—the abandonment of compassion—would occur even in the absence of the cause known as "offense. //19//

"Even now" means because he remains in that state for so long; "he does not breathe" means he does not release a breath, due to his being paralyzed. "Robbed" means one whose entire property has been taken away, since Mādhava alone was regarded as his sole possession. Recalling his own condition, he says: "O Mother! O Mother! and so forth. Since it is inevitable that every living being remembers their mother at a time of distress, he addresses his own mother in the sky, saying: "O Mother! O Mother!"

Through the repetition (*vīpsā*), the agitation caused by suffering is revealed; or rather, [the word] "Mother" addresses Mādhava’s mother, while "O Mother" again addresses his own mother, thus bringing them both face to face. "It bursts" means it splits; "it collapses" means the structural integrity of the body—the binding of its joints—loosens, or else the connection between the embodied self and the body [is severed], because the vital points (*marman*) are being pierced by agony. The world becomes empty and desolate, resembling a wilderness, with its flames burning incessantly—that is, with its light shining without interruption; [this is derived from the rule] *jvalitikasantebhyo ṇaḥ*.

(3-1-140) Thus, by the suffix *ṇa*, [the word *antaḥ* is formed]. "Within" (*antaḥ*) means inside the body; I blaze, shining like old wood kissed by fire. "Sinking" (*sīdat*) means becoming exhausted in deep darkness—according to the saying, "thick darkness is called *andhatamasa*"—in the gloom of obscurity; "distressed" (*vidhuraḥ*), meaning dependent on others, he sinks as if a boat into the ocean, that is, the inner self (*antarātmā*), the individual soul (*jīva*), or the mind (*manas*). Or, "the whole" (*viśvam*) refers to all duties or the entire world; "delusion" (*mohaḥ*), meaning mental agitation, "conceals," that is, obscures it.

The meaning is that one who, having obtained such a friend, has not been granted by fate the opportunity to experience happiness with him for a long time is one of little merit; what shall I do? In what manner shall I carry this out? Here, although the three statements—"I consider the world empty," "sinking in blind darkness," and "delusion shrouds the universe"—share a single result, there is no fault of tautology because of the variety of their modes and because they are the words of a speaker overwhelmed by the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇarasa*). The poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). //20//

Fearing that his death would be like the falling of Mount Meru—as in the expression, "A conflagration that cooks the flow of water"—he says, "O! into the sky. Addressing the world, he says, "Alas! It is improper. By the repetition (*vīpsā*), he implies that there is no suffering greater than this.

Regarding "bandhutā" and so forth: *bandhutā* is the collective group of kinsmen, such as fathers and others; [this is derived] from the rule: "The suffix *tal* is added after *grāma*, *jana*, *bandhu*, and *sahāya*."

(4-2-43) Thus, the suffix *tal* is applied in the sense of a collection (*samūha*); because it ends in *tal*, it possesses the status of a permanent feminine noun. The "Kaumudī festival" of that heart is the celebration occasioned by the full moon day of the month of Āśvayuja; because it is the cause of supreme bliss due to its possession of all excellent qualities, it is the "charming moon for Mālatī’s eyes"—that is, a charming, newly risen moon for her two eyes—or else, "charming" means eternally tender, which constitutes a figure of contrast (*vyatireka*).

The metaphorical representation (*rūpaṇa*) of the moon, which is well-known for its charm, is based on its occasional appearance and its being the cause of an excellence of coolness. "The delighter of Makaranda" (*makarandanandanaḥ*): the meaning is that whatever object is a source of prosperity (*samṛddhihetuḥ*) for Makaranda, all such things are [included here]. [This is derived from the rule: *nadi[ndi]grahipacādibhyo lyuṇinyacaḥ*.

(3-1-134) Thus, the suffix *lyu* is applied. "The ornament (*tilaka*) of the world of the living": those who live are the "living" (*jīva*), namely embodied beings; their "world" (*loka*) is the sphere that serves as their support, meaning the world of humans. He is its "ornament" (*tilaka*), its crest-jewel (*lalāma*), because he is the decoration of the highest part [of that world]. Since a *tilaka* possesses a distinction superior to other ornaments—just like a crest-jewel (*cūḍāmaṇi*)—there is here a superimposition of that status. It is perceived that he is setting; the meaning is: "What misery could be greater than this? Here, the poetic figure is *ullekha* (multiple description), because a single object is apprehended in various ways due to specific causes. //21//

"Let others be for now; [the King] says, 'My very everything has been taken away by Your Majesty,' beginning with the words *gātreṣu* and so forth. On his limbs—that is, on his body parts—there was sandalwood juice, the paste of sandalwood, because it produces the pleasure of an exceedingly cool touch.

In his vision—that is, in the faculty of sight—there was the autumnal moon, a moon occurring in the autumn season and thus free from the veil of clouds. In his heart there was bliss itself, which is embodied happiness, and not merely a means to happiness."

By the use of the past tense in "āsīt" (was), it is indicated that that state has become nothing more than a subject of legend, as in the expression, "There was once a beautiful prince. It was "exceedingly desirable," meaning an object of unsurpassed affection. Regarding this, he provides a comparison: "as if it were his own life.

Life is the supreme object of affection beyond one's vital breaths, for everyone harbors the hope for their own life, thinking, "May I always exist," and because of the attachment to sons, friends, wives, and so forth, which exists only in relation to that [life], as stated in the Śruti: "But it is for the sake of the self that everything becomes dear."

"At an untimely and improper moment"—the meaning is that even when the full span of human life ordained by the Veda, "Man has a lifespan of a hundred years," has been completed, the world cannot endure the passing away of one endowed with all virtues, much less so in the prime of youth.

By Time—the Supreme Lord who is the destroyer of all, who uproots, forcibly seizes, and plunders—He has been struck down, that is, slain. The mention of "Time" is intended to indicate His irresistible power, as seen in such scriptural statements as: "I am Time, the great destroyer of worlds," "For Time is difficult to overcome," and "The world is indeed under the sway of Time. //22//

Having touched him—that is, having grasped him with his hand—in order to save his life, he reproaches him out of an excess of affection, saying "merciless," and so forth. "Merciless" means devoid of compassion, because there is no inclination to show favor even toward me who am suffering. "Bestow" (vitara) means give back the gaze—your vision—which was formerly adorned with a gentle smile, radiant with a faint smile. "Exceedingly cruel" means the cause for the abandonment of the lives of immeasurable kinsmen, due to its being a wicked resolve. "Speech" refers to the words: "O dear friend! Why do you resort to such despondency? Are you not indeed well?"—give this speech.

The word "me" (by me) is connected to both sentences. [He is one] whose mind is devoted—meaning colored by affection—and who has never experienced separation from his companion; it is not merely a case of affection based on mere words. By the phrase "whose dear Makaranda is the object of his love," he expresses that this is well-known in the world.

"How do you not consider this companion whose heart is devoted to you? In what manner do you not understand? If at any time, in any way, even a slight trace of artificial affection had been experienced by you toward me, then this undertaking of your cruel deed would have been auspicious for you"—this is the sense. //23//

"Consciousness" (*saṃjñām*) refers to the awakening produced by the cessation of fainting. "With breath" (*socchvāsam*) means accompanied by inhalation. "Recently washed" (*aciradhautaḥ*) means freshly rinsed; the mention of being recently washed is for the purpose of demonstrating an excellence of glossiness. "Royal turban" (*rājapaṭṭaḥ*) is a specific kind of silken cloth of blue color; like that, his skin has a beautiful, radiant, fleshy, and thick luster. "By a shower of water droplets" (*toyaśīkarāsāreṇa*) means by a forceful rain of water drops.

"Āsāraḥ may mean 'spreading forth,' 'a heavy downpour,' or 'the force of a friend's army,'" according to the *Vaijayantī*. By saying "my dear friend," he highlights that a supreme service has been rendered to him by this [cloud], and thus it "revives" him. Here, one should consider that the revival brought about by the fresh rain-cloud is produced through the power of the Yoginī, and is not merely accidental; for this is further confirmed by the subsequent statements, "surely this is for him" and "as if being instantly split open from the cloud," which establish its occurrence at the appropriate time.

"He first breathed a sigh of relief" means he was restored to life; the use of the word "first" (tāvat) indicates that this breathing is not yet to be trusted as it is merely accidental until Mālatī is actually recovered, according to the maxim: "To what extent is a gain not indeed a loss? This expresses contentment, signifying: "For now, let us enjoy this happiness; as for what happens hereafter, let that be."

Now, [the poet], contemplating the unbearable onset of the rainy season—expressed by the phrase "the quarters [of the sky] are resonant with the warbling of honey-suckers and peacocks"—and thus depicting the fainting of one who is driven to madness and preoccupied with searching for a messenger for his beloved, speaks the words of that person upon awakening, under the influence of those lingering impressions: *tat* (therefore). That is to say, because the quarters of the sky are difficult to look upon without the beloved, and she, distressed by separation, must be comforted.
Whom (*kaṃ janam*), or in the reading *kim iti*, what object (*kiṃ vastu*)? Here, in this forest (*asmin vipine vane*).

"Aṭavī, araṇya, vipina, gahana, kānana, and vana" are synonyms for forest, according to Amara. By using the term *vipina*, he indicates that while in a city or a populated district one cannot be sought out due to the abundance of people, in a *vipina* (forest), because it is an unfamiliar place, one must be searched for. "A bearer of news of his beloved" (*priyāvārtāharam*) means a messenger of the beloved; he is a "bearer of news" (*vārtāharaḥ*) because he carries or brings news (*vārtām*), that is, a message. "Well done! Well done! is a joyful utterance arising from the fulfillment of his own desire; the sense is that it is "excellent" and "accomplished."

He states the reason for this with the words beginning "phalabhara" and so forth: in the *jambū* bower-groves (*jambūnikuñja*), which are dark blue in color due to the ripening (*pariṇāma*) or maturation of the abundance of fruit; in those groves where the slender, thin ripples have their momentum checked or obstructed because the fruits are blue in color. The mention of the *jambū* is because it is well known that it bears fruit during the rainy season.
[The groves are described as] being rich with fully developed juices and abundant fruits that resemble heaps of powdered charcoal.
"The branches of the Jambu trees appear as if they were being hidden by swarms of bees settling upon them"—

thus [it is said] in the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa* during the description of the rainy season (*prāvṛṭ-varṇana*). To the north (*uttareṇa*) of the river Pāṭalāvatī, which is about to be mentioned— that is, in the northern direction from it, not far away— the suffix *enap* is used according to the rule *enab anyatarasyām adūre 'pañcamyāḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.35),
and the second case ending is applied by the rule *enapā dvitīyā* (2.3.31).

(2-3-31) Thus, the accusative case [is used]. "Upon" means on the upper part; by implication, "of its own. It is as dark and glossy as a mature *tāpiñcha* flower—meaning a *tamāla* blossom that has begun to bloom, being full-grown and ripened by time—as is indicated by their association. Amara states: "The *kālaskandha* is the *tamāla*, and it is also called *tāpiñcha*. Or it may refer to the black *girikarṇikā*. It "resorts to," meaning it takes hold of it for the sake of resting.

The peak or summit of the mountain—of the hill—is [approached by] a newly arisen cloud; the construction is to be connected with the phrase "I shall make this [cloud] a bearer of news for my beloved," using the accusative case. //24//

"Impetuously" (*sarabhasam*) means with haste, agitation, or joy; according to the *Vaijayantī*, "impetuosity" (*rabhasa*) refers to both speed and joy. "With face upturned" (*unmukhaḥ*) means with the face raised, because [the object] is situated below him. "With palms joined" (*kṛtāñjaliḥ*) means having brought his hands together for the sake of worship, because of its divine nature and because he himself is full of longing.

To show his readiness for the words he intends to speak, he asks after his welfare with the words beginning "I hope" (*kaccit*), etc. "I hope" (*kaccit*) is used in a courteous inquiry. "O gentle one" (*saumya*) means one whose nature is not harsh.

The statement "I [do so] because of my desire to favor all" is intended to express her own inclination toward acting in this way. The term *priyasahacarī* suggests both a beloved companion who habitually moves along with her, and also implies a most beloved lawful wife (*dharmapatnī*). The lightning (*vidyut*, *taṭit*) embraces him of its own accord; she clings to him with passion. The underlying meaning is that when passion resides in both parties, it possesses aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

"With faces brightened by manifest affection": "manifest" (āvirbhūta) means spontaneously shimmering due to agitation and the like, rather than being artificially displayed; this highlights its sincerity. "Affection" (praṇaya) refers to friendship; thus, their faces are radiant with that. "Cātakas" are birds known as *dhārāṭas*. They are included here because they depend solely on those [clouds] and their hearts are moistened by an uncommon, liquid-like tenderness. "They resort to" means they serve them.

"Paurastya" means that which exists in the east, in the eastern direction; for it is associated with the rainy season, as seen in such usage as "his crest plumed by the forceful eastern wind. It brings happiness—that is, it makes one happy—through excellent fanning, by preventing bodily affliction and by leading one to various desired places.

Holding—that is, bearing—the rainbow of the Lord of the Gods (Indra) on all sides, in every direction, because clouds move according to the will of the Maruts; the word "or" (*vā*) is also to be supplied here [after "the rainbow"]; it spreads—that is, extends—its *lakṣmī*, meaning its beauty, as a *lakṣma*, that is, a mark or sign; [this applies] to you, by implication. The word "kaccit" is drawn into each of the three sentences. Alternatively, there is the reading "tanoṣi" (you spread). The first three sentences are in the form of questions, while the fourth sentence is in the form of a compliment (*cāṭu*).

"Carrying the mark of Indra’s bow, you spread your splendor in every direction—oh, how your wealth of beauty and fortune shines forth! The absence of the word "vā" (or) serves as the proof for this meaning. Here, the figure of speech is Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description), because from the non-contextual account of the cloud, the contextual account of the messenger is understood.

Since a dialogue consisting of questions and answers is impossible with that which is insentient, and although the literal meaning [of the words] is unestablished, this is nevertheless appropriate because there is an intended meaning (tātparya) regarding the subject at hand, because the superimposition of those [qualities] is perceived right from the outset, and because it would otherwise be the speech of a madman. Furthermore, *samāsokti* (concise expression) should be understood here, because the lightning and other elements are perceived as the heroine and so forth. In this context of the discourse of a madman, *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) is generally to be followed. //25//

Then, imagining that roar to be the answer to his own question, he said joyfully: "Aye!"—an indeclinable (*avyaya*) expressing joy. [The monkeys] were delighted—that is, filled with gladness—by the *kandarās*, the mountain caves, which were filled with echoes (*pratirava*). [This is an example of] a qualifier...

By the maxim, "When the primary [subject] is not qualified, injunctions and prohibitions apply to the qualification," the meaning is that they are delighted by echoes following after the hollows of the caves; "longing" means those who have been eager for a long time, thinking, "When indeed shall we hear the roar of our dear friend?"; or else, it refers to one by whom the blue-throated peacocks (nīlakaṇṭha) have had their necks raised.

By his beloved’s low-toned *huṅkāra*, pleasant to the ear and deep like a thunderclap—Halāyudha states that "low-toned" (*mandra*) means "deep" (*gambhīra*)—he gives his consent; the meaning is that he approves with a reply to me as I inquire. Having obtained an opportunity for the speech intended through his favorable disposition, she says: "I entreat" (or "I beg"), the word "this requested matter" being understood as the remainder of the sentence; the particle *yāvat* is used here either as a rhetorical ornament or for emphasis.

"O Blessed One," he says, expressing his own desire by means of the state of being able to assume any form at will (*kāmarūpatva*) and the state of having unimpeded movement everywhere (*sarvatrāpratihatagatitva*), due to his perfection in sovereignty and all other attributes. He then expresses his prayer to the cloud (*jīmūta*): "By fate," and so forth. "By fate" (*daivāt*) means by my good fortune. "In the world" (*jagati*) indicates that his wandering is not restricted to any particular place. By using the present participle suffix *-śatṛ* in "wandering" (*vicaran*), he indicates that this is his habitual disposition. "My beloved" (*matpriyām*) is a demonstration through dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*) of himself as characterized by his current state; the optative (*liṅ*) in "if you should see" (*paśyeś cet*) expresses a possibility: "If you should see my most dear one while I am in such a state of separation."

By the use of the word "if" (*ced*), he suggests: "I do not command you, who are honored by the three worlds, in this matter; rather, I offer only this prayer—that if it should happen by chance, then at that very moment I am to be favored. Having first comforted her, [he says]: "Child, do not grieve."

"Having made her free from agitation by saying, 'I shall reunite you with your companion,' and thereafter—following that consolation—'you should tell her condition' (the *liṅ* suffix is used here in the sense of a request); 'condition' (*avasthā*) refers to the state of Mādhava, meaning my beloved, who resides in Mādhava; this is stated as an established fact because it was indicated through dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*), specifically the condition of having only a small remnant of life."

The thread of hope is as subtle as a strand of thread; "by one who speaks" means by one describing the situation; "should speak" is a restatement of the request for him to tell [the news]; "must be cut entirely without remainder" means it is fit to be severed. When it is said, "Before seeing you, he will surely have given up his life," her life-breaths will depart instantly due to despair. When it is said, "I have consoled him so that he may live until he sees you," she too will live because of her hope—this is the meaning.

"She was wedded by Māruta [the Wind] thinking, 'He will keep her alive,'" so said Setu. He explains that very point: "The preservation of life" (*prāṇatrāṇaṃ*) means the protection of the vital breaths, that is to say, their non-departure; "somehow" means with great difficulty. "Of the long-eyed one" (*āyatākṣyāḥ*)—this is a description of her at that moment, meaning she whose eyes were wide open due to joy and wonder at your words. That very thing is the thread of hope (*āśātantu*). Here, the aesthetic sentiments (*bhāva*) of dejection (*dainya*) and longing (*autsukya*) are suggested. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic indication), because the cause is stated as the meaning of the sentence. //26//

"With joy" (saharṣam) means: perceiving that the cloud has departed of its own accord, having set out to accomplish the object he himself desired; thus, it means "filled with delight. "Aye! expresses the wonder of his benevolence. "Has moved" (pracalitaḥ) means has set out. "To another place" (anyataḥ) means to a different region.

"With agitation" (sodvegam) means with fear, because agitation is a precursor to madness, fainting, or death. "The eclipse of madness" (unmādoparāgaḥ) refers to the planet Rāhu in the form of madness.
As Amara states: "Uparāga and graha [are synonyms]; however, they refer to the moon and sun when seized by Rāhu."

"The state known as *unmāda* (madness) arises from the separation of the eldest [brother] from his beloved, the obstruction of the desires of the middle one, and the loss of wealth for the base," thus is the emotion called *unmāda* defined. [The poet] addresses Mādhava as the moon (*mādhavendu*)—that is, as the moon in the form of Mādhava—and through this superimposition of "moon-ness," he further superimposes the state of being "eclipsed. Just as the eclipse of the full-orbed moon, which gladdens the entire world, causes distress to the hearts of the sensitive (*sahṛdaya*), so too does his madness; it is to illuminate this that [the poet says the madness] "assails" or "overcomes" him.
As it is said: "He is described by means of restless lying down, sitting, rising, and weeping;

by improper prattle, stumbling, cowardice, and so forth," the meaning is that he overcomes [others] through the manifestation of his own state. "Father" is used to address Devarāta; "Mother" refers to Mādhava’s mother. "Blessed Lady" refers to Kāmandakī; the words "protect" and "save" are spoken because of her capacity for protection. By the phrase "of Mādhava," it is suggested through *dhvani* (suggestive power) that he is the object of such affection for you. "State" (*avasthā*) refers to the condition of madness.
Deluded by the sight of similar qualities, he said: "Alas, what a tragedy! This misfortune has arisen from our negligence and lack of attention.
He explains this very point with the words beginning with *naveṣu*: "In the fresh *lodhra* blossoms—those flowers of the *lodhra* tree that bloom at that very time—as it is said:
'The beauty of her face was turned pale by the pollen of the *lodhra* blossoms.'"

Although the *lodhra* tree is established as being associated with the winter season by such passages as, "He who, like Smara, desired to march his army against the worlds, and he who [is covered] with the pollen of the *lodhra*," and so forth;

here, however, there is a statement regarding its belonging to the rainy season (*prāvṛṣeṇya*) in the lines, "The expanse of forests smiles with the fragrance of *silindhra* and *lodhra* flowers," and "The splendor in the fresh blossoms of the *lodhra*. This is because it is observed that certain specific trees flower two or three times even within a single year. Furthermore, "splendor" (*kānti*) refers to an excellence of beauty (*lāvaṇya*), which is pale like that of Smara.

The mention of *lodhra* blossoms is because its whiteness is well-known from such [verses] as "the white *lodhra* pollen on the surface of her cheeks" and "the flowering *lodhra* tree on the mountain slope.
Her glances (*dṛśaḥ*) are directed toward the deer (*kuraṅgeṣu*),
and her gait (*gataṃ*) is found in the elephants (*gajeṣu*), due to the heaviness of her hips and so forth, as well as the pride of youth and passion, and her languid grace.

In the case of creepers such as the *aśoka* shrubs, "bending" (*namratvam*) refers to their nature of bowing, because they are bent down by the clusters of blossoms on their breasts, as seen in such usages as "as if slightly bent down by her two breasts" (*āvarjitā kiñcidiva stanābhyām*) and "bowed down by the clusters of blossoms that are as lovely as breasts" (*stanābhirāmastabakāvanamrām*).

The word "is seen" (*dṛśyate*) is to be supplied [as the verb]. For this reason—having violently crushed and harmed her—it is evident and certain that she has been divided, split into many parts. By the word "in the forest" (*vipine*), the absence of anyone to prevent her separation from her kinsmen is revealed; furthermore, because it is insentient, its lack of compassion due to ignorance of her qualities is shown. "O, my beloved"—alas, what misfortune is mine! That she has been thus divided while I still live is what is suggested (*dhvanyate*). Here, the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is inference (*anumāna*). //27//
Having ascertained her separation, he laments: "Alas, my dear Mālatī!

Observing his overflowing madness, he says dejectedly: "O friend"—this is a specific designation—*guṇanivāse*, meaning the abode of virtues such as modesty, sweetness, and the like; *preyasi*, meaning most beloved among all your other dear ones; *prāṇanāthe*, meaning the lord of your life-breaths, since their existence follows the presence or absence of that [beloved]; and *sahapāṃsukrīḍanaprauḍhasakhye*, meaning one with whom mature friendship was formed through playing together in the dust—that play consisting of sporting by means of dust, earth-particles, fashioned into altars and the like.

"In which [state] there is a mature, fully developed friendship"—by the word "friendship" (*sakhyam*), it is expressed that affection has been established since childhood, as between siblings. "The surge of the mental anguish and disease caused by separation from a beloved person"—the "beloved person" (*priyajanasya*) refers to the wife; "separation" (*viraha*) is the absence from her; "mental anguish" (*ādhi*) is the pain of the mind; and "surge of the disease" (*vyādhivegam*) refers to the manifestation of that illness, or of the disease rooted therein. By the phrase "bearing the surge," the continuous intensification of the condition is revealed due to its incurability.
O wretched heart! O lost mind! Why do you not burst asunder, split in two, and depart? Here, resentment toward the heart is expressed; the poetic figure is *parikara* (periphrasis). //28//

He refutes with reasoning the statement "in fresh *lodhra* blossoms" as follows: "That which has an easily imitated likeness"—that is, for which imitation (*anukāra*), meaning the following after something due to similarity, is easy to obtain; the word "indeed" (*khalu*) serves to establish both common knowledge and experience, the sense being that such is the case with the cow, the gavaya, and so forth. By saying "of the Creator" (*vedhasaḥ*), he expresses that this is not surprising for the Lord, because of His inconceivable power; "the configuration of the creation" (*nirmāṇasanniveśaḥ*) refers to a specific form of the creation (*nirmāṇa*), that is, of the world (*sṛṣṭi*). Let it be so.

Having thus determined that his beloved’s life must be preserved—concluding that she should not entertain any fear of separation from him—he says, "In this manner," which refers to the resolution of what is to be done, namely, "I shall speak exactly thus. Having prostrated himself for the sake of propitiation, he performs a salutation. By the gesture "here I am," he demonstrates his own condition and indicates that he is an object worthy of compassion. The word "O" is used to draw [the listener] toward him.

"Those who roam the mountains and forests" means those whose habit is to wander through mountainous regions and woods; the mention of "mountains and forests" is intended to demonstrate the vastness of the region and, by extension, the abundance of living beings (*sattva*). "Living beings" (*sattvān*) refers to creatures; as the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "The word *sattva* is not feminine when it denotes a creature (in the masculine), but is neuter when it denotes resolve or prowess. By speaking without specific qualification, he indicates a general prayer that anyone, wherever they may be situated, at any time, might somehow come to know some connection with his beloved.

"I inform" (*vijñāpayāmi*) means "I announce. This term is to be understood as employed here to manifest humility (*dainya*), being used in the context of making a request through prostration toward a venerable object, due to one's own wretched state and dependence. For example, as in the case of Lavaṅgikā falling at the feet of Mālatī. The indirect reference (*pārokṣyanirdeśa*) in the phrase "I inform the beings" (*sattvān vijñāpayāmi*) is indicative of great respect, just like expressions such as "Your Majesty is the authority" (*devaḥ pramāṇam*) or "As Your Majesty commands" (*yathājñāpayati devaḥ*).

Those who have been made my refuge by me—you, honorable sirs—should favor and show compassion toward the matter being requested, by granting your attention and ceasing from your respective activities, and by maintaining one-pointed concentration as the context requires.

He states the very request: "By you," and so forth. "Beautiful by nature in all her limbs" means she is captivating to the heart by her very nature or essence in every limb and through all her features. Anticipating the objection that this definition might be over-extensive (*ativyāpti*)—as it would apply to celestial nymphs (*divyāṅganā*) and others—he offers a rebuttal: "A woman of good family, a protector of the lineage. The implication is that even for such a woman, as in the case of Sītā and others, arrival here is possible due to causes such as being captured as a prisoner by an enemy.

"By those staying here"—that is, by those situated on this broad and lofty mountain slope as if on Mount Ṛśyamūka—this indicates the possibility of seeing her. The connection is: "Has she been seen? Alternatively, "iti" marks the cessation of the act of seeing; it means: "Let there be no seeing [with one's own eyes], but has news concerning her become known even through hearsay from the words of those who have seen her? Furthermore, he states a characteristic that is never-failing: "Listen to the stage of her age"—that is, the specific state of her period of life.

Fearing that the conduct of a noble wife might be disregarded by us due to its impropriety, he says: "O friends," meaning those with virtuous hearts; because they have conquered their senses and possess true friendship, there is never any impropriety on their part, as if they were brothers—this is the sense. "Wherein" means in whom [the mind] moves incessantly, being active and engaged in its own operations, having attained mastery over its own tasks such as volition and the like, through the fulfillment of its sovereign power.

"Mugdha" means unrefined, that is to say, one who has become tender; the meaning is that because of his exceedingly noble nature and the persistence of his childhood, the outward expansion of his own activities is restrained, which is to say, he is not yet fully enveloped by the intensity of youth. Alternatively, the state of the mind being stirred by aesthetic emotion (*rasa*) and the body being fit for compassionate enjoyment are being established. This is the figure of speech *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description), because the discourse proceeds by superimposing consciousness upon insentient things. //29//

Despondent due to the frustration of his hopes, he said, "Alas! The ellipsis implies: "O people, behold this which is improper. By means of the repetition (*vīpsā*), he indicates that nowhere else has such an impropriety been experienced by us.

He states the reason for this with the words beginning "kekābhiḥ" (by their cries). According to Amara, "kekā" is the cry of a peacock (*mayūra*). The plural number indicates repetition. "Nīlakaṇṭhaḥ" refers to the peacock. "Tirayati" means he causes [my speech] to disappear or be hidden. "Vacanam" refers to my words of petition. "Tāṇḍavāya" means for the sake of performing a wild dance; [this is based on the rule] *kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi sthāninaḥ*.

(2-3-14) Thus, the fourth [line]: *ucchikhaṇḍaḥ* means one whose crest of feathers (*piccha-bhāra*) is raised. He approaches his beloved—the one who is dear and filled with internal joy—because that joy is manifested through her outward expressions; he goes toward her of his own accord. His pupils are rolling with intoxication, whether produced by honey or by love. Regarding the *cakora*: "The *cakora* has moving claws and drinks [moonlight]; it is fond of moonlight," according to the *Vaijayantī*. "The black-faced monkey is called a *golāṅgūla*."

Thus says Halāyudha: [the wind] "sprinkles" (churayati), that is, mingles with the pollen (rajas) belonging to various kinds of flowers, because that [pollen] produces a secondary beauty (parabhāga-śobhā), as in the verse, "The lodhra-pollen is bright upon the surface of the cheek. Thus, among these [beings] who are preoccupied with their own diverse tasks, whom shall I entreat? The meaning is: no one among them honors our request.

By means of his own state, he imagines that even another seeker has become an object of contempt: "yatra-tatra" (here or there) means in any place whatsoever; "yadā-tadā" (then or at that time), like "yasya-tasya" (of whom or of that person), refers to the location or the person as the object. "Dhruvam" is an indeclinable particle indicating a conjecture. "Arthibhāvaḥ" (the state of being a petitioner) means the condition of begging; it is "seized by an inopportune moment" (*anavasara-grasta*), meaning it has been swallowed up or overwhelmed by the untimeliness born of the disregard shown toward the person being petitioned—in other words, it has been humiliated.

"Even a monk, though auspicious, is an object of contempt for people," by such statements. Alternatively, there is the reading *tatra yatra*; the meaning is: "In what place (*kaṃ*) shall I beg, where my state of being a petitioner remains seized by an inopportune moment? Here, the poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) are *svabhāvokti* (description of nature), *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of cause), and *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle). //30//

Looking elsewhere: "And this one—" beginning with *dantacchada* and so forth. Whose teeth are lovely—beautiful due to being free from gaps, fine, sharp, glossy, and white—and are stained as if by the dye of betel-leaf through the redness (*āruṇimna*) of his lip (*dantacchada*), that is, his lower lip; who has raised [his face] by lifting it upward with his forepaw; a "bull-faced" (*balīvadana*) or "monkey-faced" (*balīmukha*) is recognized as a specific type of monkey, red-faced and golden-hued.

"Kāmpilya, karkaśa, candra, raktāṃśa, and also rocanī"—thus says Amara. His cheeks (gaṇḍapāli), that is, the regions of his temples, were pale-red like the flower of the *kāmpilya* tree; for the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states, "That which is white and red is *pāṭala*. His luster was like that of a pomegranate flower, reddened by ripening, throbbing with bloom, or perhaps illuminated by the rays of the sun—meaning, in the areas other than the cheeks themselves.

"Kāraka, dāḍimī, and trayī"—so says the *Vaijayantī*. And the word "this" (*ayaṃ*) connects [the list] with Nīlakaṇṭha and others. Here, the poetic figure (alaṅkāra) is *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state). //31//

Looking elsewhere again, he says: "Aye!"—this expresses his joy due to his own passion for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*). "And this" (*ayaṃ ca*) connects him with those previously mentioned. A *rohiṇānokaha* is a sandalwood tree; because of its extreme coolness, the elephant (*karī*)—the word "is present" (*vartate*) being understood—is one whose neck (*kaṇṭhakāṇḍa*) is rested upon its trunk (*skandha*), meaning it has been placed there so that it is free from fatigue. Here, the word "even" (*api*) indicates that he is like an ox. This is an "inopportune moment" (*anavasara*), meaning it is not the right time for what we intend to say.

The reason for this is given by the words "kaṇḍū-kuḍmalita" and so forth. According to Amara, "kaṇḍūḥ, kharjuḥ, and kaṇḍūyaḥ" all mean itching. She is one whose eyes (īkṣaṇe) have become "mukulite"—that is, closed like buds—due to the cause of *kaṇḍū* (itching), namely, the experience of the pleasure derived from scratching with the tips of her teeth.

By the very qualifier "dear one," who cannot endure separation for even a moment, the subject [the female elephant] is established. Furthermore, by the phrase "of the tusk" rather than "of the two tusks," it is indicated that the two [tusks] stand with their sides joined together, forming a single mouth-like structure. Scratching—that is, rubbing—with the tip (koṭyā) or the point; by the word "scratching," the scratching is revealed as being done at ease through the stimulation of the path of the nail-scratches.

Fanning her ears—which were turned alternately and obliquely and were moving back and forth—with breezes that were refreshing due to their soft coolness and naturally gladdening, he performed the function of a palm-leaf fan.

By the phrase "jagdhārdhaiḥ" (half-eaten), it is suggested that [the food] was "most delicious, most delicious," having been tasted by him himself in one part; with fresh shoots of the *sallakī* tree—of which Amara states, "the *sallakī* is dear to elephants"—he provides and maintains the sustenance, that is, the bodily maintenance, of this companion. The three present participles (*śatṛ*) indicate cause. By the word "fortunate" (*dhanya*), meaning "possessed of good luck," the contrast is suggested that he alone is fortunate, whereas I am simply unfortunate.

The reason for his blessedness is as follows: the term *vanyamataṅgaja* (wild elephant) consists of *vanya*, meaning "born in the forest," which proclaims his state of unrestrained playfulness, as stated in the verse:
"The lord of elephants remembered the great festivals of his forest-dwelling, where he roamed at will with eyes half-closed.

The word *mataṅgaja* means "elephant" through a combination of etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), based on the rule *saptamyāṃ janer ḍaḥ* ("the suffix *ḍa* is applied after the root *jan* when preceded by a word in the locative case"), meaning "born on Mount Mataṅga."

(3-2-97) *Paricaya* means acquaintance; its *prārambha* or *upakrama* is that which one practices or repeats. By the word "practices" (*abhyasyati*), he indicates that because of her youth (*kalabhatva*), this is a newly initiated sexual union. Here, the emotion (*bhāva*) called joy (*harṣa*) and the erotic sentiment of union (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*) are perceived. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state). //32//

The particle *tu* indicates a distinction from what precedes it. Regarding the phrase "not within" (*nāntar*), etc.: "within" (*antar*) refers to the hollow of the throat; by this term "within," the state of being burst forth due to indignation (*amarṣa*) and its outward manifestation due to power are illuminated. "He causes to turn" means he causes to proceed. "Slightly deep" (*āmandram*) means a roar that is somewhat profound; "natural" (*svata udāttam*) means a roar arising spontaneously; "from nearby" (*āsannāt*) means from one situated close at hand—this reveals his indifference even though [the task] is easy. "Bent down" (*āvarjitaiḥ*) means drawn back. According to the *Vaijayantī*: "Śaivala is *jalaśūka*.
"Stamberama" means an elephant, according to the rule: "The roots *ram* and *jap* [take the suffix *khac*] after *stamba* and *karṇa*."

(3-2-13) Thus [the suffix] *ap* is applied; according to the rule "it should be stated that [the suffix is added] after *hasti* and *sūcaka*," when *hastinī* is the object denoted, there is no elision (*aluk*) by virtue of the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the elision of a *kṛt* suffix is frequent" (6-3-14). She languishes; she remains in a state of exhaustion. //33//

She feels compassion for him who shares her same affliction, because she herself has experienced the pain of separation—*alam* being used here in the sense of prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), meaning "enough" with *āyāsita*, i.e., being troubled by questions and the like; according to the rule: *prakṛtyādibhya upasaṅkhyānam*.

The third [case ending], *vā* (2-3-8), is used here with the sense that "there should be no effort on his part. Looking elsewhere, he says with great respect: "This," and so forth. Being heard by his female companion—who is filled with joy and delighted by hearing it—the sound of the rumbling in his throat, sweet because of its beautiful form and deep because of its magnitude, is being listened to with reverence, her ears pricked up like those of a horse, as it proceeds from the hollow of his throat with a *kuhū-kuhū* resonance.

He whose sound is that of thundering; another, who is entirely distinct from the previously mentioned distressed one, being "intoxicated" (matta) with rut having commenced—"for contentment is the cause of mental intoxication," according to the stated sequence—and thus being tranquil; he is the "protector" (pāla), meaning the guardian, of the "herd of elephants" (mātaṅgavarga), that is to say, a lordly elephant (gajendra); [he is] characterized by a resemblance to the *kadamba* flowers, which have recently blossomed, i.e., which have just now come into full bloom.

"In the *Harṣacarita*, it says: 'the world filled with the sweet fragrance resembling that of blossoming *kadamba* flowers. The reason for this is as follows: by means of that which is thick (*bahala*)—that is, dense (*sāndra*)—with a fragrance (*āmoda*) that is abundant (*parimala*), cool (*śītala*) in its favoring grace, and sweet (*surabhi*) in its gratification of the sense of smell; and by means of that which is mingled (*saṅgalita*), perfectly and incessantly flowing (*samyan-avarataṃ pravṛtta*), fleshy (*māṃsala*), and thick (*ghana*), namely the ichor (*kapolaniṣyanda*) trickling from the bursting temples (*karaṭataṭatruṭanakṣarita*), [the world] was made muddy (*kardamita*), that is to say, rendered turbid (*kaluṣita*)."

In which [place], from a cluster of lotuses (*kamalinī*) that had been uprooted and torn out, the filaments (*kesara*), stamens (*kiñjalka*), lotus stalks (*mṛṇāla*), coils of fiber (*bisavalaya*), sprouts (*kandala*), emerging leaves, shoots (*aṅkura*), and very young buds were scattered and cast hither and thither; and which was [rendered] shattered by the constant and uninterrupted *tāṇḍava*—the wild dance characterized by a charming rhythm and tempo—due to being struck by his flapping ears.

In which [place] there was a vast expanse of mist (*nīhāra*)—that is, a mass of snow (*himānī*)—spread over the broken waves and ripples of the water; by the word "mist," a multitude of water droplets is figuratively identified with it due to their subtle, cool, pure, and dense nature. In which [place] the *kurara* and *sārasa* birds were exceedingly terrified—these are adjectives qualifying that time. Alternatively, such expressions as "in this manner" (*evam yathātathā*) may be adjectives qualifying the act of play.
As it is said: "The *krauñca* is called *kruṅ*, *adhotkrośa*, and *kurara*, and it is a devourer of fish";
and "the *sārasa* is *maithunī* and *kāmī*."

According to the *Vaijayantī*: "A reservoir (*taṭāka*)—not feminine—is a pond (*kāsāra*), a lake (*sarasī*), or a pool (*sara*). Having "plunged" means having entered; he "plays" means he delights. "Let it be so" is an expression of approval for his blessedness. Because he is certain of his own contentment, there is no occasion for questions and the like; rather, in addressing him, I win him over with flattering words, as in such examples as "having addressed him, he spoke this," or "having approached [him] with respect, how many... and so forth.

O highly fortunate one! O blessed one! O Lord of Nagas! O leader of the elephant herd! Your youth is praiseworthy—a youth capable of enchanting the hearts of the sensitive. (The particle) *khalu* is used here for emphasis, because youth has distinguished enjoyment as its fruit; moreover, your engagement in it is not merely through the behavior of a beast, but rather through skillfulness in bringing about its aesthetic relish (*sarasatva*).

He says "no," because women, who share the nature of flowers, must be won over by fondling. "Skill in following the beloved" refers to the state of being clever—that is, the quality of one who is refined and discerning—in following and complying with the mind of a dear female elephant. Regarding that, he states a distinction: "but [skill] accompanied by reproach. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction; "reproach" (*apavāda*) means the state of being subject to censure by those with subtle vision; thus, the meaning is skill accompanied by such reproach.

He states the reason for this with the words beginning "līlotkhāta" (uprooted in sport), and so forth. By "līlotkhātaiḥ," meaning uprooted with playfulness, he refers to the *mṛṇāla-kāṇḍas*, or lotus stalks. Just as in the expression "mouthfuls of grass that are flavorful" (*āsvādavadbhiḥ kabalaiḥ tṛṇānām*), these are the "kabalas"—that is, mouthfuls—prepared for her by himself; at the "chedeṣu" of these, meaning at the end of their chewing, they are "puṣpyadbhiḥ," or blossoming, from the root *puṣpa* (to bloom) which takes the *śyan* suffix (*puṣpyati*). These are the "gaṇḍūṣāḥ," or mouthfuls, of the "payasaḥ," or water, which has been "vāsitasya," or rendered fragrant, by the "puṣkaraiḥ," or lotuses.
The "portions" (*aṃśāḥ*) are those parts placed upon her own face; their "transference" (*saṅkrāntayaḥ*) consists of their being offered onto her face.
This is because it has been said: "The female elephant gave mouthfuls of water, fragrant with the pollen of the lake-lotuses, to the male elephant.

The "sprinkling" (*sekaḥ*), meaning the act of moistening, was performed—carried out—by means of that which is "showering" (*śīkariṇā*), characterized by the raining down of water droplets, in order to alleviate the heat of midday. The word *kāmam* is used for emphasis, meaning that all of this is indeed entirely appropriate. By these two sentences, her cleverness (*cāturyam*) is established.

He now establishes the presence of a censure: "At the pause" (*virāme*), meaning at the conclusion of the watering; the word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates a reversal. "An uncurved-stalk lotus-leaf parasol" (*anarālanālanalinīpatrātapatram*) expresses its fitness for being held; yet, a parasol in the form of a lotus petal was not held by the hand over her head to ward off the heat. For she had hands, the lotus leaf was nearby, the affliction of the sun's heat existed for her, and your affection for her was overflowing.

Nevertheless, since there appears to be no opportunity for those of refined sensibility (sahṛdaya) to censure [the work] by saying "this was not done thus," these words are spoken with a friendly intent and accompanied by a jest. Here, the poetic figure *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause) is present, because both the skillful avoidance of censure and the cleverness [of the speaker] are established as the meaning of the sentence. //34//

"How?"—this expresses astonishment, because it was not suspected that he would become indifferent toward one whom he himself had imagined to be his dear friend. "Neglect" (*avadhīraṇā*) means he proceeds with dryness—that is, with disdain for my words—and goes elsewhere of his own accord, devoid of affection. Then, despondent, he says: "Alas! (*hanta*), expressing sorrow; "foolish" (*mūḍhaḥ*) means devoid of the discrimination between what is suitable and what is unsuitable.

"Since"—that is to say, because in this state [of intoxication], by means of dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*), he points to a hundred such misdeeds as the half-closing of the eyes due to the power of *mada*; "forest-dweller" (*vanacara*) suggests his being deprived of the company of the virtuous; "in a manner suitable for my friend Makaranda"—meaning, in whatever way is appropriate and fitting for my friend Makaranda—"I behave," that is, I act. Therefore, the connection is: "I am indeed a fool.
Even though he is insane, having been reminded of Makaranda through the incidental account of the intoxicated elephant, he says: "Ah! (*ha*).

Thinking that he was right there before him because his memory had been clouded by madness, he says: "Fie on this gasping," and so forth. "Gasping" (*ucchvasita*) refers to the experience of suffering in the form of sustaining life; from the root *śas* meaning "to injure," with the prefix *vi-* and the suffix *ac*, we get the form *viśasa*, which, with a *taddhita* suffix in the sense of the base word itself, means "a particular kind of injury. This is evident from such usages as: "Indeed, Fate has committed half the slaughter against me by releasing me after the killing of my desire. [The use of *dhik* with *ucchvasita* is justified] by the rule: "In the case of *dhik* and words beginning with *upari*..."

By the rule beginning with *vā. 1-4-48*, the accusative case is used in connection with the word *dhik*. The sense of "mine" (*mama*) is illuminated by the fact that [this state] was not abandoned by you for even a moment, even in dreams; this is what is being rejected by the word "that" (*tat*). The meaning is: "that which exists in this manner for me, who am alone—deprived of your companionship—and who am scorched by the pain of separation from you. The underlying sentiment is: "Death itself is better than such a life as this."

The reason for this is as follows: because of the experience of objects that are exceptionally delightful, specifically those things—such as mountains, rivers, and forest-dwellers—that are exceedingly heart-pleasing; and because of the cause that is "vain," meaning prone to becoming useless, the very experience together with you two constitutes the delightfulness of delightful things. Otherwise, on the contrary, they would only cause torment; such is the sense. To the question, "How can one breathe when separation arises by the power of time, which is to be loathed? he says, "By you."

It should be understood that by addressing her as "Makaranda" and saying "by you," she [Mālatī] is then included with the phrase "together with her"; this is because the heroine, the principal subject (*aṅgin*), is always to be kept in mind. The sense is: "May even that day which is not experienced by you and by her, Mālatī, come to ruin—that is, may it undergo absolute non-existence. Therefore, the separation rooted in that [day] shall also no longer exist."

The phrase "the mirage of delusion" (*pramoha-mṛgatṛṣṇikā*)—meaning the form of erroneous cognition such as "this one is my friend," "this one is dear to me"—illuminates that just as there is a futile engagement on the part of a thirsty person, deceived by the perception of water, toward the shimmering rays of the midday sun fallen upon the desert earth, so too is my attachment to the notion of kinship toward these forest-dwellers, such as the scent-elephants (*gandhasindhura*).

Elsewhere, [he speaks] regarding the human race other than yourselves, within the group of offspring of Manu Svāyambhuva, the progenitor (*prajāpati*); that is to say, among the class of living beings. [This is according to the rule: *manor jātāv añyatau ṣuk ca*.
(4-1-161) Thus, there is also the augment *ṣuk*.
"O best of the twice-born, know me to be that Virāj, the Supreme Person himself, who, having performed austerities, created this [universe]; I am the creator of all this."

According to this statement of Manu, the word *mānuṣa* (human) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for living beings in general, because it is spoken in reference to one who is detached from elephants and other such things; the connection is that "fie upon that mirage of delusion which occurs toward another human being. Here, the internal state of a friend is revealed. This is the figure of speech *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Praise of the Irrelevant). //35//

"Aye" expresses joy. "Interposed by the delusion of madness" means obscured by the mental distraction produced by intoxication. "Toward me" means with reference to me; the accusative case is used here according to the rule "it is seen in connection with words such as *prati*. "From somewhere" means from some source, such as the account of the elephant and so forth. "From a sign" (*vyañjanāt*): a sign (*vyañjana*) is that by which something is manifested or made clear, meaning a cause; from that cause, "the innate, natural predisposition for affection"—that is, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of love—residing in the mind, has been awakened or brought to light.

Therefore, for that reason, he considers [him] to be absent, situated in a remote place, and understands [this] from such statements as, "That my destruction has been so great while I am thus alone. "In front" means before him. "This one" indicates his presence; "attending at the side" means standing nearby—he who was introduced by you through recollection—that unfortunate one, meaning that due to his meager merit he still lives even today to behold such a state of yours.

Having stated that she was standing before him, he describes the result with the words "having beheld" (*samālokya*). The particle *ha* expresses the dejection born from not seeing her for a moment. "Sambhāvaya" means "honor" or "pay respect. He explains the manner of this honoring by saying "embrace her" (*pariṣvajasva*). The word *tu* indicates a contrast: while you were counted among those who were excluded by the phrase "he who is not with you [is not with her]," you yourself have fortunately been seen; however, regarding his beloved Mālatī, he is hopeless, having abandoned all hope of seeing her, since even a mere report of her has not been heard during all this time—this is the sense.

"With joy" (*saharṣam*) means accompanied by joy because he has requested exactly what was desired by [the speaker] himself. "I shall honor" (*sambhāvayāmi*) means "I shall embrace. "The lord of life" (*jīviteśvaram*) refers to the master of one's vital breaths, since life itself follows the presence and absence of that [lord]. "With compassion" (*sakaruṇam*) means with sorrow. "Manifesting a longing for my embrace" means displaying his arms with agitation. "Now," having seen him in this other state, [he speaks thus] thinking: "Through the calamity of hope, my dear friend will eventually become firm-minded.
(Abhidhāna)

[He is] bound by this form [of grief], or by suffering. The reason for this is: "in every way," that is, in every possible manner—due to the fact that Mālatī is nowhere to be seen, due to the state of his current condition, due to the intensification of time, and so forth; through all these combined modes, it is certain that he will not live—the present tense (*laṭ*) is used here according to Pāṇini 3.3.131, *vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavadvā* ("the present tense may optionally be used when there is proximity to the present"). This conclusion (*pariccheda*) is logical (*yukta*) and established (*upapanna*).

Having determined his absence, she laments with the words beginning "yat sneha" (since, through affection), etc. [The meaning is: by that heart/mind which is constantly possessed of a great disease—because it is produced by the suffering of *saṃsāra* and the impulse of the fever of affection—the constant possession being indicated by the suffix *-mat*; which has its tremors bound all around, i.e., is completely seized by shaking; even though there is an absence of the causes for calamity that might otherwise be expected due to being well-protected and possessing power, [this occurs] even without the presence of a specific cause, as in the case of "without" (*vinā*) in the sense of "separately" (*pṛthak*).

By the rule beginning with "pañcamī" (Pāṇini 2.3.42), the fifth case is used. "In you," meaning in you as the locus (*adhikaraṇe*), [occur] "calamities" (*āpadaḥ*), which are misfortunes. By the use of the plural number, [the author] reveals the diversity of calamities that are to be feared, due to the manifold nature of those fears. All—that is, the entirety—of that suffering born of such fear, whether experienced by oneself through one's own nature or by others, for all this time, [is removed] "in a single step" (*ekapade*); the meaning is: in the setting down of a single footstep (*ekapadanyāse*).

The state of suffering belonging to the stage of apprehension regarding the attainment of what is feared is indeed brought to a complete end by its cessation. The sense is that, just as when a thunderbolt strikes clearly and suddenly amidst a mass of clouds, one who fears "it will fall slowly upon my head" experiences precisely that suffering once it has fallen; thus he reflects on the popular proverb: "One who has endured much suffering becomes free from suffering. Here, the emotion of *āvega* (agitation) is suggested (*dhvani*), and the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole). //36//

*Varam* means slightly dear; as Amara states: "The word *vara* is used for the best [chosen by fate], and in the neuter, for that which is slightly dear. *Atikrāntāḥ* means passed or removed. *Muhūrtāḥ*:
"Eighteen *nimeṣas* make a *kāṣṭhā*, and thirty of those make a *kalā*... [and so forth].

"Thirty of those [kṣaṇas] constitute a muhūrta, and twelve muhūrtas make up a day and night"—thus are defined the divisions of time whose constituent parts have been characterized. During such muhūrtas, he was moving about improperly like a beast due to that kind of madness; the word "api" (even) indicates a contradiction, for even such a person is in reality unbearable [to behold]. He was "cetayamānam," meaning conscious, because although there is an absence of specific discernment (*viśeṣavijñāna*), a general consciousness (*vijñānasāmānya*) exists just as it does in a beast. Therefore, the statement "better than a state resembling wood or a clod of earth" is made; the verbal root is *citī* in the sense of "perception" (*saṃjñāne*).
Because it has been experienced and directly perceived; "now" means at this time, the particle *tu* indicating a distinction.

"The burden is the body," and so forth—the burden is a difficult-to-carry object for one who is weak; the body is the physical frame; life is the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). A "thunderbolt-stake" (*vajrakīla*) is a wedge made of the jewel called a thunderbolt (*vajra*); the term "thunderbolt" is used because it cannot be pierced by iron or other materials, as in the expression "the thunderbolt-cage for those who have sought refuge," meaning it is an exceedingly firm internal thorn. The quarters, the directions, are empty; due to the absence of all kinsmen, they are like a desolate forest.
The sense faculties are fruitless because there is an absence of seeing beautiful forms or hearing sweet sounds and so forth.

The world of living beings is everywhere and in every respect like a light that has gone out, its radiance extinguished. Here, by means of such statements as "the body is a burden," [the text] sequentially demonstrates: first, that the purpose of maintaining the body is solely the engagement in performing one's duties; second, that for all people who are most dear, it brings happiness only in his presence; third, that he alone performs the functions of a kinsman to all; fourth, that he alone delights all the senses; fifth, that he alone is beautiful through all the arts; and sixth, that he alone dispels the entirety of darkness, such as grief and delusion.
And it is thus illuminated; here, the poetic figures (alaṅkāra) are metaphor (rūpaka) and hyperbole (atiśayokti). //37//

Since this final breath is occurring, I must—indeed, I am destined to—be the witness to Mādhava’s death, the witness who sees it directly; for this reason, why indeed do I live? What purpose does my life serve? Such is the meaning.

To the question, "In that case, how should it be done? he says: "Therefore"—because being a witness to such a state is unbearable—therefore, from this nearby mountain peak, a great plateau-like summit, one should descend and plunge into the river there named Pāṭalāvatī. By the use of the words "descending" (*nipatya*) and "plunging" (*āplutya*), the sanctity of the mountain peak as the point of departure (*apādāna*) for the act of falling and of the river as the object (*karman*) of that act is established; furthermore, since the merit of leaping from a precipice (*bhṛgupatana*) is remembered in scripture, the notion that this is an ignoble death is refuted. As it is said: "In this manner, one should sacrifice the body for the sake of cows and Brahmins, or for the sake of the distressed."
He too attains merit by virtue of his regard for compassion.

"By bathing in the world-renowned and most meritorious holy site while remembering one's own deeds, even such a person immediately attains the worlds of the meritorious"—from this statement of Viśveśvara; and from the words of Māgha, "Having committed a fall like a man from the high precipices of Bhṛgu," and so forth, the meaning is: "I, the foremost among the Mādhavas, shall become a guide for Mādhava in this world as well as in the next. Having walked a little—that is, having gone a short distance—and having turned back again due to the bond of affection.

The passage beginning with "tad" means this: that which was previously experienced in such a way has now fallen among the dust of the earth due to its lack of consciousness; this is the sense. It has the luster of a blue lotus, meaning it possesses the radiance of a blue water-lily (*nīlendīvara*). He describes the very manner of that experience: "it existed in this body"—this expresses that such a state has already occurred.

There was no satiety or contentment for me from my limbs being pressed most firmly, as if they were dissolving, having been rubbed for a long time; for that touch, like an immersion in nectar, produces unsurpassed bliss.

Now, [the author] speaks of her being the locus of supramundane beauty and charm: "Because of a blossoming wonder"—that is, due to the cause of a sense of astonishment born from seeing such unprecedented loveliness and so forth; "not slight" (*atanu*) means "not small," serving as an adverbial modifier; "of insatiability" expresses the novelty [of the experience], intended to demonstrate the irresistible nature of her affection; "Mālatī’s glances"—meaning her modes of looking—agitated by the playful gestures (*vilāsa*) produced by fresh love, rippling with various modulations, have "drunk," that is, have greedily swallowed, his body.

Here, Makaranda’s feeling toward his friend and the heroine’s state known as *autsukya* (eagerness) are suggested. This constitutes the *preyaḥ* ornament, because the recollection arises from a cause other than similarity—as in the verse, "Oh, even in anger her face is lovely"—and it evokes wonder at his possession of extraordinary merit. //38//

By the phrase "in one body" (*ekasyāṃ tanau*), meaning in a single physical form, the sense is that—according to the maxim, "Generally, the Creator’s disposition regarding the assembly of qualities is averse to [placing] all [of them together]"—only some particular quality exists in a given place. By the word "to such an extent" (*etāvataḥ*), there is the manifestation of experience, eloquence, nobility, beauty, amiability, cleverness, good fortune, sovereignty, and so forth; [the question is]: how, by what manner, did the "arrangement" (*sanniveśaḥ*)—that is, the perfect placement (*samyag-nidhānam*)—of this "collection of qualities" (*guṇa-samāhāra*), the aggregate of virtues, come to be?
The sense is: "Of what name is this fruit of asceticism? That must also be diligently sought by us.

Then, fearing that for such a mass of virtues there might be a sudden shattering of life—a thorn to the hearts of the sensitive—he laments with the words beginning "āpūrṇa": "The moon, which was full—complete in its parts (kalās), meaning its fifteen digits—and possessed of a sixteenth digit that is free from waning or waxing, the support of all, stainless and unobscured by clouds of frost and the like, has reached Rāhu, the devourer of the moon; it has come to pass, it has ceased."

"‘Ghanāghana’ refers to a rutting elephant, Indra, or a rain-cloud," according to the *Vaijayantī*. The meaning is that he has become like a great rain-cloud, dark as the petal of a blue water-lily (*kuvalaya*), pervading the expanse of the sky, adorned with flashes of lightning and rainbows, and ready for a heavy downpour. "The cloud" (*jaladhara*)—referring here to a mere cloud—was shattered and scattered in every direction like the cotton-wool of a silk-cotton tree (*śālmalī*). "With speed" means with fierce velocity. According to Amara, "‘Phalegrahi’ means one who bears fruit"; that which always bears fruit is called "phalegrahi," as in the rule: "‘Phalegrahi’ and ‘ātmambhari’ [are used in the sense of bearing fruit or nourishing oneself]."

(3-2-26) By this rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the suffix *in* is applied and the vowel change to *e* occurs; thus, *drumavaraḥ* means the best of trees, such as the mango tree (*sahakāra*). According to Amara, "dava" and "dāva" refer to forest fires (*vanāraṇyavahnī*). Through the metaphorical sense (*lakṣaṇā*) that the fire of the forest is the crest-jewel (*cūḍāmaṇi*)—the head-ornament gem—for the world (*jagat*), meaning for the people residing in the world, it is established that [the tree] is carried upon the head. It has gone to, or attained, the state of [being like] lotuses with respect to its innate and acquired qualities due to the power of time.

Because the manifestation of its fragrance is appropriate at the break of day, [the phrase] "falling under the power of Death" (*mṛtyor antakasya vaśam*)—and not "Death" (*mṛtyum*) itself—avoids the inauspicious expression used by those who harbor hope. Here, through the three similes, it is revealed that [the moon] naturally gladdens the eyes of the entire world, is solely intent on benefiting others, and possesses a charming quality of service praised by refined people. This is the *prativastūpamā* (parallelism) ornament, because a single common attribute exists in each clause through a variation in its mode of presentation.

Furthermore, because the two occurrences of the word "ca" (and) establish the simultaneity of the actions in every sentence, the figure of speech *samuccaya* (accumulation), which pertains to a single substratum, should also be understood here. //39//

Because he has fallen under the power of death and an embrace will be difficult to obtain again, the meaning is that "let me embrace him first"—this indeed is the supreme gain. Thus situated, being in such a state, he was entreated—that is, requested—by this Mādhava for this object: the thing consisting of an embrace, or the purpose thereof. "O dear friend Makaranda! Commiserate with me," because it was said immediately after [the words] "embrace me."

Embracing him even now, and having ascertained his absence through his lack of consciousness, he laments: "O treasure-house of pure knowledge! O you who are the very ground for the treasury of wisdom free from doubt and error! O teacher of virtues, most weighty by virtue of your humility, sweetness, and other qualities—or rather, one who has become a master among virtues, meaning one whose virtues are envied even by others!"
