O Lord of my life, won by Mālatī’s own choice and self-choice marriage! To Kāmandakī and Makaranda especially, you are the moon of joy. In this birth, there shall be no final embrace—meaning no embrace subsequent to this one, because this very one is the last; thus is the sense. You were entreated for your final state—that is, you were petitioned by me alone during the final, ultimate stage of life.

Here, by the statement "not in this birth" (*janmanyapaścimaḥ*), it is indicated that [the result] will certainly come to pass in another birth. Anticipating the question "How so?", he says: "But now, do not think (*mā maṃsthāḥ*) that it will pass away in you. This is the second-person singular form in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense with the particle *mā*, derived from the root *man* in the sense of "to understand. The particle *eva* is for the purpose of removing doubt. He supports this restriction with a logical reason: "From what?"—if one asks for what reason—it means "from this [reason]."

"From birth," and so forth—from the time of birth, by virtue of dwelling together and not moving apart; the particle *eva* (only/even) is displaced in the sequence [of the verse]. "Together with me," that is, along with my mother, your own mother, you drank the milk from her breast (*payodhara-payaḥ*). By the word "even" (*api*), the principle of *kaimutika-nyāya* (the argument a fortiori) is introduced regarding the commonality of other objects of enjoyment; having drunk the milk in the past...

By the phrase "O Puṇḍarīkamukhī, with a face as radiant as a blooming lotus," he indicates: "The more I forcibly seize various objects of enjoyment, the more you rejoice; therefore, how can there be life for me who does not behold such a face of yours? [The suffix -tal is applied] according to the rule "from grāma, jana, bandhu, and sahāya, the suffix -tal [is used to denote a collection]. (Pāṇini 4.2.43). Bandhutayā means "by the group consisting of father and others."

According to [Pāṇini 4.2.43], the suffix *tal* is used in the sense of a collection (*samūha*). That which was "cast aside" (*nirasta*)—meaning discarded without prior deliberation due to the fear of transgressing the meaning of the scriptures because of being overwhelmed by grief—is "unfit" (*akāla-pravṛtta*) because it is improper to have acted at an inappropriate time.

"Nor did the elders perform the funeral rites for the children," according to the statement in the *Rāmāyaṇa*. "Alone, deprived of me, you drink the *nivāpa*—the *Amara-kośa* defines *nivāpa* as 'an offering to satisfy the ancestors'—that is, the water for libation, meaning that which has arrived from the other world; you drink it now, or will drink it (using the present tense to indicate immediate proximity). The particle *iti* denotes manner; this manner is improper, meaning it is untenable due to a lack of prior practice. Here, the poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) are *arthāpatti* (presumption) and *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic causality). //40//

Having released and dismissed Mādhava, [he stands] below—in the lower region—by which it is established that he has ascended to the mountain peak. Facing the Great River (Mahānadī) because of her power to grant the requested boon, he prays for his own desired object: "O Blessed One, endowed with all qualities such as sovereignty, O Āpagā, indeed a river!

Regarding 'of the beloved' and so forth: 'wherein,' that is, in whatever place there is the birth or origin of the beloved—at the end of this body, according to the Lord’s words: 'For death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died.'"

"There is nothing, O illustrious one, that turns back old age and death in all the worlds except for liberation, O lady of good vows"— from these words of Maheśvara, and from the [scriptural] statements regarding liberation, such as "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death" and "No other path exists for this journey," [it is established].

"By action a living being is bound, and by knowledge one is liberated"—since this is determined by hundreds of scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*) to be achievable through knowledge alone, it is stated that for one who abandons the body without the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the occurrence of assuming another body is certain in every respect. In the phrase "there too may there be for me," the particle *api* should also be connected here; [the meaning is: "in that very place, may there be for me also [the same]."

By the word *eva* (only), it is illuminated that if he should be born in hell due to the variety of karma, he alone would be my heaven. Furthermore, regarding *anusañcaraḥ*: he moves along after (*anu paścāt*) [the other]; he experiences association with that, thus he is an *anusañcara*. The suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). Here, the emotion (*bhāva*) of longing (*autsukya*) is suggested; the figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) is benediction (*āśīḥ*). //41//

The word *iti* marks the conclusion [of the previous thought]. The meaning is that she desires to leap from the mountain peak to descend into the river situated below, and thus she prepares herself by girding her loins and so forth. The word *sahasā* (suddenly) indicates her impulsive application toward favoring him without even thinking. *Saudāminī* is the Yoginī under discussion. By saying "having restrained her" (*vārayitvā*), meaning having seized her with her forehand and forbidden her [action], she addresses her as "child" (*vatse*)—thus indicating maternal affection while manifesting her own status as one whose word is not to be transgressed. The phrase "enough of this rashness" (*kṛtam alam sāhasena*) refers to acting without deliberation; the case ending is the third case (*tṛtīyā*) according to the rule beginning with *prakṛtyā*.

The word *atha* (now/then) serves to set aside the previous position. Whether I should commit this rash act or not, who are you? You are like a venerable teacher (*guru*) to us, having remained unknown to us for all this time; or perhaps you are a female ascetic (*liṅginī*) related to our parents—this is the meaning. For what purpose, for what motive, were we forbidden from committing this rash act? The word *kim* (what) is used here in a sense of reproach. Without the joy of fully knowing the story of Mālatī, Mādhava will not live.

"While he does not live, I shall not live. Therefore, what is the use of this futile effort—which is like bathing an elephant—without news of Mālatī that would extract the arrow [of my grief]? This is the sense. Then, wishing to give an answer in accordance with her intention and desiring to ascertain through questioning that which was already inferred by the characteristics described by Mālatī, he asks: "Api" (is it? is used in the sense of a question; "tvam" (you) refers to the one who is merely perceived [before him]; the meaning is: "Is this Makaranda—the one named Makaranda who was pointed out by Mālatī as being worthy of respect because he is the dear friend of Mādhava—the long-lived one?"

Again, acting with boldness, she says: "Release [me]," meaning "the restraint of my hands. He—Makaranda—being unfortunate and one whose merit is exhausted (*kṣīṇapuṇya*), indicates his own inability to bear witness to his friend's calamity.
She provides an answer by determining his name: "O Yoginī," thereby manifesting her own credibility through the power of her mastery in the practice of mantras, medicinal herbs, and other such means.

This is the answer to the question "Kāsī": the *mālatyabhijñāna* (the recognition token of the jasmine) is the mark given by Mālatī as proof of her own life; for the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states, "An *aṅka* is a mark or a token of recognition."

By stating "Mālatī’s recognition," it is understood that Mālatī first dispatched the Yoginī for the purpose of ascertaining this entire situation—since she had acted rashly herself, she feared her father and others and thus could not go to her father’s house; furthermore, because she did not know what her beloved was doing or where he was during her absence—rather than coming there herself along with her. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of an excessive complexity in the narrative construction.

"I hold him in my hand and carry him," he says; by this, he expresses his state of being beyond doubt, meaning that he does not say anything at all [other than this]. By this, the objection contained in the question "For what purpose? has been answered. Even upon seeing the *bakula* garland, he asks again because it is common to both life and death. The word *api* is used in the sense of a question: "Does he live? meaning "Does he maintain his vital breaths? Since the determination of life—which was initially considered utterly impossible—is now established, it is easy to subsequently ask further specific questions.

Now, what does "in that very way" mean? Fearing the consequence that there would be no opportunity for his own grace, she speaks despondently: *atyāhitam* means excessive suffering; it means the undesirable and unpleasant abandonment of life, because nothing is more cherished than one's own life by anyone. *Vyavasitaḥ* means he has resolved or determined to do it; the suffix *-ta* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari niṣṭhā*).

The syntactical connection is as follows: "I am trembling because of fear, my heart is agitated, for you have resolved upon something undesirable; what could that be so calamitous for Mādhava? The meaning is that without such a calamity, your resolution toward what is undesirable would be inexplicable. "Pramugdhaḥ" means fainted. By the word "eva" (only), it is revealed that his own effort toward death had already commenced even while he was merely left with his breath. "Vairāgyāt" means arrived at this place due to world-weariness arising from the perception of the impermanence of the body and other things. "Tūrṇam" means quickly. "Sambhāvayāvaḥ" means let us console him.

"By good fortune," that is, by the power of our luck; "one whose consciousness has returned"—according to Amara, *prekṣā*, *upalabdhi*, *cit*, *saṃvit*, *pratipad*, *jñapti*, and *cetanā* are synonyms; he is one whose consciousness—that is, knowledge—having fallen away from its own nature, has been regained.

It "corresponds," meaning it does not deviate; the bodily form of both Mādhava and Makaranda, as described by Mālatī, meaning the specific configuration of the body established through her description of complexion and other characteristics.

"Aye" expresses despondency. "Awakened" means having regained consciousness; the sense is that because the impression of his fainting persists even now, the effort of the one who awakened him was in vain—this is implied by the word "as it were" (iva). The phrase "by someone" is used because the specific person is unknown and because he is an object of aversion. He establishes what was inferred in general terms through reasoning upon a particular instance with the words "of this [person]."

"Because it fans [the fire]" (*vījamānatvāt*): this expresses the completeness of its awakening, as it has the nature of carrying forth the downpour of streams from fresh clouds—that is, the rain from new clouds—on all sides. "Of the wind" (*prabhañjanasya*): this is a reproachful statement, meaning that which thoroughly breaks or crushes the world; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent.

"Disregarding our condition" (*anavekṣitāsmadavasthaḥ*): by whom our state—either the experience of the bliss of fainting somehow regained, or the state of separation—is not observed. "Activity" (*vyāpāraḥ*): an undertaking consisting of the act of awakening.

Addressing him directly, he reproaches him: "O Blessed One, distinguished by unsurpassed knowledge—this was not done by you out of ignorance, but solely out of cruelty"; this is the meaning. For this very reason, he addresses him as "merciless" (*akaruṇa*) later on.

"Make them wander," and so forth—make them wander, that is, cause them to move about; [the phrase] "those whose wombs contain water" (*ambhogarbha*) indicates their inability to move on their own due to the weight of their burden. "Delight them" (*pramodaya*), meaning make them exceedingly joyful, because they are the cause for the multitude of clouds to appear; [the text refers to] *cātakas*, the *dhārāṭa* birds, for they too have you as their sole refuge. Alternatively, there is the reading "kokilas" (cuckoos); for it is well-known among great poets that these too experience joy during the rainy season, just as in spring. As Bhāravi says in his description of the monsoon:
"Though deeply distressed, [the cuckoo's] mind is captivated, thrilled by the consumption of ripe rose-apples and *jambu* fruits hanging from the branches."
"Make the young female cuckoos warble—a sound made charming by the fresh passion of their throats;

make the peacocks dance, for dancing is an effect of intense intoxication; make the *ketaka* flowers harden—that is, make them mature and cause them to bloom—for even they, having burst forth at the thundering of clouds and the flashing of lightning, reach their full development under your influence. [Note: The phrase "madaya tṛptān kuru" is interpreted as "make [them] intoxicated," with the sense of "cause them to dance" (*nartaya*), since dancing is an effect of excessive intoxication. "Kekotkaṇṭhān" refers to those whose necks are raised because they have greeted [the clouds] with their *kekā* cries, due to their natural friendship. "Kaṭhoraya" means "make hard," which here signifies "make ripe" or "cause to blossom," as the *ketaka* flowers reach maturity through the power of the clouds.]

The evidence for *ketaka* being used in the masculine gender (*pulliṅga*) is to be sought [elsewhere], as in: "The *ketaka* flower, possessing the luster of a bee and the hue of a deer, was perceived like the tusk of an elephant."

Because in such instances as these, the word is seen used specifically in the neuter gender (*ṣaṇḍatvena*); thus, the reading may be either *ketakīḥ* or *ketakam*. The verb form is in the imperative (*loṭ*) for the purpose of addressing or inviting. By specifying "in a person separated from a beloved" (*virahiṇi priyajanaviśleṣaviśiṣṭe jane*), rather than saying "in me" (*mayi*), the author indicates that this behavior is common to all people separated from their loved ones. By stating "having attained a swoon or delusion" (*mūrcchā moham labdhvā*), he suggests that the attainment of her, who had been long desired, is like the discovery of a great treasure.

The reason for this is as follows: "O, [you] divert" means you lead him toward that very thing. Having produced—that is, having brought about—the pain that is harsh like wallowing in the hollow of a fire, namely the disease of perception, which is a malady in the form of awakening due to the arousal of previously suppressed agony; what do you seek? What purpose do you intend? The meaning is: no purpose whatsoever will be achieved for you.

The sense is this: while the wandering of clouds and such phenomena possess purpose because they benefit the world, serve the interests of friends, and constitute their own nature (*svadharma*), this particular activity—being of the nature of an affliction to others—has only undesirable results. Here, resentment toward the wind is suggested; for it is shown that what is undertaken with the intention of helping not only lacks the quality of being helpful, but actually brings about harm. The figure of speech *viṣama* (the incongruous) is suggested. //42//

"Well done" (*sukṛtam*) means it has been beautifully performed; this is a praise out of joy because [it was accomplished] by the life-force of all living beings—that is, by the breath of every creature—[acting] as the wind (*mātariśvanā*).

The word "O God" (*deva*) illuminates the capacity for accomplishing what is desired. "Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) means: even though you have acted adversely, [I speak thus] because there is no other recourse.
"Blossoming," etc.: by the dust—that is, the pollen—of the cluster of *kadamba* flowers, the mass of *kadamba* blossoms.
"Samudāya means a collection, a cluster, or a multitude," according to the *Vaijayantī*. [The word] "saha" [indicates] ease in the act of seizing.

He said: "Take [it], lead [it] to where my beloved is—in that place. Or else, if out of compassion the taking of her life is not performed, then [lead it] to that which is cooled by the perfuming of her limbs; "perfuming" (parivāsa) means being scented by her limbs or their pervasive presence, and by that it is "cooled," meaning it removes the fever of passion, since it is logical that even what is in contact with her limbs becomes cool through the coolness of those limbs. The word "anything" (kiñcit) is used without specification, because everything of such a nature removes the fever of passion; thus, "send it" (īraya), cast it [there].

He states the reason for what was said with "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). The particle *tu* (but) serves to exclude others; the sense is that no one else has the capacity for this task. It is either the means of access (*gati-rūpa-upāya*) or the refuge (*śaraṇa*). Here, wretchedness (*dainya*) is suggested. The poetic figure is *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Praise), because the cause—the torment of separation—is revealed by way of its effect. //43//
With palms joined and both hands brought together, he bows; he prostrates himself like a staff upon the path before her.

"Well-composed" means perfectly concentrated, with the word "according to rule" (*vidhinā*) understood as the ellipsis. It also suggests "by the poet. "The occasion for the presentation of the token"—that is, the time for the giving of the bakula garland which serves as Mālatī’s identifying mark—"he releases" means he lets it fall quite indistinctly.

"With intent" means with a specific purpose, namely, intending to indicate that his beloved is alive. "With wonder and joy": wonder arises because [the garland] was delivered by the wind immediately after his prayer; joy arises because it serves as an inferential mark for the existence of his beloved. Accompanied by these two, the underlying thought is this: it would be heart-wrenching and inexplicable if the Blessed Wind-god were to deliver that identifying token, the Bakula garland, upon her destruction. "How? expresses astonishment.

This woman being seen here is the same one previously experienced, her form rendered arrogant and playful by the swelling of her breasts; she whose physical presence was made wanton by the rising of her bosoms, and who wore a garland of flowers from the *bakula* tree standing in the courtyard of the temple of the God of Love.

"Having correctly ascertained" means having examined it again minutely because its attainment was previously considered absolutely impossible. The word "kim" (what/how) is used in the sense of negation, meaning there is no room for doubt. He establishes that very point: the grammatical connection is "this very same division of hers."

"Like the charming moon," and so forth: regarding her face—which is as lovely as the charming (mugdha) and tender (komala) moon, beautiful and full of grace—in the play of gazing, that is, in the sport of looking at it, there was an unrestrained curiosity or eagerness; for the sake of concealing or hiding that, she arranged flowers in a disordered manner, a placement of blossoms made without due sequence, and thus they were unevenly strung together in a jagged composition.

The particle *api* suggests a contradiction by implying dissatisfaction, as it refers to the failure to fulfill what was begun [by saying "even"]. "Vibhāga" (division) means a portion separated from the previously knotted part; it "extended satisfaction" (*toṣaṃ tatāna*), that is, it produced joy. The root is *tanu* in the sense of "making. Furthermore, in this context, he recalls what was said before: that even though one part was unevenly fashioned due to his being distracted by gazing at Mālatī’s face, he nevertheless held it in high regard. Here, the figures of speech are *virodha* (contradiction) and *preyaḥ* (the pleasant). //44//

With joy and madness—joy arising from the recovery of the token of recognition, while madness persists—he rises up in such a state accompanied by both. Placing the garland in his joined palms, and believing his beloved to have vanished of her own accord for the sake of a jest, he says, "Mālati! Mālati! The repetition (*vīpsā*) reveals his joyful agitation. "This one"—meaning, she who stands right before him—"why are you not seen? The sense is: "What is the use of this effort to hide yourself? You are visible."

"Seeming as if with anger" means accompanied by anger, even though such anger was not manifested in her despite his own words. The word "seeming" (iva) indicates that, in reality, there was no anger; rather, because her behavior toward him proceeded from affection, it was not real. "O you who are unaware of my condition" means one who does not know my state, which is rendered wretched by extreme suffering.

Preceded by a report of her own condition, he reproaches her with irony, beginning with "as if departing" (*prayāntīva*), and so forth: "As if departing" (*prayāntī*) means as if going away, because all her vital organs (*marmans*) are being pierced. "As if perishing" (*dhvaṃsate*) means as if falling from her place, due to her lack of awareness of all things. "As if blazing" (*jvalanti*) means as if burning with fire, because she is seized by an irresistible and terrible fever. "Darkness spreads on all sides" (*samantāt tamo 'ndhakāraṃ prasarati*) means it proceeds everywhere, because of the uninterrupted state of fainting.

*Tvarā-prastāvaḥ* means the occasion for immediate engagement due to haste; *parihāsasya* means the scope or opportunity for sport. Therefore, grant—that is, bestow—joy upon my eyes through the manifestation [of your presence]. By saying "in me who has come to such a state," there is illuminated a state of total pitiability; do not be *akarunā*, devoid of compassion. Here, there is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the piercing and so forth are imagined as taking the form of the departure of life, as in the verse "Darkness, as it were, smears the limbs";
and there is also *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because the intensity of suffering is conveyed through a figurative turn of expression. //45//

Having looked everywhere in the bowers of creepers and other places out of fear of being hidden, [she speaks] with despondency—that is, accompanied by agitation due to not seeing them. "In this place, from what cause? means that my own delusion is the very root of that suspicion. By this—having placed the *bakula* garland in her joined palms—it is understood that Saudāminī and Makaranda have become invisible, as she wonders, "What will he do now?", and because their approach will be described later during the occasion of his fainting.

Recalling her supreme beneficence, she grieves, saying "without obstacle," and so forth. According to Amara, *vighna*, *antarāya*, and *pratyūha* are synonyms for "obstacle. The meaning is that prior to her full realization of my passion, they were "unimpeded"—that is, difficult to ward off due to the absence of any restrainer. She addresses her as "dear friend" (*priyasakhī*) because she is beloved by her dear one, and because she has performed the work of a friend—namely, providing consolation equal to life itself; this is the vocative case.

When, at a certain time, [the afflictions] became unbearable—unendurable due to the intensity of their pain—having arisen by fate, they were heavy with the calamity of the body’s burning; not only internally, but externally as well, they were difficult to bear due to the violent agony of the body's combustion. These were the onsets of the god of love—the unsurpassed torment and affliction—and its impulses, the expansions that produce fainting and other such states.

Embracing you is the application [of this medicine] to your heart by Lavaṅgikā, who has taken it from my hand; by the word "only" (eva), he expresses the absence of any other means of protection. The "preservation of life" (prāṇatrāṇa) is the medicine for protecting the vital breaths, according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*.

(3-3-113) The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), because it indicates my passion; "straight" (*praguṇam*) means direct (*sākṣāt*). He says it is "straight" because it was made by the hand of her most beloved one. "Almost like my embrace" (*matpariṣvaṅgakalpam*) means slightly incomplete due to my own embrace; the sense is that she had a mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) that she herself had embraced you, having placed me in between. He uses the verb *abhavat* to indicate that this occurred in the past. The *laṅ* (imperfect) tense is used to indicate a time not of today. The meaning is: "She is no longer seen now; you alone are seen. //46//

Having gazed with compassion and sorrow, and having looked closely and skillfully, he—recalling his previous experience—says, "producing bliss," and so forth. [These are] producers of supreme happiness; [the suffix *lyu* is applied] according to the rule: *nandigrahipacādibhyo lyuṇinyacaḥ*.

(3-1-134) Thus, the suffix *lyu* is used in the sense of the agent. "Kindling the fever of passion" means nourishing the burning of desire; "possessing the essence of intense affection" means being preponderant with the internally sprouted essence of love. "At various times" means by such modes as: sometimes as a reward (*pāritoṣika*), sometimes as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), sometimes as a stake in gambling and the like (*dyūtādiglaha*), and sometimes as a deposit (*nikṣepa*). "Marks of affection" are the signs of love; these were experienced through their coming and going.

I remember my goings and comings; now that these have become objects of memory, what could be more painful than this? This is the meaning. Here, memory is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), and the figure of speech is *preyaḥ* (the lovely). //47//
"In the heart" means on the chest.

Although it was made [there], because the source is unknown—that is, from Mālatī’s own hand, which is a direct token of recognition consisting of words written by her own hand; here, the word "own hand" (*svahasta*) refers by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to the mark alone—as in:
"Is it false that my beloved's own hand, marked with affection, has been taken away from you?"

This is according to the statement in the *Vikramorvaśīya*. Therefore (*tat*), do you consider this object in the form of a gain to be of the nature of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) or of the nature of illusion (*māyā*) and so forth? You reflect (*tarkayasi*) upon this. In what manner (*katham*) do you consider it? The word "iti" should be repeated; the meaning is: "What kind of form do you consider it to have, and from what person do you consider it to have come?"

He cuts through his doubt—this [gesture] is a dramatic indication (*abhinaya*) of that which stands before her. "Noble lady" (*āryā*) means auspicious, because she has rendered assistance without cause; "mistress of yoga" (*yogeśvarī*) illuminates both her venerability and her capacity for such aid. "Of the token of Mālatī" (*mālatyabhijñānasya*) excludes anything illusory or the like; the meaning is: "This very thing is what you experienced"—this is the answer to the question "Why? "The bringer" (*upanetrī*) refers to one who has brought this to our presence; the genitive case is used here with a *kṛt* suffix in the sense of the object, as in the *Kumārasambhava*: "The bringer of the rules of ritual, of water, and of sacrificial grass. "This is the bringer"—this is the answer to the question "How?"

"Having beheld her" means having seen her. "With compassion" means that his grief has increased due to the apprehension, "What will she say upon seeing this distinguished kinsman? Because she is an ascetic (liṅginī), she offers a salutation with joined palms (añjalibandha). The specific question, "Is she alive?", is asked because life is the very foundation of such an inquiry. By mentioning her being the "mistress of our lives," he implies that since our own existence depends upon hers, by speaking of her survival alone, the preservation of our lives will also be accomplished.

Knowing his intention, she gave a reply out of cleverness: "Take heart; be confident," meaning with respect to his life. By using the repetition [of the verb], she dispels his doubt. Then, once his heart was steadied by this consolation, she spoke clearly: "By good fortune—that is, through the favor of the gods—she whom you suspected otherwise is well-faring (*kalyāṇinī*), that is, auspicious (*maṅgalavatī*). And 'well-being' (*kalyāṇa*) consists of life, an unimpaired body, and the prospect of an imminent reunion."

Having sighed and become cheerful of heart due to that [news] being reliable, they said: "If he lives thus—meaning in every way and in full detail—what is this matter under discussion? What is the nature of Mālatī’s account? The sense is:

"This exists," as is understood from the context. Since the meaning of this matter was already known by you both previously, the implication is that only what follows this needs to be told. *Kapālapāṇiḥ* means one who has a skull in his hand; that is to say, a Kāpālika. *Vyāpāditaḥ* means killed.
According to the *Vaijayantī*, "killing (*vyāpādanam*) is indeed violence (*hiṃsā*)."

Having understood from the very beginning of her speech that she was about to utter what was to follow, he spoke with agitation and mental distress: "Desist! Turn back; [desist] from this further speech," is the ellipsis. By the repetition (*vīpsā*), the harshness of the words is indicated. The reason for the prohibition is: "The matter is known"—the meaning is that it has been understood by me through inference from your very proposal.
Not knowing clearly, he asks: "What kind of matter is known by you? Of what sort is it?"

He states the answer in brief: the word *kiṃ* is used in the sense of an objection, [meaning] "is another thing not another thing? She whose desire—her wish for a remedy for us—is fulfilled (*sakāmā*).
To reinforce the point already stated, she asks: *api* is used in the sense of an inquiry, meaning "in this way," "thus," or "how?
That is to say, *evaṃ* (thus) means *tathā* (in that manner), in whatever way it was known or understood by Vatsa Mādhava.

Having determined the facts of the matter, he reproaches the Creator: "This is painful; this is improper. The word "O" is used to draw the attention of the great multitude toward him. By means of repetition (*vīpsā*), the extreme impropriety of the situation is suggested.

He establishes this very point [of suchness] with the verse beginning "By the bed of night-lotuses," and so forth. By the phrase "by the bed of night-lotuses" (*kumudākareṇa kumudaṣaṇḍena*), its well-known qualities—such as being pure, soft, cool, and so on—are illuminated. By the phrase "the moonlight of the autumn moon" (*śaradinducandrikā*), which refers to the radiance of the full-moon endowed with all its qualities due to the absence of veils such as clouds, its capacity to gladden the world through its intensity, purity, and other traits is revealed. For the sake of the quality of loveliness, because of their meeting with a worthy counterpart, the bed of night-lotuses and the moonlight attain a state of unsurpassed beauty in relation to one another.

If, upon the appearance of moonlight, [the lotus] blooms, and upon its union with her, it becomes intoxicated by her beauty—should they then be joined and united, it would mean that "this person has performed a good deed" (implying *sukṛtam*); the particle *tu* serves as an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). But what kind of fate (*vidhi*) is this? Of what nature is it? It is an "unseasonable mass of clouds" (*akālameghavitati*); for since it is stated to belong to autumn, and the presence of clouds in autumn is logically inconsistent, the term refers to an "unseasonable" (*akāle*) or contrary time—the negative particle (*nañ*) here carries the sense of an opposite. As it is said: "The negative particle (*nañ*) is recorded to signify negation, existence, difference, similarity, contempt, smallness, separation, and also the opposite."

From this statement, it is understood that he "joined together" (*ayūyujat*)—that is, he brought about the expansion (*vitati*) of the clouds so that they were no longer visible to one another, as is well known to occur between them. This is the form derived from the root *yuj* (meaning "to join") in the aorist (*luṅ*) with the reduplication (*caṅ*). The meaning is that since this occurred, this rule [of the poet] is indeed to be censured like a madman, because it produced a contradiction with what preceded; this is conveyed by the interrogative particle *kim*, which expresses censure.

Here, there is the figure of speech *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description), because after first establishing the union of two heroes whose qualities are mutually compatible through a non-contextual matter, the contextual matter—the Creator—who proceeds of his own accord to obstruct that very union, is perceived through its similarity; or else, it is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because of the identification (*adhyavasāna*) of the contextual matter with a similar matter through the process of swallowing up (*nigīrya*). //48//

Then, having ascertained that she had indeed been killed by Kapālakuṇḍalā out of resentment for the murder of her guru, he, overcome by love, laments: "Alas! (he says). The sense is: "Alas" (*kaṣṭam*) signifies hardship; "most loathsome" (*atibībhatsam*) means extremely disgusting. The meaning is that the death of you, who are a mass of great fortune, from the hands of a Kāpālikī—like [the death] of Kapilā from the mouth of a tigress—is utterly contemptible.
[The term *bībhatsa* arises from the verbal root *badh* with the suffix *san*, forming the word *bībhatsā*;
that object toward which there is such loathing is called *bībhatsa*.]

"That state which is censurable, blameworthy, and contemptible is designated by the term 'vībhatsa' (the loathsome) by the wise," so says the *Bhāvaprakāśa*. You have "āpannā" means you have "prāptā" (attained).

Anticipating the misery of that situation, he says, "How indeed," and so forth. By the term "lotus-faced one" (*kamalamukhī*), he indicates that your face—distinguished by such grace and beauty—is now burning me as it is imagined to be characterized by trembling eyes and other such traits when this unsurpassed fear has arrived.

"Seized by Kapālakuṇḍalā"—meaning attacked in order to be devoured—at that time, how did you exist? In what manner did you remain? That manner was beyond the reach of speech or mind; the sense is that it was experienced by you alone. It was like a streak of smoke from a portentous omen (*utpātadhūmalekhā*)—a line of comets indicating calamity for the world.

As was previously stated: "...like a pure digit of the moon eclipsed by the eightfold smoke-grasper. Alternatively, the meaning is that you were swallowed by the smoke of the Fire of Time (*kālānala*) blazing at the dissolution of the universe.
As stated in the *Setubandha*: "Like the peak of Mount Meru polished smooth, facing the sun, it is a mass of rising dust.

Through this simile, the Kāpālikī’s quality of being a cause of terror to all people and the heroine’s quality of being pitiable to all sensitive hearts (*sahṛdaya*) are conveyed. Here, the emotion (*bhāva*) known as apprehension (*śaṅkā*) is manifested. The poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is Simile (*upamā*). //49//
Turning toward the sky with the hope for the life of her beloved, she prays: "O Venerable One.

She seeks to win her over by saying, "This is unbecoming of you," and so forth: "It is a creation," etc. "Creation" refers to the work of the Creator. The word "that" (*tat*) is a reflection upon the experience of its possession of all excellent qualities. By the particle *eva* (only/indeed), it is revealed that she is worthy of being cherished with care and worthy of being honored with great respect merely by the sight of her due to her very nature. Alternatively, the particle *eva* is displaced in order; [the meaning is: "We may indeed have offended against you, but let there be a remedy provided by you."
Nevertheless, that creation must indeed be cherished with respect, due to the inherent nature of things;
for "a position is established everywhere by means of virtues."

The sense is that, according to this principle, our relationship need not be considered there. Therefore, do not become a *pūtanā*; for you, who possess discernment, ought not to enter the state of flesh-eating *piśācas* who lack discrimination. Be her *śivatātiḥ*, the bestower of welfare; for Halāyudha says, " *śivatātiḥ* means one who brings auspiciousness. [This is derived from] the root *as* (to be) in the imperative, second person singular, where by the rule *ghvasoreddhāvabhyāsalopaśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.119), the change to *e* occurs, and by *hujhalbhyo herdhiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.101), *dhi* replaces *hi*.

(6-4-102) Thus, there is also the substitution of *dhi* for *hi*. He supports the well-known fact indicated by the word *hi*: "Inherent" (*naisargikī*) means belonging to that which is innate (*nisarga*), namely one's own nature (*svabhāva*). For a fragrant flower—one whose scent satisfies the sense of smell—it is established and well-known in the world that its "position on the head" (*mūrdhni sthitiḥ*) is its being worn upon the crown of the head. "Beatings with pestles" (*musalaiḥ avatāḍanāni*) refers to firm blows administered with clubs used as the instruments for threshing rice and other grains.

The sense is that even though a flower remains after one's own pleasure, no sane person would crush it with pestles and clubs unless they were placing it upon their head. The word "siddhāni" (perfected/accomplished) undergoes a change in gender and number; by using the plural, it is suggested: if even a single blow is improper, how much more so a series of blows? Here, the figure of speech is *Arthāntaranyāsa* (Corroboration), because a particular instance is supported by a general principle. //50//
He dispels that apprehension through reasoning: "Enough with this agitation of the mind born from the fear of her death.

Regarding the phrase "she would have done," etc.: she would have done; she will do; she is the one under discussion, desiring such retaliation for the enmity; she is evil, meaning she would have committed an undesirable act; she is exceedingly merciless, meaning her compassion has been utterly cast away—the particle *eva* (indeed) here implies that this is her habitual nature; "I would not have been" means I would not have been present there on Śrīparvata as an adversary—that is, as an opponent to that sinful cause.

Here, the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* is used when there is a cause for the conditional (*liṅ*), provided that there is a failure of action (*kriyātipatti*). The "cause for the conditional" refers to the relation of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumattā*) and so forth; "failure of action" means non-occurrence due to the intervention of a contrary action. In this case, the failure of the sinful act—which is the cause—becomes manifest due to a deficiency in the cause, namely the absence of its own presence [the speaker]. Here, the poetic figure is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic causality), because the reason for the prohibition of agitation is presented as the meaning of the entire sentence. //51//

"Having prostrated" (praṇamya): although she was previously a female ascetic (liṅginī), because she had not performed the customary salutation due to the force of her agitation, the meaning here is that she now bows down because her mind has become composed and out of an excess of great respect. "By the venerable Āryā's feet" (āryāpādaiḥ): [she is called] "Āryā" because she is worthy of honor; the word "feet" (pāda) at the end of the name signifies one who is venerable, according to the rule "the word *pāda* may also denote a deity or a lord. "Favor has been bestowed upon us" (prasannaṃ... asmadviṣaye): this is a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), meaning that grace has been shown toward us.

Therefore, the word "again" (*punar*) implies exclusion: at this time, no other resident has been seen; but you—what kind of relationship do you maintain? The meaning is: is it a relationship by learning or by birth? The reason for this question is that he is his sole kinsman, his primary relative, because he performs the duties of one.

Fearing that revealing now the connection with Kāmandakī— which, together with the minister’s secret pledge, will become manifest in her very presence and serve as a cause for the highest wonder— would result in a disruption of the aesthetic flavor (*rasabhaṅga*), he conceals it through a clever artifice:
"When questioned about all matters of news, he told the king nothing of his lineage,
by the command of the first poet who was to make [the story] famous in due time."

Thus it is stated in the *Raghuvamśa*. This—that which consists of the state of intoxication—will be known, that is, it will become understood. Then, Mādhava, having been led into her presence by the power of his magic science (*vidyā*), consoled Mālatī; and accompanied by her, with the intention of consoling his kinsmen who had been brought there, he says: "Having risen, having flown up into the sky; she who was bound by your affection."

Regarding the phrase "gurucaryā" and so forth: *gurucaryā* is service rendered to gurus—that is, to the various teachers of the sciences; *tapaḥ* is the purification of the body through ascetic practices such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*; *tantra* is medicine; *mantrāḥ* are the five-syllabled [mantra] and others; *yoga* is the application of the means for restraining the fluctuations of the mind through the eight limbs beginning with *yama*; *abhiyoga* is the persistent application toward these, from which [the power] is born—meaning, that which has become fully integrated.

Although service to the guru (*gurucaryā*) is the root of all practices beginning with austerity (*tapas*), it is mentioned separately to indicate that even without those [other practices], one may attain unsurpassed power through the grace of the guru alone—as in the case of Ekalavya and others—let alone when accompanied by them. *Tantra* [is used] in the senses of: primary principle, established doctrine, weaving, clothing, scripture, medicine, the chief [organ], and the performance of sacrificial rites.

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*. By the words "this" (*imām*), he indicates that the fruit is visible even at this very moment. "Attracting" (*ākṣepiṇīm*) means drawing [it] toward oneself; that is to say, it causes one to reach another place from one's current location. "Accomplishment" (*siddhim*) refers to the attainment of the fruit of knowledge. "I extend" (*ātanomi*) means I spread it out in every direction. "For your welfare" (*śivāya*) means for the pacification of the misfortunes of all those connected with *Mālatīmādhava*. Here, the poetic figure is *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Praise of the Unrelated), because the two causes—affection and compassion—are revealed by way of their effect. //52//
Samādha, together with Mādhava, departed for the purpose of proceeding to Śrīparvata.

Then, filled with wonder at the sight of the power of that science (*vidyā*), he said: "Like a confluence," and so forth. A *vyatikara* is a mingled mixture; it is *bhīma*, terrifying; *tāmasa*, pertaining to darkness, because its form is indistinct; and *vaidyuta*, pertaining to lightning, because only a flash of a mass of radiance is perceived. Having arisen—that is, having emerged—for a moment, which is a fraction of time, such that the activity or function of the eyes is obstructed, it then subsides and disappears.

The remainder [of the thought] is that it is some kind of phenomenon like the mingling of darkness and lightning. "With fear" means accompanied by fear due to the apprehension of misfortune. "In this place," meaning in this spot, "no friend"—that is, no companion—is seen; how is this? This expresses wonder. Therefore, "what is this?"—this refers to the present object; "what is it? expresses doubt: is it a dream, or an illusion (*māyā*), or perhaps a deception employed by this yoginī with whom I was previously unacquainted? Having reflected and examined, what else could it be?

The word *kiṃ* is used in the sense of negation, meaning "nothing else imagined by us exists. In response to the inquiry "What else [could it be]?", he says: she "prevails," meaning she exists as the most excellent sovereign (*prabhu*). By her own majesty, which is unique and not shared by others—that is, by the power of her knowledge—she is a "mistress of yoga" (*yogeśvarī*), the sovereign of yoga consisting of both action and knowledge; thus, her status as a trustworthy authority (*āpta*) is implied. By the use of the pronoun "this one" (*iyam*), her state of being directly perceptible through acts such as the presentation of the token of recognition from Mālatī, and her appearance as someone to be relied upon, are illuminated.

Here, the mental states of fear and anxiety are perceived. This is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the sudden attraction of the hero by the goddess of the weapon—herself difficult to behold—is fancied as being like the disappearance of her own form through its intermingling with darkness and lightning, just as in the case of the phrase "terrible like a confluence. This is similar to dramatic representation (*citrābhinaya*), since it has been stated that such [representations] are to be learned from both the primary manual (*hasta*) and the secondary manual (*upāṅga*). //53//

Furthermore, "with reflection" (savitarkam) means accompanied by deliberation due to being distressed by affection for a friend. Therefore (tat), because a companion is not seen here and her trustworthiness is inferred, I am bewildered—unable to reach a decision—as to whether this current event is beneficial (artha), or harmful (anartha), that is, contrary to one's interest; such is the sense.

Having considered the agitation of the mind arising from the power of delusion, he says: "Moreover—'astokavismayam' and so forth. "Astokavismayam" means one for whom there is no small amount of wonder—an extraordinary sense of amazement produced by the sight of the power of [Mādhava’s] knowledge. "Avismṛtam" means that which has not been forgotten, having ascended to the intellect; namely, Mādhava’s previous history, such as his madness resulting from the loss of Mālatī, which is being contemplated like the events of a dream. "Udbhūtena" means increased. "Bhayajvareṇa" refers to a great malady in the form of apprehension—"What will happen?"—arisen after Mādhava’s disappearance. "Jarjaram" means shattered into a thousand pieces.

In a single moment, he was broken and shattered; yet, by the thought that he would recover through skillful means, he was reassembled and joined back together. Furthermore, due to the fear of falling again into the lower realms (*apāya*), there was a stupor or fainting.

Amidst this, while he was in his final state, because he was comforted by a Yoginī who appeared unexpectedly to him, and because Mādhava was sent to bring Mālatī, his state of being variegated—meaning possessing various colors—is indicated through metonymy as being distracted by manifold emotional transformations, caused by grief and the pain of separation from his friend. Here, the figure of speech is *bhāva-śabalatva* (the mingling of emotions). //54//

Therefore, because the mind will find its suffering bearable through shared companionship in the presence of kinsmen, we shall follow the venerable Kāmandakī into this dense forest thicket near the Bṛhaddroṇī mountain—wherein "kāntāra" means an impassable path (according to Amara)—and having reached her by searching for her within this wilderness, she, being capable of discernment, shall serve as the authority for determining what is beneficial and what is harmful.

He reveals [this]—namely, the arrival of the Yoginī and the bringing of Mādhava; by the words "I shall tell," the ornament of the assembly of poets (the author) indicates the entrance of Kāmandakī and the others at the beginning of the subsequent act. Thus, all is most auspicious.
Thus, by the grace of Pūrṇajyotis, Pūrṇasarasvatī has composed this exposition on the subject matter of the ninth act of the *Mālatīmādhava*.
Thus ends the ninth act.
Now begins the tenth act.
Now, the great poet [states]:
"The prologue to an act (*aṅkāsyam*) is [presented] by the characters at the end of the preceding act, because it indicates the subject matter of the interrupted act."
Thus, with the introduction of the characters indicated by the *aṅkāsyaka* (the end of the act), he describes their entrance with the words "Then enters," and so forth.

To avoid the defect of a lack of rasa, he connects the principal sentiment (*aṅgin*) with the words "Alas, my child," and so forth. "O you who adorned my lap, you who produced the excellence of beauty through your constant presence—where are you? In what place do you dwell? This is an answer in the form of consolation for me as I lament.

"From birth," and so forth. From birth—that is, beginning from the time of birth—her movements, which were charming with particular distinctions at every moment, delightful by manifesting an excellence of qualities in every instant, and which consisted of bodily activities such as walking, laughing, and so on; those various [actions] are indicated here as being beyond description and within the range of direct experience. Her endearments—those pleasant words requested for the sake of play, union, and so forth—which were lovely, sweet, heart-pleasing, and refined, have now been recollected, having come within the range of memory.

They burn the body—that is, the physical frame—by generating a great fever. The reason for this is that they tear apart the heart, meaning they split the mind like a saw. Therefore, the burning of the body has its root in the torment of the heart. Here, the poetic figures of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) and *preyaḥ* (the pleasant) are employed. //1//

Again, remembering [the child] in another way, he says "aniyata" and so forth: "In which there is unregulated weeping and smiling"—because it is not preceded by intentional thought, and because it is interspersed at intervals due to the nature of a child, the weeping (*rudita*)—that is, crying—and the smiling (*smita*)—that is, laughter—are "unregulated" (*aniyata*), meaning devoid of fixed order; and in which the tips of a few—that is, limited, tender, and soft—"bud-like teeth" (*dantakuḍmala*), that is, sprouts of teeth, "shine forth" (*virājanti*), meaning they are beautiful, their "summits" being such because they have not yet fully emerged.

The "lotus-face" (*vadanakamalaka*) refers to the form of the face, which is like a young lotus; the suffix *-ka* is used here in the sense of "smallness" or "endearment," referring to the infant state of a suckling. His "prattle" (*jalpita*)—that is, his speech—is such that the syllables falter, meaning they proceed otherwise than intended, being inconsistent because they are governed by his own invented conventions, such as saying "cloth" for a "pot" or "fruit" for a "flower. Thus, it transcends worldly usage and is both charming (*mañju*) and sweet (*madhura*). In this verse, the poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) are *Rūpaka* (Metaphor) and *Preyaḥ* (The Pleasant). //2//
The others [say]: "O Madayantika and Lavangika! Alas, O beautiful one with a moon-like face ever serene, where are you?

What is this transformation brought about by the perverse play of fate that has befallen the jewel of your body while you were all alone? 'Serene' (suprasanna) means free from any alteration such as anger; 'moon-like face' (mukhacandra);
'beautiful one' (sundari)."

"O Śobhanā! The word 'or' (*vā*) indicates an alternative. Because the jewel in the form of her body is superior to all other bodies, it is called a 'divine jewel. Its 'misfortune' is its wicked activity; its 'consequence' is its ripening. What kind of consequence? Since she has been out of sight for so long, her destruction is already certain. The meaning is: what is the nature of that destruction—is it caused by divine forces (*ādhidevika*), or by elemental beings (*ādhibhautika*)? By saying 'alone,' the implication is that if she had experienced this together with us, it would not have been so painful."

O illustrious Mādhava! The great festival of this world of living beings has arrived and yet has already set; it has come to pass and vanished at that very moment, not remaining for even a brief time—a festival in which there was unsurpassed bliss characterized by the attainment of one’s most beloved. "Illustrious" (*mahābhāga*) means fortunate; the implication is that even the public acclaim of "Mādhava" has become a mere falsehood. "The world of living beings" (*jīvaloka*) refers to the world of humans.
Alas, my two children, Mālatī and Mādhava!

"Unseen and fresh," and so forth. "Fresh" (*abhinava*) means unrestrained because it is not stale, or else it refers to that in which the essence of passion (*rāgarasa*)—the savor of mutual love—has never before been seen elsewhere.
Regarding the term *rāga*: "Passion (*rāga*) [is found] in attachment, lac, and so on.
Regarding the term *rasa*: "Essence (*rasa*) [is found] in attachment, poison, potency, the bitter and other tastes, mercury, and liquid."

"Regarding *retasyā*, *svādane*, *hemni*, *niryāse*, and the two words for *amṛta*," so says the *Vaijayantī*. This embrace (*pariṣvaṅga*), which is an *āśleṣa* (clasp) that has aroused longing—thinking, "When will it happen that we have fulfilled our curiosity regarding you, both of you [the husband] and your ladyship?"—is present in our minds. Furthermore, as it is said: "Now, *śyāmalakā*, *lālā*, *lavalī*, and *lāvalī* are synonyms for the fruit."

"Lavaṅga, devakusuma, śrī, and varālaka"—thus says the Vaijayantī lexicon. By the phrase "like those two," the simile reveals that separation is a thorn in the hearts of the sensitive (sahr̥daya). "Destiny" (niyati) means fate; struck by destiny as if by a great whirlwind (maṇḍalīvāyu), he is forcibly oppressed. Here, wretchedness is suggested. The figure of speech is Upamā (Simile). //3//
O you whose hopes are destroyed! O you whose heart is made of adamant!
No, [it is] not a heart made of adamant.

"O, you are utterly cruel! You for whom there is the hope, 'I shall live beyond this point even though I am struck down and rendered fruitless'—you who possess a thunderbolt-like mace due to its extreme hardness! The sense is that, in every way and by every means, you do not take into account even one among our long-standing intimacy, our mutual respect, or our constant companionship. 'Cruel' (nṛśaṃsa) means devoid of affection for kinsmen; that is, merciless."

Striking her chest with both hands, she falls to the ground and prostrates herself like a staff in order to roll about. Lavaṅgikā: Indeed, I say to you: take heart for even a moment! By saying "for even a moment," the intention is that once the truth is ascertained after a moment, we shall subsequently abandon all our lives. "Take heart" means do not strike yourself and so forth.
Mother! What shall I do?

"Life, immovable due to its being bound by a firm adamantine cement—a specific kind of binding substance—does not abandon me. O Mother! 'Amba' is an address made with piteous entreaty. What else can I do other than striking myself and so forth? The meaning is that this very means of abandoning life must be diligently practiced. The reason for this is as follows: life, being immovable from its own place and free from slipping because of the bond formed by a firm adamantine cement (vajralepa), does not abandon itself; it does not release me of its own accord."

"You do not show compassion for this wretched, pitiable woman whose life is departing—whose vital breaths are escaping—as she is about to die (using the present participle *śānac* from the root *āṅ* meaning 'to go'); you do not make her a possessor of stable life by revealing yourself. He establishes her very state of being pitiable: "For (*hi*), because of this reason, this is Lavaṅgikā."

"Ujjvala," and so forth. By "ujjvalālokayā" (with a brilliant light), she is described as having radiant beauty and great splendor; "snigdhā" means possessing firm affection, while [in the secondary sense] it means soaked in oil. "Malīmasamukhī" means having a face discolored by dejection, while [in the secondary sense] it means having a tip soiled with ink. "Vartiḥ" means a wick, and "daśā" means a fringe; "pradīpaśikhayā" means by the flame of a lamp. The word "yathā" is used in the sense of "iva" (like). Here, the poetic figure is *arthaśleṣa* (semantic punning). //8//

"And how?"—the word "ca" (and) has the sense of "api" (even). "How can you even abandon Kāmandakī?"—the meaning is: "In Lavaṅgikā and the others, there is merely affection for a friend; but in me, because motherhood, respectability, and friendship coexist (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), I am the object of affection, high esteem, and confidence. Thus, my superiority over them is indeed established. Therefore, even in a dream, the abandonment of me is unthinkable. By saying "Kāmandakī" and not "me," he suggests the experience of her as possessing such distinguished affection.

He establishes that very point: "Indeed, in the case of a contradiction—O pitiless one! O you devoid of compassion for the distressed! By the warmth of the hem of my robe—that is, by the heat of the fringe (*daśā*) of the robe belonging to me, because it was held and placed incessantly upon your lap; having wiped [them] with that, meaning by making them moist with sweat; they were made smooth (*praguṇīkṛtāni*), that is, rendered beautiful, since even in childhood the physical grace of infants is maintained by their kinsmen.
As it is said in the *Daśakumāracarita*: 'From the birth of his daughter onwards, the care of her limbs...'"

And because of the summary statement, "Sweat is the cause of softness," he again expresses the impropriety of his own abandonment by manifesting his affection: "stanyanyāsād" (from the giving of breast milk). By this, starting from the relinquishing of the mother's breast-milk (*stanya*), he indicates that the nurse alone acted as a mother, performing even the mere act of suckling. According to Amara, "pāñcālikā" means a doll (*putrikā*). "Danta" refers to ivory, well-known from such usages as "bearing ivory teeth" (*dantaśapharukadhāriṇī*) and "ivory doll" (*dantaputrikā*); thus, it refers to dolls and the like made of ivory.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), activities such as playing with balls, heavy stones, molasses, and water-jars are included; the "application of means" (*yoga*) refers to the employment of methods for mastery in those games and diversions. Thereafter, having passed childhood, the meaning is that she entered into youth. Because she was a jewel among women, her teachers trained her in discipline (*vinaya*)—namely, in the sixty-four arts including dance, song, and instrumental music, in the sciences that are branches of the *Kāmasūtra*, and in the *Kāmasūtra* itself. Furthermore, because she was a Brāhmaṇī and the daughter of a minister, they trained her in the treatises on Dharma and Artha, saying:
"The teachers disciplined him (her), who was dear to his (their) elders."

This is because of the statement in the *Raghuvamśa* and the words of Kāmandaka: "Discipline (*vinaya*) is the certainty derived from the scriptures. The term "attained" (*prāpitā*) is connected to both [the girl and the woman]. Regarding this, the Teachers (*Ācāryas*) maintain: "A man should study the *Kāmasūtra* and its auxiliary sciences (*aṅgavidyā*) before his youth; a young woman, before her marriage; and a married woman, according to the will of her husband. Since it is impossible for women to grasp the scriptures [themselves], the instruction of women in this treatise is useless. Vātsyāyana, however, says: "[It is not useless] because they learn the practical application (*prayoga*), and that application is preceded by the scripture."

"An instructor for young girls may be a foster-sister, an elderly female slave, a female mendicant, or a sister"—and as stated in the *Kāmasūtra*: "For there are indeed courtesans, princesses, and daughters of high-ranking mothers whose intellects are trained in the technical treatises. By this, the eligibility of both her [the teacher] and herself in the mastery of the science is demonstrated. You have been nurtured—meaning you were raised—with foods and specific medicinal preparations that produce beauty, grace, gentleness, strength, intelligence, and good fortune. "Among the best in the world," meaning those who are preeminent according to worldly standards or within the world.

The reason for this is as follows: she was established with a husband who possesses virtues such as noble lineage; the suffix *matup* here denotes excellence. She was settled with a superior husband through the prior application of the methods taught in the scriptures, by increasing her affection so that she remained free from change until the end of her life. By the phrase "by me alone," it is illuminated that in every undertaking I did not even take account of my father or others, because they were merely servants at my command. Therefore, the pronoun *tat* (in *tena*) refers back to the entire meaning of the sentence in its totality.

And because of the fact that "I have done this for you in such a manner," for that reason, your affection toward me is even greater than toward your own mother; the meaning is that it exceeds even the love directed toward one's biological mother. [This is an example of] the ablative case in the sense of distinction (*vibhakta*).

(2-2-42) Thus [the word *ucitaḥ*] is in the ablative case. By the phrase "affection is appropriate and fitting toward those who are dear to one's own sphere," it is suggested that affection is proper toward those who are beloved, and not hatred. Therefore, the reproach, "Hence you are ungrateful," is implied; the connection is: "For this reason, why do you even abandon Kāmandakī? Here, the figure of speech is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), because the cause—the intensity of affection—is revealed through the effect; and there is also *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic causality), because the reason for not abandoning her is presented in an indirect manner. //5//

"With despondency" means with its fortitude cast out by the contemplation of hopelessness, as is the case now since not even a mere report has been obtained. "Despairing" means having abandoned all longing for the desires previously formed. He asks, "What were those desires? and answers with the words beginning with "without cause": "by affection without cause," meaning without prior intention; or rather, by natural affection, because childhood is so charming that it is unknown whether it involves love or sorrow. Alternatively, it refers to one whose face is charming on account of me through natural affection, manifesting favor by means of gentle smiles and the like.

He is one upon whose crest, head, and forehead white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*)—golden in color—are placed for the sake of protection, as described in the *Harṣacarita*: "When the mustard seeds of protection were placed upon his head, they appeared like a mass of sparks from the fire of his burgeoning majesty. He is one who sleeps on the lap (*aṅkaśāyī*), meaning he is accustomed to resting upon the chest—as the *Vaijayantī* states: "The word *aṅka* denotes a mark, the interior, or the breast"—or else he dwells in the lap, as seen in such usages as "moving from lap to lap" (*aṅkādaṅkaṃ sañcarantī*).

"By one whose fortune has turned and whose merit has changed, but not by one devoid of fortune"—the sense is that because you previously experienced, from birth until the conclusion of marriage, such a great festival, it is only now that the suffering which is the fruit of evil karma is being recognized. "Tanayaḥ" means son; "stanandhayaḥ" means one who drinks breast-milk. [This is based on the rule: *nāsikāstanayordhmādheṭoḥ*.

(3-2-29), thus [the suffix] *khaś*. Here, first there is the longing for the mere sight of a son; then, by way of restating that [longing] as being qualified by his specific attributes according to that state [of the mother], he reveals the manifold nature of such desires, like the prayer of an old maiden for a husband: "May my sons eat with ghee and milk. In this instance, the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state). //6//

"O Blessed One! Be gracious. I am now unable to sustain my life. Therefore, having cast myself down from this mountain precipice, I shall find peace. Be gracious; favor me with your permission. 'Unable' means powerless at present, due to the extreme intensity of my suffering, to sustain my life—that is, to maintain the breath of life. Since I am thus unable, [I shall do so] from this mountain precipice, from the edge of the cliff standing before me. According to the *Vaijayantī*, 'prapāta' refers to a slope or a precipice (*bhṛgu*)."

The fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used here in the sense of *lyablope* (the elision of a suffix ending in *lyap*), meaning "having ascended the precipice" (*prapātamāruhya*). Alternatively, it means "having cast herself down" (*avadhūya*), that is, having abandoned her body by falling; thus, the fifth case is used simply in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*), meaning "having cast herself down from the mountain precipice. "Nirvṛtā" means happy.
"With joy" (*saharṣam*) implies that she felt satisfaction even while imagining consent for what was actually a prohibition.

"Compassionately" (*sadayaṃ*) means with pity, due to seeing her particular state of distress, looking at Lavaṅgikā—this is the implied object. The vocative "O child" (*vatse*) is used with the intention of saying, "Restrain her."

Interpreting that intention otherwise, in accordance with his own desire, he says: "What do you command? Be my forerunner. [She replies: "I am attentive. [He explains: "Be my forerunner; proceed yourself before her toward death. "What do you command?"—the word *kim* (what) is used here in the sense of a question, meaning "command me. The plural number is used because it refers to a superior. "Attentive" means respectful toward what has been commanded. When she too has resolved upon death, he speaks to her in order to dissuade her: "Friend, be gracious; act upon my words. Desist from this self-slaughter. Desist means turn back."

The suffix *parasmaipada* is applied according to the rule *vyāṅparibhyo ramaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.43). By the phrase "from her own destruction," he reminds her of the great abundance of sin [incurred by such an act], in accordance with the Smṛti: "I see no expiation by which she might be purified along with me. Having ascertained that she intends to take her own life in order to force him to speak, he says: "Do not forget these people"—meaning both Mālatī and himself. Having understood her intention, he speaks with anger—that is, with jealousy: "How can she, who is herself striving for her own death, restrain me? For the affection between friends is equal for both."

The sense is based on the maxim: "When the fault is equal for both parties, or the remedy is likewise equal, neither should be subjected to censure in such an inquiry into the matter. The word *iva* (as if) suggests that the anger is not real (*atāttvika*), as it was produced merely out of affection. *Apehi* means "go away" or "depart. *Vaśam gatā* means "come under the sway [of control]. The meaning is: "I am not under your control; I will not do as you say."

"Hanta" expresses dejection. "The wretched one"—meaning the pitiable one—has resolved upon death, being certain of it out of affection for her friend. By this, she indicates the excellence of her friendship previously described in the words: "Through dwelling in the same house and playing together in the dust, you have been called my dear friend."

Then, by way of artful expression, the poet connects with the intended sentiment (*rasa*): "O Lord Makaranda, salutations to you! [This is an utterance directed toward the sky, establishing a visual focus. You are following Mādhava in death, and I am following Mālatī; therefore, since I cannot live while you are dead, I shall die. Thus, the meaning is: "I entreat you so that the fault of acting independently does not accrue to me. "Venerable lady! This very mountain peak has its slopes purified by the confluence of the streams of the Madhumatī river. [The word "this" (*ayam*) refers to what is perceived.]

He states the commentary: "Madhumatī" refers to the great river previously introduced; [the mountain] has a sacred girdle-like slope (*mekhalā*) on its bank due to the flowing of that river's current. "Mahīdharaviṭaṅkaḥ" means a ruggedly elevated region of a mountain;

*viṭaṅka* is a rugged peak, as seen in the usage by Bhartṛhari in his *Kāvya*: "From whose houses there shine forth, as if from the peaks of the Himālaya, images of the falling waters of the eight Ganges."

Now, because there is no remedy for consolation, the meaning is that we cannot prevent the intended self-sacrifice—which has been set in motion by Lavaṅgikā and Madayantikā—due to its feasibility. The sense is: "We do not stop it because of an obstacle or impediment. It is said that all of them, including Kāmandakī, have resolved upon death due to their shared suffering; the meaning is that they desire to quickly gird their loins and ascend a mountain peak.

The stage manager (naipathyapātra) indicates that the Yoginī has employed her magical arts (*vidyā*) to bring back Mādhava—who had been carried away by the power of those very arts—to be reunited with Mālatī: "A marvel! A marvel! Such a convergence..."

X 53) "ivetyādi" (page 538). Having heard that, he looked toward that direction, wondering, "What is this? and said with a mixture of wonder and joy—due to seeing the power of a science never seen before, and due to seeing the unexpected union of Mālatī and Mādhava—he was filled with amazement and bliss. "Here, in this place, my two children, my offspring Mālatī and Mādhava, are seen"—this is the ellipsis. "How? expresses astonishment. "Therefore, what is this present matter? is the reflection.

He refutes that thought through a change of expression. Makaranda enters and says, "What else... and so forth. By this, it is indicated by implication that what was spoken as a stage direction (*naipathyokti*) is also the speech of Makaranda himself. Furthermore, this connects with what was previously stated: "Therefore, having followed the Blessed Lady who has entered this dense forest with our group, I shall relate this account. Because the speaker is the same and there is no difference in the performance (*prayoga*), the very same verse mentioned earlier is employed here. //7//

Now, intending to bring about unsurpassed happiness and, in order to produce its aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), the poet introduces a new subject to demonstrate the ultimate limit of suffering—since the hero of the play is one whose attainment of happiness is fraught with peril—by saying, "Behind the scenes" (*naipathye*);
"public rumor" (*janavāda*) refers to hearsay.

He demonstrates the very nature of public rumor with the words "mālatyapāyam" and so forth. "Apāyam" means the departure, the disappearance, or the destruction of Mālatī; having "adhigamya" it, that is, having known it, his mind becomes dispassionate (*viraktacetāḥ*), meaning his heart is devoid of affection. This implies he has become despondent (*nirviṇṇaḥ*) through reflecting on [the world's] impermanence, its resulting in suffering, and so on. Regarding the phrase "among worldly things" (*sāṃsārikeṣu*), the sense of "pertaining to this life" (*aihikatvam*) is established here by implication; otherwise, detachment from life itself would be untenable. If one seeks liberation (*mumukṣutve*), one must indeed proceed for the sake of knowledge alone.

For it is not heard anywhere that entering the fire is a means to liberation; rather, it is heard that when performed according to scriptural injunction, it is a means to attaining heaven—the proof for which will be stated further on. Furthermore, there is detachment from sense objects, namely the enjoyment of sound and so forth, as well as from life, which has become a burden due to the experience of the suffering of losing kinsmen, and from the maintenance of the body because the body is a vessel of calamities.

Now, while the loss of sense-objects may indeed follow upon the loss of life, how can life itself be abandoned by force? For suicide is contrary to the next world. To this he says: having ascertained that it is not contrary to the next world by determining it through the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*). For it is remembered in tradition that when a child suffers from disease and other afflictions, if they abandon the body by falling into the fire of Bhṛgu or into sacred waters (*tīrtha*) after fasting in the presence of the Supreme Deity and purifying themselves through recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), and charity, they attain heaven:
"Therefore, the scripture is your authority for the determination of what ought to be done and what ought not to be done."

The meaning is that this follows from the words of the Blessed One and because dharma is characterized by injunction (*codanā*). Regarding the phrase "to fall into the fire"—that is, to fall into the fire which has been purified by mantras and has become a sacrificial offering (*havirbhūta*)—the suffix *tumun* is used according to the rule *tumarthācca bhāvavacanāt*.

(2-3-15) Thus ends the fourth [section]. Regarding the Liṅga known as Suvarṇabindu, which is established by the non-human (apauruṣeya) tradition as "purifying at the confluence of the Madhumatī and the Sindhu," he previously described the Supreme Lord as being eternally present there. By the word "approaches" (*abhyeti*), he indicates that this particular location is a means for attaining the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). In this matter, the words of Maheśvara in the *Umā-Maheśvara-saṃvāda* serve as authority: "If one desires to enter the fire, O auspicious lady, according to that very rite, one should construct a funeral pyre made of wood at a sacred field or by a river."
Having paid homage to the deities and circumambulated the fire from left to right,
being pure and resolute, he should enter the sacrificial bed of fire.
"He too shall attain the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds, according to the law.

Thus it is stated that even for one whose body is healthy, death resulting from effort such as [the application of] oils and the like is free from fault; this is also mentioned in that very same context regarding entering fire and other such acts. This is how the public rumor should be understood. Therefore, we are now "slain," meaning we are lost; for with the destruction of such a jewel among men, there will be no protector of the social orders (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas), and because the sovereignty of Padmāvatī depends entirely upon him—this is the sense.

The words of the forest-dweller are to be accepted as authoritative, because it will be stated later: "I do not see her after the words of the compassionate forest-dweller. Here, the despondency residing in the minister is suggested (*vyajyate*), as is the emotion (*bhāva*) residing in the forest-dweller directed toward him. The sentiment of pathos (*karuṇarasa*), however, is all-pervasive. This is the figure of speech *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description), since the affection for one's daughter is revealed through its effect. //8//

Suddenly there is the joyful sight of Mālatī and Mādhava; suddenly, a great calamity. By the two "suddenly" (*jhaṭiti*), simultaneity is indicated. "Calamity" (*atyāhita*) refers to the great misfortune consisting of the commencement of the minister's death. "By good fortune" (*diṣṭyā*) means by the power of fate; "a marvel has been seen" because of the attainment of the sight of Mālatī, which was considered utterly improbable.

Then, having seen a marvel, one infers from the abundance of what has been heard that "what is this? and so forth. The word "this" (*ayam*) should be supplied [to complete the sense], or rather, because both the falling [of rain] and the raining [of weapons] are being alluded to. The use of the masculine gender (*pulliṅga*) is for this reason; otherwise, it would have been referred to in the neuter as a general object (*idam*). "Sword-leaved trees" (*asipatrāḥ*) are specific trees found in hell whose leaves are shaped like swords, as in: "And the fierce Sword-Leaf Forest (*asipatravana*), as well as Kālasūtra and the rest..."

This is because of the statement [in the *Rāmāyaṇa*]: "ṛ). Of these two—the spray, meaning the mass of sandalwood juice—and that [ash], there is a "downpour," meaning a forceful rain; their "simultaneous falling" is their descent together with a single impulse. Here too, the word "cloudless" (*anabhra*) is connected [to both]. It is "cloudless"—meaning devoid of clouds—yet "thick with sparks of fire," being interspersed with fiery particles, for it is only a cloud that acts as the agent of rain. It is a "shower of nectar," a sprinkling of immortality.

Here, by means of two sentences, the simultaneity of the heart’s rending and its cooling, as well as the body’s burning and its delight, is established. The poetic ornaments (alaṅkāras) present are poetic fancy (utprekṣā), antithesis (virodha), and the description of an effect without its cause (vibhāvanā). //9//

Then, he reflects with wonder upon fate, which is skillful in bringing about the simultaneous occurrence of effects that are mutually contradictory, beginning with the words "The life-restoring herb" (*sañjīvanauṣadhi*) and so forth. "Life-restoring" (*sañjīvana*) means the act of breathing or returning to life; the "herbs" for that purpose are the *mṛtasañjīvanī* and others. "Poison" (*viṣa*) refers to the *kālakūṭa* and other such toxins. Of these two, and of light and darkness (*ālokatimira*), that is, of illumination and gloom; and of the thunderbolt and the moonbeams (*aśaniśaśadharamayūkha*), that is, of the diamond and the rays of the moon—the words *vyatikara*, *sambheda*, and *saṃvalana* are synonyms for mixing.

Fate imitates—that is, follows—the god (the moon). Because it brings about the simultaneous experience of pleasure and pain by producing their effects—consolation and torment, manifestation and concealment, and tearing asunder and nourishing—it suggests, through the reversal of what ought to have been stated in accordance with the initial metaphor of "the thunderbolt of the moonbeams," that there is no fixed rule regarding the experience of pleasure and pain, or pain and pleasure. Herein lies the figure of speech *upamā* (simile), since "imitation" (*anukaraṇa*) is synonymous with "resemblance" (*sādṛśya*). //10//
