Then, [the author] composes Mālatī’s speech from behind the scenes—she who is distressed by hearing the resolve of Bhūrivasu, whose death was announced by the words "having learned of Mālatī’s misfortune"—as a suggestion of Mālatī and Mādhava, who are seen as being present in the dressing room, thinking, "How can my child be here?"—beginning with "Hā tāta" (Alas, father! from behind the scenes: "Hā tāta! Desist, desist!"

The phrase "from this resolve" (*asmād-vyavasāyāt*) is an elliptical expression (*anukti*) that indicates haste, just as in the example "enter for the rice-ball" (*praviśa piṇḍīm*), which implies "enter the house and eat. "I am eager to behold your lotus-face" (*utsukāsmi te vadanakamaladarśanena*) means I am longing for the sight of your lotus-like mouth; [this construction is justified] by the rule: *prasitotsukābhyāṃ tṛtīyā ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.44).

(2.3.44) Thus, the instrumental case [is used]. "Be gracious; honor me; show me favor; cherish me"—this is the sense, meaning by means of embracing, holding in one's lap, sitting upon the head, smelling the crown of the head, and so forth. And why, for my sake, do you abandon yourself—who are like a single, stainless, auspicious lamp that serves as a pillar supporting the entire expanse between the worlds? The particle *ca* is used either to conjoin the meanings of the sentences or in the sense of "but. By the term *mama* (my), through a suggestion (*dhvani*) wherein the literal meaning is transferred to another, her own insignificance is revealed.

The ablative case (*kāraṇāt*) is used here in the sense of a cause (*hetu*) in connection with the genitive; it means "of the entire, without exception, terrestrial circle situated within the region of the Cakravāla mountains.
As it is said: "That much is considered the earth, including its oceans, rivers, and mountains, as far as it is illuminated by the rays of the sun and the moon."
Thus it is stated in the *Bhāgavata*,
and from the words of the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*: "Beyond that, we know nothing that is without the sun or beyond its bounds."

"Locāloka is the Cakravāla [mountain range]," according to Amara; "Viṣkambha means expansion and obstruction," according to Vaijayantī. The two qualifiers "spotless," meaning free from collyrium, and "sole," meaning without a second, are intended to distinguish it from other islands.

"O auspicious one, why do you abandon—by what manner do you relinquish—your own self, your very body, which is a lamp arisen from reality for the sake of prosperity, since it illuminates all objects? Oh, what a delusion even among the wise, that for the sake of a piece of glass they would sell the Kaustubha gem! This is the sense. Furthermore, I had presumed that you were shameless and pitiless; the word 'furthermore' (punaḥ) serves to mark a contrast."

The sense is: "By 'shameless' is meant that while you were prepared to give up your lives in my absence, I, separated from you, am still alive; oh, how shameless I am! As for the word "you": he had imagined you to be pitiless and devoid of compassion, being deluded by such affection, because he had reproached them with words such as: "The King has been offered as a gift by my father; indeed, service to the King is a heavy duty for my father, but not so for Mālatī."

Then Kāmandakī, distressed by hearing Mālatī’s most piteous words, laments for her with the verse beginning "As if from another birth" (*janmāntarāt*): "From another birth"—that is, from a particular state of existence distinct from being born from the womb of Bhūrivasu; because she has been completely out of sight for so long, and because she is seen today. The word "as if" (*iva*) does not indicate that it was actually a previous birth, since she is present [now]; rather, it suggests a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). "In some way" (*katham api*) means with great difficulty, through the scope of human effort, or simply by the favor of destiny.

"You have been found again" means "you have been recovered by us"—this is the ellipsis. The word *yāvat* is used either as a poetic ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*) or for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*); or else, it denotes a limit (*avadhi*), implying "for as long as you were lost. By saying "within that time-limit," it indicates simultaneity. This present [misfortune] is "another" (*apara*) than the calamity of not seeing you; or rather, it is "another" in the sense that there is no misfortune greater (*para*) or more excessive than this. As it is said: "The term *uparāga* (eclipse) applies to both the moon and the sun when they are seized by Rāhu."

Thus says Amara. Because of the use of the second-person form in "labdhāsī" (you have obtained), the word "tvam" (you), though not explicitly stated, naturally falls into place as the underlying subject (*sthānin*). Furthermore, due to the employment of the transitive verb "vikalayitum" (to cause to waver), this is established by the modification of the case ending to "svām" (your own).

Otherwise, there would be no connection with the standard of comparison ending in the accusative, "śaśikalām" (the crescent moon); for objections regarding matters established by the force of the usage of great poets are to be set aside, as in such passages as: "She might remain hidden by her power out of the influence of anger, but she does not stay angry for long."

Alternatively, when the speaker is overwhelmed by grief, the deficiency of words (*nyūnapadatva*) is not a fault; on the contrary, it is indeed a merit—as in the case of a speaker overwhelmed by joy, such as in the verse beginning, "Do not, O giver of honor, do not, do not overwhelm me. [The term] *vikalayitum* means to render one incapacitated or helpless (*vivaśāṃ*). The suffix *ṇic* is used in the sense of "that which causes to do" (*tatkaroti*). An "imminent misfortune" (*upasthito 'narthaḥ*) refers to a type of calamity that stands as an adversary to one's purpose. Here, the poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*) consists of a metaphor (*rūpaka*) based on a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) rooted in a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). //11//

The others, Madayantikā and Lavaṅgikā: "Alas, dear friend! [Makaranda], supporting the fainting and bewildered girl, and steadying her with his chest and arms for fear that she might fall to the ground—perceiving this other unforeseen calamity, he utters a cry of indignation toward Fate, which is cruel and beyond remedy. 'Bhā!'—this is an address directed toward the personified sky (the atmosphere) according to common worldly usage. 'Kaṣṭam' means great distress. By the repetition [of the word], a lamentation uttered with an open throat is implied."

"Esā" and so forth. By "esā" (this one), her perceptibility through the power of fortune is revealed. "Having somehow passed over"—that is, having survived—the journey abroad, which is traveling to another land, by the force of destiny; "otherwise," namely, in the form of apprehension regarding the death of her father. By the word "punaḥ" (again), it is revealed that through the cessation of their previous calamity, they for a moment considered themselves to have accomplished their purpose and felt as if they were ageless and immortal. "Doubt" refers to the uncertainty of life, the risk to one's vital breaths. The particle "eva" (only) is to be construed in a different order [with "sandeham"].

It is only doubt [that remains], and not the state of being an object of grief—such as "How has she become so emaciated and pale in our absence?"—for she has reached this time when, like rice and other grains approaching ripeness through autumn and the like, this fruit consisting of pleasure and pain must be experienced; it is by the power of time that destiny (daiva), which is the karma performed in a previous birth and is now ready to yield its fruit, brings about this result.

According to the statement of the Teacher, "Destiny is action performed in a previous birth, while human effort is that of this life," among the many merits and demerits acquired in other births, only those two which are most powerful possess the capacity to initiate the present body. Furthermore, since their exhaustion cannot occur without experience, [it is said]: "This present body has been commenced by merit and demerit for the sake of pleasure and pain; the exhaustion of those two occurs only through experience."

This is because of the statement of authoritative persons (*prāmāṇika*). "Doors" refers to the paths of entry. By the use of the plural number, it is suggested that even if there were only a single door, one would make an effort to close it with one's whole being; yet, when there are doors on all sides, what hope is there for a remedy? As it has been said: "Or rather, doors for what is destined to happen exist everywhere. [The purpose is] to close them.
According to the statement: "Bhāguri desires the elision of 'a' in the prefixes 'ava' and 'api';
and according to Śaunaka, this occurs extensively for the roots *dhā* and *kṛ*, as well as for the suffixes *tani* and *nah*," there is thus an elision of the 'a' in *api*.

"Apidhāna, tirodhāna, pidhāna, and ācchādana" [are synonyms for concealment], according to Amara. The word *ka* is used in the sense of censure; the meaning is that "no one is capable. The particle *nāma* is used in the sense of manifestation; the meaning is that this matter is well-known. Having raised the objection that the universal term *sarvanāman* (here referring to *jantu*) might lead to over-extension (*atiprasañjakatva*), he resolves it: a *jantu* is one who is subject to birth and death, being dependent on karma; the implication is that this refers to gods, humans, and so forth.

This is because the Supreme Lord alone is devoid of dependence on karma; for there are scriptural and traditional (smṛti) statements such as: "All these, beginning with the gods, are impure and have their origin in karma"; "For him, no effect or instrument exists"; and "That [power] is not born of karma, but exists for the benefit of the worlds. The form "īṣṭe" is derived from the root *īś* in the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), conjugated in the Ātmanepada, present tense (*laṭ*), third person singular.

"Who has power?"—this expresses the very absence of capability; for if there were capability, there would be a possibility of action, but that [capability] simply does not exist. Here, the figure of speech is *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle), because a specific case is supported by a general one through the statement of the inevitability of fate. By stating that fate intends his own death as well as the destruction of both [families], it is illuminated that since a great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*)—the total annihilation of all those connected to the two lineages—is intended by fate, what is the use of futile human effort? //12//

The word *atha* (now/then) serves to exclude what has been introduced; the meaning is: "let the account pertaining to this [previous] context be set aside. By the pronoun *sā* (she), there is implied the totality of her qualities, such as her experienced great majesty and her heart being moistened with compassion.

"From Śrīparvata," and so forth. "We two"—meaning myself and Mālatī—have come here to this place together with that Yoginī, following her as one who is to be honored; the word "our own" is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Immediately"—that is, at that very moment—this indicates that our arrival was accomplished in the mere twinkling of an eye through her power. Regarding the term *karuṇavanecara*: *karuṇā* means compassion (*dayā*); because it exists there, he is *karuṇa*. The suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for the *arśa-ādi* group. As it is said: "The word *karu* is declared to mean affliction (*kleśa*); since he does not tolerate affliction, his intellect is *karuṇā*, and by means of the suffix, he becomes *karuṇa*."

Thus ends the *Bhāvaprakāśa*. [The term] "karuṇānām" means of the compassionate ones, or alternatively, of the "karuṇas," that is, the forest-dwellers (*vanecara*), the sages who live in the wilderness (*araṇyavāsin*). This is according to the rule: "In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the suffix *kṛt* is frequently applied."

(6-3-14) Thus, there is no elision of the case-ending (*aluk*), as indicated by the statement from the sentence beginning with "Having learned of Mālatī’s misfortune, his mind became dispassionate. He artfully reveals that these words spoken in costume are actually the words of the sage. Immediately thereafter, by saying "I do not see him," he indicates that [Mādhava] has gone out of sight. By stating "immediately after the words of the compassionate forest-dweller," the poet suggests that she ran away in haste to rescue Bhūrivasu. //13//

Having directed [their gaze] toward the Yoginī in the sky, they said: "O Illustrious One! (mahābhāge). This means: O you whose great and unsurpassed fortune (bhāga) consists in having unconditionally performed the protection of many people's lives—a task impossible for others. Furthermore, because she previously protected them by rescuing Mālatī, and because another calamity has now befallen them, the meaning is that you alone, and no one else, are capable of protecting us from this as well. "Protect us" (paritrāyasva) means: guard us from all sides.

"Why" means for what reason; "disappeared" means concealed by magic power (vidyā). Does it mean that we are unworthy to behold you, a mass of merit, or rather for some other cause? This is the meaning.

To awaken the unconscious girl, they said, "Friend Mālatī! Seeing no sign of awakening even when addressed once, they spoke again with persistence: "Surely we are speaking! The word *nanu* is used here for emphasis. The meaning is: "Do you not hear us, friend Mālatī? Surely we two are saying [your name]," they said. Even when spoken twice, seeing no awakening from her, they cried out with trembling and agitation, fearing some calamity: "O Blessed One, protect her! Her heart is still from breaths long suppressed."

"Protect us"—the meaning is "save us by employing the means of sustaining life. Because of the breath that has been suppressed for a long time, held motionless for many moments, [the chest] is still and unshaking; for at the time of the entry and exit of inhalation and exhalation, the chest moves in accordance with them. And since the absence of the heart's throbbing creates the delusion of death, the sense is that fear arises in both of us. Alas, Minister! Alas, dear friend! You two have both become the cause of each other's end.

Because of the minister’s determination to die upon learning of Mālatī’s disappearance, and because of Mālatī’s swoon upon hearing of his resolve, there is the mention of their mutual end—their death—as the cause or reason for this. Now, wishing to bring about unsurpassed happiness for the two protagonists through their obstacle-free union, the great poet reveals the highest extreme of suffering in order to heighten its sweetness, beginning with "Alas! My child," and so forth. This is the lamentation of everyone upon realizing that Mālatī has not been restored to life.
The others, Madayantikā and Lavaṅgikā: "Alas, dear friend!
By using the suffix *lyap* in the word *upagamya* ("having approached"), the poet reveals the suddenness of regaining consciousness and indicates that this was produced by the power of the Yoginī.
[This is according to the rule: "When two actions have the same agent, the suffix *ktvā* (which becomes *lyap*) is used for the action occurring at the earlier time."
(3-4-21) This is because of the rule for the suffix *ktvā*.

He clarifies that very point through the phrasing of Kāmandakī’s speech: "What is this? What is the root of this wonder?"—the meaning is "what is its foundation? The comparison (*utprekṣā*) is based on its thickness, as if it were being split or torn open by someone. "Pariskhalan" means falling down from all sides. "Socchvāsam" means having released a breath, in the sense of having escaped the paralysis of unconsciousness. "Aye" expresses astonishment, because that matter was previously considered impossible. "Pratyāpannacetanā" means having regained consciousness once more. He establishes that very state [of her] with the words: "For thus it is with her."

"It is expanded," and so forth. In that [state], the two *payodharas*—the breasts—are "impelled" (*praṇunna*), meaning shaken, by the upward movement (*unnāha*) or upward flow of the breath (*prāṇavāyu*), which, being drawn out and long since ceased, is gathered together like the current of a river.
As it is said: "Even now, the breath, exceeding its normal measure, causes a trembling of the breasts."

The word *hṛdayam* means the chest (*vakṣas*). Then, immediately thereafter, having become "unctuous" (*snigdham*), meaning distinguished by the quality of oiliness (*sneha-guṇa*), [the eye]—which previously possessed some degree of dryness (*raukṣya*) to the touch—attained stability (*sthairya*) while remaining in its own nature (*nijaprakṛtau*), that is, in its own essential state (*svasvabhāve*) characterized by qualities such as being expansive, elongated, red, blue, or white; this is the meaning. The term "eye" (*cakṣus*) is intended to refer to the sense organ (*indriya*), and is expressed either with the singular number because it denotes a genus (*jāti*) or simply for the sake of stylistic emphasis.

Thereafter, immediately following that, his face—due to the cessation of fainting, the disappearance of delusion—became serene; it was distinguished by serenity, which is clarity, as opposed to the previous state of discoloration. At the beginning of the day, at the time of dawn, it was encompassed on all sides by beauty, like a lotus.

The statement "it was perceived in the morning" is because that [face], though in a subtle form, had already existed previously. Here, it is revealed that by its very nature, even during the time of fainting, the face did not lose its beauty, yet at the time of awakening, its beauty becomes expansive once more. The sequence of the cessation of fainting is described thus: first the heart returns, then the eyes remain fixed, and thereafter the face shines forth. In this passage, the poetic figures (alaṃkāras) are *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state) and *upamā* (simile). //14//
Then,
following the words of the forest-dweller Karuṇa— "I do not see her"— the purpose of the Yoginī’s disappearance, as indicated, is revealed by that same actress in the costume: [behind the scenes].

"Without regarding," and so forth. By "without regarding" (avigaṇayya), meaning not even considering [him] as worth a blade of grass, the previously mentioned ripening of detachment (*virakti*) is manifested; this is according to the maxim: "To one free from desire, the world is but a blade of grass. By the word "the king" (*nṛpam*), it is suggested that there is a great audacity (*sāhasikya*) in transgressing against one who is capable of both punishment and favor through anger and grace.

By the word "the king," there is expressed a state of dejection arising from the apprehension that, since the success of one authorized to protect the world depends upon the shoulders capable of bearing the burden of the earth and the jewels of his ministers, the kingdom would perish in his absence; for this very reason, it is said he was "bowed at his feet," and not that he was "dissuading him with words. The phrase "together with Nandana" means accompanied by the minister's son; the sense is that because he too was intent on following the king's will and was captivated by this host of virtues, he was equal to the king, and thus shared in the king's sorrow.

By bowing at his feet and grasping them with both hands, it is manifested that she has prostrated herself on the ground like a staff; for a mere salutation can be performed even from a distance. By falling into the fire—that is, into a fire piled with abundant fuel—it is indicated that, by the turn of fate, her vow has been fulfilled just as she was about to fall, rather than while already falling. She was turned back immediately—meaning swiftly—before she could even approach his feet, that is, before the act of falling.

Regarding how he was turned back immediately, he says: "By my words, but not by me. This means that even before [Makaranda] could see him—who was touching the very peaks of the sky—he was turned back from afar by his own deep and sweet voice speaking such words as: "Mālatī lives, and she is well; alas, alas! Do not act so rashly!"

"Intense joy and astonishment": "Guru" means intense; "sammada" means joy; "vismaya" means the sense of wonder arising from the festival of hearing news of Mālatī’s well-being, because she has appeared at this very moment quite unexpectedly. Here, the sentiment of the marvelous (*adbhuta-rasa*) is suggested. The figure of speech is the emergence of emotion (*bhāvodaya*), as it demonstrates the arising of the two emotions of joy and wonder. (15)
Then, gladdening Kāmandakī—who was distressed by the pain of longing to see her when she asked, "O noble lady, why have you vanished?"—[the text says]: "She is that yoginī," and so forth.

She is this very one standing before us, whose goodness was made manifest by her performing supreme acts of assistance without any motive; she, by whom the clouds (*jalada*) have been dispersed with excessive speed—that is, separated from one another by an extraordinary velocity of movement through the sky due to her haste to favor us and because they were tossed up by the forceful wind—is approaching us, coming toward us with us as her object.

To the question of how she can be identified as that very same person when she is seen clearly for only a moment as she rushes through the sky at a great distance—like lightning flashing by tearing through a mass of clouds—the author says: "Her speech is a torrent of the water of nectar," meaning a forceful rain of the essence of her words, which are like ambrosia; for it bestows immortality upon those of her own people who were as if dead, by reviving them.

It surpasses—that is, outshines by its own qualities—the downpour of water from clouds, which was described in the passage beginning with "as if the clouds were being instantly torn asunder," because the downpour of water from clouds merely removes the delusion that has already arisen, whereas this nectar-like downpour of speech is ever-vigilant in preventing the recurrence of such delusion; for without it, the former is like the elephant's ceremonial bath (which merely washes away the mud once it has dried). Here, the poetic figures are *rūpaka* (metaphor) and *vyatireka* (distinction/superiority). //16//
Then, her desires fulfilled, she said: "It is dear to us; our wish has been accomplished"—this is the ellipsis. The repetition [of the word] indicates joy.

"By good fortune, after a long time, I have been restored to life" means that by the power of fate, after a great length of time, my life has been re-established, because I am now almost at the end of crossing the ocean of suffering experienced for so long.

"With tears of joy" means with tears arising from the joy of seeing her restored to life, and with tears arising from the thought, "How could my dear child have experienced such suffering while I was in this state, having ceased all recollection of sorrow through that very joy? "Come, come! is a repetition used out of haste to embrace her. "How is the Blessed Lady?"—the word "is seen" is to be supplied. "How" expresses astonishment, because such a reunion was not even imagined in a dream, and because of its profound significance and the fact that it has restored her to life through that connection.

The meaning is: not tolerating the falling of her head—tender as a *śirīṣa* flower—at her feet upon the ground, she immediately raised her up, embraced her to cool her own body which was scorched by the heat of separation, and, out of maternal affection for her daughter, smelled her on the crown of her head.

She offers a blessing: "Live," and so forth—live long, may you attain a full span of life! Grant life to Mādhava, who is as dear as life itself, who is like one's own breath; restore to life your friends Makaranda and the others, and sustain their vital spirits. [Addressing her] with limbs that are most pitiable due to their extreme delicacy, limbs cooled by contact with frost and which impart a chill like plunging into icy water; [addressing] her dear friends Lavaṅgikā, Madayantikā, Avalokitā, and the rest.

First, the address "Live! (jīva) is used because it is the root of all life for that [person's] existence; subsequently, the address regarding the gift of life that gladdens one's own life is used because this [latter] life is dependent upon the former, as established by positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). This should be understood as the figure of speech called *āśis* (benediction). //17//

Now, the world of living beings—the world of humans—is to be accepted and embraced regarding the determination of Mālatī’s life; for previously, because it produced distress, it was something to be shunned. By saying "of Mādhava," he reveals his own renown as being one whose very life consists of Mālatī.
In this manner, he demonstrates the correspondence with his own experience regarding this matter, [expressing] "it is exactly so."

The others, Madayantikā and Lavaṅgikā: Dear friend! Since you appear before us even more than our desires could have imagined, honor us with an embrace. A "desire" (*manoratha*) is the mental conception of an object one longs for but finds difficult to attain—the thought, "Perhaps by the power of fortune this may happen for us. The "vision" (*darśana*) of that desire is its direct realization as such; for that is the supreme limit of the mind’s bliss in this world.
As it is said, beginning with: "O Bhārata, these eight are the very cream of joy: ... and the attainment of what is desired, and honor in the assembly of men..."
Thus, from the statement in the *Mahābhārata*, it is now shown that your vision is even more superior—that is, exceeding even that—hence the term "excess" (*atiśaya*) is established.
"Alas, my two dear friends! Alas! For, as it is said: "The suffering of one's own kin indeed arises before one as if with its doors wide open."

According to this logic, upon seeing her friends, [the embrace] expresses despondency arising from the recollection of past suffering. The meaning is that she embraces both simultaneously. By saying "she embraces both," the moment of the release from sorrow is indicated. From the words "Live, O you who are equal to life! up to "Alas, my dear friends! there is *paribhāṣaṇa* (mutual conversation) due to their speaking to one another.
Not knowing the root cause of Mālatī’s calamity, she asks: "O children, what is this?"—that is to say, what is the nature and what is the root of this matter consisting of Mālatī’s misfortune?

They gave this reply: "Kapālakuṇḍalā," and so forth. Having been brought to calamity by the wicked deed of Kapālakuṇḍalā in the form of her anger—whereby the term "we" includes all [the relatives] because Mālatī’s misfortune was common to all our kin—we have been rescued from this distress, as elephants are pulled from a mire or a danger; that is, having made a great effort (*nirbandham*) toward the rescue, facing it head-on. The ablative case is used here with the elision of the suffix *lyap*.

By this noble lady of unsurpassed goodness—just as in such expressions as "the noble lady did not speak ill of her husband" or "the noble one is truth born of lineage"—by this Yogeśvarī seen before us; here there is the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because protection is identified with rescue. //18//

He establishes, through inference, the cause of that anger expressed in the words "O Kapālakuṇḍalā, enough of your wrath! as being the manifestation—the ripening of the fruit—of the slaying of Aghoraghaṇṭa performed by Mādhava. As for the question "How so? [it is used] in the sense of wonder. The meaning is: "Alas, how terrible is the final consequence of a remnant of an enemy that was overlooked out of negligence! according to the saying: "One should not leave a remnant of fire, a remnant of debt, or a remnant of an enemy."

Oh, what a marvel! How the Creator’s dispensation, though cruel through its repetition, results in a beautiful conclusion! Though cruel through its repetition—that is, increasingly harsh due to the production of a succession of calamities—it possesses a "beauty in its final outcome" (*pariṇāmaramaṇīyatvam*), meaning it is auspicious in its ultimate result because it culminates in unhindered happiness. Such is the nature of *vidhi*, or destiny.

Having fulfilled her purpose by the complete eradication of all suffering, he introduces the Yoginī into the *samaya*—entering as "Saudāminī. The word "he" (*sa*) refers to one who, through long-standing devotion and unswerving service, has become a vessel for extraordinary grace; "this one" (*eṣa*) means the one present here before us; "of you" (*vaḥ*) uses the plural to denote the gurus; "ancient" (*cirantanaḥ*) or "primeval" (*purāṇaḥ*) excludes those who are modern; the suffixes *-tyu* and *-tyul* with the augment *tuṭ* are applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.23 (*sāyaṃ-ciraṃ-prāhṇe-prage-avyayebhyaṣṭyu-ṭyulau tuṭ ca*); "resident pupil" (*antevāsī*) means a disciple, [the suffix *-in* being used] because the word *vāsa* does not denote time [according to Pāṇini 4.2.104: *śayavāsavāsiṣvakālāt*].

(6-3-18) *Iti* indicates the elision (*aluk*). The word *janaḥ* signifies "every living being" and is a statement indicating a lack of distinction [among them]. *Aye* expresses joy arising from seeing what was not expected and from seeing what was long desired. *Bhadrā* means auspicious, because she is endowed with the grace of her elders.

Having previously reflected in many ways yet seeing no cause for the Yoginī’s intense zeal to provide such supreme benefit to their own sphere, they now, having their doubts dispelled upon hearing her name, say, "How?"—an utterance marked by joy and wonder. The word "she" (sā) implies that she has taken root in their own minds because she was previously described by the Blessed Lady at every moment during the course of their conversations with affection and great respect.

He indicates by way of an artful hint the matter already established: "The object of partiality" means the sphere of excessive affection. "The first disciple" means the initial disciple or the one who is preeminent. The name "Saudāminī" was previously invoked like a mantra; now, the meaning is that fortunately the connection with her—the bearer of that name—has been secured.

Since this Saudāminī comes from that place, now at this very moment, everything—including Mālatī’s rescue, Mādhava’s consolation, Bhūrivasu’s restoration to life, and so forth—is fitting, consistent, and logical; the sense is that this is because the great cause, namely her connection with the Goddess, exists. Regarding the form *saṅgacchate*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied to the root *gam* preceded by the prefix *sam-* when it is intransitive, according to Pāṇini 1.3.29: *samo gamyṛcchipracchisvaratyartiśruvidibhyaḥ*.

Previously, due to her exceptional service and her capacity for acquiring knowledge, she was distinguished merely by her partiality; now, however, because she has performed a supreme benefit and possesses the full power of inconceivable mantra-siddhi, she speaks with abundant affection and great respect for his many virtues, saying, "Come, come," and so forth. The repetition of "come, come" is an expression of impatience, as even a moment's delay in bowing would obstruct an embrace.

To the question, "What is this excessive regard for me, who am but a single atom among trees? he replies: "She who bears the accumulation of merit from the gift of life to many people. This means she whose nature is to maintain—that is, to possess—the collection or store of merit arising from the giving of life, the granting of breath, to many (bhūrīṇām) or numerous people. As it is said: "On one side are all sacrifices completed with the bestowal of desired gifts; on the other side is the protection of the life of a living being terrified by fear."

According to this statement from the *Mahābhārata*, great merit is earned by bestowing life upon even a single living being; what then need be said of many? This is what is illuminated by the word "sambhāra" (provision). "Hanta" expresses joy. "You have been seen after a long time"—that is, after a great interval. "Giving delight" means that joy is produced by the mere sight [of you], because the body itself is nourished by the mere sight of such a most beloved object. The particle "api" indicates that there is no satisfaction with merely that much.

"Embrace me, gladden me, and fulfill my body with the horripilation, trembling, and other signs [of joy]—thus he expresses that the pleasure of your touch, previously experienced, has been excessively robbed away by its long separation. O treasure-house of friendship, you who are like an ocean to the water of affection for your kin—a complete reservoir and place of abode for it—cease from salutations; desist from them, for they are obstacles to the pleasures of embracing, conversation, and the like. Herein lies the poetic figure of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) in the phrase "the bearer of the entire collection."
Because of the saying, "There is no difference between a virtuous son and a disciple," the disposition toward a true disciple is revealed here. //19//

Now, he clarifies the meaning suggested by the phrases "she who bears the mass of merit from granting life to many people" and "treasury of friendship" with the words: "Moreover, you alone are worthy of worship," and so forth. "Worthy of worship" means she is to be saluted and praised. By the word "alone" (eva), he indicates that those like me are not capable of such helplessness in this calamity; rather, it is you alone. "Of the world" means not merely of a few, but of the entire universe. [The suffix] *kṛtya* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

This is the genitive case [according to Pāṇini 2.3.71]. The reason for this is that her attainment of the fruit—produced by the practice of mantras and so forth—is "desirable" (*spṛhaṇīya*), meaning it is longed for by all other ascetics, who wonder, "How might such an accomplishment as ours be achieved by us? Her success is characterized by this very aspiration.

Granted that success may indeed be achieved; nevertheless, some who are merciless do not employ [mantras] in the calamities of living beings for fear of the exhaustion of their fruits. To show that you possess no such hardness, he says: "By such as these. The word "thus" (*evam*) is a gesture of experience; by this phrase—"those whose manner of bestowing favor upon us is of such a kind"—he speaks after having inferred their habitual nature of protecting the virtuous and the wretched.

By the words "with playful movements" (*vilasitaiḥ*) and "with sports" (*krīḍitaiḥ*), it is illuminated that the benefit is easily accomplished without effort and that there is an absence of pride. Furthermore, he states that there is no comparison for you in the matter of overcoming others: "by those who surpass even the Bodhisattvas," meaning those who have transcended even the Bodhisattva Jina-muni. This follows the rule: *atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā* ("words such as *ati*, when used in the sense of 'transcending' and so forth, are used with the second case").

This is a compound [formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.57]. Although he is renowned for his supreme compassion, because he commits the great sin of sacrificing his own self in order to protect Śaṅkhacūḍa and others, there exists an equality of fruit between his merit and his demerit, as well as the experience of suffering at that very moment. In your case, however, only the fruit of protecting the distressed remains, and your self is not subjected to such hardship; thus, the sense is that your deeds shine forth as far more remote [in excellence] than his legendary exploits.
[As it is said: "Buddha, Śrīghana, Śāstṛ, Bodhisattva, and Vināyaka."

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*: "In the past," meaning in a time gone by, "the seed of the obstruction to acquaintance"—acquaintance (*paricaya*) being familiarity (*saṃstava*), its "obstruction" (*pratibandha*) is its firm establishment; such is the "seed," like the seeds of rice and other grains. It "expands" (*vijṛmbhate*) in the world—that is, it becomes renowned—or it "increases," because it brings about auspiciousness higher and higher, being distinguished by abundant, mature fruits such as the preservation of life. "[Of] us" (*naḥ*) means of ourselves.

By means of the two verses beginning with "Come, come" and "You alone are to be revered," the emotion of *āvega* (agitation) arising from the excitement of attaining a desired object is suggested (*dhvani*). Furthermore, because the poet intends to transgress the conventional order [of the plot], the figure of speech *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause) is present in both instances. It should be understood that by the line, "The seed of the obstruction to former acquaintance flourishes, bearing abundant fruit," the *prakaraṇa* (episode), defined as "that which is briefly indicated but whose causal seed is expanded in many ways," is revealed; thus, the poet has artfully manifested the *bīja* (seed) through a clever stylistic turn.

Because the seed (bīja) introduced by the words "O virtuous ones" and so forth has been expanded through the development (parikara) beginning with "This vow was undertaken in the presence of Saudāminī," and because the vow is about to be revealed through the mouth of Saudāminī. //20//
This is that noble Saudāminī.
A question is implied by the tone of voice.

He states the answer to it: "Certainly" (*bāḍham*), meaning "firmly," "without a doubt. Indeed, by this lady—who, out of partiality for her connection with the Blessed One, rebuked Kapālakuṇḍalā and led me to her own dwelling—I have been comforted as if there were no difference between her and the Blessed One herself. The particle *khalu* is used here for emphasis.

Having heard that she is related to the Blessed One (the Queen), is the daughter of Kāmandakī’s friend, and is the object of unsurpassed affection; having heard this, there arose a partiality [toward her], as well as the sense of ownership [thinking], "She must indeed be cherished by us in every way. For that reason—by means of such rebukes as "Fie, you fool! What power do you have even to smell the scent of our offspring? and by threatening her in this manner, her own commencement of slaughter is indicated. [Having brought her to his own dwelling] means, having caused her to reach his house.

The adverbial phrase "in a manner indistinguishable from the Blessed Lady" means that no difference whatsoever was perceived [between her and Kāmandakī]. She was comforted by [acts such as] embracing, placing [her] on her lap, and smelling the crown of her head, with words such as: "Child, do not fear! I am Saudāminī, a female disciple of the Blessed Lady. While I am alive, who could prevail against you for any offense? Furthermore, I shall reunite you with your father and others this very day. This is the meaning.

He says that she did not merely assist with words alone, but through her actual action: "Having come here with a hand bearing the *kesarāvalī* as a token of recognition, you all have been sustained. The meaning is that she possessed a hand accompanied by the *kesarāvalī*—that is, a garland of *bakula* flowers—as a sign of recognition, because her word is trustworthy. By saying "having come here," he indicates the great distance of this region from Śrīparvata. By the word "all," there is a complete inclusion of Mādhava and the others.
"Supported" means properly established and sustained; thus, the highest limit of her beneficence is illuminated. The verbal root *dhṛ* is used in the sense of "to remain" or "to support.

"The venerable lady Kaniṣṭhā is exceedingly gracious toward us. She is designated as "Kaniṣṭhā" (the youngest) because Kāmandakī is old while she is young, or perhaps because she is slightly inferior due to being a disciple.
As the lexicon states: "The words *kaniṣṭha* and *kanīyān* denote what is small or very little, and also a younger sibling."
Thus says the *Vaijayantī*. "She is well-disposed toward us with a face bright with favor; by good fortune she has been born"—this is the ellipsis.

Now, because such an intensity of protection would otherwise be inexplicable, and according to the maxim that "in the presence of a superior, one praises [the subject]," they express his service with wonder, saying: "Aho nu khalu bhoḥ!"—thus, filled with amazement, they address all those present.

"Even the *cintāmaṇi*," and so forth. A particular kind of jewel is well known as the *cintāmaṇi* because it grants objects that fall within the scope of one's thoughts. By the word "even" (*api*), he says this: the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*) requires at least a mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*)—that is, repeated requesting with the mind of what has been resolved—and [furthermore], "only that which is churned by the internal organ do trees bearing the prefix 'kalpa' bear fruit."

This is because of the words of such great poets as [Bhāravi]. The *Kāmadhenu*, however, requires a mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*), a verbal request (*yācana*), and physical service (*paricaryā*), as is seen in the cases of Dilīpa and others. The *Kālamegha*, on the other hand, sometimes gives even when requested, sometimes does not give, and sometimes disregards the requester to give to someone else. Therefore, among all these, the wise have placed the *Cintāmaṇi* at the highest pinnacle of givers, as it depends upon nothing more than mere thought (*cintāmātra*).

When that [generosity] is also examined, it is found to be "generosity with reservation"; thus, he speaks of its very nature as being with reservation: "The fatigue of thought" means thought is a specific activity of the mind. Having first examined, "What may I request from this [person]? and subsequently established one's own request upon some object, thinking, "This thing is required by me," there follows the fatigue—the weariness—of begging, which consists of a mental state of supplication, such as, "May this be given to me by your long-lived self. That [generosity] bears fruit immediately thereafter.

If this is the nature of the *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem), then what need is there to speak of the *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-granting tree) and others? Therefore, this has been experienced—by "tu" (indeed) signifying a distinction—it was not performed (*akṛtam*) or executed by anyone else other than herself, because it was previously difficult to accomplish. Fearing that even if it were difficult, it might be something trivial, he says "no" to that possibility: it is a marvel (*āścaryam*), producing wonder because of its great fruitfulness and because it was inconceivable. It was performed (*kṛtam*) or executed by her; the word "this" (*idam*) refers to the object, as is understood from the context. This is the meaning. It was performed by the Noble One (*āryayā*), meaning by the venerable *Yogeśvarī*. The word "this" (*idam*) refers to the matter (*vastu*). Thus is the sense.
The figure of speech here is *vyatireka* (contrast); the attainment of the marvelous is embraced by such expressions as "Oh, how truly! and "Even the *cintāmaṇi* [wish-fulfilling gem]... //21//

Then, according to the maxim that "one who is being praised feels shame by performing only what is worthy of praise," she, feeling abashed by the direct praise due to her own greatness and her unsurpassed cultivation of the excellence of others, said: "Alas! (expressing regret). It causes shame; it makes one subject to embarrassment. "Excessive goodness" means an extraordinary degree of virtuousness; for gratitude is the very lifeblood of the good—this is the sense. Previously...

The apprehension arises as to what the two ministers—who have been humiliated even though they were awakened by the King himself—will do now, given that the King’s favor has not yet been manifested despite his having declared: "When Bhūrivasu and Nandana, whose faces are like the edge of a sword to the sharp point of the envious, have been awakened, will you still be dissatisfied with your son-in-law? Therefore, the King has gone inside. Thus, the matter is presented solely as the King's favor.

The poet now addresses that [objection] which has taken root within [the mind], by means of the letter, for it is precisely its resolution that remains—beginning with the words "Bhagavatī" and so forth. By the phrase "welcomed by the delighted Nandana" and "in the presence of Bhūrivasu," it is indicated that after Bhūrivasu’s recovery, the King, with a countenance bright with favor, requested the two ministers, saying, "I wish to send a letter to the venerable Mādhava through the hand of Yogeśvarī as a token of our affection," and that this was well-considered by them.

By the phrase "by the King," his approval is made manifest. By the expression "having written and bowed" (rather than simply "having written"), its status as the supreme authority is indicated through the fact that the letters were inscribed by his own hand. "Patra" refers to a palm leaf; the address "to the long-lived one" (āyuṣmat) is a formal convention used because the recipient is his son. "Preṣitam" means sent or dispatched; the meaning is "from my own hand. "Lekham" refers to a written document.

"Of those praiseworthy," and so forth. "Praiseworthy" means those who are the objects of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) for connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*). The reason for this is: "of the virtuous," meaning those who are eternally endowed with virtues such as learning (*śruta*), moral conduct (*śīla*), and the like. "Standing at the yoke" means established in the matter of the burden of duty; as it is said:
"May there be no obstacle for you; may you stand at the yoke like a father among those who have sons."

As stated in the *Raghuvamśa*, qualities that do not abide in a noble lineage are as lamentable as moonlight in the forest; however, those qualities residing in a noble person—like priceless gems fashioned from fresh gold and *jāmbūnada*—produce unsurpassed splendor. And this [splendor] belongs to you alone; thus he says: "In a preeminent lineage," meaning in a praiseworthy family (*praśasyavaṃśe*). [The suffix] *śra-* is substituted for *praśasya-* [by Pāṇini 5.3.60].

By the rule *iṣṭhan* [Pāṇini 5.3.60], the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied. In the word *mahīyasi*, meaning "one who is superior to others of great stature" by virtue of a complete abundance of wealth, friends, lands, and so forth—referring to the son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*) through the minister’s statement, "The Great King has power over his own daughters"—it gladdens us by the inference that we shall prosper through you as a suitable bridegroom for Mālatī, whom he regards as his own daughter.

Since you have cast off your calamity, and I have, by the power of fortune, encountered the calamity consisting in the non-sight of Mālatī, I am exceedingly pleased; the sense is that the kingdom is now firmly established.

By that reason of being pleased, the word "this" (*iyam*) is used because [Madayantika] is present in the mind; by the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "Madayantika also," it is illuminated that just as Mālatī is to be cherished by us in every way, so too is Madayantika not deficient even in the slightest degree—thus her status as an object of their affection, her possession of all virtues, and her connection with happiness are made manifest. To the question "How can such a one be given away?", he says: "For your pleasure"—the sense is that she is to be propitiated even at the cost of your entire life, O venerable one. "To your dearest friend"—to a friend who is dearer than life itself and the very object of your love.
"Friendship exists among those of similar character and shared interests; one should engage neither in dispute nor in friendship with the wicked, but should act in no way whatsoever with them."

From such statements as these, it is revealed that for you, O Great-Souled One, friendship proceeds only toward those possessing qualities such as noble birth equal to your own, and not elsewhere; thus, this very statement serves as our authority regarding your nobility and other such traits. It is "composed of first-love" (*prathamānurāgaghaṭitā*), meaning joined or united with a love that is foremost because it is supermundane (*lokottara*) or because it is the first [to arise]. The sense is that only such love, independent of kinsmen, is capable of bearing the entire burden [of the relationship].

By the word "api" (even), a statement with a hint of irony (*sotprāśa*) is indicated: "Even though this is so, nevertheless, due to the improper conduct of the teacher of Dharma, we—Nandana and the others—also certainly possess some degree of authority in the giving away of the maiden. Here, *api* is displaced from its logical position; the meaning is "by us, Nandana and the others as well. *Utsṛjyate* means "is given. The figure of speech here is *parikara* (poetic elaboration), because the adjectives are employed with specific intention (*sābhiprāyatva*).

From the words "by him who was delighted by the joy of Nandana" up to "of those praiseworthy and virtuous," there is *prasāda* (favor/grace) resulting from Padmāvatī’s lord’s service to Mādhava. //22//
"Uddiśya" means having directed [the attention] toward [it]. The meaning is: "Has the importance of the letter's contents been grasped through careful attention?"

"With joy" means characterized by signs of delight such as tears of bliss and so forth. "Having heard" means having attended to and grasped [the message]. He states the fruition of that which was grasped through attention to the meaning of the letter: "Now," when this investigation of the meaning of the letter has been performed, "in every way"—meaning by the attainment of his beloved, the successful accomplishment of his friend's purpose, and the pacification of suspected misfortunes—he is "one who has achieved his purpose" (*kṛtārtha*), that is, one for whom the sufficient objective has been fulfilled; for the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* denote action in general.
Through the phrases "What was heard? and "It has now been heard," there is joy arising from the attainment of what was desired.

The poet clarifies what was previously explained as a matter of apprehension through the speech of the minister’s son: "By good fortune, even this thorn of apprehension in our hearts has passed away. The phrase "even this" (*etadapi*) is used because it has been constantly present in their thoughts. The word "even" (*api*) suggests that the apprehension regarding the King's anger had already ceased prior to this. "Passed away" (*gatam*) means destroyed; by saying "in our hearts," he indicates that [the fear] was always dwelling within the hearts of all, including Mādhava and the others. It is called a "thorn of apprehension" (*āśaṅkā-śalyam*) because it is a thorn in the form of anxiety—a shaft-head—due to its painfulness and because it is difficult to remove quickly.

Now, at this moment—meaning immediately following the arrival of the letter—the desires of Mādhava have been fulfilled without remainder. "Without remainder" (*niravaśeṣam*) is an adverbial modifier meaning that no portion remains to be completed; that which was incomplete as something yet to be fulfilled has been cast aside. "Fulfilled" (*pūritāḥ*) is formed with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) used in its own sense, meaning "filled. Alternatively, it may be understood as "by fate. "Desires" (*manorathāḥ*) refers to those objects intended for attainment.

Now, the great poet—who is like a jewel-treasury for the arrangement of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—teaches by way of illustration that even the failure to connect the subordinate elements (*aṅga*), when they have been properly introduced as constituent parts, leads to the destruction of the aesthetic flavor; how much more so, then, the principal element (*aṅgin*)? Thus, he effects a connection between the subordinate elements separated by a moment: "Us—Mālatī, Mādhava, and the others—standing before you, gathered together and arrived without obstacle, [he says] 'in such a way as to be filled with joy' (*pramoda-pūrṇa*). By the transgression of rhythm and tempo (*tāla-laya*), the onset of laughter is indicated: "They have begun to dance" (*pranṛttāḥ*).
He states the fruit of the laughter: "They look on with smiles.
Who indeed does not dance at this great festival? The word *vā* (or) is used in the sense of an alternative; the meaning is that we do not see anyone who is not like that.

Approving of those words, he says: "So it is. What you have said is indeed true; the sense is that our own minds also quiver with the desire to dance. The reason for this is: "In some place (*kvacit*), in a certain region, such a thing"—that is, a performance (*abhinaya*) of the events concerning Mālatī and Mādhava as they are currently being experienced, characterized by this very manner.

To the question "What kind of manner is this?", he says: "Exceedingly variegated" means it is intensely wonderful; that is to say, because of the crookedness of its course, because of its variegation consisting of pleasure and pain arriving unexpectedly, and because it culminates in unsurpassed bliss. "Prakaraṇa" (context) means the occasion for the task, as implied by the sense. This is according to such statements as "The meaning, the context, and the indicative mark," and "Among direct assertion, indicative mark, syntactical connection, context, position, and name, each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding due to the remoteness of the meaning. And by this turn of expression: "He who has supreme devotion for the Divine, and for the Guru as for the Divine... [the following is established].

"Indeed, these objects of knowledge shine forth to that high-souled one"—according to the principle of this scriptural statement, the great poet, a supreme jewel who adorns the circle of learned and wise men, having had the impurities of his mind rubbed away by the grace of the deity and the guru, has manifested the sovereignty of the Śabdabrahman (the Word-Brahman) within himself; and with his commenced work nearly completed and in accordance with his own heart's intent, he now reveals to connoisseurs his skill in the composition of this specific dramatic form known as a *prakaraṇa*.

By stating that this work, which is composed in the manner of a *prakaraṇa* titled *Mālatīmādhava*, has been "thus made," he reveals his lack of self-aggrandizement (*avikatthanatā*) therein; for, being free from the conceit of "I" and "mine," he suggests that the composition of the *prakaraṇa* appeared to him effortlessly, as if it were the fruit of human effort arising from the grace of his guru and deity.

The meaning is that it is exceedingly wonderful, causing even Brahmā—the creator of the universe—to marvel—because he has therein arranged, in accordance with the requirements of each context, the entire essence of the nectar-ocean consisting of the collection of the eighteen branches of knowledge and the sixty-four arts.

[As it is said: "The drama (*nāṭaka*), the play-with-act (*prakaraṇa*), the monologue (*bhāṇa*), the farce (*prahasana*), the *ḍima*, the *vyāyoga*, the *samavākāra*, the *vīthī*, the *aṅka*, and the *hāmṛga*."

Thus the *prakaraṇa* has been mentioned, and its specific variety, the *rūpaka*, has been defined by the passage beginning: "Now, in the *prakaraṇa*, the plot is invented and based on worldly life," and so forth.

Now, at this point, the poet reveals through the mouth of the Yoginī—who was a witness to former events—the meaning that had been concealed for so long, beginning with the words "This" (*idam*) and so forth. "This" refers to what is about to be described in this context; "loveliness" (*rāmaṇīyakam*) means beauty, which brings about unsurpassed aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) for those of sensitive hearts (*sahṛdaya*). The sense is that this is not anything else, but rather that collection of qualities you wish to speak of; the implication is that it is far more captivating than all of those other things. To the question "What is that?", he says "That which" (*yat*) and so forth.

After a long time, from the period of serving our preceptor onwards, this [relationship] has become complete and its fruit has been realized. This is the nectar-like desire for a mutual relationship with offspring now being experienced by all of us—a proper union mediated by each other's children, namely the daughter and the son. Because the relationship is identical, there is a longing for that very nectar, the resolve: "When shall we attain this?"

Because it is to be accomplished through effort, because it produces supreme bliss at the very moment of its perfection, and because it is the means for attaining unsurpassed welfare in the future, the designation "immortality" (amṛta) is superimposed upon it.
Not understanding [the meaning], Mālatī speculates with wonder and curiosity—meaning, "How indeed? By what manner of means does she speak these words?"

"With curiosity" means possessed of an eagerness to hear that very truth. "Otherwise" means in a different manner; the matter that has occurred (*vṛtta*) refers to the reality of the action performed by transgressing against the minister Bhūrivasu—this is the meaning. "Otherwise" means intent on revealing a contrary alternative, which is consistent with the demonstration of an undertaking preceded by the minister's counsel—this is the meaning. The speech begins with "When the two ministers... and so forth. "Of the noble lady" refers to the venerable Yoginī.
From the words "This is the beauty here" up to "otherwise, the nature of things would be different," there is a contradiction due to the search for a specific effect.

Then, Lavaṅgikā, having learned the facts, fearing that revealing the truth might cause further agitation in the two princes, says: "O Blessed One! What should be done? That is to say: what thing—whether the disclosure or the non-disclosure of this matter we desire to know—should be accepted by us?

Dispelling his doubt through reasoning, she says that [the truth] must indeed be made manifest: "The meaning is that he has now received a letter indicative of the favor of the King and the Minister; because of the alliance with Madayantika—that is, on account of Madayantika—through the securing of Nandana, specifically by bringing the Minister’s son Nandana over to our side, his doubts have vanished, meaning the suspicion of treachery has been removed. The particle *khalu* is used for emphasis.

By this, it is shown that no such transformation could possibly occur in his sister who resides in our house; therefore, why is he still persisting in this habit of concealment? Having ascertained the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position, he reveals the truth: "O children, it is certainly not so. By addressing them as "children" (*vatsau*), he indicates that you, being immature, grasp things exactly as they appear, whereas in reality it is not thus; for the actual state of affairs is certainly not otherwise. This concludes the composition following the introduction of the seed-plot (*bīja*).

To the question "What then is the ultimate truth?", he says "yataḥ" (since), and so forth. In the state of being disciples (*śrāvakāvasthā*), when those two were acting as pupils through service to their teacher—at that stage, meaning precisely at the time of undertaking the life-stage of celibate studentship (*brahmacaryāśrama*)—this vow was made: "We must enter into a relationship of procreation. Therefore, the connection is: "Indeed, the reality of the matter is not otherwise than this statement of hers."

It should be understood that here the conclusion is made by means of the fulfillment of the primary seed (bīja), which was introduced at the very outset in the form of the minister’s vow; for the resolution is established through the narration of what was experienced, beginning with the words "Since [it occurred] during the stage of a Śrāvaka," as his own subsequent activity was preceded by the conduct of the minister.

Anticipating the objection—"For what purpose was such a great effort undertaken to act like a thief, when the task of establishing a relationship could have been accomplished directly without such exertion?"—he says: "In this way, however, the provocation of the primary *prakṛti* is avoided. This refers to the *prakṛti* that is primary (*pradhāna*) or principal, namely the constituent element of the kingdom (*rājyāṅga*). This is because the minister (*amātya*) is more intimate than the chaplain (*purohita*) and others. As it is said: "The sovereign, the minister, the ally, the treasury, the territory, the fort, and the army are the constituents of the kingdom; the *prakṛtis* are also the guilds of the citizens."

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*; the meaning is "of Nandana. [She speaks thus] because anger would have been directed at someone else even if Mālatī had been given openly, as that would have resulted in the King's anger as well. And by this method—this clandestine marriage—it has been avoided or averted. Because it was discovered, she says with astonishment: "The concealment of the day! The meaning is: "How wonderful is my father’s secret-keeping! By this, she recalls what was previously stated: "That is the concealment."

Filled with wonder, they said: "It is indeed marvelous! Truly, they produce a sense of astonishment. The policies (*nītayaḥ*)—meaning the employment of strategic means—are in accord even with great men such as Bhūrivasu and others; that is, they are free from contradiction (the meaning being that they do not deviate from the essential form) and are auspicious (*kalyāṇyaḥ*), being of a favorable commencement and thus possessing a nature of blessing. This constitutes the *pūrvabhāva* (the introductory stage), as seen from the passage beginning with "Ahmo saṃvaraṇam" and ending with "kalyāṇyo nītayaḥ."

Then, with her heart satisfied by the fulfillment of all desired objects through the manner of wishing expressed in the verse beginning, "May I become one who has accomplished her purpose through the efforts of my dear friend," she gladdens the hero while subtly marveling at his divine fortune and her own skill in the application of political strategy (nīti), after first enumerating the sequence of tasks already accomplished, saying: "Even before," and so forth. "Even before the birth of you two"—that is, prior to your very birth—it was "chosen" by our desires, meaning it was prayed for by us (the ellipsis being "by us").

By the use of the plural number, the manifold nature of the wish is revealed; for there are many such forms as: "When indeed will a daughter and a son be born to the two ministers? When will their promise regarding that alliance be fulfilled? When indeed shall we behold their prosperity? and so forth.

"Auspicious" (*kalyāṇam*) refers to the blessing (*maṅgalam*) consisting of the means for mutual union and so forth; "of the two long-lived ones" (*āyuṣmatoḥ*)—meaning of the long-lived one and the long-lived lady—is an affectionate mode of address. "By merits" (*puṇyaiḥ*) means by the previously performed, fully ripened good deeds of you two, and by "my undertakings" (*madupakramaiḥ*), that is, by the application of my skillful means (*upāya*). By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is suggested that there is no doubt regarding the attainment of the fruit when divine and human efforts are combined without conflict. "Bearing fruit" (*phalitam*) means that the fruit has arisen, because the tasks such as their union have been accomplished without obstacle.

Therefore, even the hardship—the exhaustion resulting from an abundance of mental, vocal, and physical exertions—experienced by my two disciples Avalokitā and Saudāminī through the performance of means such as seeing one another, as well as through the rebukes of Kapālakuṇḍalā and other events, has also borne fruit; this is to be construed by changing the gender [of the pronoun]. By this it is shown that "only one who has companions is able to attain an object that is beset with obstacles."

According to this principle, it is celebrated that my own labor has also become fruitful only through the assistance of good disciples; for, according to the statement, "At the conclusion of a task, even servants and slaves [are to be honored]," disciples who are like servants are worthy of praise when their activity results in the attainment of the fruit. It is "niṣṇāta" because it was accomplished by clever means. Alternatively, the reading is "niṣṇātam," in which case it is an adverbial modifier meaning "skillfully. [This is supported by the rule: "The suffix *ka* is added to the roots *snā* after the prefixes *ni* and *nadī* when skill is intended."

(4-3-49) Thus, there is the substitution of *ṣ*. "Abhivihitaḥ" means accomplished. By the phrase "of Makaranda, who is dearer to you than your own life," he indicates that the accomplishment of his purpose is more worthy of celebration than the accomplishment of his own. "By the beloved" means by Madayantika, the most cherished one; by this, he suggests that even the exertion of Buddharakṣitā has borne fruit.

For this reason as well, he says that the most beloved task has been accomplished: "The two princes—the Lord of Padmāvatī and the son of the minister—are perfectly delighted and well-disposed toward you. The implication is that if there were no such mutual affection between them, even the completion of every other task would be like an elephant's bath, resulting ultimately in misfortune.

Beyond this, whatever other object more dear than this—meaning, most beloved—is desired, that too shall be told; by the word "also" (api), it is indicated that like an already accomplished task, it is easily achieved and that she is solely intent upon its performance for his sake. "Let it be spoken"—that is, let it be told—and not merely "let it be undertaken"; by this, it is revealed that as soon as he says, "This is the object of my longing," he will see its fulfillment immediately thereafter.

The *kṛti* (conclusion) occurs through the stabilization of the matter already obtained by the words beginning with "That which was previously... The *kāryasaṃhāra* (conclusion of the plot) occurs through the summary of the purpose of the action by the words, "Let that other thing which is dearer [to you] also be told. And here, regarding the marriage of Mālatī and Mādhava which was introduced by the words "O auspicious one...", it is said: "If he, the brother-in-law of Mādhava, the son of Sāhara, were to marry Māraṇda’s sister Madayantī, then indeed it would be even more pleasing to Mādhava."
Because the marriage of Madayantika and Makaranda has been undertaken and both have been accomplished, the completion of the purpose of the play is established. //23//

Now, since the supreme human goal—the threefold aims of life (trivarga)—has been accomplished through the very attainment of Mālatī, and because there is no further object of desire beyond that, he rejects the pursuit of such wealth by saying, "Is there anything dearer than this? Here, "than this" refers to the already achieved goal; "anything dearer" means a superior object; "also" (*api*) implies contradiction; and by the interrogative intonation of "is there," the negation "there is nothing at all" is revealed. Alternatively, the statement "Is there anything dearer than this? constitutes a *bhāṣaṇa* (speech) because it describes the attainment of the desired object.

Nevertheless, "even from this" means even in the absence of an object for the desire to obtain another thing. "This" refers to the matter about to be stated. "Let it be" is in the *loṭ* (imperative) mood used in the sense of a prayer. By this, he indicates that even in the absence of personal desire, the favor of Great Beings must be accepted in every way because it is a means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ*). This statement follows the convention of drama; it is the *bharatavākya* (the concluding benediction).

This is the speech of one who has completely performed and concluded the *prakaraṇa* and has abandoned the role of Mādhava, remaining solely in his own natural state; the meaning is that he speaks what is about to be said. He states the manner of his prayer: "May there be auspiciousness," and so forth. "Auspiciousness" (*śivam*) means prosperity; the meaning is the attainment of the experience of objects that are not to be abandoned. [It is for] all the worlds, that is, for all embodied beings.

The reason for this is: "intent upon the welfare of others. By the word "others" (*para*), those other than oneself are meant, because they are distinct from one's own [interests], which constitute the primary purpose.

"Just as it is said: 'For thus all his qualities had as their sole fruit the welfare of others,'" so too [the sages] were "intent upon their welfare and highest good," meaning they were thoroughly devoted and diligent in that; in other words, through their own qualities such as speech and so forth, they were solely dedicated to the benefit of others. This is because if there were any deficiency or excess in those qualities, a disturbance of the world would inevitably follow. "Multitudes of beings" refers to the collections of the great elements, such as space and the rest. As it is said: "The qualities nourished the excellence of even the five elements."

Thus it has been said. "Defects" (doṣāḥ) refer to passion, hatred, greed, and so forth, according to the statement: "Passion and the rest are defects, characterized by their state of active engagement. May they go to destruction; that is, may they reach dissolution through wisdom, fortitude, self-knowledge, and the like, so as not to arise again. For it is said: "The knowledge of wisdom, fortitude, the Self, and so forth, is the supreme medicine for the defects of the mind."

According to this statement: "May he be happy everywhere—in all places and in all states—distinguished by the experience of unsurpassed bliss through the cessation of suffering without remainder; for attachment and the like, which are rooted in false knowledge, have been removed by right knowledge, and the mass of suffering rooted in attachment has likewise been dispelled by that very removal. As it is said: "When all the desires that dwell in his heart are cast away, then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman."

By such scriptural statements as, "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness," and "The knower of the Self transcends sorrow," it should be understood that the first half of this Āryā verse expresses the sage’s prayer for worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), while the second half expresses his prayer for the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) directed toward the Supreme Lord by the poet, who is moved by supreme compassion. Furthermore, because of the invocation of auspiciousness through phrases such as, "Nevertheless, may this be so: may there be welfare for all the worlds," it constitutes a benediction (*praśasti*).

Thus, these five junctures (*sandhi*) are established by means of sixty-four constituent parts (*aṅga*). In this treatise, because there is the application of "with joy" (*sānandam*) at the beginning, "O Creator, bestow what is auspicious" (*vidhātā bhadraṃ naḥ*) in the middle, and "may there be welfare for all the worlds" (*śivamastu sarvajagatām*) at the end, it begins with an auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), has an auspiciousness in the middle, and concludes with an auspiciousness; thus, for those intent on its study, the attainment of all desired goals is revealed.

Here, by the name "Mādhava," Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Lakṣmī himself, is intended; for according to the statement, "The erotic sentiment has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity," it is for the purpose of identifying that the Blessed Lord alone is the hero here as the deity of the erotic sentiment. Mālatī, however, is Lakṣmī herself due to her possession of qualities such as delicacy and fragrance. Devarāta is Kāśyapa, because he was brought down to earth by the gods for the sake of the purpose manifested by the Blessed Lord. Bhūrivasu is the Ocean of Milk, because he is a repository of infinite jewels.

Makaranda: According to such scriptural statements as "He is indeed rasa," he is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) whose nature is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). Madayantika: Because she deludes the world through her great power of illusion (*mahāmāyā*), she is Bhavānī. Kāmandakī: Because she possesses the capacity to grant desired objects, she is Devotion (*bhakti*). Buddharakṣitā: Because she is protected by the "Awakened" (*buddha*) ones—that is, the wise—she is Sarasvatī. Avalokitā: Because she is rightly observed by those possessed of discernment (*prekṣāvat*), she is Political Wisdom (*nīti*). Lavaṅgikā: Because she is full of fragrance (*parimala*), she is Fame (*kīrti*).

*Kalahaṃsa* refers to the mantra of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), characterized by its sweet and indistinct utterance. *Aghoraghaṇṭa* signifies unrighteousness (*adharma*) due to his devotion to violence not sanctioned by the scriptures. *Kapālakuṇḍalā* signifies violence itself. *Saudāminī* signifies knowledge (*vidyā*), whose nature is luminosity and which is most capable of shattering the entire mass of darkness through its instantaneous flash. Thus, even the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) employed for spiritual practice should be investigated by those who hold the Great Poet as their authority. May all be highly auspicious! //24//
Thus, by the grace of Pūrṇajyotis, Pūrṇasarasvatī has composed this commentary on the subject matter of the tenth act of the *Mālatīmādhava*.
Thus ends the tenth act.
May there be auspiciousness!
